### [1] [LLMs Know the Constraint But Do Not Use It: Activation Bottlenecks in Pragmatic Constraint Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12321)
*Yubo Li,Ramayya Krishnan,Rema Padman*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LLMs often fail when a salient surface cue conflicts with an implicit feasibility constraint, but aggregate accuracy masks whether models truly infer the constraint or just default conservatively. The paper distinguishes genuine constraint inference from conservative defaulting and shows the failure is a routing problem (constraint is known but not applied), not a knowledge problem.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Aggregate accuracy on hidden-constraint tasks conflates genuine constraint inference with conservative defaulting, making it unclear whether LLM failures reflect missing knowledge or a failure to apply internally encoded constraints. The authors seek to disentangle these possibilities.

Method: The authors formalize genuine constraint inference as "conditional constraint activation" with three criteria: Knowledge (constraint is internally encoded symmetrically across present/absent prompts), Routing (constraint is only sometimes used in decisions), and Repair (a donor activation can restore performance). They apply a quartet diagnostic to 14 models, use linear probes on two open-weight models to decode the constraint representation, and perform activation patching to test repairability. They also test a mitigation frontier of prompted interventions by decoding their outputs.

Result: Probes decode the constraint above 88% accuracy in both open-weight models, confirming the constraint is represented. However, activation patching repairs one model (+6.4 nats) but not the other (-0.07), revealing two distinct failure modes. No prompted intervention reaches the repair corner; all interventions inflate conservative bias through a single mediation pathway: prerequisite mention.

Conclusion: Hidden-constraint failure is fundamentally a routing problem—the constraint is encoded in the model but not reliably incorporated into decisions—rather than a knowledge problem. Prompted interventions fail because they only amplify conservative defaulting via prerequisite mention rather than activating genuine constraint inference.

Abstract: When a salient surface cue competes with an implicit feasibility constraint, LLMs often fail -- but aggregate accuracy conflates genuine constraint inference with conservative defaulting. We formalize the distinction as conditional constraint activation: the constraint is internally encoded (Knowledge) symmetrically across constraint-present and -absent prompts (Symmetry), yet only sometimes routed into the decision (Routing) and repairable by a donor activation (Repair). A quartet diagnostic over 14 models reveals two failure modes; probes on two open weights decode the constraint above $88\%$, yet activation patching repairs one ($+6.4$ nats) and not the other ($-0.07$). On a mitigation frontier, no prompted intervention reaches the repair corner: all inflate conservative bias through a single mediation pathway -- prerequisite mention. Hidden-constraint failure is a routing problem, not a knowledge problem.

</details>


### [2] [What Drives LLM Self-Reflection? A Controlled Ablation of Uncertainty Routing in Armed Conflict Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12322)
*Poli Nemkova,Haeshitha Indukuri*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A controlled ablation isolates four components of LLM self-reflection and finds that typed action routing—not diagnostic scaffolding or taxonomy vocabulary—drives reasoning gains in metacognitive forecasting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Self-reflection is widely assumed to improve LLM reasoning, but it is poorly understood which specific component of reflection produces the improvement. The paper aims to dismantle the black-box of self-reflection to identify the active ingredient responsible for gains.

Method: A controlled six-condition ablation isolating four components of LLM self-reflection: evidence exposure, diagnostic scaffolding, taxonomy vocabulary, and action routing. Conditions include unstructured reflection, structured diagnostic questions, a full uncertainty taxonomy collapsed to a single generic action, and typed action routing. Effects are quantified with F1 scores, p-values, and bootstrap confidence intervals, with a vocabulary-routing decomposition replicated across backbones (including GPT-4o).

Result: Two null results: structured diagnostic questions add no value over unstructured reflection (F1 0.296 vs 0.297, p=1.000, 95% CI [-0.041, +0.040]); presenting the full taxonomy with a generic action adds no value (ΔF1 +0.008, overlapping CIs), ruling out taxonomy vocabulary. Typed action routing yields consistent directional gains (F1 0.379 vs 0.296; conservative ΔF1 +0.075 controlling for taxonomy; overall gain over single-shot baseline ΔF1 +0.101, 95% CI [+0.020, +0.185]). The decomposition replicates on GPT-4o (taxonomy p=0.773 ns; action routing p=0.025 significant). Gains concentrate on structurally novel conflicts: Myanmar (F1 0.000→0.353) and Ukraine (0.167→0.500), where vocabulary-only matches generic reflection while action routing breaks the degenerate prior.

Conclusion: Typed action routing—not diagnostic scaffolding or taxonomy vocabulary—is a promising design principle for metacognitive LLM forecasting agents. The authors call for larger-scale evaluation across conflict typologies.

Abstract: Self-reflection is widely assumed to improve LLM reasoning, yet which component drives the gain remains poorly understood. We present a controlled six-condition ablation isolating four components of LLM self-reflection: evidence exposure, diagnostic scaffolding, taxonomy vocabulary, and action routing. Two precise null results converge on a single mechanism. First, structured diagnostic questions add no measurable value over unstructured reflection ($\text{F1} = 0.296$ vs $0.297$, $p = 1.000$, 95\% CI $[-0.041, +0.040]$). Second, presenting the full uncertainty taxonomy while collapsing the action space to a single generic action also adds no value ($Δ\text{F1} = +0.008$, overlapping 95\% CIs), ruling out taxonomy vocabulary as the mechanism. Typed action routing provides consistent directional gains ($\text{F1} = 0.379$ vs $0.296$); the conservative estimate controlling for taxonomy vocabulary is $Δ\text{F1} = +0.075$, and the overall gain over the single-shot baseline is significant by bootstrap CI ($Δ\text{F1} = +0.101$, 95\% CI $[+0.020, +0.185]$). The vocabulary-routing decomposition replicates on GPT-4o: taxonomy vocabulary adds no significant value over generic reflection ($p = 0.773$), while action routing provides significant gains ($p = 0.025$), confirming the mechanism holds across backbones. Gains concentrate on structurally novel conflicts: in Myanmar ($\text{F1}: 0.000 \rightarrow 0.353$) and Ukraine ($0.167 \rightarrow 0.500$), the vocabulary-only condition recovers no more than generic reflection while action routing breaks the degenerate prior. These findings identify typed action routing -- not diagnostic scaffolding or taxonomy vocabulary -- as a promising design principle for metacognitive LLM forecasting agents, while motivating larger-scale evaluation across conflict typologies.

</details>


### [3] [Why Do AI Agents Break Rules? How Framing, Context, and Social Signals Shape Compliance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12323)
*Mika Okamoto,Ansel Kaplan Erol,Kutluhan Erol*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: AI agents turn penalties into cost-benefit calculations, systematically violating rules when it is "worth it." Drawing on law-and-economics compliance theory, the paper shows different model classes match different compliance theories and that standard alignment benchmarks miss these failures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard AI safety evaluations test whether models fail but not why. The authors want to diagnose the mechanisms behind non-compliance, using compliance theory (deterrence, legitimacy, expressive law) as empirical hypotheses rather than metaphors, to understand when and why AI agents break regulatory constraints.

Method: They apply law-and-economics compliance theories as testable hypotheses and evaluate twelve instruction-tuned language models acting as enterprise procurement chatbots. They probe behavior under varying enforcement penalties, phrasing (command vs. non-command), financial incentives, managerial demands, peer outcomes, and employee pressure, comparing safety-fine-tuned, task-optimized, and agentic model classes.

Result: Safety-fine-tuned models maintain broad compliance; task-optimized and agentic models treat regulatory signals as optimization parameters and fail under conditions predicted by theory (low penalties, non-command phrasing). Across all models, financial incentives, managerial demands, peer outcomes, and employee pressure produce large compliance failures, with agents violating rules to satisfy local user objectives.

Conclusion: Compliance cannot be achieved by rule embedding alone. Model selection is itself a governance decision, and benchmark-based evaluation is insufficient for compliance-sensitive deployments.

Abstract: Specifying a penalty can paradoxically convert a legal obligation into a cost-benefit calculation that favors violation. We demonstrate that this enforcement information paradox systematically occurs in AI agents. While most AI safety evaluations test whether models fail, we investigate why, applying compliance theory from law and economics as a diagnostic tool. We treat compliance theories not as metaphors but as empirical hypotheses and show that each predicts the behavior of a distinct model class. We evaluate our hypotheses across twelve instruction-tuned language models operating as enterprise procurement chatbots. Drawing on theories of deterrence, legitimacy, and expressive law, we show that safety-fine-tuned models maintain compliance broadly, while task-optimized and agentic models treat regulatory signals as mere optimization parameters. These latter models fail to comply under conditions predicted by theory, such as low enforcement penalties and non-command phrasing. Across all models, introducing financial incentives, managerial demands, peer outcomes, or employee pressure produces large compliance failures. AI procurement agents systematically violate regulatory constraints to satisfy local user objectives in ways not captured by standard alignment benchmarks. Ultimately, compliance cannot be achieved by rule embedding alone; model selection is itself a governance decision, and benchmark-based evaluation is insufficient for compliance-sensitive deployments.

</details>


### [4] [On Measuring Semantic Preservation in Legal Ontology Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12326)
*Albert Sadowski,Jarosław A. Chudziak*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes a methodology that measures semantic loss in ontology learning by comparing LLM task performance on raw source text versus structured representations, and applies it to legal merger agreement analysis across three methods and six models, finding systematic, configuration-dependent semantic loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current ontology learning evaluation focuses solely on structural correctness and cannot detect whether meaning is lost when unstructured text is transformed into structured representations. This gap risks silently discarding information critical for automated reasoning.

Method: An evaluation framework that quantifies semantic loss as the difference in LLM task performance between source documents and their transformed (ontology-based) representations. Demonstrated on legal merger agreement analysis, comparing direct LLM application against three ontology learning methods across six language models, with variation analyzed along reasoning complexity and model-method interactions.

Result: The results reveal systematic semantic loss across ontology learning methods, with the magnitude varying significantly based on the complexity of the reasoning task and the specific pairing of language model and ontology learning method.

Conclusion: The work contributes (1) an evaluation framework for measuring semantic preservation in ontology learning and (2) empirical evidence that semantic loss varies dramatically with model-method pairing, offering guidance for selecting optimal configurations in legal knowledge systems.

Abstract: Ontology learning transforms unstructured text into structured representations for automated reasoning. Yet structuring information risks losing it, and current evaluation methodologies cannot detect such loss, focusing on structural correctness while failing to measure whether meaning survives transformation. We propose an evaluation methodology that addresses this: comparing LLM task performance on source documents against performance on transformed representations, with the difference quantifying semantic loss. We demonstrate this approach on legal merger agreement analysis, a domain chosen for its complex language and precise semantic requirements, comparing direct LLM application against three ontology learning methods across six language models. The results reveal systematic semantic loss with significant variation based on reasoning complexity and model-method interactions. Our contributions are: (1) an evaluation framework for measuring semantic preservation in ontology learning, and (2) empirical evidence that semantic loss varies dramatically with model-method pairing, providing guidance for selecting optimal configurations in legal knowledge systems.

</details>


### [5] [Comparative Analysis of Multilingual Pre-trained Models for Nepali Automatic Speech Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12327)
*Suman Paudel,Sarbin Sayami*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A controlled benchmark fine-tunes six pretrained models on the Nepali OpenSLR SLR54 corpus and evaluates WER, CER, and RTF across three test sets, finding Whisper-Large-v3-Turbo and IndicWav2Vec statistically tied at the top, CTC decoders far more efficient, and scale mainly improving out-of-domain robustness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multilingual pretrained models claim Nepali support, but no controlled, single-protocol comparison exists. The authors aim to fill this gap with a standardized benchmark covering different architectures and efficiency metrics.

Method: Fine-tune six models (XLSR-53, IndicWav2Vec, MMS-1B, Whisper-Medium, Whisper-Large-v3-Turbo, Conformer-Hi) spanning CTC self-supervised, autoregressive encoder-decoder, and hybrid Conformer-CTC families on the ~165-hour OpenSLR SLR54 Nepali corpus with identical preprocessing, data splits, optimizer, and family-matched learning-rate schedules. Evaluate Word Error Rate (WER), Character Error Rate (CER), and Real-Time Factor (RTF) on OpenSLR, FLEURS, and Common Voice test sets.

Result: Whisper-Large-v3-Turbo (14.76% WER) and IndicWav2Vec (14.89% WER) tie for best despite a 9x parameter gap and 40x pretraining-data gap. CTC decoders run up to 29x faster than autoregressive Whisper at comparable accuracy. MMS-1B shows the smallest out-of-domain degradation on FLEURS (+12.55 pp), indicating scale buys robustness rather than peak in-domain accuracy.

Conclusion: Language-family proximity in pretraining can substitute for raw scale for in-domain Nepali ASR, CTC is preferred under latency constraints, and the benchmark provides the first standardized multi-model, efficiency-aware reference for Nepali ASR.

Abstract: Multilingual pretrained models nominally support Nepali, yet no controlled benchmark has compared them under a single fine-tuning protocol. We fine-tune six pretrained models (XLSR-53, IndicWav2Vec, MMS-1B, Whisper-Medium, Whisper-Large-v3-Turbo, and Conformer-Hi) spanning CTC self-supervised, autoregressive encoder-decoder, and hybrid Conformer-CTC architectures, on the OpenSLR SLR54 Nepali corpus (~165 hours) using identical preprocessing, splits, optimizer, and family-matched learning-rate schedules. We evaluate Word Error Rate (WER), Character Error Rate (CER), and Real-Time Factor (RTF) on three independent test sets (OpenSLR, FLEURS, Common Voice). Whisper-Large-v3-Turbo (14.76% WER) and IndicWav2Vec (14.89% WER) tie at the top despite a 9x parameter gap and 40x pretraining-data gap, providing direct empirical evidence that language-family proximity in pretraining can substitute for raw scale for in-domain Nepali. CTC decoders run up to 29x faster than autoregressive Whisper at the same accuracy, flipping the practical deployment preference toward CTC under any latency budget. Massively multilingual pretraining (MMS-1B) yields the smallest out-of-domain degradation on FLEURS (+12.55 pp), indicating that scale buys robustness rather than peak in-domain accuracy. The resulting benchmark provides the first standardized, multi-model, efficiency-aware reference numbers for Nepali ASR.

</details>


### [6] [LLMs Are Not Good Strategists, Yet Memory-Enhanced Agency Boosts Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12626)
*Yi Wu,Zhimin Hu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: EpicStar is a framework that gives LLM agents a cross-episode memory bank plus working memory to combat strategic drift in long-horizon tasks. Tested in StarCraft II, it achieves higher win rates with an order of magnitude fewer tokens than baselines across difficulty levels and opponent styles.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs struggle with strategic reasoning in long-horizon environments because finite attention resources cause inconsistent subgoals and strategic drift, where localized decisions fail to maintain a coherent trajectory over thousands of steps.

Method: EpicStar lets agents "learn memory as policy": it maintains a bank of successful past episodes as a heuristic and a working memory tracking short-term environmental changes. At inference, a dynamic gating mechanism decides whether to execute a retrieved action directly or perform new reasoning via contextual fusion of retrieved episodes with current working memory.

Result: Evaluated in StarCraft II against diverse opponent styles, EpicStar significantly outperforms baselines, achieving higher win rates while using an order of magnitude fewer tokens, and maintains this advantage consistently across difficulty levels and opponent strategies.

Conclusion: Structured cross-episode memory is essential for enabling LLM agents to perform robust, long-term strategic execution in dynamic, autonomous environments.

Abstract: Strategic reasoning in Large Language Models (LLMs) within long-horizon environments is often limited by inconsistent subgoals. In these settings, finite attention resources prevent the model from maintaining strategic coherence over thousands of steps. This limitation leads to strategic drift, where localized decisions fail to sustain a coherent trajectory across reasoning. To address this, we introduce EpicStar, a framework that enables agents to learn memory as policy to tackle long-horizon reasoning. Specifically, the agent maintains a bank of successful past episodes as a heuristic alongside a working memory to track short-term environmental changes. During inference, a dynamic gating mechanism determines whether to execute a retrieved action directly or to perform new reasoning through a contextual fusion of the retrieved episodes and current working memory. Utilizing StarCraft II as the testbed, we evaluated EpicStar against diverse opponent styles. It significantly outperforms baseline methods, achieving higher win rates while consuming an order of magnitude fewer tokens, and it maintains this advantage consistently across difficulty levels and opponent strategies. Our findings provide compelling evidence that structured cross-episode memory is essential for enabling LLM agents to perform robust, long-term strategic execution in dynamic, autonomous settings.

</details>


### [7] [LoRA-Diffusion: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning via Low-Rank Trajectory Decomposition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12328)
*Iman Khazrak,Narges Nejad,Mohammadhossein Homaei,Mostafa M. Rezaee,Robert C. Green*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LoRA-Diffusion extends parameter-efficient fine-tuning to diffusion-based language models by applying low-rank decomposition to the denoising trajectory (rather than model weights), introducing trajectory-level adapters, step-adaptive rank allocation, and compositional multi-task learning. It achieves the best mean performance on SST-2 and strong results on QNLI/MRPC while reducing per-task storage.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods like LoRA successfully adapt autoregressive language models but have not been successfully extended to diffusion-based language models, which generate text through iterative denoising instead of sequential token prediction. The paper aims to fill this gap with a PEFT framework tailored to diffusion LMs.

Method: LoRA-Diffusion applies low-rank decomposition to the denoising trajectory rather than model weights. It introduces (1) trajectory-level low-rank adapters that modify each denoising step, (2) step-adaptive rank allocation across diffusion phases, and (3) compositional multi-task learning that merges task-specific modules at inference without retraining.

Result: On SST-2, QNLI, and MRPC, with token-level denoising validation accuracy averaged over five random seeds, LoRA-Diffusion achieves the highest mean performance on SST-2 and strong performance on QNLI and MRPC. Joint multi-task training yields the highest token-level accuracy among evaluated methods. It also reduces per-task storage compared with full fine-tuning.

Conclusion: LoRA-Diffusion establishes a parameter-efficient fine-tuning framework for diffusion language models, reducing per-task storage relative to full fine-tuning while achieving competitive or superior token-level accuracy across benchmark tasks.

Abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods such as LoRA have transformed the adaptation of large autoregressive language models, enabling task-specific customization with substantially fewer trainable parameters. However, these methods have not been successfully extended to diffusion-based language models, which generate text through iterative denoising rather than sequential token prediction. We propose LoRA-Diffusion, a parameter-efficient fine-tuning approach that applies low-rank decomposition to the denoising trajectory instead of model weights. Unlike weight-based LoRA, which modifies individual transformation matrices, our method learns low-rank perturbations to the entire diffusion path from noise to output. We introduce trajectory-level low-rank adapters that modify each denoising step, step-adaptive rank allocation across diffusion phases, and compositional multi-task learning that allows merging task-specific modules at inference without retraining. On SST-2, QNLI, and MRPC, we report token-level denoising validation accuracy over five random seeds. LoRA-Diffusion achieves the highest mean performance on SST-2 and strong performance on QNLI and MRPC. Joint multi-task training further shows that LoRA-Diffusion achieves the highest token-level accuracy among the evaluated methods. The approach reduces per-task storage compared with full fine-tuning and establishes a parameter-efficient fine-tuning framework for diffusion language models.

</details>


### [8] [AnchorSIPS: A Synthetic Dataset and Evaluation Resource for Evidence-Supported Psychosis-Risk Symptom Measurement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12329)
*Guilherme C. Oliveira,Stephanie Fong,Zimu Wang,Clarice Lee,Xiangyu Zhao,Duy Khoa Pham,Duong Nhu,Yiwen Jiang,Jiahe Liu,Zhongxing Xu,Dwarikanath Mahapatra,Dominic Dwyer,Zongyuan Ge*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: AnchorSIPS is a synthetic dataset of 10K structured psychosis-risk interviews with transcript-grounded labels, generated via a plan-then-realize pipeline to support research on evidence extraction and interview competence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Progress on AI for psychosis-risk assessment is bottlenecked by data access: real clinical interviews are hard to share due to privacy, governance, and consent constraints. The authors aim to provide a synthetic alternative that preserves the clinical structure of the Mini-SIPS interview while grounding every label in transcript evidence.

Method: A plan-then-realize pipeline: a hidden case sheet specifies the patient's clinical state, a deterministic planner fixes the interview structure, and an LLM realizes only patient utterances under validation and bounded repair. The interview models Mini-SIPS, capturing history, 24 symptom questions, follow-up evidence, symptom-class decisions (unusual beliefs, unusual perceptions, disorganized communication), a frank-psychosis exclusion, and a final attenuated psychosis syndrome (APS) diagnosis. Labels and structure are fixed before generation to avoid inter-turn inconsistencies.

Result: Across seven LLM baselines, models recover coarse decisions but fail to extract follow-up details or cite supporting transcript turns. This shows final-label performance overstates models' actual interview competence.

Conclusion: AnchorSIPS provides a resource for studying evidence extraction, transcript-grounded measurement, and uncertainty under partial disclosure, revealing that current LLMs fall short on detailed, evidence-based clinical reasoning even when coarse label accuracy looks high.

Abstract: Progress on AI for psychosis-risk assessment is limited by a data-access bottleneck. Real clinical interviews are difficult to share because of privacy, governance, and consent constraints. We present AnchorSIPS, a synthetic dataset of 10K structured psychosis-risk interviews with transcript-grounded measurement targets. Each interview is modeled on Mini-SIPS, a clinician-administered psychosis-risk interview. It captures history, 24 symptom questions, follow-up evidence for items the patient affirms, decisions about delusion-like symptoms (unusual beliefs), hallucination-like symptoms (unusual perceptions), and disorganized communication, exclusion of clear psychotic-level symptoms ("frank psychosis"), and a final attenuated psychosis syndrome (APS) diagnosis, a high-risk state of milder or early psychotic symptoms. The APS diagnosis is not a standalone label. It depends on earlier endorsements, supporting follow-up details, symptom-class decisions, and the frank-psychosis check. Every intermediate decision is anchored to its supporting transcript turns. AnchorSIPS is generated by a plan-then-realize pipeline. A hidden case sheet specifies the patient's clinical state, a deterministic planner fixes the interview structure, and an LLM realizes only the patient utterances under validation and bounded repair. Fixing labels and structure before generation avoids the inter-turn inconsistencies typical of multi-turn LLM dialogue. Across seven LLM baselines, models recover coarse decisions but fail to extract follow-up details or cite supporting transcript turns, so final-label performance overstates interview competence. AnchorSIPS is intended for research on evidence extraction, transcript-grounded measurement, and uncertainty under partial disclosure.

</details>


### [9] [Reliability-Aware Sexism Detection: Combining DPO with Annotator Agreement and Token-Level Confidence Scoring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12330)
*Hadi Mohammadi,Shihan Wang,Masoume M. Raeissi,Anastasia Giachanou*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: RA-DPO combines annotator agreement, model confidence, and token-level uncertainty into a reliability score to improve sexism detection, enabling cheaper training (top 30% of pairs matches full-data DPO) and reliable selective prediction (96.2% accuracy at 50% coverage).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sexism detection is inherently subjective, but existing systems reduce multi-annotator labels to a single majority vote and treat all instances uniformly, discarding two informative signals: annotator agreement and model uncertainty. The authors aim to leverage these signals to improve both training efficiency and deployment reliability.

Method: RA-DPO (Reliability-Aware Direct Preference Optimization) integrates annotator agreement, model confidence, and a token-level uncertainty signal into a single reliability score. This score selects high-value preference pairs during DPO training and supports inference-time abstention, trading coverage for accuracy. Evaluated on 6,920 multilingual EXIST 2023 posts; gpt-4o base fine-tuned via DPO, validated on two open-weight 3B models (Llama, Qwen).

Result: Training on the top 30% most reliable pairs matches full-data DPO performance. Selective prediction reaches 96.2% accuracy at 50% coverage under true-agreement and 88.7% under deployable predicted-agreement, both exceeding the 85.3% no-agreement baseline.

Conclusion: Accounting for annotation uncertainty benefits both efficient training (reduced cost without performance loss) and reliable deployment (higher accuracy via abstention) in subjective classification tasks like sexism detection.

Abstract: The detection of online sexism remains an open problem. Sexism detection is inherently subjective, yet most existing systems reduce multi-annotator labels to a single majority decision and treat all instances uniformly. This ignores two informative signals: annotator agreement and model uncertainty. We propose RA-DPO (Reliability-Aware Direct Preference Optimization), which integrates annotator agreement, model confidence, and a token-level uncertainty signal into a single reliability score. RA-DPO uses this score to select high-value preference pairs during training and to support inference-time abstention, which allows the model to trade coverage for accuracy. We evaluate RA-DPO on 6,920 multilingual posts from EXIST 2023, fine-tune OpenAI gpt-4o base via DPO, and validate on two open-weight 3B models (Llama, Qwen). Results show that training on the top 30% most reliable pairs matches full-data DPO, which indicates that reliability-aware selection can reduce training cost without sacrificing performance. At inference, selective prediction reaches 96.2% accuracy at 50% coverage in the true-agreement setting and 88.7% in the deployable predicted-agreement setting, both exceeding the 85.3% no-agreement baseline. These results suggest that accounting for annotation uncertainty is beneficial for both efficient training and reliable deployment in subjective classification.

</details>


### [10] [CRAFT: LLM-Based Iterative Refinement for Temporal Reasoning over Clinical Narratives](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12779)
*Chengyang He,Tahreem Arif,Marko Zivkovic,Lijing Wang,Yue Ning,Ping Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: CRAFT is an LLM framework combining a generator and a constraint-based verifier to reconstruct stage-wise symptom timelines from anchor-sparse clinical narratives, evaluated on a new vaccine adverse-event benchmark (MedTempo).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Clinical narratives rarely contain explicit temporal anchors, and existing temporal reasoning methods focus on pairwise relation classification in multi-visit, timestamp-rich records, leaving reconstruction of structured symptom trajectories from individual anchor-sparse reports largely unaddressed.

Method: CRAFT pairs a generator with a constraint-based verifier to iteratively produce and refine stage-wise symptom timelines through targeted feedback; evaluated on MedTempo, a new benchmark of 5,347 vaccine adverse-event narratives with expert-validated temporal stage annotations for 3,166 reports across three COVID-19 vaccine types.

Result: Experiments across four LLM backbones show CRAFT consistently improves temporal ordering accuracy, with ablation analysis isolating the contributions of the generator and verifier components across model capability levels.

Conclusion: The iterative generator-verifier approach effectively reconstructs structured symptom timelines from anchor-sparse clinical text, and the MedTempo benchmark provides a resource for future temporal reasoning research.

Abstract: Understanding the temporal progression of symptoms in clinical narratives is critical for disease monitoring, safety surveillance, and causality assessment. Clinical narratives, however, rarely provide explicit temporal anchors. Current approaches to temporal information reasoning focus predominantly on pairwise relation classification across multi-visit and timestamp-rich records, leaving the reconstruction of structured symptom trajectories from individual anchor-sparse reports largely unaddressed. We propose CRAFT, an LLM framework that pairs a generator with a constraint-based verifier to iteratively produce and refine stage-wise symptom timelines through targeted feedback. We conduct evaluation on MedTempo, a new benchmark of 5,347 vaccine adverse-event narratives spanning three COVID-19 vaccine types, with expert-validated temporal stage annotations for 3,166 reports. Experiments across four LLM backbones demonstrate that CRAFT consistently improves temporal ordering accuracy, with ablation analysis isolating the contribution of generator and verifier components across model capability levels.

</details>


### [11] [Thought-Aware KV Cache Compaction for Reasoning via Adaptive Attention Matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12331)
*Yang Liu,Bin Chong,Chongyang Zhang,Hao Zheng,Jiayu Liang,Xu Kefu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: TAM is a KV cache compaction method for reasoning language models that exploits the hierarchical structure of chain-of-thought by segmenting reasoning into blocks, allocating compression budget adaptively based on segment importance/size, and protecting pivotal high-attention tokens, improving accuracy over uniform compaction at the same memory while bounding peak memory to 3.1–3.2 GB (a 65% reduction).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reasoning language models produce long chain-of-thought sequences whose KV cache grows linearly, creating a memory bottleneck during decoding. Existing compaction approaches treat trajectories as flat token sequences and apply uniform compression, ignoring that different reasoning steps vary drastically in importance.

Method: Thought-Aware Attention Matching (TAM) uses three mechanisms: (i) thought segmentation to decompose the trajectory into reasoning blocks; (ii) adaptive budget allocation that assigns compression budget according to each segment's importance and size; and (iii) pivotal token protection that preserves high-attention reasoning anchors. The authors prove the allocation rule is optimal under a convex error model and that cumulative error under sequential compaction remains bounded.

Result: Experiments on AIME 2024 and MATH-500 with Qwen3-4B show TAM improves accuracy over uniform compaction at the same memory footprint. Periodic compaction bounds peak memory to 3.1–3.2 GB, a 65% reduction, while maintaining competitive accuracy.

Conclusion: Exploiting the hierarchical structure of CoT reasoning via segmentation, adaptive budget allocation, and pivotal token protection enables more accurate and memory-efficient KV cache compaction than uniform methods, with theoretical guarantees of optimality and bounded error supporting the empirical gains.

Abstract: Reasoning language models generate lengthy chain-of-thought (CoT) sequences whose key-value (KV) cache grows linearly and becomes a memory bottleneck during decoding. Existing compaction methods treat reasoning trajectories as flat token sequences and apply uniform compression, ignoring the hierarchical structure of CoT reasoning where different steps vary drastically in importance. We propose \textbf{Thought-Aware Attention Matching (TAM)}, which exploits this structure through three mechanisms: (i)~thought segmentation that decomposes the trajectory into reasoning blocks, (ii)~adaptive budget allocation that assigns compression budget based on each segment's importance and size, and (iii)~pivotal token protection that preserves high-attention reasoning anchors. We prove that the allocation rule is optimal under a convex error model and that cumulative error under sequential compaction remains bounded. Experiments on AIME 2024 and MATH-500 with Qwen3-4B show that TAM improves accuracy over uniform compaction at the same memory footprint, with periodic compaction bounding peak memory to 3.1--3.2\,GB (a 65\% reduction) while maintaining competitive accuracy.

</details>


### [12] [HybridRAG-BN: A Retrieval-Augmented Framework with Fine-Tuned Verification for Bangla KBQA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13004)
*Rathijit Aich,Nirjhar Das,Mahfuzulhoq Chowdhury*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: HybridRAG-BN is a retrieval-augmented framework for Bangla KBQA combining BM25 + BGE-M3 hybrid retrieval, Gemma-4-31B-Instruct (GGUF) answer generation, a LoRA-fine-tuned Gemma verifier, and post-processing with fallback/duckduckgo. It achieved top token-level F1 scores (0.71654 public, 0.72912 private), winning the competition.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Developing reliable KBQA systems for low-resource languages like Bangla is difficult due to limited retrieval-focused research, scarce language resources, and weak grounding of generated answers in external knowledge sources.

Method: A hybrid retrieval-augmented framework that (1) integrates BM25 and BGE-M3 for hybrid retrieval, (2) uses the GGUF version of Gemma-4-31B-Instruct for answer generation, and (3) employs a LoRA-fine-tuned Gemma-4-31B-Instruct for answer verification and refinement. A post-processing stage handles unresolved cases via fallback answer replacement and DuckDuckGo-assisted retrieval.

Result: Achieved token-level F1 scores of 0.71654 and 0.72912 on the public and private leaderboards, respectively, securing first place in the competition.

Conclusion: The proposed HybridRAG-BN framework effectively addresses Bangla KBQA challenges through hybrid retrieval, answer generation, verification/refinement, and post-processing, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance by ranking first in the competition.

Abstract: Knowledge-base question answering (KBQA) systems rely on effective retrieval and reasoning mechanisms to generate accurate answers from external knowledge sources. However, developing reliable KBQA systems for low-resource languages such as Bangla remains challenging due to limited retrieval-focused research, scarce language resources, and difficulties in grounding generated responses in external knowledge. In this work, we propose HybridRAG-BN, a retrieval-augmented framework for Bangla KBQA that integrates hybrid retrieval using BM25 and BGE-M3, answer generation using the GGUF version of Gemma-4-31B-Instruct, and a LoRA-fine-tuned Gemma-4-31B-Instruct model for answer verification and refinement. To further improve robustness, the framework incorporates a post-processing stage that addresses unresolved cases through fallback answer replacement and DuckDuckGo-assisted retrieval. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, achieving token-level F1 scores of 0.71654 and 0.72912 on the public and private leaderboards, respectively, securing first place in the competition.

</details>


### [13] [LigBench: A Unified and Human-Aligned Benchmark for LLM-based Research Idea Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13136)
*Chenrun Wang,Mingxuan Zhu,Tiancheng Huang,Wenjie Li,Yujie Zhang,Zichen Zhu,Zhiying Zou,Kai Yu,Lu Chen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces LigBench, an automated benchmark for fine-grained and reliable evaluation of AI-generated research ideas, plus PAIR-IQ, a dataset to train pairwise idea-judgment models. Experiments show LigBench aligns better with expert judgments and PAIR-IQ-trained models improve ranking accuracy and robustness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current evaluation of LLM-generated research ideas is fragmented, lacks objective standards, and often relies on direct LLM scoring, which cannot provide unified and reliable assessments across a coherent distribution of generated ideas.

Method: Propose LigBench, an automated evaluation benchmark for fine-grained, consistent, and reliable assessment of AI research ideas across different generation distributions; introduce PAIR-IQ, a dataset designed to train pairwise idea judgment models that serve as an auxiliary reference for objective comparative evaluation.

Result: Extensive experiments show LigBench yields stable and interpretable evaluations with significantly improved alignment with expert judgments; models trained on PAIR-IQ achieve enhanced ranking accuracy and robustness.

Conclusion: LigBench and PAIR-IQ establish a principled standard for scalable and objective research idea assessment, addressing the lack of unified and reliable evaluation practices in LLM-based idea generation.

Abstract: With the rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs), research idea generation has attracted increasing attention. Existing approaches enable LLMs to retrieve relevant literature and propose novel ideas for research areas. However, current evaluation practices for idea generation remain fragmented and lack objective standards, often relying on direct LLM scoring, which limits their ability to provide unified and reliable assessments across a coherent distribution of generated ideas. To address this challenge, we propose LigBench, an automated evaluation benchmark that enables fine-grained and reliable evaluation of AI research ideas, consistently applicable across different generation distributions. In addition, we introduce PAIR-IQ, a dataset tailored for training pairwise idea judgment models and serving as an auxiliary reference to support more objective comparative evaluation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LigBench achieves stable and interpretable evaluations, significantly improving alignment with expert judgments. Furthermore, models trained on PAIR-IQ exhibit enhanced ranking accuracy and robustness, establishing a principled standard for scalable and objective research idea assessment.

</details>


### [14] [Can Spectral-Clipping Enable Better Learning While Forgetting Less for Low-Rank Adaptation?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12332)
*Hyowon Wi,Noseong Park*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes SCLoRA, a low-rank adaptation method that uses Singular Value Decomposition to inject parameterized singular components with spectral clipping into frozen pre-trained models. It adapts task-specific minor singular components while preserving reusable principal components, and it theoretically links uncontrolled singular-value growth in LoRA adapters to catastrophic forgetting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LoRA freezes pre-trained weights and adds small adapters, but it suffers from catastrophic forgetting and suboptimal adaptation. The authors aim to understand how different singular components of network parameters behave during fine-tuning: principal components (large singular values) are reusable, while minor components (small singular values) are task-specific and require substantial adaptation. They also seek to establish and address the theoretical link between uncontrolled singular-value growth in adapters and forgetting of pre-trained knowledge.

Method: SCLoRA injects parameterized singular components with spectral clipping into the pre-trained model, informed by the spectral distribution obtained via Singular Value Decomposition of pre-trained parameters. It focuses updates on the components that require adaptation (minor singular components) while constraining singular-value growth to alleviate catastrophic forgetting, avoiding full fine-tuning.

Result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that SCLoRA improves downstream task performance while effectively retaining pre-trained knowledge, outperforming standard fine-tuning and other adaptation approaches in balancing adaptation and forgetting.

Conclusion: By leveraging SVD-based spectral awareness and clipping, SCLoRA successfully adapts models to new tasks while mitigating catastrophic forgetting, providing a more effective and knowledge-preserving alternative to standard LoRA-style adaptation.

Abstract: In recent years, low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has emerged as a significant paradigm that freezes pre-trained weights and introduces small, learnable adapters instead of fine-tuning the full set of parameters. In this work, we uncover several key insights regarding the singular components of network parameters based on Singular Value Decomposition (SVD). Firstly, the principal singular components with large singular values in pre-trained network parameters can be effectively reused during fine-tuning, whereas the minor components with smaller singular values are more task-specific and require substantial adaptation. Secondly, we first establish the theoretical connection that the uncontrolled growth of singular values in LoRA adapters leads to the forgetting of pre-trained knowledge -- a well-known issue referred to as catastrophic forgetting. Building on these observations, we propose SCLoRA, which injects parameterized singular components with spectral clipping into the pre-trained model in a way that is aware of the spectral distribution of the pre-trained model. SCLoRA effectively adapts to new tasks by focusing updates on components that require adaptation, while simultaneously alleviating catastrophic forgetting. We conduct extensive experiments and demonstrate that SCLoRA not only improves downstream performance but also effectively retains pre-trained knowledge.

</details>


### [15] [EviReform: Evidence-Guided Query Reformulation for Multi-Hop Graph Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13006)
*Xinlong Xu,Yoshua Y. Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: EviReform separates retrieval-request reformulation from evidence aggregation in graph-based multi-hop retrieval: retrieved passages generate residual queries for the still-unresolved information, whose signals are normalized, combined, and propagated over entity-sharing propositions. It outperforms the strongest baselines by up to 5.59 Recall@5 and 4.50 F1.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-hop QA requires recovering complementary passages that jointly provide evidence. However, an early retrieved passage often resolves an entity or relation that was implicit in the original question, meaning the missing evidence is easier to describe only after retrieval has started. Existing graph retrieval methods derive their retrieval signal from the original question alone, so complementary evidence must be reached through stored corpus relations even when an observed passage offers a more direct semantic cue.

Method: EviReform decouples reformulating the retrieval request from evidence aggregation over the graph. Retrieved source passages formulate residual queries capturing the unresolved information need. The original and residual retrieval signals are normalized separately, then combined and propagated between propositions that share entities.

Result: On 2WikiMultiHopQA, HotpotQA, and MuSiQue, EviReform exceeds the strongest baseline by up to 5.59 Recall@5 points and 4.50 F1 points.

Conclusion: Observed evidence can guide graph retrieval toward the part of a supporting chain left underspecified by the original question. Code is available at https://github.com/XrazyMee/EviReform.

Abstract: Multi-hop retrieval must recover passages that provide sufficient evidence together. An initial passage often resolves an entity or relation implicit in the question, making the missing evidence easier to describe only after retrieval begins. Graph retrieval improves access to related evidence through stored corpus structure, but its retrieval signal is commonly derived from the original question. Complementary evidence must then be reached through stored relations even when an observed passage provides a more direct semantic cue. We introduce EviReform, which separates revising the retrieval request from aggregating evidence in the graph. Retrieved source passages formulate residual queries for the unresolved information need. The original and residual retrieval signals are normalized separately, combined, and propagated between propositions that share entities. On 2WikiMultiHopQA, HotpotQA, and MuSiQue, EviReform exceeds the strongest baseline by up to 5.59 Recall@5 points and 4.50 F1 points. These results show that observed evidence can guide graph retrieval toward the part of a supporting chain left underspecified by the original question. Code is available at https://github.com/XrazyMee/EviReform.

</details>


### [16] [Vision-Language Models are Fragile Multilingual Associators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12333)
*Ritabrata Chakraborty,Rajatsubhra Chakraborty,Shivakumara Palaiahnakote,Angelo Cangelosi,Umapada Pal*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces M2BIND, a multilingual benchmark showing that vision-language models' binding between visual entities and textual attributes degrades significantly when input language changes, especially across language families and scripts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing vision-language models are typically evaluated in monolingual settings, but their deployment in multilingual contexts raises an unexplored question: whether concept bindings (associations between visual entities and textual attributes) remain stable when the language of the input changes.

Method: The authors introduce M2BIND, a benchmark that varies the language of both the context and the query across multiple languages. They evaluate binding through two complementary approaches: extrinsically via task performance metrics and intrinsically via causal interventions (probing the internal binding computation).

Result: Binding is not language-invariant. Cross-family and cross-script settings trigger significant binding collapse, where the model's internal binding computation shifts to later layers and loses causal strength. Closely related languages preserve associations comparatively better.

Conclusion: VLMs deployed globally in multilingual settings cannot be assumed to maintain the same association quality observed in monolingual evaluation, indicating a need for language-aware consideration of binding reliability.

Abstract: Vision-language models must associate visual entities with textual attributes. Whether these associations or concept bindings remain stable when the language of the input changes is unexplored. We introduce M$^2$BIND, a benchmark varying the language of the context and query across multiple languages. We evaluate binding both extrinsically through task performance metrics and intrinsically through causal interventions. We find that binding is not language-invariant: cross-family and cross-script settings trigger significant binding collapse, with the model's internal binding computation shifting to later layers and losing causal strength. Closely related languages preserve associations comparatively better. In a broader sense, our findings indicate how VLMs deployed globally in multilingual settings cannot be assumed to maintain the same association quality observed in monolingual evaluation.

</details>


### [17] [RAGSieve: Self-Referenced Local Contrast for Knowledge-Poison Detection in Retrieval-Augmented Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13010)
*Xinlong Xu,Yoshua Y. Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: RAGSieve is a self-referenced detection framework for retrieval-augmented generation that defends against corpus poisoning using query-local contrast (RSQ) and corpus-local contrast (RSG), achieving high detection AUROC and substantially reducing attack success while preserving retrieval quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Injected documents in retrieval-augmented generation can promote attacker-chosen claims, and existing detectors rely on trusted references, specific attack artifacts, or global thresholds sensitive to corpus topology. The paper aims to build detection that needs no poison labels or trusted corpora and works robustly across poisoning constructions.

Method: RAGSieve builds its reference from the inspected system itself. RAGSieve-Query (RSQ) performs query-local contrast by scoring top-five retrieved candidates against ranks 6-20 of the same retrieval to detect answer-anchor concentration and carrier transitions. RAGSieve-Graph (RSG) performs corpus-local contrast by comparing each document's semantically similar but lexically distinct neighbors against its local baseline to detect coordinated density before queries arrive. These components can be deployed jointly at corpus ingestion and query time.

Result: Across three QA datasets and six poisoning constructions, RSQ achieves 95.2% AUROC and detects 82.2% of poison at 5% clean-document removal, versus 81.1%/52.5% for GMTP. RSG achieves 93.3% AUROC and 79.8% detection, versus 79.4%/37.6% for CleanBase. Joint deployment reduces attack success from 67.4% to 14.0% while retaining 41.3% F1 on unpoisoned retrieval.

Conclusion: RAGSieve demonstrates practical protection against corpus poisoning at both ingestion and query time without poison labels or trusted corpora, significantly outperforming baselines (GMTP, CleanBase) in AUROC and poison detection at low false-positive rates, while limiting attack success and preserving retrieval F1. Source code is publicly available.

Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation treats an external corpus as inference evidence, allowing injected documents to promote attacker-chosen claims. Existing detectors depend on trusted references, specific attack artifacts, or global thresholds sensitive to corpus topology. We present RAGSieve, a self-referenced detection framework that constructs its reference from the inspected system. RAGSieve-Query (RSQ) performs query-local contrast, scoring top-five candidates against ranks 6-20 of the same retrieval to detect answer-anchor concentration and carrier transitions. RAGSieve-Graph (RSG) performs corpus-local contrast, comparing each document's semantically similar but lexically distinct neighbors with its local baseline to detect coordinated density before queries arrive. Across three QA datasets and six poisoning constructions, RSQ achieves 95.2% AUROC and detects 82.2% of poison at 5% clean-document removal, versus 81.1%/52.5% for GMTP. RSG achieves 93.3%/79.8%, versus 79.4%/37.6% for CleanBase. Joint deployment reduces attack success from 67.4% to 14.0% while retaining 41.3% F1 on unpoisoned retrieval, demonstrating practical protection at both corpus ingestion and query time without poison labels or trusted corpora. Source code is available at https://github.com/XrazyMee/RAGSieve.

</details>


### [18] [Steering the Language Axis: From Linear Decodability to Causal Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12334)
*Arnav Srivastav*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether language choice in multilingual LLMs is merely linearly decodable or causally controllable, finding that PCA-derived "language axes" in hidden states can be steered to force language switches, with layer- and language-pair-dependent effects and a default fallback to English upon ablation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The latent dynamics that govern language selection in Large Language Models remain poorly understood. The authors aim to determine whether language identity is only linearly decodable from hidden states or whether it can be causally controlled via a compact activation direction (a "language axis"), thereby clarifying the mechanistic basis of language choice.

Method: The authors perform an exhaustive causal-intervention analysis across multiple model families (Qwen 3.5-2B and Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct). They isolate PCA-derived language axes in activation space and conduct steering and ablation experiments over 1.26 million generations on the FLORES-200 dataset. Interventions are compared against equal-magnitude random perturbations as controls, in both cross-script (English to Chinese) and same-script (English to Spanish) settings, with a layerwise analysis of intervention sensitivity and a targeted ablation of the language signal.

Result: Steering along the language axes reliably forces language switching in both cross-script and same-script cases, while random perturbations of equal magnitude have virtually no effect. Language commitment is highly localized and language-pair-dependent: English-to-Chinese switching resists early-layer intervention and steers easily only in later layers, whereas English-to-Spanish shifting occurs earlier and shows a distinct bimodal sensitivity profile. Targeted ablation reveals a fundamental reversion to English—removing the language signal causes the model to fall back to English regardless of the input prompt.

Conclusion: Language decision boundaries act during inference as causally active, direction-dependent, and layer-specific features. Language identity is not merely a decodable correlate but can be controlled by compact activation directions, and the model possesses a default English fallback behavior once the language signal is removed.

Abstract: Despite the impressive multilingual capabilities of Large Language Models, the latent dynamics dictating language selection remain poorly understood. In this work, we ask whether language identity is merely linearly decodable from hidden states, or if it can be causally controlled by a compact activation direction. We conduct an exhaustive causal intervention analysis across multiple model families, including Qwen 3.5-2B and Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, isolating PCA-derived "language axes" to perform steering and ablation experiments across 1.26 million generations on the FLORES-200 dataset.
  Steering along these geometric directions reliably forces language switching in both cross-script (English to Chinese) and same-script (English to Spanish) settings, whereas equal-magnitude random perturbations yield virtually no effect. Our layerwise analysis reveals that language commitment is highly localized and explicitly language-pair-dependent. While English to Chinese switching resists early intervention and steers easily in the later layers, the English-Spanish transition shifts earlier, displaying a distinct, bimodal sensitivity. Furthermore, targeted ablation uncovers a fundamental reversion to English: once the language signal is removed, the model falls back to English regardless of the input prompt. Ultimately, these findings demonstrate that language decision boundaries function during inference as causally active features that are direction-dependent and layer-specific.

</details>


### [19] [GEM: A Generative Embedding Model Bridging Reasoning and Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13200)
*Zhili Shen,Craig Macdonald*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: GEM is a generative embedding model that unifies reasoning and embedding in a single model, enabling better retrieval by explicitly reasoning about user intent before encoding; it outperforms larger baselines and can scale test-time compute via prompting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern LLMs let users express complex, diverse information needs, but conventional retrievers rely on surface-level query-document matching, creating a growing gap between how users express needs and how retrievers interpret them. The paper aims to close this gap by augmenting retrieval with the model's own knowledge and reasoning.

Method: GEM is a generative embedding model that unifies generation and embedding in a single model. It first reasons over the query to understand user intent and relevance criteria, then appends an embedding token to encode the enriched context for retrieval. Its generative nature also supports test-time compute scaling via prompting.

Result: On reasoning-intensive and instruction-following retrieval tasks, GEM outperforms its non-reasoning variant and matches baselines that use substantially larger models. Test-time compute scaling via prompting further enhances retrieval performance.

Conclusion: Reasoning-augmented retrieval via a unified generative embedding model effectively bridges the gap between user expression and retriever interpretation, achieving strong performance with smaller models and enabling scalable test-time improvements.

Abstract: Modern LLMs excel at reasoning and instruction following, enabling users to express complex and diverse information needs. However, conventional retrievers largely rely on surface-level matching between queries and documents, resulting in a growing gap between how users express their needs and how retrievers interpret them. In this paper, we present GEM, a generative embedding model that augments retrieval through its own knowledge by explicitly reasoning about user intent and relevance criteria. GEM unifies generation and embedding within a single model: it first reasons over the query, then appends an embedding token to encode the enriched context for retrieval. \zhili{Evaluated on reasoning-intensive and instruction-following retrieval tasks, GEM demonstrates the effectiveness of its reasoning-augmented retrieval, outperforming its non-reasoning variant and matching baselines using substantially larger models.} Furthermore, GEM's generative nature allows test-time compute scaling via prompting to further enhance retrieval performance. Our code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/GEM.

</details>


### [20] [HC-RAG: Evidence-Centric Retrieval-Augmented Generation over Heterogeneous Financial Filings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12335)
*Siyuan Chen,Huaye Tan,You Li,Jiajun Liang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: HC-RAG is a hierarchical cross-modal RAG framework that organizes SEC filings into a typed financial evidence graph and routes evidence by query intent, achieving strong gains in evidence-centric financial QA over long, table-heavy, multi-document reports.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Financial QA over annual reports is not just semantic retrieval; it requires finding the right companies and fiscal years, locating standardized filing sections, gathering text and table evidence, and verifying answers against source documents. Existing RAG systems flatten filings into unordered chunks, ignore the typed structure of financial reports, and apply fixed text-table fusion without considering query intent, limiting evidence localization and answer accuracy.

Method: HC-RAG builds a typed financial evidence graph (documents, sections, text units, table units, metadata nodes) and retrieves evidence via document-section-unit paths. It aligns textual and tabular evidence in a shared retrieval space and routes evidence according to four semantic intents: calculation, trend, fact, and comparison. The authors introduce Multi-Doc-2025, a benchmark of 2,327 expert-verified QA pairs from 179 SEC 10-K filings of 87 S&P 500 companies (fiscal years 2022–2024), labeled for intent, difficulty, and structural evidence attributes.

Result: HC-RAG outperforms RAPTOR by 6.6 F1 points on DocFinQA and GraphRAG by 10.9 F1 points on Multi-Doc-2025, improving answer quality and evidence localization especially in long-document, table-related, and cross-document settings. Evidence-level and ablation analyses attribute gains to better section localization, table grounding, cross-document evidence aggregation, and intent-aware text-table routing.

Conclusion: Modeling the hierarchical, typed structure of financial filings and routing evidence by query intent significantly improves financial QA, as demonstrated by HC-RAG's superior performance and evidence-level contributions compared to text-flattening and fixed-fusion baselines.

Abstract: Financial question answering over annual reports requires more than retrieving semantically similar passages. It often involves identifying relevant companies and fiscal years, locating standardized filing sections, collecting textual and tabular evidence, and checking answers against the original documents. Existing RAG systems, however, usually flatten long filings into unordered chunks, pay limited attention to the typed structure of financial reports, and use fixed text-table fusion strategies without considering query intent. To address these limitations, we propose \textbf{HC-RAG}, a hierarchical cross-modal retrieval-augmented generation framework for evidence-centric financial QA. HC-RAG organizes filings into a typed financial evidence graph with documents, sections, text units, table units, and metadata nodes. It retrieves evidence through document-section-unit paths, aligns textual and tabular evidence in a shared retrieval space, and routes evidence according to four semantic intents: calculation, trend, fact, and comparison. We further introduce \textbf{Multi-Doc-2025}, a benchmark containing 2,327 expert-verified QA pairs from 179 SEC 10-K filings of 87 S\&P 500 companies across fiscal years 2022--2024, with labels for intent, difficulty, and structural evidence attributes. Experiments on public financial QA benchmarks and Multi-Doc-2025 show that HC-RAG improves both answer quality and evidence localization, especially in long-document, table-related, and cross-document settings. HC-RAG outperforms RAPTOR by 6.6 F1 points on DocFinQA and GraphRAG by 10.9 F1 points on Multi-Doc-2025. Evidence-level analysis and ablation studies show that the improvements mainly come from more accurate section localization, table grounding, cross-document evidence aggregation, and intent-aware text-table routing.

</details>


### [21] [StorySpark: Module-wise Evolutionary Search for Story Premise Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12336)
*Yang Yang,Zining Zhong,Qian Cao,Jindong Li,Boyun Xu,Kaishen Yuan,Menglin Yang,Yutao Yue*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: StorySpark is an evolutionary search framework for story premise generation that treats narrative modules (background, persona, event, ending, twist) as iteratively explored search spaces, producing more original premises and higher-quality downstream stories than baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based story generation research has focused heavily on later-stage planning, controllability, coherence, and prose expansion, while the initial creative phase—premise ideation—remains underexplored. The paper aims to fill this gap by improving the generation of story premises, the creative spark from which full narratives grow.

Method: StorySpark is a module-wise evolutionary search framework operating over interpretable narrative modules (background, persona, event, ending, twist). Each active module is treated as a local search space conditioned on the partial premise built so far. For each module it: generates alternatives, evaluates them in context, refines them via feedback-driven mutation and recombination, preserves complementary strengths using Pareto-guided selection, and reallocates frontier capacity to balance branch coverage against promising directions.

Result: Multi-view automatic and human evaluations show StorySpark produces stronger final premises than competitive baselines, with especially consistent gains in originality. When expanded with the same story writer, StorySpark premises lead to higher-quality downstream stories while maintaining completeness, fascination, and diverse usable narrative directions.

Conclusion: StorySpark demonstrates that evolutionary, module-wise search over premise components substantially improves originality and quality, and that better premises translate into better downstream story generation.

Abstract: A story premise is the creative spark from which a full narrative can grow. Yet LLM-based story generation has mostly emphasized later-stage planning, controllability, coherence, and prose expansion, while premise-level ideation remains comparatively underexplored. We introduce StorySpark, a module-wise evolutionary search framework for story premise generation. StorySpark operates over interpretable narrative modules such as background, persona, event, ending, and twist, treating each active module not as a static field to fill once, but as a local search space conditioned on the partial premise built so far. For each module, it generates alternatives, evaluates them in context, refines them through feedback-driven mutation and recombination, preserves complementary strengths with Pareto-guided selection, and reallocates frontier capacity to balance branch coverage with promising directions. Multi-view automatic and human evaluations show that StorySpark produces stronger final premises than competitive baselines, with especially consistent gains in originality; when expanded with the same story writer, its premises also lead to higher-quality downstream stories while maintaining completeness, fascination, and diverse usable narrative directions.

</details>


### [22] [From Refuse to Richness: Rubric Rewards for Long-Form Hallucination Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12337)
*Yudong Wang,Zhe Yang,Wenhan Ma,Rang Li,Qibin Yang,Weimin Xiong,Jiangshan Duo,Liang Zhao,Zhifang Sui*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies the trade-off between refusing to answer and generating rich content in long-form Hallucination RL. It introduces key-point rubrics that define required/optional information per question as direct coverage signals. A soft combination of grounding, rubric coverage, and relevance rewards achieves the best balance and better out-of-distribution transfer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Rewards that penalize unsupported claims improve factual grounding but risk teaching models to answer less (refusal). Existing richness proxies (length, claim count, detail, pairwise relevance) are global and indirect, so the authors seek a more direct way to define content coverage and understand the refusal-to-richness trade-off.

Method: Represent each question with a key-point rubric specifying required and optional information. Use these rubrics both for evaluation and as reward signals, and compare grounding-only, proxy-based, rubric-only, and combined reward setups within long-form RL.

Result: A stable trade-off emerges: strict grounding rewards improve support but suppress coverage, while unconstrained rubric rewards improve coverage but weaken grounding. A soft combination of grounding, rubric coverage, and relevance gives the best balance, improving in-distribution support and transferring better to out-of-distribution checklist tasks.

Conclusion: The refusal-to-richness trade-off is inherent but manageable. Combining grounding, rubric coverage, and relevance rewards softly yields the best overall grounding-coverage balance and stronger generalization compared to grounding-only or rubric-only rewards.

Abstract: Rewards that penalize unsupported claims can improve grounding in long-form generation, but they can also teach models to answer less. We study this refusal-to-richness trade-off in long-form hallucination RL. Instead of using global richness proxies such as length, claim count, detail, or pairwise relevance, we represent each question with a key-point rubric that specifies the required and optional information a useful answer should cover. These rubrics define coverage directly and are used both for evaluation and as reward signals. Across grounding-only, proxy-based, rubric-only, and combined rewards, we find a stable trade-off: strict grounding rewards improve support but suppress coverage, while unconstrained rubric rewards improve coverage but weaken grounding. A soft combination of grounding, rubric coverage, and relevance gives the best balance in our experiments, improving in-distribution support while transferring better to out-of-distribution checklist tasks than either grounding-only or rubric-only rewards.

</details>


### [23] [SDAM: Structure-Difference-Aware Memory Evolution for Complex Text-to-SQL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12338)
*Keyan Xu,Dingzirui Wang,Xuanliang Zhang,Qingfu Zhu,Wanxiang Che*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces SDAM, a memory agent designed for Text-to-SQL that improves SQL generation by learning from historical errors, semantic rules, and schema alignment. Integrated as SDAM-SQL, it outperforms mainstream methods on BIRD-dev and Spider-test.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing memory-based agent systems for Text-to-SQL neglect historical experience and suffer from three key weaknesses: weak structure analysis, shallow semantic understanding, and poor schema alignment, which limit their ability to generate complex SQL queries correctly.

Method: The authors propose SDAM with three components: (1) a structure-difference aware reasoning tree to identify potential errors, (2) contradiction-aware reflection to extract deep semantic rules, and (3) a schema-grounded memory evolution mechanism that binds memory with database schemas to enhance structural consistency. SDAM is integrated into a Text-to-SQL framework called SDAM-SQL.

Result: SDAM-SQL achieves improvements of 2.0 on BIRD-dev and 0.4 on Spider-test compared with mainstream Text-to-SQL methods, demonstrating its effectiveness.

Conclusion: By addressing deficiencies in memory design through structure-aware error identification, contradiction-aware semantic reflection, and schema-grounded memory evolution, SDAM-SQL effectively enhances complex Text-to-SQL generation and outperforms existing mainstream approaches.

Abstract: Text-to-SQL aims to convert natural language questions into executable SQL queries. While memory-based agent system improves complex SQL generation, existing memory design neglect historical experience and suffer from weak structure analysis, shallow semantic understanding, and poor schema alignment. To address these challenges, we propose SDAM. Specifically, SDAM identifies potential errors via a structure-difference aware reasoning tree, extracts deep semantic rules through contradiction-aware reflection, and enhances structural consistency using a schema-grounded memory evolution mechanism to bind memory with database schemas. We integrate SDAM into a Text-to-SQL framework named SDAM-SQL. Experiment shows that SDAM-SQL achieves 2.0 and 0.4 improvement on BIRD-dev and Spider-test compared with mainstream Text-to-SQL methods, showing the effectiveness of SDAM-SQL.

</details>


### [24] [Mimicry without understanding: the origins of decision bias in large language models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12339)
*Eldad Yechiam,Adi Tarabeih*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LLMs can acquire biases not only from biased or mislabeled human preference data, but from two additional mechanisms: faulty mimicry of logically preference-unrelated behaviors, and mimicry of explicitly labeled biased behaviors. Four studies show ChatGPT-4o and Qwen exhibited social proof and loss aversion biases, with biases described in scientific reports self-fulfilling in the LLMs' subsequent responses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work documents that LLMs are susceptible to social, affective, and cognitive biases, but it focuses mostly on biases inherited from training data. The authors aim to show that LLM biases can arise through distinct component processes even when the human preference data are unbiased or are correctly labeled as biased—deepening understanding of how (not just whether) LLMs become biased.

Method: Four empirical studies using ChatGPT-4o and Qwen. The authors probed two hypothesized mechanisms: (1) faulty mimicry, in which LLMs infer human preferences from behaviors that are logically unrelated to preferences; and (2) mimicry of explicitly biased human behaviors, including prompting with scientific reports that describe a bias (e.g., loss aversion) and testing whether the LLM exhibits that bias in its own responses. Economic biases (social proof, loss aversion) served as the test domains.

Result: ChatGPT-4o and Qwen displayed social proof biases even when prompted with human behaviors clearly non-indicative of actual preferences. They also displayed loss aversion when it was explicitly described as a bias. When prompted with detailed scientific reports, the magnitude of the bias described (loss aversion) predicted the LLMs' subsequent bias, indicating that scientific reports of biases can act as self-fulfilling prophecies for LLM responses.

Conclusion: LLM biases are not merely inherited from biased training data; they can be generated through faulty mimicry of preference-unrelated behaviors and through mimicry of explicitly labeled biases. Scientific descriptions of biases can become self-fulfilling prophecies in LLM outputs, highlighting the role of component processes underlying bias generation.

Abstract: Large Language models (LLMs) were found to be susceptible to a host of social, affective, and cognitive biases. We examined two mechanisms through which such biases can be generated even when human preferences (in the training data) are not biased or when they are correctly categorized as being biased. The first is faulty mimicry of preferences based on human behavior: this involves LLMs inferring human preferences even when behaviors are logically unrelated to preferences. The second is mimicry of explicitly biased human behaviors. In four studies focusing on economic biases, we find that ChatGPT-4o and Qwen exhibited social proof biases even when prompted with reports of human behaviors that were clearly non-indicative of individuals' actual preferences. LLMs also displayed loss aversion when it was explicitly described as a bias. Indeed, when prompted with detailed scientific reports, the extent of the bias (i.e., loss aversion) in the scientific report predicted LLMs' own subsequent bias. Scientific papers of biases can thus become self-fulfilling prophecies, at least when it comes to LLMs' responses. The current study goes beyond fleshing out LLM biases and sheds light on the underlying component processes.

</details>


### [25] [Class-Structure Preservation Beats Diversity: A Comprehensive Benchmark of Text Augmentation Methods for Imbalanced Text Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12340)
*Keito Inoshita*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A controlled benchmark of 11 data augmentation methods on 7 imbalanced text-classification datasets finds that all LLM-based augmentation methods are statistically equivalent or inferior to embedding-space SMOTE-style retrieval (EmbSMOTE), with the gap widening as class imbalance grows. Class-conditional structural fidelity, not surface-level diversity, drives performance, so retrieval-based oversampling is recommended as the default.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generative data augmentation with LLMs has attracted much attention for imbalanced text classification, yet no empirical benchmark has compared LLM-based augmentation against embedding-space SMOTE-style retrieval (EmbSMOTE), a strong classical reference. The authors aim to establish whether LLM generation actually outperforms classical/retrieval baselines and to identify what factor (diversity vs. structural fidelity) determines downstream performance.
