Method: A controlled benchmark of 11 augmentation methods (classical perturbation, embedding-space retrieval, and LLM-based generation) was constructed across seven public text classification datasets spanning K=2–28 classes and imbalance ratios from 1.1 to over 500. Each cell was evaluated with five random seeds using macro F1, Welch's t-tests, five distributional metrics, and an LLM-family sensitivity analysis based on Qwen3-8B. Correlation analyses were performed between surface-level uniqueness/LLM artifacts and downstream accuracy.

Result: All LLM-based methods were statistically equivalent or inferior to EmbSMOTE, with the performance gap widening monotonically as imbalance increased, reaching ΔF1_macro ≈ 0.063 on GoEmotions-28. Surface-level uniqueness had negligible correlation with downstream performance, while LLM-specific artifacts (text elongation and label-distribution uniformization) were negatively associated with classification accuracy. EmbSMOTE outperformed six LLM-based and four classical baselines.

Conclusion: The effective variable is not surface-level diversity but class-conditional structural fidelity—the degree to which augmented samples preserve the class-conditioned geometry of the training distribution. Retrieval-based oversampling should be adopted as the default for imbalanced multi-class classification, and a higher empirical bar should be required before LLM-based augmentation is deployed in practice.

Abstract: With the rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs), generative data augmentation has attracted considerable attention for imbalanced text classification in natural language processing. However, no empirical benchmark to date has compared LLM-based augmentation against the embedding-space SMOTE-style retrieval (EmbSMOTE), a strong classical reference for imbalanced classification. In this study, a controlled benchmark of 11 augmentation methods, spanning classical perturbation, embedding-space retrieval, and LLM-based generation, is newly constructed on seven public text classification datasets covering class counts $K=2$-$28$ and imbalance ratios of 1.1 to over 500, evaluated with five random seeds per cell using macro F1, Welch's $t$-tests, five distributional metrics, and an LLM-family sensitivity analysis based on Qwen3-8B. The experimental results reveal that all LLM-based methods are statistically equivalent or inferior to EmbSMOTE, with the performance gap widening monotonically as imbalance increases and reaching $Δ\text{F1}_\text{macro}\!\approx\!0.063$ on GoEmotions-28. Furthermore, it is observed that surface-level uniqueness has negligible correlation with downstream performance, whereas LLM-specific artifacts, such as text elongation and label-distribution uniformization, are negatively associated with classification accuracy. Compared with six LLM-based and four classical augmentation baselines, these results demonstrate that the effective variable is not surface-level diversity but class-conditional structural fidelity, namely the degree to which augmented samples preserve the class-conditioned geometry of the training distribution. Accordingly, retrieval-based oversampling should be adopted as the default for imbalanced multi-class classification, and a higher empirical bar should be required before LLM-based augmentation is deployed in practice.

</details>


### [26] [The "Knowledge-Behavior Gap" in Cultural Taboo Safety of Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12341)
*Ying He,Sihang Jiang,Xingzhou Chen,Zhouhong Gu,Yiwei Gu,Minggui He,Shimin Tao,Hongxia Ma,Yanghua Xiao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: CulShield is the first public benchmark for evaluating and improving LLMs' cultural taboo safety, covering 77 countries and over 2,020 taboos, and revealing a "knowledge-behavior gap" alongside sensitivity to linguistic context.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing cultural benchmarks only assess cultural knowledge or value biases and overlook whether LLMs can recognize and respect cultural taboos, especially when taboos are implicitly embedded in seemingly harmless questions. Cultural taboos are also implicit and context-dependent, making reliable evaluation challenging.

Method: The authors build CulShield, a benchmark spanning 77 countries/territories with over 2,020 taboos, and evaluate models along two dimensions: explicit knowledge (knowing the taboo) and implicit behavior (respecting it in interaction). They test advanced LLMs such as GPT-4o-mini and Gemini-2.5-pro and analyze how linguistic context variations affect safety.

Result: Experiments reveal a clear "knowledge-behavior gap": models often possess the relevant taboo knowledge yet fail to apply it during interaction. Linguistic context variations were also shown to significantly affect LLMs' cultural taboo safety.

Conclusion: CulShield addresses a critical gap in cultural evaluation, demonstrating that LLMs need improvement in applying cultural taboo knowledge in practice, and provides a public benchmark (code and data available) to support evaluation and improvement of cultural taboo safety.

Abstract: Cultural taboo safety is essential for deploying large language models (LLMs), as culturally insensitive outputs may cause offense or even social harm. However, existing cultural benchmarks primarily assess cultural knowledge or values biases, while overlooking whether LLMs can recognize and respect cultural taboos, especially when taboos are implicitly hidden in seemingly harmless questions. Besides, cultural taboos are implicit, and context-dependent, thus poss unique challenges for reliable evaluation. To address these gaps, we introduce \textbf{CulShield}, the first public benchmark dedicated to evaluating and improving the cultural taboo safety of LLMs. CulShield spans 77 countries and territories, and includes over 2,020 taboos. It evaluates models along both explicit knowledge and implicit behaviors. Experiments on several advanced LLMs (e.g., GPT-4o-mini, Gemini-2.5-pro) reveal a clear ``knowledge-behavior gap'': models often fail to apply known taboos during interaction. We further show that variations in linguistic context can significantly affect LLMs' cultural taboo safety. Code and data is accessible here: https://github.com/hedyHe/CulShield.

</details>


### [27] [Are Large Language Models Reliable Reviewers? A Benchmark for Error Detection in Financial Documents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12342)
*Ying He,Zhouhong Gu,Zhecheng Hu,Yubo Zhou,Hao Shen,Jiaqing Liang,Zhaoqian Dai,Shuguang Ma,Fei Yu,Yanghua Xiao,Zhixu Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces FinED-Bench, the first public benchmark for financial error detection, featuring over 900 real-world 2025 documents across nine scenarios and three cognitive complexity levels. Evaluation shows current LLMs struggle, especially on high-complexity cases, though supervised fine-tuning notably improves weaker models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Financial document accuracy is crucial for economic analysis, regulatory compliance, and corporate decisions. While LLMs excel at many financial tasks like stock prediction and analytics, their ability to detect errors in financial documents remains unexplored, creating a gap the paper aims to address.

Method: The authors construct FinED-Bench, a benchmark with over 900 financial documents from 2025 (unseen by existing models), spanning nine real-world scenarios and three levels of cognitive complexity. They evaluate advanced LLMs (e.g., GPT-4o, Qwen3-14B) on this error-detection task requiring both financial domain knowledge and reasoning, and additionally apply supervised fine-tuning to weaker models.

Result: Current LLMs struggle with financial error detection, with performance degrading notably on high-complexity cases. Supervised fine-tuning significantly improves the performance of weaker LLMs on this task.

Conclusion: Financial error detection is a challenging, underexplored task where existing LLMs remain insufficient, particularly for complex cases. The released FinED-Bench benchmark, data, and code aim to spur further research, with fine-tuning shown as an effective means to boost weaker models.

Abstract: Ensuring the accuracy of financial documents is critical for economic analysis, regulatory compliance, and corporate decision-making. Several studies have shown that Large Language Models (LLMs) perform well in many financial tasks, such as stock price movements and financial analytics. However, a critical task remains unexplored: the ability of LLMs to identify errors in financial documents. In this paper, we introduce \textbf{FinED-Bench}, the first publicly \textbf{Bench}mark for \textbf{Fin}ancial \textbf{E}rror \textbf{D}etection across three levels of cognitive complexity. FinED-Bench covers nine real-world financial scenarios, and includes over 900 documents reported in 2025 that are unseen by existing language models. We detail the benchmark construction process and evaluate several advanced LLMs (e.g., GPT-4o, Qwen3-14B) on this tasks, which requires both financial domain knowledge and reasoning capabilities. Experimental results show that current LLMs still struggle with this task, especially in high-complexity cases. Besides, supervised fine-tuning can significantly improve the performance of weaker LLMs on this task. Our data and code are available at https://github.com/hedyHe/FinED-Bench.

</details>


### [28] [Large Language Models Pass the History Exam But Miss the <<History>>: A Polish High School Exit Exam Matura Benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12343)
*Adrian Trzoss,Kacper Dudzic,Wiktor Werner,Marcin Moskalewicz*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Eight leading LLMs were tested on the Polish high school history exit exam (Matura, 2023–2025), where all models outperform humans, but aggregate scores hide unstable rankings and consistent weakness on Polish (vs. Global) content, with recurring failures of source conflation and temporal disorientation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI chatbots are widely used by students as knowledge sources, yet existing LLM benchmarks rarely assess interpretative historical reasoning, leaving a gap in evaluating how well models handle the skills tested in real educational settings.

Method: The authors evaluated eight leading LLMs on three official Polish Matura history papers (2023–2025), covering short-answer questions and extended essays. Model performance was compared against the human examinee population, with analysis across task type, source modality, and geographical scope, plus qualitative error analysis.

Result: All eight models dramatically outperform human examinees, but rankings are unstable across task type, source modality, and geographical scope. Models consistently perform worse on Polish history content than on Global history content. Qualitative analysis identifies two recurring failure modes: source conflation (reasoning from source content rather than treating it as an object of analysis) and temporal disorientation (historically misplacing responses).

Conclusion: The study introduces the first LLM history benchmark grounded in the Polish national curriculum, showing that aggregate scores obscure distinct competency profiles and that current models exhibit systematic weaknesses in interpretative historical reasoning, particularly on localized content.

Abstract: AI chatbots are widely used by students as knowledge sources, yet LLM benchmarks rarely assess interpretative historical reasoning. We evaluate eight leading LLMs on the Polish high school exit exams (Matura) in history - three official papers from 2023-2025, comprising short-answer questions and extended essays - comparing model performance against the human examinee population. Every model dramatically outperforms human examinees, yet aggregate scores mask distinct competency profiles: rankings are unstable across task type, source modality, and geographical scope, with a consistent penalty on Polish versus Global history content. Qualitative error analysis reveals two recurring failure modes - source conflation, in which models reason from source content rather than treating it as an object of analysis, and temporal disorientation, in which responses are historically misplaced. This study introduces the first LLM history benchmark grounded in Polish national curriculum.

</details>


### [29] [Predicting consumer-technology ownership without a diffusion history](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12344)
*Irina Vartanova,Niels Selling,Jennifer Viberg Johansson,Pontus Strimling*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper tests whether perceived attributes of consumer technologies (rated by humans and by frontier language models) can predict ownership prevalence, finding attribute-based models outperform a years-since-launch baseline in cross-sectional prediction but not short-horizon change prediction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine whether subjective, perceived attributes of consumer technologies (drawn from the UTAUT2 acceptance framework) predict how widely those technologies are owned, and whether frontier language models can substitute for costly human survey ratings in generating these attribute scores.

Method: A 2022 Prolific survey of 678 US adults rated 65 consumer technologies on six attributes; the same ratings were elicited from two frontier language models (Anthropic Claude Opus 4.7 and OpenAI GPT-5.5). Ownership prevalence was regressed on four UTAUT2 acceptance attributes plus a log-age covariate using a sign-constrained penalized regression, evaluated by leave-one-technology-out cross-validation against a years-since-launch baseline and, for the 2022-2025 change, a no-change baseline. The paper also includes a deployment illustration with 2027 ownership predictions for eleven products launched in 2025-2026.

Result: The attribute model reduces mean absolute error by 17% over the years-since-launch baseline using human ratings, with further improvement using language-model ratings (most with Claude Opus 4.7). Over the short 2022-to-2025 window, where ownership changed little, the attributes did not improve on a no-change baseline.

Conclusion: Perceived attributes meaningfully predict cross-sectional ownership prevalence, and language-model ratings perform at least as well as human ratings, though the authors caution that language models may be recalling prior knowledge rather than independently reasoning about attributes. The approach has limited value for short-horizon change prediction.

Abstract: We test whether the perceived attributes of a consumer technology predict how widely it is owned. In a 2022 Prolific survey of US adults (n = 678), respondents rated 65 consumer technologies on six attributes. We then elicited the same ratings from two frontier language models, Anthropic Claude Opus 4.7 and OpenAI GPT-5.5. We regress ownership prevalence on four UTAUT2 acceptance attributes plus a log-age covariate with a sign-constrained penalized regression and evaluate it by holding out one technology at a time. The attribute model improves on a baseline of years-since-launch: mean absolute error falls by 17% with the human ratings, and by more with either model, most with Opus 4.7. Over the short 2022-to-2025 window, where ownership moved little, the same attributes do not improve on a no-change baseline. We set out the limitations of the approach, including the possibility that language-model ratings reflect prior knowledge of these technologies rather than independent attribute reasoning. We include a deployment illustration: 2027 ownership predictions for eleven products launched in 2025 and 2026.

</details>


### [30] [New Terms, New Toxicity: Consensus-based Chinese Neologism Toxicity Detection via Search-Augmented LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12361)
*Shiyao Cui,QingLin Zhang,Di Wang,Yida Lu,Zhexin Zhang,Jinhua Gao,Jinglin Yang,Min He,Han Qiu,Minlie Huang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper addresses implicit toxicity expressed through "toxic neologisms" (new terms that appear benign but carry toxic public-consensus meanings). It proposes a taxonomy and lexicon of toxic neologisms, then introduces SeTox, a search-augmented framework that lets static LLMs incorporate real-time web evidence for detection, outperforming larger models even at 3B scale.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Toxic expressions increasingly hide behind neologisms—terms new in form or meaning that look benign but gain stigmatizing or harmful usage through public consensus (e.g., "country girl" as an anti-feminist slur). These evade existing moderation systems built on static lexicons/models, and implicit toxicity via neologisms remains underexplored.

Method: The authors (1) propose a taxonomy describing the origins of toxic neologisms and criteria for verifying toxicity via public consensus; (2) build a lexicon of toxic neologisms across broad risk categories; and (3) develop SeTox, a search-augmented detection framework that enables static LLMs to retrieve and incorporate real-time web context in order to ground toxicity judgments in public consensus rather than in fixed training knowledge.

Result: Experiments show that SeTox, even using small 3B-scale models, outperforms recent large-scale language models on neologism toxicity detection, demonstrating that augmenting static LLMs with real-time, real-world web knowledge is effective and scalable for this task.

Conclusion: Toxic neologism detection can be substantially improved by grounding judgments in public consensus through search-augmented retrieval, and the proposed taxonomy, lexicon, and SeTox framework provide effective, scalable tools for moderation systems to catch implicit toxicity that static approaches miss.

Abstract: Neologisms, emerging terms in meaning or form, can serve as new vehicles for toxic expression, like "country girl" as a stigmatizing label targeting feminism. Such toxic neologisms appear benign but have evolved into toxic usage in public consensus, posing challenges to moderation systems and remaining underexplored. In this paper, we investigate how to detect implicit toxicity expressed via neologisms. We first propose a taxonomy that captures the origins and consensus-verification criteria of toxic neologisms, followed by the construction of a lexicon spanning widely observed risk categories. To capture toxicity grounded in public consensus, we introduce SeTox, a search-augmented framework that enables static large language models (LLMs) to incorporate real-time web context for neologism toxicity detection. Experiments show that SeTox, even with 3B-scale models, outperforms recent large-scale models, demonstrating its scalability to incorporate real-world knowledge for toxic neologism detection. Disclaimer: this paper has offensive contents that may be disturbing to some readers.

</details>


### [31] [Are you Talking Logic to Me? Assessing Language Models Syllogistic Reasoning Capabilities](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12374)
*Hanna Abi Akl,Fabien Gandon,Catherine Faron,Pierre Monnin*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how different Knowledge Representation (KR) notations affect syllogistic reasoning in language models, introduces a categorization method (SEF) to enrich zero-shot prompts, and releases CLGC, a Python library for generating syllogisms in KR notations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Language models struggle with logical tasks like syllogistic reasoning, and prior work shows KR improves input expression for solving these tasks. This motivates investigating whether different formal KR notations impact performance, inference speed, and reasoning.

Method: The authors extend the FOLIO and P-FOLIO datasets to cover multiple formal KR notations; evaluate Small Language Models (SLMs) under Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Zero-Shot (ZS) settings; propose a syllogistic categorization method called SEF used to add logical definitions to ZS prompts; and build the Common Logic Grammar Construction (CLGC) framework for automatic syllogism generation.

Result: Choice of input notation can match natural language performance while enabling faster inference. SEF-based logical definitions in zero-shot prompts boost reasoning in small models.

Conclusion: Formal KR notations are a viable, efficient alternative to natural language for syllogistic reasoning, and prompt enrichment with SEF categories improves small-model performance. The open-sourced CLGC library supports reproducible generation and categorization of syllogisms.

Abstract: Language models (LMs) struggle with logical tasks like reasoning on syllogisms. It has been shown that Knowledge Representation (KR) plays a crucial role in expressing input information to help models solve tasks. This observation motivates our study of the impact of different formal KR notations on syllogistic reasoning by extending the FOLIO and P-FOLIO datasets. Our experiments on Small Language Models (SLMs) in Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Zero-Shot (ZS) settings show that the choice of input notation can yield performances competitive with natural language while enabling faster inference. We also propose a syllogistic categorization method (SEF) and use it to enrich ZS prompts with logical definitions, which boost reasoning in small models. We open-source our framework, Common Logic Grammar Construction (CLGC), as the first Python library for automatically generating syllogisms in KR notations and defining their SEF categories.

</details>


### [32] [Query Timing Produces Opposite Positional Biases Between LLMs and Humans](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12387)
*Jasin Cekinmez,Addison J. Wu,Thomas L. Griffiths*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper investigates positional biases (primacy and recency effects) in large language models, examining how belief-updating timing influences these effects and finding that newer LLMs exhibit more exacerbated biases than older ones.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Positional biases in LLMs are documented but poorly understood mechanistically. Prior human studies show that primacy/recency effects depend on whether belief updating occurs during evidence presentation or only at the end. The authors aim to test whether this phenomenon holds for LLMs and understand the underlying mechanism.

Method: The authors investigate whether the timing of belief updating (during evidence presentation versus only at the end) influences positional biases in LLMs, mirroring recent human-judgment research, and compare behavior across different model generations.

Result: LLMs diverge from human behavior with respect to how belief-updating timing influences primacy/recency effects. Additionally, these positional biases are more exacerbated in newer models compared to their predecessors.

Conclusion: The belief-updating mechanism in LLMs does not mirror human behavior regarding positional biases, and newer models show stronger primacy/recency biases, indicating biases worsen with model advancement.

Abstract: Positional biases such as recency and primacy effects have been documented in large language models (LLMs), yet the underlying mechanism by which these models make their evaluations remains poorly understood. Both primacy and recency biases have been observed in human judgments in response to evidence, but recent work suggest that \emph{when} the listener updates their beliefs -- during the presentation of evidence or only at the end -- influences the presence of such effects. We investigate whether a similar phenomenon holds for LLMs, finding divergence from human behavior. These biases are more exacerbated in newer models compared to their predecessors.

</details>


### [33] [PatientAct: Theory-Grounded Mental Health Client Simulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12750)
*Sahand Sabour,TszYam NG,Yaqian Chen,Guanqun Bi,Jialu Zhao,Minlie Huang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: PatientAct is a framework for simulating therapy clients that grounds client profiles in the 5Ps clinical formulation and uses a trust-thresholded memory layer to produce realistic resistance, yielding more clinically plausible and behaviorally realistic responses than existing overly-cooperative LLM simulators.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM-based client simulators are unrealistically cooperative: they disclose too readily, accept therapeutic reframes without resistance, and resolve core issues within a single session. The authors trace these shortcomings to (1) profiles lacking causal depth and (2) behavioral mechanisms that treat all content as equally accessible regardless of the therapeutic relationship.

Method: PatientAct introduces (1) client profiles built on the 5Ps clinical case formulation to provide causal depth in a modality-agnostic way, and (2) a dynamic memory layer in which each memory item carries a trust threshold (e.g., symptoms surface early, while formative memories require a sustained therapeutic alliance). Each turn models the client's emotional reaction and behavior before generating a response, and when the therapist approaches gated content, the client expresses resistance along three dimensions—quantity, content, and style—rather than defaulting to cooperation or a single resistance pattern.

Result: Evaluated on 40 clinical situations, PatientAct generates diverse profiles with high clinical plausibility and significantly outperforms baselines, achieving substantial gains in resistance quality and behavioral realism.

Conclusion: Grounding simulation in established clinical theory (5Ps formulation) and modeling trust-gated memory produces more realistic, resistant client behavior, addressing a key weakness of prior LLM simulators. Code and data will be released publicly at github.com/Sahandfer/PatientHub.

Abstract: LLM-based simulated clients are increasingly used to train novice counselors, evaluate LLM therapists, and generate synthetic data. However, current simulators produce overly cooperative clients that disclose too readily, accept therapeutic reframes without resistance, and resolve core issues within a single session. We trace these issues to profiles that lack causal depth and behavioral mechanisms that treat all content as equally accessible. We present PatientAct, a framework for client simulation grounded in established clinical theories. Our profiles integrate the 5Ps clinical case formulation, providing causal depth without tying the design to any single therapeutic modality. During simulation, profiles include a dynamic memory layer in which items carry trust thresholds (e.g., symptoms are available early, whereas formative memories require a sustained therapeutic alliance). At each turn, the client's emotional reaction and behavior are modeled before generating a response. If the therapist approaches gated content, PatientAct expresses resistance in terms of quantity, content, and style rather than defaulting to cooperation or a single resistance pattern. We evaluate our framework on 40 clinical situations and demonstrate that it generates diverse profiles with high clinical plausibility. Moreover, PatientAct significantly outperforms the baselines, yielding substantial gains in resistance quality and behavioral realism. Our code and data will be publicly available via github.com/Sahandfer/PatientHub.

</details>


### [34] [Unified Multi-Dimensional Benchmark for Complex Graph Reasoning in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12391)
*Fali Wang,Ali Al-Lawati,Iliyas Bektas,Jinxuan Fang,Alek Melenski,Tianxiang Zhao,Yao Ma,Suhang Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces GraphGym, a five-stage semi-automatic framework for building complex graph reasoning benchmarks that expands coverage across five dimensions and evaluates LLMs under text-based, code-based, and augmented reasoning settings, revealing limitations not visible in existing benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing graph reasoning benchmarks have limited coverage of data complexity, rely heavily on manual construction, and lack unified evaluation across text-based and code-based reasoning modes. Graph reasoning is a promising testbed because graphs can be programmatically generated, structurally controlled, and naturally scaled to long inputs.

Method: The authors propose a five-stage semi-automatic framework that expands benchmark coverage along five dimensions: Graph Size, Task Complexity, Task Description, Graph Loading, and Task Source. An LLM-based data generator automatically produces task descriptions, graph data, reference solutions, graph-loading scripts, question forms, and evaluation scripts, while human validation is retained at key quality-control stages. The framework yields a benchmark of 202 tasks evaluated under text-based, code-based, and augmented reasoning settings.

Result: The complexity dimensions reveal model limitations that are less visible in existing benchmarks. Existing fine-tuned models struggle to generalize to GraphGym. Retrieval-augmented methods show scenario-dependent adaptability, improving textual reasoning but not consistently improving coding reasoning.

Conclusion: GraphGym serves as a challenging and diagnostic benchmark for graph reasoning and provides empirical guidance for future enhancement methods. Code and dataset will be published soon.

Abstract: Graph reasoning provides a promising testbed for evaluating the reasoning ability of large language models (LLMs), as graph instances can be programmatically generated, structurally controlled, and naturally scaled to long-input settings. However, existing graph reasoning benchmarks have limited coverage of data complexity, rely heavily on manual construction, and lack unified evaluation across text-based and code-based reasoning modes. To address these limitations, we propose {\dataset}, a five-stage \textit{semi-automatic} framework for constructing complex graph reasoning benchmarks. It expands benchmark coverage along five dimensions: \textit{Graph Size}, \textit{Task Complexity}, \textit{Task Description}, \textit{Graph Loading}, and \textit{Task Source}. The framework uses an LLM-based data generator to automatically produce task descriptions, graph data, reference solutions, graph-loading scripts, question forms, and evaluation scripts, while retaining human validation at key quality-control stages. Based on it, we construct a benchmark with $202$ tasks and evaluate LLMs under text-based, code-based, and augmented reasoning settings. Experiments show that the complexity dimensions reveal model limitations that are less visible in existing benchmarks; existing fine-tuned models struggle to generalize to GraphGym, whereas retrieval-augmented methods show scenario-dependent adaptability, improving textual reasoning but not consistently improving coding reasoning. These findings suggest that ours serves as a challenging and diagnostic benchmark for graph reasoning and provides empirical guidance for future enhancement methods. Code and dataset will be published soon.

</details>


### [35] [DIVE: Unlocking Self-Improvement in Frozen Language Models Through Diversity-Driven Skill Evolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12486)
*Siheng Xiong,Ali Payani,Oguzhan Gungordu,Faramarz Fekri*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: DIVE is a diversity-driven framework that lets frozen LLMs self-improve by evolving persistent natural-language skills from experience and verifier feedback, with no parameter updates. It evolves multiple skill populations independently to avoid overfitting, then selects a complementary skill set. DIVE outperforms existing reasoning, prompt-optimization, skill-development, and memory baselines across six reasoning tasks, achieving larger gains with fewer rollouts than SFT, GRPO, and GEPA, and its skills transfer across model scales/families.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs cannot retain post-deployment experience without parameter updates. Natural-language skill evolution is a stochastic, non-convex search process, so optimizing a single skill trajectory risks overfitting to sampled experience or converging to suboptimal solutions. This motivates a diversity-driven approach that reduces optimization variance.

Method: DIVE evolves persistent, interpretable natural-language skills (encoding reasoning procedures, verification strategies, failure modes, and output constraints) that are executed and revised by the same frozen model without a teacher model. It independently evolves multiple skill populations from bootstrapped experience, adaptively refines them through diverse transformations, and jointly selects a complementary set of skills using verifier feedback.

Result: Across six mathematical and logical reasoning tasks and multiple model families, DIVE consistently outperforms existing reasoning methods, prompt-optimization approaches, skill-development frameworks, and memory-based baselines. It achieves rapid self-improvement with substantially larger performance gains using fewer rollouts than parameter-based methods (SFT, GRPO) and prompt optimization (GEPA). Evolved skills transfer across model scales and families, letting smaller models like GPT-5-nano match or outperform larger models like GPT-5 under conventional prompting.

Conclusion: Diversity-driven skill evolution is an effective, interpretable, and parameter-free approach to LLM self-improvement, enabling frozen models to retain and exploit experience through evolved natural-language skills.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) cannot retain post-deployment experience without parameter updates. We introduce DIVE, a diversity-driven framework that enables frozen LLMs to improve by evolving persistent natural-language skills from task experience and verifier feedback. These skills encode reusable reasoning procedures, verification strategies, common failure modes, and output constraints and are both executed and revised by the same underlying model without access to a teacher model. Since natural-language skill evolution is a stochastic, non-convex search process, optimizing a single skill trajectory can overfit to sampled experience or converge to a suboptimal solution. DIVE mitigates this optimization variance by independently evolving multiple skill populations from bootstrapped experience, adaptively refining them through diverse transformations, and jointly selecting a complementary set of skills. Across six mathematical and logical reasoning tasks and multiple model families, DIVE consistently outperforms existing reasoning methods, prompt-optimization approaches, skill-development frameworks, and memory-based baselines. It achieves rapid self-improvement from accumulated experience, obtaining substantially larger performance gains with fewer rollouts than parameter-based methods such as SFT and GRPO, and prompt optimization with GEPA. Further, the resulting skills transfer across model scales and families, enabling smaller models such as GPT-5-nano to match or outperform larger counterparts, i.e., GPT-5, under conventional prompting. These results establish diversity-driven skill evolution as an effective, interpretable, and parameter-free approach to LLM self-improvement.

</details>


### [36] [Intensional Anaphora](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12598)
*Ezra Keshet,Steven Abney*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes a description-based (rather than value-based) account of anaphora into intensional contexts, formalized in a new logic (PIP) that extends prior work by Keshet and Abney & Keshet.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing accounts (Stone 1999; Stone & Hardt 1999; Brasoveanu 2010) explain the infelicity of anaphora from non-veridical intensional contexts by requiring pronoun referents to exist in the world of evaluation. The authors show this value-based condition is both too strong (anaphora is disallowed even when referents clearly exist) and too weak (anaphora is allowed even when referents might not exist), motivating a new account.

Method: A description-based account: a pronoun presupposes that its antecedent description is instantiated in every world of the context set. This is implemented in a new logic, Plural Intensional Presuppositional predicate calculus (PIP), building on Keshet (2018) and Abney and Keshet (2022). Each PIP formula translates directly into standard first-order predicate calculus with set abstraction.

Result: The description-based presuppositional account correctly predicts both cases where intensional anaphora is disallowed despite existing referents and cases where it is permitted despite possibly non-existing referents, unifying data that value-based accounts could not handle.

Conclusion: Intensional anaphora is best captured by a description-based account requiring the antecedent description to be instantiated in each world of the context set, with PIP providing a classical, first-order foundation for the proposal.

Abstract: Intensional operators are often treated as quantifiers over possible worlds, parallel to the treatment of determiners as quantifiers over individuals. Yet individuals introduced in intensional contexts cannot serve as antecedents to later pronouns as easily as those introduced in merely quantificational contexts. For instance, "Everyone is eating a cheeseburger" may be followed by "They are large", where "they" refers to the cheeseburgers being eaten. However, as Stone (1999) points out, the similar "Andrea might be eating a cheeseburger" does not support later anaphoric references such as "It is large" or "They are large". Stone (1999), Stone and Hardt (1999), and Brasoveanu (2010) address this by requiring a pronoun's value (its referents) to exist in the world of evaluation, ruling out anaphora from non-veridical intensional contexts. We show, however, both cases where such anaphora is disallowed even when the pronoun's referents clearly exist and cases where it is allowed even though they might not exist. We argue that intensional anaphora is best captured using a description-based rather than value-based account. A pronoun presupposes that its corresponding antecedent description is instantiated in each world of the context set. Thus, there must be a cheeseburger being eaten by Andrea in every candidate world for "It is large" to be felicitous after "Andrea might be eating a cheeseburger". We implement our proposal via a new logic, building on Keshet (2018) and Abney and Keshet (2022), called Plural Intensional Presuppositional predicate calculus (PIP). Each PIP formula translates directly into standard first-order predicate calculus with set abstraction, providing a classical foundation for this work.

</details>


### [37] [When Explanations Betray Backdoors: Black-Box Auditing for Language Model Classifiers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12623)
*Yang Liu,Ran Zou*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: For black-box auditing of language model classifiers with explanations, the paper introduces Groundedness Drift, a lightweight score measuring whether the answer summary remains grounded in the input; it outperforms all compared detectors on backdoor attack detection, and a multi-probe escalation (Unsupported Groundedness) further improves signals under explanation-camouflage stress cases but does not fully close the adaptive gap.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Language model classifiers with explanations are widely deployed for moderation, routing, topic triage, and low-resource annotation, but they are vulnerable to backdoor attacks. The defender may only have clean calibration data (no trigger information) and is limited to black-box queries returning a label plus a short rationale/quoted evidence. The paper aims to audit such models for backdoors using only these explanation-level signals.

Method: The authors propose Groundedness Drift, a lightweight score that measures whether the classifier's answer summary remains grounded in the input after a clean calibration set. They evaluate it across two 7B backbones, five datasets, and four common non-adaptive OpenBackdoor-style attack families, benchmarking against other detectors at a nominal 5% clean-FPR budget using AUROC and residual target ASR. They also introduce Unsupported Groundedness, a multi-probe escalation designed for explanation-camouflage stress cases.

Result: Groundedness Drift achieves higher AUROC and lower residual target ASR than every compared detector in all cases at a nominal 5% clean-FPR budget. Unsupported Groundedness improves detection signals under explanation-camouflage stress cases but does not close the adaptive gap.

Conclusion: Explanation-groundedness can serve as an effective black-box signal for auditing backdoored language model classifiers, with Groundedness Drift beating existing detectors under a clean-data-only setting. However, adaptive attackers exploiting explanation camouflage remain a challenge, as Unsupported Groundedness improves but does not close the gap.

Abstract: Language model classifiers with explanations are used for moderation, routing, topic triage, and low-resource annotation. We study black-box auditing when the defender has only clean calibration data without trigger information but can ask the classifier for a label plus a short rationale or quoted evidence. We introduce Groundedness Drift, a lightweight score measuring whether the answer summary remains grounded in the input. Across two 7B backbones, five datasets, and four common non-adaptive OpenBackdoor-style attack families, Groundedness Drift achieves higher AUROC and lower residual target ASR than every compared detector in all cases at a nominal 5\% clean-FPR budget. We then evaluate Unsupported Groundedness, a multi-probe escalation for explanation-camouflage stress cases. Unsupported Groundedness improves signals but does not close the adaptive gap.

</details>


### [38] [Novels generated by language models show compressed formal variation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12630)
*Mehdy Sedaghat Payam,Justin Quinn*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Repeated AI novel generation produces far less formal (stylistic) variation than human-written corpora, a phenomenon the paper terms "variance overclosure," alongside a distinct "correlational overclosure" where cross-measure relationships are unstable across models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Little is known about the level of formal variation across many AI generations, so rather than detecting individual AI passages, the study asks whether repeated AI generation can match the diversity range found across human corpora.

Method: Contrasts six corpora: 20 novels each from GPT-5.5 Thinking and Qwen3-14B in a nineteenth-century British realist style, 20 novels each from both models in a contemporary zero style, 205 nineteenth-century human British novels, and 65 contemporary human Zero-Style novels. Document-level measures include MATTR-500, Shannon entropy, average sentence length, readability, punctuation rate, and sentence-length variability.

Result: The most robust finding is compression of sentence structure: AI-generated novels vary far less from one another in sentence structure than human novels. Compression also appears in readability, punctuation, and within-novel sentence-length variability. Lexical measures are similarly compressed except Qwen Zero-Style MATTR. GPT and Qwen show distinct mean stylistic profiles but lack stable cross-measure correlations, motivating a distinction between "variance overclosure" (limited formal range between novels) and "correlational overclosure."

Conclusion: An individual AI-generated novel may resemble human fiction stylistically, but a collection of AI-generated novels occupies a much narrower formal range, due to variance overclosure and correlational overclosure.

Abstract: While large language models can generate entire novels, there is little information about the level of formal variation in their output over many generations. Rather than asking whether individual passages can be identified as AI-generated, this study asks whether repeated AI generation can produce the same range of diversity which is found across human corpora. This paper contrasts six corpora based on generation source and target style: twenty novels generated using GPT-5.5 Thinking in a nineteenth-century British realist style, twenty novels generated using Qwen3-14B in a nineteenth-century British realist style, twenty novels generated using each of these models in a contemporary zero style, 205 nineteenth-century human-written British novels, and sixty-five contemporary human-written Zero-Style novels. At the document level, the research includes MATTR-500, Shannon entropy, average sentence length, readability, and punctuation rate measurements. The most robust and reliable result is compression of sentence structure. Repeated generations produce novels that vary far less from one another in sentence structure than human novels do. Compression is also present in the measures of readability, punctuation, and sentence length variability within novels. Lexical measures tend to be similarly compressed, with the exception of Qwen Zero-Style MATTR. Despite having distinct mean stylistic profiles, GPT and Qwen lack a stable pattern of cross-measure correlation. This article therefore distinguishes between variance overclosure, which represents a limited formal range between novels, and a more specific phenomenon of correlational overclosure. This means that an individual AI-generated novel may resemble human fiction stylistically, while a collection of AI-generated novels occupies a much narrower formal range.

</details>


### [39] [Excess Separability: Nuisance-Controlled Residual-Stream Probing for Benchmark Contamination Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12652)
*Florian Braun*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper audits contamination detection via linear probes on transformer activations, showing the naive approach fails and proposing a protocol with a zero-sum depth-profile contrast, placebo baseline, and label-permutation null that reliably controls false positives.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing contamination detection methods (n-gram overlap, likelihood membership inference, canary strings) each require unavailable resources: the training corpus, a well-chosen test statistic, or foresight at dataset release. A newer probe-based alternative is appealing but its natural implementation is unreliable, so the authors aim to find a probe protocol whose false-positive rate actually tracks the analyst's control set and survives empirical measurement.

Method: The authors systematically measure and reject simpler probe-based alternatives, then specify a protocol that reports a zero-sum contrast on the depth profile of probe accuracy, recentered on a level-matched placebo baseline, tested against a label-permutation null with the reference set twice the size of the suspect set. Each design choice replaces a rejected simpler alternative; robustness is verified via item bootstrap, flat-profile contrasts, half-size baselines, and audits on real transformers including Pile arms and a temporal split.

Result: The naive approach fails in measured ways: reporting the level rather than the shape of excess separability makes the false-positive rate range 0.03-0.99 under a true null; contrasting against a flat depth profile fails in both directions (rejecting a true null 0.72 of the time when surface decodability rises with depth, losing all power when it falls); a fixed-probe item bootstrap rejects up to 0.09 vs 0.02 for the refitting permutation null; a half-size baseline triples error. On real transformers, baseline depth profiles are measurably non-flat (up to 29.1 accuracy points on a temporal split), and non-flatness tracks surface differences between item sets (correlation 0.87 over 6 audits). All 4 well-matched Pile arms return null, and the protocol refuses a verdict on the temporal split. No positive familiarity direction is established; the only positive occurs where exchangeability fails.

Conclusion: A reliable probe-based contamination-detection protocol requires a zero-sum depth-profile contrast with a level-matched placebo and label-permutation null, and the paper cannot establish that transformers encode a familiarity direction under exchangeable settings; implementation, tests, and audits are released.

Abstract: Benchmark contamination is diagnosed today with n-gram overlap, with likelihood-based membership inference, or with canary strings, and each needs something usually unavailable: the training corpus, a well-chosen test statistic, or foresight at dataset release. A recent alternative reads contamination off a linear probe on internal activations. We show that the natural way to do this does not work, and specify one that survives measurement.
  The protocol reports a zero-sum contrast on the depth profile of probe accuracy, recentred on a level-matched placebo baseline, tested against a label-permutation null, with the reference set twice the size of the suspect set. Each choice replaces a simpler alternative we measured and rejected. Reporting the level of excess separability rather than its shape makes the false positive rate track the size of the analyst's own control set, from 0.03 to 0.99 under a true null. Contrasting against a flat depth profile fails in both directions, rejecting a true null 0.72 of the time when surface decodability rises with depth and losing all power when it falls. An item bootstrap holds the fitted probe fixed and rejects up to 0.09 of the time where a permutation null that refits it holds 0.02. A half-size baseline triples the error rate.
  On real transformers, baseline depth profiles are measurably not flat, spanning up to 29.1 accuracy points on a temporal split, and their non-flatness tracks the surface difference between the item sets (correlation 0.87 over 6 audits), so the correction is largest exactly where it is needed. All 4 well-matched Pile arms return null, and the protocol refuses a verdict on the temporal split rather than reporting one. What this does not establish is whether transformers carry a familiarity direction at all: the only positive sits on the split where exchangeability fails. Implementation, tests and audits are released.

</details>


### [40] [ERSkill: Evolving for Skill-Guided Adaptive Memory Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12720)
*Haolong Chen,Liang Zhang,Zhuo Li,Lei Xue,Guanrxu Zhu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ERSkill is a retrieval-centric framework that treats memory retrieval as evolvable, skill-guided components for LLM agents. It represents retrieval behaviors as executable skills, matches queries to skills via a trained router, and continuously co-evolves skills and router through an experience trie and a double-frontier mechanism, achieving large gains over non-evolving and self-evolving baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents increasingly depend on long-term memory for persistent interactions, but existing retrieval mechanisms are static and not treated as evolvable components. This limits performance on heterogeneous memory queries that require diverse evidence construction strategies.

Method: ERSkill compiles interaction histories into a structured memory store and represents retrieval behaviors as executable skills built from fundamental primitives. At inference, a trained router dynamically matches each query to the optimal skill to construct tailored evidence. During training, it co-evolves the skill set and router, using an experience trie to efficiently record explored retrieval paths and a double-frontier mechanism to safely decouple expansion of new skill capabilities from stable, router-facing deployment.

Result: Across multiple agent memory benchmarks, ERSkill substantially outperforms strong non-evolving and self-evolving baselines, improving the overall average of F1, BLEU-1, and LLM-judge scores by 31.3% with Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct and 28.1% with GPT-5.4-nano.

Conclusion: Treating memory retrieval as self-evolving, skill-guided components enables continuous improvement and significantly boosts LLM agent performance on heterogeneous memory queries, outperforming both non-evolving and existing self-evolving approaches.

Abstract: While Large Language Model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on long-term memory for persistent interactions, the retrieval mechanisms governing this memory are rarely treated as evolvable components. This static approach limits performance on heterogeneous memory queries, which often demand diverse evidence construction strategies. To address this, we introduce \textbf{ERSkill}, a retrieval-centric framework for self-evolving, skill-guided memory access. ERSkill compiles interaction histories into a structured memory store and represents retrieval behaviors as executable skills composed of fundamental primitives. At inference time, a trained router dynamically matches each query to the optimal skill to construct tailored evidence for answer generation. To enable continuous improvement, ERSkill co-evolves the skill set and the router during training. It employs an experience trie to efficiently record explored retrieval paths, alongside a double-frontier mechanism that safely decouples the expansion of new skill capabilities from stable, router-facing deployment. Experiments across multiple agent memory benchmarks demonstrate that ERSkill substantially outperforms strong non-evolving and self-evolving baselines. Notably, it improves the overall average across F1, BLEU-1, and LLM-judge scores by 31.3\% with Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct and by 28.1\% with GPT-5.4-nano.

</details>


### [41] [ReconSpan: Reconstruction-Guided Adaptive Latent Tokenization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12756)
*Lixing Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ReconSpan introduces adaptive latent tokenization that segments text into chunks, each represented by a single latent token that a backward decoder can use to reconstruct the chunk, enabling variable average chunk lengths (6.5–12.2 tokens).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To develop a latent tokenization method that produces shorter, input-dependent continuous representations while preserving as much reconstructable content as possible compared to random chunk boundaries.

Method: ReconSpan divides text into chunks that a backward decoder can reconstruct from a single contextual prefix code, retaining one such code as the latent token per chunk. The reconstruction criterion is applied at chunk formation, allowing a single trained autoencoder to produce varying average chunk lengths.

Result: At matched average length, reconstruction-guided boundaries preserve more text than random boundaries; readers of the latent sequence recover topic information reliably but struggle to extract exact details. The method achieved average chunk lengths ranging from 6.5 to 12.2.

Conclusion: ReconSpan supports flexible, reconstruction-driven text chunking that trades off sequence length against fidelity, preserving high-level topic information while sacrificing fine-grained details.

Abstract: Adaptive latent tokenization maps a fine-grained input to a shorter sequence of continuous representations associated with input-dependent spans. We introduce ReconSpan, which divides text into chunks that a backward decoder can reconstruct from a single contextual prefix code and retains one such code as the latent token for each chunk. The reconstruction criterion is applied when chunks are formed, allowing one trained autoencoder to produce average chunk lengths from 6.5 to 12.2. At matched average length, reconstruction-guided boundaries preserve more text than random boundaries. Readers of the resulting latent sequence recover topic information reliably but struggle to extract exact details.

</details>


### [42] [ViTOED: A Dataset for Target-Oriented Emotion Detection on Vietnamese Social Media Texts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12776)
*Chanh Vo,Son T. Luu,Ngan Luu-Thuy Nguyen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces ViTOED, a Vietnamese dataset for target-oriented emotion detection containing 10,985 comments and 21,244 annotated opinion quadruples, along with a graph-based baseline evaluated on Vietnamese PLMs that reveals substantial room for improvement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is a lack of datasets and baselines for fine-grained, target-oriented emotion detection in Vietnamese social media, which exhibits unique linguistic phenomena (implicit sources/targets, vocabulary ambiguities) not captured by existing resources.

Method: The authors construct the ViTOED dataset with 10,985 user comments and 21,244 manually annotated opinion quadruples (source, target, expression, polarity) under strict guidelines. They propose a baseline using structured sentiment graphs and evaluate it with various Vietnamese pre-trained language models.

Result: Empirical results show that span detection and relation extraction remain challenging, indicating the task is difficult for current Vietnamese pre-trained language models and there is significant room for improvement in Vietnamese target-oriented emotion detection.

Conclusion: ViTOED provides a valuable resource for Vietnamese target-oriented emotion detection, and while the proposed graph-based baseline establishes initial benchmarks, the gap in span detection and relation extraction suggests future work is needed to improve model performance on this task.

Abstract: This paper introduces ViTOED, a novel dataset for target-oriented emotion detection in Vietnamese social media texts. The ViTOED comprises 10,985 user comments and 21,244 manually annotated opinion quadruples (source, target, expression, polarity) that follow strict guidelines. The dataset reveals Vietnamese-specific phenomena, such as implicit sources and targets and vocabulary ambiguities, enabling deeper analysis of user emotions toward entities. We propose a baseline using structured sentiment graphs and evaluate various Vietnamese pre-trained language models. The empirical results highlight challenges in span detection and relation extraction and indicate substantial room for model improvement in Vietnamese Target-Oriented Emotion Detection tasks.

</details>


### [43] [FastThaiG2P: Lightning-fast Thai Grapheme-to-phoneme Conversion for Voice Agent Pipelines](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12814)
*Charin Polpanumas*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: FastThaiG2P is a fast, sub-millisecond Thai grapheme-to-phoneme (G2P) converter that uses a PyThaiNLP-tokenized dictionary plus normalization rules to produce IPA/Kokoro-TTS phonemes, enabling real-time Thai TTS when paired with an 82M-parameter StyleTTS 2 model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Thai text-to-speech pipelines need accurate and fast grapheme-to-phoneme conversion, but existing approaches struggle with Thai script specifics (no explicit word boundaries, complex tone/orthography rules), motivating a lightweight, extensible, dictionary-and-rule-based G2P that is fast enough for real-time synthesis.

Method: FastThaiG2P uses PyThaiNLP tokenization, an extensible dictionary, and normalization rules for common Central Thai speech to convert graphemes into IPA and Kokoro-TTS phoneme conventions. Out-of-vocabulary tokens are handled via a fallback (0.5% OOV rate). The converter was used to phonemize the Som-TTS dataset (20 hours of grapheme/audio pairs), which then trained an 82M-parameter StyleTTS 2 model based on a Kokoro-TTS recipe, deployed via ONNX inference on CPU.

Result: FastThaiG2P achieved an average latency of 0.15 ms per utterance on 27,242 synthetic utterances: 30% tokenization, 12% normalization, 58% OOV fallbacks (0.5% OOV rate). The resulting StyleTTS 2 model vocalizes intelligible Thai speech at a 0.25 real-time factor (4x real-time) with ONNX CPU inference, suitable for prototyping and development.

Conclusion: FastThaiG2P delivers sub-millisecond, accurate Thai G2P conversion, and when integrated into a Kokoro-TTS-based StyleTTS 2 pipeline it produces intelligible Thai speech in real time (4x), making it a practical solution for prototyping and development of Thai TTS systems.

Abstract: FastThaiG2P provides sub-millisecond Thai grapheme-to-phoneme conversion for text-to-speech pipelines (International Phonetic Alphabet and Kokoro-TTS conventions) using a PyThaiNLP-tokenized, extensible dictionary and normalization rules for common Central Thai speech. The approach achieves an average latency of 0.15 ms per utterance on a benchmark of 27,242 synthetically generated utterances, of which 30\% is spent on tokenization, 12\% on normalization, and 58\% on out-of-vocabulary fallbacks (0.5\% OOV rate). To demonstrate its effectiveness, we used FastThaiG2P to phonemize Som-TTS, an open dataset containing 20 hours of grapheme-and-audio pairs, then trained an 82M-parameter StyleTTS 2 model based on a Kokoro-TTS recipe. The resulting model vocalizes intelligible Thai speech suitable for prototyping and development at 0.25 real-time factor (4x real-time) with ONNX inference on CPU.

</details>


### [44] [From Atomic Evidence to Logical Composition: Structured Compositional Reasoning over Compound Answer Options](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12836)
*Obed Junias,Maria Leonor Pacheco*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LLMs fail to compose atomic judgments under logical operators (AND/OR/NEITHER-NOR), so the paper decomposes compound options into atomic hypotheses, scores each atom independently, and recombines the calibrated scores via an operator-constrained ILP. It improves Macro-F1 substantially on LOGICAL-COMMONSENSEQA and a new LOGICAL-SATA benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large language models often answer individual atomic judgments correctly but fail when those atoms must be combined under explicit logical operators such as AND, OR, and NEITHER/NOR. Existing approaches require the model to evaluate whole compound options, which causes errors even when the underlying atomic judgments are correct.

Method: The paper introduces a framework that decomposes each compound answer option into its constituent atomic answers. For each atom, the model scores contrastive hypotheses, and since the model never sees the full compound option, it avoids compound-induced errors. The calibrated atomic scores are then composed into a single prediction using an operator-constrained integer linear program (ILP) that respects the logical structure (AND, OR, NEITHER/NOR) of the options.

Result: The framework improves Macro-F1 from 48.3 to 77.0 on the human-validated LOGICAL-COMMONSENSEQA split, and from 47.0 to 75.6 on LOGICAL-SATA, a newly introduced reading-comprehension benchmark derived from SATA-Bench. The largest gains occur on NEITHER/NOR options.

Conclusion: Decomposing compound options into atomic judgments and recombining calibrated scores with an operator-constrained ILP substantially improves logical composition in LLMs, particularly for NEITHER/NOR constructions, demonstrating the value of separating atomic scoring from logical composition.

Abstract: Large language models often fail when answer options require combining atomic judgments under explicit logical operators, even when they judge the individual atoms correctly. We study compound options connected by AND, OR, and NEITHER/NOR, introducing a framework that decomposes each option into atomic answers and scores contrastive hypotheses about each one, so the model never sees a compound option. An operator-constrained integer linear program then composes the calibrated scores into a single prediction. We evaluate on LOGICAL-COMMONSENSEQA and introduce LOGICAL-SATA, a reading-comprehension benchmark derived from SATA-Bench. Our framework improves Macro-F1 from 48.3 to 77.0 on the human-validated LOGICAL-COMMONSENSEQA split and from 47.0 to 75.6 on LOGICAL-SATA, with the largest gains on NEITHER/NOR.

</details>


### [45] [AQuA: Recursively Self-Improving Quantitative Trading Research Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12841)
*Jiacheng Guo,Suozhi Huang,Yunlong Gao,Zihao Li,Jian Ge,Xu Kuang,Mengdi Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: AQuA consists of two independent language-model-driven research systems—one for symbolic factor discovery and one for trainable model development—that each close their own research loop by using validated evidence to guide later proposals, implementing a bounded form of recursive self-improvement in quantitative-investment research.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper investigates whether an autonomous system can use evidence from earlier experiments to improve the hypotheses and candidates it proposes in later iterations—i.e., recursive self-improvement at the level of the quantitative-investment research process rather than at the level of a single model.

Method: AQuA comprises two separate LM-driven systems that share no agents, memories, candidate spaces, or research state. Each runs inside its own sealed sandbox with fixed data splits, feature/label definitions, and evaluator, and can act only via constrained factor expressions or configuration diffs. The factor system is a manager-mediated multi-agent pipeline that discovers and combines factors into a signal; the model system is a config-driven loop over a hybrid time-series architecture. Both close their own research loop by retaining validated evidence to guide subsequent proposals.

Result: The factor system reaches a combined information coefficient of about 0.190 on a crypto universe. The model system reaches a per-stock information coefficient of +0.0843 on US equities and converts it into a threshold long/short strategy with a held-out Sharpe of up to +2.50 at a two-leg cost; the strategy is positive in every year from 2021 to 2025.

Conclusion: Two independent, sandboxed research systems can each implement recursive self-improvement at the process level, producing signals and strategies with competitive information coefficients and Sharpe ratios, validating the feasibility of autonomous evidence-driven research loops in quantitative investing.

Abstract: We study recursive self-improvement at the level of quantitative-investment research: whether an autonomous system can use evidence from earlier experiments to improve the hypotheses and candidates proposed in later iterations. We present AQuA, which comprises two separate language-model-driven research systems: one for symbolic factor discovery and one for trainable model development. The two systems do not share agents, memories, candidate spaces, or research state. Instead, each independently closes its own research loop by retaining validated evidence and using it to guide subsequent proposals. In this bounded sense, both systems implement recursive self-improvement at the level of the research process. Each system also uses its own sealed sandbox, which fixes the data splits, feature and label definitions, and evaluator while allowing the model to act only through constrained factor expressions or configuration diffs. The factor system, a manager-mediated multi-agent pipeline, discovers and combines factors into a signal that reaches a combined information coefficient of about $0.190$ on a crypto universe. The model system, a config-driven loop over a hybrid time-series architecture, reaches a per-stock information coefficient of $+0.0843$ on US equities and converts it into a threshold long/short strategy with a held-out Sharpe of up to $+2.50$ at a two-leg cost. The strategy is positive in every year from 2021 to 2025.

</details>


### [46] [Falsehood and Impossibility Are Different Directions in an AI's Representation of Language](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12852)
*Yoon Pyo Lee*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: An activation study of Gemma 3 4B IT finds that, despite verbally conflating contingent falsehood with contradiction, the model's internal activations sharply separate necessary falsehoods from contingent falsehoods, instead placing impossibility closer to semantic anomaly.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine whether a multimodal language model internally distinguishes false statements whose states of affairs could not obtain (necessary/impossible falsehoods) from merely false ones, given that language can describe both false and impossible states of affairs and the model's overt answers conflate these categories.

Method: Exploratory activation study of Gemma 3 4B IT using 85 prompts across 17 philosophical families and 15 topics, each expressed as truth, contingent falsehood, improbable claim, semantic anomaly, and necessary falsehood. Probes include a linear truth probe, an impossibility probe evaluated on held-out topic families, overlap analysis with a semantic anomaly direction, orthogonalization checks, and sparse autoencoder feature analysis at matched layers.

Result: Model answers label 12 of 15 false statements as "contradiction," conflating contingent falsehood with contradiction. Activations: truth probe separates impossible from true (AUC 0.93) but not impossible from false (AUC 0.20). Impossibility probe separates necessary from contingent falsehood at AUC 1.00 (layer 15, balanced accuracy 0.97, Bonferroni-adjusted P=0.018). Truth and impossibility directions are near-orthogonal; impossibility direction partially overlaps semantic anomaly but stays distinguishable. Sparse autoencoder features selective for impossibility also fire on anomalous sentences but rarely on contingent falsehoods.

Conclusion: In this model's activation space, necessary falsehoods are not extreme instances of contingent falsehood but lie closer to semantic anomaly, though this proximity does not imply impossible statements are intrinsically meaningless. These correlational findings from one small model serve as an empirical footnote to a longstanding philosophical distinction.

Abstract: Language can describe states of affairs that are false and states of affairs that could not be the case at all. Whether an AI model internally distinguishes these failures remains unclear. I report an exploratory activation study of the multimodal open-weight model Gemma 3 4B IT using 85 prompts from 17 philosophical families and a topic-matched modality set of 15 topics, each expressed as a truth, contingent falsehood, improbable claim, semantic anomaly, and necessary falsehood. In its answers, the model conflates contingent falsehood with contradiction, labeling 12 of 15 false statements "contradiction." Its activations show a different pattern. A linear truth probe separates impossible from true statements (AUC 0.93) but not impossible from false statements (AUC 0.20). An impossibility probe evaluated on held-out topic families separates necessary from contingent falsehood at AUC 1.00, peaking at layer 15 with balanced accuracy 0.97 (Bonferroni-adjusted P=0.018). The truth and impossibility directions are close to orthogonal, whereas the impossibility direction partially overlaps a semantic anomaly direction while remaining distinguishable from it. Sparse autoencoder features at the same layer repeat this geometry. Features selective for impossibility also fire on anomalous sentences but rarely on contingent falsehoods. In this model's activation space, necessary falsehoods are not extreme cases of contingent falsehood but lie closer to the experimentally defined category of semantic anomaly. This representational proximity does not imply that impossible statements are intrinsically meaningless. These correlational observations from one small model offer an empirical footnote to an old philosophical distinction.

</details>


### [47] [The Embedder's Dilemma: LLMs Are Better, but at What Cost?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12875)
*Adnan El Assadi,Niklas Muennighoff,Jinhyuk Lee*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A controlled, cost-aware comparison of ten LLMs and 26 embedding models across 37 tasks finds the two paradigms roughly tied overall, but LLMs excel at reasoning-heavy retrieval while embedding models win on classification; LLMs are far more expensive, suggesting a task-based division of labor.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To answer whether text-embedding pipelines should be replaced by LLMs, given the rise of LLMs as general-purpose encoders and the lack of a systematic, cost-aware comparison between the two paradigms.

Method: A controlled, cost-aware benchmark comparing ten LLMs from six families and 26 embedding models (118M to 14B parameters) on 37 tasks spanning classification, semantic textual similarity (STS), clustering, pair classification, and retrieval, plus an ablation on reasoning budget and a Pareto-frontier analysis.

Result: The best LLM (Gemini 3.1 Pro, 77.6) and best embedding model (77.2) differ by only 0.4 points; LLMs lead on reasoning-heavy retrieval, embedding models lead on classification, and they match on clustering, STS, and pair classification. LLMs cost up to 1,431x more (USD 154 vs. USD 0.11 per benchmark pass), and open LLMs process tokens 2.5–736x slower. Reasoning tokens account for 28–81% of LLM inference cost, though lower reasoning budgets preserve or improve retrieval quality for most models.

Conclusion: The two paradigms are effectively tied in aggregate but have complementary strengths, supporting a division of labor: use embedding models for similarity, classification, and clustering, and reserve LLMs for reasoning-intensive retrieval. Code, datasets, and results are publicly available.

Abstract: Should you replace your text-embedding pipeline with a large language model? We answer this with a controlled, cost-aware comparison of ten LLMs across six families and 26 embedding models (118M to 14B parameters) on 37 tasks spanning classification, semantic textual similarity (STS), clustering, pair classification, and retrieval. In aggregate the two paradigms are effectively tied: the best LLM (Gemini 3.1 Pro, 77.6) and the best embedding model (77.2) differ by 0.4 points. Their strengths differ by task: LLMs lead on reasoning-heavy retrieval, embedding models lead on classification, and the two match on clustering, STS, and pair classification. Reaching that parity is expensive. An LLM costs up to 1,431x more than an embedding model of comparable quality (USD 154 vs. USD 0.11 per benchmark pass), and the open LLMs tested process tokens 2.5 to 736x more slowly on the same GPU. Reasoning tokens account for 28 to 81% of LLM inference cost; lower reasoning budgets preserve or improve retrieval quality for most models in our ablation. The Pareto frontier contains the leading embedding models and one LLM, Gemini 3.1 Pro. These results support a division of labour: use embedding models for similarity, classification, and clustering, and reserve LLMs for reasoning-intensive retrieval. Our code, datasets, and results are publicly available at https://github.com/embeddings-benchmark/embedders-dilemma.

</details>


### [48] [When Your Agent Opens the Chat App: Agent-Controlled Search over Raw Chat Logs Rivals Structured Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12888)
*Ruizhe Li,Licheng Zhang,Benfeng Xu,Mingxuan Du,Zheren Fu,Weidong Chen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ReFind introduces an agent-controlled search interface that skips semantic memory structures entirely, indexing raw conversation history lexically at turn granularity. Combined with four chat-native search controls and a separate reasoning stage, it beats graph- and tree-based memory systems on conversational-memory tasks, showing that much of structured memory's benefit can be recovered with controllable search over the unmodified record.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agent-memory systems increasingly invest in structured representations (summaries, embeddings, trees, knowledge graphs) to improve retrieval quality. The authors question how much of this benefit actually comes from the structure itself versus from competent retrieval over the raw conversation history, hypothesizing that elaborate structure may be unnecessary for precise, evidence-grounded questions.

Method: ReFind builds no semantic structure. It leaves the conversation archive unmodified, indexes it lexically at turn granularity, and combines a generic iterative keyword-search loop with four chat-native controls grounded in empirical refinding work: (1) session-aware rank fusion, (2) local context expansion, (3) temporal narrowing, and (4) skipping already-inspected sessions. A separate reasoning stage then answers from the collected evidence. Comparisons include single-shot BM25, a matched generic-agentic BM25 control, component ablations, and agentic dense/hybrid variants, all using a GPT-4o-mini backbone matched to reused baselines.

Result: Across roughly 2,800 conversational-memory questions (single- and multi-hop QA, event ordering, fact consolidation) under MemoryAgentBench's incremental multi-turn setting, ReFind achieved the highest mean accuracy (58.2), surpassing the strongest graph- and tree-based systems (HippoRAG 2 at 53.2). On LongMemEval-S/M, it reached 93.2 ± 3.3 and 89.3 ± 6.0 with GPT-5-mini. Ablations supported the roles of agent control, chat-native controls, and lexical retrieval.

Conclusion: For precise, evidence-grounded questions over chat archives, much of the benefit credited to elaborate memory structures is recoverable by giving an agent controllable search over the unmodified record, requiring no LLM-based index construction at all.

Abstract: Agent-memory systems increasingly buy retrieval quality with structure, transforming raw conversation histories into summaries, embeddings, trees, or knowledge graphs before any question is asked. We ask how much of that benefit comes from the structure itself, rather than from competent retrieval over the raw history. We present ReFind, an agent-controlled search interface that builds no semantic structure at all: it leaves the conversation archive unmodified, indexes it lexically at turn granularity, and combines a generic iterative keyword-search loop with four chat-native controls grounded in empirical refinding work: session-aware rank fusion, local context expansion, temporal narrowing, and skipping already-inspected sessions. A separate reasoning stage answers from the collected evidence. Across a broad suite of conversational-memory tasks (single- and multi-hop QA, event ordering, and fact consolidation), roughly 2,800 questions on precise-retrieval and fact-tracking capabilities evaluated under the incremental multi-turn setting of MemoryAgentBench, ReFind attains the highest mean accuracy (58.2) of any system compared, above the strongest graph- and tree-based memory systems (HippoRAG 2, 53.2), all under a GPT-4o-mini backbone matched to every reused baseline. Controlled comparisons to single-shot BM25, a matched generic-agentic BM25 control, component removals, and agentic dense/hybrid variants separately support the roles of agent control, chat-native controls, and lexical retrieval. On LongMemEval-S/M, the same interface reaches 93.2 +/- 3.3 and 89.3 +/- 6.0 with GPT-5-mini.
