The results indicate that for precise, evidence-grounded questions over chat archives, much of the benefit credited to elaborate memory structures is recoverable by giving an agent controllable search over the unmodified record, with no LLM-based index construction at all.

</details>


### [49] [BavGround: A Benchmark for Regional Cultural Grounding and Dialect Competence in Bavarian](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12894)
*Jophin John,Michael Hoffmann,Jan Fillies,Michael A. Hedderich,Barbara Plank*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: BavGround is a benchmark of 618 multi-parallel multiple-choice questions (206 per language, across 8 cultural domains) for evaluating Bavarian regional cultural grounding and dialect competence in English, German, and Bavarian, tested on fifteen 7B–10B open-weight models plus one closed model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cultural evaluation of LLMs typically targets high-resource standard languages, underrepresenting regional cultures and dialect communities; the authors address this gap by focusing on Bavarian culture and dialect.

Method: They construct BavGround with 206 source-grounded multiple-choice questions across eight cultural domains, rendered in English, German, and Bavarian (618 instances), combining broadly accessible and source-grounded regional knowledge from journalism, historical sources, and specialist literature. They evaluate fifteen 7B–10B open-weight instruction-tuned models and one closed model under multiple protocols: raw answer-letter scoring, shuffled-letter scoring, option-text likelihood, generated-answer parsing, and semantic matching.

Result: Strong multilingual models perform best overall, but accuracy declines on Bavarian and source-grounded items, revealing persistent difficulty with dialect and localized knowledge. Evaluation protocol strongly affects absolute scores and rankings, especially for regionally adapted models. An exploratory analysis of GENBA-10B checkpoints shows continued pretraining improves answer-content likelihood unevenly across domains, while dialect competence stays comparatively weak.

Conclusion: BavGround provides localized, protocol-aware evaluation of cultural representation in LLMs, highlighting both the underperformance on dialectal/localized content and the sensitivity of conclusions to evaluation methodology.

Abstract: Cultural evaluation of large language models (LLMs) often focuses on high-resource standard languages, leaving regional culture and dialect communities underrepresented. We introduce BavGround, a benchmark for evaluating Bavarian regional cultural grounding and dialect competence across English, German and Bavarian. BavGround contains 206 multiple-choice source questions across eight cultural domains per language, yielding 618 multi-parallel instances, with items covering both broadly accessible cultural knowledge and source-grounded regional knowledge from journalism, historical sources, and specialist literature. We evaluate fifteen 7B-10B open-weight instruction-tuned models and one closed-model reference. Strong multilingual models perform best overall, but performance drops on Bavarian items and source-grounded questions, indicating persistent difficulty with dialectal and localized cultural knowledge. We further show that conclusions depend strongly on evaluation protocol: raw answer-letter scoring, shuffled-letter scoring, option-text likelihood, generated-answer parsing, and semantic matching can produce different absolute scores and rankings, especially for regionally adapted models. Finally, an exploratory analysis of GENBA-10B checkpoints suggests that continued pretraining improves answer-content likelihood unevenly across domains, while dialect competence remains comparatively weak. BavGround supports localized, protocol-aware evaluation of cultural representation in LLMs.

</details>


### [50] [Prompts in the Wild: A Large Analyzed Collection of Transactional Prompts in Code](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12905)
*Victoria Basmov,Yoav Goldberg,Reut Tsarfaty*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper collects 57.5K unique transactional prompts (reproducible natural language instructions embedded in software) from GitHub, introduces a structured ontology to annotate them, and analyzes their diversity, revealing Zipf-like distributions across languages, domains, tasks, and modalities, with an error analysis validating annotation quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prompt engineering is central to LLM behavior, yet prompts themselves—as linguistic objects—have not been systematically studied empirically. The authors argue prompts deserve investigation in their own right and that a structured, quantitative foundation is needed to enable such research.

Method: The authors collect 57.5K unique prompt samples from GitHub, focusing on transactional prompts (reproducible natural language instructions integrated into software). They introduce a structured ontology capturing prompt properties and their formal and semantic components, then transform raw unstructured prompt texts into richly structured linguistic objects. They analyze the resulting data for usage-pattern diversity and perform a comprehensive error analysis across all ontology fields to validate annotation reliability. The dataset and a browsing/exploration interface are released.

Result: Analysis reveals significant diversity of usage patterns across languages, domains, tasks, and modalities, following a typical Zipf-like distribution: some prompt types clearly prevail while more diverse ones appear in the long tail. The error analysis provides a detailed assessment of annotation quality across all fields.

Conclusion: Prompts are linguistic objects worthy of independent study; structuring them via a defined ontology enables quantitative empirical analysis, and the released dataset plus exploration interface provides a foundation for future research on prompt structure and usage.

Abstract: The behavior of contemporary generative Large Language Models (LLMs) is directly shaped by prompts, unstructured texts that describe the desired output and model behavior. In this paper we argue that prompts are linguistic objects that merit investigation in their own right. To this end, we collect 57.5K unique samples of prompts from GitHub. Specifically, we focus on transactional prompts: reproducible natural language instructions that are integrated into software. To enable the empirical, quantitative study of prompts, we introduce a structured ontology, capturing the properties of prompts as well as their formal and semantic components. Based on this ontology, we transform prompts from unstructured raw texts into richly structured linguistic objects. Analysis of these structured data reveals significant diversity of usage patterns across languages, domains, tasks, and modalities, in a typical Zipf-like distribution where some clearly prevail and others, more diverse, appear in the long tail. To validate the reliability of the ontology-based annotation of the prompts, we perform a comprehensive error analysis across all fields, providing a detailed assessment of annotation quality. We release the dataset together with a browsing and exploration interface (https://github.com/OnlpLab/transactionalPromptsCollection ).

</details>


### [51] [Decoupled Contrastive Decoding via Expert-Aligned Drafting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12913)
*Zhixuan Liu,Zhichen Dong,Yuanfu Wang,Chao Yang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper shows that contrastive-aware drafting does not reliably beat expert-aligned drafting for accelerating Contrastive Decoding, and introduces Decoupled Contrastive Decoding (DCD), which drafts expert-aligned and reserves the amateur only for verification, achieving 1.65–1.95x speedups over vanilla CD.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Contrastive Decoding improves generation quality but is expensive because it requires an amateur-model forward pass. Speculative decoding could accelerate it, but it is unclear whether the contrastive signal should influence the drafter (contrastive-aware drafting) or be applied only during verification. The paper aims to resolve this proposal-alignment question, especially in the lightweight feature-level drafter regime.

Method: The authors run two controlled diagnostics: matched Cross-alpha training (aligning the drafter under different contrastive mixing coefficients) and an Approximate Dual-Drafter decomposition that separates expert-aligned and contrastive components. Both diagnose whether contrastive-aware drafting helps. They then propose Decoupled Contrastive Decoding (DCD), which drafts using an expert-aligned lightweight proposer (e.g., EAGLE3) and applies the amateur model only in the unchanged Contrastive Decoding verification step, with standard speculative verification preserving the vanilla-CD output distribution.

Result: Both diagnostics converge on the same finding: contrastive-aware drafting does not consistently improve over expert-aligned drafting, because the contrastive correction is usually weaker than drafter error and reconstruction can amplify that error. On main 8B settings, EAGLE3-based DCD achieves average greedy speedups of 1.65–1.95x over vanilla CD and reduces MMLU proposal-path latency by roughly 5–12x compared to amateur-coupled proposal paths.

Conclusion: The contrastive signal should remain confined to verification rather than shape the drafter. Decoupled Contrastive Decoding provides efficient, distribution-preserving acceleration of Contrastive Decoding by expert-aligning the drafter and keeping the amateur only in verification.

Abstract: Contrastive Decoding (CD) improves generation quality, but its amateur-model pass makes decoding expensive. Accelerating CD with speculative decoding raises a proposal-alignment question: should the contrastive signal shape the drafter, or should it remain only in verification? We study this question in the lightweight feature-level drafter regime. Two controlled diagnostics, matched Cross-alpha training and an Approximate Dual-Drafter decomposition, give the same diagnosis: contrastive-aware drafting does not consistently improve over expert-aligned drafting because the contrastive correction is usually weaker than drafter error, and reconstruction can amplify that error. We introduce Decoupled Contrastive Decoding (DCD), which drafts with an expert-aligned lightweight proposer and applies the amateur only in unchanged CD verification. Standard speculative verification preserves the vanilla-CD output distribution. Across the main 8B settings, EAGLE3-based DCD achieves average greedy speedups of 1.65 to 1.95x over vanilla CD and reduces MMLU proposal-path latency by about 5 to 12x relative to amateur-coupled proposal paths.

</details>


### [52] [Unifying Depth and Width Pruning for LLMs via Binary Knapsack Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12953)
*Palaash Goel,Ayan Sengupta,Akshay Nambi,Tanmoy Chakraborty*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: SNIPER is a two-stage structured pruning framework for LLMs that uses knapsack optimization for conditionally optimal coarse-grained parameter allocation, followed by fine-grained pruning to meet strict budget constraints. It introduces CRAFT to measure compression ratio adherence and consistently outperforms six state-of-the-art pruners across 4 architectures and 18 tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing structured pruning methods rely on greedy heuristics that produce myopic (short-sighted) decisions, and they often fail to precisely meet target compression budgets. There is a need for a principled, budget-faithful pruning approach that generalizes across architectures.

Method: SNIPER is a two-stage framework: (1) a knapsack optimization over coarse-granularity components to yield conditionally optimal parameter allocations with respect to fixed importance estimates, and (2) a fine-grained pruning stage to meet strict budget constraints. It also introduces the Compression Ratio Adherence Factor (CRAFT) to quantify budget fidelity.

Result: Existing pruners deviate from target compression ratios by up to 33%, while SNIPER achieves near-exact adherence with a CRAFT score of 0.98. Across 4 architectures and 18 tasks in 5 domains, SNIPER shows consistent improvements in average performance retention and task-level stability over 6 SOTA pruners, achieving a mean rank of 1.25 across all pruning configurations.

Conclusion: SNIPER delivers near-exact budget adherence, robust cross-architectural generalizability, and excellent reliability, outperforming six state-of-the-art structured pruners in average performance retention and stability. Its optimization-based allocation overcomes the myopic limitations of greedy heuristics.

Abstract: Structured pruning is a promising approach for compressing large language models (LLMs), yet existing methods rely heavily on greedy heuristics that produce myopic decisions, and often fail to precisely meet target compression budgets. We present SNIPER, a two-stage structured pruning framework that solves a knapsack optimization over coarse-granularity components to yield conditionally optimal parameter allocations with respect to fixed importance estimates, followed by a fine-grained pruning stage to meet strict budget constraints. We introduce the Compression Ratio Adherence Factor (CRAFT) to quantify budget fidelity, showing that while existing pruners deviate from target compression ratios by up to 33%, SNIPER achieves near-exact adherence with a CRAFT score of 0.98. Evaluations across four diverse architectures over a set of 18 tasks spanning five domains demonstrate SNIPER's consistent improvements in average performance retention and task-level stability over six state-of-the-art pruners. Across all pruning configurations, SNIPER achieves an excellent mean rank of 1.25, indicating its robust cross-architectural generalizability and excellent reliability.

</details>


### [53] [LycheeMemory V2: Efficient Long-Term Memory for LLM Agents via Semantic Segment-Level Consolidation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12990)
*Dongfang Li,Zixuan Liu,Junmai Wang,Jiahe Huang,Fuhao Li,Bonian Jia,Baotian Hu,Min Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LycheeMemory V2 is an efficient long-term memory framework for LLM agents that replaces per-turn consolidation with semantic segment-level consolidation, batching exchanges into segments and encoding each into context-independent typed memory records. It achieves state-of-the-art accuracy (89.22% on LoCoMo, 92.20% on LongMemEval-S) while cutting construction tokens by 86.0% and 75.9% versus A-Mem, without increasing query-time tokens.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing memory systems use eager, turn-level consolidation, which invokes LLMs after every interaction and makes memory construction increasingly costly as conversations grow. Coarse summarization reduces cost but loses fine-grained context, while larger retrieval contexts or multi-hop reasoning merely shift overhead to query time. This motivates a method that lowers construction cost without sacrificing accuracy or inflating query-time cost.

Method: LycheeMemory V2 batches multiple exchanges into semantic segments and encodes each finalized segment into context-independent typed memory records, rather than consolidating every turn. Semantic boundary detection preserves coherent event-level and temporal evidence versus fixed-window batching. The records are organized with lightweight structured indexes enabling query-planned evidence retrieval.

Result: Using GPT-4.1-Mini, LycheeMemory V2 reaches state-of-the-art results of 89.22% on LoCoMo and 92.20% on LongMemEval-S. Compared with A-Mem, it reduces construction tokens by 86.0% on LoCoMo and 75.9% on LongMemEval-S, with no increase in query-time token usage.

Conclusion: The accuracy–cost trade-off of long-term agent memory depends not only on what information is retained but also on the granularity at which it is consolidated. Segment-level consolidation offers an efficient compromise between turn-level and coarse consolidation, cutting construction cost while preserving accuracy and query-time efficiency.

Abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents must preserve information from past interactions to support future tasks. Existing memory systems typically rely on eager consolidation, invoking LLMs after each interaction to extract, summarize, or update memories. This design makes memory construction increasingly costly as conversations grow. Coarse summarization can reduce construction cost but risks discarding fine-grained contextual evidence, whereas larger retrieval contexts or multi-hop LLM reasoning shift the overhead to query time. We present LycheeMemory V2, an efficient long-term memory framework that replaces turn-level consolidation with semantic segment-level consolidation. Instead of consolidating every interaction, LycheeMemory batches multiple exchanges into segments and encodes each finalized segment into context-independent typed memory records. Segment-level batching lowers LLM encoding frequency, while semantic boundary detection helps preserve coherent event-level and temporal evidence compared with fixed-window batching. The resulting records are organized with lightweight structured indexes for query-planned evidence retrieval. Experiments using GPT-4.1-Mini show that LycheeMemory achieves state-of-the-art performance, reaching 89.22% on LoCoMo and 92.20% on LongMemEval-S. Compared with A-Mem, it reduces construction tokens by 86.0% on LoCoMo and 75.9% on LongMemEval-S without increasing query-time token usage. More broadly, our results suggest that the accuracy--cost trade-off of long-term agent memory depends not only on what information is retained, but also on the granularity at which it is consolidated.

</details>


### [54] [CASA: Content-Acoustic Speaking Assessment with Speech Encoder and Large Language Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13101)
*Nhan Phan,Ilona Lähteenmäki,Anna von Zansen,Olli-Pekka Pauna,Yaroslav Getman,Tamás Grósz,Mikko Kurimo*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: CASA combines Whisper-medium and Qwen3.5-2B into a simpler multimodal speech LLM architecture that achieves state-of-the-art automatic speaking assessment (RMSE 0.358 on Speak & Improve 2025) while offering clearer separation between delivery and content, using roughly half the inference parameters of the prior best model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multimodal speech LLM approaches for automatic speaking assessment (ASA) lack analysis of how acoustic vs. content information drives predictions and how stable performance is across runs; the authors aim to close this gap with an interpretable, robust, and efficient architecture.

Method: CASA pairs Whisper-medium (acoustic encoder) with Qwen3.5-2B (LLM) in a simplified architecture with three handcrafted fluency features. Evaluated on the Speak & Improve Corpus 2025, with ablations and repeated runs to isolate acoustic and content contributions and measure variability, plus LLM-reasoning experiments for training-free content validation.

Result: CASA achieves RMSE 0.358, outperforming the previous state of the art while using about half the estimated inference parameters. Ablations reveal the individual and complementary roles of acoustic and content information; repeated runs characterize performance variability; LLM reasoning shows promise for content validation without fine-tuning.

Conclusion: A simpler, general-purpose architecture can match or exceed prior ASA performance while improving interpretability and parameter efficiency, and it is adaptable to other ASA corpora without structural changes.

Abstract: Research on automatic speaking assessment (ASA) has increasingly adopted multimodal speech large language models to assess learners' speaking performance. However, existing studies provide limited analysis of how acoustic and content information contribute to predictions and how stable the resulting performance is. We propose CASA, a simpler architecture combining Whisper-medium and Qwen3.5-2B that achieves state-of-the-art performance while providing a more interpretable separation between speech delivery and content.
  On the Speak & Improve Corpus 2025, CASA achieves a root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.358, improving on the previous best RMSE while using approximately half the estimated inference parameters. The general-purpose architecture is designed for adaptation to other ASA corpora without structural changes and relies on three handcrafted fluency features. Through ablations and repeated runs, we analyze the individual and complementary contributions of acoustic and content information, examine performance variability, and demonstrate the potential of large language model reasoning for training-free content validation.

</details>


### [55] [Better Decomposition, Free Aggregation: A Synthesizer-Folding Framework for Multilingual Multi-Hop Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13160)
*Yilin Wang,Yuchun Fan,Weidong Bao,Zili Wei,Shi Feng,Tong Xiao,Zhengtao Yu,Jingbo Zhu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Syfer is a synthesizer-folding framework for multilingual multi-hop QA that defers translation by default, only activating an English translation pathway with bilingual sub-question graph alignment when a decomposition-quality check fails, achieving competitive accuracy at lower computational cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multilingual retrieval-augmented generation (mRAG) approaches suffer from two limitations: (1) one-size-fits-all translation alignment — blanket translation discards culturally and linguistically native information, introduces translation noise, and inflates cost; (2) greedy decomposition and aggregation — uncontrolled decomposition generates redundant sub-questions that compound errors during step-wise reasoning, and final aggregation over reasoning paths amplifies these errors.

Method: Syfer performs: (1) a format-constrained decomposer that builds a sub-question graph in the original language; (2) a decomposition-quality check; (3) when the check passes, sub-questions are answered sequentially via a retrieve-then-answer policy in the target language; (4) when the check fails, an English translation pathway with bilingual sub-question graph alignment is activated. This defers translation instead of applying it by default.

Result: Experiments across multiple languages show Syfer attains competitive accuracy while striking a favorable balance between performance and computational cost compared to prior translation-alignment and decomposition-aggregation approaches.

Conclusion: Deferring translation and imposing decomposition-quality control lets Syfer preserve native language information and avoid compounding reasoning errors, yielding competitive multilingual multi-hop QA accuracy with reduced computational overhead.

Abstract: Multilingual retrieval-augmented generation (mRAG) equips large language models with access to globally distributed external knowledge for complex multilingual question answering. Recent approaches either translate retrieved documents into English or the query language to bridge the cross-lingual semantic gap, or decompose a complex query into sub-questions and aggregate the intermediate reasoning process. However, both lines of work suffer from two limitations. First, one-size-fits-all translation alignment, blanket translation discards culturally and linguistically native information unique to the target language, introduces translation noise, and inflates system cost. Second, greedy decomposition and aggregation, uncontrolled decomposition produces redundant sub-questions that compound errors during step-wise reasoning, and the final aggregation over reasoning paths further amplifies these errors. We address both with our method Syfer, a synthesizer-folding framework for multilingual multi-hop question answering that defers translation rather than applying it by default. Syfer first invokes a format-constrained decomposer to produce a sub-question graph in the original language, followed by a decomposition-quality check; when the check passes, sub-questions are answered sequentially under a retrieve-then-answer policy in the target language, and the English translation pathway with bilingual sub-question graph alignment is activated only when the check fails. Experiments across multiple languages show that Syfer attains competitive accuracy while striking a favourable balance between performance and computational cost.

</details>


### [56] [Which LLM Is Your Ideal Companion? Evaluating Emotional Companion Capabilities of LLMs Based on Adult Attachment Theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13168)
*Junkai Zhou,Shiting Guan,Zhaoyi Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper applies adult attachment theory (ECR-R scale) to evaluate LLMs' emotional companionship, introducing the ECBench benchmark spanning four scenarios across friendship and romantic relationships, and assessing 32 LLMs to examine how attachment tendencies manifest and can be shaped via prompting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM evaluations focus on general personality traits, offering limited insight into behavior in intimate, emotionally sensitive contexts. As LLMs are increasingly used for emotional companionship, there is a pressing need for theory-grounded evaluation of their behavior within intimate relationships.

Method: The authors integrate adult attachment theory into LLM evaluation using the Experiences in Close Relationships-Revised (ECR-R) scale to quantify attachment anxiety and avoidance. They construct ECBench, an emotional companionship benchmark covering four scenarios—emotional support, collaborative tasks, conflict resolution, and social guidance—across friendship and romantic relationships. Model behavior is assessed via 11 dialogue-quality metrics and three evaluation methods. They evaluate 32 LLMs, select representative models, and probe how attachment tendencies appear in multi-turn interactions and respond to prompting.

Result: The study characterizes the attachment anxiety/avoidance tendencies of 32 LLMs, identifies representative models, and demonstrates that these tendencies manifest in contextualized multi-turn interactions and can be modified through prompting.

Conclusion: The work offers a psychological (adult attachment) theoretical lens together with practical tools (ECBench) to better understand and select LLMs for emotional companionship, bridging psychology and AI evaluation.

Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied for emotional companionship, evaluating their behavior and capabilities in intimate relationships has become a pressing issue. However, existing assessments primarily characterize general personality traits, providing limited insight into model behavior within intimate and emotionally sensitive contexts. Therefore, we introduce adult attachment theory into LLM evaluation and use the Experiences in Close Relationships-Revised (ECR-R) scale to characterize attachment anxiety and avoidance. To evaluate emotional companionship capabilities of LLMs in realistic interaction scenarios, we present an emotional companionship benchmark, ECBench, spanning four scenarios including emotional support, collaborative tasks, conflict resolution, and social guidance, across friendship and romantic relationships. ECBench is utilized to assess model behavior using 11 dialogue-quality metrics and three evaluation methods. We evaluate the attachment tendencies of 32 LLMs and select representative models to investigate how these tendencies manifest in contextualized multi-turn interactions and whether they can be shaped through prompting. Our study provides a theoretical lens from psychology, along with practical tools to understand and select LLMs for emotional companionship.

</details>


### [57] [Localize, Then Reason: Visual Latent Structural Reasoning for Molecular Properties and Edits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13244)
*Xingqiao Lin,Junmei Wang,Haocheng Tang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: VLSR is an end-to-end framework that localizes chemically meaningful regions in molecular images before reasoning in a latent workspace, improving throughput by 9.6X over textual-reasoning baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understanding how molecular structure determines properties requires both local chemical perception (identifying meaningful substructures) and property reasoning. Existing LLM-based methods either combine SMILES/molecular images with textual descriptions of local motifs or reason directly from images, but neither lets the model first focus on chemically meaningful regions before reasoning.

Method: VLSR uses a localize-then-reason strategy: it jointly learns localization and reasoning from molecular images. The model first learns to locate chemically meaningful regions in a molecular image, then reasons about their property effects in a compact latent workspace before generating the final answer, all end-to-end.

Result: Under the same inference setup, VLSR achieves 9.6X higher throughput than a comparable textual-reasoning baseline.

Conclusion: By decoupling localization from reasoning and conducting reasoning in a compact latent workspace, VLSR enables chemically grounded perception and efficient property reasoning from molecular images.

Abstract: Local chemical perception and property reasoning are both essential for understanding how molecular structure determines properties. Current LLM-based chemical reasoning methods either receive SMILES/molecular images together with descriptions of local motifs, or reason directly from molecular images. Neither approach enables the model to focus on chemically meaningful regions before reasoning. To address this gap, we propose Visual Latent Structural Reasoning (VLSR), an end-to-end framework that jointly learns localization and reasoning from molecular images. Central to our approach is a localize-then-reason strategy. VLSR first learns to locate chemically meaningful regions in a molecular image. It then reasons about their property effects in a compact latent workspace before producing the final answer. Under the same inference setup, this design achieves 9.6X higher throughput than a comparable textual-reasoning baseline.

</details>


### [58] [Self-Referential Induction Increases Response Instability Relative to Unresolvable and Verifiable Questions in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13258)
*Paras Balani,Subhrakanta Panda*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper measures how unstable LLM responses are across repeated trials, comparing self-referential prompts, unresolvable philosophy questions, and verifiable questions, finding self-referential prompts produce the least consistent responses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work showed self-referential prompting reliably induces first-person subjective-experience reports, but no one had measured how consistent these reports are across repeated independent trials or compared that consistency to other open-ended question types.

Method: The authors define response instability as one minus the mean pairwise cosine similarity of sentence embeddings of a compressed core claim extracted from each response. They collect 30 independent responses per question (360 total, Gemini API, temperature 0.7) across four questions in each of three groups: self-referential prompts, unresolvable philosophical questions unrelated to self-reference, and questions with verifiable correct answers.

Result: Self-referential questions show the highest instability (0.343 +/- 0.047), unresolvable philosophy questions show intermediate, tightly clustered instability (0.192 +/- 0.008), and verifiable questions show the lowest instability (0.105 +/- 0.058).

Conclusion: The induced subjective-experience report occupies a distinct, less stable position in the model's output distribution compared to ordinary open-ended philosophical uncertainty, providing a quantitative baseline for this phenomenon.

Abstract: Self-referential prompting has been shown to reliably induce large language models to produce first-person reports resembling subjective experience, but no prior work measures how consistent these reports are across repeated, independent trials, or how that consistency compares to the model's behavior on other kinds of open-ended questions. We measure response instability, defined as one minus the mean pairwise cosine similarity of sentence embeddings computed over a compressed core claim extracted from each response, for three groups of questions: self-referential prompts eliciting a subjective-experience report, unresolvable philosophical questions unrelated to self-reference, and questions with a verifiable correct answer. Using 30 independent responses per question (360 responses total, Gemini API, temperature 0.7) across four questions per group, we find that self-referential questions show the highest instability (0.343 +/- 0.047), unresolvable philosophy questions show intermediate and tightly clustered instability (0.192 +/- 0.008), and verifiable questions show the lowest instability (0.105 +/- 0.058). This provides a quantitative baseline for the induced subjective-experience report, showing that it occupies a distinct, less stable position in the model's output distribution than ordinary open-ended philosophical uncertainty.

</details>


### [59] [How Do VLMs Behave When Blind or Misled? Behavioral Evaluation of VLMs on Scientific Figures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13267)
*Paul Osemudiame Oamen,Owusu-Banahene Osei,Ananya Mukherjee,Christian Greisinger,Steffen Eger,Pius Onobhayedo,Wei Zhao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: SciFigBench is a diagnostic benchmark for scientific figure understanding that evaluates not only VLM perception and reasoning but also behavioral reliability under uncertainty. Built from 250 annotated figures and over 34,000 stress-test setups, it reveals that high accuracy does not imply trustworthy behavior: GPT-5.2 scores highest on description/reasoning yet hallucinates unreadable content 96% of the time, while Gemini 3.1 Pro admits uncertainty far more often.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing VLM benchmarks focus mainly on perception and reasoning accuracy, ignoring behavioral reliability under uncertainty—how models act when visual evidence is missing or misleading. This gap matters for scientific workflows, where hallucination and overconfidence can be harmful.

Method: The authors build SciFigBench, a benchmark of 250 scientific figures with high-quality human annotations (600+ hours) across three evaluation aspects. They extend the data with image transformations, reasoning questions, resistance probes, caption-bias probes, and confirmed selective-blur targets, generating over 34,000 evaluation setups. They also propose the Admittance-Resistance-Inductance (A-R-I) framework measuring whether models acknowledge insufficient evidence (Admittance), resist misleading context (Resistance), and infer cautiously from partial information (Inductance).

Result: Models show substantial behavioral differences. GPT-5.2 reaches the highest description quality (MQM 91.6) and strong reasoning accuracy (78.4%) but hallucinates unreadable content in 96% of cases. Gemini 3.1 Pro is comparably capable (MQM 90.2, reasoning 81.0%) yet admits uncertainty in 71% of such cases and achieves the strongest resistance score (0.91). These results demonstrate that high perception and reasoning accuracy alone do not guarantee behavioral reliability.

Conclusion: Behavioral reliability under uncertainty is a distinct, critical dimension that benchmarks must measure separately from accuracy. The findings argue for evaluating and improving uncertainty-aware behaviors (admitting ignorance, resisting misleading context, inferring cautiously) to make VLMs safe and dependable in scientific deployment.

Abstract: Existing vision-language model (VLM) benchmarks emphasize perception and reasoning accuracy (how well VLMs describe and reason about what they see in an image), with limited attention to behavioral reliability under uncertainty (how they behave when visual evidence is missing or misleading). We introduce SciFigBench, a diagnostic VLM benchmark for scientific figure understanding that jointly evaluates perception, reasoning, and behavioral reliability under uncertainty. It contains 250 figures with high-quality human annotations across three evaluation aspects, totaling 600+ hours of annotation effort. We further extend these figures via image transformations, reasoning questions, resistance probes, caption-bias probes, and confirmed selective-blur targets, producing over 34,000 evaluation setups for stress testing.
  We further propose the Admittance-Resistance-Inductance (A-R-I) framework to evaluate whether models acknowledge insufficient evidence, resist misleading context, and infer cautiously from partial information. Our results reveal substantial behavioral differences among models. GPT-5.2 achieves the highest description quality (MQM 91.6) with strong reasoning accuracy (78.4%), yet hallucinates unreadable content in 96% of cases, whereas Gemini 3.1 Pro, a comparably capable model (MQM 90.2, reasoning 81.0%), admits uncertainty in 71% of such cases and achieves the strongest resistance score (0.91). These findings show that high perception and reasoning accuracy alone do not guarantee behavioral reliability, a dimension critical for deployment in scientific workflows.

</details>


### [60] [Mixture of Training: Recombining Small-Scale Scaffolded Pretraining Runs into a Larger Language Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13277)
*Mohammed Sabry,Sean Augenstein,Keith Rush,Lucio Dery*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces Mixture of Training (MoT), a scaffolded modular pre-training method that splits a Transformer into layer blocks, trains each block independently within a frozen pretrained aligner, and reassembles them; on a 1.3B model it matches monolithic perplexity at small scale, with compute advantages depending on aligner reuse.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine whether language-model pre-training can be decomposed into smaller, independently trainable jobs that can later be recomposed into a coherent larger model, enabling modular and potentially reusable training units.

Method: Mixture of Training (MoT) partitions a target Transformer into contiguous layer blocks, trains each block inside a frozen pretrained aligner scaffold, and recomposes the trained blocks, with an optional short end-to-end adaptation pass. Evaluated on a 1.3B-parameter Gemma-style model trained on C4.

Result: On a 1.3B Gemma-style model, MoT provides a small-scale proof of mechanism: independently trained depth slices recompose into a usable language model, and a quality-parity schedule reaches the same reported perplexity as the monolithic baseline, though it processes more aggregate tokens and has a shorter idealized layer-equivalent critical path after aligner preparation.

Conclusion: MoT is not a general replacement for monolithic pre-training but a small-scale framework for studying whether scaffolded sub-runs can act as reusable training units; its effective compute advantage depends on reusing the aligner across runs.

Abstract: We ask whether language-model pre-training can be decomposed into smaller, independently trainable jobs that can later be recomposed into a coherent larger model. We introduce Mixture of Training (MoT), a scaffolded modular pre-training procedure that partitions a target Transformer into contiguous layer blocks, trains each block inside a frozen pretrained aligner scaffold, and then recomposes the trained blocks with an optional short end-to-end adaptation pass. On a 1.3B-parameter Gemma-style model trained on C4, MoT provides a small-scale proof of mechanism: independently trained depth slices can be recomposed into a usable language model, and a quality-parity schedule reaches the same reported perplexity as the monolithic baseline. This parity setting processes more aggregate tokens and has a shorter idealized layer-equivalent critical path after aligner preparation; its effective compute advantage depends on reusing the aligner across runs. We therefore present MoT not as a general replacement for monolithic pre-training, but as a small-scale framework for studying whether scaffolded sub-runs can act as reusable training units.

</details>


### [61] [Refusing Intent, Not Form: Wrapper-Based Intent-Group Supervision for LLM Safety](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13304)
*Ping Wu,Haibo Tong,Feifei Zhao,Han Shen,Yu Shi,Yilin Zhao,Sicheng Shen,Guobin Shen,Yun Luo,Yi Zeng*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Safety-tuned models often learn superficial wrapper shortcuts, bypassing safety for wrapped harmful prompts while over-refusing wrapped benign ones. The authors introduce WIFA, an automatic intent-group data augmentation that pairs wrapped harmful examples with structurally matched benign counterexamples, and use it in two fine-tuning routes (WIFA-Boost and A-GCRT) to improve refusal accuracy and reduce over-refusal.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Safety tuning improves harmful refusal but can cause models to learn surface-form wrappers rather than intent, leading to two failure modes: wrapped harmful prompts bypass safety (under-refusal), while similarly wrapped benign prompts are over-refused. The goal is to disentangle wrapper form from underlying intent so models refuse based on intent consistently across wrappers.

Method: WIFA (Wrapper-Based Intent-Form Augmentation) automatically groups examples by intent, pairing wrapped harmful examples with structurally matched wrapped benign counterexamples, requiring no external teacher or manual per-wrapper intent labels. WIFA serves as a data layer for two complementary fine-tuning routes: (1) WIFA-Boost, a two-stage high-safety recipe; and (2) Anchored Group-Consistent Refusal Training (A-GCRT), which regularizes refusal/compliance decision scores across same-intent wrappers and anchors harmful vs. benign groups on opposite sides of a margin.

Result: On Qwen, WIFA-Boost achieves the strongest transformed-harmful refusal, while A-GCRT reduces OR-Bench over-refusal from 25.7% (base model) to 17.4%; reproduced baselines do not match these operating points. Llama results and ablations over data structure, two-stage order, and A-GCRT components support the intent-group interpretation, without claiming universal below-base over-refusal.

Conclusion: Intent-group augmentation (WIFA) with paired harmful/benign wrapped counterexamples improves safety tuning by making refusal behavior intent-consistent across wrappers. WIFA-Boost maximizes transformed-harmful refusal and A-GCRT lowers over-refusal, with evidence supporting the intent-group view while remaining modest about universally beating base-model over-refusal.

Abstract: Safety tuning can improve harmful refusal, but models may learn surface-form shortcuts: wrapped harmful prompts bypass safety, while similarly wrapped benign prompts are over-refused. We propose Wrapper-Based Intent-Form Augmentation (WIFA), an automatic intent-group augmentation method that pairs wrapped harmful examples with structurally matched wrapped benign counterexamples, requiring no external teacher or manual per-wrapper intent labels. We use WIFA as a common data layer for two complementary fine-tuning routes: WIFA-Boost, a two-stage high-safety recipe, and Anchored Group-Consistent Refusal Training (A-GCRT), which regularizes refusal/compliance decision scores across same-intent wrappers and anchors harmful and benign groups on opposite sides of a margin. In the Qwen setting, WIFA-Boost reaches the strongest transformed-harmful refusal, while A-GCRT reduces OR-Bench over-refusal from 25.7\% for the base model to 17.4\%; reproduced baselines do not match these operating points. Llama results and ablations over data structure, two-stage order, and A-GCRT components support this intent-group interpretation without claiming universal below-base over-refusal.

</details>


### [62] [Beyond Local Accuracy: A Protocol-Level Identifiability Audit for Controlled LLM Reasoning Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13326)
*Junhao Luo,Ning Huang,Ziqi Sha,Wenxuan Tang,Wei Deng*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes a structural, model-free protocol-level identifiability audit for LLM benchmarking. It formalizes when an observation support can separate behavioral policies with different estimands, resolves a case where base-only observation collapses distinct policies, and demonstrates empirically that base correctness does not guarantee intervention-response fidelity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM benchmark scores can appear precise while the observation protocol fails to identify the intended behavioral property. The authors want to diagnose and structurally verify, before any model inference, whether an evaluation design can actually discriminate the target estimand across policies.

Method: In a controlled, solver-grounded setting, the authors formalize a protocol-level identifiability audit over a finite behavioral policy class H. Given policies H, observation support O, and estimand τ, the audit tests whether O separates every policy pair with different τ values. It uses zero model calls and relies on equivalence classes, collision witnesses, and a synthesized minimum identifying support O*.

Result: Base-only observation collapses seven frozen deterministic policies into one equivalence class; full support yields seven classes with no cross-estimand collisions; every leave-one-out support retains a constructive collision witness. Empirically, both constrained-generation variants have pair-validity 1.0, yet base accuracy (0.620, 95% CI [0.600, 0.642]) and selective-response fidelity (0.324, 95% CI [0.304, 0.345]) diverge, with the gap recurring on a second deterministic source (0.646 vs 0.331). The audit synthesizes a minimum identifying support O* of two cells instead of the full 36-cell tensor.

Conclusion: Evaluation-design validity can be checked structurally before model inference. Base correctness does not determine intervention-response fidelity; distinct policies may be benchmark-indistinguishable under insufficient observation supports.

Abstract: LLM benchmark scores can be precise even when the observation protocol does not identify the behavioral property they are intended to measure. In a controlled, solver-grounded setting, we formalize a protocol-level identifiability audit over a finite behavioral policy class: given policies H, observation support O, and estimand $τ$, we test whether O separates every pair with different $τ$. The audit requires zero model calls and resolves our diagnostic case: base-only observation collapses seven frozen deterministic policies into one equivalence class; full support yields seven classes and no cross-estimand collisions; every leave-one-out support retains a constructive collision witness. Empirically, both constrained-generation variants have pair-validity 1.0, yet base accuracy and selective-response fidelity diverge - 0.620 versus 0.324 across six balanced oracle-transition directions (cluster-bootstrap 95% CI [0.600, 0.642] vs. [0.304, 0.345]) - and the gap recurs on a second deterministic source (0.646 vs. 0.331). The audit also synthesizes a minimum identifying support $O^*$ for the frozen policy class: two cells instead of the full 36-cell tensor. This case shows how evaluation-design validity can be checked structurally before model inference and why base correctness does not determine intervention-response fidelity.

</details>


### [63] [It's How You Ask: Gender-Associated Linguistic Bias in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13328)
*Katherine Van Koevering,Anjalie Field*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LLMs produce shorter, less sophisticated, and less formal responses to prompts using linguistic features common among women (hedges, tag questions, collective reference), an effect that persists across document types and models and is hard to mitigate post-hoc.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Professional communication is increasingly mediated by LLMs, raising the question of whether these models serve all users equally. The authors investigate whether gendered linguistic variation in prompts leads to different response quality, aiming to uncover potential disparate impacts in LLM-mediated workplace communication.

Method: The authors tested prompts containing feminine-associated linguistic features (hedges, tag questions, collective reference) across three document types and four models, controlling for prompt complexity and feature carry-over. They compared these effects against explicit gender cues (sign-off names), examined representational similarity between names and linguistic dialect, and performed mechanistic analysis of transformer layers to understand how linguistic features are encoded and whether they can be avoided.

Result: Feminine-linguistic features systematically elicit shorter, less sophisticated, and less formal responses across all document types and models, even after controlling for complexity and carry-over. Explicit gender cues (names) map to the same representational space as linguistic dialect but produce no effects, while linguistic register produces large, consistent effects. Post-hoc mitigation is difficult because the patterns are culturally embedded and outside conscious control, and mechanistic analysis shows linguistic features are encoded in early transformer layers and entangled with other features.

Conclusion: To mitigate disparate impacts of LLM-mediated workplace communication, the field should address linguistic variation upstream rather than relying on user-level avoidance strategies, since these patterns are culturally embedded and not easily controllable by users.

Abstract: Professional communication is increasingly mediated by LLMs - but do these models serve all users equally? We show that when prompts contain linguistic features more commonly used by women (hedges, tag questions, collective reference), they systematically elicit shorter, less sophisticated, and less formal responses across three document types and four models. These effects persist after controlling for prompt complexity and feature carry-over. Explicit gender cues like sign-off names are encoded in the same representational space as linguistic dialect - suggesting shared underlying mechanisms - yet linguistic register is far more influential, producing large, consistent effects where names produce none. Our results further reveal that post-hoc mitigation is challenging: because these patterns are culturally embedded and outside conscious control, users cannot easily avoid them through strategic self-presentation, and mechanistic analysis reveals that linguistic features are encoded in early transformer layers and entangled with other features. Our work calls for upstream consideration of the influences of linguistic variation to mitigate disparate impacts of LLM-mediated workplace communication.

</details>


### [64] [RippleMem: From Isolated Retrieval to Associative Recollection for Long-Term Agent Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13334)
*Jingbo Ji,Lingyi Li,Xilong Cheng,Yuhao Zhou,Wenji Zhang,Yuting Tan,Yunxiao Qin*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: RippleMem is a long-term memory system for LLM agents that replaces one-shot retrieval with adaptive associative recollection using cue-rich episodic memory units organized in an event-centric graph, outperforming baselines while cutting graph construction cost ~30x.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The key bottleneck in LLM agent memory is not storing experience but retrieving the correct evidence set when relevant information is spread across many interactions. Existing methods fail: full-context approaches need noisy long-context search, flat retrieval returns isolated/incomplete records, and graph-based memory is expensive to build and compresses rich event context.

Method: RippleMem stores interaction history as cue-rich episodic memory units in an event-centric memory graph. Given a query, it first recalls relevant memory anchors using hybrid cues, then expands from these anchors along semantic and structural associations to recover missing supporting evidence. Recalled memories thus serve both as answer context and as cues for completing needed evidence.

Result: RippleMem achieves the best overall performance across evaluated settings, improving LLM-as-a-Judge accuracy by 3.95% on LoCoMo and up to 11.87% on LongMemEval-S, while reducing graph construction cost by about 30x.

Conclusion: Adaptive associative recollection via cue-rich episodes and an event-centric graph effectively solves the evidence-retrieval problem in long-term agent memory, delivering higher accuracy and dramatically lower construction cost than existing approaches.

Abstract: LLM-based agents increasingly rely on external memory to support long-horizon reasoning and interaction. However, the main bottleneck is not simply storing past experience, but recovering the right set of evidence when relevant information is distributed across many interactions. Existing approaches struggle with this access problem. Full-context methods require noisy long-context search, flat retrieval often returns isolated and incomplete records, and graph-based memory systems can be expensive to construct while compressing rich event context. We introduce RippleMem, a long-term memory system that replaces one-shot retrieval with adaptive associative recollection. Inspired by cue-dependent episodic retrieval and associative completion, RippleMem stores interaction history as cue-rich episodic memory units and organizes them in an event-centric memory graph. Given a query, it first recalls relevant memory anchors through hybrid cues, then expands from these anchors along semantic and structural associations to recover missing supporting evidence. In this way, initially recalled memories serve not only as answer context, but also as cues for completing the evidence needed to answer. Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S show that RippleMem achieves the best overall performance across evaluated settings, improving LLM-as-a-Judge accuracy by 3.95% on LoCoMo and up to 11.87% on LongMemEval-S, while reducing graph construction cost by about 30x.

</details>


### [65] [CROP: Task Relevance via Counterfactuals for Selective On-Policy Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13387)
*Enhan Li,Junhao He,Hongyang Du*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces CROP, a method that improves selective on-policy distillation by allocating token-level supervision according to task relevance, measured via a paraphrase-calibrated counterfactual sensitivity margin, outperforming existing selectors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: On-policy distillation (OPD) assigns equal credit to all response tokens, yet tokens have unequal supervision value. Existing selective OPD criteria focus mostly on optimization need (uncertainty, teacher-student disagreement) but under-characterize task relevance—whether supervision is tied to the semantic content of the current input. The authors argue task relevance is a complementary dimension needing direct operationalization.

Method: CROP operationalizes task relevance using a paraphrase-calibrated counterfactual sensitivity margin. For each source prompt, it builds a validated original-paraphrase-counterfactual triplet, keeps the student rollout fixed, and scores each response position by its sensitivity to a task-relevant condition change, normalized/calibrated by its sensitivity to a meaning-preserving rewrite. Supervision is then allocated non-uniformly across tokens based on these relevance scores.

Result: Matched selection controls show CROP identifies more useful supervision positions than random or lowest-relevance baseline selectors. Ablations confirm the contribution of both counterfactual sensitivity and paraphrase calibration. Across two teacher-student settings, CROP improves aggregate performance by 1.92 and 2.96 points over the strongest non-CROP selector.

Conclusion: Task relevance is a valid complementary criterion for selective OPD. CROP offers a model-internal, contrast-specific method for allocating token-level supervision, and its empirical gains support the value of relevance-aware supervision in on-policy distillation.

Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) supervises a student language model on trajectories sampled from its current policy, but assigns equal credit to response tokens with unequal supervision value. Selective OPD addresses this limitation by allocating supervision non-uniformly across response tokens according to their estimated training value. Most existing criteria, however, focus primarily on optimization need, such as uncertainty or teacher-student disagreement, while task relevance, namely whether the supervision is tied to the semantic content of the current input, remains less directly characterized as a complementary dimension. To address this gap, we introduce Counterfactual Relevance for On-Policy Distillation (CROP), which operationalizes task relevance through a paraphrase-calibrated counterfactual sensitivity margin. For each source prompt, CROP constructs a validated original-paraphrase-counterfactual triplet, holds the student rollout fixed, and measures each response position by its sensitivity to a task-relevant condition change calibrated by its sensitivity to a meaning-preserving rewrite. Matched selection controls show that CROP identifies more useful supervision positions than random or lowest-relevance selection, while component comparisons confirm the value of both counterfactual sensitivity and paraphrase calibration. Across two teacher-student settings, CROP improves aggregate performance by 1.92 and 2.96 points over the strongest non-CROP selector. These results support task relevance as a complementary criterion for selective OPD and establish CROP as a model-internal, contrast-specific method for allocating token-level supervision.

</details>


### [66] [Motor, Cognitive, or Corpus? What Survives Cross-Lingual Transfer in Speech-Based Parkinsons Disease Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13425)
*Serli Kopar,Sam Gijsen,Abner Hernandez,Paula Andrea Perez-Toro,Kerstin Ritter*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A layer-wise analysis of nine self-supervised speech models shows that optimal layers for Parkinson's disease detection are corpus-dependent, not architecture-dependent, and that the learned discriminative signal lacks pathological specificity (also flagging dementia as PD), limiting clinical reliability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SSL speech representations perform well for PD detection within single corpora, but it is unclear whether they capture true disease-related characteristics or dataset-specific confounds, especially as most SSL backbones are pretrained only on healthy speech. The authors aim to clarify this uncertainty.

Method: They perform a layer-wise analysis of nine SSL speech backbones using a low-capacity logistic regression probe across three languages. Evaluation is structured into multiple scenarios that progressively introduce distribution shifts in participant identity, recording conditions, language, and pathology (including dementia as a confounding pathology).

Result: Two key findings: (1) layer selection is highly corpus-dependent—the optimal representation layer is determined by the source dataset rather than the SSL architecture; (2) the transferred discriminative signal lacks pathological specificity—classifiers trained to detect PD assign similarly high PD probabilities to dementia speech in the target corpus.

Conclusion: Critical limitations exist in current SSL-based speech pathology recognition; these must be addressed before such models can be reliably deployed in clinical settings.

Abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) speech representations achieve strong performance for Parkinson's disease (PD) detection within individual corpora. However, it remains unclear whether these models capture disease-related characteristics or exploit dataset-specific confounds, particularly since most SSL backbones are pretrained exclusively on healthy speech. To investigate this question, we perform a layer-wise analysis of nine SSL speech backbones using a low-capacity logistic regression probe across three languages. We structure the evaluation as multiple scenarios that progressively introduce distribution shifts in participant identity, recording conditions, language, and pathology. Our results reveal two key findings. First, layer selection is highly corpus-dependent: the optimal representation layer is determined primarily by the source dataset rather than by the SSL architecture itself. Second, the transferred discriminative signal lacks pathological specificity: classifiers trained to detect PD assign similarly high probabilities to both PD and dementia speech in the target corpus. These results highlight critical limitations that must be addressed before speech-based pathology recognition models can be reliably deployed in clinical settings.

</details>


### [67] [Are You Sure You're Sure? On the Impact of Instruction Tuning on Confidence and Lexical Diversity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13430)
*Irina Proskurina,Mayank Kumar,Oyindolapo O. Komolafe*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Instruction tuning alters model confidence and rationale diversity in distinct ways: confidence consistently changes (despite little accuracy change and worse likelihood calibration), cross-rationale diversity consistently decreases, and surface lexical diversity varies; these effects persist after controlling for answer selection and rationale length.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Instruction-tuned language models show verbalized overconfidence in generation tasks, and this overconfidence may relate to the consistency of generated supporting rationales in question answering. The authors aim to understand how instruction tuning affects both model confidence and the lexical diversity of generated rationales, and whether these two effects are related or distinct.

Method: They evaluate three matched pairs of base and instruction-tuned models across question-answering benchmarks. They measure changes in answer confidence, predictive accuracy, likelihood-based calibration, and two dimensions of rationale diversity: cross-rationale diversity and surface-level lexical diversity. They further control for answer selection and rationale length to isolate the effects of instruction tuning.

Result: Instruction tuning consistently alters answer confidence despite limited changes in predictive accuracy and decreased likelihood-based calibration. Its effect on rationale diversity is non-uniform: cross-rationale diversity consistently decreases, while surface-level lexical diversity varies in direction and magnitude across models and benchmarks. These differences persist after controlling for answer selection and rationale length, indicating that confidence and rationale diversity capture distinct effects of instruction tuning.

Conclusion: Instruction tuning induces distinct, largely independent changes in model confidence and rationale diversity, suggesting that verbalized overconfidence and rationale generation behavior are separate phenomena that should be studied accordingly.

Abstract: Instruction-tuned language models achieve strong performance across a range of generation tasks, but have also recently been shown to exhibit verbalized overconfidence. In question answering, verbalized model overconfidence may be associated with the consistency of the generated supporting rationales. In this paper, we study whether corresponding changes in the lexical diversity of generated answer rationales accompany changes in model confidence induced by instruction tuning. We evaluate three matched base and instruction-tuned models across question-answering benchmarks and find that instruction tuning consistently alters answer confidence, despite limited changes in predictive accuracy and decreases in likelihood-based calibration. Secondly, we observe a non-uniform effect of instruction tuning on rationale diversity: cross-rationale diversity consistently decreases, whereas surface-level lexical diversity varies in both direction and magnitude across models and benchmarks. Finally, we find that these differences persist after controlling for answer selection and rationale length, confirming that confidence and rationale diversity capture distinct effects of instruction tuning.

</details>


### [68] [Toward a Gricean Retreat: Probing LLMs for Knowledge Boundaries and Referent Specificity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13484)
*Dananjay Srinivas,Saksham Khatwani,Maria Pacheco*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LLMs can internally detect knowledge gaps and anticipate referent specificity, but they fail to act on these signals and still fabricate specific details instead of retreating to safer generic claims.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs fabricate plausible-sounding specifics when asked about entities they do not know, rather than backing off to truthful generic claims. The authors frame this as a Gricean failure—a cooperative speaker should retreat up the specificity hierarchy when uncertain—and investigate whether models possess the internal ingredients for this retreat.

Method: Using a T-REx-based benchmark that varies entity familiarity and referent specificity, the authors probe model activations to test two questions: whether activations encode whether a referent falls inside the knowledge boundary, and whether they anticipate the specificity of the referent about to be generated. They also examine generation behavior to see whether models reconcile these signals, including offering correct generic alternatives.

Result: Both activations encode knowledge-boundary membership and anticipate referent specificity ("yes" to both), but these signals are not reconciled during generation. Models overwhelmingly prefer specific referents even for unknown entities, and do so even when correct generic alternatives are offered.

Conclusion: The substrate for a Gricean retreat is present in LLMs, but the policy needed to act on it is missing. The findings are positioned as a first step toward "Gricean alignment"—training or steering objectives that couple knowledge-boundary awareness to referent-specificity during generation.

Abstract: When asked about entities outside their knowledge boundary, LLMs routinely fabricate plausible-sounding details rather than backing off to safer, more general claims. We frame this failure through a Gricean lens: a cooperative speaker who is uncertain about a referent retreats up the specificity hierarchy, trading informativeness for truthfulness. We ask whether LLMs have the ingredients to perform this retreat. Using a T-REx-based benchmark that varies entity familiarity and referent specificity, we probe models to answer two questions: (i) do their activations encode whether a referent falls inside the knowledge boundary, and (ii) do they anticipate the specificity of the referent they are about to generate? We find that the answer to both is yes, but the two signals are not reconciled in generation. Models overwhelmingly prefer specific referents even when the entity is unknown to them, and do so even when offered correct generic alternatives. The substrate for a Gricean retreat is present, but the policy that would act on it is not. We position our findings as a first step toward Gricean alignment, training or steering objectives that couple knowledge-boundary awareness to referent-specificity during generation.

</details>


### [69] [Measuring Task-Agnostic Training Data Influence Across Language Model Pretraining](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13515)
*Yuto Nishida,Hirokazu Kiyomaru,Yusuke Oda,Takashi Kodama,Chaoran Liu,Daisuke Kawahara,Yusuke Miyao,Max Müller-Eberstein,Masaru Isonuma*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces a task-agnostic measure of training data influence in language model pretraining, defined via how much each example's gradient update reduces distance to the final parameters, and finds a systematic shift from literature-heavy to STEM-heavy influential data over training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing influence methods require choosing downstream tasks or validation sets as attribution targets, which is difficult to make representative of general capabilities and complicates fair comparisons across training runs due to reliance on intermediate task performance.

Method: Define an example's influence as the reduction in squared distance to the final parameters of a pretraining run caused by its gradient update, estimated from intermediate checkpoints without retraining. Applied to 18 Pythia and PolyPythia configurations.

Result: Influential data exhibit systematic temporal changes: early in training, literature-related data align more strongly with the trajectory toward final parameters, while STEM data become more strongly aligned in later stages. The literature-to-STEM crossover holds broadly across model configurations.

Conclusion: The method offers a tractable, trajectory-level view of how influential training data change throughout pretraining, complementing downstream-task- or validation-set-based influence analyses without requiring an attribution target.

Abstract: Measuring training data influence consistently across language model pretraining is challenging. It is difficult to select downstream tasks or validation sets representative of a model's general capabilities, and reliance on task performance at intermediate checkpoints complicates comparisons across training. We propose a measure of training data influence that does not require selecting a downstream task or validation set as the attribution target. Specifically, we define an example's influence by how much its gradient update reduces the squared distance to the final parameters of a given pretraining run, and estimate this quantity from intermediate checkpoints without retraining. Applying the method to 18 configurations from the Pythia and PolyPythia suites, we find systematic temporal changes in influential data. Early in training, literature-related data are more strongly aligned with the trajectory toward the final parameters, whereas STEM data become more strongly aligned in later stages. This qualitative crossover is broadly consistent across model configurations. Our results provide a tractable trajectory-level view of how influential data change throughout pretraining, complementing influence analyses defined with respect to specific downstream tasks or validation sets.

</details>


### [70] [DFM Mimir v1: An Open HRM Delivering Frontier Performance at 1B Parameters Using Only Permissible Post-Training Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13517)
*Peter Schneider-Kamp,Jacob Nielsen,Gianluca Barmina,Kenneth Enevoldsen,Lukas Galke Poech*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Mimir v1 is a 1B-parameter language model trained from scratch on only permissible data, achieving strong English performance and state-of-the-art Danish results while competing with much larger frontier models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM development relies on massive, often non-permissible datasets, which creates a high barrier for researchers committed to open-source and ethically sourced data. The paper aims to show that competitive performance can be achieved using only permissible post-training data.

Method: Mimir v1 is based on the Hierarchical Reasoning Model (HRM) architecture and trained from scratch on a mixture of 161 datasets (post-training only, permissible data). It was evaluated across 20 benchmarks covering English, Math & Code, and Danish, and compared against HRM-Text 1B, Qwen 3.5 4B, and Gemma 4 E2B.

Result: Mimir v1 outperforms the original HRM-Text 1B and competes with larger frontier models (Qwen 3.5 4B and Gemma 4 E2B). It delivers highly competitive performance for English and sets a new state of the art for Danish.

Conclusion: A 1B-parameter model trained from scratch exclusively on permissible data can rival larger frontier models, demonstrating that ethical, open-source data does not preclude competitive performance. The model is openly released on the Hugging Face Hub.

Abstract: Current large language model development relies on massive, often non-permissible datasets, creating a high barrier for researchers committed to open-source and ethically sourced data. We introduce Mimir v1, a 1-billion-parameter language model based on the Hierarchical Reasoning Model (HRM) architecture, that is trained from scratch and delivers highly competitive performance for English and sets a new state of the art for Danish using only permissible post-training data. Trained on a mixture of 161 datasets, Mimir v1 outperforms the original HRM-Text 1B and competes with larger frontier models like Qwen 3.5 4B and Gemma 4 E2B, tested across 20 benchmarks for English, Math & Code and Danish. The model is available on the Hugging Face Hub: https://huggingface.co/danish-foundation-models/DFM-Mimir

</details>


### [71] [SAEVerbalizer: Generating Explanations for Sparse Autoencoder Features via Representation Verbalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13538)
*Weihan Meng,Hongzhu Guo,Yi Jing,Dewen Liu,Zijun Yao,Xiaozhi Wang,Lei Hou,Juanzi Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: SAEVerbalizer trains an LLM to generate natural-language explanations of SAE features directly from decoder directions, replacing external behavioral observation; the capability generalizes to unseen features, transfers across SAEs, and adapts to different LLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Explaining SAE-extracted features in LLMs currently relies on external observation, which yields superficial explanations inferred from behavior and is computationally expensive to collect at scale. The authors aim to overcome both limitations by explaining features directly from their internal representations.

Method: SAEVerbalizer injects SAE decoder directions into an LLM's representations and fine-tunes the LLM's downstream layers to produce natural-language explanations of the injected features. Intervention experiments inject multiple directions and reverse individual directions to validate the resulting explanations.

Result: The learned verbalization generalizes to unseen features, transfers across separately trained SAE dictionaries, and extends to features from different LLMs with a lightweight adapter. Injecting multiple directions yields combined-meaning explanations, and reversing directions produces corresponding meaning shifts.

Conclusion: SAEVerbalizer enables direct, efficient, and scalable natural-language explanation of SAE features from decoder directions, addressing the superficiality and computational cost of behavior-based explanations while showing strong generalization and transferability.

Abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are proposed to extract numerous features from large language model (LLM) representations, yet explaining these features still relies primarily on external observation. This reliance leads to superficial explanations inferred from observed model behavior and computational inefficiency from collecting such behavioral evidence at scale. We introduce SAEVerbalizer, a framework that injects SAE decoder directions into an LLM's representations and fine-tunes the LLM's downstream layers to generate natural-language explanations of the injected features. Once trained, the resulting verbalizer explains SAE features directly from decoder directions, addressing both limitations. Our experiments show that the learned verbalization capability generalizes to unseen features, transfers across separately trained SAE dictionaries, and, with a lightweight adapter, extends to SAE features from different LLMs. Intervention experiments show that injecting multiple directions yields an explanation combining their meanings, while reversing individual directions produces corresponding meaning shifts.

</details>


### [72] [LittleLearner: Language Models Under Pedagogically Controlled Knowledge Exposure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13545)
*Fanfei Li,Jana Zeller,Manuel Prada-Corral,Thaddäus Wiedemer,Prasanna Mayilvahanan,Ryan Cotterell,Wieland Brendel*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces LITTLECURRICULUM, an 88B-token pretraining corpus limited to U.S. elementary school (through Grade 5) content, and LITTLELEARNER, a 5B-parameter LLM trained on it from scratch, providing a developmentally restricted sandbox for studying knowledge/skill acquisition under a controlled scope.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Studying how language models acquire knowledge and skills is hard because web-scale training corpora are heterogeneous, making prior exposure to related content difficult to characterize. A controlled, curriculum-scoped corpus is needed to map model capabilities to interpretable training boundaries.

Method: Curate LITTLECURRICULUM (88B tokens of U.S. elementary school material, excluding above-Grade-5 concepts/facts/vocabulary); train a 5B-parameter LLM from scratch to obtain LITTLELEARNER; then test knowledge injection via post-training and in-context learning.

Result: LITTLELEARNER has enough language competence for open-ended evaluation while its knowledge/capability boundaries align with Grade-5 curriculum guidelines. Post-training and in-context learning improve utilization of existing knowledge but do not raise out-of-scope capabilities.

Conclusion: The controlled environment is valuable for future investigations into how models acquire, represent, and use data under a well-defined scope, as evidenced by the initial knowledge-injection experiments.

Abstract: Modern language models are trained on heterogeneous web-scale text corpora. Consequently, studying knowledge and skill acquisition is difficult, as prior exposure to related content is hard to characterize. To address this challenge, we introduce LITTLECURRICULUM, a curated 88B-token pretraining corpus tailored to U.S. elementary school material, explicitly excluding concepts, facts, and vocabulary taught above Grade 5. Training a 5B-parameter LLM from scratch on LITTLECURRICULUM yields LITTLELEARNER, a model with sufficient language competence for open-ended evaluation, yet with clear knowledge and capability boundaries mapped to interpretable curriculum guidelines. We release LITTLECURRICULUM and LITTLELEARNER as a developmentally restricted sandbox to study how models acquire, represent, and use data under a well-defined training scope. We illustrate the sandbox's utility in a first suite of experiments on injecting new knowledge through post-training and in-context learning. These methods let LITTLELEARNER better utilize existing knowledge, but do not raise out-of-scope capabilities. Our findings underscore the value of this controlled environment for future investigations.
