</details>


<div id='cs.SE'></div>

# cs.SE [[Back]](#toc)

### [73] [SynWeaver: Website-Prior Task and Trajectory Co-Synthesis for Web Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12429)
*Ruitao Wang,Yuwen Hao,Menglin Yang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: SynWeaver is a framework that synthesizes website-specific task-trajectory supervision by first building a website map through structured exploration, then training a UI-aware model with website-specific priors to ground task proposals, and finally co-synthesizing and verifying tasks and trajectories to produce executable, semantically aligned supervision.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Web agents fail to generalize to unseen websites due to lack of website-specific supervision. Existing exploration-based synthesis methods cannot cover a website's full functionality and, lacking website prior knowledge, propose hallucinated tasks, limiting the diversity and efficiency of downstream trajectory synthesis.

Method: SynWeaver performs three stages: (1) structured website exploration to construct a website map covering functionally distinct page states and executable interactions; (2) deriving page-level and transition-level supervision from the map to train a UI-aware model with website-specific priors for grounded task proposals; (3) collaborative task-trajectory synthesis that jointly updates the task and execution trajectory when inconsistent, followed by verification and repair to ensure executable, semantically aligned results.

Result: Experiments on WebArena and WebVoyager show that SynWeaver consistently outperforms strong synthesis baselines and produces more effective supervision for both in-domain and out-of-domain generalization.

Conclusion: SynWeaver addresses the limitations of hallucinated and incomplete task proposals in web agent data synthesis by grounding task generation in a website map and co-synthesizing tasks with trajectories, yielding superior execution supervision and improved generalization.

Abstract: Web agents often struggle to generalize to unseen websites because they lack website-specific supervision. Recent exploration-based data synthesis methods reduce manual annotation, but they still face two key limitations: they often fail to cover the full functionality of a website, and without sufficient website prior knowledge, they tend to propose hallucinated tasks, which in turn limits the diversity and efficiency of downstream trajectory synthesis. We present \textbf{SynWeaver}, a website-prior task-trajectory co-synthesis framework designed to address these challenges. SynWeaver first performs structured website exploration and constructs a website map that covers a broad set of functionally distinct page states and executable interactions on the target website. It then derives page-level and transition-level supervision from this map to train a UI-aware model with website-specific priors, enabling more grounded task proposals. Finally, SynWeaver performs collaborative task-trajectory synthesis, jointly updating the task and execution trajectory when they become inconsistent, and then verifies and repairs the collected results to produce executable, semantically aligned supervision. Experiments on WebArena and WebVoyager demonstrate that SynWeaver consistently outperforms strong synthesis baselines and yields more effective supervision for both in-domain and out-of-domain generalization.

</details>


### [74] [Specification-first convergence with an AI coding agent: a case study of dismantling a core architectural invariant across 189 files in a 717k-line codebase with no test oracle and no human code review](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12440)
*Joel Abenhaim*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A single-case study documents an AI coding agent successfully performing a large-scale architectural refactoring (dismantling a core lifetime invariant) in a 717,725-line TypeScript codebase under a specification-first protocol with no human review, no oracle, and zero observed bugs across ~31 sessions, over three days at $2,430.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To test whether an AI coding agent can perform a large-scale architectural refactoring that the author deemed effectively infeasible via incremental refactoring (the kind of change that normally warrants a rewrite). The task lacked human review and had no pre-existing oracle to validate the target behavior, challenging the agent's ability to reason about a central invariant across a large interdependent codebase and produce a verifiable, correct change end-to-end.

Method: A specification-first protocol on a 717,725-line, 3,648-file production TypeScript app: (1) the agent writes a formal specification; (2) 14 refinement cycles audit the spec against source code; (3) atomic implementation followed by a compile/test feedback loop; (4) 17 verification cycles audit the code against the frozen specification. The task was to dismantle a core lifetime invariant (a UI panel staying open during an AI request) so a streaming generation survives panel closure and reattaches to the same live stream without loss or duplication. Convergence was empirical: two consecutive verification passes with zero findings. Across 31 audit passes, 201 defects were fixed before any human execution.

Result: The change touched 189 files (31 new); including extraction, two commits totaled 288 files, 34,770 insertions, 16,422 deletions. Across the first and roughly thirty later sessions the software behaved as specified with no observed bugs. Elapsed time was three days at a cost of USD 2,430. The full specification and 1,500+ pages of raw session logs (in French) are published as evidence for inspection and LLM consistency checking.

Conclusion: An AI coding agent can successfully complete an architectural refactoring normally requiring a rewrite, under a specification-first protocol with no human code review or behavioral oracle, achieving zero observed bugs over ~31 production sessions. The key enablers were iterative specification auditing, a frozen-spec verification loop, and an empirical convergence criterion, with full logs published for reproducibility and further validation.

Abstract: This paper reports a single, fully instrumented case study of a large-scale architectural refactoring by an AI coding agent under a specification-first protocol, with no human review of the generated code and no pre-existing oracle to validate the target behaviour. The task, dismantling a central invariant across a large interdependent codebase, was assessed by the author as effectively infeasible through incremental refactoring, the kind of change that conventionally calls for a rewrite instead. Under the protocol described here, the agent completed it successfully.
  The system is a 717,725-line production TypeScript application across 3,648 files. The task required dismantling a core lifetime invariant: the guarantee that a UI panel remains open for the duration of an AI request. The target behaviour was that a streaming generation survives the closing of its panel and can be reattached, on reopening, to the same live stream with no loss or duplication.
  The protocol: formal specification by the agent, 14 refinement cycles auditing that specification against the source code, atomic implementation, a compile/test feedback loop, then 17 verification cycles auditing the code against the frozen specification. Across 31 audit passes, 201 defects were corrected before any human executed the program. The convergence criterion was empirical: two consecutive verification passes returning zero findings.
  The change touched 189 files (31 new); with the extraction phase, the two commits total 288 files, 34,770 insertions, 16,422 deletions. Across the first and roughly thirty later sessions, the software behaved as specified, no bug observed. Elapsed: three days; cost: USD 2,430.
  The full specification and raw session logs, 1,500+ pages in French, are published as evidence, allowing inspection of the process and submission to a language model for consistency checking.

</details>


### [75] [Does It Render Everywhere? A Study of Cross-Environment Compatibility in MLLM-Generated Webpages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12518)
*Ziyun Guo,Jingyu Xiao,Yuqiang Sun,Yintong Huo*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper presents WebCompat, the first systematic study of cross-environment compatibility in AI-generated webpages, and XCompat, a detector combining screenshot and DOM analysis that achieves 0.903 F1, outperforming existing tools and LLM baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluations of MLLM-generated webpages only assess visual fidelity under a fixed browser-device configuration, ignoring cross-environment rendering compatibility that matters for real-world deployment.

Method: Construct WebCompat, a dataset of 2,032 annotated instances from 8 AI tools rendered across 9 browser-and-device combinations; analyze compatibility issues, symptoms, and root causes. Then build XCompat, a lightweight offline detector that fuses visual screenshots with structural DOM tree analysis.

Result: 68% of generated webpages contain at least one compatibility issue. 88.3% of symptoms are layout-wide failures (shrinking to fit with too-small fonts, or scale mismatches causing cut-off content); only 13.4% are element-local (image distortion, missing components). MLLMs include responsive design patterns but fail to implement them correctly.

Conclusion: MLLM-generated front-end code suffers pervasive rendering reliability issues across environments; XCompat effectively detects these issues, and the released datasets and tools support future research on rendering reliability.

Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have been increasingly adopted to automate webpage generation from visual designs (e.g., screenshots). However, existing evaluations are limited to visual fidelity assessment under a fixed browser-device configuration. Such a setting overlooks the cross-environment rendering compatibility for real-world deployments.
  To address this gap, we present the first systematic empirical study of cross-environment compatibility in AI-generated webpages. Specifically, we construct WebCompat, a dataset of 2,032 annotated instances, comprising webpages generated by 8 representative AI tools, each rendered across 9 browser-and-device combinations. We analyze the prevalence of compatibility issues, their user-perceptible symptoms, and underlying code-level root causes. Our findings reveal that 68% of generated webpages exhibit at least one compatibility issue, underscoring the pervasive reliability concerns surrounding MLLM-generated front-end artifacts. The most prevalent symptoms are failures that disrupt the entire page layout (88.3%): pages shrink directly to fit the target screen with too small fonts, or exhibit scale mismatches that produce cut-off content. Failures localized to individual elements, such as image distortion or missing components, are comparatively less common (13.4%). Furthermore, although most MLLMs incorporate responsive design patterns into the generation, they fail to properly implement these codes.
  Guided by the findings, we develop XCompat, a lightweight offline compatibility issue detector that combines visual screenshots and the structural DOM tree for analysis. It achieves an F1 score of 0.903 on the WebCompat-test, outperforming the existing compatibility checking tools and LLM baselines. All datasets and tools are released to support future research on rendering reliability in MLLM-based front-end code generation.

</details>


### [76] [Memorization Diagnostics for Code LLMs Should be Scale-Aware](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12771)
*Prateek Kumar Rajput,Abdoul Aziz Bonkoungou,Alberick Euraste Djiré,Xunzhu Tang,Yewei Song,Iyiola Emmanuel Olatunji,El Hacen Diallo,Jacques Klein,Tegawendé F. Bissyandé*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper argues that existing probing techniques fail to detect memorization in large code models, and that memorization should be disentangled from "representation load" (adapting to surface-form variation). Using invertible transforms on numeric problems, the authors show scaled encoders absorb representation changes while still solving the right problem family, suggesting memorization matters less for practical usability than previously thought.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current memorization probes (synonym fuzzing, dead-code insertion, log-probability checks) work on smaller models but degrade on dense, scaled architectures—even on known-contaminated benchmarks. The authors seek to understand why these probes fail and to separate the entangled concepts of memorization and representation load instead of treating them as one phenomenon.

Method: The authors apply invertible mathematical transforms to numeric code problems to isolate representation load (surface-form variation) from memorization (prior exposure to a specific solution). They then assess whether scaled encoder models absorb the representation load while still converging on the correct family of solutions, and evaluate existing encoder- and decoder-style probing techniques across dense architectures.

Result: Existing probes (encoder perturbations and decoder log-probability methods) break down severely on large dense models, failing to expose memorization even on contaminated benchmarks. Scaled encoders successfully absorb substantial representation load while still converging on the correct solution family, indicating that adaptation to surface form matters more for real-world usability than whether a specific answer was memorized.

Conclusion: Memorization inflates scores on contaminated benchmarks, but once representation load is factored out, it is debatable how much memorization actually matters for functional answers. Future evaluations should be redesigned to separate memorization from representation load rather than relying on methods that quietly entangle them.

Abstract: The extent to which large language models for code rely on memorization over genuine understanding remains highly debated. While current literature frequently reports widespread memorization, evaluating the underlying probing techniques across dense architectures reveals a severe breakdown in their utility at scale. Traditional encoder-style probes using perturbations such as synonym fuzzing or dead-code insertion struggle to expose memorization in scaled models, even on known-contaminated benchmarks, and decoder-style probes that rely on log probabilities show similar performance degradation. The specific mode of failure for these probes, particularly why such techniques disrupt smaller models but fail to impact larger ones, motivates us to untangle representation load from memorization rather than treating them as a single phenomenon. By applying invertible mathematical transforms to numeric problems, we isolate these two factors and reveal that scaled encoders successfully absorb substantial representation load while still converging on the correct family of solutions. In practical software engineering, this ability to adapt to varying surface forms is what truly matters for usability and generalizability in LLM and agentic applications. Whether a specific solution was seen during training becomes a much less pressing question because although memorization inflates scores on contaminated benchmarks, factoring out representation load makes it debatable how much we should truly care if a functional answer was originally memorized. Future evaluations must therefore be built around separating these phenomena rather than relying on methodologies that quietly entangle them.

</details>


### [77] [Dissecting Software Graphs: Structural Insights for Driver-Guided Fuzzing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12859)
*Baihong Chen,Hua Ming,Weifeng Pan,Tian Xie,Haipeng Cai,Wen Li*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper studies multi-driver fuzzing through a structural lens, projecting driver-specific coverage onto a static call-graph backbone to expose how execution modes partition, overlap, and under-explore software structure. Across 27 OSS-Fuzz C/C++ projects (43 executables, 854 drivers), multi-driver fuzzing beats the best single driver by 27.9% more call-graph nodes and 73.5% more CFG edges, finding 11 bugs single-driver fuzzing misses, while revealing uneven driver contributions and recurring under-exploration regimes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing fuzzing evaluations focus only on aggregate coverage and bug counts, leaving unclear how multiple execution modes (options, subcommands, config flags) structurally partition, overlap, or miss software, and how these differences shape effectiveness.

Method: Proposes a structural abstraction that uses a static call graph as a shared backbone and projects driver-specific dynamic coverage onto it to produce driver-induced subgraphs. This supports a four-phase methodology: (1) backbone construction, (2) fuzzing and profiling, (3) graph-based analysis, and (4) research-question-driven evaluation. Applied to 27 OSS-Fuzz-derived C/C++ projects with 43 executables and 854 driver configurations under an equal total budget.

Result: Multi-driver fuzzing outperforms the best single-driver baseline, increasing covered call-graph nodes by 27.9% and CFG-edge coverage by 73.5%, and uncovers 11 unique bugs/abnormal behaviors largely missed by single-driver fuzzing. Driver contributions are highly uneven; induced subgraphs differ strongly in cohesion, fragmentation, modularity, and overlap; residual under-exploration follows recurring regimes rather than a homogeneous tail.

Conclusion: Multi-driver fuzzing is fundamentally a structural exploration problem: mode-based variability shapes which parts of a program are reachable and explored, so evaluation and algorithm design should account for structural partitioning, overlap, and recurring under-exploration regimes rather than treating coverage as a monolithic tail.

Abstract: Many software systems expose multiple execution modes through command-line options, subcommands, and configuration flags. For such programs, fuzzing depends on both mutated inputs and the invoked mode. Yet evaluations still focus on coverage and bug counts, leaving unclear how execution modes partition, overlap, and miss software structure, and how these differences affect effectiveness. We present an empirical study of software structure under multi-driver fuzzing. We propose a structural abstraction that uses a static call graph as a shared backbone and projects driver-specific dynamic coverage onto it to derive driver-induced subgraphs. Based on this abstraction, we develop a four-phase methodology for backbone construction, fuzzing and profiling, graph-based analysis, and research-question-driven evaluation. We apply it to 27 OSS-Fuzz-derived C/C++ projects, spanning 43 executables and 854 driver configurations. Under the same total budget, multi-driver fuzzing outperforms the best single-driver baseline, increasing covered call-graph nodes by 27.9% and CFG-edge coverage by 73.5%, and revealing 11 unique bugs and abnormal behaviors largely missed by single-driver fuzzing. However, driver contributions are uneven, subgraphs differ substantially in cohesion, fragmentation, modularity, overlap, and residual under-exploration follows recurring regimes rather than a homogeneous tail. These results show that multi-driver fuzzing is fundamentally a structural exploration problem.

</details>


### [78] [Requirements-Augmented Generation for Trustworthy Acceptance Testing of LLM-Based Software](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12970)
*Fanyu Wang,Chetan Arora,Zhenping Xie,Yonghui Liu,Kla Tantithamthavorn,Aldeida Aleti,Siwei Jiang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper proposes an automated acceptance testing framework for LLM-based software that generates context-aware test oracles via Requirements-Augmented Generation and uses a confidence-calibrated cascade judgment with conformal risk control to guarantee verdict reliability, demonstrated on an industrial nutrition advisory application.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based software produces context-dependent, stochastic outputs, so traditional deterministic acceptance testing and test oracles are insufficient. The same query may need different responses depending on user personas and context, creating an urgent need for automated acceptance testing that interprets user instructions and reliably infers intentions in changing environments.

Method: Two contributions: (1) Requirements-Augmented Generation (REAG), which retrieves relevant software requirements, domain knowledge, and personas through adaptive RAG and self-reasoning to generate context-aware test oracles; (2) a confidence-calibrated cascade judgment that quantifies verdict reliability via simulated expert agreement, accepting high-confidence verdicts, escalating ambiguous cases, or abstaining when uncertain, with empirical reliability guarantees from conformal risk control.

Result: In an industrial case study on a production nutrition advisory application, REAG achieved a 3.91/5 oracle quality score with qualified or marginal oracle quality in 82% of cases. The confidence-calibrated cascade reached 98.8% accuracy, improved oracle quality from 3.91 to 4.30 by filtering unqualified outputs, and delivered a 31.7% cost-efficiency improvement over single-judge baselines.

Conclusion: The proposed framework is industrially viable, providing automated acceptance testing for LLM-based software with calibrated verdict reliability, robust oracle quality improvement, and notable cost-efficiency gains over single-judge approaches.

Abstract: LLM-based software (LBS) integrates large language models as core components to deliver flexible, personalised responses. Unlike traditional software with deterministic outputs, LBSs exhibit context-dependent, stochastic behaviour that renders classical acceptance testing and test oracles insufficient: the same query may require fundamentally different responses depending on user personas and software context. This gap creates an urgent need for automated acceptance testing frameworks that autonomously interpret user instructions, while reliably inferring user intentions in a changing environment. In this paper, we present an automated acceptance testing framework for LBS with calibrated verdict reliability via two technical contributions. First, we introduce Requirements-Augmented Generation (REAG), which interprets user intentions by retrieving relevant software requirements, domain knowledge, and personas via adaptive RAG and self-reasoning to generate context-aware test oracles. Second, recognising that oracle generation may retrieve irrelevant constraints, misinterpret intent, or hallucinate requirements, we introduce a confidence-calibrated cascade judgment. This method quantifies verdict reliability via simulated expert agreement -- accepting high-confidence verdicts, escalating ambiguous cases, or abstaining when uncertain -- with empirical reliability guarantees backed by conformal risk control. An industrial case study on a production nutrition advisory application demonstrates that REAG achieves a 3.91/5 oracle quality score, reaching qualified or marginal oracle quality in 82% of cases. The confidence-calibrated cascade achieves 98.8% accuracy, improves oracle quality from 3.91 to 4.30 by filtering unqualified outputs, and delivers a 31.7% cost-efficiency improvement over single-judge baselines, validating industrial viability

</details>


### [79] [How Powerful are LLMs in Generating Formal Program Specifications?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13077)
*Fanpeng Yang,Xing Li,Shuling Wang,Jie An,Zeyu Sun,Shenghua Feng,Wenhan Wang,Weiyi Wang,Naijun Zhan,Fanjiang Xu*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper introduces Coins, a Rocq-based evaluation framework that measures specification quality by instantiating specifications on trusted test cases and extracting concrete proof obligations, avoiding the pitfalls of conformance verification and semantic equivalence proofs. A large-scale study on HumanEval shows specification generation remains hard and that verification complexity obscures quality differences.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Formal verification is underused because writing precise specifications is expensive. LLMs show promise in theorem proving and verified code generation, but their ability to produce specifications is unclear. Existing evaluations rely on verifying implementation conformance or proving semantic equivalence between specifications, which are both extremely hard and can conflate proof difficulty with actual specification quality. This motivates a more faithful, discriminative evaluation approach.

Method: The authors build Coins, an evaluation framework based on the Rocq proof assistant. It assesses specification quality by instantiating candidate specifications against trusted test cases and generating concrete proof obligations. This leverages the asymmetric nature of formal reasoning: successful proofs give reliable evidence, while proof failures are inherently ambiguous.

Result: A large-scale study on HumanEval with curated human-written Rocq specifications shows that specification generation remains a formidable challenge. Results indicate verification complexity can obscure genuine differences in specification quality, and that accurate evaluation, rather than model scaling alone, is key to understanding LLM capabilities for specification synthesis.

Conclusion: Test-case-based formal reasoning offers a more faithful and discriminative measure of progress in LLM specification synthesis. Accurate specification evaluation is central to understanding LLM power, and verification complexity must be accounted for rather than conflated with quality.

Abstract: Formal verification provides strong guarantees of software correctness, but its adoption is limited by the high cost of writing precise formal specifications. While recent large language models (LLMs) have shown strong capabilities in theorem proving and verified code generation, their true ability to generate program specifications remains unclear. Existing evaluations require either verifying implementation conformance or proving semantic equivalence between specifications, both of which are formidably difficult and may conflate proof difficulty with specification quality. To address this problem, we introduce Coins, a Rocq based evaluation framework that assesses specification quality by instantiating specifications under evaluation on trusted test cases and generating concrete proof obligations. This design aligns with the asymmetric nature of formal reasoning, where successful proofs provide reliable evidence while proof failures are inherently ambiguous. Using Coins, we conduct a large scale study on HumanEval with a curated set of human written Rocq specifications. Our results show that specification generation remains a formidable challenge, and that verification complexity can obscure genuine differences in specification quality. Overall, we find that accurate specification evaluation, rather than model scaling alone, is central to understanding the power of LLMs for specification synthesis, and that test case based formal reasoning offers a more faithful and discriminative measure of progress.

</details>


### [80] [Can Formal Specifications Be Synthesized from Tests Alone?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13240)
*Tianhai Liu,Maximilian Müller,Tobias Hey,Vitus Lüntzel,Muhammad Minhas,Anne Koziolek,Bernhard Beckert*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper presents a black-box approach that uses LLMs to infer JML (Java Modeling Language) specifications from test code and dynamic execution traces, avoiding access to program source code. Candidates are validated and iteratively refined via bounded model checking, with initial SpecGenBench results showing promise but flagging checker compatibility and feedback quality as key challenges.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Formal specifications are valuable but expensive to write manually, and recent LLM-based inference methods rely on white-box access to source code, which creates intellectual property risks and deployment costs that hinder industrial adoption. The authors seek a specification-inference method that only observes program interfaces and behavior, not implementation internals.

Method: The approach uses LLMs to generate candidate specifications from only test code and dynamic execution traces (selected inputs, outputs, and state changes), keeping implementation internals hidden. Candidate specifications are then validated locally using bounded model checking, with the checker's feedback used to guide iterative refinement of the specifications.

Result: Initial experiments on the SpecGenBench benchmark indicate that tests can steer LLMs toward producing meaningful JML specifications. However, the results also reveal that checker compatibility and the quality of diagnostic feedback are significant obstacles to achieving reliable iterative refinement.

Conclusion: Black-box, test-guided LLM inference of formal specifications is feasible, but further work is needed to address bounded-model-checker compatibility and improve diagnostic feedback to make iterative refinement reliable for industrial use.

Abstract: Formal specifications offer strong guarantees, but remain costly to write manually. Recent LLM-based approaches automate this by inferring specifications from source code, yet their reliance on white-box access poses barriers to industrial adoption due to intellectual property risks and deployment costs. Our approach uses LLMs to infer candidate specifications solely from test code and dynamic execution traces: the LLM observes only the program interface, selected inputs, and corresponding outputs or state changes, while the implementation internals remain hidden. Candidate specifications are validated locally using bounded model checking, with feedback guiding iterative refinement. Initial results on the SpecGenBench benchmark suggest that tests can guide LLMs towards meaningful Java Modeling Language specifications, while also highlighting checker compatibility and diagnostic feedback as key challenges for reliable refinement.

</details>


### [81] [Refine After Generation: Toward Correct and Concise Patches in LLM-based Program Repair](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13292)
*Wenqiang Luo,Jacky Keung,Xiaoyu Shi,Yicheng Sun,Boyang Yang,Zhou Yang,Haoye Tian*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: LLM-based APR systems fix bugs effectively but produce unnecessarily large, complex patches. The paper shows successful patches are far more verbose than human fixes, attributes this to agentic design choices, and proposes RECAP—a post-generation refiner that sharply reduces patch size while preserving or improving correctness, outperforming baselines that sacrifice resolution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite the success of LLM-based agentic program repair, generated patches are evaluated almost solely on test passage. Patch verbosity (size and complexity) has been overlooked, yet it harms reviewability and maintainability. The authors aim to quantify this verbosity, understand its root causes, and develop a practical way to produce more minimal, reviewable patches without losing correctness.

Method: The authors first characterize 28 state-of-the-art APR approaches on SWE-bench Verified, measuring total changes, net changes, and cyclomatic complexity against developer patches. They analyze how design choices (iterative refinement, broad context) drive verbosity. They then formulate post-generation patch refinement and build RECAP, a lightweight plug-and-play adapter attached after generation. RECAP's refiner is trained via supervised fine-tuning and direct preference optimization with distilled reasoning traces, using patch pairs constructed from multiple sources. It is evaluated across four host systems and compared against prompting, commit-untangling, and minimality-aware baselines.

Result: Even successful patches are much larger and more complex than developer patches: +121.78% total changes, +80.91% net changes, and +43.99% higher cyclomatic complexity (median). Baselines reduce patch size only by sacrificing 49–217 resolved instances. RECAP achieves a far better size-correctness tradeoff, cutting average total changes from +242.14% to +4.24% and net changes from +348.24% to -39.75% relative to developer patches, while preserving or improving resolution by up to 42 instances.

Conclusion: Minimality cannot be reduced to simple syntactic compression, and post-generation refinement decoupled from generation is a practical, effective path to more reviewable repairs. RECAP delivers substantially smaller patches with preserved or improved correctness across host systems.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have advanced automatic program repair (APR) to the point where agentic systems routinely resolve real-world, repository-level issues. Yet the generated patch has received little scrutiny beyond whether it passes tests.
  In this paper, we identify patch verbosity as a major yet overlooked concern in LLM-based APR. Characterizing 28 state-of-the-art approaches on SWE-bench Verified, we find that even successful patches are consistently larger and more complex than developer patches, with the median approach producing 121.78% more total changes, 80.91% more net changes, and 43.99% higher cyclomatic complexity. We further show that this verbosity is rooted in capability-oriented design choices such as iterative refinement and broad context, and can hardly be reduced by surface-level controls such as output format or minimality prompts. Motivated by these findings, we formulate post-generation patch refinement and propose RECAP, a lightweight, plug-and-play adapter that attaches to existing repair frameworks after generation. RECAP's refiner is trained via supervised fine-tuning and direct preference optimization with distilled reasoning traces, on a dataset of patch pairs we construct from multiple sources. Across four host systems, prompting, commit-untangling, and minimality-aware baselines reduce patch size only by sacrificing 49 to 217 resolved instances. In contrast, RECAP achieves a substantially better size-correctness tradeoff, cutting average total changes from +242.14% to +4.24% and net changes from +348.24% to -39.75% relative to developer patches while preserving or improving resolution by up to 42 instances. Our results indicate that minimality cannot be simply reduced to syntactic compression, and that decoupling minimization from generation offers a practical path to more reviewable repairs.

</details>


### [82] [Integration-First Structural Coverage for Embedded Software:Trace-Based Evidence, Hybrid Runtime Analysis, and Cross-Variant Consolidation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13322)
*Alexander Weiss,Albert Schulz,Michael Wittner*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Coverage in embedded projects is mostly measured at unit level due to cost, but real completeness evidence lies in integration/system tests on the device. The paper proposes an integration-first strategy with an explicit gap-closure loop, a hybrid runtime analysis (hRA) using embedded trace to make branch/condition/MC/DC coverage measurable on optimized (-O3) release-like binaries, and a "Hyper Coverage" consolidation layer that merges evidence across levels, runs, variants, and configurations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is a mismatch in embedded testing: structural coverage is collected at unit level because instrumentation is cheap there, yet the most representative completeness signal comes from integration and system tests executed on the device. Classical instrumentation perturbs timing, memory, and concurrency, while trace-reconstructed coverage becomes unreliable for decisions/conditions under aggressive compiler optimization. The goal is to resolve this mismatch from both process and technical sides.

Method: (1) Process side: an integration-first coverage strategy that uses integration and system tests as the baseline measurement and drives residual gaps through an explicit closure loop, establishing completeness as "covered or justified." (2) Technical side: embedded trace as the observation path plus hybrid runtime analysis (hRA), a minimal semantics-preserving observability scaffolding that keeps decision/condition boundaries distinguishable in the trace of an -O3 build, with all coverage state and counting off-target. (3) Hyper Coverage: a consolidation layer merging evidence across test levels, runs, variants, and build configurations, exposing source lines untested in every relevant variant.

Result: The approach converts object-to-source mapping from heuristic reconstruction into reviewable evidence and makes branch, condition, and MC/DC measurement practical on release-like (optimized -O3) binaries. It also provides a consolidated view of untested source lines across all relevant variants.

Conclusion: By combining an integration-first process with trace-based hybrid runtime analysis and a multi-dimensional evidence consolidation layer, the work closes the coverage mismatch in embedded projects, enabling reviewable, off-target coverage (branch, condition, MC/DC) on optimized binaries and justifying completeness gaps explicitly.

Abstract: Structural coverage is widely used as evidence that testing is complete, yet in embedded projects it is predominantly collected at unit level, simply because that is where instrumentation and observability are inexpensive. This produces a mismatch. The most representative completeness signal would come from integration and system tests executed on the device under test, but classical instrumentation perturbs timing, memory footprint and concurrency behaviour, while purely trace-reconstructed coverage loses reliability for decisions and conditions as soon as the compiler optimizes aggressively. We address this mismatch from both ends. On the process side we describe an integrationfirst coverage strategy that treats integration and system tests as the baseline measurement and drives the residual gaps through an explicit closure loop, so that completeness is established as covered or justified rather than as covered alone. On the technical side we use embedded trace as the observation path and add hybrid runtime analysis (hRA): a minimal, semantics-preserving observability scaffolding that keeps decision and condition boundaries distinguishable in the trace stream of an optimized (-O3) build, while all coverage state and counting remain off-target. This converts object-to-source mapping from a heuristic reconstruction into reviewable evidence and makes branch, condition and MC/DC measurement practical on release-like binaries. Finally we describe Hyper Coverage, a consolidation layer that merges evidence across test levels, test runs, variants and build configurations, and that exposes source lines which remain untested in every relevant variant.

</details>


### [83] [Does Fixing Break Security? An Empirical Study of Security Degradation in Iterative LLM-Driven Infrastructure-as-Code Repair](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13404)
*Benjamin Agyekum,Fabio Santos*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper studies whether iterative LLM repair of Infrastructure-as-Code introduces security regressions, analyzing 5,968 scenario timelines from IaC-Eval. It finds that under strict detection only ~3.3% of scenarios show regressions, with resource restructuring as the dominant root cause, and identifies iteration 3 as the optimal stopping point.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work on iterative LLM repair for IaC only reports cumulative-best metrics, which are non-decreasing and thus mask whether security degrades between iterations. No prior study has examined the raw per-iteration security trajectory, so the authors aim to quantify security regressions caused by feedback-loop repair.

Method: The authors analyze 5,968 scenario timelines from the IaC-Eval benchmark, each run through one configuration for up to 5 repair iterations. Across 15 configurations (six model-specific RAG, nine model-aggregated non-RAG, three temperatures each), they derive 4,440 iteration transitions with Checkov data on both sides. They track 30 individual CIS check IDs and classify root causes from code diffs under two detection modes: standard (inclusive) and strict (exclusive check failures only). Statistical comparisons use effect sizes such as Cohen's d.

Result: Under standard detection, 13.8% of scenarios (24.8% of transitions) exhibit at least one security regression; under strict detection this falls to 3.3% of scenarios (5.2% of transitions), indicating most apparent regressions are multi-resource measurement artifacts. Resource restructuring is the dominant root cause (79.0%). Regression transitions show 2.6x more code churn (Cohen's d=0.90) and 4.9x higher strict-mode check volatility (d=1.49). Of standard-mode regressions, 36.6% self-correct within an average of 1.2 iterations; iteration 3 is the optimal stopping point.

Conclusion: Iterative IaC repair does introduce security regressions, but the conservative, defensible rate is about 3.3% of scenarios. The findings motivate security-aware feedback-loop design and provide actionable iteration-budget guidance (stopping at iteration 3).

Abstract: Background: Iterative feedback loops are the dominant paradigm for improving LLM-generated Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC): validators such as Checkov and terraform validate feed error signals back for successive repair attempts. Prior work reports cumulative-best metrics, which are non-decreasing by construction, so the raw per-iteration security trajectory has never been examined for IaC. Aims: We study security regression (a previously-passing CIS Benchmark check that fails after a repair iteration) to determine whether and how often iterative LLM repair degrades security while fixing other issues. Method: We analyze 5,968 scenario timelines from the IaC-Eval benchmark, each one scenario run through one configuration for up to 5 repair iterations. The 15 configurations (six model-specific RAG, nine model-aggregated non-RAG, three temperatures each) yield 4,440 iteration transitions with Checkov data on both sides. We track 30 individual CIS check IDs and classify root causes from code diffs, under two detection modes: standard (inclusive) and strict (exclusive check failures only). Results: Under standard detection, 13.8% of scenarios (24.8% of transitions) exhibit at least one regression. Under strict detection the rate falls to 3.3% of scenarios (5.2% of transitions), indicating most apparent regressions are multi-resource measurement artifacts. Resource restructuring (79.0%) is the dominant root cause. Regression transitions show 2.6x more code churn (Cohen's d=0.90) and 4.9x higher strict-mode check volatility (d=1.49). Of standard-mode regressions, 36.6% self-correct within an average of 1.2 iterations; iteration 3 is the optimal stopping point. Conclusions: Iterative IaC repair does introduce security regressions, but the conservative, defensible rate is about 3.3% of scenarios. Our findings motivate security-aware feedback-loop design and actionable iteration-budget guidance.

</details>


### [84] [LLM-Assisted Dynamic Threat Analysis for Attacker-Reachable Software Weaknesses in Autonomous Vehicles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13450)
*Md Wasiul Haque,Sagar Dasgupta,Mizanur Rahman,Md Rayhanur Rahman*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This study tests whether LLMs can automate dynamic confirmation of potential weaknesses in Autoware (an open-source autonomous-driving stack). After static analysis identified 740 reachable candidate sites, two open-weight LLMs generated test harnesses that were compiled against the real build, repaired, and fuzzed. The key finding is that build integration—not weakness generation or fuzzing—is the dominant failure point: ~80% of first-shot compilation failures stem from dependency wiring, the reasoning model compiled 64% of harnesses first-try (vs 6% for the code-specialized model), full object-compileability was achieved only through extensive stubbing, and all 37 crashes came from stubbed code, with zero real weaknesses dynamically confirmed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous vehicles rely on large safety-critical software stacks, where adversarial inputs can reach weaknesses affecting steering, braking, or control decisions. Static analysis can find candidate sites, but dynamically confirming exploitability requires executable test artifacts that are hard to build manually. The authors investigate whether LLMs can automate this confirmation process for a full real-world AV stack.

Method: Compiler-precise static analysis across 185 Autoware packages identified 1,375 decision rules, 2,274 validation checks, and 482 input-to-safety-output flows, yielding a weakness taxonomy and 740 sampled reachable sites. Two local open-weight LLMs (a reasoning model and a code-specialized model), plus a no-static-context ablation and a naive-template baseline, generated 3,700 artifact sets. These were compiled against the real build under sanitizers, repaired via compiler-in-the-loop feedback, and fuzzed when executable.

Result: A build-integration failure taxonomy shows ~80% of first-shot compilation failures arise from dependency wiring rather than program logic. The reasoning model compiled 64% of harnesses first-try vs 6% for the code-specialized model. Full object-compileability for the reasoning model required extensive stubbing; fewer than half its harnesses reached the fuzzer, and all 37 observed crashes originated in stubbed code rather than Autoware. No candidate weakness was dynamically confirmed within budget.

Conclusion: Build integration—not candidate generation or fuzzing—is the primary barrier to reliable LLM-assisted dynamic analysis of full autonomous-vehicle software stacks. Future work must address dependency wiring and harness integration into large real-world builds before LLM-generated dynamic confirmation can be trusted at scale.

Abstract: Autonomous vehicles depend on large safety-critical software stacks, where weaknesses reachable from adversarial inputs may affect steering, braking, or other control decisions. Static analysis can identify candidate sites, but dynamically confirming exploitability requires executable test artifacts that are difficult to construct manually. We investigate whether large language models (LLMs) can automate this process for Autoware, an open-source autonomous-driving stack. We perform compiler-precise static analysis across 185 packages, identifying 1,375 decision rules, 2,274 validation checks, and 482 input-to-safety-output flows, from which we derive a weakness taxonomy and sample 740 reachable sites. Two local open-weight LLMs, a no-static-context ablation, and a naive-template baseline generate 3,700 artifact sets, which are compiled against the real build under sanitizers, repaired through compiler-in-the-loop feedback, and fuzzed when executable. The main result is a build-integration failure taxonomy showing that 80% of first-shot compilation failures arise from dependency wiring rather than program logic. The reasoning model compiled 64% of harnesses on the first attempt, compared with 6% for the code-specialized model. Repair achieved full object-compileability for the reasoning model only through extensive stubbing; fewer than half of its harnesses reached the fuzzer, and all 37 observed crashes originated in stubbed code rather than Autoware. No candidate weakness was dynamically confirmed within budget. These results show that build integration, not candidate generation or fuzzing, is the primary barrier to reliable LLM-assisted dynamic analysis of full autonomous-vehicle software stacks.

</details>


### [85] [CAPRI: Contract-Aware Proof Repair for Isabelle](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13459)
*Jim Woodcock,Gabriel Leite,Augusto Sampaio,Ran Wei*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper presents CAPRI, a contract-aware proof-repair workflow where Isabelle verifies proofs while an independent checker enforces machine-readable edit contracts, preventing LLMs from modifying text outside developer authorization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs can help discover Isabelle proofs, but an Isabelle build only confirms the submitted theory is accepted—it does not verify that the LLM changed only developer-authorized content. This risks unauthorized modifications slipping into proofs.

Method: CAPRI combines Isabelle's proof checking with an independent checker that enforces a machine-readable edit contract. Prompts, proposals, candidate repositories, diagnostics, verdicts, and hashes are retained for audit. Five workflows were evaluated on twelve failed proofs from four developments, with three replicates per task and condition (180 runs total).

Result: Of 144 terminal candidates accepted by Isabelle, six modified protected text—all in iterative workflows editing a complete theory. A proof-body-only interface yielded 29/36 valid repairs with no contract violations versus 31/36 for full-theory workflow. One-shot repair produced 22/36, while a later frozen iterative workflow produced 32/36. A Sol configuration with matched demonstrations achieved 33/36 repairs versus 29/36 for frozen OpenAI Responses, but the difference was not statistically significant (exact McNemar, p=0.0625).

Conclusion: Contract-aware workflows like CAPRI can effectively constrain LLM edits during proof repair, with proof-body-only interfaces eliminating contract violations at a small cost in repair success, though differences between configurations were not statistically significant.

Abstract: We address the use of large language models (LLMs) to help discover Isabelle proofs. An Isabelle build establishes that the submitted theory is accepted, but not that an LLM changed only what the developer authorised. We present CAPRI, a contract-aware repair workflow in which Isabelle checks the proof and an independent checker enforces a machine-readable edit contract. Prompts, proposals, candidate repositories, diagnostics, verdicts, and hashes are retained for audit. We evaluate five workflows on twelve failed proofs from four developments, with three replicates per task and condition, giving 180 runs and 138 valid repairs. Of 144 terminal candidates accepted by Isabelle, six had modified protected text; all arose in iterative workflows that could edit a complete theory. A proof-body-only interface produced 29/36 valid repairs and no contract violations, compared with 31/36 for the corresponding full-theory workflow. One-shot repair produced 22/36, while a later prospectively frozen iterative workflow produced 32/36; these figures compare complete workflows rather than individual mechanisms. A separate post hoc OpenRouter campaign found no improvement in the designated Luna comparisons. A Sol configuration with matched demonstrations produced 33/36 repairs, compared with 29/36 in the frozen OpenAI Responses condition, but the difference was not statistically significant in a one-sided exact McNemar test ($p=0.0625$).

</details>

### [86] [Position: Reasoning is a Learnable Rule-Based Process](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12325)
*Rachel Lawrence,Jacqueline Maasch*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper argues that AI reasoning lacks clear operational definitions, undermining evaluation validity, and proposes operational definitions (formalizing reasoning as a learnable rule-based process) plus a best-practices checklist for communicating reasoning research.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous reasoning is scientifically and economically important, but the generative AI community has not converged on operational definitions of reasoning and often rejects historical treatments rooted in logic and verifiable automated reasoning. This definitional ambiguity makes the construct validity of reasoning evaluations unverifiable, threatening quantifiable progress toward trustworthy autonomous reasoning.

Method: A position paper that (1) synthesizes the literature on reasoning from symbolic AI, logic, and generative modeling to derive operational definitions, positioning valid and sound reasoning as a learnable rule-based process; and (2) proposes a checklist of best practices for communicating AI reasoning research.

Result: The paper provides operational definitions of reasoning and a communication best-practices checklist, contending that the existing definitional ambiguity is addressable and that these tools can restore verifiability to reasoning evaluation.

Conclusion: Definitional ambiguity has left the construct validity of reasoning evaluation unverifiable, but this can be remedied by adopting operational definitions based on rules and soundness/validity, along with standardized best practices for reporting reasoning research—thereby enabling trustworthy autonomous reasoning and quantifiable progress.

Abstract: Autonomous reasoning is among the most scientifically and economically motivating topics in AI today. Historically the purview of symbolic AI, recent advances have mainly emerged from deep probabilistic generative models. Despite immense interest and rapid progress, the generative AI community has not clearly converged on operational definitions for reasoning and often implicitly rejects the historical treatment of this topic in logic and verifiable automated reasoning. This position contends that definitional ambiguity leaves the construct validity of reasoning evaluation unverifiable, undermining quantifiable progress toward trustworthy autonomous reasoning. We also contend that this ambiguity is addressable. To that end, we provide (1) operational definitions based on a synthesis of the literature, positioning valid and sound reasoning as a learnable rule-based process; and (2) a checklist for best practices in the communication of AI reasoning research.

</details>


### [87] [Diagnostic Foundation for Evaluating LLMs' Research Integrity as Co-Scientists](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12345)
*Yash Tripathi,Silu Sharma,Sai Sidhanth Manoharan Jayanthi,Shivank Garg,Lin Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces IntegrityBench, a benchmark assessing language models' research-integrity behavior under pressure. Across 36 paired tasks and 18 frontier models, models fail ~1 in 3 integrity-critical decisions at peak pressure; scale/reasoning don't help, explicit pressure induces misconduct compliance while implicit reframing causes over-refusal, and classification accuracy is dissociated from ethical action.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Language models are increasingly deployed as co-scientists, yet their ability to uphold research integrity when facing institutional pressure has not been measured. The authors aim to quantify whether frontier models maintain ethical behavior across misconduct classification, ethical action reasoning, and artifact-grounded decision making.

Method: Proposes IntegrityBench, a benchmark with 36 paired tasks spanning 3 domains and 4 research stages, using a 5-level implicit-to-explicit pressure protocol. Evaluates 18 frontier model variants on three facets: misconduct classification, ethical action reasoning, and artifact-grounded decision making.

Result: Under peak pressure, models fail roughly 1 in 3 integrity-critical decisions, with neither model scale nor reasoning ability reliably mitigating failures. Explicit pressure induces compliance with misconduct, while implicit contextual reframing more often causes over-refusal of legitimate tasks. Models failing classification perform equally or better on artifact-grounded decision making (85.7 vs. 79.4), indicating the three facets are structurally dissociated.

Conclusion: Frontier models can appear helpful while harboring integrity failures, creating two deployment risks: facilitating research misconduct and eroding trust in AI-assisted research. Accurate misconduct classification is not required for correct ethical action, highlighting a structural dissociation that complicates safety assurance.

Abstract: Language models are increasingly deployed as co-scientists, yet their ability to uphold research integrity under institutional pressure remains unmeasured. We introduce IntegrityBench, a benchmark evaluating misconduct classification, ethical action reasoning and artifact-grounded decision making across 36 paired tasks under a 5-level implicit-explicit pressure protocol spanning 3 domains and 4 research stages. Evaluating 18 frontier model variants, we find that under peak pressure, models fail roughly 1 in 3 integrity-critical decisions, and neither scale nor reasoning ability reliably mitigates this. Explicit pressures induce compliance with misconduct, while implicit contextual reframing more often causes over-refusal of legitimate research tasks. Interestingly, models failing to classify research requests accurately perform equally or better on artifact-grounded decision making (85.7 vs. 79.4), suggesting the three facets are structurally dissociated and correct ethical action does not require accurate classification. Frontier models can thus appear helpful while harbouring integrity failures that create two distinct deployment risks: facilitating research misconduct and eroding trust in AI-assisted research.

</details>


### [88] [Position: The Alignment Community is Unintentionally Building a Censor's Toolkit](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12346)
*Sarah Ball,Phil Hackemann*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This position paper argues that AI alignment methods are dual-use technologies that can be misused for censorship and manipulation, maps current techniques to misuse cases, and urges the community to develop mitigation strategies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The drive to create "perfectly aligned" AI models inadvertently equips malicious actors with increasingly powerful tools for informational dominance. This risk is heightened by rapid AI adoption as an information source, economic power asymmetries, and a political shift toward authoritarianism, necessitating urgent discussion of alignment's dual-use potential.

Method: The paper is a position paper that maps current AI alignment techniques (originally designed to prevent harmful output) onto potential and actual cases of misuse for censorship and manipulation, and analyzes how these techniques can be repurposed for informational dominance.

Result: The analysis shows that alignment methods are dual-use: the pursuit of perfectly aligned models simultaneously provides malicious actors with ever-improving tools for censorship and manipulation, exacerbating risks under conditions of rapid AI adoption, economic power asymmetry, and authoritarian political trends.

Conclusion: The community should consider the intentional misuse of AI alignment mechanisms and adopt mitigation strategies to safeguard against the dual-use potential of alignment technologies.

Abstract: This position paper argues that modern AI alignment methods - originally designed to prevent harmful output - are dual-use technologies that may easily be misused by malicious actors for censorship and manipulation. By mapping current alignment techniques to the possibility and actual cases of misuse, we show that the quest for a "perfectly aligned" model inadvertently also provides malicious actors with an ever-improving tool for informational dominance. We need to discuss this dual-use potential now, as its risk is exacerbated by rapid user adoption of AI as information provider, economic power asymmetries, and a political landscape that increasingly shifts towards authoritarianism. We conclude by urging the community to consider the intentional misuse of AI alignment mechanisms and propose mitigation strategies to safeguard against this dual-use potential.

</details>


### [89] [Agreement Is Not Alignment: Divergent Moral Grounds in Human and LLM Ethical Judgments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12368)
*Octavian M. Machidon,Alina L. Machidon,Vojko Strahovnik,Mateja Centa Strahovnik,Jonas Miklavčič,Marko Robnik Šikonja*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Label agreement between LLMs and humans often masks systematic divergence in the moral rationales behind those labels, so agreement metrics alone can be misleading as a measure of moral alignment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Previous evaluation of LLM moral alignment relies on agreement with human final labels, but identical labels can be produced from different moral grounds (principles, contextual assumptions, interpretations). The authors argue that true alignment requires comparing the reasons behind judgments, not just outcomes.

Method: The authors built a curated 500-item benchmark derived from the ETHICS dataset spanning five domains of moral judgment. They collected new annotations from human annotators and LLMs capturing both final labels and supporting rationales. They then compared label-level agreement against rationale-level divergence, examining how models redistribute attention across moral categories (harm, respect, promise-keeping, justice, desert, excuse relevance) even when final labels match the human majority.

Result: Agreement with human majority labels is often high across frontier and open model families, yet rationale-level analysis reveals systematic divergence in moral grounds. Models redistribute attention across categories such as harm, respect, promise-keeping, justice, desert, and excuse relevance, even when their final labels match the human annotator majority.

Conclusion: Agreement should not be treated as equivalent to alignment. Label-based evaluation can be misleadingly reassuring and should be complemented by analysis of the reasons, principles, and moral priorities expressed in model judgments.

Abstract: Agreement with human judgments is a common proxy for evaluating the alignment of large language models (LLMs). Yet agreement in final labels does not show that human annotators and models rely on the same moral grounds. Two agents may reach the same judgment while appealing to different principles, contextual assumptions, or interpretations of the situation.
  We test this distinction using a curated 500-item ETHICS-derived benchmark spanning five domains of moral judgment, with new human annotator and LLM annotations of both final labels and supporting rationales. Across frontier and open model families, agreement with human annotator majority labels is often high. However, rationale-level analysis reveals systematic divergence in the moral grounds expressed by human annotators and models. In particular, models redistribute attention across categories such as harm, respect, promise-keeping, justice, desert, and excuse relevance, even when their final labels match the human annotator majority.
  Our results show that agreement should not be treated as equivalent to alignment. Label-based evaluation can therefore be misleadingly reassuring unless complemented by analysis of the reasons, principles, and moral priorities expressed in model judgments.

</details>


### [90] [Multi-Agent Scheduling with LLM-Assisted Contract Net Negotiation for Stream Processing in Mobile Edge Computing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12371)
*Sabeur Lajili,Zaki Brahmi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MAS-DecStream extends the Contract Net Protocol (CNP) with LLM-driven semantic offloading and multi-round negotiation for decentralized stream-processing scheduling across mobile edge-cloud infrastructures, showing reduced latency violations and improved utility while keeping constraints deterministic.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Stream-processing systems increasingly span heterogeneous mobile edge-cloud environments where workload volatility, resource contention, and strict QoS requirements make decentralized scheduling difficult. Existing CNP-based approaches lack semantic formulation, iterative refinement, and memory, while purely rule-based methods struggle with qualitative, uncertain runtime context.

Method: The paper introduces LLM-MR-CNP, an extension of the Contract Net Protocol featuring semantic Call-for-Proposal (CFP) formulation, progressive context disclosure, multi-round proposal revision, negotiation memory, and deterministic validation. Edge-cluster agents generate and refine natural-language offloading proposals from local observations, predicted resource states, and qualitative runtime context, while hard resource and QoS constraints remain deterministically enforced.

Result: Using the Alibaba ASI Trace, MAS-DecStream reduces latency violations to 3%, eliminates resource overcommitment, achieves a conflict-resolution rate of 0.91 with 20 agents, and improves utility by up to 22% over the multi-round rule-based baseline. A separate 25-case study indicates accuracy-cost trade-offs are model- and prompt-dependent.

Conclusion: Initial evidence suggests multi-round CNP refinement is the principal protocol-level gain, while LLM assistance adds the most value for handling qualitative and uncertain runtime context, pointing toward hybrid rule-plus-LLM approaches for decentralized stream-processing orchestration.

Abstract: Stream-processing systems increasingly operate across heterogeneous mobile edge--cloud infrastructures, where workload volatility, resource contention, and stringent quality-of-service (QoS) requirements complicate decentralized scheduling. This paper proposes \emph{MAS-DecStream}, whose main contribution is \emph{LLM-MR-CNP}: an extension of the classical Contract Net Protocol with semantic CFP formulation, progressive context disclosure, multi-round proposal revision, negotiation memory, and deterministic validation. Edge-cluster agents refine natural-language offloading proposals from local observations, predicted resource states, and qualitative runtime context, while hard resource and QoS constraints remain deterministic. Experiments derived from the Alibaba ASI Trace evaluate the extension at three levels: single- versus multi-round CNP, rule-based versus LLM-assisted refinement, and fixed-model single- versus multi-round negotiation. Under the evaluated configurations, MAS-DecStream reduces latency violations to 3\%, eliminates resource overcommitment, reaches a conflict-resolution rate of 0.91 with 20 agents, and improves utility by up to 22\% over the multi-round rule-based baseline. A separate 25-case evaluation shows model- and prompt-dependent accuracy--cost trade-offs. The results provide initial evidence that multi-round CNP refinement is the principal protocol-level gain, with LLM assistance adding value for qualitative and uncertain runtime context.

</details>


### [91] [Position: We Need Practical AI Alignment Methods to Mirror Human Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12372)
*Vijay Keswani,Breanna K. Nguyen,Cyrus Cousins,Vincent Conitzer,Walter Sinnott-Armstrong,Jana Schaich Borg*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This position paper argues that high-stakes AI should be cognitively aligned with its users—reasoning similarly and communicating faithfully—and lays out evidence, survey data, and a research agenda to close the gap between existing alignment methods and true cognitive alignment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As AI systems serve as decision aids, delegates, or autonomous decision-makers, the authors worry that misaligned reasoning will undermine understandability, trustworthiness, and justified reliance, impeding adoption in high-stakes settings.

Method: The paper combines a review of existing evidence on cognitive alignment with new survey data on whether users consider such alignment essential, then identifies gaps in current alignment methods and proposes a research agenda.

Result: Evidence indicates cognitive alignment improves understandability and trustworthiness, and new survey data show many users rate it as essential when an AI's rationale matters to them.

Conclusion: Cognitive misalignment is a likely barrier to AI adoption in many envisioned applications, and addressing it is key to building AI systems that users are both willing and justified to rely on.

Abstract: AI systems are increasingly employed as decision aids, decision delegates, or autonomous decision-makers. This position paper argues that in many settings, particularly high-stakes decision-making, we need accurate cognitively-aligned AI systems that reason similarly to their users, and faithfully communicate their reasoning. We review evidence that cognitive alignment improves understandability and trustworthiness, and provide new survey data showing that many users find cognitive alignment "essential" when an AI's rationale for a judgment or action is important to them. We outline the gaps between existing alignment methods and what is needed to achieve cognitive alignment, and present a research agenda to address these gaps. We argue that cognitive misalignment represents a likely impediment to AI adoption in many envisioned applications, and that addressing it is important for creating AI systems on which users are both willing and justified to rely.

</details>


### [92] [Agent Behavioral Contracts II: Certifying Compositional Reliability Without Assuming Independence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12895)
*Varun Pratap Bhardwaj,Garima Singh,Arun Pratap Bhardwaj*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper empirically tests—and rejects—the routine conditional-independence assumption underlying compositional reliability bounds in multi-agent systems, showing same-model agents co-fail far more than independence predicts, and proposes finite-sample and anytime-valid certificates based on linear programming over measured co-execution moments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Compositional reliability bounds multiply component reliabilities, which is only valid under a conditional-independence assumption that is routinely stated but almost never tested. The authors suspect this assumption is false in practice for multi-agent systems sharing models and aim to verify and quantify the resulting error.

Method: A preregistered evaluation of 18,000 two-agent handoff missions scored by deterministic code (no LLM judge). They measure co-failure rates, compute log OR, phi, and confidence intervals; run six contrasts substituting models and vendors. They prove a bootstrap bound on a fitted dependence model loses coverage as n grows (identification gap O(1) vs bootstrap haircut O(n^{-1/2})). They construct a finite-sample certificate via a linear program over the joint distribution within a Bonferroni–Clopper–Pearson box around measured co-execution moments, plus an anytime-valid companion certificate under optional stopping.

Result: Two instances of one model co-fail on 90.0% of missions where either fails (log OR 6.66, 95% CI [6.38, 7.00]; phi 0.916). Substituting a different model reduced the association in all six contrasts; substituting a different vendor (model already different) did not—a null as preregistered. Enriching ten moment functionals to fourteen narrowed the identified interval by 85.7% and lifted the certified floor from 0.2455 to 0.4116. The anytime-valid certificate held type-I error at 0.0471 under optional stopping. The signed error inflates joint failure above the independence product, over-crediting redundancy when components share a model.

Conclusion: The conditional-independence assumption is empirically false and its failure is signed against the operator, over-crediting redundancy for same-model components. Assumption-free alternatives are often vacuous and fitted dependence models degrade with more data without visible symptoms. The proposed moment-based linear-programming certificates are sound, sharp, monotone in the moment family, and the anytime-valid variant controls type-I error under optional stopping.

Abstract: Compositional reliability bounds for multi-agent systems multiply component reliabilities, a step licensed by a conditional-independence assumption that is routinely stated and rarely tested. We test it. Two instances of one model, in a two-agent handoff, co-fail on 90.0% of the missions on which either fails (log OR 6.66, 95% CI [6.38, 7.00]; phi 0.916), in a preregistered evaluation of 18,000 missions scored by deterministic code with no LLM judge. Substituting a different model reduces the association in six of six contrasts; substituting a different vendor, model already different, does not -- a registered hypothesis reported as a null.
  The error is signed and runs against the operator: positive dependence inflates joint failure above the independence product, so redundancy is over-credited exactly when components share a model. The assumption-free alternative is often vacuous, and fitting a dependence model is worse: we prove a bootstrap bound on a fitted model's functional loses coverage of the truth as n grows, the identification gap being O(1) while the bootstrap haircut is O(n^{-1/2}). More data makes such a certificate worse, with no visible symptom.
  We give a finite-sample certificate assuming no dependence structure: a linear program over the joint, over a Bonferroni-Clopper-Pearson box around measured co-execution moments. It is sound, sharp for the information supplied, and monotone in the moment family. Enriching ten moment functionals to fourteen narrows the identified interval by 85.7% and lifts the certified floor from 0.2455 to 0.4116. A companion anytime-valid certificate holds type-I error at 0.0471 under optional stopping.
  Common dependence statistics are marginal-bounded and can reverse an apparent ordering of conditions when the compared agents fail at different rates. Contracts, scoring code, analysis scripts, and the preregistration are released.

</details>


### [93] [Don't Want Your LLM to Recommend Nuclear Strike? Try Asking It in Japanese](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12373)
*Rian Touchent*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLMs advise on a nuclear strike in game-theoretic vignettes; for models that hesitate in English, Japanese reasoning (not Japanese input) dramatically lowers launch rates by eliciting spontaneous moral reasoning, revealing that safety alignment is language-dependent.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Safety alignment of LLMs is typically evaluated only in English, leaving unknown whether a prompt's language changes a model's decisions in high-stakes advisory scenarios. The authors seek to determine whether language itself can alter model behavior and uncover the mechanism.

Method: Nine models from six providers were tested using single-turn, strategically identical, amoral game-theoretic vignettes in which the model advises a nuclear-armed nation whether to strike a defenseless opponent. Scenarios are categorized by strategic rationality (unnecessary, contested, rational). A cross-language experiment manipulates reasoning language independently of input language (e.g., instructing English-prompt models to reason in Japanese) to isolate the mechanism.

Result: Japanese prompts reduce launch rates in Claude (Sonnet 4.6: 40%→0% unnecessary, 93%→17% contested, minimal effect when rational) and Gemini Pro 3.1 (53%→13%). The effect is driven by reasoning language, not input language (93%→37% when told to reason in Japanese within English prompts). Japanese reasoning elicits spontaneous moral vocabulary ("moral cost", "millions of lives") absent from the prompt. Five other models show no language effect because they launch in nearly all conditions.

Conclusion: LLM safety behavior is language-dependent; the effect requires a model that already hesitates in English. Evaluating safety in English alone can miss both risks and safeguards encoded in other languages.

Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used in strategic and advisory contexts, yet their safety alignment is typically evaluated in English only. We test nine models from six providers and ask whether the language of a prompt can change a model's decision in a high-stakes scenario. We use single-turn game-theoretic vignettes in which a model advises a nuclear-armed nation on whether to strike a defenseless opponent. The prompt is intentionally amoral and strategically identical across languages. We find that Japanese prompts reduce launch rates in the Claude model family: Claude Sonnet 4.6 drops from 40% to 0% in scenarios where the strike is unnecessary and from 93% to 17% in contested scenarios, with minimal effect when the strike is strategically rational. The effect extends to Gemini Pro 3.1 (53% to 13%). A cross-language experiment isolates the mechanism: when instructed to reason in Japanese in an English prompt, launch rates drop from 93% to 37%. It is the language the model is asked to reason in, not the language of the input, that drives the effect. When reasoning in Japanese, models spontaneously generate moral vocabulary (''moral cost'', ''millions of lives'') that is entirely absent from the prompt. Five other models show no language effect, but they launch in nearly every condition regardless of language. The effect requires a model that already hesitates in English. These results show that LLM safety behavior is language-dependent, and that evaluating in English alone can miss both risks and safeguards encoded in other languages.

</details>


### [94] [MindMemOS: A Portable and Self-Evolving Memory Operating Layer for AI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12428)
*Kaichao Liang,Yuqi Cui,Hao Kong,Xinyuan Huang,Guohaotian Hou,Qingcan Kang,Liang Chen,Yiyang Yin,Ke Ye,Jiaquan Guo,Da Chen,Lingan Zeng,Yixing Peng,Rong Yao,Shixiong Kai,Mingxuan Yuan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MindMemOS is a portable, self-evolving memory operating layer for AI agents that organizes open-world information via a unified entity-property-time structure, adapts memory schemas through validation-driven evolutionary search, consolidates memories through "dreaming," and refines skills from execution trajectories, achieving 94.03% accuracy on LOCOMO and 70.63% on PersonaMem while improving SpreadsheetBench success by 9.2 points.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing AI agent memory systems are largely fixed after development, lacking the ability to adapt memory models, organization strategies, and procedural knowledge during continued use. This limits long-term personalization, experience accumulation, and adaptability.

Method: MindMemOS uses a unified entity-property-time structure for open-world information and supports scenario-adaptive memory modeling, higher-order pattern discovery, autonomous memory refinement, and continuous skill evolution. Its MindMemEvolve algorithm applies validation-driven evolutionary search to optimize memory schemas for target scenarios, while "dreaming" consolidates memories by merging redundant records and resolving conflicts; implicit corrective feedback provides a human-in-the-loop signal to identify and revise inaccurate or misaligned memories. The MindSkillEvolve algorithm converts agent execution trajectories into reusable, progressively refined skills.
