Result: MindMemOS achieves 94.03% accuracy on LOCOMO and 70.63% on PersonaMem. MindSkillEvolve improves SpreadsheetBench success by 9.2 percentage points over the initial-skill baseline.

Conclusion: A self-evolving, portable memory operating layer can effectively adapt AI agents' memory schemas, organization, and skills over time, yielding strong benchmark performance and demonstrable improvements in skill-based task success.

Abstract: Memory is a core component of AI agents, enabling them to accumulate experience, maintain personalization, and adapt over long-term interactions. However, existing memory systems often remain fixed after development, limiting their ability to adapt their memory models, organization strategies, and procedural knowledge through continued use. We present MindMemOS, a portable and self-evolving memory operating layer that organizes open-world information using a unified entity property timestructure. MindMemOS supports scenario-adaptive memory modeling, higher-order pattern discovery, autonomous memory refinement, and continuous skill evolution. Its MindMemEvolve algorithm employs validation-driven evolutionary search to optimize memory schemas for target scenarios, whiledreaming consolidates accumulated memories by merging redundant records and resolving conflicts. In addition, implicit corrective feedback serves as a human-in-the-loop signal for identifying and revising potentially inaccurate or misaligned memories. Its MindSkillEvolve algorithm further transforms agent execution trajectories into reusable and progressively refined skills. MindMemOS achieves 94.03% accuracy on LOCOMO and 70.63% on PersonaMem. MindSkillEvolve improves SpreadsheetBench success by 9.2 percentage points over the initial-skill baseline.

</details>


### [95] [OGR-MARL: Option-Guided Residual Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous USV Cooperative Pursuit in Constrained Port Waterways](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12995)
*Mao Jiayang,Wang Lanfeng,Peng Zhao-Han*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OGR-MARL is an option-guided residual multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for heterogeneous USV cooperative pursuit in constrained port waterways, achieving 75.0% capture rate with MASAC backbone and promising zero-shot transfer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Heterogeneous USV cooperative pursuit in constrained port waterways is difficult because evader interception must respect navigation, traffic, and role constraints. Existing MARL algorithms would need to explore these constrained environments from scratch, making learning inefficient and unsafe.

Method: OGR-MARL is a framework decoupled from a specific MARL algorithm, integrating four components: (1) shared evader belief, (2) role-conditioned option targets, (3) adaptive rule penalties, and (4) residual policy learning. It allows MARL algorithms to learn corrective actions on top of rule-guided behaviors. Four instantiations were created using MADDPG, MATD3, MAPPO, and MASAC backbones.

Result: In an abstract Xiazhimen port-waterway scenario, OGR-MASAC achieves a 75.0% capture rate with promising mission-effective rule compliance and the best heterogeneous coordination among tested methods. Zero-shot transfer to a QGIS/AIS-informed Xiazhimen map without retraining yields promising results, demonstrating generalization potential.

Conclusion: OGR-MARL effectively enables heterogeneous USV cooperative pursuit under multiple constraints by decoupling rule guidance from MARL learning, with OGR-MASAC performing best and showing strong generalization to more complex port scenarios.

Abstract: Heterogeneous USV cooperative pursuit in constrained port waterways requires evader interception under navigation, traffic, and role constraints. This paper proposes OGR-MARL, an option-guided residual multi-agent reinforcement learning framework that is decoupled from a specific MARL algorithm. OGR-MARL integrates shared evader belief, role-conditioned option targets, adaptive rule penalties, and residual policy learning, allowing different MARL algorithms to learn corrective actions on top of rule-guided behaviors rather than exploring constrained port environments from scratch. We instantiate OGR-MARL with representative continuous-control MARL backbones, including MADDPG, MATD3, MAPPO, and MASAC, yielding OGR-MADDPG, OGR-MATD3, OGR-MAPPO, and OGR-MASAC. Experiments in an abstract Xiazhimen port-waterway scenario show that the OGR-MASAC instantiation achieves a 75.0% capture rate, promising mission-effective rule compliance, and the best heterogeneous coordination among the tested methods. Without retraining, zero-shot transfer to a QGIS/AIS-informed Xiazhimen map achieves promising results, demonstrating the generalization potential of OGR-MARL in more complex port scenarios.

</details>


### [96] [Dual-Flow Transformers: Decoupling the Primary Prefill Path from Additional Decode Computation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12385)
*Liming Liu,Mingze Wang,Tuo Zhao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes the Dual-Flow Transformer, which separates prefill (compute-bound) from decode (memory-bandwidth-bound) computation. It keeps a single primary causal flow that handles prompts and the KV cache, while an auxiliary flow activates only during continuation prediction, adding computation without extra persistent state. This lowers validation loss and, in MoE models, enables independent control over prefill vs. decode expert allocation, exposing a prefill-decode-quality trade-off.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLMs serve more requests, cumulative inference cost rivals training cost. Prefill and decode stress hardware differently (parallel/compute-bound vs. sequential/memory-bandwidth-bound), yet conventional width/depth scaling increases both costs together since every added layer runs in both phases. The authors want to allocate extra learned computation specifically to continuation prediction while preserving the prompt-wide primary computation and a single KV cache.

Method: Introduce the Dual-Flow Transformer with a primary flow (a complete causal LM that processes the prompt and writes the KV cache) and an auxiliary flow (skipped during prompt processing, activated from the final prompt position onward). The auxiliary flow adds continuation-prediction computation without writing persistent state or influencing the primary flow. The two flows share attention, MLP, and output matrices, but use separate token embeddings and lightweight coupling. For MoE models, primary and auxiliary expert fan-outs become independent controls. Two regimes are studied: increasing decode computation at fixed prefill expert computation, and reallocating a fixed decode expert budget between the flows.

Result: Across matched-token comparisons, Dual-Flow achieves lower validation loss across architectures and data configurations. MoE experiments expose a prefill-decode-quality trade-off and show the potential of phase-specific expert allocation, with independent control over prompt cost, continuation cost, and predictive quality.

Conclusion: Dual-Flow demonstrates that separating prefill and decode computation is effective — extra learned computation can be targeted at continuation prediction without additional KV cache or impacting the primary flow, yielding better validation loss and flexible phase-specific expert allocation in MoE models.

Abstract: As large language models serve more requests, cumulative inference cost is becoming increasingly important relative to one-time training cost. The two inference phases stress hardware differently: prompt prefill is parallel and typically compute-bound, whereas autoregressive decode is sequential and often memory-bandwidth-bound. Conventional width or depth scaling increases both costs together because every added layer is evaluated in both phases. We ask whether additional learned computation can instead be allocated to continuation prediction while preserving the prompt-wide primary computation and a single persistent key-value (KV) cache. We introduce the Dual-Flow Transformer. Its primary flow is a complete causal language model that processes the prompt and writes the KV cache. The auxiliary flow is omitted during prompt processing and activated only from the final prompt position onward, adding continuation-prediction computation without writing persistent state or influencing the primary flow. The two flows share major attention, MLP, and output matrices, while using separate token embeddings and lightweight coupling. Sharing weights and the primary cache also creates opportunities to reuse loaded weights and cached keys and values during grouped execution. Across matched-token comparisons, Dual-Flow achieves lower validation loss across architectures and data configurations. In MoE models, the separation makes primary and auxiliary expert fan-outs independent controls over prompt cost, continuation cost, and predictive quality. We study two regimes: increasing decode computation at fixed prefill expert computation, and reallocating a fixed decode expert budget between the two flows. These experiments expose a prefill-decode-quality trade-off and demonstrate the potential of phase-specific expert allocation.

</details>


### [97] [Learning to Adapt Cross-Domain Preferences via Meta-LoRA for LLM Personalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12389)
*Xuefei Wang,Jun Han,Zixuan Wang,Qingkai Zeng,Xiao Wang,Ruijie Wang,Jianxin Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes PAC-Bayes-regularized Meta-LoRA combined with functional decomposition of personalization priors to improve cross-domain zero-/few-shot personalization, reducing overfitting under sparse evidence and negative transfer from entangled user/domain preferences.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cross-domain zero- or few-shot personalization is hard because adaptation methods overfit under sparse target-domain evidence, and history-transfer methods entangle user preferences with source-domain artifacts, causing unreliable priors and negative transfer.

Method: The method has two components: (1) PAC-Bayes-regularized Meta-LoRA uses a meta-learned LoRA initialization that serves as both adaptation starting point and prior center, and adjusts update magnitude based on support-set size and predictive uncertainty to calibrate adaptation to evidence quality; (2) functional decomposition of personalization priors into user and domain components, using a human-readable prompt for stable preferences and topology-preserving soft tokens for domain-specific hidden-space conditioning.

Result: Experiments across multiple benchmarks and personalization tasks show consistent gains over strong baselines. On HiCUPID, the method reduces cross-domain win-rate degradation by 47.9% relative to the best competing baseline and improves win rate by 110.2% under unseen-user cold start.

Conclusion: Calibrating adaptation magnitude to evidence quality via PAC-Bayes regularization, combined with functionally separating user and domain priors, effectively mitigates overfitting and negative transfer, yielding substantial improvements in cross-domain personalization.

Abstract: Cross-domain zero- or few-shot personalization aims to generate user-preferred responses in unseen conversational domains from only a handful of target-domain interactions. Existing adaptation methods struggle to calibrate update magnitude under sparse evidence and thus overfit, whereas history-transfer methods often entangle user preferences with source-domain artifacts, yielding unreliable personalization priors and negative transfer. To calibrate adaptation to evidence quality, we propose PAC-Bayes-regularized Meta-LoRA, which uses a meta-learned LoRA initialization as both the adaptation start and prior center, while adjusting update strength according to support-set size and predictive uncertainty. This limits overfitting under sparse or ambiguous evidence while permitting stronger personalization as evidence grows. Controlled adaptation alone does not determine which preferences should transfer across domains or how they should be expressed. We therefore functionally decompose personalization priors into user and domain components, using a human-readable prompt for stable preferences and topology-preserving soft tokens for domain-specific hidden-space conditioning. Experiments across multiple benchmarks and personalization tasks show consistent gains over strong baselines. On HiCUPID, our method reduces cross-domain win-rate degradation by 47.9% relative to the best competing baseline and improves win rate by 110.2% under unseen-user cold start.

</details>


### [98] [Research Assistant: AstraZeneca's Agentic System for R&D](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12395)
*Piotr Grabowski,Mohamed Alameen,Jorge Bretones,Sabina Cardell,Miguel Carmona,Gavin Edwards,Ben Grainger,Sameh Hassan,Erik Jansson,Artur Kuziakhmetov,Albert Maristany,Hebatallah Mohamed,Andriy Nikolov,Sebastian Nilsson,Mark O'Donoghue,James Pacileo,Ashiq Sultan,Alex Voegele,Michael Ughetto*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AstraZeneca built "Research Assistant," an internal LLM-based chat system that lets scientists and clinicians query biomedical questions across literature, knowledge graphs, chemistry, clinical trials, safety data, expression data, and internal experiments, in either fast or multi-step modes, with answers grounded in and linked to source evidence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To help scientists and clinicians explore biomedical questions across many disparate data sources efficiently, and to support day-to-day R&D workflows at scale within AstraZeneca.

Method: A chat-style LLM interface integrating evidence from scientific literature, knowledge graphs, chemistry, clinical trials, safety resources, expression data, and internal experimental systems. It offers a fast mode for direct question answering and a multi-step mode for complex research tasks, with responses grounded in retrieved evidence and linked back to original sources.

Result: The system was deployed at scale to support daily R&D workflows across AstraZeneca; the paper is a technical note describing the architecture, design choices, and deployment lessons learned rather than reporting novel benchmarks.

Conclusion: An internal LLM-based assistant can be productively integrated into large pharma R&D workflows by combining retrieved evidence from multiple data sources, offering fast and multi-step answering modes, and grounding responses with traceable source links.

Abstract: We describe Research Assistant, an internal LLM-based system developed at AstraZeneca to help scientists and clinicians explore biomedical questions across a broad range of data sources. The system provides a chat-style interface that brings together evidence from scientific literature, knowledge graphs, chemistry, clinical trials, safety resources, expression data, and internal experimental systems. It supports both a fast mode for direct question answering and a multi-step mode for more complex research tasks. Responses are grounded in retrieved evidence and linked back to the original sources, allowing users to review and further explore the underlying data. In this technical note, we outline the system architecture, the main design choices behind the product, and lessons learned from deploying it at scale to support day-to-day R&D workflows across AstraZeneca.

</details>


### [99] [Large Language Models Can Follow Instructions, But Not Many at Once: Phase Transitions in Compositional Constraint Satisfaction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12426)
*Mariya I. Vasileva*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces Constraint Saturation Evaluation (CSE), a procedurally generated benchmark that systematically varies the number of simultaneous constraints (k) an LLM must satisfy, using deterministic rule-based verifiers across 15 models, 36 constraint types, and 369,753 checks. It finds per-constraint pass rate decays gradually but all-k success collapses multiplicatively, that structural constraints degrade ~2x faster than lexical ones due to a comprehension-maintenance gap, and that failures are nearly independent with residual coupling from shared output features. Reliable instruction following breaks down beyond 5-6 simultaneous constraints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly required to satisfy multiple explicit constraints simultaneously (reasoning structure, safety boundaries, output schemas), but the compositional regime—where many constraints must hold jointly—is poorly characterized. The authors aim to quantify how rapidly performance degrades with constraint count, what governs the degradation, and whether the collapse can be mitigated.

Method: They introduce Constraint Saturation Evaluation (CSE), a procedurally generated benchmark that systematically varies the number of simultaneous constraints k from 1 to 12. Each constraint is scored by a deterministic, rule-based verifier with zero LLM-judge involvement. The study covers 15 models, 36 constraint types, and 369,753 checks, enabling analysis of per-constraint decay, all-constraint joint success, constraint-type asymmetries, and failure independence.

Result: Three key findings: (1) per-constraint pass rate decays gradually and predictably, while the chance of satisfying all k constraints collapses—models passing individual constraints at ~41% at k=8 succeed on all eight only 5.7% of the time; (2) constraints degrade unequally, with structural constraints losing 2x more baseline capability per added constraint than lexical ones, explained by a comprehension-maintenance gap separating constraints requiring sustained tracking from binary decisions; (3) failures are nearly independent, making the accumulation multiplicative, while the residual coupling tracks shared output features rather than pairwise interference (e.g., a wrong sentence count fails every constraint that reads it). Overall, probe-level success falls below 50% at 7 constraints for the strongest model and at 3 or fewer for 12 of 15 models.

Conclusion: Reliable instruction following breaks down beyond roughly 5-6 simultaneous constraints, and the collapse is primarily multiplicative accumulation of near-independent failures driven by shared output features rather than direct constraint interference. The comprehension-maintenance gap indicates structural constraints are disproportionately fragile under composition.

Abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed in settings that require simultaneous adherence to multiple explicit constraints - reasoning structure, safety boundaries, output schemas. Individual constraints are handled proficiently, but the compositional regime, where many must hold jointly, remains poorly characterized: how rapidly does performance degrade, what governs the degradation, and can the collapse be mitigated? We introduce Constraint Saturation Evaluation (CSE), a procedurally generated benchmark that systematically varies the number of simultaneous constraints (k), with every constraint scored by a deterministic, rule-based verifier and zero LLM-judge involvement: 15 models, 36 constraint types, 369,753 checks at k=1-12. Three findings emerge. First, per-constraint pass rate decays gradually and predictably, while the chance of satisfying all k constraints collapses - a model passing individual constraints at ~41% at k=8 succeeds on all eight just 5.7% of the time. Second, constraints do not degrade equally: structural constraints lose 2x more baseline capability per added constraint than lexical ones, ordered by a comprehension-maintenance gap that separates constraints requiring sustained tracking from binary decisions immune to composition. Third, failures are nearly independent, which is what makes the accumulation multiplicative; the residual coupling that does exist tracks shared output features rather than pairwise interference - a wrong sentence count fails every constraint that reads it. Reliable instruction following breaks down beyond 5-6 simultaneous constraints: probe-level success falls below 50% at 7 constraints for the strongest model, and at 3 or fewer for 12 of 15.

</details>


### [100] [Governed Persistent Memory: Source-Bound State Semantics and Fail-Closed Release for Long-Horizon Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12476)
*Guodong Xu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces Governed Persistent Memory (GPM), an auditable bitemporal state-transition model for long-term agent memory that constrains which records may support released claims, and validates it through a frozen benchmark, a sealed service evaluation, finite-state model checking, and differential testing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard select--store--retrieve agent memory pipelines do not decide whether contradictory, superseded, retracted, deleted, or stale records may support an outgoing claim, creating a governance gap between stored data and released outputs.

Method: GPM uses source-bound admission, derived lifecycle state, current public barriers, and fail-closed structured release, formalized in five executable clauses covering ledger integrity, source binding, conflict isolation, non-revival after retraction/deletion, and exact claim closure over a fresh verified view. Evaluation spans a hash-frozen 3,600-case GPM-ReleaseBench, a sealed end-to-end service evaluation across eight query families, finite-state model exploration (331,776 semantic and 1,990,656 query states), and a 100,000-trace three-engine differential test.

Result: GPM matches all complete outcomes on GPM-ReleaseBench, while the strongest simple complete policy matches only 1,800/3,600 and makes unmatched releases on 50% of violation cases. In the sealed evaluation's public V3 arm, the governed lane is correct on 2,400/2,400 clusters versus 600/2,400 for ungoverned Qwen2.5-7B, repairing all 1,800 baseline failures with no regression (one-sided 95% lower bounds 99.875% and 99.834%). A V5 reseal with Chinese/English arms and generation-date pinning again obtains 2,400/2,400 per arm. Model checking found no full-contract counterexample, and differential testing yielded zero mismatches.

Conclusion: These are bounded contract and implementation results, not open-world model accuracy or evidence of world truth; the governed answers are deterministic service outputs, while the 7B result is only an ungoverned comparison, not a claim that a language model became perfectly accurate.

Abstract: Long-term agent memory is usually treated as select--store--retrieve, but retrieval does not decide whether contradictory, superseded, retracted, deleted, or stale records may support an outgoing claim. We introduce Governed Persistent Memory (GPM), an auditable bitemporal state-transition model with source-bound admission, derived lifecycle state, current public barriers, and fail-closed structured release. Five executable clauses cover ledger integrity, source binding, conflict isolation, non-revival after retraction or deletion, and exact claim closure over a fresh view at one verified head.
  On a prespecified hash-frozen 3,600-case GPM-ReleaseBench, GPM matches all complete outcomes; the strongest of three intentionally simple complete policies matches 1,800/3,600 and makes unmatched releases on 50% of violation cases. A separate sealed end-to-end service evaluation exercises real ingestion and release across eight query families. In its publicly disclosed V3 arm, the governed lane is correct on 2,400/2,400 clusters versus 600/2,400 for ungoverned local Qwen2.5-7B; it repairs all 1,800 baseline failures with no regression (one-sided 95% lower bounds 99.875% and 99.834%). A later V5 reseal over Chinese- and English-command arms, with generation-date pinning and no post-freeze reducer amendment, again obtains 2,400/2,400 per arm. A production-code-independent finite model explores 331,776 semantic and 1,990,656 query states without a full-contract counterexample, and a 100,000-trace three-engine differential yields zero mismatches.
  These are bounded contract and implementation results, not open-world model accuracy or evidence of world truth. Governed answers in the sealed service evaluation are deterministic service outputs; the 7B result is the ungoverned comparison, not a claim that a language model itself became perfectly accurate.

</details>


### [101] [$\varepsilon$-MemEvo: Adaptive Cross-Task Memory Transfer for LLM Program Evolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12522)
*Aofan Liu,Shiyuan Song,Yiyan Qi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ε-MemEvo is a framework enabling cross-task knowledge transfer in LLM program evolution by storing prior search experience as task-agnostic tactic memories (natural-language strategy summaries) with an adaptive injection gate to prevent negative transfer, achieving +8.7% mean AUCC gain over AdaEvolve across 8 benchmarks at <1% overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based program evolution systems (FunSearch, AlphaEvolve) optimize each task in isolation and discard search experience after completion, wasting reusable algorithmic knowledge. The goal is to transfer prior successful strategies across tasks with different APIs and evaluators while avoiding negative transfer from mismatched memories.

Method: ε-MemEvo stores past experience as compact, task-agnostic natural-language tactic summaries (not raw code) so they transfer across differing APIs/evaluators. An adaptive injection gate decides whether and how intensely to inject retrieved memories, preventing negative transfer from semantically mismatched content. Evaluation uses an 8-benchmark suite (mathematical optimization + systems engineering) under a content-level Leave-One-Out protocol excluding target-task memory entries, compared against AdaEvolve on a primary GPT-5 backbone.

Result: On the primary GPT-5 backbone, ε-MemEvo improves AUCC over AdaEvolve on all 8 tasks (mean relative gain +8.7%) and improves early-stage convergence by +9.4% on average. Ablations show naive memory injection can fail catastrophically, while adaptive gating remains safe across all five ablation tasks. The data-updated posterior is interpretable: it favors skip during improving search and shifts from skip to hint across early and late plateaus. Overhead is under 1%.

Conclusion: ε-MemEvo demonstrates effective, safe cross-task knowledge transfer in LLM program evolution via task-agnostic tactic memories and adaptive gating, yielding consistent gains with negligible computational cost.

Abstract: LLM-based program evolution systems such as FunSearch and AlphaEvolve have shown strong ability to discover novel algorithms, but typically optimize each task in isolation, discarding search experience after completion. We introduce $\varepsilon$-MemEvo, a framework for cross-task knowledge transfer in LLM program evolution. $\varepsilon$-MemEvo stores prior experience as task-agnostic tactic memories: compact natural-language summaries of successful algorithmic strategies rather than raw code, enabling transfer across tasks with different APIs and evaluators. To avoid negative transfer from semantically mismatched memories, $\varepsilon$-MemEvo uses an adaptive injection gate that decides whether retrieved memories should be injected, and at what intensity. We evaluate $\varepsilon$-MemEvo on 8 diverse optimization benchmarks spanning mathematical optimization and systems engineering, using a content-level Leave-One-Out protocol that excludes target-task memory entries. On the primary GPT-5 backbone, $\varepsilon$-MemEvo improves AUCC over AdaEvolve on all 8 tasks, with a mean relative gain of +8.7%, and improves early-stage convergence by +9.4% on average. Ablations show that naive memory injection can fail catastrophically, while adaptive gating remains safe across all five ablation tasks. The data-updated posterior is interpretable in observed states: it favors skip during improving search and shifts from skip to hint across early and late plateaus. These gains incur less than 1% computational overhead.

</details>


### [102] [CAS: A Causal Attribution Score for Local and Global Explainable Artificial Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12555)
*Michael Georgiades,Charalambia Varnava*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces the Causal Attribution Score (CAS), an architecture that attributes intervention effects rather than model outputs, using causal Shapley contributions on an identified interventional coalition game, and adds a local-to-global causal reporting layer. Benchmarks show CAS outperforms one-at-a-time and global normalisation methods, especially under interactions, and differs materially from predictive SHAP rankings in real causal datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing predictive explanation methods (e.g., SHAP) attribute a model's output, not the effect of an intervention on a real-world outcome. There is a need to separate "what predicts the outcome" from "what explains heterogeneity in an estimated causal effect," and to provide explanations anchored to an explicit intervention target.

Method: CAS starts from an identified interventional coalition game, allocates the joint intervention contrast using causal Shapley contributions, and converts raw outcome-scale effects into Local CAS, Signed Local CAS, and two complementary Global CAS summaries. The key innovation is a local-to-global causal reporting layer with an explicit intervention target, rather than a new Shapley formula.

Result: In a known-truth benchmark (8 repeated primary-interaction simulations, n=2,200 each, three actions), coalition-aware CAS achieved mean Local CAS MAE of 0.107, versus 0.173 for one-at-a-time normalisation and 0.213 for a global normalised absolute ATE vector. The paired advantage over one-at-a-time normalisation grew from -0.003 under additivity to 0.091 under strong interactions. On DoubleML datasets (401(k): n=9,915; Pennsylvania reemployment: n=5,099), predictive SHAP/TreeSHAP rankings differed materially from Feature-CAS rankings of treatment-effect modifiers. In Pennsylvania, dep1 moved from predictive global rank 13 to Feature-CAS rank 2 and was the leading local Feature-CAS modifier.

Conclusion: The results isolate the added value of separating what predicts the outcome from what explains heterogeneity in an estimated causal effect. CAS provides a more accurate and causally grounded attribution of intervention effects, outperforming normalisation-based baselines, particularly in the presence of strong interactions.

Abstract: Predictive explanation methods attribute a model output; they do not, by themselves, attribute an intervention effect on the real-world outcome. We introduce the Causal Attribution Score (CAS), a compact score architecture for causal explanation. CAS starts from an identified interventional coalition game, allocates the joint intervention contrast with causal Shapley contributions, and converts those raw outcome-scale effects into Local CAS, Signed Local CAS, and two complementary Global CAS summaries. The innovation is not a new Shapley formula, but a local-to-global causal reporting layer with an explicit intervention target. In the known-truth benchmark, eight repeated primary-interaction simulations (n = 2,200 each, three actions) gave mean Local CAS MAE of 0.107 for coalition-aware CAS, compared with 0.173 for one-at-a-time normalisation and 0.213 for a global normalised absolute ATE vector. The paired advantage over one-at-a-time normalisation increased from -0.003 under additivity to 0.091 under strong interactions. On both empirical DoubleML datasets, 401(k) eligibility/net financial assets (n = 9,915) and Pennsylvania reemployment bonus/unemployment duration (n = 5,099), predictive SHAP/TreeSHAP rankings differed materially from Feature-CAS rankings of treatment-effect modifiers. In Pennsylvania, dep1 (exactly one dependent) moved from predictive global rank 13 to Feature-CAS rank 2 and was the leading local Feature-CAS modifier. These results isolate the added value of separating what predicts the outcome from what explains heterogeneity in an estimated causal effect.

</details>


### [103] [Trie Automata for Constrained Decoding over Large Finite Sets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12574)
*Xingzi Xu,Karim Bouyarmane*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces a trie automaton using Aho-Corasick multi-pattern matching to precompute per-node token masks for schema-constrained decoding, dramatically speeding up valid-token computation and compilation while guaranteeing 100% output validity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs increasingly must generate structured outputs constrained to a finite set of valid strings. Existing constrained decoding systems use general-purpose grammar compilation, which becomes prohibitively slow as the number of valid values grows into the thousands — a "cardinality wall" in per-step computation and compilation latency.

Method: A specialized trie automaton exploits finite-set structure (shared prefixes, bounded depth, known cardinality) via Aho-Corasick multi-pattern matching to precompute per-node token masks. Precomputed masks enable a stateless serving path that bypasses the guided decoding pipeline.

Result: Achieves 7X faster per-step valid-token computation (0.65 us vs. 5.8 us) versus XGrammar, and 2–6.5X faster compilation at K >= 300. End-to-end vLLM throughput reaches 219 req/s vs. XGrammar's 7.5 req/s at batch size 256 (29X). Maintains sub-100ms compilation up to K = 10,000 and flat per-step cost regardless of set size across seven tokenizer families (32K–262K vocabulary), with 100% output validity.

Conclusion: The trie automaton overcomes the cardinality wall by combining an algorithmic speedup with integration-path savings only precomputed masks can unlock, delivering large speedups over grammar-based backends while guaranteeing fully valid structured outputs.

Abstract: Large language models increasingly need to generate structured outputs that conform to predefined schemas, with one common constraint being selection from a finite set of valid strings. Current constrained decoding systems handle this through general-purpose grammar compilation, which becomes prohibitively slow as the number of valid values grows into the thousands, a cardinality wall. We introduce the trie automaton, a specialized mechanism that exploits finite-set structure (shared prefixes, bounded depth, known cardinality) via Aho-Corasick multi-pattern matching to precompute per-node token masks. The trie achieves 7X faster per-step valid-token computation (0.65 us vs. 5.8 us) compared to XGrammar, one of the primary backends in vLLM and SGLang, and 2--6.5X faster compilation at K >= 300. Because precomputed masks enable a stateless serving path that bypasses the guided decoding pipeline, this advantage compounds in batch serving: end-to-end vLLM throughput reaches 219 req/s vs. XGrammar's 7.5 req/s at batch size 256 (29X). The 29X combines the algorithmic speedup with integration-path savings that only precomputed masks can unlock. Across seven tokenizer families (32K--262K vocabulary), the trie maintains sub-100ms compilation up to K = 10,000 and flat per-step cost regardless of set size, while guaranteeing 100% output validity.

</details>


### [104] [QuoteBench: How Matched Scores Can Hide Command-Path Failures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13547)
*Shangao Li,Yao Zhang,Volker Tresp,Yuanyuan Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: QuoteBench measures where LLM Bash-command failures originate by validating exact final state across 56 one-shot tasks from 14 incident-derived families, revealing that serialization/parsing boundaries—not raw command generation—cause most mismatched failures, and that models compensate for parser damage when boundaries are disclosed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Matched execution scores cannot distinguish whether a failure comes from flawed command generation by the model or from errors introduced after generation (serialization, wrapping, reparsing of output). The paper aims to isolate and quantify this boundary between generation and execution transport.

Method: Constructs QuoteBench with 56 one-shot tasks across 14 incident-derived task families. It crosses the generation contract with the execution transport around one deliberately unescaped added parser (an interpolation point). Each replayed reply is run through the added parser, and exact final-state validation measures outcomes. Eight same-window configurations are tested, comparing raw-path outcomes against parser-injected outcomes, with and without boundary disclosure.

Result: Replaying identical replies through the added parser lowers success by 55.4–73.2 percentage points across eight configurations. Disclosing the boundary recovers 30.4–60.7 points for six configurations, but zero or slightly negative for two. Raw generation is nearly saturated at the frontier, so boundary adaptation separates models. GPT-5.6-sol's matched gap of -3.6 points masks -64.3 points of damage offset by +60.7 points of compensation. The deployment configuration reorders models: one unambiguous reversal among 26 comparable pairs and four more on single-task margins.

Conclusion: Evaluations of command-issuing agents must report the model configuration, generation contract, execution path, operating point, and final-state validator, rather than treating a matched score as an intrinsic model property, because parsing/serialization boundaries dominate failure and disclosure-driven compensation.

Abstract: LLM coding agents issue Bash commands through interfaces that may serialize, wrap, and reparse model output. Matched execution scores alone cannot distinguish command-generation errors from failures introduced after generation. QuoteBench measures this boundary with exact final-state validation on 56 one-shot tasks from 14 incident-derived families, crossing the generation contract with the execution transport around one deliberately unescaped added parser. Escaping at the interpolation point reproduces each replayed reply's raw-path outcome, so any recovery under a disclosed boundary must come from the model changing its generation. Across eight same-window configurations, replaying the same reply through the added parser lowers success by 55.4 to 73.2 percentage points; disclosure recovers 30.4 to 60.7 points for six configurations, and zero or slightly negative for the other two. Raw generation is nearly saturated at the frontier; boundary adaptation is what still separates models. GPT-5.6-sol's matched gap of -3.6 points hides -64.3 points of damage and +60.7 points of compensation. The deployment configuration reorders models: one reversal among 26 comparable pairs is unambiguous and four more sit on single-task margins. Evaluations of command-issuing agents should report the model configuration, generation contract, execution path, operating point, and final-state validator rather than treat a matched score as an intrinsic model property.

</details>


### [105] [Reasoning Jury: Multi-Model Consensus for Evaluating Reasoning Traces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12585)
*Congchao Wang,Diwakar Singh,Qiaozi Gao,Spyros Matsoukas,Yang Liu,Mahdi Namazifar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Reasoning Jury replaces a single LLM judge with a jury of open-weight models plus a moderated consensus/deliberation mechanism, significantly outperforming frontier models at identifying reasoning defects at only 8–15% of the cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Judging the quality of long reasoning traces is essential for reasoning data curation, RL training signals, performance evaluation, and runtime feedback. However, single-model judges (even frontier models) struggle with this complex task, and using frontier models during online training is often prohibited by usage guardrails.

Method: Introduces Reasoning Jury: a jury of LLMs (open-weight models such as gpt-oss-120b) with a moderated consensus mechanism. A moderator facilitates deliberation among jurors, who critique each other's judgments and may revise their initial votes; the moderator then derives a consensus via deliberation or consolidation of judgments, surfacing both reasoning defects and their severity.

Result: Reasoning Jury with open-weight models significantly outperforms frontier models (opus-4.6, sonnet-4.6, gemini-3.1-pro) at correctly identifying reasoning defects, while its aggregated cost (initial verdicts, deliberations, consolidation) is only 8–15% of the cost of frontier LLM-as-a-judge setups. The judgments also enable deeper understanding of failure modes of reasoning LLMs on benchmarks.

Conclusion: A jury-of-open-weight-models approach with moderated deliberation is both more accurate and cheaper than single frontier-model judging, providing high-fidelity reasoning-defect identification useful for training signals, data curation, evaluation, and runtime feedback.

Abstract: Improving reasoning LLMs requires the ability to judge the quality of long reasoning traces for effective reasoning data curation, strong training signals during reinforcement learning, and an in-depth understanding of reasoning behaviors during model performance evaluation. Additionally, surfacing reasoning mistakes that the model makes would enable improving the model's performance at runtime through providing feedback. Due to the difficulty of this complex task on long reasoning traces, single-model judges (even frontier models) do not do well at identifying reasoning defects. Additionally, leveraging frontier models during online training of reasoning LLMs is generally prohibited due to guardrails in terms of use. In this work, we introduce Reasoning Jury, a system that replaces the single judge with a jury of LLMs and a moderated consensus mechanism, to improve the fidelity of judgments for identifying reasoning defects. In reasoning jury, defects of a reasoning trace and their severity are surfaced through a deliberation where a moderator conducts a discussion amongst the jury where the jurors critique each other's judgments and get to modify their initial votes. The moderator derives a consensus through deliberation amongst jurors or consolidation of judgements. We show that Reasoning Jury with a jury of open-weight models (e.g., gpt-oss-120b) is able to significantly outperform frontier models (opus-4.6, sonnet-4.6, and gemini-3.1-pro) at correctly identifying reasoning defects. Besides accuracy performance improvements, the aggregated cost of the jury (initial verdicts, deliberations, consolidation, etc.) is a fraction (8 to 15%) of the cost of running frontier models in LLM-as-a-judge setup. We also show how these judgements can be leveraged to understand failure modes of reasoning LLMs on benchmarks, which allows much deeper understanding of a model's performance.

</details>


### [106] [Auditable agentic AI for evidence-grounded thyroid ultrasound diagnosis and reporting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12590)
*Haifan Gong,Shiyu Chen,Bodong Wang,Yuqi Wang,Shijie Wang,Guoliang You,Xinyu Xiong,Haowei Wang,Mingzhi Mao,Dexing Kong,Qinghua Liu,Wei Lou,Fei Chen,Guanbin Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ThyroidXAgent is a clinician-interactive agentic AI system that coordinates multiple thyroid ultrasound diagnostic tools (segmentation, classification, metastasis prediction, reporting) into an auditable evidence record, developed on ~0.3M images/24K reports and validated across 28,458 cases, improving physician accuracy, report consistency, and workflow efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Thyroid ultrasound diagnosis requires coordinated lesion localization, measurement, risk stratification, and reporting, yet most AI systems tackle these tasks in isolation and offer limited support for clinical review. The authors aim to build an integrated, auditable, clinician-correctable system that coordinates specialized tools rather than leaving them siloed.

Method: Developed ThyroidXAgent, a clinician-interactive agentic AI system that coordinates specialized diagnostic tools and stores outputs as an auditable case-level evidence record. It was built using OpenThyroidDB (multicentre, multitask, ~0.3M ultrasound images and 24,000 paired reports) and evaluated on 28,458 non-overlapping test cases (including 8,721 cases from 35 centres in the private NHC-MISD-TUS cohort). The system performs nodule segmentation, benign-malignant classification, lymph-node metastasis prediction, follicular vs papillary carcinoma classification, and evidence-grounded report generation. A lesion-level clinical semantic metric, ThyClinScore, was introduced and correlated with a location-aware language-model judge.

Result: Mean Dice of 87.21% for nodule segmentation and mean AUROC of 0.9466 for benign-malignant classification. Lymph-node metastasis prediction AUROC 0.864; follicular vs papillary classification AUROC 0.805. Evidence-grounded report generation outperformed multimodal language-model baselines across three cohorts; ThyClinScore showed the strongest correlation with the location-aware judge. Clinically, ThyroidXAgent improved physician classification accuracy, raised report diagnostic consistency from 70.3% to 86.2%, and reduced segmentation and reporting time by 35.9% and 27.4%, respectively.

Conclusion: The results support auditable, clinician-correctable agentic AI for thyroid ultrasound diagnosis and reporting, demonstrating that coordinating specialized tools into an evidence-grounded workflow improves diagnostic performance, consistency, and efficiency while remaining reviewable by clinicians.

Abstract: Thyroid ultrasound diagnosis requires coordinated lesion localization, measurement, risk stratification and reporting, yet most AI systems address these tasks in isolation and provide limited support for clinical review. We present ThyroidXAgent, a clinician-interactive agentic AI system that coordinates specialized diagnostic tools and stores their outputs as an auditable case-level evidence record. The system was developed using OpenThyroidDB, a multicentre, multitask resource integrating approximately 0.3 million ultrasound images and 24,000 paired reports, and was evaluated on 28,458 non-overlapping test cases, including 8,721 cases from 35 centres in the private NHC-MISD-TUS cohort. Across heterogeneous datasets, ThyroidXAgent achieved a mean Dice score of 87.21 percent for nodule segmentation and a mean AUROC of 0.9466 for benign-malignant classification. The same workflow supported lymph-node metastasis prediction and follicular versus papillary thyroid carcinoma classification, with AUROCs of 0.864 and 0.805, respectively. For report generation, evidence-grounded assembly outperformed multimodal language-model baselines across three cohorts. ThyClinScore, a lesion-level clinical semantic metric introduced here, showed the strongest correlation with a location-aware language-model judge. ThyroidXAgent improved physician classification accuracy, increased report diagnostic consistency from 70.3 percent to 86.2 percent, and reduced segmentation and reporting time by 35.9 percent and 27.4 percent, respectively. These findings support auditable, clinician-correctable agentic AI for thyroid ultrasound diagnosis and reporting.

</details>


### [107] [DiG-bench: Discovery in Games](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12593)
*Ruairidh M. Battleday,Kai Sandbrink,Jimi Cullen-Drohan,Zihan Yan,Timothy Muller,Clare Maguire,Ales Kubicek,Fraser Greenlee-Scott,Sukrit Sumant,Tri Dao,Jürgen Schmidhuber,Michal Valko,Joshua Tenenbaum,Thomas L. Griffiths,Zeb Kurth-Nelson,James C. R. Whittington*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DiG-bench is a new benchmark of 70 games designed to test an AI agent's ability to discover novel rules and solve challenges through interaction, where objectives and win conditions are unknown. Games span seven difficulty tiers, with 21 released publicly and the rest held out for secure evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is a gap in current AI benchmarks: few directly probe the capacity for discovering new knowledge through experimentation in controlled environments where the objective is unknown. The authors aim to address this by providing a benchmark focused on discovery, a central part of the scientific process.

Method: The benchmark consists of 70 independent games, each encoded as a short string with unique transformation rules that must be discovered through interaction and experimentation. Each game presents a series of levels (challenges) that test whether the rules have been discovered, with even the win conditions left unknown. Games are organized into seven tiers of difficulty for AI agents. A subset of 21 games is publicly released, while the remaining 49 are held private for secure evaluation.

Result: The lowest difficulty tier is routinely solvable by multiple models, whereas the highest tier challenges the best models in agentic harnesses. All 70 games were solved by at least one human on first attempt, establishing a human baseline of success across the full benchmark.

Conclusion: DiG-bench fills a notable gap in AI evaluation by providing a controlled, experimentation-based benchmark for assessing agents' ability to discover novel rules and achieve unknown objectives, with difficulty tiers that differentiate model capabilities and private held-out games enabling secure, reliable evaluation.

Abstract: Discovery---formulating novel generalizations---is a central part of the scientific process. Despite its importance, there is a gap in the current AI benchmark landscape, with few benchmarks directly probing the capacity for discovering new knowledge with experimentation in controlled environments where the objective is unknown. To address this gap, we release a new benchmark: DiG-bench (Discovery in Games). DiG-bench consists of a set of 70 independent games. Each game is encoded as a short string and has unique transformation rules that must be discovered through interaction and experimentation. The levels of the game present a series of challenges to test whether the rules have been discovered, where the win conditions for each level are also unknown. We provide games at seven tiers of difficulty for AI agents. The lowest tier is routinely solvable by multiple models, while the highest tier challenges the best models in agentic harnesses. All 70 games were solved by at least one human on first attempt. A subset of 21 games is released publicly, and the remainder is held private for secure evaluation.

</details>


### [108] [Dead text or binding clause? Measuring and restoring constraint influence in black-box LLM dialogues](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12599)
*Haoyuan Zhu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces a system that measures, predicts, and repairs "behavioral relapse" (revocation inertia) in multi-turn dialogue models, where withdrawn constraints continue to influence outputs. It uses a contract ledger with executable checkers and tombstones, a sequential ablation probe for per-clause adherence measurement, and a repair ladder under matched budgets. Results show ahead-of-time compilation significantly reduces relapse, the probe predicts relapse reliably (AUROC high), and a one-sentence tombstone note partially recovers the compilation effect.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-turn dialogues allow users to revoke constraints as easily as impose them, but models often keep enacting withdrawn requirements—sometimes even beneath comments claiming their removal. This "behavioral relapse" (revocation inertia) is a real failure mode, yet no existing instrument measures its per-clause influence, predicts it before delivery, or repairs it under matched budgets. The authors aim to close these three gaps so that revocation failure becomes measurable, predictable, and repairable rather than invisible.

Method: The system (sysname) uses only the model API. (1) A contract ledger pairs every constraint with an executable checker, records revocations as tombstones, and compiles the net constraint state ahead of time into a single specification. (2) A sequential ablation probe measures per-clause adherence and incremental behavioral effect. (3) A repair ladder operates under token- and attempt-matched budgets, including adaptive ladder interventions stacked on top and a one-sentence tombstone note (with a placebo control). Evaluation is conducted on dataname (NTasks HumanEval tasks, NClauses verified checkers) against a no-ledger verifier-retry baseline, with a stronger-model comparison at an 8B operating point.

Result: Relapse at an 8B operating point climbs from ScaleDelayedMTwo to ScaleDelayedMEight as constraint load grows, while stronger models sit at floor. Under matched checkers, model, and budget, ahead-of-time compilation significantly reduces relapse versus the no-ledger verifier-retry baseline (RestoreDiff, 95% CI RestoreDiffCI, p RestoreDiffP); adaptive ladder interventions add no detectable gain (95% confidence excludes gains ≥ LadderExcludedGain). The probe predicts relapse before delivery with AUROC AurocPrimary. A one-sentence tombstone note recovers about one third of the compilation effect and survives a placebo control. Costs are CostDeliveryFactor delivery overhead and CostTotalHedged of API compute per result.

Conclusion: Revocation failure (behavioral relapse) can be transformed from an invisible property of dialogue state into one that is measurable, predictable, and repairable—using only the model API. Ahead-of-time compilation of the net constraint state is the primary effective intervention, while adaptive ladder repairs add no detectable benefit under matched budgets, and a lightweight tombstone note offers partial, placebo-surviving recovery at modest cost.

Abstract: Multi-turn dialogues let users revoke constraints as easily as impose them, but revocation does not reliably take effect: models keep enacting withdrawn requirements (occasionally beneath comments asserting their removal), a failure we call \emph{behavioral relapse}, or revocation inertia. No existing instrument measures this influence per clause, predicts it before delivery, or repairs it under matched budgets. \sysname{} closes the three gaps through the model API alone: a contract ledger pairs every constraint with an executable checker, records revocations as tombstones, and compiles the net constraint state ahead of time into a single specification; a sequential ablation probe measures per-clause adherence and incremental behavioral effect; a repair ladder operates under token- and attempt-matched budgets. On \dataname{} (\NTasks{} HumanEval tasks, \NClauses{} verified checkers), relapse at an 8B operating point climbs from \ScaleDelayedMTwo{} to \ScaleDelayedMEight{} as constraint load grows, while stronger models sit at floor. Under matched checkers, model, and budget, ahead-of-time compilation significantly reduces relapse against a no-ledger verifier-retry baseline (\RestoreDiff{}, 95\% CI \RestoreDiffCI{}, $p$ \RestoreDiffP{}); adaptive ladder interventions stacked on top add no detectable gain (95\% confidence excludes gains $\geq$ \LadderExcludedGain{}). The probe predicts relapse before delivery (AUROC \AurocPrimary{}); a one-sentence tombstone note recovers about a third of the compilation effect and survives a placebo control. At \CostDeliveryFactor{} delivery overhead and \CostTotalHedged{} of API compute for every result, revocation failure becomes a measurable, predictable, and repairable property of dialogue state rather than an invisible one.

</details>


### [109] [@skills: Attention is all you have](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12610)
*Li Yin,Zhi Li,Zhan Shi,Haoran Zhang,Haebin Seong,Zhangyang,Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: @skills is an open protocol that decouples skill installation into three separable functions—content, persistence, and triggering—so agents can use skills via paths without prompt residency, with an optional hub for discovery and authoring.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The current delivery model (installation) bundles content, persistence, and automatic triggering together, forcing every installed skill's description to occupy scarce prompt trigger slots (<100 reliable). This leaves the long tail of skills unusable and makes teams' own playbooks compete for the same limited space.

Method: @skills separates the three bundled functions. Paths address any skill, subtree, or collection; reading a skill suffices to use it (no installation/residency). The 'vendor' operation copies a skill at the same path into a Git-tracked tree for adaptation and ownership. The 'add' operation contributes one .gitignore-style line, the sole element costing prompt residency. Directories act as menus so bundles are ordinary directories. No manifest, lockfile, or registration; SKILL.md unchanged. Ships as an installable package with a single instruction file to turn any file/command-capable agent into a client. Paired with an optional hub (atskills.one) for search, ranking, repository-free hosting, collections, and authoring; gh: and local paths work without the hub.

Result: A protocol that removes the need for prompt residency for skill content and persistence, reserving prompt slots only for explicit trigger lines, while making bundles plain directories and enabling any agent to act as a client. Companion implementations: the AdaL CLI and the atskills.one hub.

Conclusion: By separating content, persistence, and triggering, @skills lets the long tail of skills be used without competing for scarce prompt slots, summarized in the motto "Install less, use more."

Abstract: There are 56,804 public agent skills today, and teams write many more privately. The dominant delivery model is installation: once installed, a skill's description remains in the system prompt, competing for fewer than 100 reliable trigger slots. This leaves the long tail with no practical path to use and forces teams' own playbooks to compete for the same scarce space. We observe that installation bundles three separable functions: content, persistence, and automatic triggering. Only the last requires prompt residency. We therefore propose @skills, an open protocol that separates them. A path addresses any skill, subtree, or collection, and reading a skill is sufficient to use it, so nothing is installed or made resident. The operation vendors a copy at the same path into a project's Git-tracked tree for adaptation and ownership. The operation adds one .gitignore-style line, the only element that costs prompt residency. A directory is a menu, making bundles ordinary directories rather than all-or-nothing units. The protocol requires no manifest, lockfile, or registration, and SKILL.md remains unchanged. @skills is additive, ships as an installable package, and turns any agent that can read files and run commands into a client through a single instruction file. Its open specification is at https://github.com/SylphAI-Inc/atskills and it is implemented in the AdaL CLI at https://adalagent.ai . Because paths address skills well but cannot find them, the protocol is paired with a free hub at https://atskills.one for corpus-wide search and ranking, repository-free hosting, private and team collections, and one-screen authoring. The hub is optional: gh: and local paths resolve without it, and indexed GitHub skills retain their gh: identities. Install less, use more.

</details>


### [110] [Jagged Judges: Epistemic Stability Under Silence, Pressure, and Persistence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12645)
*Justin Zhao,Himaghna Bhattacharjee,Hannah Korevaar,Bhaktipriya Radharapu,Khalid El-Arini*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces the Wiggle Framework, a stress test for LLM judges' epistemic stability, showing that frontier judges flip verdicts 25–71% under static pushback and 62–91% under adversarial persuasion, with most flips being net-corrupting relative to ground truth.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM judge validation relies on accuracy over golden data, which does not reveal whether judges are stable under re-prompting, challenge, or pushback. There is a need for a unified framework to measure epistemic stability beyond accuracy.

Method: Proposes the Wiggle Framework, decomposing judge robustness into three dimensions: Mechanical Consistency (stability under re-prompting/reframing), Single-turn Conviction (stability under a single challenge), and Multi-turn Persistence (stability under sustained/adaptive pressure). Applied to 9 frontier models across 14 judging tasks covering safety, toxicity, AI-writing detection, and political-response evaluation.

Result: Every model shows substantial wiggle: verdicts flip 25–71% under static pushback and 62–91% with an adversarial LLM persuader. Pressure that changes a judge's verdict is almost always net-corrupting with respect to ground truth. Baseline jury majority strength is the most effective single-shot signal for predicting which items wiggle.

Conclusion: Epistemic instability is pervasive across frontier LLM judges, and accuracy-based validation is insufficient. The framework enables the first apples-to-apples cross-dataset comparison of mechanical, conformity, and persuadability tests, with jury majority strength as a practical predictor of instability.

Abstract: LLM judges have become central infrastructure for model evaluations, online grading, and reward modeling. Judges are typically validated by accuracy on golden data, but accuracy says little about whether they are stable under re-prompting, challenge, or sustained pushback. We introduce the \emph{Wiggle Framework}, a unified stress test for epistemic stability in LLM judges. The framework decomposes judge robustness along three dimensions: Mechanical Consistency (stability under re-prompting and reframing), Single-turn Conviction (stability under a single challenge), and Multi-turn Persistence (stability under sustained or adaptive pressure). We use the framework to study 9 frontier models across 14 judging tasks spanning safety, toxicity, AI writing detection, and political-response evaluation. Every model exhibits substantial wiggle as a judge --- flipping verdicts 25--71\% of the time under static pushback, and 62--91\% with an adversarial LLM persuader. Critically, we find that pressure that succeeds in changing a judge's verdict is almost always net-corrupting with respect to ground truth. Beyond the framework itself, we identify baseline jury majority strength as the most effective single-shot signal for anticipating which items wiggle. Taken together, this is the first apples-to-apples cross-dataset comparison of mechanical, conformity, and persuadability tests in a judging context.

</details>


### [111] [Privacy-Preserving RAG by Concealing Sensitive Information from External LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12675)
*Saleh Almohaimeed,Saad Almohaimeed,Mousa Jari,Fahad Alotaibi,Khalid A. Alobaid*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes SEAG, a privacy-preserving RAG framework that replaces sensitive entities with aliases in both queries and retrieved documents before sending them to an external generator, and evaluates it on two newly constructed datasets, achieving over 80% response accuracy and ~75–78% entity-hiding accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RAG privacy research focuses on preventing unauthorized user access to sensitive data, but overlooks that external generators see the raw query and retrieved documents, which may expose confidential information. The authors aim to let users benefit from third-party generators without leaking sensitive content.

Method: SEAG uses a lightweight model that locates sensitive entities, generates corresponding aliases, and builds an entity replacement table. This table is then used to replace sensitive words in the user's query and retrieved documents before forwarding them to the external generator. Two datasets were created: one for fine-tuning SEAG models to produce entity replacement tables, and another for end-to-end framework evaluation.

Result: All SEAG models achieved over 80% accuracy on the User metric (correct response while hiding sensitive information). In additional analysis, Qwen-3, LLaMA-3.2, and Phi-4 successfully hid all sensitive entities with total accuracies of 77.83%, 76.73%, and 74.91%, respectively.

Conclusion: The SEAG framework successfully enables privacy-preserving use of third-party generators by preventing the disclosure of sensitive entities, validated through strong experimental results and a dedicated evaluation methodology.

Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is widely used to improve the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) in answering user queries. Existing privacy research on RAG has focused on preventing unauthorized users from accessing sensitive data. However, another important problem that is often overlooked in RAG privacy research is that external generators have access to the query and the retrieved documents, which may contain confidential information that could potentially be misused or accessed for unintended purposes. In this paper, we introduce the Sensitive Entity Alias Generator (SEAG), a privacy-preserving framework that empowers users to utilize powerful third-party generators without disclosing sensitive information. SEAG introduces a lightweight model that locates sensitive entities, generates corresponding aliases, and constructs an entity replacement table. The table is used to replace sensitive words in the user's query and in the retrieved documents before they are forwarded to an external generator. For this purpose, two datasets were constructed: one for fine-tuning SEAG models to generate entity replacement tables, and another for evaluating the entire SEAG framework. The experimental results demonstrate the success of the SEAG framework. As for the User metric, which measures the ability of the model to provide a correct response to the user while hiding sensitive information from the external generator, all SEAG models achieved over 80% accuracy. Additional analysis further evaluated the ability of SEAG models Qwen-3, LLaMA-3.2, and Phi-4 to hide all sensitive entities within given documents. The results show good performance with total accuracies of 77.83%, 76.73%, and 74.91%, respectively.

</details>


### [112] [SteerBench-Work: A Benchmark for Agent Steering at Action Boundaries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12654)
*Oguz Serdar,Cuneyt Mertayak*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SteerBench-Work is an incident-anchored benchmark measuring whether LLM workplace agents correctly decide to proceed or hold at high-stakes tool-use boundaries. Across 30 model conditions, models mostly err by over-refusing (28.1%) rather than wrongly allowing unsafe actions (1.0%), and higher capability does not guarantee better steering calibration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents performing real-world actions (emailing, merging PRs, wiring payments) must make pre-commit gate decisions: proceed or hold for review. Prior evaluation lacks a balanced, incident-grounded measure of this steering decision, especially the asymmetry between false-allow and false-hold errors.

Method: Introduce SteerBench-Work, a bidirectional benchmark across seven domains (devops, customer service, finance, legal, medical, HR, security). Release v2026-05 has 106 scenarios anchored in public incidents, with paired evidence-reversed mirrors, calibration controls, and near-even proceed/hold label splits. Models view the proposed action and evidence, return a gate decision, and are scored by whether they cross or hold the boundary correctly.

Result: Failures are highly asymmetric: models wrongly hold authorized, evidence-cleared work on 28.1% of opportunities vs. wrongly allowing unsafe work on only 1.0%. Hardest cases are risk-resolved commits (where evidence clears a real risk trigger). On evidence-reversed mirrors of famous incidents, models score 63.8% versus 98.5% on original incidents. More reasoning repairs a weak gate but leaves a calibrated one flat, showing capability ≠ steering calibration.

Conclusion: LLM workplace agents are poorly calibrated at commit boundaries, predominantly over-refusing safe work. Steering calibration is a distinct capability from general performance, and the benchmark provides a public leaderboard (steerbench.com) to track and improve gate decisions.

Abstract: Long-running LLM agents act through tools, and a single step can send an email, merge a pull request, or wire a payment. The steering decision is the pre-commit choice at that boundary: proceed, or hold for human or policy review. We introduce SteerBench-Work, an incident-anchored, bidirectional benchmark for that decision in workplace agents across developer operations, customer service, finance, legal, medical, HR, and security.
  Release v2026-05 contains 106 scenarios anchored in public incidents, paired evidence-reversed mirrors, and calibration controls, with labels split nearly evenly between proceed and hold so the two error directions get near-identical numbers of chances. A model sees the proposed action and the available evidence, returns a gate decision, and is scored on whether it crosses or holds the boundary correctly. Across 30 model conditions the failures run almost entirely in one direction: models wrongly hold authorized, evidence-cleared work on 28.1% of opportunities and wrongly allow unsafe work on 1.0%. The hardest cases are risk-resolved commits, where signed or structured evidence has already cleared a real risk trigger, and models score markedly worse on evidence-reversed mirrors of famous incidents (63.8%) than on the incidents themselves (98.5%). General capability is not the same as steering calibration: higher-capability models often over-refuse at the commit boundary, and more reasoning can repair a weak gate while leaving a calibrated one flat. The public leaderboard is at steerbench.com.

</details>


### [113] [Correct Is Not Governed: Provenance Integrity in Agentic Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12761)
*Jesus Salas*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces Matrix, a deterministic causal-state layer that adds governed execution to agentic workflows by recording authority and fact dependencies, verifying completion evidence, and selectively invalidating stale work, so that agentic work becomes auditable and independently verifiable in institutional settings rather than simply outcome-correct.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluating agentic workflows solely by whether they reach the correct outcome is insufficient in institutional contexts, where a correct action may rely on the wrong authority, claim completion without evidence, or become stale after later changes. This motivates a need for governed execution whose decisions, completion, and change-response are supported by inspectable provenance.

Method: The authors present Matrix, a deterministic causal-state layer that records authority and fact dependencies, verifies completion evidence, and selectively invalidates work affected by later changes. They evaluate it through controlled comparisons between governed and direct workflows, plus a role-separated transfer challenge involving a deterministically enforced completeness contract.

Result: Governed and direct workflows often reached identical outcomes, but only the governed path consistently preserved governing evidence, refused unsupported closure, and limited recovery to dependent tasks. However, the role-separated transfer challenge failed: the completeness contract severely over-blocked synthetic packets produced outside its authoring context.

Conclusion: The results show Matrix is not a general accuracy enhancer; instead, it serves primarily as an institutional integrity layer for making agentic work auditable and independently verifiable.

Abstract: Agentic workflows are commonly evaluated by whether they reach the correct outcome. That is insufficient in institutional settings, where a correct action may rely on the wrong authority, an unsupported completion claim, or work made stale by a later change. We define governed execution as work whose decisions, completion, and response to change are supported by inspectable provenance. We present Matrix, a deterministic causal-state layer that records authority and fact dependencies, verifies completion evidence, and selectively invalidates affected work. Across controlled comparisons, governed and direct workflows often reached the same outcomes, but only the governed path consistently preserved governing evidence, refused unsupported closure, and limited recovery to dependent tasks. A role-separated transfer challenge then failed: a deterministically enforced completeness contract severely over-blocked synthetic packets produced outside its authoring context. These results do not establish Matrix as a general accuracy enhancer; they support its primary role as an institutional integrity layer for making agentic work auditable and independently verifiable.

</details>


### [114] [General Probabilities of Causation with Causal Knowledge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12657)
*Xin Shu,Zhen Lei,Ang Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper derives tighter bounds for multivalued probabilities of causation (PoCs) by incorporating causal information from covariates and mediators, building on prior work on binary and nonbinary PoC bounds.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Probabilities of causation (PN, PS, PNS) cannot be directly observed and require partial identification via bounds. While sharp bounds exist for binary cases (Tian & Pearl) and improvements were made for binary PNS using covariates/mediators (Mueller et al.), and multivalued settings have theoretical bounds (Li & Pearl; Shu et al.), it remains open whether additional causal knowledge can further tighten bounds in multivalued settings.

Method: The authors extend the covariate- and mediator-informed bounding strategy from the binary setting to multivalued PoCs, deriving tighter bounds by incorporating causal information encoded in covariates and mediators. Results are illustrated with toy examples and validated through simulation studies.

Result: The paper derives tighter bounds for multivalued probabilities of causation. Toy examples illustrate the theoretical results, and simulation studies demonstrate that the proposed bounds are tighter than existing nonbinary bounds.

Conclusion: Additional causal knowledge from covariates and mediators can further tighten the bounds for multivalued probabilities of causation, improving on existing nonbinary bounds as confirmed by simulations.

Abstract: Probabilities of causation (PoCs) characterize individual causal responses that cannot be directly observed and therefore generally require partial identification. Tian and Pearl first derived theoretically sharp bounds for binary PoCs, including the probability of necessity (PN), the probability of sufficiency (PS), and the probability of necessity and sufficiency (PNS). Mueller et al. subsequently tightened the bounds for binary PNS by incorporating causal information encoded in covariates and mediators. More recently, Li and Pearl, as well as Shu et al., extended PoCs to multivalued settings and derived corresponding theoretical bounds. These developments naturally raise the question of whether additional causal knowledge can further tighten the bounds in multivalued settings. This paper addresses this question by deriving tighter bounds for multivalued PoCs through the incorporation of causal information encoded in covariates and mediators. We illustrate the theoretical results with toy examples, while simulation studies further demonstrate that the proposed bounds are tighter than existing nonbinary bounds.

</details>


### [115] [Designing AI Pipelines for Decision-Ready ITSM Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12670)
*Archan Dutta,Yash Dharmadhikari,Marat Valiullin,Rahul Guha,Alexander Liss*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents a sociotechnical AI pipeline that converts raw ITSM ticket exports into a multilevel decision-support artifact, using LLM normalization, HDBSCAN sub-topic clustering, and hierarchical agglomerative clustering to produce executive-facing Main-topics and granular Sub-topics, with stakeholder evaluation showing all metrics exceeding 4.0/5.0.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: ITSM systems generate large volumes of heterogeneous ticket data that sales and executive stakeholders struggle to turn into actionable intelligence, creating a need for automated transformation of raw exports into interpretable, human-centered decision-support outputs.

Method: A design science research (DSR) approach was used to build and evaluate a sociotechnical AI pipeline. The pipeline combines (1) LLM-based schema normalization to harmonize heterogeneous ticket data, (2) HDBSCAN clustering to extract sub-topics, and (3) hierarchical agglomerative clustering to aggregate these into executive-facing Main-topics. The artifact was evaluated across six artifacts by five raters from Sales Engineering and customer success roles using four decision-support metrics.

Result: Stakeholder evaluation shows that all four decision-support metrics—interpretability, actionability, trust, and likelihood of use—average above 4.0 out of 5.0. Trust emerged as the most consistent signal across raters, indicating strong confidence in the generated artifacts.

Conclusion: ITSM analytics should be framed as an Information Systems (IS) problem of transformation, abstraction, and human-centered design rather than a purely technical machine learning task, and the proposed pipeline offers an effective sociotechnical solution for turning ticket data into actionable decision support.

Abstract: IT service management (ITSM) systems accumulate large volumes of heterogeneous ticket data that are difficult for sales and executive stakeholders to convert into actionable intelligence. This paper presents a sociotechnical AI pipeline, designed and evaluated following design science research principles, that transforms raw ITSM exports into a multilevel decision-support artifact. The pipeline combines LLM-based schema normalization, HDBSCAN sub-topic clustering, and hierarchical agglomerative clustering to generate executive-facing Main-topics and granular Sub-topics. A stakeholder evaluation across six artifacts and five raters from Sales Engineering and customer success roles shows that all four decision-support metrics, interpretability, actionability, trust, and likelihood of use, on average exceed 4.0 out of 5.0, with trust as the most consistent signal. The findings position ITSM analytics as an Information Systems (IS) problem of transformation, abstraction, and human-centered design.

</details>


### [116] [On the Expressive Power of Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12671)
*Phokion Kolaitis,Rik Sengupta*

Main category: cs.AI
