TL;DR: This paper surveys how circuit complexity provides the right framework for precisely characterizing the expressive power of multi-layer transformers as language recognizers, by mapping transformer resources (attention, precision) onto circuit resources (gates, size, depth).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-layer transformers are the core of all modern LLMs, yet their exact computational boundaries remain unclear. The goal is to rigorously calibrate what languages transformers can recognize by comparing them against well-studied models of computation from theoretical computer science, specifically circuit complexity.

Method: The authors present an overview of selected results that translate between transformers and circuit classes. They parameterize transformers by resources such as the number of attention heads and numerical precision, and show these map to circuit complexity parameters like gate type, circuit size, and depth, yielding exact or tight correspondences between transformer families and circuit classes (e.g., TC0, AC0, logspace-uniform classes).

Result: The survey establishes that circuit complexity is the appropriate lens for analyzing transformer expressiveness, showing direct equivalences and separations between different transformer parameterizations and classical circuit classes, thereby delimiting which languages transformers can and cannot recognize.

Conclusion: Circuit complexity has emerged as the correct branch of computational complexity for calibrating transformer expressiveness, since resource-based parameterizations of transformers correspond cleanly to resource-based parameterizations of circuits, providing a principled framework for understanding the theoretical limits of LLM architectures.

Abstract: Multi-layer transformers form the critical component of essentially all large language models (LLMs) in use today. Because of their ubiquity and computational capability, there is a rapidly growing body of work that aims to precisely calibrate the expressive power of transformers as language recognizers by comparing them against standard models of computation studied for decades by the theoretical computer science community. In this endeavor, circuit complexity has by and large emerged as the "correct" branch of computational complexity to analyze the expressive power of transformers; the reason is that parameterizing transformers by the various resources they use, such as attention and precision, leads to direct comparisons with different classes of circuits parameterized by resources such as type of gates, size, and depth. Here, we present an overview of selected results that delineate the expressive power of transformers using concepts and methods from circuit complexity.

</details>


### [117] [Multi-Layer Context Camouflaging: A Semantic Superposition and Contextual Lamination Framework for Malpractice-Resilient Online Assessment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13100)
*Gupta Lovi Raj,Kaur Kamalpreet,Dama Sri Ram,Parani Prajithaa*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces the Multi-Layer Context Camouflaging Theory (MCCT), a mathematical framework extending MSCCM within MARS that protects online assessment content from extraction attacks by semantically superposing real content with synthetic camouflage, recoverable only by legitimate candidates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Contemporary online assessment systems (browser lockdown, webcam monitoring, behavioural analytics) remain vulnerable to content-extraction attacks—screenshots, screen sharing, OCR, and automated scraping—that steal the assessment content itself rather than the delivery channel. A principled, mathematically rigorous mechanism is needed to secure rendered content while preserving readability for legitimate users.

Method: The paper develops MCCT as a semantic-superposition framework that renders authentic content and synthetic camouflage as a unified output. It models adversarial extraction via an explicit extraction-channel operator and constructs six coupled components: Context Inversion Operator, Contextual Lamination Operator, Separation Channel, Human Readability Functional, Computational Ambiguity Functional, and Context Camouflage Tensor. Computational ambiguity is formalized using conditional entropy to yield a closed-form uncertainty expression, with legitimate recovery guaranteed by an exact filtering identity. Theoretical properties cover ambiguity, camouflage density, semantic preservation, multi-observation leakage, and temporal multiplexing, complemented by a rendering algorithm with complexity analysis and a pre-registered evaluation protocol.

Result: The framework yields a closed-form conditional-entropy expression quantifying uncertainty during unauthorized extraction, an exact filtering identity ensuring legitimate recovery, and formal theorems governing ambiguity, camouflage density, semantic preservation, multi-observation leakage, and temporal multiplexing. A rendering algorithm with specified computational complexity and a pre-registered evaluation protocol are also provided.

Conclusion: MCCT establishes a mathematically rigorous foundation for behaviorally adaptive, accessibility-aware, and computationally resilient digital assessment by securing rendered content against extraction attacks while preserving readability for legitimate users.

Abstract: Contemporary online assessment systems rely primarily on browser lockdown, webcam monitoring, and behavioural analytics, yet remain vulnerable to attacks that extract the assessment content itself through screenshots, screen sharing, optical character recognition, and automated scraping. This paper extends the Multi-dimensional Spatio-Temporal Context Camouflaging Model (MSCCM) within the MARS (Multi-modal Assessment Resilience Suite) by introducing the Multi-Layer Context Camouflaging Theory (MCCT), a mathematical framework that protects rendered assessment content through semantic superposition. Authentic assessment content and synthetically generated camouflage are represented as a unified rendering while remaining recoverable only by legitimate candidates. The framework models the adversarial extraction process through an explicit extraction-channel operator and develops six coupled constructs: the Context Inversion Operator, Contextual Lamination Operator, Separation Channel, Human Readability Functional, Computational Ambiguity Functional, and Context Camouflage Tensor. Computational ambiguity is formulated using conditional entropy, yielding a closed-form expression that quantifies uncertainty during unauthorized extraction, while legitimate recovery is guaranteed through an exact filtering identity. We further establish theoretical properties governing ambiguity, camouflage density, semantic preservation, multi-observation leakage, and temporal multiplexing, and present a rendering algorithm with computational complexity and a pre-registered evaluation protocol. MCCT provides a mathematically rigorous foundation for behaviorally adaptive, accessibility-aware, and computationally resilient digital assessment by securing rendered assessment content while preserving readability for legitimate users.

</details>


### [118] [Lines and Ladders: A Context-Aware Multi-Agent Framework for Large-Scale Retail Price Taxonomy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12674)
*Ravi Teja Chunduri,Srikaran Reddy Boya,Deep Narayan Mishra,Ajay Kumar B,Karthik Kumaran,Pranay Kona*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents a scalable, context-aware Multi-Agent Framework using specialized LLM agents to automate the construction of "Lines and Ladders" pricing taxonomies for global retailers, achieving strong precision/recall and outperforming single-agent baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Global retailers must maintain price consistency and execute an Every Day Low Price strategy, but catalogs with millions of items make manual governance infeasible. Inconsistent pricing across item variants distorts customer value perception and cannibalizes sales, motivating automated construction of pricing taxonomies.

Method: A scalable, context-aware Multi-Agent Framework using specialized LLM agents that build "Lines and Ladders" pricing structures by identifying key attributes, extracting multi-modal values, and applying hierarchical grouping logic. The implementation is a 3-Agent system evaluated on real-world enterprise data.

Result: The 3-Agent system achieves an F1-score of 0.83 for Lines, outperforming single-agent baselines by reducing cognitive overload. It attains >90% precision and >75% recall in Food & Consumables, and 80.2% assignment accuracy in the unstructured General Merchandise catalog, and is deployed in production.

Conclusion: A multi-agent LLM framework with specialized agents effectively automates pricing taxonomy construction at scale, mitigating cognitive overload versus single agents and delivering production-grade accuracy across both structured and unstructured catalogs.

Abstract: Maintaining price consistency and executing an Every Day Low Price strategy is critical for global retailers. However, with catalogs spanning millions of active items, manual governance of price relationships is infeasible. Inconsistent pricing across item variants distorts customer value perception and cannibalizes sales. To address this, we present a scalable, context-aware Multi-Agent Framework designed to automate the construction of "Lines and Ladders" pricing taxonomies. Our framework employs specialized LLM agents to construct these coherent pricing structures by identifying key attributes, extracting multi-modal values, and applying hierarchical grouping logic. Evaluated on real-world enterprise data and deployed in production, our 3-Agent system achieves an F1-score of 0.83 for Lines, outperforming single-agent baselines by mitigating cognitive overload. The system achieves >90% precision and >75% recall in Food & Consumables, and 80.2% assignment accuracy in the unstructured General Merchandise catalog.

</details>


### [119] [Sovereign by necessity? Frontier AI export controls, cyber security, and the limits of national AI capability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13272)
*Alan Woodward,Andrew Rogoyski*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: As frontier AI concentrates in a few firms in two states, access to these models is becoming a lever of national power. Using the 2026 US licensing case as a pivot, the article argues that frontier AI access is now part of cyber defence, can be revoked, and that true sovereign capability is only partly feasible for all but a few states. It proposes a layered strategy—negotiated access, inference-level sovereignty, open-weight hedging, regional pooling, talent development, and basic cyber resilience—noting the open-weight hedge is more capable but also more politically exposed than assumed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper is motivated by the convergence of two developments: the first largely autonomous AI-run cyber espionage campaign and mounting evidence that frontier models shift the economics of cyber attack and defence, combined with the unusual market dynamics (few firms, two states) that concentrate control over frontier AI. A concrete trigger is the June 2026 US requirement that a leading developer obtain licences before releasing its most advanced models to any foreign person, which led to worldwide withdrawal and highlighted that access can be politically revoked.

Method: The article is an analytical/argumentative policy piece rather than an empirical study. It situates the licensing case within market dynamics, examines how AI-driven cyber capability and access control interact, and draws on evidence about training costs, the concentration of computing power, and national AI programmes to assess what sovereignty can realistically mean for small, middle, and large powers. It then develops and evaluates a layered strategy for managing access and building capability.

Result: The analysis finds that access to frontier AI is becoming part of national cyber defence and is revocable, while sovereign capability remains only partly feasible outside a handful of states. The proposed layered remedy includes negotiated access guarantees, inference-level sovereignty, open-weight hedging, pooled regional capability, sustained talent development, and continued investment in basic cyber resilience. The open-weight hedge is found to be both more capable and more politically exposed than commonly assumed, and near-term risk is located in deployment and containment of capable models rather than their apparent performance.

Conclusion: Frontier AI access is emerging as a component of national cyber defence that can be politically withdrawn, and genuine sovereign AI capability is only partly achievable for most states. Policy should therefore pursue a layered strategy combining negotiated access, inference-level sovereignty, open-weight hedging, regional pooling, talent development, and basic cyber resilience. The key near-term risk to manage is how capable models are deployed and contained, not their raw performance.

Abstract: A small number of firms based in two states produce the most capable frontier AI models. The governments of those states have shown both the legal power and the political will to decide which other countries may use these systems. In June 2026 the United States required a leading developer to obtain licences before releasing its most advanced models to any foreign person, including foreign nationals resident in the United States. The affected models were withdrawn worldwide at short notice, partly because the restriction proved impractical to administer. This followed within months of the first documented case of a largely autonomous, AI-run cyber espionage campaign, and coincided with mounting evidence that frontier models alter the economics of both cyber attack and cyber defence. This article examines how these two developments interact, and situates them within the unusual market dynamics now driving large-scale AI development. It argues that access to frontier AI is becoming part of national cyber defence, that such access can be revoked, and that the obvious remedy of sovereign capability remains only partly feasible for all but a handful of states. Drawing on evidence about training costs, the concentration of computing power and the support offered by national AI programmes, it asks what sovereignty can realistically mean for small and middle powers, and for large powers as well. The article proposes a layered strategy: negotiated access guarantees, sovereignty at the level of inference, hedging with open-weight models, pooled regional capability, sustained talent development and continued investment in basic cyber resilience. The open-weight hedge proves at once more capable and more politically exposed than is commonly assumed. Much of the near-term risk lies in how capable models are deployed and contained rather than in their apparent performance.

</details>


### [120] [TopoIntent: Compiling Security Intent into Executable, Compliance-Checked Network Topologies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13389)
*Xiaokang Qu,Jianliang Ma,Zao Fan,Tianshu Chu,Tianlong Fan,Linyuan Lü*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TopoIntent compiles underspecified natural-language security requirements into executable, compliance-checked network topologies by constraining LLM generation with a schema, retrieving reference architectures via dense-vector search, applying staged fusion for intent-template alignment, and repairing gaps additively before exporting Mininet scripts with iptables ACLs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing NetOps automation tools operate only after a security topology design is fixed and cannot generate structured security topologies from underspecified natural-language requirements. There is also no public benchmark for the requirement-to-topology task, motivating both a new system and a custom evaluation set.

Method: TopoIntent uses (1) a schema contract to constrain generation, (2) dense-vector retrieval of reference architectures from a curated template library, (3) staged fusion to align intent with templates and complete security details, (4) compliance checking against CIS Controls v8.1.2 topology-visible safeguards with unresolved cases flagged for manual review, (5) additive schema-preserving edits to repair structural gaps, and (6) export to Mininet scripts with kernel-level iptables ACLs for reachability and allow/deny testing. Evaluation uses 22 retrieval templates and 44 synthetic intents across five scenarios, plus a held-out set of 7 templates and 14 intents from finance and government scenarios excluded from retrieval.

Result: On the held-out set, additive repair improved topology-visible CIS satisfaction from 0.78 to 1.00 in fewer than 1.5 rounds on average, and one feedback round raised the post-ACL policy pass rate from 0.78 to 0.88.

Conclusion: TopoIntent demonstrates that LLM generation constrained by a schema, template retrieval, staged fusion, and additive repair can produce executable, compliance-checked security topologies from natural-language intent, achieving near-complete CIS compliance and improved post-ACL policy pass rates on held-out scenarios.

Abstract: Enterprise security topology design requires translating business intent, regulatory requirements, and risk assumptions into zones, boundary devices, inter-zone paths, and access-control policies. Existing NetOps automation tools mainly operate after this design is fixed, providing limited support for generating structured security topologies from underspecified natural-language requirements. We present TopoIntent, a system that compiles security intent into executable, compliance-checked network topologies. It uses a schema contract to constrain generation, retrieves reference architectures from a curated template library via dense-vector search, and applies staged fusion for intent-template alignment and security completion. The generated topology is checked against CIS Controls v8.1.2 safeguards visible at the topology layer, while unresolved cases are marked for manual review. Structural gaps are repaired through additive schema-preserving edits. The final topology is exported to Mininet scripts with kernel-level iptables ACLs, enabling executable reachability and allow/deny tests. Because no public benchmark exists for this requirement-to-topology task, we construct an evaluation set from reference security architecture diagrams. The retrieval set contains 22 templates and 44 synthetic intents across five scenarios, while the held-out set contains 7 templates and 14 intents from finance and government scenarios excluded from retrieval. On the held-out set, additive repair improves topology-visible CIS satisfaction from 0.78 to 1.00 in fewer than 1.5 rounds on average, and one feedback round raises the post-ACL policy pass rate from 0.78 to 0.88.

</details>


### [121] [The Role of Natural Language Understanding in Multimodal Video-Based Dengue Diagnosis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12677)
*Danial Sharifrazi,Saadat Behzadi,Julakha Jahan Jui,Mojtaba Mohammadi,Nouman Javed,Roohallah Alizadehsani,Prasad N. Paradkar,Asim Bhatti*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A YOLO + CLIP vision-language framework classifies video frames of DENV2-infected vs. uninfected mosquitoes, achieving 98.54% accuracy and 99.91% sensitivity at frame level and 100% video-level performance after temporal aggregation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Detecting infection-related behavioral changes in mosquitoes from video is hard because mosquitoes are small, move rapidly and irregularly, and are affected by environmental factors (background, lighting, shadows), making reliable feature extraction difficult.

Method: A YOLO- and CLIP-based vision-language framework is proposed. YOLO isolates mosquito regions from background. Visual features from video frames are aligned with biologically meaningful textual prompts in a shared embedding space. The model is fine-tuned via supervised bidirectional contrastive learning and evaluated using frame-level image-text similarity-based classification, followed by temporal aggregation for video-level results. Ablation studies assess fine-tuning, CLIP-based representations, and the textual branch.

Result: 98.54% accuracy and 99.91% sensitivity at frame level; 100% (complete) video-level performance after temporal aggregation. Ablations show fine-tuning and CLIP representations are essential for this domain, while the textual branch mainly provides semantic image-text alignment without an accuracy gain over a vision-only model.

Conclusion: Vision-language models provide a useful framework for analyzing infection-related biological behaviors from video data, with fine-tuning and CLIP-based representations being critical to performance.

Abstract: Detecting infection-related behavioral changes in mosquitoes from video data is challenging because mosquitoes are small, move rapidly and irregularly, and are affected by environmental factors such as background, lighting, and shadows, which can make reliable feature extraction difficult. In this study, a YOLO- and Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP)-based vision-language framework is proposed to classify mosquito flight frames of uninfected and Dengue virus serotype 2 (DENV2)-infected mosquitoes. First, YOLO is used to isolate mosquito regions from the background. Then, visual features extracted from video frames are aligned with biologically meaningful textual prompts in a shared embedding space. The multimodal model was fine-tuned using supervised bidirectional contrastive learning and evaluated through frame-level image-text similarity-based classification. The results show that the proposed method achieved 98.54% accuracy and 99.91% sensitivity at the frame level. After temporal aggregation of frame-level information, the model achieved complete video-level performance. The ablation results showed that fine-tuning and CLIP-based representations were essential for this domain, while the textual branch provided semantic image-text alignment rather than an accuracy advantage over the vision-only model. These findings suggest that vision-language models can provide a useful framework for analyzing infection-related biological behaviors from video data.

</details>


### [122] [Beyond the Best Guess: Improving LLM Solution Coverage with Evolution Strategies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12679)
*Conor F. Hayes,Elliot Meyerson,Kajetan Schweighofer,Roberto Dailey,Babak Hodjat,Risto Miikkulainen,Xin Qiu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper argues that post-training LLMs with Evolution Strategies (ES) instead of Reinforcement Learning (RL) yields higher pass@k by preserving diverse solution coverage, which matters for discovery domains like math and science.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are used to propose solutions in discovery domains, but using only a single best-guess answer underutilizes test-time compute. The pass@k approach lets models generate diverse candidates, yet standard RL post-training narrows the output distribution around high-reward outputs, causing solution-coverage collapse and limiting pass@k.

Method: The authors use Evolution Strategies (ES), a population-based, gradient-free post-training method that optimizes directly in weight space through random perturbations, and compare it against Reinforcement Learning (RL).

Result: ES achieves consistently higher pass@k than RL and produces a broader output distribution with greater solution coverage, which translates into better results on standard math benchmark applications.

Conclusion: ES provides a better foundation for post-training in discovery problems and other domains where diverse solution coverage is critical.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in discovery domains such as math and science. The usual approach is to present the problem to the model and use its answer as the proposed solution. However, beyond this best guess, discovery can be enhanced by increasing test-time compute. In a process called pass@k, the model is allowed to explore the solution space and generate diverse candidate solutions. Unfortunately, the standard approach to post-training LLMs through Reinforcement Learning (RL) may limit pass@k: the model's output distribution narrows around high-reward outputs, causing the solution coverage to collapse. The alternative is to use Evolution Strategies (ES), a population-based, gradient-free post-training method that optimizes directly in weight space through random perturbations. As this paper shows, ES achieves consistently higher pass@k than RL and produces a broader output distribution with greater solution coverage. This coverage in turn makes it possible to achieve better results in e.g. standard math benchmarks. Thus, ES provides a better foundation for post-training in discovery problems and other domains where diverse solution coverage is critical.

</details>


### [123] [Spatial Memory Agent: Experience-Grounded Procedure Memory for Spatial Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12743)
*Haokai Zhang,Yuhang Ding,Yunshu Zhou,Xinze Du,Shengtao Zhang,Zhiyue Zhao,Yuling Xi,Hao Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SMA is a parameter-update-free framework that lets frozen VLMs self-evolve their spatial reasoning by distilling verified experiences into transferable lessons, ranked by a Transfer Reliability Score, and retrieving them at inference time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing work improves VLM spatial reasoning via post-training (SFT/RL) or agentic external tools, but both are costly or depend on external spatial tools at inference. The authors explore a complementary, underexplored route: enabling a frozen VLM to improve spatial reasoning through parameter-update-free self-evolution without external expert tools at inference time.

Method: SMA is an experience-grounded runtime framework. In a verifiable spatial environment, it queries the frozen VLM for a prediction and reward, then applies verifier-guided reflection to distill compact transferable lessons from the spatial experience. Each lesson gets a Transfer Reliability Score (TRS), initialized uniformly and later calibrated from retrieval outcomes as evidence of future transfer reliability. During read-only deployment, SMA retrieves lessons via semantic filtering combined with similarity-TRS ranking to guide frozen model inference.

Result: Across five spatial benchmarks and four base VLMs, SMA achieves the highest macro average in every base-model block and the best accuracy in most of the 20 evaluations, validating a practical parameter-update-free self-evolution path across frozen model scales and environments.

Conclusion: Parameter-update-free self-evolution via experience-grounded memory and transfer-reliability-aware retrieval is a viable and practical way to improve spatial reasoning in frozen VLMs without external spatial tools at inference time.

Abstract: Spatial intelligence is becoming a foundation for embodied agents, robotic planning, and multimodal assistants. To improve the spatial reasoning ability of VLM agents, existing work has mainly followed two lines. One line uses post-training methods, such as supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. Another line adopts an agentic paradigm in which the model calls external spatial tools, such as depth estimation and 3D reconstruction tools, to gather intermediate spatial evidence. We study a complementary and underexplored route: Can a frozen VLM agent improve its spatial reasoning through \textbf{parameter-update-free self-evolution}, without depending on external expert spatial tools at inference time? We present \textbf{Spatial Memory Agent (SMA)}, an \textbf{experience-grounded runtime framework} that converts verified spatial experience into reusable transferable lessons. In a verifiable spatial environment, SMA queries the frozen VLM, obtains a predicted answer and reward, and uses \textbf{verifier-guided reflection} to distill compact transferable lessons from spatial experience. SMA further assigns each lesson a \textbf{Transfer Reliability Score (TRS)}, which is initialized uniformly and calibrated from later retrieval outcomes as visit evidence of future transfer reliability. During \textbf{read-only deployment}, SMA retrieves lessons by semantic filter and similarity-TRS combined ranking, allowing the retrieved memory to guide frozen model inference. Across five representative spatial benchmarks and four base VLMs, SMA achieves the highest macro average in every base-model block and the best accuracy among the evaluated methods in most of the 20 evaluations, establishing a practical parameter-update-free path for spatial self-evolution across the evaluated frozen model scales and environments.

</details>


### [124] [PROVE-RT: Generating Mechanized Theorem Prover Scripts for Real-Time Systems using LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12762)
*Sadat Shahriyar,Shareef Ahmed,Abdullah Al Arafat*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PROVE-RT is an LLM-assisted framework that generates PROSA/ROCQ scripts for mechanizing real-time schedulability analyses, using dependency-aware sketches, retrieval, staged skeleton generation, and proof completion, achieving a 44.7% success rate where direct prompting fails.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Schedulability analysis is critical for certifying real-time systems, but existing tests rely on pen-and-paper proofs that are hard to scale, validate, and maintain. Mechanical verification in PROSA/ROCQ offers rigor, yet manually writing such proofs demands deep domain expertise and proof-engineering effort. While LLMs are promising for generating PROSA/ROCQ scripts, state-of-the-art models typically lack the PROSA-specific knowledge needed to correctly use its modeling abstractions and proof patterns.

Method: PROVE-RT guides LLM generation through four components: (1) dependency-aware informal sketches, (2) retrieval from processed PROSA documentation, (3) staged skeleton generation, and (4) proof completion. The authors construct a mechanization-oriented corpus from 1,191 real-time systems papers containing 13,134 informal sketches with dependency information, and evaluate on a curated test set.

Result: Direct prompting of state-of-the-art LLMs fails to reliably generate valid PROSA mechanizations, whereas PROVE-RT achieves a success rate of 44.7% on the curated evaluation set.

Conclusion: Retrieval-guided and staged LLM assistance can substantially improve the automated mechanization of schedulability analysis in PROSA/ROCQ, demonstrating a viable path toward more scalable and maintainable formal certification of real-time systems.

Abstract: Schedulability analysis is essential for certifying real-time systems, but existing tests are often developed through pen-and-paper proofs that are difficult to scale, validate, and maintain. Mechanized verification in PROSA/ROCQ offers a rigorous alternative, yet manually constructing such proofs requires substantial domain expertise and proof-engineering effort. Recent successes of large language models (LLMs) across a wide range of tasks make them promising candidates for generating PROSA/ROCQ scripts for mechanized theorem provers. However, state-of-the-art LLMs often lack the PROSA-specific knowledge required to correctly use its modeling abstractions and proof patterns.
  This paper introduces PROVE-RT, an LLM-assisted framework for generating PROSA/ROCQ scripts to mechanize schedulability analyses in real-time systems literature. PROVE-RT guides generation through dependency-aware informal sketches, retrieval from processed PROSA documentation, staged skeleton generation, and proof completion. We construct a mechanization-oriented corpus from 1, 191 real-time systems papers, containing 13, 134 informal sketches with dependency information. On a curated evaluation set, direct prompting of state-of-the-art LLMs fails to reliably generate valid PROSA mechanizations, whereas PROVE-RT achieves a success rate of 44.7%. These results show that retrieval-guided and staged LLM assistance can improve automated mechanization of schedulability analysis in PROSA/ROCQ.

</details>


### [125] [ARAC: Benchmarking Auto-Research's Alignment and Completeness on End-to-End Researchs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12788)
*Jiale Cui,Yueyao Yuan,Kaixi Zhong,Xiaogang Xu,Jiafei Wu,Zhe Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ARAC-Bench is a researcher-mimicking evaluation framework that measures Auto-Research systems by how well they reproduce high-quality human research processes across Proposal, Experiment, and Synthesis, rather than merely matching final answers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Auto-Research advances rapidly, but existing evaluation only checks whether final answers match, failing to assess alignment, logical coherence, and evolutionary completeness of the research trajectory relative to human research behavior.

Method: The framework combines two synergistic components: (1) the Academic Cognition Skills system, which converts implicit reviewer expertise into stage-calibrated, quantifiable rubrics; and (2) a three-stage capability diagnostic protocol that decomposes the research process under strict modular constraints into three traceable, mutually independent dimensions—Proposal, Experiment, and Synthesis.

Result: Systematic evaluation of 11 SOTA frameworks yields a best alignment score of only 67.9 out of 100, revealing a significant gap in simulating rigorous human methodology. Validation against Ph.D. candidate rankings shows a strong correlation of 0.8141, confirming ARAC-Bench reliably reflects dimensions researchers value.

Conclusion: ARAC-Bench provides a fine-grained diagnostic tool and a scalable reward signal for training the next generation of autonomous research systems, while exposing a substantial gap between current Auto-Research systems and rigorous human research methodology.

Abstract: The rapid advancement of Auto-Research has surfaced a fundamental evaluation challenge: how can we measure the alignment, logical coherence, and evolutionary completeness of its research trajectory with human research behavior? We propose Auto-Research's Alignment and Completeness, ARAC-Bench: a Researcher-Mimicking Evaluation framework that shifts the objective from matching final answers to reproducing high-quality human research processes. The framework operates through two synergistic components: the Academic Cognition Skills system, which is the first to transforms implicit reviewer expertise into stage-calibrated, quantifiable rubrics; and a three-stage capability diagnostic protocol, which decomposes the research process under strict modular constraints into three traceable, mutually independent dimensions: Proposal, Experiment, and Synthesis. Systematic evaluation of 11 SOTA frameworks yields a best alignment score of only 67.9 of 100, revealing a significant gap in simulating rigorous human methodology. Validation against Ph.D. Candidates rankings shows a strong correlation of 0.8141, confirming that ARAC-Bench reliably reflects the dimensions researchers truly value. ARAC-Bench provides not only a fine-grained diagnostic tool but also a scalable reward signal for training the next generation of autonomous research systems.

</details>


### [126] [CABS+: Efficient and Scalable Model Merging via Conflict-Aware Sparsification and Adaptive Weight Allocation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12842)
*Yuchen Liu,Zongzhen Yang,Binhang Qi,Hailong Sun,Xiang Gao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes CABS+, an extension of CABS for multi-task model merging that replaces grid-search coefficient tuning with a gradient-free Adaptive Weight Allocation (AWA) scheme, adds an asymmetric fitness function for balanced task gains, and introduces a Relative Synergy Score (RSS) to quantify model mergeability. Across 27 datasets and 5 models (large/small language and vision), CABS+ outperforms CABS, AdaMerging, and WUDIMerging, improving overall performance by 16.97% and 12.93% over AdaMerging and WUDIMerging respectively, while using under 25% of AdaMerging's GPU memory and achieving ~4x faster merging than WUDIMerging.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Model merging enables unified multi-task models without retraining, but suffers from parameter conflicts and knowledge interference. The prior CABS method mitigates interference via structured pruning and sequential masking, yet it relies on grid search for scaling coefficients (exponential time complexity) and its objective can be dominated by high-performance tasks, causing suboptimal overall performance.

Method: CABS+ extends CABS with three contributions: (1) Adaptive Weight Allocation (AWA), which optimizes merging coefficients using a gradient-free search to cut time complexity; (2) an asymmetric fitness function that promotes more balanced performance gains across tasks rather than favoring high-performance ones; and (3) a Relative Synergy Score (RSS) to quantify model mergeability and guide model selection. A systematic empirical study of key merging factors is also conducted.

Result: On 27 datasets and 5 models across large language, small-scale language, and vision domains, CABS+ improves overall performance by 16.97% over AdaMerging and 12.93% over WUDIMerging. It shows stronger stability and robustness across varying task numbers and model architectures, uses less than 25% of AdaMerging's GPU memory, and achieves nearly a 4x speedup in merging time over WUDIMerging.

Conclusion: CABS+ addresses the efficiency and imbalance limitations of CABS through AWA and an asymmetric fitness function, and provides RSS as a principled measure of mergeability. Extensive experiments confirm its effectiveness, efficiency, stability, and robustness, establishing CABS+ as a strong baseline for multi-task model merging.

Abstract: Model merging has recently attracted significant attention as a promising paradigm for constructing unified multi-task models without requiring additional retraining. However, parameter conflicts and knowledge interference across tasks often degrade merged-model performance. Prior work introduced Conflict-Aware and Balanced Sparsification (CABS), which reduces parameter interference through structured pruning and sequential masking. However, CABS relies on grid search to determine scaling coefficients, resulting in exponential time complexity, while its optimization objective can be dominated by high-performance tasks, leading to suboptimal overall performance. To address these limitations, we extend CABS and propose CABS+. Specifically, Adaptive Weight Allocation (AWA) optimizes merging coefficients via a gradient-free search scheme to reduce time complexity, while an asymmetric fitness function promotes more comprehensive performance gains across tasks. Moreover, we conduct a systematic empirical study of key factors influencing model merging performance and propose Relative Synergy Score (RSS) to quantify model mergeability and guide model selection. We compare CABS+ with state-of-the-art model merging methods, including CABS, AdaMerging, and WUDIMerging, across 27 datasets and 5 models covering large language, small-scale language, and vision models. Extensive experiments verify the effectiveness and efficiency of CABS+. Compared with AdaMerging and WUDIMerging, CABS+ improves overall performance by 16.97% and 12.93%, respectively, exhibits stronger stability and robustness across varying task numbers and model architectures, uses less than 25% of the GPU memory required by AdaMerging, and achieves nearly a 4x speedup in merging time over WUDIMerging.

</details>


### [127] [Beyond Retrieval: Query-Conditioned Reuse of Long-Horizon Agent Trajectories](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12847)
*Yifei Li,Heng Wang,Lingling Zhang,Muye Huang,Xinyu Zhang,Jiashuai Liu,Hang Yan,Rongman Xu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper identifies post-retrieval reuse as a distinct bottleneck in long-horizon trajectory memory for LLM agents, proposes an evaluation framework isolating reuse from retrieval, and introduces Query-Conditioned Reuse (QCR), a simple target-bound note format that achieves 62.3% average success (10.7 points above Full Trajectory) while using 48.9% fewer online tokens across WebArena, WorkArena, and AppWorld.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work on trajectory-based memory focuses on retrieving relevant past trajectories, but retrieval alone does not tell an agent how to reuse that trajectory when users, entities, constraints, or environment state have changed. The authors argue this post-retrieval reuse step is the actual bottleneck for long-horizon trajectory memory and is under-evaluated.

Method: The authors formulate an evaluation framework that holds candidate retrieval, target state, model, decoding, and tool budget fixed while varying the support delivered to the agent, thereby isolating reuse quality from retrieval quality. They instantiate it with Query-Conditioned Reuse (QCR), a deliberately simple target-bound note recording a reusable procedure, bindings to recover, applicability conditions, and verification requirements. They also compare against Full Trajectory injection and an oracle reusable selector, and analyze effects of trajectory length and source-target binding shift.

Result: Across 2,391 target instances in WebArena, WorkArena, and AppWorld, QCR reaches 62.3% average Success, 10.7 points above Full Trajectory, using 48.9% fewer online tokens. Summary reranking selects a reusable memory for 94.8% of targets, placing end-task Success within 1.8 points of an oracle selector. Analyses show direct trajectory injection loses utility as traces grow longer or source-specific values change, while target-bound support preserves a larger share of the gain.

Conclusion: The proposed framework separates retrieval quality from the task of turning retrieved experience into safe, useful support for a new task. Target-bound reuse support like QCR substantially improves success while reducing token cost, showing that how retrieved trajectories are reformulated for reuse matters more than prior work assumed.

Abstract: Retrieval can identify a past trajectory that may matter, yet it does not specify how an acting agent should use that trajectory after users, entities, constraints, or environment state have changed. We identify this post-retrieval reuse step as a distinct bottleneck for long-horizon trajectory memory and formulate an evaluation framework that holds candidate retrieval, target state, model, decoding, and tool budget fixed while varying the support delivered to the agent. We instantiate the framework with query-conditioned reuse (QCR), a deliberately simple target-bound note that records a reusable procedure, bindings to recover, applicability conditions, and verification requirements. QCR serves to test the reuse hypothesis rather than to claim a universally preferred memory format. Across 2,391 target instances in WebArena, WorkArena, and AppWorld, QCR reaches 62.3% average Success, 10.7 points above Full Trajectory, while using 48.9% fewer online tokens. Summary reranking selects a reusable memory for 94.8% of targets, placing end-task Success within 1.8 points of an oracle reusable selector. Analyses by trajectory length and source--target binding shift show that direct trajectory injection loses much of its utility as traces grow longer or source-specific values change, whereas target-bound support preserves a larger share of the measured gain. The resulting framework separates retrieval quality from the problem of turning retrieved experience into safe, useful support for a new task.

</details>


### [128] [Practice Makes Unsafe: Skill Misevolution in Self-Improving LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12851)
*Xutao Mao,Liangjie Zhao,Xiang Zheng,Cong Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper identifies a security failure mode in self-improving LLM agents: unsafe task successes get distilled into reusable cross-task "skills," and these can persist and cause harm even after the original malicious input is gone. The authors introduce SkillMisevo-Gym (a lifecycle-aware evaluation harness) and SkillMisevo-Bench (a benchmark with nine lifecycle metrics) to measure risk across skill authoring, retrieval, and execution, plus SafeEvolve (a wrapper that repairs unsafe content and governs reuse). Experiments show evolved agents author unsafe artifacts and can transfer harm to fresh sessions, but SafeEvolve substantially reduces unsafe retrieval and harm with minimal loss to benign utility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Self-improving LLM agents convert successful trajectories into persistent, cross-task skills/skill libraries. If an agent ever succeeds at an unsafe task, that "success" can be distilled into a reusable procedure, turning a one-off exploit into durable unsafe policy. Because skill evolution optimizes task outcomes rather than procedure safety, compromised experience leads to "skill misevolution." Existing benchmarks only measure current behavior or static artifacts and cannot attribute risk across the full lifecycle (authoring, retrieval, later execution), so the authors seek to expose and measure this gap.

Method: The authors build a lifecycle-aware evaluation framework. SkillMisevo-Gym versions skill state across agent frameworks to track how skills are authored, stored, retrieved, and executed over time. SkillMisevo-Bench is a frozen evaluation design spanning malicious exposure to carryover tasks, with concept-aligned benign tasks and nine lifecycle metrics that attribute risk across authoring, retrieval, and execution. They also propose SafeEvolve, a wrapper that repairs unsafe skill content and governs subsequent reuse. Evaluation covers 25 agent-method configurations, each running 525 tasks over 25 episodes, plus an exposure sweep varying the number of malicious tasks.

Result: All 21 evolved configurations author unsafe artifacts, yet only 15 lead to fresh-session harm, showing authoring risk does not always translate to execution harm. In the exposure sweep, adding three malicious tasks raises carryover attack success rate from 16.0% to 35.3%, demonstrating skill misevolution transfers harm across tasks. SafeEvolve reduces unsafe retrieval and fresh-session harm by 26.7 and 17.3 percentage points respectively, while mean benign utility changes by only 0.4 points across representative skill evolution methods.

Conclusion: Persistent-adaptation safety must govern both what skill updates write and what future executors reuse; measuring only current behavior or static artifacts is insufficient. Lifecycle-aware evaluation (authoring, retrieval, execution) is necessary to attribute and mitigate skill misevolution risk, and SafeEvolve offers a practical mitigation with negligible cost to benign utility.

Abstract: Self-improving LLM agents convert successful trajectories into persistent cross-task state. An unsafe success can thereby become reusable policy after its triggering input disappears. Skill evolution makes this failure measurable by distilling operational trajectories into executable, transferable, and inspectable procedures. Because evolution optimizes task outcomes rather than procedure safety, compromised experience can cause skill misevolution. Existing benchmarks measure current behavior or static artifacts but cannot attribute risk across authoring, retrieval, and later execution. To expose this lifecycle, we introduce SkillMisevo-Gym, a lifecycle-aware harness that versions skill state across agent frameworks, and SkillMisevo-Bench, a frozen design from malicious exposure to carryover tasks, with concept-aligned benign tasks and nine lifecycle metrics. We also introduce SafeEvolve, a wrapper that repairs unsafe content and governs subsequent reuse. Across 25 agent-method configurations, each covering 525 tasks in 25 episodes, all 21 evolved configurations author unsafe artifacts, while only fifteen lead to fresh-session harm. In the exposure sweep, three malicious tasks raise carryover ASR from 16.0% to 35.3%. Across representative skill evolution methods, SafeEvolve reduces unsafe retrieval and fresh-session harm by 26.7 and 17.3 percentage points, respectively, while mean benign utility changes by only 0.4 points. Together, persistent-adaptation safety must govern what updates write and what future executors reuse. Code is available at https://github.com/henrymao2004/misevolve.

</details>


### [129] [AI and Consumer Rights in India Working Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12863)
*Omir Kumar,Sriya Sridhar,Vibhav Mithal,Balaraman Ravindran*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This working paper evaluates whether India's Consumer Protection Act, 2019 adequately covers AI-related harms and allocates liability across the AI value chain, finding that while its definitions are technology-agnostic and potentially applicable, causation and multistakeholder attribution remain major unresolved gaps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As AI systems spread through consumer-facing applications, liability for AI-related harms remains legally unresolved. The paper seeks to determine whether India's Consumer Protection Act, 2019 can adequately address harm caused by defective AI products and services and proportionately assign liability across the AI value chain.

Method: Doctrinal/legal analysis of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, examining its definitions of product liability, harm, and deficiency in light of AI-specific characteristics such as design-driven failures, biased outputs, and overlapping roles of data providers, model developers, deployers, and users.

Result: The Act's broad, technology-agnostic definitions appear potentially applicable to AI-related incidents (personal injury, psychological harm, biased outputs, loss of control). However, significant gaps remain: proving causation is technically difficult because AI failures often stem from design choices rather than discrete defects; and the Act's assumption of distinct manufacturer/seller/service-provider roles does not map to the overlapping responsibilities in the AI value chain. Current frameworks lack proportionate mechanisms to address complex multistakeholder harms.

Conclusion: Although the Act may cover AI entities, enforcement requires clarification on sector-specific overlaps. Proportionate liability mechanisms are needed to address complex, multistakeholder AI harms, as existing frameworks fall short.

Abstract: As AI systems proliferate in consumer facing applications, questions about liability for AI related harms remain unresolved. This working paper examines whether India's Consumer Protection Act, 2019, adequately addresses harm caused by defective AI products and services, and whether it proportionately allocates liability across the AI value chain.
  The Act's broad definitions of product liability, harm, and deficiency appear technology agnostic and potentially applicable to AI related incidents including personal injury, psychological harm, biased outputs, and loss of control. However, significant gaps remain. Proving causation between AI defects and consumer harm presents a technical challenge, as AI failures often stem from design choices rather than discrete defects. Additionally, the Act's framework assumes distinct roles for manufacturers, sellers, and service providers, yet the AI value chain involves overlapping responsibilities among data providers, model developers, deployers, and users that do not neatly map to these categories. Current liability frameworks lack proportionate mechanisms to effectively address complex, multistakeholder AI harms. While the Act may cover AI entities, enforcement requires clarification on sector specific overlaps.

</details>


### [130] [ReflectFact: Self-Reflective Agents for Improving Comprehension and Reasoning in Multi-Hop Fact Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12877)
*Runze Zhao,Zixin Tang,Xiaoshuai Hao,Leyuan Chang,Xiaopeng Fu,Boyu Qiao,Dongyang Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ReflectFact is a self-reflective agent framework for multi-hop fact verification that uses explicit reasoning path planning, evidence-drift verification, and reasoning reflection verification to keep agents aligned with a global objective and grounded in evidence, outperforming baselines on HOVER and EX-FEVER.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-hop fact verification is critical for fighting misinformation but existing multi-agent methods suffer from (1) agents lacking awareness of the global verification objective, causing reasoning drift, and (2) conflicts between parametric knowledge and provided evidence that undermine evidence-grounded reasoning and produce wrong verdicts.

Method: ReflectFact introduces three tasks: (1) Explicit Reasoning Path Planning, which builds an evidence-grounded reasoning path by resolving implicit entities, decomposing the claim into sub-questions, and integrating verified facts into a verdict; (2) Evidence-Drift Verification, which makes the agent re-answer by quoting supporting evidence when a grounded answer merely echoes its parametric prior, calibrating evidence deviation; and (3) Reasoning Reflection Verification, which re-examines each reasoning step and regenerates inconsistent steps to correct flaws such as location bias and replacement bias from a global task perspective. Validated reasoning chains are then aggregated to produce reliable verdicts.

Result: Experiments on HOVER and EX-FEVER show ReflectFact remedies comprehension and reasoning defects of existing methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance, outperforming the strongest baseline by 3.32% on HOVER and 2.78% on EX-FEVER.

Conclusion: ReflectFact effectively addresses the comprehension and reasoning limitations of existing multi-agent fact verification methods through self-reflection, achieving state-of-the-art results and substantially surpassing prior baselines on both benchmark datasets.

Abstract: Multi-hop fact verification, which verifies claims by reasoning over multiple pieces of evidence, is critical for combating misinformation on social media yet remains highly challenging. Recent methods primarily rely on multi-agent collaboration to decompose fact verification into specialized subtasks. However, these methods face two critical limitations: (1) agents may perform individual subtasks without sufficient awareness of the global verification objective, causing their reasoning to deviate from the intended direction; and (2) conflicts between parametric knowledge and the provided evidence may undermine evidence-grounded reasoning and lead to incorrect verdicts. To address these challenges, we propose ReflectFact, a novel self-reflective agent framework for multi-hop fact verification. ReflectFact introduces three key tasks. Explicit Reasoning Path Planning builds an evidence-grounded reasoning path by resolving implicit entities, decomposing the claim into sub-questions, and integrating the verified facts into a verdict. Evidence-Drift Verification makes the agent re-answer by quoting the supporting evidence when a grounded answer merely echoes its parametric prior, thereby calibrating evidence deviation to ensure grounded comprehension. Reasoning Reflection Verification re-examines each reasoning step and regenerates it once an inconsistency is detected, correcting reasoning flaws such as location bias and replacement bias through a global task perspective. Subsequently, the agent aggregates validated reasoning chains to yield reliable verdicts. Extensive experiments on HOVER and EX-FEVER demonstrate that ReflectFact effectively remedies the comprehension and reasoning defects of existing methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance and respectively outperforming the strongest baseline by 3.32\% and 2.78\% on the two datasets.

</details>


### [131] [Predictive Memory Localization: Forecasting Selective Intervention Paths from Internal Signals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12892)
*Jinhao Jing,Tian Zeyu,Lucas Qingyang Fang,Zhisheng Chen,Shuang Chen,Yuhao Luo,Qiannian Zhao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PML reframes memory localization as a predictive, falsifiable task: it measures whether an intervention direction has a selective operating regime by using low-dose causal responses to forecast outcomes at disjoint strengths, and shows a predictor-driven selector can choose coefficients or abstain while reducing semantic-neighbor damage.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Activation steering turns localized representations into control directions, but finding a localized representation does not tell us whether that direction actually has a selective operating regime (i.e., whether it moves the target without damaging semantic neighbors or general capability). The paper aims to turn memory localization into a predictive forecast of margin-level selective outcomes, rather than a static geometric claim.

Method: Introduces Predictive Memory Localization (PML), treating the measured-grid intervention path as the predictive object. It separates random-calibrated target movement from semantic-neighbor and capability damage, and compares static localization and supervised geometry (RFM/AGOP) with a strength-disjoint low-dose causal response. Frozen study covers 3,000 records, nine datasets, fourteen domains, producing 30,000 record-direction-layer paths and 210,000 path-strength evaluations. Analyses use record-paired bootstrap, record/dataset/domain-grouped splits, low-dose responses at |α|=0.1 to forecast outcomes at |α|∈{0.25,0.5}, and a predictor-driven selector that chooses a coefficient or abstains. Three residual-norm-matched base models are used.

Result: At layer 7, the geometry-derived RFM/AGOP direction reaches 13.1% target-any and 12.3% clean-any, exceeding random by 3.6 and 3.4 percentage points. Low-dose responses at |α|=0.1 are the strongest signal for outcomes at disjoint strengths. The predictor-driven selector improves utility, reduces semantic-neighbor damage versus a train-tuned fixed-strength policy, and avoids most evaluations in a dense scan. Across three residual-norm-matched base models, learned directions retain selective-path gains, and low-dose responses yield 0.801-0.828 record-held-out macro AUROC.

Conclusion: PML converts memory localization into a falsifiable forecast of margin-level selective outcomes and a risk-aware intervention decision, showing that low-dose causal responses can predict selectivity and that a learned selector can trade off utility against semantic-neighbor damage while avoiding dense scanning.

Abstract: Activation steering turns localized representations into control directions, but localization alone does not reveal whether a direction has a selective operating regime. We introduce Predictive Memory Localization (PML), which treats the measured-grid intervention path as the predictive object of memory localization. PML separates random-calibrated target movement from semantic-neighbor and capability damage, and compares static localization and supervised geometry with a strength-disjoint low-dose causal response. Our frozen study covers 3,000 records from nine datasets and fourteen domains, yielding 30,000 distinct record-direction-layer paths and 210,000 distinct path-strength evaluations. At layer 7, the geometry-derived RFM/AGOP direction reaches 13.1% target-any and 12.3% clean-any, exceeding random by 3.6 and 3.4 percentage points under a record-paired bootstrap. Across record-, dataset-, and domain-grouped splits, responses at $|α|=0.1$ are the strongest signal for outcomes at disjoint strengths $|α|\in\{0.25,0.5\}$. On held-out records, a predictor-driven selector chooses a coefficient or abstains, improves utility and reduces semantic-neighbor damage relative to a train-tuned fixed-strength policy, and avoids most evaluations in a dense scan. Across three residual-norm-matched base models, learned directions retain selective-path gains and low-dose responses yield 0.801-0.828 record-held-out macro AUROC. PML therefore turns memory localization into a falsifiable forecast of margin-level selective outcomes and a risk-aware intervention decision.

</details>


### [132] [Polish Medical Visual Question Answering: Vision-Language Models Underutilize Visual Evidence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12928)
*Jakub Pokrywka,Łukasz Grzybowski,Antoni Lasik,Marek Kubis,Jeremi Ignacy Kaczmarek,Wojciech Kusa*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces a Polish medical visual question answering (VQA) benchmark built from Polish Board Certification Examination questions, evaluates Polish-oriented, open-weight, and commercial vision-language models, and finds the task challenging with a best model accuracy of 79.0%; ablations show models rely more on question text than images and achieve above-chance accuracy from answer choices alone.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is a lack of medical VQA benchmarks in low-resource languages like Polish, limiting evaluation of vision-language models in non-English clinical settings. The authors aim to fill this gap using authentic Polish medical licensing examination questions and to probe whether models genuinely ground answers in visual content.

Method: They construct a VQA benchmark from image-containing items of the Polish Board Certification Examination for physicians and dentists, spanning specialties and visual domains, plus a text-only QA control set. They evaluate Polish-oriented, general-purpose open-weight, and commercial vision-language models, compare accuracy against an approximate human reference, and perform ablation configurations (omitting image, question, or both) with categorization by image importance to assess visual grounding.

Result: The best model reaches 79.0% accuracy on the full VQA set; only GPT-5.6 surpasses human reference on the subset with available candidate responses, while all other models underperform humans. Models extract more useful information from the question text than from the image and perform worse on image-dominant questions. Across QA and VQA, models still achieve above-chance accuracy from answer choices alone.

Conclusion: Polish medical VQA remains unsolved and challenging even for strong models. Current models rely more on textual cues and answer-choice artifacts than on visual grounding, highlighting the need for benchmarks that stress genuine image understanding in medical applications.

Abstract: We introduce a Polish-language medical visual question answering (VQA) benchmark, built from Polish Board Certification Examination questions for licensed physicians and dentists pursuing specialist certification. The benchmark comprises image-containing questions spanning diverse medical specialties and visual domains, together with a text-only question answering (QA) control set. We evaluate Polish-oriented, general-purpose open-weight, and commercial vision-language models. The task remains challenging: the best model achieves 79.0\% accuracy on the full VQA set, and only GPT-5.6 surpasses the approximate human reference on the subset with available candidate responses; all other evaluated models perform worse than humans. To assess visual grounding, we compare complete inputs with configurations omitting the image, the question, or both, and categorize questions by image importance. Models derive more useful information from the question text than from the image and perform worse on image-dominant questions. Across both QA and VQA, they nevertheless achieve above-chance accuracy from the answer choices alone, showing that non-trivial performance can persist even when key task components are missing.

</details>


### [133] [FlashDrive: Flash Vision-Language-Action Inference for Autonomous Driving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12932)
*Zekai Li,Yihao Liang,Hongfei Zhang,Jian Chen,Yesheng Liang,Zhijian Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FlashDrive is an algorithm-system co-design framework that simultaneously accelerates all four inference stages of Vision-Language-Action models for autonomous driving, cutting end-to-end latency from 717ms to 151ms (4.7x) on Alpamayo 1.5-10B with no meaningful accuracy loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: VLA models promise end-to-end reasoning for autonomous driving, but their computational cost is far too high for real-time control. The bottleneck is structural: inference is a cascade of four stages—visual encoding, language-model prefill, autoregressive reasoning-token generation, and flow-matching denoising—each of which wastes compute in a distinct way. Addressing any single stage in isolation leaves the others untouched, so a holistic acceleration is required.

Method: FlashDrive targets all four bottlenecks with lightweight algorithmic shortcuts: (1) streaming KV-cache reuse across temporally overlapping video frames to reduce visual encoding waste; (2) a non-autoregressive diffusion drafter exploiting the low per-token entropy and strong intra-block correlations of driving-domain reasoning for speculative decoding; (3) adaptive step caching for flow-matching denoising that exploits the velocity field's structure—sharp at endpoints, flat in the middle—to concentrate compute where it matters. These are layered on CUDA Graph compilation and kernel fusion. Evaluation uses Alpamayo 1.5-10B with W4A8 quantization.

Result: End-to-end latency drops from 717ms to 151ms (4.7x). Accuracy stays essentially unchanged: minADE6@6.4s shifts by only 0.08m, minADE1 improves, and closed-loop collision and off-road rates improve in simulation. Throughput rises from 1.4 Hz to 6.6 Hz on a single GPU.

Conclusion: By compounding algorithmic shortcuts with system-level optimizations, FlashDrive raises a 10B-parameter reasoning VLA from 1.4 Hz to 6.6 Hz on one GPU while preserving or improving accuracy, moving end-to-end autonomous driving substantially closer to real-time deployment.

Abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models promise to bring end-to-end reasoning to autonomous driving, but their computational cost remains far too high for real-time control. The core challenge is structural: VLA inference is not a single bottleneck but a cascade of four. Visual encoding wastes compute on overlapping video frames; language-model prefill recomputes context that could be carried over from the previous timestep; reasoning tokens are generated serially despite low entropy; and flow-matching denoising applies uniform compute to a non-uniform velocity field. Addressing any one stage in isolation leaves the others untouched. We propose FlashDrive, an algorithm-system co-design framework that targets all four stages simultaneously. Our key insight is that each bottleneck admits a distinct, lightweight algorithmic shortcut: temporal overlap enables streaming KV-cache reuse across frames; the low per-token entropy and strong intra-block correlations of driving-domain reasoning make a non-autoregressive diffusion drafter highly effective for speculative decoding; and the velocity field's structure---sharp at the endpoints, flat in the middle---permits adaptive step caching that concentrates compute where it matters. Layered on system-level CUDA Graph compilation and kernel fusion, these techniques compound. Applied to Alpamayo 1.5-10B with W4A8 quantization, FlashDrive reduces end-to-end latency from 717ms to 151ms (4.7x) while leaving accuracy essentially unchanged: minADE6@6.4s shifts by only 0.08m, minADE1 improves, and closed-loop collision and off-road rates improve in simulation. By raising a 10B-parameter reasoning VLA from 1.4~Hz to 6.6~Hz on a single GPU, FlashDrive moves end-to-end autonomous driving substantially closer to real-time deployment.

</details>


### [134] [Decomposition of Evidence, Contradiction, and Fragility in Perturbation Responses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12935)
*Lei You*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DECAF decomposes a model's response magnitude to perturbed inputs into three endpoint-relative components—evidence E, contradiction C, and fragility F—that sum exactly to the original magnitude (Abs = E + C + F), uniquely under its axioms. Tracking how the contrast develops as paired inputs are progressively revealed (via trajectory) resolves the ambiguity where equal magnitudes can mean different things.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing perturbation methods measure only how much a model reacts (response magnitude), not what that reaction means. The same magnitude can support, oppose, or be endpoint-null relative to the final factual-counterfactual difference, so magnitude alone is ambiguous and often misaligned with actual model behavior.

Method: Introduce DECAF, which progressively reveals paired inputs and defines an endpoint-relative decomposition that routes the total response into aligned responses (evidence E), opposed responses (contradiction C), and responses that occur along the path but vanish at the endpoint (fragility F). The decomposition satisfies Abs = E + C + F and is unique under endpoint-relative axioms, where the final contrast is used to interpret the trajectory.

Result: Across controlled vision and tabular settings, the three DECAF components track independently measured behavior. In a 72-model ImageNet-9 audit comparing cases with nearly identical response magnitude but different observed behaviors, the largest DECAF component agrees with observed behavior in 96.4% of cases versus 35.0% for magnitude alone. Changing only the reveal path raises total response by ~80%, yet evidence barely changes while fragility grows by >4x. Short forward-only DECAF trajectories outperform tested general-purpose attribution baselines on FunnyBirds and ImageNet-1k, and on a 1B-scale DINOv2 model match a strong gradient-based baseline with 4.75x lower wall time and 2.36x lower peak memory.

Conclusion: Magnitude-based perturbation explanations are inherently ambiguous; decomposing the response trajectory endpoint-relatively into evidence, contradiction, and fragility yields an exact, interpretable explanation that significantly better tracks true model behavior and is computationally cheaper than gradient baselines at scale.

Abstract: Perturbation methods explain model decisions by measuring prediction changes under altered inputs, but response magnitude tells us only how much a model reacts, not what that reaction means. The same magnitude can support the final factual-counterfactual difference, oppose it, or arise strongly along the perturbation path yet vanish at the endpoint. We therefore track how the contrast develops as paired inputs are progressively revealed, using the final contrast to interpret the trajectory. We introduce DECAF (Decomposition of Evidence, Contradiction, And Fragility), which routes aligned, opposed, and endpoint-null responses into evidence E, contradiction C, and fragility F. The decomposition preserves ordinary magnitude exactly, Abs = E + C + F, and is unique under endpoint-relative axioms. Across controlled vision and tabular settings, the three components track independently measured behavior. In a 72-model ImageNet-9 audit, we compare cases with nearly identical response magnitude but different independently measured behaviors. The largest DECAF component agrees with an observed behavior in 96.4% of cases, compared with 35.0% for magnitude alone. Changing only the reveal path increases total response by nearly 80%, yet evidence barely changes while fragility grows by more than 4x. On FunnyBirds and ImageNet-1k, short forward-only DECAF trajectories outperform the tested general-purpose attribution baselines. On a 1B-scale DINOv2 model, a short trajectory matches a strong gradient-based baseline with 4.75x lower wall time and 2.36x lower peak memory.

</details>


### [135] [Moose: Latent concept learning with reasoning-shortcut awareness in $\mathcal{EL}^{++}$](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12961)
*Olga Mashkova,Asaad Mohammedsaleh,Fernando Zhapa-Camacho,Robert Hoehndorf*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Moose compiles OWL 2 EL ontologies (TBox + finite ABox) into Sentential Decision Diagrams to enable differentiable neuro-symbolic learning, adds closure clauses for exhaustive families, proves termination/soundness/completeness in Lean, and outperforms propositional, fuzzy, and embedding baselines while providing the first reasoning-shortcut analysis in OWL EL.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large production ontologies (e.g., Gene Ontology, SNOMED CT) use the OWL 2 EL profile, but existing neuro-symbolic (NeSy) learning methods only support propositional theories or Datalog, and reasoning-shortcut (RS) awareness has never been studied in ontology settings. This gap motivates integrating OWL EL reasoning into differentiable learning.

Method: Moose compiles an EL++ TBox and finite ABox into a Sentential Decision Diagram (SDD), which serves as a differentiable weighted-model-counting layer. To overcome EL++'s limited expressivity under partial supervision, closure clauses are added outside the EL++ profile over declared exhaustive families. Formal properties (termination, soundness, completeness, polynomial intermediate sizes) are proven and validated in the Lean proof assistant. The authors also define the first formal partial-supervision latent-concept-learning task over an OWL EL ontology, learning per-individual classifiers for latent concepts from observed ABox literals.

Result: On MNIST-with-ontology and Pizzaïolo benchmarks, Moose improves over propositional-NeSy, fuzzy-logic, and ontology-embedding baselines. It further provides the first reasoning-shortcut analysis in an OWL EL setting, showing RS awareness in ontology-based NeSy learning.

Conclusion: Moose bridges OWL 2 EL reasoning and neuro-symbolic learning by compiling ontologies into SDDs as differentiable weighted-model-counting layers, with proven and formally verified correctness properties. It establishes the first formal latent-concept-learning benchmark over OWL EL and demonstrates superior performance plus the first reasoning-shortcut analysis in this ontology setting.

Abstract: The OWL 2 EL profile is used in some of the largest production ontologies, including the Gene Ontology and SNOMED CT. Existing neuro-symbolic (NeSy) learning methods accept propositional theories or Datalog, and reasoning-shortcut (RS) awareness has not been investigated in ontology settings. We present Moose, a method that compiles an $\mathcal{EL}^{++}$ TBox and finite ABox to a Sentential Decision Diagram (SDD). The SDD acts as a differentiable weighted-model-counting layer, and we add closure clauses outside the $\mathcal{EL}^{++}$ profile on declared exhaustive families to overcome the limited expressivity of $\mathcal{EL}^{++}$ under partial supervision. We show termination, soundness, completeness, and polynomial intermediate sizes, and validate the proofs in Lean. We then define the first formal partial-supervision latent-concept-learning task over an OWL EL ontology, i.e., learning per-individual classifiers for latent concepts from observed ABox literals, and evaluate Moose on MNIST-with-ontology and Pizzaïolo. Moose improves over propositional-NeSy, fuzzy-logic, and ontology embedding baselines, and presents the first reasoning-shortcut analysis in an OWL EL setting.

</details>


### [136] [Foundations of MT-PDCL: Measure-Theoretic Probabilistic Definite Clause Logic](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13018)
*Costin Bădică,Amelia Bădică*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MT-PDCL extends probabilistic definite clause logic to continuous measurable domains by replacing discrete grounding with measure-theoretic Lebesgue integration over Borel σ-algebras, enabling exact continuous inference while preserving declarative syntax.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard probabilistic logic programming frameworks require grounding into discrete propositional representations, which restricts exact inference to finite domains and discrete probability distributions. The authors aim to remove this limitation to support continuous variables and distributions natively.

Method: The paper introduces Measure-Theoretic Probabilistic Definite Clause Logic (MT-PDCL). It defines stochastic variables over bounded index domains and equips the interpretation space with standard Borel σ-algebras, so logical variables operate over continuous measurable spaces. Building on Continuous Distribution Semantics, probabilistic rules are modeled as mutually independent causal events. Declarative entailment is defined via exact Lebesgue integration over the continuous measure space, and a continuous immediate consequence operator is introduced that unifies integration of continuous priors with evaluation of exact continuous observations.

Result: The approach replaces the combinatorial bottleneck of discrete grounding with exact, algebraic, and structurally differentiable inference, achieving the expressive power of continuous probabilistic models while retaining the pure declarative syntax of definite clause logic.

Conclusion: The transition from discrete combinatorics to continuous measure-theoretic integration trades one challenge for another—the geometric curse of dimensionality—but successfully generalizes probabilistic logic programming to continuous domains with exact and differentiable inference.

Abstract: Standard probabilistic logic programming frameworks typically rely on grounding logic programs into discrete propositional representations. This operational requirement restricts exact inference to finite domains and discrete probability distributions. In this paper, we introduce Measure-Theoretic Probabilistic Definite Clause Logic (MT-PDCL), a generalized foundational framework that eliminates this finite-domain restriction. By explicitly defining stochastic variables over bounded index domains and equipping the interpretation space with standard Borel $σ$-algebras, MT-PDCL allows logical variables to operate natively over continuous measurable spaces. Building on Continuous Distribution Semantics, MT-PDCL models probabilistic rules as mutually independent causal events. However, rather than aggregating these derivations via finite boolean circuits, declarative entailment is formally defined through exact Lebesgue integration over the continuous measure space. We introduce a continuous immediate consequence operator that unifies the integration of continuous prior distributions with the evaluation of exact continuous observations. We demonstrate that this approach replaces the combinatorial bottleneck of discrete grounding with exact, algebraic, and structurally differentiable inference. While this transition trades discrete combinatorics for the geometric curse of dimensionality, it achieves the expressive power of continuous probabilistic models while preserving the pure declarative syntax of definite clause logic.

</details>


### [137] [From Local Mismatch to Global Impact: Optimizing Cache Reuse Policy for Efficient Diffusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13043)
*Xichen Ye,Yifan Wu,Zhikang Xie,Xiangyu Yue,Cheng Jin,Weizhong Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI
