TL;DR: GCache improves cache-based acceleration for diffusion models by replacing local similarity heuristics with a global error-impact-aware policy, formulated as a bilevel optimization that aligns error weighting with generation quality, yielding large quality gains (LPIPS 0.1095→0.0316) at 2.17× speedup on Wan2.1.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion models are expensive at inference time, and existing cache-based acceleration methods rely on local similarity heuristics that are misaligned with final generation quality because errors propagate and accumulate non-uniformly along the denoising trajectory. This motivates a caching policy that accounts for global error impact rather than local similarity.

Method: GCache first derives a rigorous upper bound on error propagation along the denoising trajectory, then reparameterizes the propagation exponent in Bernstein form to avoid overly conservative bounds for non-convex models. Cache policy search is reformulated as a bilevel optimization: the inner objective finds an optimal reuse policy, while the outer objective aligns the error-weighting function with generation quality loss.

Result: Extensive experiments on video and image generation show GCache consistently outperforms prior caching strategies. On the Wan2.1 video diffusion model, it achieves a 2.17× speedup while reducing LPIPS from 0.1095 to 0.0316, significantly enhancing generation quality.

Conclusion: By reconciling theoretical error-propagation analysis with empirically learned error weighting via bilevel optimization, GCache reallocates computation toward the most quality-critical steps, achieving state-of-the-art speed-quality trade-offs for diffusion model acceleration.

Abstract: Diffusion models have achieved dominant performance in visual generation but suffer from substantial inference overhead. While cache-based acceleration has emerged as a promising solution, existing policies rely on local similarity heuristics, which we identify as being significantly misaligned with final generation quality. This discrepancy stems from the non-uniform propagation and accumulation of errors along the denoising trajectory. To address this, we propose Global-Impact Cache (GCache). We first establish a rigorous theoretical characterization of the error propagation upper bound. Recognizing that this bound can be overly conservative for complex, highly non-convex diffusion models, we further reparameterize the propagation exponent with a Bernstein form and reformulate cache policy search as a bilevel optimization problem. In detail, GCache identifies an optimal reuse policy in the inner objective while aligning the error-weighting function with generation quality loss in the outer objective. This framework effectively reconciles theoretical rigor with empirical performance, learning to prioritize computation where it most impacts visual fidelity. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GCache consistently outperforms prior caching strategies on both video and image generation. Notably, on the state-of-the-art Wan2.1 video diffusion model, GCache maintains a 2.17x speedup while significantly enhancing generation quality, reducing LPIPS from 0.1095 to 0.0316.

</details>


### [138] [BoardroomAI: Dependency-Aware Human-Steerable Multi-Agent Deliberation through Evolving Decision Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13046)
*Sanjeev Manivannan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: BoardroomAI is a multi-agent framework that treats humans as persistent participants in decision-making, using a typed decision graph and dependency-aware propagation to let interventions selectively update only affected parts. In tests, propagation matched exhaustive impact computation while inspecting only 14.59% of nodes, though selective repair abstained in half of the pilot cases, motivating a "decision-sufficient context closure."


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional transcript-based multi-agent systems assume a one-shot human-to-agent handoff: humans supply an initial problem, agents deliberate internally, and a final answer is returned. However, real organizational decisions are co-created while evidence, constraints, and priorities continue to evolve, so the human should be able to intervene (challenge assumptions, change constraints/priorities, introduce evidence, redirect the process) during deliberation rather than only at the start.

Method: Four components: (i) a typed decision graph encoding evidence, assumptions, constraints, claims, objections, alternatives, risks, decisions, semantic dependencies, and specialist responsibility; (ii) an intervention compiler that turns confirmed human actions into explicit graph updates; (iii) dependency-aware propagation that finds affected subgraphs, preserves unaffected artifacts, and selectively reactivates relevant specialists; and (iv) an evaluation framework measuring intervention impact, repair coverage, preservation, recomputation, and decision validity. Evaluation used 600 generated decision-DAG interventions plus a 12-case exploratory pilot.

Result: Across 600 generated decision-DAG interventions, propagation matched exhaustive impact computation while inspecting only 14.59% of nodes. In the 12-case pilot, selective repair recomputed 62.11% of canonical nodes, preserved all gold-unaffected nodes, and produced valid updated decisions in six cases while abstaining in six. The abstentions indicate correct intervention routing may still provide insufficient context for synthesis.

Conclusion: The system demonstrates correct and efficient intervention routing and selective repair, but the abstentions reveal a gap: identifying affected nodes is not enough for synthesis. This motivates a "decision-sufficient context closure" for human-steered multi-agent deliberation. All results are synthetic and prototype-level.

Abstract: Organizational decisions are co-created while evidence, constraints, and human priorities continue to evolve. In conventional transcript-based multi-agent systems, humans typically provide an initial problem, agents deliberate internally, and the system returns a final response. BoardroomAI instead treats the human as a persistent participant who can intervene by challenging assumptions, modifying constraints, changing priorities, introducing evidence, or redirecting the decision process. We operationalize this human--agent coexistence through four components: (i) a typed decision graph representing evidence, assumptions, constraints, claims, objections, alternatives, risks, decisions, semantic dependencies, and specialist responsibility; (ii) an intervention compiler that converts confirmed human actions into explicit graph updates; (iii) dependency-aware propagation that identifies affected subgraphs, preserves unaffected artifacts, and selectively reactivates relevant specialists; and (iv) an evaluation framework measuring intervention impact, repair coverage, preservation, recomputation, and decision validity. Across 600 generated decision-DAG interventions, propagation matched exhaustive impact computation while inspecting only 14.59% of nodes. In a 12-case exploratory pilot, selective repair recomputed 62.11% of canonical nodes, preserved all gold-unaffected nodes, and produced valid updated decisions in six cases while abstaining in the remaining six. These abstentions show that correct intervention routing may still provide insufficient context for synthesis, motivating a \emph{decision-sufficient context closure} for human-steered multi-agent deliberation. All results are synthetic and prototype-level.

</details>


### [139] [DMDIntel: Interpreting Large Language Models via Dynamic Mode Decomposition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13048)
*Amogh Joshi,Animesh Mukherjee,Sergey Utyuzhnikov*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DMDIntel introduces dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) to make LLM classification predictions interpretable by decomposing hidden states into modes and ranking input tokens by their projection onto those modes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing interpretability methods for LLMs (such as PCA, integrated gradients, and SHAP) have limitations in capturing the relevant dynamics of hidden states; the paper seeks a more effective way to attribute predictions to input tokens.

Method: DMDIntel builds an input attribution pipeline that decomposes an LLM's hidden states into prominent dynamic patterns (modes) via dynamic mode decomposition, then assigns ranks/attributions to input tokens based on their projection values onto these modes.

Result: Experiments across three datasets and three model families consistently show that DMDIntel's ranked token attributions outperform state-of-the-art baselines, including principal component analysis, integrated gradients, and SHAP.

Conclusion: DMD provides a superior foundation for interpreting LLM classification decisions, and DMDIntel offers a reliable input attribution method that surpasses established interpretability techniques.

Abstract: In this work, we introduce DMDIntel which uses dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) to make the predictions made by LLMs in a classification task interpretable. It develops an input attribution pipeline, that first decomposes the hidden states of an LLM into prominent patterns, also known as modes, and then associates ranks to the input tokens based on the projection values on those modes. Rigorous experiments across three datasets and three model families consistently show that the ranked attribution of input tokens obtained using DMDIntel by far outperforms state-of-the-art techniques such as principal component analysis, integrated gradients and SHAP.

</details>


### [140] [VALG: An Agentic System for ML Theory Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13060)
*Dechen Zhang,Xuan Tang,Xinxiang Yin,Xingwu Chen,Jian Qian,Difan Zou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: VALG is an agentic system for autonomous machine-learning theory research that combines multi-level verification, adaptive problem formulation, and graph-structured proof development, and it is evaluated on nine subproblems from five COLT 2026 open problems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: ML theory research requires jointly developing the problem formulation, theorem target, and proof mechanism, typically through iterative hypothesis testing and refinement. The authors investigate whether this process can be organized as an autonomous agentic workflow.

Method: VALG combines multi-level Verification, Adaptive formulation of Learning-theory problems, and Graph-structured proof development. Each source-relative theorem branch maintains a fixed mathematical specification, checks theorem-level composition of a typed proof-dependency graph, and constructs and reviews local proofs in dependency order. On failure, it classifies obstructions as derivation-level, proof-structure-level, or formulation-level, routing the next attempt accordingly; formulation-level obstructions trigger explicitly related variants or relaxations that preserve the mathematical relation to the source problem.

Result: Across nine subproblems from five COLT 2026 open problems, two runs produced internally finalized theorem candidates matching the scope of their source briefs, while seven yielded restricted-method results, special cases, or conditional theorems. The case studies show VALG keeps source-scope matches, relaxations, conditional results, and blocked attempts mathematically distinct.

Conclusion: An autonomous agentic workflow for ML theory research is feasible, and VALG demonstrably maintains clear mathematical distinctions among theorem variants while producing meaningful partial results on open problems. The system is open source.

Abstract: Machine learning theory studies learning procedures through mathematical setups in which the data model, training protocol, oracle access, loss, metric, and randomness define the phenomenon that a theorem is meant to explain. Solving an open problem therefore requires the problem formulation, theorem target, and proof mechanism to be developed in concert. Researchers formulate hypotheses, test them through preliminary theoretical or empirical analysis, and refine both assumptions and proofs. We investigate whether this process can be organized as an autonomous agentic workflow for ML theory research.
  We develop VALG, an agentic system that combines multi-level Verification, Adaptive formulation of Learning-theory problems, and Graph-structured proof development. Within each source-relative theorem branch, VALG maintains a fixed mathematical specification, checks the theorem-level composition of a typed proof-dependency graph, and constructs and reviews local proofs in dependency order. When a proof attempt fails, VALG identifies whether the obstruction lies in a derivation, the proof structure, or the theorem formulation and routes the next attempt accordingly. Formulation-level obstructions initiate an explicitly related variant or relaxation, preserving the mathematical relation between the resulting theorem and the source problem.
  We evaluate VALG on nine subproblems from five COLT 2026 open problems. Two runs produce internally finalized theorem candidates that match the scope of their source briefs; the remaining seven yield restricted-method results, special cases, or conditional theorems. These case studies show how VALG keeps source-scope matches, relaxations, conditional results, and blocked attempts mathematically distinct. VALG is open source at https://github.com/DechenZhang/VALG-ML-Theory-Agent.

</details>


### [141] [Uniform Herding: Exemplar Replay with Representation Refresh](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13061)
*Krishna Subedi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes Uniform Herding, a replay method for class-incremental learning that evenly allocates a bounded active exemplar set across observed classes and uses a bounded candidate pool to refresh exemplars in the current feature representation. On CIFAR-100, it outperforms iCaRL in final accuracy and forgetting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In class-incremental learning, replay must preserve earlier classes as the feature representation changes, but only a bounded active exemplar set can be stored and replayed. Existing methods such as iCaRL leave room for improvement in final accuracy and forgetting, motivating a better allocation and refresh strategy.

Method: Uniform Herding allocates the current active exemplar set evenly across observed classes and uses a bounded candidate pool to refresh the chosen exemplars in the current feature representation. It is evaluated against alternatives for exemplar selection (NME, herding) and distillation, with an end-to-end comparison to iCaRL on CIFAR-100 with ten class-incremental tasks.

Result: With a ResNet-18 backbone, active budget M=2000, retrieval budget b=64, and three seeds, Uniform Herding achieves 44.00±0.51% final average accuracy and 17.22±0.43% forgetting, versus 42.33±1.20% and 24.87±1.11% for iCaRL. Replacing NME or herding decreased final accuracy, while removing distillation increased forgetting. The retrieval budget had a smaller effect than the active budget.

Conclusion: Uniform Herding improves accuracy and reduces forgetting relative to iCaRL under the tested protocol. However, the comparison is end-to-end and does not isolate the effect of refresh from other protocol differences, and the findings are limited to the tested protocol.

Abstract: As the feature representation changes, replay must preserve the earlier classes. However, only a bounded active exemplar set can be replayed. We propose Uniform Herding, which allocates the current active set across observed classes and uses a bounded candidate pool to refresh their chosen exemplars in the current representation. On CIFAR-100 with ten class-incremental tasks, a ResNet-18 backbone, active budget $M=2{,}000$, retrieval budget $b=64$, and three seeds, Uniform Herding obtains $44.00\pm0.51\%$ final average accuracy and $17.22\pm0.43\%$ forgetting, compared with $42.33\pm1.20\%$ and $24.87\pm1.11\%$ for iCaRL. Within the Uniform Herding protocol, final accuracy decreased when NME or herding was replaced with the tested alternatives, while forgetting increased when distillation was removed. Changing the retrieval budget has a smaller effect across the tested range than changing the active budget. The comparison with iCaRL is end-to-end. It does not isolate the effect of refresh from the other protocol differences. These results are limited to the tested protocol.

</details>


### [142] [Explanatory Engagement Under Rare Anomalous Failure: Asymptotic Rarity in Model Behavior (or: The Asymptotic AI)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13063)
*Sam Mao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper investigates whether an LLM's explanatory engagement (length, specificity, confidence) changes as tool-call failures become increasingly rare, using a local harness on three open-weight models across eight failure probabilities and five elicitation conditions. Pooled results show a flat monotonic decline, but splitting by condition reveals that elicitation structure strongly moderates the predicted "rise-then-collapse" pattern, with the clearest rise (followed by a plateau, not collapse) appearing under immediate forced explanation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work on abnormal LLM behavior asks only whether models notice anomalies. The paper narrows this to: once a model sits in a workflow with a low, controllable failure rate, does its explanatory engagement change as failures grow asymptotically rarer? It hypothesizes a rise in engagement as failures become rarer, then a collapse near a detectability threshold.

Method: A local, zero-cost harness runs a repeated tool-call task on three open-weight models (qwen3:8b, llama3.1:8b, mistral:7b), where one call fails with probability p swept across eight rates (0.2 to 0.0001), under five elicitation conditions (from immediate prompting to none). Engagement is measured via explanation length, specificity, and self-reported confidence. A companion guaranteed-failure run (72 cells) backfills rates where random sampling produced zero real failures.

Result: Pooled across conditions, the hypothesized rise-then-collapse was false: length fell in a flat, monotonic pattern. Splitting by condition overturned this. Under immediate_forced, the rise was confirmed but followed by a plateau, not a collapse (length peaks at 28.4 words at p=0.05, settles at 17.4-19.0 at rarest rates; confidence rises unevenly from ~53% to the 70s-90s). Under grouped_runs, no collapse appears. Under passive_unprompted, aggregate magnitude is a floor artifact, but a recovered logging gap revealed model-specific self-monitoring: llama3.1:8b volunteers structured confidence reports unprompted (sometimes eroding its own confidence as trials accumulate), while the other two do so only once as boilerplate. The guaranteed-failure run shows models differ in whether they recognize an anomaly, distinct from engagement once recognized.

Conclusion: Elicitation structure is a first-class moderator of collapse observability; the predicted engagement rise appears only under forced explanation and plateaus rather than collapses. Models also differ in anomaly recognition independently of engagement. A key limitation is that discrete rate points cannot capture behavior between them, a direction for future work.

Abstract: Prior work on LLM behavior under anomalous conditions asks whether a model notices anomalies. We ask a narrower question: once a model sits in a workflow with a low, controllable failure rate, does its explanatory engagement - length, specificity, self-reported confidence - change as failure grows asymptotically rarer? We built a local, zero-cost harness on three open-weight models (qwen3:8b, llama3.1:8b, mistral:7b) running a repeated tool-call task where one call fails at probability p, swept across eight rates from 0.2 to 0.0001, under five elicitation conditions from immediate prompting to none. We hypothesized a rise in engagement as failures grew rarer, then a collapse near a detectability threshold. Pooled across conditions this appeared false: length fell in a flat, monotonic pattern. Splitting by condition overturned that. Under immediate_forced, where the model must explain every failure instantly, the predicted rise is confirmed but followed by a plateau, not a collapse: length peaks at 28.4 words at p=0.05, settles to 17.4-19.0 words at the rarest rates, and confidence rises unevenly from about 53% to the 70s-90s. Under grouped_runs, explanation batched to run-end, no collapse appears. Under passive_unprompted, aggregate magnitude is a floor artifact, but a recovered logging gap revealed real, model-specific self-monitoring: llama3.1:8b volunteers structured confidence reports unprompted, sometimes eroding its own confidence as trials accumulate; the other two do so only once, as boilerplate. Elicitation structure is a first-class moderator of collapse observability. A companion guaranteed-failure run (72 cells, backfilling rates where random sampling gave zero real failures) shows models differ in whether they recognize an anomaly, distinct from engagement once recognized. Limitation: discrete rate points cannot capture behavior between them, a direction for future work.

</details>


### [143] [Behavioral Reprogramming of Open-Weights Models: Cognitive Plasticity and Alignment Bounds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13069)
*Lucia Malíčková*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper empirically re-programs open-weight LLMs from passive assistants into proactive, Socratic questioners using parameter-efficient fine-tuning and DPO, mapping precise compute/rank/epoch bounds across 405 HPC jobs and testing cross-lingual persona transfer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are predominantly aligned as passive, sycophantic assistants. The authors challenge this default paradigm by testing whether open-weight model behavior can be reprogrammed into a proactive, Socratic conversational framework that generates questions at high frequency, under strictly constrained HPC conditions for compute efficiency.

Method: A massively parallelized hyperparameter sweep of 405 HPC jobs defines bounds for parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT). They identify a LoRA rank threshold at r=16, run extensive epoch ablations establishing an optimal training window e∈[2,3], scale model capacity to 14B parameters, and apply Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) to decouple assertive behavior from localized syntax. Cross-lingual stress testing evaluates zero-shot persona transfer.

Result: Minimum validation loss of 0.919 within e∈[2,3] depending on dataset density; 14B model achieved lower localized evaluation perplexity of 1.414. DPO successfully decoupled assertive behavior from localized syntax. Cross-lingual tests showed robust persona transfer in closely related linguistic families but degradation in morphologically distant targets.

Conclusion: The findings establish a rigorous empirical framework for compute-efficient, cross-lingual behavioral modification of LLMs, demonstrating that open-weight architectures can be reprogrammed from passive to proactive Socratic behavior with well-defined mathematical and computational bounds.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are predominantly aligned to function as passive, sycophantic assistants. We challenge this default paradigm by empirically evaluating the cognitive plasticity of open-weight architectures when subjected to rigorous behavioral reprogramming. Our objective is to induce a proactive, Socratic conversational framework, characterized by high-frequency question generation under strictly constrained high-performance computing (HPC) conditions. Through a massively parallelized hyperparameter sweep comprising 405 HPC jobs, we define precise mathematical bounds for parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT). We identify an architectural threshold at LoRA rank $r=16$ and demonstrate via extensive epoch ablation that generalization capacity strictly reaches its optimal convergence within an optimized training window of $e \in [2, 3]$ depending on dataset density (minimum validation loss of 0.919). Furthermore, scaling model capacity to 14B parameters yielded a lower localized evaluation perplexity (1.414). Subsequent Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) successfully decoupled the underlying assertive behavior from localized syntax, while rigorous cross-lingual stress testing reveals both the capabilities and the structural boundaries of zero-shot persona transfer, demonstrating robust alignment in closely related linguistic families alongside identifiable degradation pathways in morphologically distant targets. These findings establish a rigorous empirical framework for compute-efficient, cross-lingual behavioral modification.

</details>


### [144] [EEG-PRIME: Prototype-Aligned Representation Learning with Multi-Level Conditioning for EEG Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13072)
*Shuailei Zhang,Muyun Jiang,Wei Zhang,Jinbo Chen,Zhiwei Guo,Yong Li,Yi Ding,Cuntai Guan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EEG-PRIME is a two-stage EEG foundation model combining masked pretraining with prototype-aligned instruction tuning to achieve instruction-aware, subject-invariant, cross-dataset multi-task decoding, showing strong zero-shot transfer on held-out datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: EEG decoding models generalize poorly across datasets and subjects due to domain shifts from differing acquisition protocols and individual neurophysiology. The goal is a foundation model that performs robust multi-task decoding across heterogeneous BCI paradigms without per-target fine-tuning.

Method: EEG-PRIME uses two stages: (1) pretraining an EEG encoder via masked reconstruction with frequency-cutoff spectral augmentation to learn transferable representations; (2) instruction tuning with task-semantic, dataset-specific, and subject-invariant conditioning, where the conditioning signal modulates a Q-Former through Layer-wise Query Modulation. Frozen text embeddings of class labels act as prototypes for cosine-similarity-based prediction across heterogeneous label spaces.

Result: Across sixteen datasets covering motor imagery, emotion recognition, ADHD detection, covert speech, and mental workload, EEG-PRIME consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines and prior EEG foundation models under cross-subject settings. On two held-out datasets, it achieves balanced accuracy comparable to within-session calibration models without target-domain optimization, calibration, or linear probing.

Conclusion: EEG-PRIME demonstrates effective zero-shot transfer by leveraging instruction conditioning and prototype-based prediction, enabling strong cross-dataset, cross-subject decoding without any target-domain adaptation, positioning it as a promising foundation model for EEG-based BCI.

Abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) decoding models often generalize poorly across datasets and subjects due to domain shifts in acquisition protocols and individual neurophysiology. We propose EEG-PRIME, a two-stage EEG foundation model for cross-dataset multi-task decoding. EEG-PRIME combines masked pretraining with prototype-aligned instruction tuning to enable instruction-aware and subject-invariant decoding across diverse BCI paradigms. During pretraining, an EEG encoder learns transferable representations through masked reconstruction with frequency-cutoff spectral augmentation. During instruction tuning, EEG-PRIME incorporates task-semantic, dataset-specific, and subject-invariant conditioning. The resulting conditioning signal modulates the Q-Former through Layer-wise Query Modulation, while frozen text embeddings of class labels serve as prototypes for cosine-similarity-based prediction across heterogeneous label spaces. Experiments on sixteen datasets covering motor imagery, emotion recognition, ADHD detection, covert speech, and mental workload show consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines and prior EEG foundation models under cross-subject settings. On two additional held-out datasets, EEG-PRIME achieves balanced accuracy comparable to within-session calibration models without target-domain optimization, calibration, or linear probing, demonstrating promising zero-shot transfer capability.

</details>


### [145] [SPADE: Speculative Decoding for Precise and Low Cost Distributed Edge Cloud Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13076)
*Divya Jyoti Bajpai,Kishan Kumar Upadhyay,Manjesh Kumar Hanawal*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A distributed speculative-decoding framework splits LLM inference between an edge-based compact draft model and a cloud-based large verifier model, cutting cloud calls by 76% with no accuracy loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM deployment faces a trade-off: edge-only smaller models reduce compute/cost but lose accuracy, while cloud-only big models preserve accuracy but incur expensive per-token computation. The authors seek a framework that achieves big-model accuracy while reducing inference time and cloud cost.

Method: The framework integrates speculative decoding (SD) across edge and cloud. A compact draft model deployed on the edge generates candidate tokens rapidly; a large verifier model on the cloud validates these tokens in parallel. Accepted tokens are kept, and only rejections trigger verifier correction, drastically reducing cloud queries. The design is plug-and-play (no retraining) and shifts most computation to the edge.

Result: Experiments on SpecBench and CNN/Dailymail across multiple NLP tasks show the approach reduces cloud model calls by 76% with zero accuracy loss compared to running the full (big) model.

Conclusion: The framework provides a practical, scalable, cost-efficient, and accurate path for deploying LLMs in real-world settings, preserving big-model accuracy while lowering inference time and cloud cost without retraining.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success in natural language understanding and generation, but their deployment is constrained by high computational demands. Deploying smaller LLMs directly on the edge can circumvent this, but with degraded accuracy. Deploying smaller cloud-based big LLMs preserves performance, but at the cost of expensive per-token computation. We present a distributed inference framework, \our{}, that integrates speculative decoding (SD) across edge and cloud. A compact draft model deployed on the edge generates candidate tokens rapidly, and a large verifier model on the cloud validates these tokens in parallel. Accepted tokens are retained, while only rejections trigger verifier correction, substantially reducing the number of cloud queries. Our plug-and-play design shifts the bulk of computation to the edge, significantly lowers inference time and cloud cost, and preserves the accuracy of the big model without any retraining requirement. Our approach demonstrates a practical path toward scalable, cost-efficient, and accurate deployment of LLMs in real-world environments. Experimental results across multiple Natural Language Processing tasks using SpecBench and CNN/Dailymail datasets demonstrate that \our{} reduces the cloud model calls by $76\%$ with zero loss in accuracy as compared to the full model.

</details>


### [146] [Robust Dempster-Shafer Evidence Fusion with Chaos-Conflict Measurement and Historical-Experience Weighting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13108)
*Huiyu Li,Weibo Liu,Xinru Xu,Dongchen Gao,Meng Zhang,Junhua Hu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a unified Dempster-Shafer evidence fusion framework that jointly measures conflict/non-specificity and leverages historical reliability via regret theory, achieving state-of-the-art classification performance across 16 benchmark datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing conflict measures assess inter-evidence inconsistency and intra-evidence uncertainty independently, giving incomplete evaluations. Moreover, current fusion methods evaluate evidence sources only through instantaneous comparisons, ignoring long-term reliability across diverse decision contexts.

Method: The framework introduces: (1) a chaos-conflict measurement that jointly quantifies cross-evidence conflict and intra-evidence non-specificity, with five formally proven properties; (2) a historical-experience-driven weighting scheme that partitions the decision space via spectral clustering and applies regret theory to compute context-specific reliability profiles from past fusion outcomes; (3) a hybrid combination rule that adaptively balances uncertainty preservation against weighted consensus based on global conflict level; and (4) a belief-interval decision strategy enabling robust classification while preserving epistemic uncertainty.

Result: On 16 real-world benchmark datasets, the framework achieves an average F1 score of 85.78 and mean AUC of 93.30, outperforming eight DST-based baselines and three gradient boosting methods. Ablation analysis confirms the contribution of each proposed component.

Conclusion: The framework offers an effective approach for adaptive evidence fusion in multi-source decision making, addressing both incomplete conflict assessment and the lack of long-term reliability modeling.

Abstract: Multi-source evidence fusion under Dempster-Shafer theory faces two persistent challenges: existing conflict measures assess inter-evidence inconsistency and intra-evidence uncertainty independently, yielding incomplete evaluations, and current fusion methods evaluate evidence sources exclusively through instantaneous comparisns without exploiting their long-term reliability across diverse decision contexts. This paper proposes a unified evidence reasoning framework that addresses both limitations. Specifically, a chaos-conflict measurement is introduced to jointly quantify cross-evidence conflict and intra-evidence non-specificity, with five formally proven properties ensuring consistent assessment. A historical experience driven weighting scheme partitions the decision space via spectral clustering and applies regret theory to compute context-specific reliability profiles from past fusion outcomes. These mechanisms feed into a hybrid combination rule that adaptively balances uncertainty preservation against weighted consensus, controlled by the global conflict level, followed by a belief-interval decision strategy that enables robust classification without discarding epistemic uncertainty. Experiments on 16 real-world benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves an average F1 score of 85.78 and a mean AUC of 93.30, outperforming eight DST-based baselines and three gradient boosting methods. Ablation analysis confirms the contribution of each component we proposed. The framework offers an effective approach for adaptive evidence fusion in multi-source decision making.

</details>


### [147] [SkillEvo: Self-Renewing Evolution Gradients from Multi-Turn Interaction Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13120)
*Qianxi Yan,Chunrong Chen,Jiuzhou Zhao,Min Zhang,Yongzhou Xu,Xiaochuan Xu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SkillEvo proposes a two-component framework for sustained Agent Skill evolution: multi-turn user simulation as a trustworthy feedback generator (to keep supplying evolution gradients), plus an independent governance layer that actively repairs factual degradation and structural bloat rather than passively rejecting candidates. It outperforms self-reflection evolution by 23.0 points and single-turn QA-driven evolution by 15.4 points across 6 cloud-service categories, 9 production Skills, and 98 skill-reference files.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current Agent Skills are hand-authored or produced in a single LLM generation pass with no closed loop for improvement from real interaction failures. Recent closed-loop work relies on single-turn QA evaluation, whose evolution gradient decays after the first round patches immediately visible gaps, leaving multi-turn defects invisible and causing evolution to stall. Additionally, governance relies only on an end-to-end scalar verification score that can reject degraded candidates but cannot localize or repair their structural causes. The authors argue the binding constraint on sustained skill evolution is not editing capability or iteration count, but whether evaluation feedback keeps supplying trustworthy evolution gradients.

Method: SkillEval comprises two components: (1) Trustworthy feedback generation: it recasts multi-turn user simulation from a mere evaluation endpoint into a feedback generator, where follow-up questions expose defects layer by layer so each revision round both consumes and produces new feedback. (2) Controllable governance: it replaces passive scalar-gate rejection with an independent governance layer that actively repairs factual degradation and structural bloat, preventing the evolution gradient from drifting as degradation accumulates.

Result: Across six categories of cloud services, 9 production Skills, and 98 skill-reference files, SkillEvo surpasses self-reflection-based evolution by 23.0 points and single-turn-QA-driven evolution by 15.4 points.

Conclusion: The key to sustained skill evolution is maintaining trustworthy evolution gradients through multi-turn feedback generation, complemented by an active governance layer that constrains the gradient's direction, enabling SkillEvo to significantly outperform prior self-reflection and single-turn-QA evolution baselines.

Abstract: Agent Skills are today either hand-authored or produced in a single LLM generation pass, and consequently possess no closed loop through which they might improve from the interaction failures they actually cause. Recent work does close this loop, but derives its feedback from single-turn question-answering evaluation. The consequence is a sharp asymmetry: once the first round has patched the gaps that a single exchange can reveal, the evolution gradient decays, the defects that surface only across multiple turns remain invisible, and evolution stalls. Governance in these systems is likewise driven by an end-to-end verification score, a scalar gate that can reject a degraded candidate but can neither localize nor repair its structural cause. We argue that the binding constraint on sustained skill evolution is neither editing capability nor the number of iterations, but whether the evaluation feedback keeps supplying trustworthy evolution gradients. We introduce SkillEvo, in which trustworthy feedback generates the gradient and controllable governance constrains its direction. The first component recasts multi-turn user simulation from an evaluation endpoint into a feedback generator: follow-up questions expose defects layer by layer, so that every round of revision both consumes feedback and produces new feedback. The second replaces the passive rejection of a scalar gate with an independent governance layer that actively repairs factual degradation and structural bloat, preventing the gradient from drifting as degradation accumulates. Across six categories of cloud services, 9 production Skills, and 98 skill-reference files, SkillEvo surpasses self-reflection-based evolution by 23.0 points and single- turn-QA-driven evolution by 15.4 points.

</details>


### [148] [Numeracy in Large Language Models: Fundamental Limitations and Paths to Improvement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13129)
*Aoxin Ni*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This survey analyzes LLMs' unreliable basic numerical skills (separate from high-level math reasoning), proposes the Numerical Grounding Framework (RG + PG) to organize diagnostics, failure modes, explanations, and mitigations, and evaluates three frontier model families. It finds architectural fixes help only from-scratch models, while practitioners must rely on fine-tuning, reasoning scaffolds, and external tools.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Although LLMs perform well on mathematical reasoning benchmarks, they remain unreliable on elementary numerical tasks (magnitude comparison, large-integer arithmetic, fractions, scientific notation). The authors argue basic numeracy is a distinct capability from high-level reasoning and needs dedicated analysis and mitigation.

Method: The paper introduces the Numerical Grounding Framework (NGF), decomposing numeracy into Representational Grounding (RG: mapping numeral forms to value, magnitude, and equivalent representations) and Procedural Grounding (PG: executing arithmetic operations per their mathematical definitions). Using NGF, it organizes diagnostic benchmarks, failure modes, structural explanations (tokenization, positional encoding, embedding geometry, pretraining-data distribution), and mitigation strategies. It also applies NGF to evaluate three frontier model families across Number Cookbook, NumericBench, and GSM-Symbolic, comparing atomic, contextual, and reasoning-assisted numeracy.

Result: Architectural interventions (digit-aware tokenization, Abacus Embeddings) improve models trained from scratch but are unavailable to users of pretrained systems. For those users, supervised fine-tuning, reasoning scaffolds, and external tools are more practical mitigations.

Conclusion: The authors provide deployment recommendations and research directions for more reliable numerical behavior in foundation models, emphasizing the need to treat basic numerical grounding as a first-class capability distinct from high-level mathematical reasoning.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve strong results on mathematical reasoning benchmarks yet remain unreliable on elementary numerical tasks, including magnitude comparison, large-integer arithmetic, fractions, and scientific notation. This survey examines basic numerical understanding as a capability distinct from high-level mathematical reasoning. We propose the Numerical Grounding Framework (NGF), which decomposes numeracy into Representational Grounding (RG), mapping numeral forms to value, magnitude, and equivalent representations, and Procedural Grounding (PG), executing arithmetic operations in accordance with their mathematical definitions. Using NGF, we organize recent diagnostic benchmarks, failure modes, structural explanations, and mitigation strategies. We review evidence concerning tokenization, positional encoding, embedding geometry, and pretraining-data distribution. We also apply NGF in a coordinated evaluation of three frontier model families across Number Cookbook, NumericBench, and GSM-Symbolic, comparing atomic, contextual, and reasoning-assisted numeracy. Architectural interventions such as digit-aware tokenization and Abacus Embeddings can improve models trained from scratch but are generally unavailable to users of pretrained systems, for whom supervised fine-tuning, reasoning scaffolds, and external tools are more practical. We conclude with deployment recommendations and research directions for more reliable numerical behavior in foundation models.

</details>


### [149] [Rethinking Normalization Placement for LLMs: Post-Norm under Curriculum Depth Growing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13156)
*Sheng Ren,Yadong Wang,Naiqiang Tan,Jiangang Kong,Jun Fang,Rui Liu,Jun Wang,Kai Chen,Lipeng Liang,Xiang Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether normalization placement (pre-norm vs. post-norm) interacts with training curriculum in Transformers, challenging the standard pre-norm assumption when depth is introduced gradually via curriculum growth.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pre-norm is the standard choice for modern Transformers under joint (full-depth) training, but the paper questions whether this holds when depth is added via curriculum. In curriculum depth growth, each appended block receives the boundary representation from a trained prefix, so normalization placement affects forward conditioning of new blocks—a regime where pre-norm's advantages may not persist.

Method: A controlled distillation study using a Qwen3-8B teacher and a nine-layer student. The authors compare pre-norm and post-norm under joint training versus curriculum depth growth, with controls: (1) matching student active-layer tokens (post-joint control), (2) single-block and freeze controls to isolate the effect of block appending, and (3) boundary diagnostics (residual scale and identity-mapping measurements) on a fixed batch.

Result: Under joint training, pre-norm and post-norm are nearly identical (0.0004 validation CE difference). Under curriculum growth, post-norm beats pre-norm by 0.0328 validation CE—an order of magnitude larger. The ranking crosses over during the curriculum once blocks are appended. Controls rule out compute and shallow-block quality/retraining as explanations. Boundary diagnostics show post-norm maintains stable residual scales while pre-norm exhibits structural-token scale drift, and the final pre-grow block is nearly identity-mapped.

Conclusion: Normalization placement and training curriculum interact and should be treated as coupled design choices in distillation settings. Post-norm is preferable when depth is introduced through curriculum growth, consistent with boundary-scale conditioning after new blocks are appended.

Abstract: Pre-norm is the standard normalization placement in modern Transformers because it facilitates joint optimization of full-depth models. We ask whether this preference persists when depth is introduced through a curriculum. In curriculum depth growth, each appended block receives the boundary representation produced by a trained prefix, making normalization placement relevant to forward conditioning. We therefore test whether placement and training curriculum interact. In a controlled distillation study with a Qwen3-8B teacher and a nine-layer student, pre-norm and post-norm are indistinguishable under joint training, differing by $0.0004$ validation CE, while post-norm improves over pre-norm by $0.0328$ under curriculum growth, an order of magnitude larger. A post-joint control matched by student active-layer tokens remains worse than post-grow, which rules out compute as the sole explanation. The ranking crosses over during the curriculum: post-norm takes the lead once blocks are appended. Single-block and freeze controls localize the ranking change to block appending rather than shallow-block quality or retraining. Boundary diagnostics associate post-norm with stable residual scales and pre-norm with structural-token scale drift; on a fixed batch, the final pre-grow block is also nearly identity-mapped. Together with the phase-wise crossover, these observations are consistent with boundary-scale conditioning after new blocks are appended. The results motivate treating normalization placement and training curriculum as coupled design choices in this distillation setting.

</details>


### [150] [SkillShapley: Boundary-Adaptive Shapley Valuation for Skill Step Attribution in LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13173)
*Chang Liu,Yuqi Zhang,Yiman Zhong,Boyi Liu,Hengjun Wang,Shuyue Wei*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SkillShapley is a two-phase, Shapley value-based framework that attributes contributions to individual steps in agent skills, enabling efficient identification of high- and low-value steps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agent skills (external instructions for long procedural tasks) are typically created manually or from execution traces, but there is no principled way to quantify how much each step contributes to overall skill performance on a specific task. The paper addresses this open problem of step-level contribution attribution.

Method: SkillShapley models skill-step attribution as a Shapley value-based contribution estimation problem. It adopts a two-phase design driven by two empirical insights: (1) discretized benchmark rewards create sharp performance cliffs, and (2) step interactions are largely additive rather than synergistic. Phase one identifies informative coalitional regions; phase two adaptively samples new coalitions that yield reusable marginal evidence for efficient Shapley value estimation.

Result: Experiments on skills from the SkillsBench benchmark show that SkillShapley effectively and efficiently identifies high-value and low-value skill steps, and yields several key takeaways for agent skill creation.

Conclusion: SkillShapley demonstrates that Shapley value-based step-level attribution is a practical and efficient approach for understanding agent skill contributions, offering actionable insights to improve how agent skills are created.

Abstract: Agent skills are crucial external instructions that enable language agents to execute long procedural tasks such as coding or document processing. Existing agent skills are primarily created through human manual crafting or agent execution traces, with limited understanding of how each step contributes to overall skill performance on specific tasks; i.e., there remains an open problem in quantifying the contribution of individual steps within an agent skill. To address this issue, we first model skill-step attribution as a Shapley value-based contribution estimation problem, and then propose SkillShapley, a step-level attribution framework for agent skills. Notably, SkillShapley operates in two phases, motivated by key empirical insights, i.e., discretized benchmark rewards that create sharp performance cliffs, and step interactions that are largely additive rather than synergistic. Specifically, it first identifies informative coalitional regions, and then adaptively samples new coalitions that can yield reusable marginal evidence. Experiments on skills from the widely adopted SkillsBench demonstrate that our SkillShapley can effectively and efficiently identify high- or low-value skill steps, providing several key takeaways for agent skill creation.

</details>


### [151] [Teach the Magnitude, Not the Direction: Verifier-Bounded Credit Assignment for Multi-Turn Multi-step LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13179)
*Zechuan Wang,Siyuan Lu,Hongxuan Zhang,Linjian Mo,Chenyi Zhuang,Leilei Gan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CrEST is a hierarchical credit assignment framework for training multi-turn tool-use agents that combines RLVR's verifier-bounded ceiling with dense token-level signals from a privileged self-teacher, resolving credit at both turn and token levels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RLVR has a verifier-bounded performance ceiling but conflates heterogeneous per-turn outcomes into a single trajectory-level reward signal (credit assignment dilution). On-policy distillation offers dense per-token supervision but is teacher-bounded or suffers from gradient concentration collapse. The paper seeks dense credit assignment without losing the verifier-bounded ceiling.

Method: CrEST resolves credit hierarchically: (1) turn-segmented verified advantages address inter-turn dilution by segmenting the trajectory into turns; (2) entropy-gated self-teacher modulation refines intra-turn token contributions, demoting the teacher from determining update directions to only modulating update magnitudes.

Result: CrEST consistently outperforms both RL and distillation baselines on BFCL V3 and WildToolBench across two model scales, with the largest gains on long-trajectory and strict session-level metrics.

Conclusion: The teacher's role in policy optimization can be reduced from determining update directions to modulating update magnitudes, enabling dense credit assignment without sacrificing the verifier-bounded ceiling.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) offers a verifier-bounded performance ceiling for training multi-turn tool-use agents, yet its trajectory-level credit assignment conflates heterogeneous per-turn outcomes into a single reward signal. On-policy distillation provides dense per-token supervision but is either teacher-bounded or prone to gradient concentration collapse. We introduce $\textbf{CrEST}$, a hierarchical credit assignment framework that retains RL's verifier-bounded ceiling while incorporating dense token-level signals from a privileged self-teacher. $\textbf{CrEST}$ resolves credit at two levels: turn-segmented verified advantages address inter-turn dilution, while entropy-gated self-teacher modulation refines intra-turn token contributions. Experiments on BFCL V3 and WildToolBench show that $\textbf{CrEST}$ consistently outperforms both RL and distillation baselines across two model scales, with the largest gains on long-trajectory and strict session-level metrics. Our work demonstrates that the teacher's role in policy optimization can be reduced from determining update directions to modulating update magnitudes, unlocking dense credit assignment without sacrificing the verifier-bounded ceiling.

</details>


### [152] [TsuGO: Probing Search Efficiency in LLM Reasoning via Go Life-and-Death Problems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13221)
*Shunwen Bai,Ziping Ma,Chaoyang Zhang,Yarong Wang,Jiale Liu,Zhen Qin,Qingpei Guo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TsuGO is a process-level benchmark that uses Go life-and-death (tsumego) problems to measure how efficiently LLMs organize search—specifically candidate generation, verification, branch comparison, and backtracking—reporting Search Efficiency, Token Efficiency, and diagnostic visualizations rather than only final-answer accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM reasoning evaluation focuses on final-answer accuracy or CoT coherence/redundancy, and most benchmarks have single objectives solvable by static capabilities (derivation, tool use), leaving search organization and reasoning-resource allocation unmeasured. The authors argue that how models plan reasoning paths and allocate resources is a missing evaluation dimension.

Method: TsuGO constrains the solution space to closed, verifiable tsumego problems with inherent adversarial structure, which force candidate generation, response checking, branch comparison, and backtracking. It disentangles domain knowledge from search organization, parses the CoT into a structured search tree, and computes Search Efficiency, Token Efficiency, plus diagnostic metrics and visualizations.

Result: Experiments show current LLMs remain far from stable tsumego solving: stronger models succeed by finding the correct candidate earlier and sustaining effort on productive branches, but most models behave closer to unguided search than to neural-guided KataGo. Longer CoT or higher Token Efficiency does not necessarily imply better search.

Conclusion: Search organization and reasoning-resource allocation are missing dimensions in LLM reasoning evaluation, and TsuGO provides a rigorous, verifiable framework for measuring search efficiency in process-level reasoning.

Abstract: The evaluation of LLM reasoning is moving from final-answer accuracy to process-level assessment, yet existing methods still fail to capture how models plan reasoning paths and allocate reasoning resources--that is, how they organize search. Prior process-level methods focus on the coherence and redundancy of chain-of-thought (CoT), and most benchmark tasks have a single objective solvable by static capabilities such as derivation and tool use, leaving search organization unmeasured. We introduce TsuGO, a process-level reasoning benchmark for evaluating Search Efficiency in LLM reasoning through Go life-and-death problems. These problems provide closed and verifiable solution spaces with an inherent adversarial structure, making candidate generation, response checking, branch comparison, and backtracking necessary parts of reasoning rather than incidental trace patterns. By constraining the solution space, TsuGO disentangles domain knowledge from search organization, parses CoT into a structured search tree, and reports Search Efficiency together with Token Efficiency and other diagnostic metrics and visualizations. Experiments show that current LLMs remain far from stable tsumego solving: stronger models succeed by finding the correct candidate earlier and sustaining effort on productive branches, but most models still behave much closer to unguided search algorithms than to neural-guided KataGo. Longer CoT or higher Token Efficiency does not necessarily imply better search. Our results identify search organization and reasoning-resource allocation as missing dimensions in LLM reasoning evaluation.

</details>


### [153] [Capability Sheaves for Compositional Agent-Harness Repair: Controlled Quotients and a Real-Repository Stress Test](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13228)
*Saveliy Batruin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper uses a finite "capability sheaf" to model conflicts among agent components over shared state, with an exact CSP defining acceptance and a relative cohomology class serving as a diagnostic/search feature. A controlled experiment confirms the method is merely invariant to stale representatives (not superior to exact CSP), while a larger SWE-bench-derived discovery test shows no statistically supported real-world cohomological advantage; the confirmatory split remains sealed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agent harnesses combine many components (retrieval, routing, state, provenance, verification) that may each succeed locally yet disagree over shared state. The paper seeks a rigorous, finite mathematical model of this consistency failure, with a principled way to detect and search across coherent global configurations.

Method: Model component behavior as a finite capability sheaf: stalks carry typed behavior signatures, restriction maps retain shared fields, and valid runs are global sections. Acceptance is defined by an exact finite constraint-satisfaction problem (CSP), while a linearized relative cohomology class supplies diagnostics/search. Experiments include a controlled 20-task-cluster setup with hidden interior mediators (nuisance raw states, quotienting coboundaries) and a discovery split from SWE-bench Multilingual (PatchFuseBench) with 160 issues, 20 repos, 875 candidate patches, 2,579 edit atoms, and 153 newly executed patches.

Result: Controlled experiment: quotienting coboundaries cuts candidate budget from 2,000 to 1,000 per cluster; aligning hidden state closes the gap; exact CSP matches the quotient, showing invariance to stale representatives rather than superiority. Discovery split: a pool-level construction is constant (since [b-Dx]=[b] in coker D) and cannot rank configurations; a candidate-indexed repair is nontrivial on 848/875 candidates, varies within 120/160 issues, resolves 118 vs 116 issues for a matched noncohomological selector (sign-flip p=0.75, unsupported across repos). A leave-one-repository-out abstention gate reaches 127/160, tying the strong anchor and exceeding its matched gate by one issue (p=1.0). The discovery gate fails and the confirmatory split remains sealed.

Conclusion: The capability-sheaf/CSP/cohomology framework cleanly captures a controlled invariance mechanism and an identifiability correction, but it does not demonstrate a real-world cohomological advantage; the confirmatory split is left unopened.

Abstract: Agent harnesses combine retrieval, routing, state, provenance, and verification, but locally successful components may disagree on shared state. We model this failure with a finite \emph{capability sheaf}: stalks encode typed behavior signatures, restriction maps retain shared fields, and accepted runs are useful global sections. An exact finite constraint-satisfaction problem (CSP) defines acceptance, while a linearized relative cohomology class provides a diagnostic and search feature.
  A controlled experiment over 20 task clusters introduces hidden interior mediators whose raw states are nuisance variables. Quotienting their coboundaries reduces the candidate budget from 2,000 to 1,000 per cluster; aligning the hidden state removes the gap. Exact CSP matches the quotient, so the result demonstrates invariance to stale representatives, not superiority over exact reasoning.
  We then test the method on a discovery split from the SWE-bench Multilingual pool of PatchFuseBench: 160 issues from 20 repositories, 875 real candidate patches, 2,579 source-aware edit atoms, and 153 newly executed patches. A first pool-level construction is constant because $[b-Dx]=[b]$ in $\operatorname{coker}D$ and therefore cannot rank configurations. A candidate-indexed repair is nontrivial on 848/875 candidates and varies within 120/160 issues. It resolves 118 issues versus 116 for a matched noncohomological selector, but the difference is not supported across repositories (exact sign-flip $p=0.75$). A leave-one-repository-out abstention gate reaches 127/160, tying the strong anchor and exceeding its matched gate by one issue ($p=1.0$). The discovery gate therefore fails and the confirmatory split remains sealed. The study supports the controlled invariance mechanism and an identifiability correction, but not a real-world cohomological advantage.

</details>


### [154] [vToken: Token-Level Virtualization for Reclaimable KV Caches](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13263)
*Yuanhang Gao,Xiangrui Yang,Yuanfeng Chen,Hongjia Chen,Qianru Lv,Wenfei Wu,Dongsheng Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: vToken is a token-level virtualization layer for LLM serving that separates logical token lifetimes from physical KV-cache block placement, enabling finer-grained eviction than PagedAttention's block-level management. It reduces retained KV blocks by 27.2%–72.3%, improves SLA-constrained throughput up to 1.37×, and doubles maximum feasible concurrency under constrained KV budgets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM serving is bottlenecked by KV-cache memory, which grows with sequence length and batch size. PagedAttention reduces allocator-level fragmentation using fixed-size blocks, but modern KV eviction algorithms operate at token granularity, which mismatches block-level management and creates intra-block fragmentation—leaving large fractions of allocated KV memory unreclaimable.

Method: vToken introduces a lightweight token-level virtualization layer that decouples logical token liveness from physical block placement. It maintains a stable logical token view via token-table indirection and reclaims physical memory by asynchronously repacking live tokens. The design preserves PagedAttention kernels and CUDA Graph compatibility, and is implemented in vLLM, evaluated with H2O, Random, and Scissorhands eviction policies.

Result: Compared to a paired Naive-Evict baseline, vToken reduces retained KV blocks per request by 27.2%–72.3% and improves SLA-constrained throughput by up to 1.37×. Under a constrained active-KV budget, it extends maximum feasible concurrency by up to 2×, while reducing the per-policy integration footprint from 500+ lines to under 50 lines.

Conclusion: By virtualizing token liveness at a finer granularity than physical block management while preserving existing kernels and CUDA Graph compatibility, vToken effectively eliminates intra-block fragmentation, enabling more aggressive KV eviction, higher throughput, and greater concurrency with minimal integration overhead.

Abstract: Large language model serving faces a critical memory bottleneck: the KV cache grows with sequence length and batch size. PagedAttention uses fixed-size memory blocks to reduce allocator-level fragmentation, but recent KV eviction algorithms operate at a token granularity finer than block-level management. This mismatch causes intra-block fragmentation, leaving a large fraction of allocated KV memory unreclaimable. We present vToken, a lightweight token-level virtualization layer that decouples logical token liveness from physical block placement. vToken maintains a stable logical token view through token-table indirection and realizes physical reclamation by repacking live tokens asynchronously. The design preserves PagedAttention kernels and CUDA Graph compatibility. We implement vToken in vLLM and evaluate it with H2O, Random, and Scissorhands across models. Compared with a paired Naive-Evict baseline, vToken reduces retained KV blocks per request by 27.2\%--72.3\% and improves SLA-constrained throughput by up to 1.37$\times$. Under a constrained active-KV budget, it extends the maximum feasible concurrency by up to 2$\times$, while reducing the per-policy integration footprint from 500+ lines to under 50.

</details>


### [155] [Towards Context-Aware Clinical Motion Understanding in Daily Living at Home: Freezing of Gait Detection with Egocentric Vision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13283)
*Vayalet Stefanova,Diwas Lamsal,Margot Genbrugge,Maxim Yudayev,Christian Schlenstedt,Moran Gilat,Bart Vanrumste,Benjamin Filtjens*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether egocentric vision can add contextual information to wearable IMU sensing for detecting freezing of gait (FOG) in Parkinson's disease during daily living. Using synchronized ego-video, IMUs, and expert annotations from 13 PD participants at home, it compares frozen representations from pretrained ego-video and time-series foundation models against an IMU-based TCN. The IMU TCN performed best (42.3 F1, 83.0 AUROC), while V-JEPA2 ego-video features reached 32.6 F1 and 77.2 AUROC, showing above-chance but weaker discrimination, with qualitative evidence that vision captures complementary FOG-relevant information.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motion during activities of daily living is ambiguous from kinematics alone: similar inertial patterns can arise from intentional stopping, object interaction, or pathological impairment. FOG in Parkinson's disease is strongly context-dependent, so the authors hypothesize that egocentric vision can provide task-related context to help disambiguate these cases and improve wearable-sensor-based clinical motion understanding.

Method: Data were collected from 13 PD participants in their homes with synchronized egocentric video, wearable IMUs, and expert-annotated FOG labels. The authors evaluated frozen (non-finetuned) representations from pretrained ego-video and time-series foundation models, alongside an IMU-based temporal convolutional network (TCN) trained from scratch, all under leave-one-subject-out evaluation. Performance was measured with F1 and AUROC for event detection, complemented by qualitative analyses.

Result: The IMU-based TCN achieved the strongest event-detection performance (42.3 F1, 83.0 AUROC), outperforming V-JEPA2 ego-video features (32.6 F1, 77.2 AUROC). Ego-video alone did not beat IMU sensing but showed above-chance discrimination, and qualitative analyses suggest egocentric vision captures FOG-relevant information independent of IMUs.

Conclusion: Although ego-video alone underperforms IMU-based sensing, its above-chance discrimination and complementary information support using pretrained ego-video representations to add contextual information to wearable-sensor-based clinical motion understanding in daily living.

Abstract: Understanding motion in daily living requires context beyond kinematics, because similar inertial patterns during activities of daily living (ADLs) can reflect intentional stopping, object interaction, or pathological movement impairment. Egocentric vision provides task-related context that may help disambiguate these cases. We investigate this challenge through freezing of gait (FOG) detection in Parkinson's disease (PD), a symptom strongly influenced by contextual factors during ADLs. Using synchronized egocentric video, wearable IMUs, and expert-annotated FOG labels collected from 13 PD participants in their homes, we evaluate frozen representations from pretrained ego-video and time-series foundation models, alongside an IMU-based TCN trained from scratch, under leave-one-subject-out evaluation. The IMU-based TCN achieved the strongest event-detection performance, reaching 42.3 F1 and 83.0 AUROC, compared with 32.6 F1 and 77.2 AUROC for V-JEPA2 ego-video features. Although ego-video alone did not outperform IMU-based sensing, it showed above-chance discrimination, and qualitative analyses suggest that egocentric vision may capture FOG-relevant information independent of IMUs. Together, these results support the use of pretrained ego-video representations to add contextual information to wearable-sensor-based clinical motion understanding in daily living.

</details>


### [156] [NAS-Driven Hardware Accelerator Exploration for Edge AI and Quantization Effects on the Pareto Space](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13293)
*Eleftherios Mylonas,Angelos Kouprizas,Michael Birbas,Alexios Birbas*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a three-stage pipeline combining NAS, INT4 post-training quantization (PTQ), and evolutionary hardware mapping on a reconfigurable accelerator, and empirically characterizes how quantization perturbs the NAS-Bench-201 Pareto space. A key finding is that an FP32 zero-shot surrogate outperforms a dedicated INT4-trained surrogate in Pareto coverage.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Edge AI requires architectures that are accurate, efficient, and hardware-deployable. Hardware-aware NAS often integrates quantization directly into the search loop, which increases search complexity and couples architecture/quantization design. The simpler post-search PTQ strategy is under-analyzed: its effects on the NAS Pareto structure are uncharacterized, and no framework combines quantized architecture mapping onto reconfigurable accelerators with automated hardware exploration.

Method: A three-stage pipeline: (1) a hardware-agnostic Pareto-rank surrogate frontend on NAS-Bench-201; (2) a quantization bridge with Pareto-aware filtering and feedback control; (3) an evolutionary Domain Space Exploration (DSE) backend on CGRA4ML for optimal hardware mapping. An empirical study uses formal stability metrics on ground-truth data for all 15,625 architectures to characterize INT4 PTQ perturbations, comparing FP32 vs. INT4-trained surrogates across two standard search strategies.

Result: INT4 PTQ perturbations of the NAS-Bench-201 Pareto space are formally characterized via stability metrics over all 15,625 architectures. The FP32 zero-shot surrogate outperforms the dedicated INT4-trained surrogate in Pareto space coverage across two standard search strategies.

Conclusion: The proposed pipeline and empirical analysis address the gaps in post-search quantization analysis for NAS, showing that a simpler FP32-based surrogate can be more effective than a quantization-specific surrogate, and that quantized architecture mapping onto reconfigurable accelerators can be automated within an evolutionary DSE framework.

Abstract: Edge AI deployment demands neural architectures that are simultaneously accurate, computationally efficient, and hardware-deployable - a challenge addressed by hardware-aware Neural Architecture Search (NAS). While recent works incorporate quantization directly into the NAS loop, these approaches expand search complexity and tightly couple architecture and quantization design. The simpler post-search quantization strategy has received little analytical attention: the effects of Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) on the NAS-discovered Pareto structure remain uncharacterised, and no framework combines quantized architecture mapping onto reconfigurable accelerators with automated hardware exploration. This paper addresses both gaps. First, a three-stage pipeline is proposed: a hardware-agnostic Pareto rank surrogate frontend on NAS-Bench-201, a quantization bridge with Pareto-aware filtering and feedback control, and an evolutionary Domain Space Exploration (DSE) backend on CGRA4ML for optimal hardware mapping. Second, an empirical study characterises how INT4 PTQ perturbs the NAS-Bench-201 Pareto space through formal stability metrics on ground-truth data for all 15,625 architectures, and demonstrates that an FP32 zero-shot surrogate outperforms a dedicated INT4-trained surrogate in Pareto space coverage across two standard search strategies.

</details>


### [157] [StateBridge: Training-free Hidden-state Alignment for Latent Communication in LLM Multi-Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13317)
*Yanwen Peng,Delvin Ce Zhang,Xi Wang,Nikolaos Aletras*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: StateBridge is a training-free latent communication method for multi-agent LLM systems that aligns a sender's final hidden states to a receiver's input space via a closed-form orthogonal transformation plus norm calibration and vocabulary anchoring, outperforming baselines on 22/26 model-task pairs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Text-based communication between LLM agents introduces a discrete bottleneck because converting continuous hidden states into discrete tokens discards information. Existing latent communication methods either inject working memory layer-by-layer across transformers or require trained projectors, which hurts portability. The goal is latently transferring richer continuous information without training.

Method: StateBridge aligns the sender's final-layer hidden states to the receiver's input space using a closed-form orthogonal transformation (a rotation/alignment computable without gradient training). Lightweight norm calibration and vocabulary anchoring further make the aligned states compatible with the pretrained input distribution. The resulting continuous states are prepended to the receiver's input as a prefix.

Result: Evaluated on math reasoning, code generation, and question answering across four models from two families, StateBridge achieves the best or tied-best score on 22 out of 26 model-task pairs, consistently outperforming the strongest baseline.

Conclusion: StateBridge offers a training-free, portable latent communication mechanism that transfers richer continuous information than text tokens, demonstrating consistent and superior performance across diverse multi-agent tasks.

Abstract: Large language model based multi-agent systems usually communicate in text, i.e., using discrete tokens. However, text introduces a discrete bottleneck. Converting the sender's continuous hidden states into discrete tokens discards information that token identities alone cannot capture. Recent work proposes latent communication as an alternative, where agents transmit hidden representations directly without converting them to text. However, existing latent methods either inject working memory layer by layer across the transformers, or require trained projectors that limit portability. We propose StateBridge, a training-free latent communication approach that aligns the sender's final-layer hidden states to the receiver's input space via a closed-form orthogonal transformation. Lightweight norm calibration and vocabulary anchoring ensure compatibility with the pretrained input distribution. The aligned states are prepended to the input of the receiver agent as a continuous prefix. We evaluate StateBridge on math reasoning, code generation, and question answering with four models from two families. StateBridge achieves the best or tied-best score on 22 out of 26 model-task pairs, consistently outperforming the strongest baseline.

</details>


### [158] [LLM-Guided Graph Generation for Structure-Based Local Improvement Methods](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13333)
*Hai Xia,Vaidyanathan Peruvemba Ramaswamy,Stefan Szeider*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes an automatic, problem-agnostic pipeline that uses an LLM to generate graph representations (semantic graphs) of constraint optimization problems in the MiniZinc format. These graphs guide a structure-based local improvement framework (SLIM) in variable selection and enable shared graph features for configuration selection, achieving a 44.0% win rate against Gurobi across 20 MiniZinc problems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large neighborhood search typically selects a random subset of decision variables, and existing variable selection strategies rely on hand-crafted, domain-specific structural features. The authors aim to automate structural feature extraction in a problem-agnostic way for all MiniZinc-format problems, avoiding per-domain manual design.

Method: An LLM is prompted with semantic guidelines to produce a graph generator that maps any problem instance to a uniform weighted graph, where nodes represent decision variables and edges represent constraint relationships. These problem-agnostic graphs drive SLIM's variable selection. The uniform weighted graph representation lets all instances share the same graph features, which are extracted and used for configuration (algorithm) selection.

Result: Evaluated on instances across 20 MiniZinc competition problems, algorithm selection achieved a 39.5% average problem-weighted win rate against a one-shot Gurobi baseline, more than doubling the best single configuration (19.3%). Configuration and feature ablation further improved performance to 44.0%.

Conclusion: LLM-based semantic generation enables effective automated structure and feature extraction for constraint optimization, significantly outperforming single configurations and demonstrating the value of problem-agnostic graph-guided variable and configuration selection.

Abstract: Large neighborhood search normally selects a random subset of decision variables for iterative optimization. For efficiently solving different problems, researchers tend to design variable selection strategies by taking into account structural features from different domains. In this paper, we build an automatic pipeline that is problem-agnostic to all problems in the MiniZinc format. By prompting an LLM with our semantic guidelines, we guide the LLM to produce a graph generator that maps any instance of a problem type to a uniform weighted graph, where nodes represent decision variables and edges represent constraint relationships. These problem-agnostic graphs guide our structure-based local improvement framework (SLIM) in variable selection. Meanwhile, the weighted graph enables all problem instances to share the same generic graph representation, from which the same graph features can be extracted and used for configuration selection. We evaluated our pipeline on instances across 20 MiniZinc competition problems, finding that algorithm selection achieves a 39.5% average problem-weighted win rate against a one-shot Gurobi baseline, more than doubling the best single configuration (19.3%). Configuration and feature ablation boost the performance further to 44.0%, demonstrating that LLM-based semantic generation enables effective automated structure extraction and feature extraction for constraint optimization.

</details>


### [159] [LongEarth-R1: Benchmarking and Aligning Vision-Language Models for Long-Horizon Earth Observation Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13344)
*Yupan Ding,Jing Xiao,Zhenyuan Zhang,Chaofeng Chen,Liang Liao,Gui-Song Xia,Mi Wang*

Main category: cs.AI
