TL;DR: The paper introduces LongEarth-Bench, a ~120k-sample benchmark for long-horizon Earth observation reasoning over image sequences (avg. 15.14 frames, up to 30), spanning 12 tasks, plus two models: LongEarth (SFT with sequence identifiers and chain-of-thought supervision) and LongEarth-R1 (GRPO with format/temporal/spatial rewards), which leads on all 12 long-sequence tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing remote sensing vision-language models focus on isolated images, pairs, or short sequences, failing to support multi-stage geographic evolution, spatial change localization, temporal anomaly detection, and future inference over extended image sequences. This limits reliable grounding in relevant frames and regions.

Method: The authors construct LongEarth-Bench with ~120k QA samples from 117k images (sequences averaging 15.14 frames, up to 30), covering 12 tasks: evolution summarization, spatial reasoning, anomaly identification, and logical prediction, with a 30k-sample subset providing structured reasoning traces linking key frames/regions to answers. LongEarth is trained via supervised fine-tuning with explicit sequence identifiers and structured chain-of-thought supervision. LongEarth-R1 extends this using group relative policy optimization (GRPO) with format, temporal, and spatial rewards.

Result: LongEarth-R1 achieves the best performance on all 12 long-sequence tasks while remaining competitive on standard remote sensing benchmarks.

Conclusion: LongEarth-Bench and the LongEarth/LongEarth-R1 models advance long-horizon Earth observation reasoning, establishing new state-of-the-art results on long-sequence tasks without sacrificing performance on conventional remote sensing benchmarks.

Abstract: Long-horizon Earth observation reasoning requires models to organize multi-stage geographic evolution, localize spatial changes, detect temporal anomalies, and infer future from extended image sequences. However, existing remote sensing vision-language models mainly focus on isolated images, image pairs, or short sequences, limiting reliable grounding in the relevant frames and regions. We introduce LongEarth-Bench, a benchmark containing approximately 120k question-answering samples derived from 117k unique images. Its sequences average 15.14 frames and extend to 30 frames, covering 12 tasks across evolution summarization, spatial reasoning, anomaly identification, and logical prediction. A 30k-sample subset further provides structured reasoning traces linking key frames and changed regions to final answers. We develop LongEarth through supervised fine-tuning with explicit sequence identifiers and structured chain-of-thought supervision. Building on LongEarth, LongEarth-R1 applies group relative policy optimization with format, temporal, and spatial rewards. LongEarth-R1 achieves the best results on all 12 long-sequence tasks while remaining competitive on standard remote sensing benchmarks.

</details>


### [160] [Rules or Character? Scaling Laws for AI Safety Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13345)
*Satoshi Takahashi,Nobuji Kouno,Masaaki Komatsu,Ryuji Hamamoto*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A formal comparative-statics model shows that the optimal balance between character shaping (training-time) and rule enforcement (inference-time) in AI safety shifts only weakly toward shaping as deployment scale grows, and is dominated far more by the baseline character fragility rate than by scale or other parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite AI safety systems combining character shaping (e.g., RLHF, Constitutional AI) with rule enforcement (e.g., output filters, safety classifiers), little formal analysis exists on how their optimal balance should change as deployment scale increases. The authors aim to fill this gap given scale-dependent filter degradation, common-mode failures, and the risk that shaped behavior collapses under novel conditions (character fragility).

Method: They introduce a stylized comparative-statics model parameterizing safety design as a resource allocation alpha in [0,1] between shaping and enforcement. Using a multiplicative Pareto damage model, they derive closed-form expected harm and supplement it with tail-risk (CVaR) analysis via Monte Carlo simulation across three scenarios (optimistic, moderate, pessimistic).

Result: The optimal alpha* is interior or at the rules-only boundary and shifts weakly toward character shaping as deployment scale T grows, from negligible (Delta alpha* = +0.01) to pronounced (Delta alpha* = +0.21) depending on scenario. The baseline character fragility rate p^(0)_frag is the dominant parameter, shifting alpha* by 0.50 across its range — far exceeding the effect of tail severity, filter quality, or common-mode failure probability. CVaR and expected-harm optima converge at large T.

Conclusion: Safety architecture decisions depend less on deployment scale per se than on the reliability of character shaping under distributional shift, indicating that improving shaping robustness matters more than scale-based rebalancing.

Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) safety systems combine character shaping (e.g., Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback [RLHF], Constitutional AI), which modifies behavioral distributions at training time, with rule enforcement (e.g., output filters, safety classifiers), which blocks harmful outputs at inference time, yet little formal analysis exists on how their optimal balance should change as deployment scales increase. We introduce a stylized comparative-statics model that parameterizes safety design as a resource allocation alpha in [0,1] between these two approaches, incorporating scale-dependent filter degradation, common-mode failures, and character fragility -- the risk that shaped behavior degrades or collapses under novel conditions. Under a multiplicative Pareto damage model, we derive closed-form expected harm and supplement it with tail-risk (CVaR) analysis via Monte Carlo simulation. Across three scenarios (optimistic, moderate, pessimistic), the optimal alpha* is interior or at the rules-only boundary and shifts weakly toward character shaping as deployment scale T grows, from negligible (Delta alpha* = +0.01) to pronounced (Delta alpha* = +0.21) depending on scenario. The dominant parameter is the baseline character fragility rate p^(0)_frag, which shifts alpha* by 0.50 across its range -- far exceeding the effect of tail severity, filter quality, or common-mode failure probability. CVaR and expected-harm optima converge at large T. These results suggest that safety architecture decisions depend less on deployment scale per se than on the reliability of character shaping under distributional shift.

</details>


### [161] [Jointly Predicting Courses and Grades Using a Transformer-Based Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13409)
*Paul Savala*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TRACE is a Transformer-based model that jointly predicts a student's upcoming course set and course grades per semester, treating courses as concurrent rather than sequential, and achieves nearly 50% MAE reduction over grade-only models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing learning-analytics models treat student academic history as a simple sequence and ignore course concurrency within a semester, leading to poor grade predictions—especially for students with heavy or difficult course loads.

Method: TRACE encodes courses on a per-semester basis to capture course concurrency and uses a novel loss function combining course-set prediction with grade prediction (joint prediction). It is trained on ten years of institutional data.

Result: Jointly predicting courses taken plus grades reduces mean absolute error by nearly 50% compared to an identical grade-only architecture, and outperforms LSTM-based sequential models and graph neural network approaches. The model also naturally incorporates student attribute data.

Conclusion: Modern neural architectures can produce interpretable, transferable models (via retraining and recalibration) for academic prediction, and predicting courses taken during training is a key technique. The model could support early detection systems in higher education.

Abstract: Existing predictive models in learning analytics often treat student academic history as a simple sequence, overlooking the concurrent nature of courses taken within a semester. This simplification can lead to inaccurate performance predictions, particularly for students with heavy or challenging course loads. This paper introduces a TRansformer for Academic Course-grade Estimation (TRACE) that addresses this limitation by jointly predicting both the set of courses a student will take and their corresponding grades for an upcoming semester. Our approach encodes courses on a per-semester basis to capture the effects of course concurrency and utilizes a novel loss function combining course-set prediction with grade prediction. We demonstrate that predicting courses taken in addition to the grades in those courses leads to significant improvements in prediction quality. Trained on ten years of institutional data, our joint prediction model reduces mean absolute error by nearly 50% compared to an identical architecture that predicts grades alone. The model also outperforms traditional LSTM-based sequential models, as well as graph neural network-based approaches, and offers natural ways to incorporate student attribute data. This work demonstrates the utility of modern neural architectures for creating interpretable models that can be adapted to new institutions via retraining and recalibration, as well as the importance of key techniques, such as predicting courses taken during training. We discuss how this model could be incorporated into early detection systems at institutions of higher education.

</details>


### [162] [Who Speaks Matters: Authority-Aware Multi-View RAG over Italian Parliamentary Proceedings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13410)
*Mirko Tritella,Riccardo Pozzi,Matteo Palmonari*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ParliamentRAG is a retrieval-augmented generation system for the Italian Chamber of Deputies that mitigates speaker-dominance, expertise-weighting, and citation-misattribution risks via a query-dependent, topic-aware authority model; it outperforms Google NotebookLM on coverage, quotation faithfulness, and source-related expert preferences.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Parliamentary proceedings are a large, fragmented record of democratic deliberation, making multi-perspective access difficult for citizens, journalists, and researchers. Directly applying RAG risks dominance of frequent speakers, inability to weight speakers by topical expertise, and citation misattribution in politically sensitive text.

Method: ParliamentRAG contributes a topic-dependent authority model that estimates each speaker's authority as a function of the query by combining interpretable components (profession, education, prior interventions). For a query, it retrieves relevant speech chunks, identifies topic-relevant experts across parliamentary groups, and generates a synthesis with supporting quotations. Evaluation uses 15 policy topics with automated metrics plus blind A/B human evaluation by six domain experts against Google NotebookLM.

Result: ParliamentRAG achieves higher political-group coverage (0.97 vs. 0.95), perfect quotation faithfulness (1.00 vs. 0.95), and stronger expert preferences on source-related dimensions, while NotebookLM remains stronger on prose-oriented dimensions.

Conclusion: A topic-dependent authority model that jointly addresses speaker dominance, topical expertise weighting, and faithful citation enables RAG to produce more balanced, reliable parliamentary summaries, with trade-offs in prose fluency relative to NotebookLM.

Abstract: Parliamentary proceedings are a primary record of democratic deliberation, yet their volume and fragmentation make multi-perspective access difficult for citizens, journalists, and researchers. Applying Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to parliamentary transcripts introduces three specific risks: dominance of the most frequent speakers, inability to weight speakers according to topical expertise, and citation misattribution in politically sensitive text. We present ParliamentRAG, a RAG system for the Italian Chamber of Deputies that addresses these risks jointly. Its core contribution is a topic-dependent authority model that estimates each speaker's authority as a function of the current query, combining interpretable components such as profession, education, and previous interventions. Given a user query, the system retrieves relevant speech chunks, identifies topic-relevant experts across parliamentary groups, and generates a summary synthesizing their perspectives, accompanied by supporting quotations. ParliamentRAG is evaluated against Google NotebookLM on 15 policy topics via a two-level protocol combining automated metrics and blind A/B human evaluation by six domain experts. The system achieves higher coverage across political groups (0.97 vs. 0.95), perfect quotation faithfulness (1.00 vs. 0.95), and stronger expert preferences on source-related dimensions, while NotebookLM remains stronger on prose-oriented dimensions.

</details>


### [163] [Beyond Final Scores: A Systematic Evaluation of Agents for Long-Horizon AI Research and Development](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13417)
*Yiwei Li,Wanli Yang,Hexiang Tan,Xiangzhou Huang,Zhengyu Chen,Ziran Li,Borun Chen,Shanglin Lei,Huaisheng Zhu,Hao Tian,Fei Sun,Xunliang Cai,Jingang Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper systematically evaluates seven frontier models on 36 long-horizon experimentation tasks, analyzing within-run behavior and experience reuse. It finds that current agents act more like engineering optimizers than autonomous researchers, with high run-to-run variance, limited novelty, and experience reuse that can both help and mislead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluation of autonomous agents focuses on final scores, which hide where progress is gained or lost during long-horizon experimentation and fail to reveal whether accumulated experience improves later decisions. The authors aim to characterize within-run behavior and experience reuse to better understand current capabilities.

Method: A new evaluation framework applying rule-based metrics to 36 long-horizon tasks. It characterizes within-run behavior along three dimensions: Solution Framing, Execution, and Feedback Control. It also uses controlled comparisons to assess experience reuse both within and across tasks, and evaluates seven frontier models under different harness designs.

Result: Current agents behave like engineering optimizers rather than fully autonomous researchers: they can formulate and implement practical solutions, but performance varies substantially across runs; their strongest solutions mainly adapt or combine established techniques; and genuine methodological novelty is rare. Observed performance is shaped by distinct process bottlenecks behind similar final outcomes, by experience reuse that can help or mislead subsequent decisions, and by harness designs that affect performance stability.

Conclusion: The findings point to concrete directions for improving model training, inference-time strategies, experience management, and harness design to move agents closer to autonomous research capability.

Abstract: Autonomous agents are increasingly capable of improving models, systems, and other technical artifacts through long-horizon experimentation. To understand the current state of this capability, however, evaluation must go beyond final scores, which neither reveal where progress is gained or lost nor indicate whether accumulated experience improves later decisions. We therefore present a systematic evaluation of seven frontier models on 36 long-horizon tasks based on a new framework that uses rule-based metrics to characterize within-run behavior through Solution Framing, Execution, and Feedback Control and controlled comparisons to assess experience reuse within and across tasks. The results show that current agents operate more like engineering optimizers than fully autonomous researchers: they can formulate and implement practical solutions, but their performance varies substantially across runs, their strongest solutions mainly adapt or combine established techniques, and genuine methodological novelty remains rare. Detailed analysis reveals that observed performance is shaped by multiple factors, including distinct process bottlenecks behind similar final outcomes, experience reuse that can help or mislead subsequent decisions, and harness designs that affect performance stability. These findings suggest concrete directions for improving model training, inference-time strategies, experience management, and harness design.

</details>


### [164] [Enhancing Virtual Agents through SLMs and Edge-Computing: An Exploratory Evaluation of Think and Memory Processes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13420)
*Aimilios Hadjiliasi,Louis Nisiotis*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents an edge-based virtual agent gateway that uses Small Language Models (e.g., Qwen2.5 on NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX) to implement selected Cognitive Embodied Agent Architecture (CEAA) components—specifically "Think" and "Memory"—enabling lightweight, context-aware embodied agents for virtual and Metaverse worlds.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Embodied intelligent virtual agents need to be persistent, adaptive, and context-aware in complex virtual/Metaverse worlds, but implementing cognitively capable agents is conceptually and technologically challenging. Recent advances in edge computing and generative AI motivate exploring Small Language Models as a lightweight alternative to support edge-based operation of CEAA cognitive components.

Method: The authors developed an edge-based virtual agent gateway system running on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX using Qwen2.5 SLMs of different sizes. They focused on the CEAA "Think" and "Memory" processes and conducted simulation experiments to evaluate routing accuracy, memory-read performance, and latency, including handling memory-driven conversations.

Result: The simulation experiments demonstrated an SLM-driven prototype agent system that partially implements selected CEAA processes. The system was evaluated on routing accuracy, memory-read performance, and latency, showing that the cognitive "brain" of embodied agents can operate efficiently and contextually on edge hardware for interactive immersive virtual worlds.

Conclusion: Small Language Models on edge devices can feasibly support core cognitive orchestration and persistence functions of embodied virtual agents, providing an efficient and contextual foundation for developing embodied agents in immersive virtual and Metaverse environments.

Abstract: Embodied intelligent virtual agents are expected to operate as persistent, adaptive, and context-aware entities within complex virtual and Metaverse worlds. However, implementing cognitively capable agents in such environments is conceptually and technologically challenging. Among a range of blueprints and development approaches, the Cognitive Embodied Agent Architecture (CEAA) has been developed as an implementation-oriented framework for architecting components of perception, memory, reasoning, planning, and embodied action. Considering the recent advances in edge computing and generative AI language models, this paper explores the use of Small Language Models (SLMs) to support edge-based operation of selected CEAA components, focusing on "Think" and "Memory" as processes central to cognitive orchestration and persistence of virtual agents in interactive virtual worlds. An edge-based virtual agent gateway system was developed and evaluated on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX using Qwen2.5 models of different sizes, exploring the system's capability to process service requests and handle memory-driven conversations. A series of simulation experiments evaluated routing accuracy, memory-read performance, and latency, demonstrating an SLM-driven prototype agent system that partially implements selected CEAA processes to support the development of embodied agents whose cognitive "brain" can operate efficiently and contextually for interactive experiences in immersive virtual worlds.

</details>


### [165] [RAIL: An Automatic Classifier of the Artificial Intelligence Readiness Level](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13428)
*Juan Irving Vasquez,Juan Terven,Laura-Ivoone Garay-Jimenez*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces the Unified AI Readiness Level (AIRL), a nine-level ordinal scale merging three existing readiness frameworks, and RAIL, a panel-of-experts LLM classifier that assesses AI maturity from natural-language descriptions alone while preventing overestimation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing AI readiness frameworks are heterogeneous and hard to apply automatically: Technology Readiness Levels lack AI-specific gating, Machine Learning Technology Readiness Levels require internal process artifacts, and AI/data readiness dimension models use scales that resist direct comparison. A decidable, comparable scale assessable from external descriptions is needed.

Method: First, the authors unify three frameworks into AIRL: a nine-level ordinal scale based on an environmental evidence ladder with dimensional caps (specification, data existence, data quality, data legality, expert knowledge, algorithmic maturity), a generality-anchoring rule, and explicit assignment disciplines. Second, they build RAIL, a panel-of-experts classifier using one evidence agent and six independent dimension agents (each a narrowly scoped LLM), whose verdicts are aggregated by a deterministic minimum rule and reviewed by a chief expert with asymmetric authority that can confirm or lower—but never raise—the recommendation.

Result: Testing on several research works showed the method is consistent and avoids the overestimation typical of monolithic LLM classifiers.

Conclusion: AIRL and RAIL provide a decidable, automatically applicable, and comparable measure of AI maturity that remains conservative against overestimation.

Abstract: Assessing the maturity of artificial intelligence technologies is essential for investment decisions, project management, and policy monitoring, yet the available readiness frameworks are heterogeneous and difficult to apply automatically: the adaptation of Technology Readiness Levels to AI lacks AI-specific gating criteria, the Machine Learning Technology Readiness Levels presuppose access to internal process artifacts, and AI/data readiness dimension models employ scales that resist direct comparison. This paper makes two contributions. First, we unify these three frameworks into the Unified AI Readiness Level (AIRL), a nine-level ordinal scale built on an environmental evidence ladder and complemented by dimensional caps (covering specification, data existence, data quality, data legality, expert knowledge, and algorithmic maturity) together with a generality-anchoring rule and explicit assignment disciplines, so that a readiness level becomes decidable from a natural-language description of the work alone. Second, we propose RAIL (Readiness Assessment via Independent LLM-experts), a panel-of-experts classifier that operationalizes the scale: one evidence agent and six independent dimension agents, each a large language model with a narrowly scoped mandate, deliver verdicts that a deterministic minimum rule aggregates and a chief expert reviews under asymmetric authority, confirming or lowering the panel's recommendation but never raising it above the caps. The method was tested in the analysis of several research works showing consistency and avoiding overestimation from monolithic LLM classifiers.

</details>


### [166] [Academic League of Artificial Intelligence - An Integrative Perspective of Teaching, Research, and Extension](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13447)
*Alison R. Panisson,Maria Eduarda W. M. Vianna,Italo Firmino da Silva,Heitor Henrique da Silva,Rafaela Fernandes Savaris,Bernardo Pandolfi Costa,Martin Augusto Gagliotti Vigil,Jim Lau,Agenor Hentz,Andréa Sabedra Bordin,Alexandre Leopoldo Gonçalves,Roberto Rodrigues-Filho*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper describes the organizational framework of the Academic League of Artificial Intelligence (LIA) at UFSC, which integrates teaching, research, and extension through a student-centered, project-based model, and shows it as a flexible and replicable blueprint for academic leagues in engineering and computing education.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Academic leagues have become important for extracurricular education and for strengthening ties between universities and society, but there is a need for a structured organizational model that effectively unifies the three university pillars—teaching, research, and extension—in a student-driven context.

Method: The paper presents an organizational framework combining democratic governance, collaborative learning, and dynamic project organization. It is illustrated through representative initiatives such as competition teams, study groups, open lectures, knowledge repositories, and socially impactful AI applications, all developed within a common student-centered, project-based structure.

Result: The framework successfully supports diverse educational, scientific, and extension activities while promoting leadership, scientific production, community engagement, and knowledge preservation. The reported experience indicates the model is flexible and replicable for integrating the three university pillars into engineering and computing education.

Conclusion: The LIA framework offers a practical, adaptable, and replicable model for academic leagues and similar student organizations seeking to integrate teaching, research, and extension, providing actionable guidance for engineering and computing education.

Abstract: Academic leagues have become important mechanisms for promoting extracurricular education and strengthening the integration between universities and society. This paper presents the organizational framework adopted by the Academic League of Artificial Intelligence (LIA) at the Federal University of Santa Catarina (UFSC), designed to integrate teaching, research, and university extension through a student-centered, project-based approach. The framework combines democratic governance, collaborative learning, and dynamic project organization to foster both technical and transversal competencies. The framework is illustrated through representative initiatives, including competition teams, study groups, open lectures, knowledge repositories, and AI-powered applications with social impact. These projects demonstrate how diverse educational, scientific, and extension activities can be developed within a common organizational structure while promoting leadership, scientific production, community engagement, and knowledge preservation. The reported experience indicates that the proposed framework provides a flexible and replicable model for integrating the three university pillars into engineering and computing education, offering practical guidance for academic leagues and similar student organizations.

</details>


### [167] [A Unifying Perspective on Causal World Models: From Observations to Representations to Structure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13456)
*Avinash Kori,Fabrizio Russo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes Causal World Models (CWMs), arguing that useful world models must go beyond generation to capture causal structure—entity properties, entity-to-entity interactions, and entity-to-environment interactions—and provides a formal, task-grounded definition tied to causal representation learning, object-centric learning, causal discovery, SCMs, and model-based decision-making, including identifiability analysis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: World Models are increasingly seen as foundational for intelligent agents that predict, plan, and act out-of-distribution. However, current WMs focus heavily on generative capability and lack the causal structure needed to explain dynamics. The authors argue WMs should capture entity properties and interactions that determine and explain system dynamics, enabling causal reasoning and informed decision-making rather than mere generation.

Method: The paper takes a conceptual/formal approach: it studies WMs from a causal perspective across multiple abstraction levels (from perceptual observations to conceptual representations of environment structure), provides a formal definition of Causal World Models grounded in the tasks they support, and connects them to causal representation learning, object-centric learning, causal discovery, structural causal models, and model-based decision-making. It further relates CWMs to identifiability results to clarify when and up to which equivalence components can be recovered from data.

Result: The paper delivers a formal definition of CWMs linking world modelling to established causal frameworks, and clarifies identifiability conditions—specifying when WM components can be recovered from data and up to which equivalence class—thereby grounding WMs in representations and structures that support causal reasoning and informed decision-making.

Conclusion: Useful World Models must capture causal structure (entity properties and interactions), not just generative ability. By formalizing Causal World Models and connecting them to identifiability literature, the work grounds WMs in representations and structures that enable causal reasoning and informed decision-making.

Abstract: World Models (WM) are increasingly seen as a foundation for intelligent agents that can predict, plan, and act beyond their training distribution. In this paper, we study WMs from a causal perspective across multiple levels of abstraction, ranging from perceptual observations to building a conceptual representation of the structure governing the environment dynamics. We argue that useful WMs must go beyond generative capabilities alone: they should also capture entity properties, entity-to-entity interactions, and entity-to-environment interactions that determine and explain the dynamics of a system. We provide a formal definition of Causal WMs (CWMs) grounded in the tasks they are intended to support, connecting world modelling with existing work in causal representation learning, object-centric learning, causal discovery, structural causal models, and model-based decision-making. Finally, we relate CWMs to the literature on identifiability, clarifying when the components of a WM can be recovered from data and up to which equivalence. With this, we ground WMs in representations and structures that support causal reasoning and informed decision-making.

</details>


### [168] [MARC v1: An Open-Source Multi-Agent Framework for Clinical AI Reasoning and Coordination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13476)
*Saisha Shetty,Satvik Tripathi,Austin Lin,Colin Zhao,Theodore Kim,Don Enwerem,Jacinta Arnold,Shahriar Faghani,Tessa S Cook*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MARC is an open-source, YAML-configurable multi-agent framework that replaces monolithic LLM prompting with deterministic, role-specialized orchestration for interpretable clinical reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Clinical reasoning via single monolithic LLM prompts lacks interpretability and makes it hard to attribute failures to specific reasoning stages. The authors aim to enable stage-wise failure attribution and eliminate manual prompt engineering, while making the system accessible to non-programming clinical experts.

Method: MARC orchestrates role-specialized agents for extraction, reasoning, answer generation, and evaluation, using explicit context passing and traceable intermediate outputs. A Decomposer module auto-generates task-specific agent prompts from plain-language descriptions, removing manual prompt engineering. The framework is model-agnostic, supports API-based and local CPU deployments, and is fully configured via YAML without code changes.

Result: The framework provides deterministic multi-agent orchestration with traceable intermediate outputs enabling stage-wise failure attribution, plus automatic prompt generation. It is available as open source at https://github.com/Penn-RAIL/MARC-v1.

Conclusion: MARC offers an interpretable, model-agnostic, and accessible approach to clinical reasoning, designed for easy use by clinical domain experts without programming expertise.

Abstract: We present Multi-Agent Reasoning and Coordination (MARC), an open-source framework that replaces monolithic LLM prompting with deterministic multi-agent orchestration for clinical reasoning. MARC coordinates role-specialized agents for extraction, reasoning, answer generation, and evaluation, with explicit context passing and traceable intermediate outputs, enabling stage-wise failure attribution. We additionally introduce a Decomposer module that generates task-specific agent prompts from a plain-language description, eliminating manual prompt engineering. The framework supports both API-based and local CPU-compatible deployments and is entirely configurable via YAML, without code modifications. MARC is designed to be model-agnostic, interpretable, and accessible to clinical domain experts without programming expertise. The full framework is available at https://github.com/Penn-RAIL/MARC-v1.

</details>


### [169] [AlayaWorld: Interactive Long-Horizon World Modeling - Full Technical Report (v1.1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13492)
*AlayaWorld Team,Kaipeng Zhang,Chuanhao Li,Yifan Zhan,Yongtao Ge,Yuanyang Yin,Jiaming Tan,Kang He,Liaoyuan Fan,Mingliang Zhai,Ruicong Liu,Xiaojie Xu,Xuangeng Chu,Zhen Li,Zhengyuan Lin,Zhixiang Wang,Zian Meng,Zihui Gao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: An improved version of AlayaWorld that keeps its backbone, generation scheme, and data fixed, but overhauls how conditioning signals are represented and integrated—aligning conditions with generated content in latent space and temporal structure via a streaming 3D point-cache renderer and a redesigned causal-VAE conditioning pipeline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The previous AlayaWorld relied on depth-warping-based spatial memory and static-frame conditioning, causing a mismatch between conditioning signals and generated content. The guiding principle is that conditioning signals should match the generated content as closely as possible in both latent representation and temporal structure.

Method: Keeps backbone architecture, chunk-wise autoregressive generation, and training data unchanged. Replaces depth-warping spatial memory with a streaming 3D point-cache renderer and redesigns conditioning so visual conditions are encoded in the same causal-VAE latent space with temporally consistent statistics. Six concrete modifications: (1) motion-aware latent conditioning instead of static-frame image conditioning; (2) causally encoding re-rendered spatial memory as a continuous sequence; (3) aligning the temporal-memory window in pixel space; (4) hard memory dropout that removes memory tokens rather than zeroing them; (5) unifying VAE encode/decode protocol across training and inference; (6) removing the camera AdaLN branch so viewpoint control comes entirely from the re-rendered spatial condition.

Result: The report describes the architectural and conditioning-pipeline redesign of the new AlayaWorld release and the rationale behind it, but does not present quantitative experimental results.

Conclusion: The redesign unifies conditioning with generated content in latent representation and temporal structure, simplifying viewpoint control while improving the consistency between conditioning signals and generation.

Abstract: This report presents an improved version of AlayaWorld. While the backbone architecture, chunk-wise autoregressive generation scheme, and training data remain unchanged from the previous release, we substantially revise how conditioning signals are represented and integrated into the model. The new design is guided by a simple principle: conditioning signals should match the generated content as closely as possible in both latent representation and temporal structure. To this end, we make two major changes. First, we replace the previous depth-warping-based spatial memory with a streaming 3D point-cache renderer. Second, we redesign the conditioning pipeline so that visual conditions are encoded in the same causal-VAE latent space, with temporal statistics consistent with those of the generated video. Concretely, the new version introduces six modifications: (1) replacing static-frame image conditioning with motion-aware latent conditioning; (2) causally encoding re-rendered spatial memory as a continuous sequence; (3) aligning the temporal-memory window in pixel space; (4) adopting hard memory dropout that removes memory tokens rather than zeroing them; (5) unifying the VAE encoding and decoding protocol across training and inference; and (6) removing the camera AdaLN branch, such that viewpoint control is provided entirely through the re-rendered spatial condition.

</details>


### [170] [OmniScientist: An Omni-Modal Omni-Discipline AI Scientist](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13558)
*Bobo Li,Hao Fei,Tianjie Ju,Mong-Li Lee,Wynne Hsu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OmniScientist is an end-to-end, omni-modal AI scientist that conducts research directly from heterogeneous raw evidence (images, signals, audio, video, 3-D structures, trajectories, tables, formulae, graphs). A deterministic pipeline with a perception layer and three autonomous agents (ideation, experiment, writeup) runs idea, rigour, and claim checks in code to enforce novelty, validity, provenance, and traceability. On 36 real-data cases across 5 discipline families, it completes the full raw-data-to-manuscript path in all cases, scoring a mean of 6.3, and direct perception improves all 7 evaluation dimensions, winning 85% of paired comparisons against a blind precomputed-features variant.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing AI scientists typically reason over text, code, labels, or precomputed summaries, which omits scientifically decisive spatial, temporal, cross-channel, and procedural relations needed for full evidence-grounded discovery. The authors argue workflow coverage alone is insufficient; agents need lifecycle-wide access to raw, heterogeneous evidence to make observations that shape research questions, experiments, and claims.

Method: OmniScientist combines a perception layer with three autonomous agents (ideation, experiment, writeup) in a deterministic end-to-end pipeline operating directly on raw evidence across multiple modalities. It enforces scientific integrity through idea, rigour, and claim checks executed in code, covering novelty screening, statistical validity, execution provenance, and numerical traceability. Evaluation uses 36 real-data cases spanning 5 discipline families, 4 evidence families, and 9 modalities, including paired (head-to-head) comparisons against a blind variant receiving only precomputed scalar features.

Result: The system completed the full path from raw data to a compiled manuscript in all 36 cases, achieving a mean overall paper score of 6.3 with the reference reasoning backbone. Direct perception improved all 7 evaluation dimensions relative to the blind precomputed-features variant and won 85% of head-to-head judgments.

Conclusion: Lifecycle-wide perception of raw, heterogeneous evidence is essential for evidence-grounded scientific discovery. OmniScientist demonstrates a practical path toward broadly capable AI scientists that ground their hypotheses, experiments, and claims in the full available evidence rather than precomputed summaries.

Abstract: Recent advances in foundation models have enabled AI scientists to automate increasingly complete research workflows, from hypothesis generation and code execution to manuscript preparation. Yet workflow coverage alone does not provide access to the full evidence on which scientific discovery depends. Existing systems typically reason over text, code, labels, or precomputed summaries, leaving scientifically decisive spatial, temporal, cross-channel, and procedural relations unavailable to the agent. We introduce OmniScientist, an end-to-end, omni-modal AI scientist that conducts multidisciplinary research directly from heterogeneous raw evidence. A perception layer and 3 autonomous agents for ideation, experiment, and writeup operate within a deterministic pipeline, allowing observations to shape research questions, experimental decisions, and final claims throughout the research lifecycle. By running idea, rigour, and claim checks in code, the system enforces novelty screening, statistical validity, execution provenance, and numerical traceability. We evaluate OmniScientist on 36 real-data cases spanning 5 discipline families, 4 families of scientific evidence, and modalities including images, signals, audio, video, 3-D structures, trajectories, tables, formulae, and graphs. The system completes the full path from raw data to a compiled manuscript in all 36 cases and achieves a mean overall paper score of 6.3 with the reference reasoning backbone. In paired comparisons against a blind variant that receives only precomputed scalar features, direct perception improves all 7 evaluation dimensions and wins 85% of head-to-head judgments. These results show that lifecycle-wide perception is essential for evidence-grounded scientific discovery and provides a practical path toward broadly capable AI scientists.

</details>

### [171] [Entropy-Augmented Multi-Objective Policy Optimization in Multiagent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12534)
*Jamie Santos,Ayhan Alp Aydeniz,Raghav Thakar,Kagan Tumer*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: The paper proposes adding an entropy-based behavior-space diversity bonus to NSGA-II-style multi-objective evolutionary optimization for multiagent teams, and shows up to 48% hypervolume improvement over baseline in rover-domain experiments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-objective evolutionary algorithms like NSGA-II optimize for diversity in the objective space but ignore behavioral diversity. In multiagent settings, this can cause premature convergence and a collapse of behaviors that would otherwise distinguish policies under different external conditions, producing suboptimal coordination outcomes. The authors aim to correct this by explicitly promoting behavioral diversity during policy evaluation.

Method: The authors introduce an entropy-augmented policy evaluation strategy that adds an entropy bonus to agent fitness scores, penalizing behavioral homogeneity across the evolving population. This behavior-space diversity signal is integrated into the existing Pareto optimization framework (NSGA-II) rather than replacing it, so Pareto optimality is preserved while encouraging exploration of behaviorally distinct policies. The approach is evaluated in rover-domain experiments with qualitatively distinct reward structures.

Result: Experiments in rover-domain environments with qualitatively different reward structures show hypervolume improvements of up to 48% relative to the NSGA-II baseline, indicating that the entropy-augmented, behavior-diverse method yields better-performing and more diverse policy sets.

Conclusion: Behavioral diversity is a promising and underexplored direction for improving multi-objective multiagent evolutionary optimization. Augmenting policy evaluation with a behavior-space entropy bonus, while retaining the Pareto framework, substantially improves hypervolume and encourages behaviorally distinct policies.

Abstract: Autonomous agent teams deployed in settings such as marine and extraterrestrial outposts must coordinate actions to achieve optimal outcomes across multiple competing objectives. Multi-objective evolutionary algorithms such as NSGA-II optimize for diversity in the objective space, but neglect diversity in the behavior space, possibly leading to premature convergence and a collapse in behaviors that may differentiate policies in different external conditions. To address this, we introduce an entropy-augmented policy evaluation strategy that incorporates an entropy bonus into agent fitness scores, discouraging behavioral homogeneity across the evolving population. By augmenting policy evaluation with a behavior-space diversity signal while preserving the underlying Pareto optimization framework, our method is designed to encourage exploration of behaviorally distinct policies in multiagent domains. We evaluate our approach across rover-domain experiments with qualitatively distinct reward structures and observe hypervolume improvements of up to 48% relative to the NSGA-II baseline, suggesting that behavioral diversity is a promising and underexplored direction for improving multi-objective multiagent evolutionary optimization.

</details>


### [172] [Do LLMs Beat Nash? Testing Decentralized Coordination in Self-Play Multi-Agent Games](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12547)
*Deborah Sinishaw,Qile Zhu,Edwin Meriaux,Gregory Dudek*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: The paper studies whether independent, non-communicating instances of the same language model can implicitly coordinate in one-shot games, benchmarking 13 LLMs against the Nash equilibrium. Frontier-hosted models exceed Nash baselines in two-player games, but performance collapses in larger multi-agent team games.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Investigate whether LLMs can coordinate without explicit communication, relying solely on reasoning about identical counterparts, and whether this capability generalizes beyond dyadic games to larger multi-agent teams.

Method: Constructs a benchmark of one-shot, no-communication games across seven archetypes with two to ten actions per player. Thirteen language models play as all agents (self-play), told only that counterparts run the same model, and performance is evaluated against the Nash equilibrium (and optimal joint outcome) of each game.

Result: Two frontier-hosted models consistently exceed their Nash benchmark, approaching the optimal joint outcome in several archetypes, while most open-weight models achieve only partial gains that vary sharply by game structure. Performance degrades substantially in team-based games with four or more interchangeable agents, particularly as the action space grows.

Conclusion: Whatever capability drives self-play gains in dyadic games does not transfer to larger multi-agent teams, suggesting LLM implicit coordination is limited to small settings and may not provide the assumed coordination mechanism in decentralized multi-agent systems.

Abstract: Large language model agents deployed without a central controller are often assumed to require communication to coordinate their actions. We ask what remains possible without it: when independent instances of the same model cannot communicate, can they still reason about their counterparts well enough to exceed the standard game-theoretic baseline for uncoordinated play? We introduce a benchmark of one-shot, no-communication games in which each of thirteen language models is told only that its counterparts are running the same model and is evaluated against the Nash equilibrium of the underlying game. In two-player matrix games spanning seven archetypes and two to ten actions per player, two frontier-hosted models consistently exceed their Nash benchmark, approaching the optimal joint outcome in several archetypes, while most open-weight models achieve only partial gains that vary sharply by game structure. Performance degrades substantially in team-based games with four or more interchangeable agents, particularly as the action space grows, suggesting that whatever capability drives self-play gains in dyadic games does not transfer to larger multi-agent teams.

</details>


### [173] [Discovering Efficient and Explainable Communication Topologies for LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems via Causal Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12921)
*Junzhi Li,Peng He,Qirui Ji,Wei Wang,Lixiang Liu,Chuxiong Sun*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: E2-Explainer is a model-agnostic framework that explains communication topologies in LLM-based multi-agent systems by identifying compact, task-preserving communication subgraphs, using a Granger-style edge-level objective, then distilling them into an amortized explainer for efficient post-hoc explanation and communication pruning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing topology generation methods rely on black-box optimization driven only by task-level rewards, offering little insight into why specific communication edges are chosen. This opacity makes it hard to identify the critical communication subgraphs that underlie successful collaboration.

Method: E2-Explainer formulates topology explanation as a causal attribution problem that finds compact communication subgraphs supported by edge-level evidence of task preservation. It uses a Granger-style objective measuring how masking each communication channel changes task outcome and final-response stability. The resulting budgeted subgraphs are distilled into an amortized explainer, enabling efficient post-hoc explanation without repeated edge-level evaluations at deployment.

Result: Experiments on multiple reasoning and coding benchmarks show E2-Explainer identifies critical communication subgraphs preserving successful collaboration. These subgraphs can be executed directly to prune redundant communication edges, substantially reducing communication costs while maintaining competitive task performance.

Conclusion: E2-Explainer provides interpretable, causal explanations of communication topologies in LLM-based multi-agent systems, enabling the identification and pruning of redundant edges to cut communication costs while keeping task performance competitive.

Abstract: The performance of large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) largely depends on effective communication topologies. Existing topology generation methods, however, typically learn communication topologies through black-box optimization driven solely by task-level rewards. While effective, such optimization provides little insight into why particular communication edges are selected, making it difficult to identify the critical communication subgraphs responsible for successful collaboration. To address this limitation, we propose E2-Explainer, a model-agnostic framework for providing interpretable explanations of communication topologies produced by arbitrary topology generators. Specifically, we formulate topology explanation as a causal attribution problem that identifies compact communication subgraphs supported by edge-level evidence of task preservation. We obtain this evidence with a Granger-style objective that measures how masking each communication channel changes the task outcome and the stability of the final response. The resulting budgeted subgraphs are then distilled into an amortized explainer, enabling efficient post-hoc explanation without repeated edge-level evaluations at deployment. Extensive experiments on multiple reasoning and coding benchmarks demonstrate that E2-Explainer identifies critical communication subgraphs that preserve successful collaboration. These subgraphs can also be executed directly to prune redundant communication edges, substantially reducing communication costs while maintaining competitive task performance.

</details>


### [174] [Reconcile Once, Write Anytime: A Trust-Tiered Librarian and a Multi-Agent Writer for Drift-Free, Point-in-Time Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12984)
*Xing Zhang,Yanwei Cui,Guanghui Wang,Peiyang He*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: The paper introduces a two-tier agentic system that decouples a maintained, trust-tiered knowledge library from report writing, enabling contradiction-free, provenance-grounded, point-in-time reports without look-ahead, validated by deterministic quality gates and a defect-injection meta-evaluation at perfect precision/recall.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-generated long-form reports drift, self-contradict, and lose provenance—metrics appear with inconsistent values and rumor is cited as confidently as audited filings. The authors argue the fix is not per-query RAG over raw chunks but a persistent, always-current source of truth that separates knowledge maintenance from writing.

Method: A deterministic "librarian" ingests timestamped sources into a trust-tiered ontology comprising evidence cards, an authoritative metric ledger, and a claim graph. A portable multi-agent "writer" runtime composes reports at any knowledge cutoff T, reading only evidence with as_of <= T to prevent look-ahead, and red-team verdicts flow back into the librarian. Evaluation uses 6,130 public sources yielding 555,926 evidence cards (SEC EDGAR filings for 295 issuers/11 sectors, BLS releases, Wikipedia), four point-in-time reports, and eight reproducible experiments.

Result: The shared metric ledger eliminated 6,845 cross-section contradictions to zero. Tier-first selection scored 22/22 on gold cases versus 9/22 for a popularity-first baseline; trust tiering leaked zero media-sourced numbers and no government statistic displaced a company filing. A red-team refutation self-corrected a later run with zero manual edits. Replay showed zero look-ahead violations across seven cutoffs while the library grew from 235,373 to 555,312 cards. Difficulty-tiered model routing exceeded the all-Opus quality ceiling while running 3.7x faster than serial.

Conclusion: Separating a deterministic, trust-tiered knowledge library from a multi-agent writing runtime yields contradiction-free, evidence-grounded, provenance-preserving point-in-time reports, with quality verified by deterministic gates and validated via defect-injection meta-evaluation.

Abstract: Long-form research reports generated by large language models drift, contradict themselves, and lose provenance: the same metric appears with different values, and rumor is quoted as confidently as an audited filing. We present a two-tier agentic system that separates a maintained, point-in-time knowledge library from report writing. A deterministic "librarian" ingests timestamped sources into a trust-tiered ontology, layering evidence cards, an authoritative metric ledger, and a claim graph into an always-current source of truth, not per-query RAG over raw chunks. A portable multi-agent "writer" runtime then composes a contradiction-free, evidence-grounded report at any knowledge cutoff T, reading only evidence with as_of <= T (no look-ahead); red-team verdicts flow back into the librarian. We evaluate on a self-collected, public corpus of 6,130 sources yielding 555,926 evidence cards (SEC EDGAR filings across 295 issuers and 11 sectors, U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics releases, and Wikipedia). From the one library we compose four point-in-time reports on distinct theses and run eight reproducible experiments, whose headline metrics come from a deterministic quality-control gate, itself validated by defect-injection meta-evaluation at recall 1.0 and precision 1.0. A shared metric ledger removes 6,845 cross-section contradictions to zero. Tier-first selection is correct on 22/22 gold cases where a popularity-first baseline scores only 9/22; trust tiering leaks zero media-sourced numbers, and no government statistic displaces a company's own filing. A red-team refutation propagates back and self-corrects a later run with zero manual edits. Replay exhibits zero look-ahead violations across seven cutoffs while the library grows from 235,373 to 555,312 cards. Difficulty-tiered model routing exceeds the all-Opus quality ceiling while running 3.7x faster than serial.

</details>

### [175] [The Affordance is the Message: Creative Media as Complex Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12349)
*Ane Espeseth,Elias Najarro*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: The paper proposes a formalisation of computational creativity (CC) media using complex systems (CS) concepts—nine properties (emergence, collective intelligence, self-organisation, non-linear dynamics, criticality, multi-scale hierarchy, phase transitions, diversity of attractors, path dependence, open-endedness)—to describe and compare creative media at the system level, linking medium affordances to creative outputs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Creative media strongly condition what artefacts they can produce through their affordances, yet computational creativity lacks a systematic vocabulary for describing media at the system level. The authors aim to bridge this gap by formalising CC media using complex systems concepts and connecting medium affordances to the realised creative practices they enable.

Method: The authors introduce nine complex systems properties (emergence, collective intelligence and self-organisation, non-linear dynamics, criticality, multi-scale hierarchy, phase transitions, diversity of attractors, path dependence, and open-endedness), connect each to existing computational creativity literature, and position medium affordances as the design-level mechanisms determining each medium's complex system properties. They then apply this vocabulary to characterise a diverse set of media (r/place, Minecraft, cellular automata, Twitter, Boids, etc.).

Result: The result is a shared vocabulary of nine CS properties that enables creative media to be described and compared at the system level. This formalisation establishes an explicit link between a medium's affordances (design-level mechanisms) and its realised creative practices, and is demonstrated through the characterisation of diverse example media.

Conclusion: The proposed formalisation serves a dual purpose: establishing a conceptual link between medium affordances and the creative practices they realise, and offering a shared lens for characterising and comparing existing creative media through complex systems concepts.

Abstract: The affordances of a creative medium strongly condition the creative artefacts the medium will produce. In this work, we present a formalisation of computational creativity (CC) media using the conceptual toolbox of complex systems (CS). We introduce the notions of emergence, collective intelligence and self-organisation, non-linear dynamics, criticality, multi-scale hierarchy, phase transitions, diversity of attractors, path dependence, and open-endedness, and connect them to the existing CC literature. Together these nine properties form a vocabulary with which creative media can be described and compared at the system level, while medium affordances are the design-level mechanisms that determine each medium's complex system properties. The formalisation emphasises the influence of each medium's affordances in determining what the medium can produce in creative processes. To demonstrate the proposed theoretical approach, we characterise a diverse set of media (r/place, Minecraft, cellular automata, Twitter, Boids, ...) using this vocabulary. The proposed formalisation under the CS concepts serves a dual purpose: it establishes a link between the affordances and realised practices of the medium, and it offers a shared lens for characterising existing creative media.

</details>


### [176] [Visibility Asymmetry: How Vendor Attention Shapes Which EdTech Breakdowns Become Product-Visible](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12353)
*Lucan Li*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Introduces "visibility asymmetry" to explain why some local breakdowns in vendor-managed EdTech systems become actionable while others do not, tracing a four-stage mechanism and discussing surveillance-light feedback designs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: CSCW infrastructure research treats breakdown as the moment infrastructures become visible, but in vendor-managed sociotechnical systems many breakdowns never become visible to the actors who could repair them. The paper seeks a concept to understand this uneven visibility and action.

Method: A retrospective qualitative study of a Chinese K-12 EdTech deployment, comprising 11 interviews, 5 classroom observations, and more than 28 days of field notes, analyzed inductively to trace how breakdowns are routed, recognized, and acted upon.

Result: Finds a four-stage mechanism: procurement categories sort schools into attention tiers; staffing and visit cadence follow those tiers; only some local problems travel through staff or administrator channels; and dashboards re-code unresolved repair labor as evidence of adoption. Together these produce visibility asymmetry.

Conclusion: Shifts CSCW attention from breakdown occurrence to the organizational channels through which breakdown becomes actionable, extending work on infrastructure, articulation work, and repair, and discusses feedback systems that surface repair needs without expanding surveillance.

Abstract: Infrastructure scholarship in CSCW often treats breakdown as the moment when infrastructures become visible. However, in vendor-managed sociotechnical systems, not all breakdowns become visible to actors who have the capacity to repair them. Drawing on a retrospective qualitative study of a Chinese K-12 EdTech deployment, including 11 interviews, 5 classroom observations, and more than 28 days of field notes, this paper introduces visibility asymmetry: a sensitizing concept for understanding how similar local breakdowns encounter uneven conditions for being routed, recognized, and acted upon. The analysis traces a four-stage mechanism through which procurement categories sort schools into attention tiers; staffing and visit cadence follow those tiers; only some local problems travel through staff or administrator channels; and dashboards can re-code unresolved repair labor as evidence of adoption. By shifting attention from the occurrence of breakdown to the organizational channels through which breakdown becomes actionable, this paper extends CSCW work on infrastructure, articulation work, and repair. It concludes by discussing implications for feedback systems that can surface repair needs without expanding surveillance.

</details>


### [177] [Humans are Missing from AI Coding Agent Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12355)
*Zora Z. Wang,John Yang,Kilian Lieret,Alexa Tartaglini,Valerie Chen,Yuxiang Wei,Zijian Wang,Lingming Zhang,Karthik Narasimhan,Ludwig Schmidt,Graham Neubig,Daniel Fried,Diyi Yang*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This position paper argues that AI coding agent research should shift from autonomous task-solving toward human-centered collaboration, identifying four interaction-level dimensions—task alignment, verifiability, steerability, and adaptability—and proposing research directions such as user-involved coding environments, verification mechanisms, and measures of human-agent interaction quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As AI coding agents become increasingly capable of autonomously handling complex software engineering tasks, the main bottleneck to practical usefulness is no longer raw task-solving ability but rather challenges in how users communicate with, supervise, and trust these agents. This motivates a reorientation from autonomous to human-centered coding agents.

Method: The paper takes a position-paper approach: it argues for a conceptual shift from autonomous to human-centered coding agents, introduces four core interaction-level dimensions (task alignment, verifiability, steerability, and adaptability) to characterize the human-agent task-solving loop, and outlines concrete research directions for advancing them.

Result: The paper defines a framework of four interaction dimensions—task alignment, verifiability, steerability, and adaptability—and proposes future research directions including user-involved coding environments, comprehensive verification mechanisms, and principled measures of human-agent interaction quality.

Conclusion: Coding agent research should be reoriented from autonomy toward human-centered collaboration, with progress measured and driven by improvements in task alignment, verifiability, steerability, and adaptability rather than task-solving capability alone.

Abstract: Recent progress in AI coding agent research has led to rapid improvements in agents' ability to autonomously perform complex software engineering tasks, from editing large codebases to executing long-horizon development workflows. As these systems make strides, however, the primary bottleneck to practical usefulness increasingly shifts away from pure task-solving capability, and toward challenges in how users communicate with, supervise, and trust agents. In this position paper, we argue for a reorientation from autonomous to human-centered coding agents: systems designed not only to complete tasks, but to collaborate effectively with people. We identify four core interaction-level dimensions that characterize the human-agent task-solving loop: task alignment, verifiability, steerability, and adaptability. Finally, we outline concrete research directions to advance these dimensions, including user-involved coding environments, comprehensive verification mechanisms, and principled measures of human-agent interaction quality.

</details>


### [178] [DrawTalking It Out: Creativity-Support Research as Creative Process Itself](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12357)
*Karl Toby Rosenberg*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: The author argues that the creative, open-ended process behind creativity-adjacent research—including abandoned ideas and pivots—deserves more emphasis, and proposes bridging projects and reaching broader audiences by focusing on interaction techniques, building a community around shared creative experiences, using "DrawTalking" as an example.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Creative research is often presented only through its final polished outputs, while the messy, winding creative process (ideation, pivots, tangents) that produced the work remains hidden. The author wants this process to receive greater emphasis, and seeks ways to connect multiple open-ended projects and communicate them to broader non-technical audiences to open new directions.

Method: The author proposes three strategies: (1) emphasize interaction techniques rather than presenting singular tools in isolation; (2) grow a community grounded in shareable experiences of "creativity interactions" to assemble more complete pictures of how creativity problems are solved; and (3) illustrate these ideas through the example of DrawTalking, a drawing-plus-talking interaction project that emerged from a winding creative process of exploring spontaneous interactive world-building and storytelling.

Result: DrawTalking is presented as evidence of the claim: it resulted from a non-linear creative process of exploring spontaneous interactive world-building and storytelling when drawing and talking together, demonstrating that valuable work can emerge from tangents and pivots that are usually excluded from final publications.

Conclusion: Emphasizing interaction techniques and building a community around shared creative interaction experiences can bridge multiple open-ended projects, serve broader audiences, and lead to new research directions in creativity research.

Abstract: I think the creative process in conducting open-ended creativity-adjacent research is itself part of the creative process (including ideation, pivots, and tangents excluded from the final work) that deserves greater emphasis. how might we bridge multiple open-ended projects and serve broader non-technical audiences? We may choose to emphasize interaction techniques rather than singular tools in isolation. We may grow a community based on our shareable experiences in creativity interactions, to draw more complete pictures of how we creatively solve creativity problems (or satisfy curiosities). This may lead to new directions. I briefly elaborate on this using the example of "DrawTalking" a drawing+talking interactions work. DrawTalking itself resulted from a winding creative process exploring spontaneous interactive world-building and storytelling when drawing and talking.

</details>


### [179] [Interaction Readiness: A Framework for Building and Evaluating AI Agents in Human Roles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12358)
*Sudhir Alladi Venkatesh*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: The paper proposes "Interaction Readiness" as a framework to close the gap between an agent's content quality (accuracy, safety, fluency) and its behavioral fit to an assigned role, separating content from interaction specifications, and demonstrates via the StudyChat dataset that content accuracy and interaction quality are independent, with authority miscalibration as the most persistent failure.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Product and engineering teams building role-bearing AI agents lack a way to evaluate whether an agent behaves appropriately for its role, since an agent can be accurate, safe, and fluent yet still fail the role's behavioral requirements. This motivates separating content quality from interaction quality and creating a specification and evaluation framework for the latter.

Method: The authors introduce the Interaction Readiness framework, which separates content specifications (what an agent knows and says) from interaction specifications (how it conducts itself in a role-governed exchange). Interaction specifications require defining role purpose, authority boundaries, recurring situations, boundary cases, repair behaviors, and audit criteria before deployment. The framework is operationalized through four agent operations: understanding purpose, calibrating authority, managing tone, and repairing breakdowns. It is applied to StudyChat, a public dataset of student interactions with an AI tutoring agent, to measure and diagnose interaction failures.

Result: Content accuracy and interaction quality are shown to be independent dimensions: an agent can be factually correct while failing as a tutor, or interactionally sound while technically wrong. The most persistent failure is authority miscalibration, where the agent knows how to answer but not whether, when, or how the tutor role permits it to answer.

Conclusion: The findings are translated into a specification template and audit procedures that product and engineering teams can apply before and after deployment, providing a practical framework for specifying and evaluating role-appropriate agent behavior beyond content quality.

Abstract: Product and engineering teams building role-bearing AI agents face an evaluation gap: an agent can produce accurate, safe, and fluent content while still failing the behavioral requirements of its assigned role. This paper introduces Interaction Readiness as a framework for specifying and evaluating that missing layer of performance. The framework separates content specifications, which govern what an agent knows and says, from interaction specifications, which define how an agent should conduct itself in a role-governed exchange. Interaction specifications require teams to define role purpose, authority boundaries, recurring situations, boundary cases, repair behaviors, and audit criteria before deployment. We operationalize interaction readiness through four agent operations: understanding purpose, calibrating authority, managing tone, and repairing breakdowns. Using StudyChat, a public dataset of student interactions with an AI tutoring agent, we show that content accuracy and interaction quality are independent dimensions: an agent may be factually correct while failing as a tutor, or interactionally sound while technically wrong. The most persistent failure is authority miscalibration: the agent often knows how to answer, but not whether, when, or how the tutor role permits it to answer. The paper translates these findings into a specification template and audit procedures that product and engineering teams can apply before and after deployment

</details>


### [180] [What Do We Mean When We Talk About Infographics?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12370)
*Xiaoyu Liu,Vishnu Sreekanth,Vraj Patel,Shalin Muzumdar,Diego Lopez,Fumeng Yang,Zhicheng Liu*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: The paper investigates what "infographics" means by systematically reviewing literature and surveying practitioners, identifying key conceptual disagreements and offering recommendations for future work.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is limited clarity and consistency regarding what the term "infographics" (or information graphics) refers to in visualization research and practice, and little is understood about where people's conceptualizations converge or diverge.

Method: Conducted a systematic literature review with inductive coding of 487 sentences from 111 visualization and HCI papers, combined with a practitioner survey analyzing questionnaire responses from 44 domain practitioners.

Result: The study reveals recurring dimensions of conceptual disagreement on infographics: the role of text, the relationship with data visualization, and the relationships with statistical charts and data comics.

Conclusion: The authors recommend that future work explicitly reports assumptions along these diverging conceptualizations, investigates the cognitive origins of these disagreements, and develops more holistic design component frameworks for infographics. Supplementary materials are available via OSF and an interactive web application.

Abstract: There has been limited clarity and consistency regarding what the term infographics, or information graphics, refers to in visualization research and practice. In particular, little is understood about where people's conceptualizations of infographics converge or diverge. To address this gap, we conducted a systematic literature review and a practitioner survey to identify and contrast different perspectives on infographics. We performed inductive coding on 487 sentences from 111 visualization and HCI papers, and analyzed questionnaire responses from 44 domain practitioners. Our findings reveal recurring dimensions of conceptual disagreement on infographics: role of text, relationship with data visualization, and relationships with statistical charts and data comics. Based on the results, we recommend future work to explicitly report any assumptions made along these diverging conceptualizations, to investigate the cognitive origins of these disagreements, and to develop more holistic design component frameworks for infographics. The supplementary materials are available via OSF and as an interactive web application.

</details>


### [181] [Transforming Interactions in Thesis Supervision: An Exposé-First Workflow in Higher Education](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12546)
*Lin-Yin Huang,Dennis Zyska,Iryna Gurevych*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: An exposé-first workflow (proposal-writing before thesis phase) made thesis preparation more structured for students but redistributed rather than reduced work, shifting supervisors toward feedback/feasibility checks and leaving administrators with underrecognized coordination across two digital platforms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: A single professorship oversees ~20 theses per semester with day-to-day supervision delegated to doctoral/postdoctoral researchers, creating heavy supervision demand. The institute adopted an exposé-first workflow to manage this load, and the paper investigates how this structured early-preparation process is experienced and how it redistributes responsibility, supervision, and coordination work across roles and platforms.

Method: Mixed-methods study framed through Frauenberger et al.'s four reflective design lenses (four lenses for reflective design), analyzing experiences of students, supervisors, and administrators with the exposé-first workflow and its use of two digital platforms.

Result: The exposé-first model structured thesis preparation by turning early research planning into staged proposal writing, feedback, and approval. Students clarified research goals and took early ownership of their plans. However, work was redistributed, not reduced: supervisors moved toward iterative feedback, feasibility checking, and preliminary quality assurance, while administrators absorbed most cross-platform coordination of deadlines, submissions, and feedback.

Conclusion: The paper contributes an analysis of exposé-first thesis preparation as a sociotechnical workflow, showing that workflow redesign can improve structure while essential administrative coordination work remains underrecognized.

Abstract: At the studied research institute, one professorship oversees approximately 20 theses per semester, while day-to-day supervision is distributed among doctoral and postdoctoral researchers. To manage this supervision demand, the institute uses an exposé-first workflow in which students prepare a research proposal before entering the main thesis-writing phase. This paper asks how students, supervisors, and administrators experience the exposé-first workflow as a structured process for early thesis preparation, and how it redistributes responsibility, supervision, and administrative coordination work across roles and two digital platforms. Based on a mixed-methods study analyzed through Frauenberger et al.'s four reflective design lenses, the findings show that the exposé-first model made thesis preparation more structured by turning early research planning into a staged process of proposal writing, feedback, and approval. Students reported that this process helped them clarify research goals and take ownership of their research plans at an early stage. However, the workflow redistributed rather than reduced work: supervisors shifted toward iterative feedback, feasibility checking, and preliminary quality assurance, while administrators carried much of the coordination across platforms, deadlines, submissions, and feedback. The paper contributes an analysis of exposé-first thesis preparation as a sociotechnical workflow, showing how workflow redesign can improve structure while leaving essential administrative coordination work underrecognized.

</details>


### [182] [Analysis of Motor Signatures of Social Adaptation in Autism for Efficient Human-Centric Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12548)
*Lara Pereira,Teresa Sousa,Miguel Castelo-Branco,João Ruivo Paulo*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Using 3D motion capture and Dynamic Time Warping on dance imitation data, the study introduces a Social Context Sensitivity Index (SCSI) showing neurotypical adults increase movement variability under social framing while autistic adults do not, enabling 79.2% balanced classification accuracy and proposing social context sensitivity as a biomarker for autism-related motor behavior.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
