Motivation: Dance imitation integrates motor planning, sensorimotor integration, and social cognition, providing a sensitive framework to characterize motor behavior in autism. The goal is to identify computational biomarkers that can improve medical and human-machine systems, particularly by capturing how social context modulates motor behavior.

Method: The authors analyzed 3D motion capture data from autistic and neurotypical adults performing dance imitation in solo and socially-framed duo conditions. They applied Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) to quantify movement consistency and proposed the Social Context Sensitivity Index (SCSI) to measure how social framing modulates movement variability. These extracted features were then fed into a classifier to discriminate autistic versus neurotypical groups.

Result: Neurotypical adults showed increased movement variability in socially-framed imitation (especially in upper and lower limbs), while autistic adults maintained consistent movement across contexts. Classification using these features achieved 79.2% balanced accuracy in distinguishing the two groups.

Conclusion: Social context sensitivity in motor imitation constitutes a robust biomarker of autism-related motor behavior. The findings highlight the importance of social modulation in motor assessments and inform the development of inclusive, human-centric technologies.

Abstract: Dance imitation integrates motor planning, sensorimotor integration, and social cognition, offering a sensitive framework to characterize motor behavior in autism. In this work, we explore a computational analysis framework to identify potential biomarkers that allow the design and development of improved medical and human-machine systems. We analyzed 3D motion capture data from autistic and neurotypical adults performing dance imitation under solo and socially-framed duo conditions. Methodologically, using Dynamic Time Warping, we quantified movement consistency and propose the Social Context Sensitivity Index (SCSI) to measure modulation of variability by social framing. These features were then used on a classifier to discriminate subjects into autistic or neurotypical groups. Results show that neurotypical adults exhibited increased movement variability in socially-framed imitation, especially in upper and lower limbs, whereas autistic adults maintained consistent movement across contexts. Classification achieved 79.2% balanced accuracy in distinguishing groups. These findings suggest that social context sensitivity in motor imitation constitutes a robust biomarker of autism-related motor behavior, highlighting the importance of social modulation in motor assessments and informing the development of inclusive human-centric technologies.

</details>


### [183] [Legally Mandated, but Still Inaccessible: Digital Tensions in Older Adults' Use of Norwegian Web Services](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12552)
*Yavuz Inal,Sujay Shalawadi,Eleftherios Papachristos*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This paper examines why digital accessibility for older adults remains inadequate despite legal universal design requirements, analyzing 294 Norwegian adults (55–90) and identifying four accessibility tensions that show checklist compliance does not ensure lived usability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Norway is highly digitalized and legally mandates universal design of ICT, yet older adults still face barriers to essential digital services. The authors argue that cognitive accessibility cannot be guaranteed by technical compliance alone, motivating a study of real-world barriers experienced by older users.

Method: The study analyzed responses from 294 participants aged 55 to 90 to examine barriers encountered when using digital services. The analysis surfaced four types of tensions—navigational, semantic, procedural, and temporal—that arise from misalignments between service design, underlying system assumptions, and older adults' capabilities.

Result: Four tensions were identified: navigational, semantic, procedural, and temporal. These reveal how accessibility barriers emerge from misalignments among service design, system assumptions, and older adults' capabilities, demonstrating that checklist-based compliance does not translate into lived accessibility for mandatory or near-mandatory digital services.

Conclusion: The paper calls for moving beyond minimum compliance frameworks toward accessibility approaches that more effectively support older adults' independent participation in digital society.

Abstract: Norway is among the most digitalized countries in the world, where access to essential services increasingly depends on digital systems. Although universal design of ICT is legally required across public and private sectors, ensuring cognitive accessibility for older adults involves more than technical compliance. We analyzed responses from 294 participants aged 55 to 90 to examine the barriers they encounter when using digital services. Our findings identify four tensions, namely navigational, semantic, procedural, and temporal, which reveal how accessibility barriers emerge through misalignments between service design, system assumptions, and older adults' capabilities. Together, these tensions show that checklist-based compliance does not necessarily translate into lived accessibility when engaging with mandatory or near-mandatory digital services. We discuss the need to move beyond minimum compliance frameworks toward accessibility approaches that better support older adults' independent participation in digital society.

</details>


### [184] [InvisIto: Weaving Unobtrusive Infrared Markers for Ubiquitous Textile Interaction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12580)
*Hsuanling Lee,Hal Sugiyama,Tian Min,Hanako Fujino,Mayuka Kuwana,Yuta Sugiura,Mustafa Doga Dogan,Liang He,Koya Narumi*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: InvisIto weaves machine-readable near-infrared (NIR) markers invisibly into fabrics using NIR-absorbing yarns, preserving aesthetic and tactile qualities while enabling camera-based decoding and tracking across hand weaving, Jacquard weaving, and industrial production.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing textile-digital interaction methods rely on visible tags, printed overlays, or electronic modules that compromise the fabric's appearance and feel, creating a need for unobtrusive machine-readable marking.

Method: InvisIto uses NIR-absorbing yarns (visually similar to standard fibers yet high-contrast in NIR imaging) to weave infrared markers into fabrics. It comprises (1) a design tool for embedding infrared markers into weaving drafts, (2) five disguising strategies to reduce ambient-light visibility, and (3) a camera-based detection pipeline for decoding and tracking woven markers. It supports woven QR codes (data encoding) and woven ArUco markers (binary input and deformation tracking).

Result: The method achieves visually unobtrusive woven markers that decode and track reliably in NIR imaging, demonstrated across hand weaving, Jacquard weaving, and industrial fabrication, scaling from bespoke artifacts to mass production.

Conclusion: InvisIto enables scalable, aesthetically unobtrusive textile-digital interaction by embedding invisible NIR-readable markers directly into fabric, validated across multiple fabrication workflows and application scenarios.

Abstract: Textiles are increasingly explored as media for interacting with digital information. However, many of the existing approaches rely on visible tags, printed overlays, or electronic modules that compromise the fabric's aesthetic and tactile qualities. To address this, we present InvisIto, a method for weaving visually unobtrusive yet machine-readable infrared markers directly into fabrics using near-infrared (NIR)-absorbing yarns. Although these yarns look similar to standard fibers in ambient light, they produce strong contrast in NIR imaging. Our method includes: (1) a design tool that helps users easily embed infrared markers into weaving drafts, (2) five disguising strategies that further reduce marker visibility under ambient light, and (3) a camera-based detection pipeline for decoding and tracking the woven markers. InvisIto supports both woven QR codes for data encoding and woven ArUco markers for binary input and deformation tracking. We demonstrate applications across hand weaving, Jacquard weaving, and industrial fabrication, showing that InvisIto supports scalable interaction and fabrication from bespoke artifacts to mass production.

</details>


### [185] [Not All Nudges Land: Behavioral Controllability and Elaboration Quality in AI-Supported Journaling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12582)
*Nadia Mehjabin,Henry Kautz,Subigya Nepal*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: An exploratory eight-week passive sensing study of AI journaling found that whether a stated behavior-change intention improves depends mainly on whether the behavior involves other people: solo behaviors improved up to 50–63% of cases, while other-dependent behaviors improved only 15–22%. Writing features carried only behavior-specific signal.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI journaling tools can personalize prompts based on a user's sensed behavior, but it is unclear which kinds of behaviors actually respond to such interventions. The authors aim to understand where AI journaling nudges are most likely to be effective.

Method: Analyzed 369 journal entries from an eight-week passive sensing study. An LLM labeled each entry as expressing an intention to change a behavior or not. Follow-through was measured against 26 sensor features using a 3-day before/after comparison to see which behaviors improved after the intention was expressed.

Result: Responsiveness depended most on whether the behavior involves other people. Behaviors depending on others improved in only 15–22% of cases, whereas behaviors a person can act on alone improved more often (up to 50–63%), though unevenly. How users wrote mattered less: no single text feature separated improved from unimproved entries, and writing carried signal only within specific behaviors—most clearly for text messaging and for longer, more personal intention entries.

Conclusion: Given the small sample size, the findings are treated as exploratory patterns rather than definitive results, but they point to where AI journaling nudges are most likely to work—namely, behaviors that a person can act on alone rather than those depending on others.

Abstract: AI journaling tools can tailor prompts to a person's own sensed behavior, but it is unclear which behaviors respond to them. We analyzed 369 journal entries from an eight-week passive sensing study. An LLM labeled each entry as expressing an intention to change a behavior or not, and we measured follow-through against 26 sensor features with a 3-day before/after comparison. Responsiveness depended most on whether a behavior involves other people. Behaviors that depend on others improved in only 15 to 22% of cases, while behaviors a person can act on alone improved more often, up to 50 to 63%, though unevenly. How users wrote mattered less. No single text feature separated improved from unimproved entries; writing carried signal only within specific behaviors, most clearly for text messaging and for longer, more personal intention entries. The sample is small, so we treat these as exploratory patterns that point to where AI journaling nudges are most likely to work.

</details>


### [186] [Surprise2Refine: Axis-Centered Exploration-To-Refinement for Agent-Assisted Creative Scaffolding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12605)
*Yuzhe You,Gromit Yeuk-Yin Chan,Shunan Guo,Anlan Zhang,Eunyee Koh,Jian Zhao,Tongyu Zhou*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This paper presents Surprise2Refine, an agent-driven design tool that adaptively broadens and narrows an n×n design space via axis-centered interactions, supporting structured exploration and refinement based on evolving creative intent, and demonstrates through a user study that it improves control, scaffolding tracking, and perceived creativity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Designers need different design-space sizes at different creative stages—broad during exploration and targeted during refinement—yet existing agent-driven tools assume a fixed or continuously expanding space, forcing designers to manage and navigate the space themselves. A formative study with five designers informed the need for an adaptive, axis-centered workflow.

Method: After a formative study with five designers, the authors propose an axis-centered workflow that adaptively broadens and narrows the design space. They implemented it in the Surprise2Refine prototype, allowing users to build and reshape an n×n design space through axis-centered interactions as creative intent evolves. A within-subjects study with 14 designers evaluated the prototype.

Result: Surprise2Refine enhances users' sense of control, supports tracking of scaffolding paths, and improves the perceived creativity of design outcomes.

Conclusion: The authors distill design insights to guide future agent-assisted tools for creative scaffolding, showing that adaptively managing the design space axis-by-axis better aligns tools with designers' evolving needs across creative stages.

Abstract: Designers require different design spaces across creative stages: broad during exploration, and targeted during refinement. Yet existing agent-driven tools assume a fixed or continuously expanding space, leaving designers to manage and navigate it themselves. Informed by a formative study with five designers, we propose an axis-centered workflow that adaptively broadens and narrows the design space to support structured exploration and refinement. We implemented this workflow in Surprise2Refine, a prototype that allows users to build and reshape an nxn design space through a set of axis-centered interactions as their creative intent evolves. A within-subjects study with 14 designers shows that Surprise2Refine enhances users' sense of control, supports tracking of scaffolding paths, and improves the perceived creativity of design outcomes. We further distill design insights to guide future agent-assisted tools for creative scaffolding.

</details>


### [187] [NavSight in the Wild: Understanding Real-World Use of a Mobile Augmented Reality Application for People with Low Vision in Outdoor Navigation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12759)
*Yuheng Wu,Kexin Zhang,Ben Kosa,Ru Wang,Sanbrita Mondal,Yuhang Zhao*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: NavSight is a mobile AR app that helps people with low vision navigate outdoors by recognizing key objects and overlaying visual augmentations. A seven-day real-world diary study with 12 users reveals its benefits, how users configure it, how they handle recognition errors, social acceptability issues, and the environmental factors (weather, lighting, road conditions) that affect recognition and usability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: People with low vision face significant challenges in safe, independent outdoor navigation. Existing AR assistive systems have only been evaluated in ideal lab conditions, leaving a gap in understanding their real-world feasibility, limitations, and design needs.

Method: The authors built NavSight, a mobile augmented reality application that recognizes important outdoor objects (e.g., curbs, vehicles) and renders real-time visual augmentations. They evaluated it through a seven-day diary study with 12 people with low vision in real-world settings, collecting qualitative data on usage, configuration, errors, and social acceptability.

Result: The study characterized NavSight's impact on scene perception; users' configuration strategies for which objects to augment and how to augment them across scenarios; how users interpreted and responded to recognition errors; and the social acceptability of the system in public. It also identified environmental factors that affect recognition—weather conditions, lighting and shadows, and nonstandard road markings and textures—along with usability issues in daily use.

Conclusion: Real-world use of assistive AR for low-vision navigation introduces challenges not seen in lab settings. The authors synthesize these findings into design implications for future AI-powered assistive AR systems intended for outdoor use.

Abstract: The ability to navigate outdoors safely and independently is crucial yet challenging for people with low vision (PLV). While various augmented reality (AR) systems for low vision have been designed and evaluated in ideal lab environments, no research has investigated their real-world feasibility and challenges. We present NavSight, a mobile AR application that assists PLV in outdoor navigation by recognizing important outdoor objects (e.g., curb, vehicle) and rendering real-time visual augmentations. Through a seven-day diary study with 12 PLV in real-world settings, we characterize the impact of NavSight on scene perception, users' configuration strategies on what objects to augment and how to augment them across scenarios, how users made sense of and responded to recognition errors, and the social acceptability of using NavSight in public. We further identify environmental factors affecting recognition, such as weather conditions, lighting and shadows, and nonstandard road markings and textures, as well as usability issues in daily use. We discuss these real-world challenges and derive design implications for future AI-powered assistive AR systems for outdoor use.

</details>


### [188] [Considering Contribution Statements in Visualization and HCI Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12792)
*Mara Solen,Wesley Willett,Andrew M McNutt*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: The paper investigates why contribution statements remain uncommon in visualization and HCI research. Through an online study with 21 researchers, it uncovers tensions around ill-fitting contribution frameworks, power dynamics, authorship bias, and documentation burden. It offers modest recommendations to authors and institutions, aiming to spark dialogue on authorship and transparent attribution in these communities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Contribution statements can make research labor visible, reduce malfeasance, and increase transparency, yet they are rare in visualization and HCI. The authors seek to understand this gap and open a dialogue about authorship, attribution, and equity in these fields.

Method: An online study was conducted with N=21 visualization and HCI researchers to gather perspectives on the utility, limitations, and practical implications of contribution statements.

Result: Researchers hold differing opinions on contribution statements, shaped by tensions including contribution frameworks that poorly fit HCI and visualization contribution types, power dynamics between authors, bias in authorship perceptions, and the tedium of additional documentation. The study surfaces both contexts where statements are useful and those where they cause conflict or burden.

Conclusion: The authors recommend that authors consider contribution statements contextually, noting their value for accountability and internal alignment. To institutions, they recommend exempting contribution statements from page/word limits and providing flexible templates and examples, while continuing not to require them. The work seeks to advance equitable, transparent attribution practices in visualization and HCI.

Abstract: Contribution statements are an increasingly common way to make research labor visible, reduce academic malfeasance, and provide broader transparency. Despite this potential value, they remain uncommon in visualization and HCI. To explore this gap, we conducted an online study with (N=21) visualization and HCI researchers. We find a range of differing opinions about the utility of contribution statements, which are set against a background of tensions relating to contribution frameworks that inadequately fit contribution types in HCI and especially visualization, power dynamics between authors, bias in authorship perceptions, and the tedium of providing yet another form of documentation. From these factors, we offer a modest recommendation to authors: consider contribution statements. There are contexts when they may usefully explicate work, and others where they can cause author-team conflict or become a burdensome chore. Regardless of whether they are used by readers or not, we suggest that scaffolded mechanisms for reflecting on contribution roles are valuable both for public accountability and internal alignment. To institutions, we recommend that contribution statements be exempt from page or word limits, and that flexible templates and examples be provided to authors, but that they continue to not be required. By surfacing these perspectives, we seek to open a dialogue about what constitutes authorship, how our community might move toward more equitable and transparent attribution practices, and where the visualization and HCI communities might be uniquely equipped to help.

</details>


### [189] [PolyPresentation: A Multimodal AI Platform for Slide-Aware Iterative Presentation Practice](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12857)
*Chen Chen,Jihao Li,Zhiyuan Wen,Tianhui Zhang,Di Zou,Jiannong Cao*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: PolyPresentation is a multimodal AI platform that supports slide-aware, iterative presentation practice by linking slide-by-slide rehearsal, Q&A, and feedback into a unified loop, providing more actionable and practice-oriented guidance than existing baseline tools.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Effective presentation delivery requires repeated, coordinated practice of content, delivery, visuals, and audience interaction. Existing AI rehearsal tools treat presentations as single-run performances and fail to connect feedback to the slide deck or guide planning of subsequent practice iterations.

Method: The authors develop PolyPresentation, a multimodal AI platform that integrates slide-by-slide practice, full rehearsals, audience Q&A, and feedback into a unified iterative practice loop using slide-grounded evidence. It is evaluated through a rubric-based comparison against four baseline systems on 20 academic presentation rehearsals, plus assessment of alignment with human ratings.

Result: PolyPresentation outperforms four baselines in rubric-based evaluation, offering more actionable, context-aware, and practice-oriented support, and its assessments align well with human ratings.

Conclusion: PolyPresentation demonstrates that structuring AI feedback around slides within an iterative practice loop improves the usefulness of presentation rehearsal tools, helping presenters diagnose issues and prepare for subsequent practice more effectively.

Abstract: Presentations are essential for students, researchers, and professionals to communicate ideas persuasively, yet delivering them effectively requires repeated practice that coordinates content, delivery, visual materials, and audience interaction. Existing AI-assisted rehearsal tools provide scalable feedback, but they often treat presentations as single-run delivery performances, offering limited support for linking feedback to the slide deck or planning what to practice in the next iteration. To address this gap, we introduce PolyPresentation, a multimodal AI platform for slide-aware iterative presentation practice. PolyPresentation organizes slide-by-slide practice, full rehearsal, audience Q&A, and feedback into a unified practice loop, using slide-grounded evidence to help presenters diagnose performance issues and prepare for subsequent practice. We evaluate PolyPresentation through a rubric-based comparison with four baseline systems on 20 academic presentation rehearsals, and additionally assess its alignment with human ratings. Results suggest that PolyPresentation provides more actionable, context-aware, and practice-oriented support for improving presentations. The demonstration video is available at https://youtu.be/MmWj9O_PJxw.

</details>


### [190] [How LLMs Respond to Escalating Delusions: Four Longitudinal Trajectories of Model Behavior](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13017)
*Anna Sterna,Kacper Dudzic,Karolina Drożdż,Hubert Plisiecki,Marcin Rządeczka,Marcin Moskalewicz*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: The study longitudinally evaluates 15 mainstream LLMs over 30 days using a fixed script simulating progression from mild anomalous experiences to psychotic ideation. Four raters assessed 449 model-days on recognition stage, interpretative confidence, and intervention profile, supplemented by two automated metrics (entrainment and modality). Four distinct response trajectories were identified, ranging from premature disengagement to active delusion co-construction. Results show LLMs' capacity to exacerbate AI psychosis should be operationalized via recognition timing, stability, and intervention accuracy, assessed longitudinally.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Widespread LLM use among psychiatric populations raises safety concerns about iatrogenic effects in the context of AI psychosis. Although emerging literature conceptualizes AI psychosis and reports case studies, empirical evidence tracing whether and how LLM interactions can exacerbate psychotic processes remains scarce.

Method: A longitudinal qualitative evaluation design supported by automated metrics was developed and tested. Fifteen widely used LLMs were prompted daily for 30 days using an identical 30-message script that simulates progression from mild anomalous experiences to psychotic ideation. Four trained evaluators independently rated 449 model-days on three dimensions: recognition stage, interpretative confidence, and intervention profile. Two computational metrics (entrainment and modality) were devised to increase evaluation reliability, and direct disengagement recommendations were flagged and re-coded through adjudication with a strict two-level definition.

Result: Four response trajectories emerged: (1) premature medicalization and disengagement (Claude Haiku 4.5); (2) recognition without safeguarding, marked by LLM self-sufficiency in offering help (GPT Instant/Thinking); (3) delayed and unstable recognition with late, non-progressive conceptualization (Claude Opus 3/4/4.1, Claude Haiku 3.5, GPT-4o, Gemini 3.1 Pro); and (4) delusion co-construction via active engagement with delusional content (Gemini 2.5 Pro/Flash, DeepSeek-V3, Claude Sonnet 4).

Conclusion: LLMs' potential to exacerbate AI psychosis should be operationalized as a combination of recognition timing, recognition stability, and intervention accuracy, and should be evaluated longitudinally with a focus on temporal dynamics rather than isolated responses.

Abstract: The widespread use of LLMs among psychiatric populations has raised concerns regarding their safety and potential iatrogenic impact in the context of AI psychosis. While growing literature conceptualizes AI psychosis and documents case studies, empirical evidence tracing AI-exacerbated psychotic processes remains scarce. We propose and test a longitudinal qualitative evaluation design, supported by automated metrics, to assess mainstream LLMs' potential to exacerbate psychosis. Fifteen widely used LLMs were prompted across 30 days using the same 30-message script, simulating progression from mild anomalous experiences to psychotic ideation. Four trained evaluators independently rated 449 model-days, assessing (1) recognition stage (from naive engagement to stabilized clinical framing), (2) interpretative confidence, and (3) intervention profile (from education to treatment recommendation). Two computational metrics-entrainment and modality-were devised to increase evaluation reliability. Direct recommendations to disengage from the LLM were flagged and re-coded via adjudication using a strict two-level definition. Across model generations and vendors, we identified four response trajectories: (1) premature medicalization and disengagement (Claude Haiku 4.5); (2) recognition without safeguarding, marked by LLM self-sufficiency in offering help (GPT Instant/Thinking); (3) delayed and unstable recognition, marked by late, non-progressive conceptualization (Claude Opus 3/4/4.1, Claude Haiku 3.5, GPT-4o, Gemini 3.1 Pro); and (4) delusion co-construction through active engagement with delusional content (Gemini 2.5 Pro/Flash, DeepSeek-V3, Claude Sonnet 4). Our findings indicate that LLMs' potential to exacerbate AI psychosis should be operationalized as a combination of recognition timing, stability, and intervention accuracy and evaluated longitudinally, focusing on temporal dynamics.

</details>


### [191] [Tracing Methamphetamine abuse in under-treatment drivers: How biomechanical and oculomotor features help detect at-risk drivers?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13054)
*Hamed Salmanzadeh,Alireza Mortezapour,Iman Tahbazzadeh Moghaddam,Farshid Ipackchi,Payam Abedinzadeh,Samira Teimoori*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This study uses driving-simulator data (eye-tracking and Kinect biomechanics) to compare healthy drivers with stimulant-abuse patients in two treatment phases, training a KNN classifier that detects high-risk driving patterns with 90% accuracy for potential integration into ADAS safety systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While the dangers of driving under the acute influence of stimulants (e.g., methamphetamine) are well-documented, little research exists on the driving performance of individuals during stimulant-abuse treatment. The authors aim to fill this gap and enable proactive, real-time identification of at-risk drivers.

Method: The study collected oculomotor data via an eye-tracker and biomechanical data via a Kinect sensor from participants driving in a simulator. Participants included healthy controls and individuals with a stimulant-abuse history in two distinct treatment phases. A K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) classifier was trained on these parameters, and various feature combinations and neighborhood (k) configurations were evaluated to optimize discrimination of high-risk behavioral patterns.

Result: The optimized KNN model successfully discriminated between normal drivers and drivers with a history of stimulant abuse with 90% accuracy.

Conclusion: Continuously monitoring physiological and behavioral parameters—through technologies embedded in Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS)—can detect at-risk drivers and issue real-time alerts to the driver, passengers, and external monitoring networks, thereby proactively reducing the risk of traffic collisions.

Abstract: While the detrimental impacts of driving under the influence of stimulants such as methamphetamine are well-documented, the driving performance of individuals currently under-treatment has received considerably less attention. This study compared the behavior of individuals with a history of stimulant abuse (across two distinct treatment phases) with a control group of healthy drivers using a driving simulator. Oculomotor and biomechanical data were continuously collected via an eye-tracker and a Kinect sensor, respectively. These parameters were utilized to train a K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) classification model designed to detect high-risk behavioral patterns in drivers undergoing methamphetamine rehabilitation. Through the evaluation of various feature combinations and neighborhood configurations, the optimized model successfully discriminated between normal drivers and those with a history of abuse with an accuracy of 90%. Detecting at-risk drivers through technologies embedded in Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) by continuously monitoring physiological and behavioral parameters, facilitates a proactive safety strategy. Issuing real-time alerts to the driver, passengers, and external monitoring networks can ultimately mitigate the risk of traffic collisions.

</details>


### [192] [CogChat: Knowledge Graph-Augmented Conversational AI with Heterogeneous Graph Transformer for Cognitive Grounding in Design Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13216)
*Jiin Choi,Kyung Hoon Hyun*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: CogChat is a real-time chat framework that grounds LLM conversation in a personal heterogeneous knowledge graph built from a designer's utterances, using a Heterogeneous Graph Transformer to select relevant nodes and generate probing questions, improving context retention and conversational depth.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM chat systems treat designer utterances as generic sequences and rely on recency for context, lacking a model of how the speaker organizes knowledge. In design conversations this causes relational context to decay between turns, identical terms to remain unresolved across designers, and conversations to loop or restart rather than deepen.

Method: CogChat extracts typed entities and relations from each designer's input into a heterogeneous knowledge graph, then applies a Heterogeneous Graph Transformer (HGT) to select structurally relevant nodes for response generation and to produce both intentional and exploratory probing questions.

Result: Technical evaluation shows HGT-based entity selection outperforms ungrounded LLM interaction and naive KG augmentation (which introduces noise degrading response quality). A within-subjects study with nine professional designers shows improved context retention, personalized intent interpretation, and conversational depth, with reduced cognitive load.

Conclusion: Structuring a designer's expressed concepts and relations as a dynamic knowledge graph preserves relational context that fades across turns, pointing toward a graph-grounded approach to long-term context management in LLM-based interaction.

Abstract: LLM-based chat systems have become valuable tools for design practice, enabling rapid ideation and flexible task support. Yet these systems process designer utterances as generic sequences, maintaining context through recency rather than through any model of how the speaker organizes knowledge. In design conversation, this gap compounds as relational context decays between turns, identical words go unresolved across designers, and the conversation loops or restarts rather than deepens. We present CogChat, a real-time chat framework that grounds conversational AI in a personal heterogeneous knowledge graph constructed from each designer's input. The system extracts typed entities and relations into a heterogeneous graph, then applies a HGT (Heterogeneous Graph Transformer) to select structurally relevant nodes for response generation and to generate both intentional and exploratory probing questions. Technical evaluation shows that HGT-based entity selection outperforms both ungrounded LLM interaction and naive KG augmentation, which introduces noise that degrades response quality. A within-subjects study with nine professional designers indicates that grounding conversation in a relationally structured, designer-specific semantic context improves context retention, personalized intent interpretation, and conversational depth while reducing cognitive load. These findings suggest that structuring a designer's expressed concepts and relations as a dynamic knowledge graph can preserve relational context that fades across turns, pointing toward a graph-grounded approach to long-term context management in LLM-based interaction.

</details>


### [193] [Print&Fold: Printing and Folding Shape-accurate 3D Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13279)
*Archit Kumar,Zachary Grimm,Mingsheng Xu,Shlok Rathi,Martin Nisser*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Print&Fold is a design tool that lets users print 3D models flat using FDM and then manually fold them into shape, reducing print time and material while keeping surface detail intact.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: FDM 3D printing of complex models is costly in time and material, and prior folding methods discretize the surface, producing low-fidelity prints that lose surface features.

Method: The tool uses a folding algorithm that planarizes faces internal to a 3D model, allowing the model to be unfolded and printed flat, then manually folded into its target shape while preserving surface features.

Result: The authors demonstrate a variety of applications and evaluate material and time savings across a range of 3D models, showing reduced printing cost with preserved shape accuracy.

Conclusion: Print&Fold enables faster, cheaper FDM printing of complex models without sacrificing surface fidelity, advancing folding-based fabrication techniques beyond surface-discretizing approaches.

Abstract: This paper introduces Print&Fold, a tool to allow FDM 3D printing of complex models with less time and material while preserving shape accuracy. Key to this work is a folding algorithm that planarizes foldable faces internal to the 3D model. While folding techniques typically discretize a target model's surface, thereby fabricating low fidelity counterparts, our method preserves the surface features in the physical print. Our design tool allows users to unfold 3D models to be FDM-printed flat before manually folding these into their target shapes. We showcase a variety of applications and evaluate the material and time savings across a range of 3D models.

</details>


### [194] [More Than 63% of IEEE VIS Research Liable to be Retracted?! Ethics Approval Statements Protect Participants (and Researchers!)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13295)
*Lonni Besançon,Tobias Isenberg*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: An analysis of 255 IEEE VIS papers (2024–2025, TVCG) finds that 74.1% involved human participants, yet only 3.2% fully reported ethics approval, an approval identifier, and informed consent; the paper calls for standardized ethics-reporting practices in visualization research.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors observed, as readers and reviewers, that ethics reporting in IEEE VIS papers is frequently incomplete or missing. They also faced challenges themselves when needing to demonstrate ethics approval for their own work. Since visualization research often involves human participants, the lack of explicit reporting makes ethical approval difficult to assess and potentially puts authors at risk.

Method: The authors conducted a corpus analysis of 255 IEEE VIS papers published in TVCG in 2024 and 2025, examining whether each paper reported involving human participants and, where applicable, whether it reported obtaining ethics approval, an approval identifier, and informed consent from participants.

Result: 189 of 255 papers (74.1%) involved human participants. Only 6 (3.2%) reported ethics approval, an approval identifier, and informed consent together; 26 (13.8%) reported at least ethics approval and informed consent. The authors emphasize these omissions do not prove unethical conduct but show that current reporting practices make ethics approval hard to assess.

Conclusion: The VIS community should adopt clearer, more standardized ethics-reporting practices to protect participants, authors, reviewers, and editors, and to safeguard authors against risks arising from inadequate ethics reporting.

Abstract: We analyzed the ethics reporting in 255 IEEE VIS papers from 2024 and 2025, as published in TVCG. This analysis arose from our experience as readers and reviewers of IEEE VIS papers that such reporting is frequently incomplete or missing, as well as from investigations in which we ourselves had to answer challenges regarding ethics approval in our own work. Visualization research naturally often involves human participants, yet ethics approval and informed-consent procedures are not always explicitly reported. In our corpus, 189 papers (74.1%) reported on work involving human participants. Only 6 of them (3.2%) reported to have obtained ethics approval, an approval identifier, and having received informed consent from the participants, while 26 (13.8%) reported at least ethics approval and informed consent. These omissions do not imply that the empirical work was unethical or lacked approval. They rather show that current reporting practices make ethical approval difficult to assess. Beyond our alarming - yet true - paper title, we wish to raise awareness on how authors themselves may eventually be at risk for not properly reporting ethics. We argue that VIS should adopt clearer and more standardized ethics-reporting practices to protect participants, authors, reviewers, and editors.

</details>


### [195] [Sensorimotor Stickies: A Reconfigurable On-Body Platform for Closed-Loop Sensorimotor Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13412)
*Tianhong Catherine Yu,Jiwei Zheng,Chi-Jung Lee,Qifeng Yang,Tingyu Cheng,Qiuyue,Xue,Cheng Zhang,Yiyue Luo*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Sensorimotor Stickies is a reconfigurable, modular on-body platform that packages IMU sensing, optional tactile sensing, and vibrotactile feedback as adhesive "stickies," supported by BLE firmware and a mobile app, to enable closed-loop sensorimotor training across tasks without task-specific hardware rewrites.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing closed-loop sensorimotor training systems are built as rigid, task-specific implementations, despite sharing the same core technologies (inertial/tactile sensing, vibrotactile cueing, rule-based logic). This limits reusability and reconfiguration across tasks, users, and feedback designs.

Method: The authors build a reconfigurable on-body platform comprising miniaturized adhesive modules (IMU sensing, optional tactile sensing, vibrotactile actuation), low-power firmware with BLE infrastructure for raw streaming and motor control requiring no task-specific rewrites, and a companion mobile app providing a shared body-centered model for placement, calibration, and feedback authoring. Evaluation includes technical characterization, configured application demonstrations, practitioner-mediated configuration sessions, and an end-user study.

Result: The platform demonstrates technical feasibility, broad reconfiguration across training scenarios, and end-user configurability for first-time setup, calibration, and within-task feedback reconfiguration.

Conclusion: A modular, reconfigurable stickies-based approach can generalize closed-loop sensorimotor training infrastructure across diverse tasks and users, avoiding the need for fixed, task-specific system implementations.

Abstract: Closed-loop sensorimotor training systems can improve learning by sensing movement and delivering real-time feedback, yet most are built as fixed implementations tied to a single task, even though the core technology (inertial and tactile sensing, vibrotactile cueing, rule-based logic) remains the same. We present Sensorimotor Stickies, a reconfigurable on-body platform that treats sensing and vibrotactile feedback as modular stickies that can be patched onto the body as needed. The platform includes miniaturized adhesive modules for IMU sensing, optional tactile sensing, and vibrotactile actuation; low-power firmware and BLE infrastructure for raw streaming and motor control without task-specific rewrites; and a companion mobile app that provides a shared body-centered model for placement, calibration, and feedback authoring. Together, these components enable reconfiguration across training scenarios, user needs, and feedback setups. We evaluate the platform through technical characterization, configured application demonstration, practitioner-mediated configuration sessions, and an end-user study, demonstrating technical feasibility, reconfiguration breadth, and end-user configurability for first-time setup, calibration, and within-task feedback reconfiguration.

</details>


### [196] [Before You Say It: Anticipating Verbal Behavior from Longitudinal Everyday Conversations with LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13454)
*Yasith Samaradivakara,Valdemar Danry,Paul Liang,Pattie Maes*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: The paper introduces an LLM-based predictive behavioral modeling approach that anticipates a user's likely behavior in everyday conversations, using over 1000 hours of naturalistic longitudinal data from 14 participants collected via a wearable smartwatch, and validates predictions against ground truth plus qualitative interviews on future behavioral support.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most interactive systems model users for personalization but cannot predict how an individual will think, react, or behave across situations, since such behavioral prediction typically requires longitudinal observation of behaviors unfolding across varied everyday contexts.

Method: The authors (1) collected a longitudinal dataset of over 1000 hours of naturalistic conversations from 14 participants using a wearable smartwatch; (2) evaluated LLM-based predictions of user behavior against ground truth behaviors; and (3) used semi-structured interviews to explore participants' perceptions of behavioral predictions and possible future forms of behavioral support.

Result: The findings provide evidence that person-specific verbal behavior can be predicted from longitudinal conversational data, confirming the feasibility of LLM-based behavioral prediction from everyday conversational streams.

Conclusion: Predicting person-specific verbal behavior opens new possibilities for future context-aware, anticipatory, proactive, and personalized AI systems, such as anticipating goal deviation, catching regrettable behaviors, and surfacing blind spots before they take hold.

Abstract: Knowing someone deeply means not just understanding what they say or do but also how they will likely think, react, and engage across situations. Such predictions could eventually inform systems to anticipate when the individual is about to deviate from their goal, catch regrettable behaviors before they are made, and surface blind spots before they take hold. While many interactive systems model users to enable more personalized interactions, most cannot make such behavioral predictions, as this often requires longitudinal observation and inference of how the individual's behaviors unfold across various everyday situations. In this work, we introduce a novel LLM-based predictive behavioral modeling approach that anticipates a user's likely behavior across everyday conversational situations. We (1) collect a longitudinal dataset of over 1000 hours of naturalistic conversations from 14 participants using a wearable smartwatch; (2) evaluate LLM-based predictions against ground truth behaviors; and (3) use semi-structured interviews to explore participants perceptions of behavioral predictions and their views on possible forms of future behavioral support. Altogether, our findings provide evidence that person-specific verbal behavior can be predicted from longitudinal conversational data. This opens up new possibilities for potential future context-aware, anticipatory, proactive and personalized AI systems.

</details>


### [197] [Safety vs. Social Image: Co-Designing Protection Mechanisms Against Ableist Harassment with People with Disabilities in Social Virtual Reality](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13532)
*Kexin Zhang,Daniel Killough,Xinran Adeline Li,Yaxing Yao,Yuhang Zhao*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: The paper co-designs harassment-protection mechanisms for people with disabilities (PWD) in social VR, using Hall's Proxemics Theory to structure four social zones and offering mechanism probes (Inform, Educate, Consent, Combat). It finds social proximity shapes PWD's harassment perceptions and preferences, revealing values like resilience, optimism, and prioritizing social image over safety, and proposes design recommendations that protect PWD without harming their desired social image.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: PWD increasingly use avatars to express disability identities in social VR, but this visibility invites targeted harassment. Existing safety features are often insufficient because they overlook PWD's unique experiences and needs, motivating a co-design process to surface their values and preferences.

Method: The authors co-designed protection mechanisms with 11 PWD participants. They applied a social lens, drawing on Hall's Proxemics Theory to divide social VR space into four proxemic zones (Intimate, Personal, Social, Public) that structured the co-design. They used protection mechanism probes—Inform, Educate, Consent, and Combat—to elicit participant preferences.

Result: The study showed that social proximity shapes PWD's harassment perception and protection preferences. It revealed PWD's distinctive social values and needs, including managing harassment with optimism and resilience and prioritizing social image over safety, which differ from assumptions embedded in existing safety tools.

Conclusion: Design recommendations are proposed for protection mechanisms that safeguard PWD while preserving their desired social images, grounded in proxemic zones and PWD's expressed values, rather than generic one-size-fits-all safety features.

Abstract: People with disabilities (PWD) increasingly use avatars to express disability identities in social virtual reality (VR), but greater visibility also invites targeted harassment. Existing safety features are often insufficient, overlooking PWD's experiences and needs. To address this gap, we co-designed protection mechanisms with 11 PWD to reveal their values and needs. Our research employed a social lens to interpret harassment behaviors and protection mechanisms. Inspired by Hall's Proxemics Theory that interpersonal distances indicate social intent and boundaries, we divided social VR spaces into four proxemic zones (Intimate, Personal, Social, and Public) and used them to structure our protection mechanism co-design. We also provided different protection mechanism probes (Inform, Educate, Consent, and Combat) to elicit participant preferences. Our study highlighted the role of social proximity in shaping PWD's harassment perception and protection preferences and revealing PWD's unique social values and needs (e.g., managing harassment with optimism and resilience, prioritizing social image over safety). We proposed design recommendations for protection mechanisms that protect PWD while maintaining their desired social images.

</details>


<div id='cs.CR'></div>

# cs.CR [[Back]](#toc)

### [198] [DCBA: Detection of Collaborative Black-Hole Attacks in Connected Dominated Set using Baiting Process](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12347)
*Lata B T,Venugopal K R*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper proposes LW-CBH, a lightweight technique that enhances the AODV routing protocol to detect and isolate collaborative black-hole attacks in MANETs using a timer-based baiting process and reverse tracing via MAC-layer control status messages (R-SEQ and C-SEQ).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MANETs lack central administration and rely on cooperative multihop forwarding, making them vulnerable to malicious nodes. Black-hole attacks—especially collaborative ones—falsely advertise short routes to drop packets and degrade network performance. Existing AODV cannot detect malicious nodes during dynamic topology changes, so a lightweight detection/isolation mechanism is needed.

Method: The authors propose a timer-based baiting process combined with reverse tracing setup to detect malicious nodes using control status messages at the MAC layer: Reply Sequence (R-SEQ) and Code Sequence (C-SEQ) from the connected dominated set of nodes. The technique is integrated as an enhancement to the AODV routing protocol and simulated in NS-2.35.

Result: Simulation results show the proposed LW-CBH improves network performance measured by throughput, packet delivery ratio, average end-to-end delay, and normalized routing overhead compared to existing AODV under collaborative black-hole attacks.

Conclusion: The LW-CBH scheme effectively detects and isolates collaborative black-hole attacks in MANETs while remaining lightweight, overcoming AODV's inability to handle malicious nodes during dynamic topology changes and improving overall network reliability and performance.

Abstract: Mobile Ad-hoc Network (MANET) is temporary and dynamic network topology, wherein nodes are mobile in nature and distributed randomly in a network area. In MANET, nodes cooperate with each other to operate and forward data through multihop communication between source and destination. MANET is exposed to different types of attacks due to absence of central administration. However, some nodes decline to cooperate, misbehaves and appears to be malicious affecting network functionality and connectivity. Providing security and identifying malicious node has become one of the challenging research topics in MANET. Black-hole attack is considered to be most popular attack that degrades the overall network performance. Black-hole node falsely advertises the shortest path to destination intentionally to disrupt the network communication resulting in packet drop. In collaborative black-hole attacks, multiple black-hole nodes cooperate and launch attacks in order to degrade network reliability. In this article we propose a Lightweight technique to detect and isolate Collaborative Black-Hole attacks (LW-CBH) by enhancing existing AODV routing protocol. In this scheme a timer based baiting process and reverse tracing setup is used to detect malicious node through control status message in MAC layer which are Reply Sequence (R-SEQ) and Code Sequence (C-SEQ) message of connected dominated set of nodes. However existing AODV routing protocol fails to detect malicious node during dynamic topology changing in MANET. Simulation of proposed technique is performed using discrete event simulator tool NS-2.35. The simulation results are evaluated for throughput, packet delivery ratio, average end-to-end delay and normalized routing overhead.

</details>


### [199] [The energetic cost of mitigating AI attacks in cellular networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12431)
*Adrián Losada,Hao Qiang Luo-Chen,David Segura,Carlos S. Alvarez-Merino,Milan Groshev,Emil J. Khatib,Raquel Barco*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper explores how integrating ML-driven AI into cellular networks (e.g., O-RAN's Radio Intelligence Controller) introduces data-dependent security vulnerabilities, and examines how defending against these attacks incurs an often-overlooked energy cost, framing a trade-off among ML accuracy, robustness, and energy efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While data-driven ML algorithms deliver substantial benefits to cellular networks, their reliance on data exposes them to adversarial attacks that degrade model performance. Existing mitigation strategies work but impose computational overhead whose energy cost is generally ignored, despite the current emphasis on energy awareness in network operations.

Method: The work characterizes the energy consumption of a specific defence technique and systematically outlines the challenges arising from the interplay (triad) of ML accuracy, robustness against attacks, and energy efficiency.

Result: Defence techniques generate a measurable computational load that translates into a non-negligible energy cost, revealing a concrete trade-off among accuracy, robustness, and energy efficiency that is typically overlooked in current solutions.

Conclusion: Achieving secure and efficient AI-driven cellular networks requires jointly considering accuracy, robustness, and energy consumption, rather than treating security defence as cost-free; this triad must guide future design of ML-based network functions.

Abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI), generally as Machine Learning (ML) algorithms, in all levels and aspects of cellular networks demonstrates the success of data-driven algorithms; for example, the Radio Intelligence Controller (RIC) of the O-RAN paradigm bestows the network with optimised radio resource allocation, load balancing or energy efficiency functions, among others. Nevertheless, this dependency on data opens new security vulnerabilities, as attackers can alter data properties and steer ML models to underperform or degrade. Conversely, the developed mitigation strategies are effective, but they generate a computational load which, in consequence, results in an energy cost generally overlooked, even in the current energy-awareness context. In this work, consumption of a defence technique is characterised, and the challenges raised by the triad of ML accuracy, robustness and energy efficiency are outlined.

</details>


### [200] [Non-Degenerate Risk Certification for Automated Security Decisions: A Decision-Contract Theory with ATT\&CK-Aligned Triage as a Worked Instance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12444)
*Zhenpeng Li*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper addresses a "vacuity failure" in risk-based certification of automated decision systems: an all-abstain (never-acting) selector trivially satisfies a risk bound while providing zero utility. It develops a decision-contract theory with an error-conservation law, a capacity diagnostic separating recoverable from structural incapacity, and a non-degenerate actionability certificate, then validates the framework on LLM-based intrusion-detection alert triage.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Unconditional risk bounds can be satisfied vacuously by systems that never act, so existing certification approaches fail to distinguish meaningful automation from trivially safe abstention. The authors aim to expose this as a structural property of "decision contracts" (inputs acted on plus the semantic relation defining correctness), rather than a fixable quirk, and to build certificates that rule out all-abstain solutions.

Method: They formulate decision-contract theory around an error-conservation law stating that base-classifier error is only redistributed among three channels: harmful automation, human deferral, and semantic masking (error hidden by weakening the correctness relation). They introduce (1) a label-free singleton capacity to certify structural incapacity, with a risk-feasible refinement that distinguishes recoverable threshold misalignment from risk-constrained incapacity, and (2) a non-degenerate actionability certificate that excludes all-abstain solutions by construction. The framework is instantiated on ATT&CK-aligned alert triage for LLM-based intrusion detection across 3 IDS datasets, 6 LLMs, and 4 error-rate thresholds.

Result: Empirical false-attribution risk stayed at or below target in 90.3% of configurations, with 83.4% mean correct automation. The capacity diagnostic explained every low-utility configuration; its refinement separated genuine threshold misalignment from risk-constrained incapacity, confirmed by an exhibited alternative threshold. A training-stability re-run found no confirmed structural-incapacity instance. Real fine-grained attack-subtype labels confirmed the coarsening-transfer identity under a genuine many-to-one map, with small but non-zero masking mass.

Conclusion: Risk certificates are only meaningful relative to an explicit decision contract, and the vacuity failure is structural rather than incidental. The decision-contract theory provides certificates (capacity, refinement, actionability) that give non-vacuous guarantees while empirically achieving near-target risk and substantial correct automation on LLM intrusion detection, and the diagnostics reliably explain low-utility outcomes.

Abstract: An unconditional risk bound on automated decisions can be satisfied without automating anything, since a selector that never acts drives the bound to zero. We show this is structural: any risk certificate is defined over a decision contract, the inputs a system acts on plus the semantic relation under which an output counts correct, and weakening either hides base-classifier error. We develop a decision-contract theory: an error-conservation law showing error is only reassigned among harmful automation, human deferral, and semantic masking; a label-free singleton capacity certifying structural incapacity, with a risk-feasible refinement separating recoverable threshold misalignment from risk-constrained incapacity; and a non-degenerate actionability certificate excluding all-abstain solutions by construction. We instantiate this on ATT\&CK-aligned alert triage for LLM-based intrusion detection, the setting that exposed the vacuity failure. Across 3 IDS datasets, 6 LLMs, and 4 error-rate thresholds, empirical false-attribution risk stays at or below target in 90.3% of configurations, with 83.4% mean correct automation. The capacity diagnostic explains every low-utility configuration; its refinement separates genuine misalignment from risk-constrained incapacity, confirmed by an exhibited alternative threshold; a training-stability re-run finds no confirmed structural-incapacity instance; and real fine-grained attack-subtype labels confirm the coarsening-transfer identity under a genuine many-to-one map, with small but non-zero masking mass.

</details>


### [201] [SoK: From Generation to Consumption of Privacy Documents in Software Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12511)
*Shidong Pan,Clark LaChance,Zhen Tao,Sepideh Ghanavati*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A Systematization of Knowledge (SoK) reviewing 290 papers (2010–2025) on privacy documents, organized into a lifecycle-oriented framework covering definition, generation, analysis/extraction, consistency/compliance checking, and usability evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Research on privacy documents has grown rapidly and fragmentedly, spanning privacy policies, short notices (e.g., privacy labels), and interface-level transparency mechanisms. It has become difficult to obtain a coherent, unified view of how privacy documents are created, analyzed, evaluated, and maintained across their lifecycle.

Method: A systematic literature review of 290 papers published between 2010 and 2025 from a software engineering perspective, structured around five research questions: (1) definition and scoping, (2) generation, (3) analysis and extraction, (4) inconsistency and noncompliance checking, and (5) usability evaluation and improvement. Findings are synthesized into trends, open opportunities, and broader research directions.

Result: Identified 15 key research trends and 21 open opportunities, and charted four broader research directions: (i) emerging challenges in AI-centric platforms, (ii) diverse and up-to-date data foundations, (iii) LLM-based unified policy-code analysis, and (iv) dual usability for end-users and developers.

Conclusion: The SoK offers a shared, lifecycle-oriented foundation for future research on privacy policies and privacy documents, helping the community navigate the field's diversity and identify promising directions.

Abstract: Privacy documents (e.g., privacy policies) are a central mechanism through which digital services disclose data practices and seek user consent. Over the past decades, research on privacy documents has expanded significantly, encompassing not only traditional privacy policies but also short notices (e.g., privacy labels) and interface-level transparency mechanisms. As this research area continues to grow, it has become increasingly difficult to obtain a coherent view of how privacy documents are created, analyzed, evaluated, and maintained across their lifecycle. This SoK provides a unified, lifecycle-oriented view of privacy documents from a software engineering perspective. We systematically review and analyze 290 papers published between 2010 and 2025, organizing them around five research questions that examine how privacy documents are (1) defined and scoped, (2) generated, (3) analyzed and extracted, (4) checked for inconsistencies and noncompliance, and (5) evaluated and improved for usability. Building on our findings, we identify 15 key research trends and 21 open opportunities. We further chart four broader research directions that highlight (i) emerging challenges in AI-centric platforms, (ii) the need for diverse and up-to-date data foundations, (iii) LLM-based unified policy-code analysis, and (iv) dual usability for end-users and developers. We hope this SoK provides a shared foundation for future research on privacy policies and privacy documents.

</details>


### [202] [Tracing Provenance and Detecting Tampering with Complementary LLM Watermarks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12713)
*Xiaoyan Feng,Yanjun Zhang,He Zhang,Leo Yu Zhang,Shirui Pan*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper proposes a dual-signal LLM watermark that co-embeds a robust signal (for provenance/attribution) and a fragile signal (for tamper evidence) into each token, enabling a three-state detector (Intact / Tampered / No-Watermark) that resists piggyback spoofing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM watermarks preserve provenance under editing, but this same robustness lets adversaries alter critical content while retaining attribution—a vulnerability called piggyback spoofing. The motivation is to provide both provenance and tamper evidence simultaneously, so that edited text can be flagged as tampered rather than still attributed to the original author.

Method: The method co-embeds two signals into each generated token using the same mechanism but independent keys and different seeding windows over normalized text. One signal is robust to edits (provenance), while the other is fragile/sensitive to reader-visible changes (tamper evidence). Multiple rounds of unbiased tournament reweighting preserve the expected generation distribution, and a periodic round-allocation pattern controls the trade-off between the two signals. At detection, the two scores form a two-dimensional space supporting three decisions: Intact, Tampered, and No-Watermark.

Result: Across two large language models and two prompt datasets, the method achieves the highest tamper-detection rate among evaluated methods while maintaining competitive attribution robustness and perplexity. Ablations show that reliable three-state detection requires a well-defined notion of intactness, co-embedding of the two signals, and complementary sensitivity to edits.

Conclusion: The proposed watermark successfully combines provenance and tamper evidence, achieving superior tamper detection without sacrificing attribution robustness or text quality, and demonstrates that the three-state detection framework depends on intactness definition, co-embedding, and complementary edit sensitivity.

Abstract: Watermarking LLM-generated text is an important task for tracing its provenance. Existing LLM watermarks preserve provenance under editing, but this same robustness allows an adversary to alter critical content while retaining attribution, a vulnerability known as piggyback spoofing. We introduce an innovative watermark that jointly provides provenance and tamper evidence. It co-embeds a robust signal and a fragile signal into each generated token. The signals share the same mechanism but use independent keys and different seeding windows over normalized text, making one resilient to edits and the other sensitive to reader-visible changes. Multiple rounds of unbiased tournament reweighting preserve the expected generation distribution, while a periodic round-allocation pattern controls the trade-off between the two signals. At detection, their scores form a two-dimensional space supporting three decisions: Intact, Tampered, and No-Watermark. Across two large language models and two prompt datasets, our method demonstrates the highest tamper-detection rate among the evaluated methods while maintaining competitive attribution robustness and perplexity. Ablation studies show that reliable three-state detection requires a well-defined notion of intactness, co-embedding of the two signals, and complementary sensitivity to edits.

</details>


### [203] [PIPES: Securing Agent Perception with Provenance and Priors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12789)
*Sanjay Kariyappa,Severin Klingler,G. Edward Suh*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Tool responses lack provenance about who produced each component, enabling state-corruption attacks that manipulate an agent's perceived environment. The paper introduces PIPES, a provenance-informed screening defense that reduces attack success from 84.7% to 2.3% while preserving benign utility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tool-using agents consume external data from sources with varying trust levels, but tool responses rarely identify the producer or intended meaning of each component. This provenance gap allows attacker-controlled content to make claims beyond its informational authority, corrupting the agent's perceived environment and making malicious actions appear justified to existing guardrails.

Method: PIPES (Provenance-Informed, Prior-Enforced Screening) screens response units using semantic priors and source provenance. It applies static field contracts when schemas provide stable expectations, and conditions screening of open-ended content on the pre-response trajectory and trusted provenance metadata. It marks units that violate their semantic prior or the provenance hierarchy; deployments may remove, warn, block, or escalate violations. The authors instantiate atomic removal and evaluate PIPES against adaptive PAIR-style attacks.

Result: Across three VitaBench and three AgentDyn splits with Gemma 4 31B IT as the target agent, PIPES reduces average attack success from 84.7% to 2.3%, while preserving average benign utility (92.5% with PIPES versus 90.6% without defense).

Conclusion: PIPES effectively mitigates state-corruption attacks on tool-using agents by enforcing semantic priors and provenance hierarchies during response screening, dramatically lowering attack success while maintaining benign utility.

Abstract: Tool-using agents consume external data from sources with different levels of trust, yet tool responses rarely identify who produced each component or what it should convey. We show that this gap enables state-corruption attacks, in which attacker-controlled content makes environmental claims beyond the informational authority of its response component and corrupts the agent's perceived environment, making the resulting action appear justified to existing guardrails. We introduce PIPES (Provenance-Informed, Prior-Enforced Screening), which screens response units using semantic priors and source provenance. PIPES uses static field contracts when schemas provide stable expectations, and conditions screening of open-ended content on the pre-response trajectory and trusted provenance metadata. It marks units that violate their semantic prior or the provenance hierarchy; deployments may remove, warn, block, or escalate detected violations. We instantiate atomic removal and evaluate PIPES against adaptive PAIR-style attacks. Across the three VitaBench and three AgentDyn splits with Gemma 4 31B IT as the target agent, PIPES reduces average attack success from 84.7% to 2.3%, while preserving average benign utility (92.5% with PIPES versus 90.6% without defense).

</details>


### [204] [RealmEye: Virtual Machine Introspection for Arm CCA Realm VMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12822)
*Ruofei Qu,Wei Feng,Hongzhan Ma,Menghan Jia,Muyan Shen,Yu Qin*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: RealmEye is the first VM introspection (VMI) system for Arm CCA Realm VMs, placing all introspection logic inside the Realm Management Monitor (RMM) at R-EL2 to achieve hardware-enforced separation without any in-VM agent or VM modification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Confidential VMs (CVMs) protect workloads from a malicious cloud but blind owners to what runs inside, leaving them vulnerable to kernel rootkits planted via network or supply-chain attacks. Existing CVM-VMI solutions like 00SEVen depend on AMD SEV-SNP's privileged in-VM agent (VMPL0), a mechanism unavailable on Arm CCA, leaving Realm VMs with no introspection capability.

Method: RealmEye embeds the full introspection logic in the RMM at R-EL2. It reads Realm memory and registers, suspends the VM for consistent snapshots, and traps page-level accesses without any in-VM interface. A periodic self-driven trigger mode keeps scan timing internal to the RMM, preventing Hypervisor collusion with in-Realm rootkits. Results reach the remote owner over a hardware-attested channel, and a CCA driver backend allows existing tools like LibVMI and DRAKVUF to interoperate unchanged.

Result: On the Arm FVP, RealmEye detects process hiding and syscall-table hooking by Diamorphine, and its in-RMM cost is linearly predictable from primitive invocation counts.

Conclusion: RealmEye restores VMI for Arm CCA Realm VMs by moving introspection into the RMM, providing hardware-enforced isolation with no in-VM agent, and enabling compatibility with existing introspection tooling while keeping timing secure against a colluding Hypervisor.

Abstract: Confidential VMs (CVMs) have become the dominant substrate for sensitive cloud workloads, from financial services to privacy-preserving AI inference. The hardware isolation that protects these CVMs from a malicious cloud also blinds their owners to what runs inside them: kernel rootkits planted via network or supply-chain attacks can hide processes, tamper with kernel data, and exfiltrate model weights under the cover of the same isolation that defends the VM. Tenants therefore need to inspect a running CVM from outside, yet classical VM introspection (VMI) presupposes a trusted Hypervisor, which CVMs exclude from the TCB. The state-of-the-art CVM-VMI system, 00SEVen, restores introspection on AMD SEV-SNP via an in-VM agent at a privileged tier (VMPL0), a mechanism that does not exist on Arm CCA, leaving Realm VMs without any introspection solution.
  We present RealmEye, the first VMI system for Arm CCA Realm VMs. RealmEye places the entire introspection logic inside the Realm Management Monitor (RMM) at R-EL2, achieving hardware-enforced separation between the monitor and the monitored VM: no agent runs inside the Realm, and the Realm remains unmodified. RealmEye reads Realm memory and registers, suspends the VM for consistent snapshots, and traps page-level accesses, without relying on any in-VM interface. A periodic, self-driven trigger mode keeps scan timing internal to the RMM, preventing the Hypervisor from colluding with in-Realm rootkits. Results are returned to the remote owner over a hardware-attested channel, and a CCA driver backend lets existing tools such as LibVMI and DRAKVUF interoperate with RealmEye unchanged. On the Arm FVP, RealmEye detects process hiding and syscall-table hooking by Diamorphine, and its in-RMM cost is linearly predictable from primitive invocation counts.

</details>


### [205] [Beyond Source: An Empirical Study of Python Bytecode Security Risks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12853)
*Baihong Chen,Tian Xie,Wen Li*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: An empirical study of Python bytecode (.pyc/marshalled code) as a security artifact, showing it is widespread in PyPI, practically decompilable but not robustly, and can drive CPython runtimes into memory-corruption-like failures unreproducible from source.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Python package security is source-centric, yet runtimes can execute bytecode directly and there is an inspection-execution gap: analysts inspect source but the interpreter may execute different bytecode behavior. The authors want to determine whether bytecode is a meaningful, measurable security artifact.

Method: Large-scale empirical measurement across 1,034,843 PyPI artifacts: (1) quantify bytecode exposure (counts of .pyc files and artifact-local source-less .pyc files); (2) evaluate decompilability using version-aware tooling on CPython 3.8-3.14 bytecode; (3) assess CPython runtime robustness by feeding observed PyPI bytecode and adversarially mutated/fuzzed bytecode to decompilers and the runtime; (4) attempt source-level reproduction of bytecode findings.

Result: Found 7,388 bytecode-containing artifacts with 228,578 .pyc files, including 28,193 source-less .pyc files. Decompilers emitted source for 204,901 of 204,904 in-scope files (emission, not verified equivalence). Tools are non-robust: PyPI bytecode caused managed-code exceptions/timeouts, mutated bytecode caused native process failures, yielding 17 distinct robustness signatures. Fuzzing produced 1,009 stack-deduplicated runtime findings dominated by pointer-dereference symptoms; 261 groups show potential memory-corruption characteristics, and ≥91.7% of groups execute past the documented-unsafe ingestion boundary. None reproduce from ordinary Python source.

Conclusion: Bytecode is a visible ecosystem artifact, a practical analysis target, and a security-relevant interpreter input whose runtime behavior need not match source-level behavior, exposing a gap between source-centric analysis and actual execution.

Abstract: Python package security is largely source-centric, yet Python runtimes can execute bytecode directly through .pyc files, compiled-only modules, and marshalled code objects, creating an inspection-execution gap. We present an empirical study of Python bytecode as a security artifact. We measure bytecode exposure in PyPI distributions, evaluate practical analyzability using version-aware tooling, assess CPython runtime robustness under adversarial bytecode, and test source-level reproduction of bytecode findings. Across 1,034,843 collected PyPI artifacts, we identify 7,388 bytecode-containing artifacts, including 228,578 .pyc files and 28,193 artifact-local source-less .pyc files. For modern CPython 3.8-3.14 bytecode, at least one selected decompiler emits source for 204,901 of 204,904 in-scope files, a result measuring emission rather than verified functional equivalence. Tools are non-robust: observed PyPI bytecode triggers managed-code exceptions and timeouts, while adversarial mutated bytecode also drives decompilers into native process failures; together these outcomes yield 17 distinct robustness signatures. Fuzzing produces 1,009 stack-deduplicated runtime findings dominated by pointer-dereference symptoms; 261 groups exhibit potential memory-corruption characteristics, and at least 91.7% of groups reach execution beyond the documented-unsafe ingestion boundary. None reproduce from ordinary Python source. Bytecode is thus a visible ecosystem artifact, a practical analysis target, and a security-relevant interpreter input whose behavior need not match source-level behavior.

</details>


### [206] [InterSAGE: The Secure and Verifiable Interoperability Protocol for An Internet of Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13030)
*Zhenhua Zou,Sheng Guo,Qiuyang Zhan,Lepeng Zhao,Shuo Li,Zhuotao Liu*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: InterSAGE is a trust-native protocol suite that adds a missing security substrate (identity, authorization, capability negotiation, accountability) to existing agent communication protocols, structured as four layers and built on four core primitives.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
