Motivation: The emerging Internet of Agents lets LLM-powered agents discover peers, invoke tools, and delegate tasks across organizational boundaries. Existing protocols define how agents exchange messages but do not specify how an agent proves identity, authorization, advertised capabilities, or accountability after delegation. This gap leaves trust semantics implicit and unenforceable.

Method: InterSAGE supplies a four-layer trust-native protocol suite that complements (not replaces) communication protocols. Its four layers are Persistent Identity, Discovery, Trust Negotiation, and Accountability. Its four core primitives are: (1) Agent Identity Cards binding developer, code package, operator, and deployment context; (2) capability-aware discovery via DID-bound Verifiable Credential manifests; (3) trust negotiation combining monotonic capability attenuation with two-tier access control; and (4) kernel-mediated cryptographic audit trails binding usage, delegation, and execution traces to agent identity without a consensus ledger. It is compared against more than 50 related efforts across agent protocols, decentralized identity, OAuth/OIDC extensions, zero-trust governance, delegation, and audit architectures.

Result: The comparison with 50+ efforts shows that no prior architecture jointly enforces persistent identity, capability-aware discovery, trust negotiation, and accountability as a unified four-layer trust substrate for secure agent interoperability. InterSAGE is designed to work alongside MCP, A2A, ANP, and AG-UI so communication protocols evolve independently while trust semantics remain explicit, portable, and verifiable.

Conclusion: InterSAGE fills a critical gap in the Internet of Agents by providing a unified, four-layer trust substrate that operates alongside existing communication protocols, ensuring explicit, portable, and verifiable trust semantics for secure agent interoperability.

Abstract: The emerging Internet of Agents enables LLM-powered agents to discover peers, invoke tools, and delegate tasks across organizational boundaries. Existing protocols increasingly define how agents exchange messages, but not how an agent proves its identity, authorization, advertised capabilities, or accountability after delegation. We present InterSAGE, a trust-native protocol suite that supplies this missing security substrate alongside, rather than in place of, communication protocols. InterSAGE comprises four layers: Persistent Identity, Discovery, Trust Negotiation, and Accountability. Its four core primitives are: (1) Agent Identity Cards that bind developer, code package, operator, and deployment context; (2) capability-aware discovery using DID-bound Verifiable Credential manifests; (3) trust negotiation combining monotonic capability attenuation with two-tier access control; and (4) kernel-mediated cryptographic audit trails that bind usage, delegation, and execution traces to agent identity without a consensus ledger. InterSAGE is designed to complement MCP, A2A, ANP, and AG-UI, allowing communication protocols to evolve independently while keeping trust semantics explicit, portable, and verifiable. We compare InterSAGE with more than 50 efforts spanning agent protocols, decentralized identity, OAuth/OIDC extensions, zero-trust governance, delegation, and audit architectures. We show that no prior architecture jointly enforces persistent identity, capability-aware discovery, trust negotiation, and accountability as a unified four-layer trust substrate for secure agent interoperability.

</details>


### [207] [Discovering Persistent Behavioural Patterns for Interpretable Blockchain Forensics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12864)
*Dorottya Zelenyanszki,Zhe Hou,Kamanashis Biswas,Vallipuram Muthukkumarasamy*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper proposes a scalable, application-agnostic framework for discovering persistent behavioural patterns in blockchain activity using behaviour sentences and two-step embeddings, evaluated on 30M+ Ethereum transactions to uncover routine and malicious behaviours.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing DeFi-related blockchain analysis approaches are application-specific, difficult to scale, or hard to interpret. There is a need for a general, interpretable method that can discover both routine and malicious long-term behavioural patterns from large-scale blockchain data.

Method: The framework constructs "behaviour sentences" enriched with contract, token, and market context, then applies a two-step embedding process: sentence-level embeddings capture individual actions and sequence-level embeddings capture user behaviour over time. An interpretable behavioural profiler characterizes discovered communities via behavioural motifs, routines, temporal dynamics, entity exposure, and suspiciousness evidence.

Result: Evaluation on Ethereum using over 30 million transactions uncovered both routine and malicious behavioural patterns, including DEX trading, NFT activity, phishing, bot operations, oracle manipulation, and rug-pull schemes. Many patterns remained stable across independent observation windows, enabling identification of long-term behaviours.

Conclusion: The framework combines scalability, interpretability, and persistence analysis, supporting blockchain forensic investigation, behavioural attribution, and threat discovery.

Abstract: Public blockchain data enables large-scale DeFi-related analysis, but many existing approaches are application-specific, difficult to scale, or hard to interpret. This research proposes a scalable, application-agnostic framework for \emph{persistent behavioural pattern discovery} from large-scale blockchain activity. It constructs behaviour sentences enriched with contract, token and market context, then applies a two-step embedding process: sentence-level embeddings capture individual actions, while sequence-level embeddings capture user behaviour over time. An interpretable behavioural profiler characterizes discovered communities through behavioural motifs, routines, temporal dynamics, entity exposure, and suspiciousness evidence. Evaluation on Ethereum using over 30 million transactions shows that the framework uncovers both routine and malicious behavioural patterns, including decentralised exchange (DEX) trading, NFT activity, phishing, bot operations, oracle manipulation, and rug-pull schemes. Importantly, many patterns remain stable across independent observation windows, enabling the identification of long-term behaviours beyond a single analysis period. The proposed framework combines scalability, interpretability, and persistence analysis, supporting blockchain forensic investigation, behavioural attribution, and threat discovery.

</details>


### [208] [Labels Are Not Endpoints: Treatment Leakage and Construct Validity in MCP Agent Security Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12880)
*Rana Muhammad Ahmed,Sabahat Abbas*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper audits a preserved tool-using agent security campaign by tracing execution rows to model-bound requests, semantic requests, and stimuli. It finds the historical grader leaked treatment metadata into labels (ATTACK_SUCCESS gated by treatment info), enabling class flips under relabeling. A treatment-blind reconstruction reclassifies 58 historical ATTACK_SUCCESS/HIJACK_ATTEMPT labels as benign while preserving three verified protected-data transfers and one unauthorized-forwarding case, which remains a HIJACK_ATTEMPT boundary case. The locked v2 census has zero ATTACK_SUCCESS records. A blinded dual-reviewer concordance review matched reviewer consensus on 96 interpretable requests but diverged from the locked codebook on four construct-boundary cases. Contributions include a seven-link Integrity Chain and an executable scope-bounded endpoint-integrity linter.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Security evaluations of tool-using agents often conflate stored labels with actual behavioral facts, risking invalid conclusions. The authors seek to test whether a preserved campaign's labels correspond to genuine agent behavior and to correct systematic grading errors (e.g., treatment leakage) that could misstate attack outcomes.

Method: A campaign-level measurement audit. The authors traced 10,200 execution rows back to 180 model-bound requests, 45 semantic requests, and 15 observable stimuli. They delivered two schema treatments but not the planned external payload-family corpus. They identified direct treatment leakage in the historical grader (treatment metadata gating ATTACK_SUCCESS). They performed a treatment-blind reconstruction of labels, applied a locked v2 census, and ran a dual-reviewer blinded concordance review over all 96 structurally interpretable requests. They also built a seven-link Integrity Chain and a scope-bounded endpoint-integrity linter.

Result: The treatment-blind reconstruction corrected 58 historical ATTACK_SUCCESS or HIJACK_ATTEMPT labels to authorized benign completions, while preserving three verified protected-data transfers and one separate unauthorized-forwarding case. The locked v2 census contains exactly zero ATTACK_SUCCESS records; the forwarding case remains a HIJACK_ATTEMPT at a semantic boundary regarding objective completion. The blinded dual-reviewer concordance review produced identical reviewer-consensus classes but differed from the locked codebook on four construct-boundary cases.

Conclusion: The result is a campaign-bounded measurement audit, explicitly not a population attack-rate, model-ranking, defense-efficacy, or causal estimate. The work contributes the seven-link Integrity Chain and the executable linter to support reproducible, treatment-blind integrity checks within that campaign scope.

Abstract: Security evaluations of tool-using agents often equate stored labels with behavioral facts. We audit a preserved campaign by tracing 10,200 execution rows to 180 model-bound requests, 45 semantic requests, and 15 observable stimuli. Two schema treatments were delivered, but the planned external payload-family corpus was not. The historical grader exhibited direct treatment leakage: treatment metadata gated the ATTACK_SUCCESS class, so fixed behavior could change class under treatment relabeling. A treatment-blind reconstruction corrects 58 historical ATTACK_SUCCESS or HIJACK_ATTEMPT labels to authorized benign completions while preserving three verified protected-data transfers and one separate unauthorized-forwarding case. The locked v2 census contains exactly zero ATTACK_SUCCESS records, while the forwarding case remains a HIJACK_ATTEMPT at a semantic boundary concerning objective completion. A dual-reviewer blinded concordance review of all 96 requests deemed structurally interpretable by locked v2 produced identical reviewer-consensus classes but differed from the locked codebook on four construct-boundary cases. We contribute a seven-link Integrity Chain and an executable, scope-bounded endpoint-integrity linter. The result is a campaign-bounded measurement audit, not a population attack-rate, model-ranking, defense-efficacy, or causal estimate.

</details>


### [209] [Adversarial Robustness in Smishing Detection: A Comparative Analysis of Adversarial Fragility in Classical vs. Transformer-Based Detection Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12889)
*Denzel Chiuseni,Athanase Bahizire,Silva Hama,Jema David Ndibwile*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This study benchmarks the adversarial robustness of five smishing-detection models (Random Forest, XGBoost, CNN+BiLSTM, mBERT, XLM-RoBERTa) against character obfuscation, code-switching, and structural perturbation attacks, showing that transformers are far more resilient than classical lexical models and that clean-text accuracy does not predict robustness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Smishing detectors are usually built and tested on clean, monolingual text, but in low-resource settings attackers evade them via character obfuscation, cross-lingual code-switching, and structural perturbation. The authors aim to quantify how different model architectures degrade under such adversarial conditions and determine whether clean-text performance predicts robustness.

Method: The authors evaluate five architectures—three classical lexical models (Random Forest, XGBoost, CNN+BiLSTM) and two multilingual transformers (mBERT, XLM-RoBERTa)—on a dataset of 27,037 messages. Classical models receive black-box generic attacks, while transformers receive attention-guided targeted attacks. Each model is tested across three attack types and intensity levels, with performance measured by the Robustness Degradation Ratio (RDR). Statistical validation uses Mann-Whitney U and Friedman tests, and effect size is quantified with Cliff's d.

Result: Classical models suffer near-catastrophic failure under character obfuscation and structural perturbation (RDR up to 0.988), while transformers are markedly more resilient (RDR up to 0.351), with structural perturbation as their biggest weakness. Cliff's d indicates a substantial gap between the two model categories. Within transformers, XLM-RoBERTa degrades more than mBERT despite a higher clean-text baseline, showing clean-text accuracy is not a reliable predictor of robustness. Statistical tests confirm these patterns stem from architecture, not sampling.

Conclusion: There is a clear architectural boundary in adversarial robustness: transformers substantially outperform classical lexical models, and clean-text performance does not guarantee robustness. The authors argue for architecture-specific defenses and for reframing smishing detection as an adversarial cybersecurity problem rather than a static classification task.

Abstract: Smishing detection systems are commonly trained and evaluated on clean, monolingual text. In low-resource settings, however, attackers frequently circumvent these systems through character obfuscation, cross-lingual code-switching, and structural perturbation. This study evaluates adversarial robustness for five model architectures: three classical lexical models (Random Forest, XGBoost, CNN+BiLSTM) and two multilingual transformers (mBERT, XLM-RoBERTa), using a dataset of 27,037 messages. Classical models are subjected to black-box generic attacks, while transformers are evaluated with attention-guided targeting. Each model is tested across three attack types and intensity levels, with performance measured by the Robustness Degradation Ratio (RDR). The results reveal a distinct architectural boundary: classical models experience near-catastrophic failure under character obfuscation and structural perturbation (RDR up to 0.988), whereas transformers demonstrate significantly greater resilience (RDR up to 0.351), with structural perturbation representing their most pronounced vulnerability. Effect-size analysis (Cliff's d) indicates a substantial difference between the two model categories. Within the transformer group, XLM-RoBERTa, despite achieving a higher clean-text baseline, exhibits greater degradation than mBERT. These findings demonstrate that clean-text performance is not a reliable predictor of adversarial robustness. Statistical validation using Mann-Whitney U and Friedman tests confirms that these patterns are attributable to model architecture rather than sampling. The results underscore the necessity for architecture-specific defences and frame smishing detection as an adversarial cybersecurity challenge rather than a static classification task.

</details>


### [210] [Beyond Handcrafted Security: Towards Self-Evolving Defense for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12977)
*Jiajun Ruan,Peiyang Li,Yukun Chen,Fengting Li,Chao Feng*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper introduces a harness-level formulation of runtime defense for LLM agents and proposes HARD, a self-evolving framework that autonomously identifies intervention strategies and improves defense artifacts from failure traces, outperforming handcrafted defenses while maintaining benign task utility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents face growing security threats, and existing runtime defenses depend on manually designed interventions without a principled construction/maintenance framework. This motivates a systematic harness perspective and autonomous evolution to replace manual engineering.

Method: First, the authors develop a harness-level formulation of runtime defense that characterizes how harness mechanisms enable defense construction and unify existing interventions. Building on this, they propose HARD (Harness-based Autonomous Runtime Defense Evolution), which automatically identifies appropriate intervention strategies and iteratively refines defense artifacts using observed failure traces.

Result: Extensive experiments show HARD improves security performance over existing handcrafted defenses while preserving benign task utility, transforming runtime defense development into an autonomous evolution process.

Conclusion: Autonomous defense evolution is a promising new paradigm for securing deployed LLM agents, enabling agents to identify defense weaknesses and continuously enhance their protection mechanisms.

Abstract: The expanding operational capabilities of large language model (LLM) agents introduce sophisticated security threats. Runtime defenses have emerged as an effective approach to mitigating these risks by integrating security mechanisms into the agent execution loop. However, existing runtime defenses rely heavily on manually designed interventions and lack a principled framework for their construction and maintenance. In this work, we first develop a harness-level formulation of runtime defense that systematically characterizes how harness mechanisms enable defense construction and provides a unified view of existing runtime defense interventions from a harness perspective. Building on this formulation, we propose HARD (Harness-based Autonomous Runtime Defense Evolution), a self-evolving runtime defense framework that automatically identifies appropriate intervention strategies and iteratively improves defense artifacts based on observed failure traces. HARD transforms runtime defense development from manual engineering into an autonomous evolution process, and extensive experiments demonstrate that it improves security performance over existing handcrafted defenses while preserving benign task utility. Our findings highlight autonomous defense evolution as a promising new paradigm for securing deployed LLM agents, enabling agents to identify defense weaknesses and continuously improve their protection mechanisms.

</details>


### [211] [ATOBench: Tracing How Autonomous Penetration-Testing Agents Verify Vulnerabilities When Target Evidence Lies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12996)
*Qiyang Chen,Yixi Li,Fengwei Zhang,Junlin Liu*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: ATOBench is an evaluation framework that makes the verification process of autonomous penetration-testing agents observable by injecting deceptive target responses at runtime, aligning transformed and native episodes, and tracing how actions, evidence recovery, stopping, and reporting evolve from the first affected response.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous pentest agents rely on target responses to guide actions and final reports, and deceptive responses can redirect both attack trajectory and verification. However, final reports reveal little about how an agent interprets conflicting evidence, changes course, decides to stop, or converts observations into vulnerability claims, leaving the verification process opaque.

Method: ATOBench injects registered response transformations at runtime and pairs each transformed episode with a native episode under the same environment, aligned at the first affected response. A source-linked reconstruction follows later actions, evidence recovery, stopping, and report support. Three frozen observation contracts cover exploit proof, resource ownership, and reusable artifacts. Five model routes are evaluated over 450 episodes.

Result: Analysis over 450 episodes across five model routes shows that increased activity can mask a broken verification chain, while successful recovery depends on finding usable evidence and preserving it through reporting.

Conclusion: ATOBench turns deceptive target observations into a reproducible probe of evidence handling in autonomous penetration testing, extending offensive pentest agent evaluation beyond final outcomes to reveal how untrusted observations shape actions, verification, and reporting.

Abstract: Autonomous penetration-testing agents rely on target responses. These responses guide both subsequent actions and the final report. A deceptive response can therefore redirect both the attack trajectory and the agent's verification process. However, final reports reveal little about how an agent interprets conflicting evidence, changes course, decides to stop, or turns observations into a vulnerability claim. We introduce ATOBench, an evaluation framework that makes this verification process observable. ATOBench injects registered response transformations at runtime and pairs each transformed episode with a native episode under the same environment. Each pair is aligned at the first affected response. A source-linked reconstruction then follows later actions, evidence recovery, stopping, and report support. Three frozen observation contracts cover exploit proof, resource ownership, and reusable artifacts. We evaluate five model routes over 450 episodes. The analysis shows that increased activity can mask a broken verification chain, while successful recovery depends on finding usable evidence and preserving it through reporting. ATOBench turns deceptive target observations into a reproducible probe of evidence handling in autonomous penetration testing. This process-level view extends offensive pentest agent evaluation beyond final outcomes by revealing how untrusted observations shape actions, verification, and reporting.

</details>


### [212] [OmniSphinx: Active Mix Networks (Extended Version)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13008)
*Daniel Schadt,Christoph Coijanovic,Shabi Shabani,Thorsten Strufe*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper introduces OmniSphinx, a new packet format for mix networks that lets senders embed processing code in packets, enabling a single deployment to emulate any other mix format instead of maintaining incompatible, format-specific infrastructures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing mix network packet formats are incompatible with one another and are typically designed around a single, specific goal, which forces operators to set up separate software and infrastructure for each format. The authors aim to unify these formats under one active mix network deployment.

Method: OmniSphinx is an active mix network format in which senders embed executable code in their packets. This code determines how the packet is processed by the mix nodes, allowing the network to emulate the behavior of any other mix packet format within a single deployment.

Result: Empirical evaluation shows emulation incurs reasonable overhead versus native execution for typical use cases. For Sphinx (the most compact format), computation time increases by about 90μs while header size grows by roughly 33%.

Conclusion: OmniSphinx demonstrates that a single active mix network deployment can flexibly emulate diverse existing mix formats with only modest overhead, reducing the need for separate software and infrastructure.

Abstract: Mix networks are an important tool to implement anonymous communication, which protects not just the content but also the metadata of messages. Over time, various packet formats for mix networks have been proposed, usually with single, specific goals in mind. These formats are incompatible with each other, requiring separate software and infrastructure to be set up. In this paper, we propose a new format, OmniSphinx, which solves this issue. In OmniSphinx, senders embed code in their packets that determines how they must be processed. The resulting active mix network can emulate any other mix format within a single deployment. Our empirical evaluation shows that emulation in OmniSphinx incurs reasonable overhead compared to native execution for typical mix network use cases: For Sphinx, the most compact format, computation time increases by around 90μs, while headers increase by 33% in size.

</details>


### [213] [Smart Contract Invariants Protect Against Cybercriminals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13191)
*Sofia Bobadilla,Humaira Afrin,Angela Novelli,Martin Monperrus*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper argues that program invariants are the most powerful defense against smart contract exploits. It introduces INVARIANTEVAL (28 real Ethereum exploits with human-authored invariants) and PONDEREPLAY (a replay framework), validating invariants against 108,637 historical transactions and showing they block all attacks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Blockchains are highly adversarial environments where cybercriminals exploit smart contract vulnerabilities to steal billions of dollars. Existing concepts and techniques have not reliably solved this open problem.

Method: The authors devise an experimental protocol with two goals: studying whether invariants would have prevented past attacks, and whether state-of-the-art automated tools can find them. They build INVARIANTEVAL, a benchmark of 28 real Ethereum exploits each paired with a human-authored invariant, and PONDEREPLAY, a replay framework that re-executes transactions to verify the correctness and soundness of invariants.

Result: Smart contract invariants blocked all 28 cybercriminal attacks in INVARIANTEVAL, fully validated by replaying 108,637 historical transactions.

Conclusion: Large-scale experiments demonstrate that smart contract invariants effectively protect against cybercriminal attacks.

Abstract: Blockchains are among the most adversarial environments in computing. Billions are stolen by cybercriminals who exploit vulnerabilities. This is an open problem and no concept or technique has proven to really make a difference. In this paper, we claim that the classical notion of program invariant is perhaps the most powerful solution to the problem. We devise anoriginal experimental protocol to 1) study how invariants would have protected against past real-world attacks and 2) whether state-of-the-art automated tools can find them. The experimental toolchain is sophisticated. It is based on INVARIANTEVAL, a benchmark of 28 real Ethereum exploits, each paired with a human-authored invariant that blocks the attack. We validate every invariant with PONDEREPLAY, a replay framework that re-executes transactions in order to prove the correctness and soundness of smart contract invariants. We demonstrate that smart contract invariants block all the cybercriminal attacks in INVARIANTEVAL, fully validated by replaying 108,637 historical transactions. Our large-scale experiments clearly demonstrate that smart contract invariants protect against cybercriminals.

</details>


### [214] [InSPECtor: Improving SLEIGH Processor Specification Veracity via Proxy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13042)
*Michael Chesser,Paul Quirk,Douglas Cooke,Guy Farrelly,Surya Nepal,Damith C. Ranasinghe*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: InSPECtor is a testing framework that, for the first time, systematically validates open-source SLEIGH processor specifications (used by Ghidra) using differential testing against hardware references, uncovering 38,920+ discrepancies and 125 unique bugs across five architectures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Processor specifications underpin security and program-analysis tools (disassemblers, decompilers, emulators), yet their correctness is rarely examined. Specification errors distort program behavior, hide vulnerabilities, and enable analysis-evasion techniques. Validating these specifications is difficult, and no prior systematic validation approach existed for SLEIGH specifications.

Method: The authors design and implement InSPECtor, a testing framework using automated oracle validation "by proxy." It leverages the structure encoded in a specification to enumerate decodable instruction forms and generate targeted initial states, then differentially tests successful decoding and emulation by comparing emulators built on the SLEIGH specification against hardware references.

Result: Across five open-source specifications (x86-64, AArch64, ARM/Thumb, RISC-V, MSP430) with differing styles and designs, InSPECtor found over 38,920 discrepancies leading to 125 unique bugs with proposed fixes, including decoding and semantic defects as well as cross-vendor inconsistencies. Findings were distilled into 8 concrete recommendations.

Conclusion: Specification correctness is critical, and InSPECtor substantially improves the fidelity of SLEIGH processor specifications, strengthening the reliability of downstream security and analysis tools.

Abstract: Processor specifications underpin critical security and program- analysis tools such as disassemblers, decompilers, and emulators, yet, their correctness is rarely examined. Errors in specifications distort program behaviour, obscure vulnerabilities, and enable analysis-evasion techniques. Validating processor specifications is a non-trivial task. Our study is a significant undertaking to enable, for the first time, the systematic validation of open-source SLEIGH language specifications, predominantly used by Ghidra. We design and implement a testing framework based on an automated oracle validation strategy by proxy. Our approach leverages the structure encoded in a specification itself to enumerate decodable instruction forms and generate targeted initial states. Then differentially test the successful decoding and emulation of those instructions by comparing emulators exercising the processor specification against hardware references.
  Applying InSPECtor across diverse, open-source specifications---x86-64, AArch64, ARM/Thumb, RISC-V, MSP430---embedding differences in specification styles, author preferences, and instruction set architecture designs, we uncovered over 38,920 discrepancies that led to 125 unique bugs with proposed fixes, identifying decoding and semantic defects as well as cross-vendor inconsistencies. We distill our findings into 8 concrete recommendations to drive future improvements. Our work underscores the importance of specification correctness and provides a practical tool to substantially improve the fidelity of SLEIGH processor specifications, strengthening the reliability of downstream security and analysis tools.

</details>


### [215] [Operationalizing Cyber Threat Intelligence with GraphRAG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13050)
*Atul Kabra,Prakhar Paliwal,Manjesh K. Hanawal*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper compares Microsoft GraphRAG (knowledge-graph retrieval) against Naive RAG (vector-similarity retrieval) for turning cyber threat intelligence reports into detection plans, as measured by the Pyramid of Pain. GraphRAG plans rely on more durable, top-of-pyramid indicators and keep firing after simple IOCs are rotated, while Naive RAG plans collapse. Results across nine CTI reports support GraphRAG as the architecturally correct foundation, though prompt wording matters nearly as much.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Automated extraction of detections from threat reports typically captures only the simplest, shortest-lived clues (IPs, domains, hashes), which attackers can change quickly, so detections fail soon after deployment. The authors seek a retrieval approach that produces detection plans leveraging durable, high-pyramid indicators rather than trivial block-list artifacts.

Method: The study feeds a security report into two retrieval systems—Microsoft GraphRAG (knowledge-graph retrieval) and Naive RAG (vector-similarity retrieval)—keeping the report, generation instructions, and final language model identical so that only the retrieval step differs. It evaluates the resulting detection plans using the Pyramid of Pain, measuring how many detections still fire (and at what pyramid level) after rotating all IP addresses, domains, and file hashes. The comparison includes a detailed APT28 case study and is repeated across nine real CTI reports from four vendors.

Result: In the APT28 case study, after rotating all simple IOCs, the GraphRAG plan kept firing at 100% of its detections while the Naive RAG plan kept firing at only 29%. Across nine CTI reports from four vendors, GraphRAG plans consistently reached higher, harder-to-evade pyramid levels than Naive RAG plans, even when total scores were close. Prompt wording was also found to matter almost as much as the choice of retrieval back-end.

Conclusion: Knowledge-graph-aware retrieval is the architecturally correct foundation for automatically generating SOC-deployable hunting plans. However, the wording of the generation prompt is almost as important as the retrieval back-end, so both the retrieval architecture and prompt design must be considered.

Abstract: When a security researcher publishes a report on a cyberattack, detection engineers are supposed to turn it into working detection rules. In practice, most automated attempts at this only extract the simplest clues from the report --- bad IP addresses, domain names, and file hashes --- and turn them into block lists. This is a weak strategy, because attackers can change these simple clues within hours or days, so the resulting detections stop working almost as soon as they are deployed. Security teams describe this idea with the Pyramid of Pain. This project asks whether feeding a report into a knowledge-graph retrieval system, Microsoft GraphRAG, rather than a standard vector-similarity retrieval system (Naive RAG), produces detection plans that rely more on these durable, top-of-pyramid clues. Both systems are given the same report, the same generation instructions, and the same language model to write the final plan; only the retrieval step differs. In a detailed case study of one APT28 report, the GraphRAG plan kept firing at 100\% of its detections after every IP address, domain, and file hash in the report was rotated, while the Naive RAG plan kept firing at only 29\%. Repeating the comparison across nine real CTI reports from four vendors confirms the same pattern: GraphRAG plans consistently reach higher, harder-to-evade levels of the pyramid, even when the two systems end up close on total score. The results support treating knowledge-graph-aware retrieval as the architecturally correct foundation for automatically generating SOC-deployable hunting plans, while showing that the wording of the generation prompt matters almost as much as the retrieval back-end itself.

</details>


### [216] [A Commitment-Based Hybrid Post-Quantum Cryptographic Model for Multi-File Cloud Storage](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13138)
*Lemdi Frank Prikutse,Regina Esi Turkson,Alimatu-Saadia Yussiff,Abdul-Lateef Yussiff,Maame G. Asante-Mensah*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A hybrid post-quantum cloud-storage model uses a SHA3-256 batch commitment so that only one post-quantum signature is needed per batch of files, dramatically reducing signing-phase latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cloud storage clients need authentication that stays secure against future quantum adversaries, so classical schemes are combined with standardized post-quantum ones. However, naively extending these hybrid constructions to multi-file uploads means paying a per-file lattice-based signing cost that dominates total authentication time and becomes prohibitive at realistic batch sizes.

Method: The paper proposes a commitment-based hybrid post-quantum model. It combines AES-256-GCM for bulk encryption, a hybrid X25519 + ML-KEM-768 key encapsulation mechanism, and a hybrid Ed25519 + ML-DSA-65 dual signature computed over a SHA3-256 batch commitment. The commitment binds all ciphertexts in a batch to one fixed-size digest that is signed only once, reducing post-quantum signature invocations per batch from n to one.

Result: On a commodity client, averaged over 20 repetitions, signing-phase time stays near-constant as batch size grows, while the per-file baseline scales linearly. At n = 1000, the model cuts signing-phase time by factors of 629, 606, and 725 for 100 KB, 1 MB, and 10 MB files respectively, versus a per-file dual-signing baseline sharing all other primitives.

Conclusion: Batch commitment sign-once authentication removes the per-file post-quantum signing bottleneck, making hybrid post-quantum protection practical for large multi-file uploads while preserving quantum-resistant security.

Abstract: Cloud storage clients increasingly require authentication that remains secure against future quantum-capable adversaries, motivating hybrid constructions that combine classical primitives with standardized post-quantum alternatives. Extended naively to multi-file upload, such constructions incur a per-file lattice signing cost that dominates authentication time and becomes prohibitive at realistic batch sizes. This paper presents a commitment-based hybrid post-quantum model that addresses this bottleneck. It comprises AES-256-GCM bulk encryption, a hybrid X25519 with ML-KEM-768 key encapsulation mechanism, and a hybrid Ed25519 with ML-DSA-65 dual signature, computed over a SHA3-256 batch commitment. The commitment binds all ciphertexts in a batch to a single fixed-size digest that is signed once, reducing the number of post-quantum signature invocations per batch from n to one, independent of batch size; the remaining encryption and hashing is bounded by fast symmetric throughput. On a commodity client platform, averaged over 20 repetitions, this holds signing-phase time near-constant as the batch grows while the per-file baseline scales linearly. At n = 1000, the model reduces signing-phase time by factors of 629, 606, and 725 for 100 KB, 1 MB, and 10 MB files respectively, against a per-file dual-signing baseline sharing every other primitive.

</details>


### [217] [Slow and Steady: Preventing MEV with Verifiable Delays](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13271)
*Zeta Avarikioti,Dimitris Karakostas,Karl Kreder,Shreekara Shastry*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper proposes a defense against Maximal Extractable Value (MEV) in distributed ledgers by enforcing a verifiable delay during transaction generation, preventing block creators from reacting to MEV opportunities without breaking liveness. It provides positive results in both Byzantine and rational (game-theoretic) settings, negative bounds showing the approach's limits, and real-world analysis suggesting the mechanism could mitigate most existing MEV threats based on historical data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MEV allows block creators to exploit their ability to observe and reorder transactions for profit, undermining fairness and security in distributed ledgers. The authors seek a defense that makes it impossible for a block creator to take advantage of newly visible MEV opportunities in time, without sacrificing the system's liveness guarantees.

Method: The defense enforces a verifiable delay in the transaction generation process, so that any block creator attempting to react to a freshly emerged MEV opportunity would fail to meet liveness requirements. The approach is analyzed under a Byzantine adversary model and a game-theoretic model of rational participants, with both positive (security) and negative (limitation) bounds derived, and evaluated using historical MEV data for practicality of real-world verifiable-delay implementations.

Result: The mechanism achieves positive security results under both Byzantine and rational-participant models. The negative bounds outline fundamental limitations of this delay-based line of defense. Real-world implementation analysis combined with historical MEV data suggests the mechanism could realistically prevent most existing MEV threats.

Conclusion: Enforcing verifiable delays in transaction generation is a promising, practical defense against MEV, providing security in both adversarial and rational settings, though with identifiable theoretical limits. Based on historical data, it could realistically mitigate the majority of current MEV threats.

Abstract: Our work presents a defense mechanism against Maximal Extractable Value (MEV) opportunities in distributed ledgers. The mechanism relies on the idea of enforcing a verifiable delay when generating transactions, such that a block creator cannot react to the appearance of a MEV opportunity without breaking liveness. We present positive results both in the Byzantine setting and in a game theoretic model of rational participants. We additionally present negative bounds that outline the limitations of this line of defense. Finally, we explore real-world implementation details of verifiable delays and show that, based on historical MEV data, our mechanism could realistically help prevent most existing MEV threats.

</details>


### [218] [VR-Themis: A Scalable Framework for Virtual Reality Application Clone Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13290)
*Gengyang Xu,Hanyang Guo,Hong-Ning Dai,Weizhi Meng*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: VR-Themis is a two-stage framework for detecting cloned (repackaged) VR apps using hierarchy-object-behaviour (HOB) metrics. A coarse-grained clustering stage ensures scalability, and a fine-grained similarity-analysis stage identifies clones with high accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: App cloning threatens user security/privacy and developers' copyright, yet existing clone detectors focus on mobile platforms like Android and miss VR-specific features, making them ineffective for cloned VR apps that are frequently targeted in the VR market.

Method: A two-stage detection framework named VR-Themis based on Hierarchy-Object-Behaviour (HOB). Stage 1 (coarse-grained) clusters apps using retrievable statistical features for scalability on large datasets. Stage 2 (fine-grained) analyzes suspicious apps by computing similarity through HOB metrics.

Result: VR-Themis detected 307 suspected clone apps from 4,277 collected VR apps with no false positives.

Conclusion: VR-Themis is an effective and scalable solution for detecting cloned VR apps, outperforming platform-agnostic or mobile-focused methods by leveraging VR-specific features.

Abstract: Repackaging of mobile applications (aka app cloning) not only threatens the security and privacy of mobile users but also infringes upon the copyright of the original app developers. However, existing detection methods that primarily focus on mobile platforms (such as Android) fail to capture the essential features of virtual reality (VR). Consequently, they are inadequate for effectively detecting cloned VR apps, which have often been targeted by illegal users in the VR market. Considering the unique features of VR apps, this paper proposes a two-stage app clone detection framework, namely VR-Themis, based on \emph{Hierarchy-Object-Behaviour} (HOB). Firstly, VR-Themis exploits the coarse-grained stage to cluster apps based on their retrievable statistical features, making this tool scalable to large-scale VR app datasets. Then, in the fine-grained stage, VR-Themis performs in-depth analysis of the suspicious apps (identified in the first stage) by calculating similarity using our defined \emph{HOB metrics}. Our extensive experiments indicate that VR-Themis successfully detects 307 suspected clone apps from the collected 4,277 VR apps without false positives, demonstrating its effectiveness and scalability.

</details>


### [219] [TeleGapper: On the (un)reliability of Privacy Policies in Telegram Mini apps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13390)
*Luca Ferrari,Mariano Ceccato,Luca Verderame*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: TeleGapper is a black-box dynamic analysis framework that examines Telegram Mini Apps' privacy by capturing network traffic and comparing observed third-party data flows against disclosed privacy policies. Evaluating 278 working Mini Apps, it finds 59.4% contact at least one undisclosed third party, 78.8% rely solely on Telegram's default privacy policy, and none offer consent or opt-out mechanisms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Telegram Mini Apps are widely used but their privacy properties are largely unexplored. Because they run in a WebView with standard Web capabilities and unrestricted outbound networking, they can transmit sensitive context to third parties (analytics, advertising, trackers) with limited visibility. Privacy disclosures are critical for transparency, but the platform allows apps to use a generic default policy that may not match actual data practices, creating potential compliance gaps.

Method: The authors propose TeleGapper, a black-box dynamic analysis framework that assesses Mini App privacy posture by (1) capturing runtime network traffic, (2) identifying third-party communications, and (3) comparing observed data flows against disclosed privacy information. They evaluate 278 working Mini Apps collected from tApps Center, a community-driven catalogue for Telegram third-party applications.

Result: 59.4% of evaluated Mini Apps contact at least one undisclosed third party; 78.8% rely exclusively on Telegram's default privacy policy rather than an app-specific one; and none provide a consent or opt-out mechanism.

Conclusion: The findings reveal a substantial transparency and compliance gap in the Telegram Mini App ecosystem, a widely used yet understudied platform. The reliance on generic default privacy policies and the prevalence of undisclosed third-party data flows indicate that current disclosure mechanisms inadequately reflect actual data practices.

Abstract: Telegram Mini Apps are Web applications embedded within the Telegram client, forming an ecosystem of third-party services within one of the world's most widely used messaging platforms. Despite their growing adoption and access to Telegram-provided context, their privacy properties remain largely unexplored. Unlike ecosystems such as WeChat, which rely on tightly controlled, proprietary execution frameworks, Telegram adopts a different model: Mini Apps run inside a WebView, combining platform-provided context with standard Web capabilities and unrestricted outbound networking. This enables applications to transmit sensitive information to analytics, advertising, tracking, or other third parties through ordinary Web requests, often with limited visibility.
  Privacy disclosures are therefore critical for transparency. Telegram allows Mini Apps either to define an application-specific privacy policy or to rely on a platform-provided default policy. While the latter reduces the developer's disclosure burden, it may lead to generic statements that do not accurately capture actual data practices of individual Mini Apps.
  In this paper, we present TeleGapper, a black-box dynamic analysis framework to assess the privacy posture of Mini Apps by capturing runtime network traffic, identifying third-party communications, and comparing observed data flows against disclosed privacy information. We evaluate 278 working Mini Apps collected from tApps Center, a community-driven catalogue for discovering third-party applications in Telegram. We find that 59.4% contact at least one undisclosed third party, 78.8% rely exclusively on Telegram's default privacy policy, and none provides a consent or opt-out mechanism. These findings expose a substantial transparency and compliance gap in a widely used yet understudied ecosystem.

</details>

### [220] [LoKiFormer: Locality-aware Attention with Decoupled Knowledge Memory for Efficient Large Language Model Pretraining](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12419)
*Qiuwu Chen,Zimo Liu,Yuchen Li,Ying Sun,Yifan Zhang,Zhijie Qiu,Zeng You,Ryan Dong,Simeng Ma,Yaofo Chen,Mingkui Tan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LoKiFormer is a novel LLM architecture that adds two modules to a standard decoder—Local Fusion Attention (LFA) for explicit local pattern capture and a Knowledge Memory Module (KMM) for decoupled global knowledge retrieval—enabling 1.33x faster pretraining convergence than baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM architectures are inefficient in pretraining due to two limitations: (i) self-attention lacks an explicit inductive bias for locality, causing redundant modeling of sequence-internal local information; and (ii) mixture-of-experts (MoE) implicitly couples knowledge storage with computational pathways, restricting flexible access to sequence-external global knowledge.

Method: The authors propose LoKiFormer, which augments a standard decoder with two modules: (1) Local Fusion Attention (LFA), integrating convolutional fusion into attention to explicitly capture local patterns and let attention operate on more informative representations; and (2) Knowledge Memory Module (KMM), a parametric key-value memory storing global knowledge in addressable slots, decoupling storage from computation and enabling direct knowledge retrieval.

Result: Experimental results show LoKiFormer converges 1.33x faster during pretraining compared to baseline models, demonstrating superior efficiency and effectiveness over existing LLM architectures.

Conclusion: By explicitly integrating local and global information through LFA and KMM, LoKiFormer overcomes the locality and knowledge-storage limitations of standard LLMs, achieving notably faster pretraining convergence and highlighting its architectural advantage.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable breakthroughs across various applications. However, their architectures remain inefficient in pretraining due to two main limitations: (i) self-attention lacks an explicit inductive bias for locality, leading to redundant modeling of sequence-internal local information; (ii) mixture-of-experts (MoE) implicitly couples knowledge storage with computational pathways, hindering flexible access to sequence-external global knowledge. To overcome these limitations, we propose LoKiFormer, a novel LLM architecture that augments the standard decoder with two dedicated modules: 1) Local Fusion Attention (LFA), which incorporates a convolutional fusion to attention, explicitly capturing local patterns and allowing the attention to operate on more informative representations; 2) Knowledge Memory Module (KMM), which introduces a parametric key-value memory that explicitly stores global knowledge in addressable slots, decoupling storage from computation and enabling direct knowledge retrieval. Together, these modules enable LoKiFormer to achieve more efficient and effective integration of information at both levels. Experimental results show that LoKiFormer converges 1.33x faster in pre-training than baseline models, underscoring its superiority over existing LLM architectures.

</details>


### [221] [Which Site, and When: A Free-Satellite-Data Test of Himalayan Glacial Lake Bursts, Landslides, and Ice Floods](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12422)
*Matthew Kahn,Milan Arjel,Nirmala Adhikari,Mingmar Sherpa,James Pope*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Using only free satellite data, the authors build and test models that predict both which Himalayan site is susceptible to glacial-lake outbursts/landslides (susceptibility) and when a trigger will arrive (timing). Weather signals time triggers well (ROC 0.73–0.83), but terrain-based susceptibility is barely above chance once compared against nearby similar sites (0.54–0.76), and deep learning does not beat a simple gradient-boosted baseline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: A prior feasibility study showed that free signals—radar interferometry detecting moraine-dam sagging and satellite weather data—indicate which lake is destabilizing and when it is at risk, but it proposed no predictive model. This paper fills that gap by proposing and evaluating models that predict susceptibility and trigger timing for three related hazards using free data alone.

Method: Using 589 dated outbursts from HMAGLOFDB and several thousand catalogued landslides, events are matched against similar but unfailed sites. Models are evaluated against a strong simple baseline under spatial cross-validation that withholds whole map tiles to prevent leakage from recognizing trained-on neighborhoods. Two questions are asked separately for each hazard: susceptibility ranking (terrain) and trigger timing (antecedent weather). Five deep-learning models are compared with a gradient-boosted baseline, supplemented by a three-rule decision tree on ruggedness and monsoon rainfall.

Result: Antecedent weather times triggers at ROC 0.73 (big bursts), 0.83 (landslides), 0.82 (small floods). Terrain susceptibility scored naively near 0.9 due to clustered cataloging in wetter ranges, but honest matched figures drop to 0.76, 0.71, and 0.54 (chance-level for small floods). The burst signal holds within single regions, reaching 0.89 in Nepal alone. Deep-learning models do not decisively beat the gradient-boosted baseline; three score marginally higher on landslides (inconclusive), while the baseline wins outright on lake hazards, reproduced by a three-rule decision tree.

Conclusion: Susceptibility from terrain alone is weak once spatial clustering is controlled, whereas weather-based trigger timing is the stronger signal. Simple models match or beat deep learning. The authors close with a ranked Nepal watchlist as a prioritisation aid (not a prediction) and note the limits of free data.

Abstract: Two free satellite signals carry real information about glacial-lake outburst risk in the Nepal Himalaya: radar interferometry sees a moraine dam slowly sagging, and satellite weather marks the weeks when a primed lake is under stress. A companion feasibility study found that deformation indicates which lake is destabilizing and weather indicates when it is at risk, but proposed no predictive model. To address this gap, we propose and evaluate models that predict which site is susceptible and when a trigger arrives. We test three related hazards on free data alone: large moraine- and ice-dammed bursts, rainfall-triggered landslides, and smaller floods from ponds on and around a glacier. Each hazard gets two questions, never blended. Using 589 dated outbursts from HMAGLOFDB and several thousand catalogued landslides, we match each event against similar but unfailed sites, and hold every model to a strong simple baseline under spatial cross-validation that withholds whole map tiles, so no model succeeds by recognising a trained-on neighbourhood. Antecedent weather times the trigger at ROC 0.73 for big bursts, 0.83 for landslides, and 0.82 for small floods. Terrain ranks susceptibility only in part: scored naively it appears near 0.9, largely because catalogued failures cluster in wetter ranges; matched against comparable nearby sites the honest figures are 0.76, 0.71, and 0.54 (no better than chance). The burst signal holds within single regions, reaching 0.89 in Nepal alone. Five deep-learning models do not decisively beat a simple gradient-boosted baseline. Three score marginally higher on landslides, a hint too small to confirm. For the lake hazards the baseline wins outright, reproduced by a three-rule decision tree on ruggedness and monsoon rainfall. We close with a ranked Nepal watchlist, a prioritisation aid, not a prediction, and note where free data reaches its limits.

</details>


### [222] [MARCH: Scaling Recurrent Memory with Content-Routed State Anchors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12435)
*Ming Zhang,Kaisen Yang,Shu Yu,Ermo Hua,Ning Ding,Xia Hu,Bowen Zhou,Chaochao Lu,Youbang Sun*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MARCH introduces a recurrent architecture that improves long-context retrieval by periodically caching recurrent-state checkpoints as "state anchors" and routing attention over them, scaling state-space models beyond fixed-size states while keeping decoding efficient.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Transformers achieve strong long-context retrieval via token-level memory but suffer quadratic training cost and linear key-value cache growth. Recurrent models decode efficiently with fixed-size states, yet underperform on recall-intensive tasks because later updates overwrite earlier associations. The paper seeks to scale state-space models beyond a fixed-size dimension while preserving computational efficiency over long sequences.

Method: MARCH periodically stores cumulative recurrent-state checkpoints as state anchors, each paired with a compact, content-conditioned anchor key, forming a growing memory bank. At each token, MARCH generates an anchor query that attends over all causally available state anchors, and the output is an attention-style aggregation over historical anchors combined with the current state. This provides a controllable trade-off between historical resolution and memory cost.

Result: After standard pretraining, MARCH consistently outperforms multiple linear attention variants on commonsense reasoning, LongBench, and in-context retrieval benchmarks.

Conclusion: Content-routed state caching substantially strengthens recurrent long-range memory while preserving its native computation path, demonstrating that fixed-size state bottlenecks can be relaxed without sacrificing efficiency.

Abstract: Transformers owe much of their strong long-context retrieval capability to a token-level memory that grows with context length. This flexibility, however, incurs a quadratic computation complexity during training and a key--value cache that grows linearly during autoregressive inference. Recurrent alternatives offer efficient decoding by compressing the entire history into a fixed-size state, but often underperform on recall-intensive tasks since earlier associations usually get overwritten by subsequent updates, and only the most recent contextual information is retained. In this paper, we introduce Memory-Anchor Routing across Context History (MARCH), a network architecture that effectively scales state-space models beyond a fixed-size dimension, while maintaining computational efficiency over long-sequences. MARCH periodically caches cumulative recurrent-state checkpoints as state anchors and associates each anchor with a compact, content-conditioned anchor key. This lets MARCH maintain a memory bank, which can grow as context length increases, providing a controllable trade-off between historical resolution and memory cost. At each token, MARCH produces an anchor query to attend all causally available state anchors, and the output is calculated as an attention-style aggregation over all historical anchors along the current state. We show that after standard pretraining, MARCH consistently outperforms multiple linear attention variants across commonsense reasoning, LongBench, and in-context retrieval. These results demonstrate that content-routed state caching substantially strengthens recurrent long-range memory while preserving its native computation path.

</details>


### [223] [Multi-AUV Ad-hoc network-based Target Tracking: A Value Gradient Guidance Multi-Agent Diffusion Reinforcement Learning Approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12436)
*Jiaao Ma,Chuan Lin,Guangjie Han,Shengchao Zhu,Qian Zhu,Ying Liu,Zhenyu Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes VGG-MADiffRL, a value-gradient-guided multi-agent diffusion reinforcement learning algorithm, together with MDCA, a diffusion-based hierarchical control architecture, to enable cooperative target tracking in multi-AUV ad-hoc networks under acoustic communication constraints, dynamic topology, and ocean disturbances. It models cooperative tracking as an MDP incorporating sonar detection and ocean currents, and shows improved convergence, accuracy, and training stability over existing MARL methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-AUV ad-hoc target tracking requires decentralized cooperation under constrained acoustic communication, dynamic topology, and uncertain ocean disturbances. Existing MARL methods rely on high-dimensional joint state-action modeling and noise-sensitive policy generation, causing unstable training and degraded tracking performance. The authors aim to overcome these limitations.

Method: The authors model cooperative tracking for multi-AUV ad-hoc networks as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) that incorporates sonar detection mechanisms and ocean current disturbances. They propose MDCA, a three-tier closed-loop control architecture comprising a global intelligent control layer, a local online training layer, and a physical action execution layer, enabling synergistic optimization across task allocation, local decisions, and execution feedback. Within MDCA, the local online training layer uses VGG-MADiffRL, which builds on diffusion policies and injects value gradients into the reverse denoising process to steer generated actions toward higher expected returns. It uses twin value networks with joint optimization and soft target updates to reduce overestimation and training oscillations.

Result: Experiments show that VGG-MADiffRL achieves faster convergence, higher tracking accuracy, and smoother training dynamics compared to baseline methods in cooperative tracking scenarios, validating its effectiveness and engineering value in dynamic underwater environments.

Conclusion: VGG-MADiffRL combined with the MDCA hierarchical architecture effectively addresses unstable training and degraded tracking in multi-AUV cooperative target tracking, providing stable convergence and strong practical value in dynamic underwater settings.

Abstract: Multi-AUV ad-hoc network-based target tracking requires networked autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) to cooperatively track maneuvering targets under constrained acoustic communication, dynamic topology, and uncertain ocean disturbances. Although multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) enables decentralized coordination through centralized training, existing methods suffer from high-dimensional joint state-action modeling, noise-sensitive policy generation, leading to unstable training and degraded tracking. To address these issues, we propose VGG-MADiffRL, a value-gradient-guided multi-agent diffusion RL algorithm, and MDCA, a diffusion?based hierarchical control architecture. Leveraging underwater mission characteristics, we model sonar detection mechanisms and ocean current disturbances, formulating cooperative tracking for multi-AUV ad-hoc networks as an MDP. The proposed MDCA constitutes a three-tier closed-loop control framework: a global intelligent control layer, a local online training layer, and a physical action execution layer. This structure enables synergistic optimization across task allocation, local decision processes, and execution feedback. Within MDCA, the local online training layer is the policy learning framework; VGG-MADiffRL builds on diffusion policies and incorporates value gradients to guide action generation in the reverse denoising process, steering the generated actions towards higher expected returns. It employs twin value networks with joint optimization and soft target updates to mitigate overestimation and training oscillations, promoting more stable convergence. Experimental results show that VGG-MADiffRL consistently achieves faster convergence, higher tracking accuracy, and smoother training dynamics in cooperative tracking scenarios, validating its effectiveness and practical engineering value in dynamic underwater settings.

</details>


### [224] [Unifying Generative Models with Path Integrals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12438)
*Ramon Winterhalder*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper unifies flow, diffusion, variational, and adversarial generative models as different evaluation principles of a single path-integral action, then uses diagrammatic perturbation theory to derive corrections (e.g., a one-loop fix for deterministic samplers) and principled training objectives such as response-weighted score matching.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing generative modeling approaches (flow-based, diffusion-based, variational, adversarial) are typically treated as distinct methods. The authors seek a unifying framework that reveals their common structure and enables systematic, perturbative corrections and principled objective design using tools from statistical field theory.

Method: Generative modeling is reformulated as a path integral with a single master action, whose Martin-Siggia-Rose-Janssen-de Dominicis (MSRJD) form separates free and interacting probability flows. This enables diagrammatic perturbation theory: a one-loop expansion corrects deterministic samplers without stochastic sampling, imperfect learned scores enter as insertions giving a response-weighted score-matching objective, and symmetry-equivariant drift design is treated as an operator expansion with effective field theory (EFT) power counting.

Result: The one-loop correction reduces deterministic-sampler error from a 53% tree-level error to 1.6% on solvable and nonlinear drift problems, at no stochastic-sampling cost.

Conclusion: Path-integral/field-theoretic formulations offer a unifying lens on generative modeling, yielding perturbative systematic corrections and new objectives, and placing symmetry-equivariant design within an EFT power-counting framework, with strong empirical error reduction demonstrated.

Abstract: We formulate generative modeling as a path integral in which flow-based, diffusion-based, variational, and adversarial models arise as different evaluation principles for a single master action. Its Martin-Siggia-Rose-Janssen-de~Dominicis (MSRJD) form separates free from interacting probability flows and opens them to diagrammatic perturbation theory. The expansion yields a one-loop correction to deterministic samplers at no stochastic-sampling cost, which we validate on solvable and nonlinear drifts, where it reduces a 53 % tree-level error to 1.6 %. Imperfect learned scores enter as insertions and yield a response-weighted score-matching objective, and symmetry-equivariant drift design becomes an operator expansion with EFT power counting.

</details>


### [225] [Dual Spatial-Temporal Attribution: Architecture-Aligned Post-Hoc Explainability for Recurrent Graph Anomaly Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12441)
*Iyad Assaad Nekka,Hamida Seba,Khaled Walid Hidouci,Karima Amrouche*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: X-AddGraph is a strictly post-hoc explainability framework for the AddGraph GCN+GRU dynamic-graph anomaly detector, using Dual Spatial-Temporal Attribution (spatial gradient, zero-cost short-term temporal attention, and long-term temporal gradient rollback) to explain edge-level anomaly flags while preserving detection performance exactly.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: High-accuracy deep learning anomaly detectors for dynamic graphs are opaque, returning only scores without reasons, which is unacceptable in cooperative regulated systems requiring auditable and trustworthy automated decisions. AddGraph, the foundational GCN+GRU framework for edge-level dynamic-graph anomaly detection, has never had any form of explainability.

Method: A strictly post-hoc framework, X-AddGraph, built on a Dual Spatial-Temporal Attribution (DSTA) mechanism with three components each aligned to an AddGraph module: (1) gradient-based relevance attribution over the current adjacency structure (spatial); (2) direct reading of contextual attention weights computed during inference (short-term temporal, zero additional cost); and (3) gradient rollback through recurrent hidden states (long-term temporal). The detector remains frozen, preserving performance exactly.

Result: Detection performance is preserved exactly (Delta AUC = 0, verified to ten decimal places). On UCI Message, the trained AddGraph baseline achieves an average per-snapshot AUC of 0.8705, exceeding the originally published result; X-AddGraph reproduces every score identically. Across four edge populations (confident true positives, low-confidence true positives, false positives, random samples), long-term attribution identifies historical snapshots with more counterfactual signal than random selection (0.127 vs. 0.074).

Conclusion: X-AddGraph provides the first explainability for AddGraph, adding explanations where none existed while exactly preserving detection performance, and introduces a spatially-blind capability (long-term counterfactual snapshot identification) that spatially-only explainers cannot provide. The implementation is released for reproducibility.

Abstract: Deep learning detectors for anomalies in dynamic graphs have reached strong accuracy, yet they remain opaque: when an edge is flagged, the analyst receives a score but no reason. This opacity is untenable in the cooperative, regulated information systems where such detectors are deployed, where automated decisions must be auditable and trustworthy. We address this gap for AddGraph, the foundational GCN+GRU framework for edge-level anomaly detection in dynamic graphs, which to our knowledge has never been equipped with any form of explainability. We present a strictly post-hoc explainability framework, X-AddGraph, built on a Dual Spatial-Temporal Attribution (DSTA) mechanism whose three components are each aligned with one of AddGraph's architectural modules: a gradient-based relevance attribution over the current adjacency structure (spatial), a direct reading of the contextual attention weights already computed during inference (short-term temporal, at zero additional cost), and a gradient rollback through the recurrent hidden states (long-term temporal). Because the detector is frozen, detection performance is preserved exactly (Delta AUC = 0, verified empirically to ten decimal places). On the UCI Message benchmark, our trained AddGraph baseline reaches an average per-snapshot AUC of 0.8705, exceeding the originally published result; X-AddGraph reproduces every score identically while adding explanations where none existed. Evaluated across four edge populations - confident true positives, low-confidence true positives, false positives, and random samples - the long-term attribution identifies historical snapshots carrying significantly more counterfactual signal than random selection (0.127 vs. 0.074), a capability that no spatially-blind explainer can provide. We release our implementation for full reproducibility.

</details>


### [226] [Personalized Scorer Modeling: A Learning-Based Framework for Deriving Robust Sleep Stage Labels from Multiple Experts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12446)
*Seyyed Ali Hoseini,Javad Baseri,Hamid Saadatfar,Edris Hoseini Gol,AmirHossein Eshghi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a learning-based hypnogram (LBH) method that combines multiple expert scorers' labels via confusion-matrix-derived probabilities, improving sleep stage classification accuracy and reliability beyond single-reference hypnograms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most automatic sleep staging studies evaluate against a single reference hypnogram despite known inter-scorer variability among experts. The authors investigate whether multi-scored datasets can yield more reliable reference labels by leveraging the collective behavior of multiple experts rather than discarding individual scorer information.

Method: Using the public DOD-H and DOD-O datasets, EEG (C3-M2) and chin EMG signals were segmented into 30-s epochs, with 30 features extracted per modality (60 for EEG+EMG). The proposed LBH (learning-based hypnogram) models each scorer's stage-specific behavior using confusion matrices from machine-learning classifiers. After column normalization, these matrices estimate the probability of each true sleep stage given a scorer's label; probabilities are aggregated across scorers to assign the final label per epoch. LBH was evaluated with random forest, support vector machine, and multilayer perceptron classifiers under EEG-only and EEG+EMG settings, and compared against the dataset hypnogram (DH) and best-scorer hypnogram (BSH).

Result: LBH consistently improved overall performance. Best results used random forest with EEG+EMG: 86.07% accuracy, 85.46% precision, 85.29% F1-score on DOD-H; and 86.04% accuracy, 85.21% precision, 84.70% F1-score on DOD-O.

Conclusion: Personalized scorer modeling improves reference hypnogram construction without discarding information from individual experts, suggesting that aggregating multiple scorers' behavior can produce more reliable labels for automatic sleep staging.

Abstract: Sleep stage classification is important for the diagnosis and management of sleep disorders, yet most automatic staging studies evaluate models against a single reference hypnogram despite known inter-scorer variability. This study investigates whether multi-scored datasets can be used to construct more reliable reference labels from the collective behavior of multiple experts. We use the publicly available DOD-H and DOD-O datasets. EEG (C3-M2) and chin EMG signals were segmented into 30-s epochs, and 30 features were extracted from each modality, yielding 60 features for EEG+EMG. We propose a learning-based hypnogram (LBH) that models the stage-specific behavior of each scorer using confusion matrices derived from machine-learning models. After column normalization, these matrices estimate the probability of each true sleep stage given each scorer's label; probabilities are aggregated across scorers to assign the final label for each epoch. LBH was evaluated with random forest, support vector machine, and multilayer perceptron classifiers under EEG-only and EEG+EMG settings, and compared with the dataset hypnogram (DH) and best-scorer hypnogram (BSH). LBH consistently improved overall performance. The best results were obtained with random forest and EEG+EMG, reaching 86.07% accuracy, 85.46% precision, and 85.29% F1-score on DOD-H, and 86.04% accuracy, 85.21% precision, and 84.70% F1-score on DOD-O. These findings suggest that personalized scorer modeling can improve reference hypnogram construction without discarding information from individual experts.

</details>


### [227] [Geometric and Behavioral Stratification in Transformer Residual Streams](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12447)
*Nelson Guda*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper shows that a transformer's current prediction direction acts as a privileged, content-defined anchor in the residual stream. Residual-stream variation stratifies by proximity to this anchor: a narrow "prediction interface" concentrates readout-relevant, highly structured, prompt-clustering geometry, while a large prediction-distal complement expands with scale and is flatter but still causally and temporally load-bearing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work revealed that transformers develop "privileged bases" (coordinate axes with exceptional statistics), but it was unclear what kind of direction such a basis selects. The authors investigate whether the prediction direction—the unembedding direction of the currently predicted token—serves as a content-defined privileged anchor, and how residual-stream geometry and behavior organize relative to it. They also address why variance-based (principal component) analyses only partially recover this organization.

Method: Across eighteen models (dense and mixture-of-experts, 7B–120B parameters, base and instruction-tuned), the authors measure residual-stream variation with respect to the prediction direction as an anchor. They decompose the space into prediction-proximal and prediction-distal regions, analyze the geometric gradient (structure, prompt clustering, anti-discrimination), and run causal interventions by disrupting variance directions at different proximity levels to the prediction direction, observing divergence timing and task-frame shifts.

Result: A narrow, scale-invariant "prediction interface" concentrates readout-relevant structure and clusters related prompts; the large prediction-distal complement expands with model scale, is flatter, and anti-discriminates among prompt groups. The prediction direction is nearly orthogonal to the principal variance axes, so variance-based analyses recover this organization only partly—and worse with prompt heterogeneity. Disrupting variance directions closest to the prediction causes immediate divergence and frequent task-frame shifts; disrupting the next level down delays divergence but preserves framing. The complement is weakly readout-aligned per direction yet causally and temporally load-bearing, with behavior driven by direction rather than magnitude.

Conclusion: The prediction direction is a privileged anchor distinct from previously described coordinate axes, and it provides a geometric account of how high-dimensional computation coexists with linear readout: a narrow, decisive prediction interface plus a large load-bearing complement.

Abstract: Trained transformer models develop privileged bases: coordinate axes whose statistics differ from the rest of the residual stream. But what kind of direction does such a basis select? We investigate the prediction direction, the unembedding direction of the token a model currently predicts, and find that it functions as a content-defined privileged anchor. Measured with respect to this anchor, residual-stream variation is geometrically and behaviorally stratified by proximity to the prediction.
  The stratification holds in all eighteen models tested (dense and mixture-of-experts, 7B-120B, base and instruction-tuned). A narrow, scale-invariant prediction interface concentrates readout-relevant structure, while the vast prediction-distal complement expands with model scale. Because the prediction direction sits nearly orthogonal to the principal variance axes, variance-based analyses recover this organization only partly, and the shortfall grows with prompt heterogeneity.
  Anchoring reveals a steep geometric gradient: prediction-proximal regions are highly structured and cluster related prompts, while the complement is flatter and anti-discriminates among prompt groups. The interface is a narrow slice but functionally decisive. Disrupting the variance directions closest to the prediction causes immediate divergence and frequent task-frame shifts; disrupting the next level down delays divergence and preserves framing. The complement is weakly readout-aligned per direction yet causally and temporally load-bearing, and behavior is driven by direction rather than magnitude.
  These results establish the prediction direction as a privileged anchor distinct from previously described coordinate axes, and give a geometric account of how high-dimensional computation coexists with linear readout.

</details>


### [228] [Exemplar-based objective classification of gust-induced loads across multiple flight conditions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12448)
*Paolo Olivucci,Kowshik Srivatsan,David E. Rival*

Main category: cs.LG
