TL;DR: The paper proposes a machine-learned, similarity-based method to objectively classify gust-induced aerodynamic load data into a small set of interpretable exemplars, demonstrated on 3480 pressure-load measurements across six flight attitudes of a flying-wing model, finding nine recurring fundamental response types.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To find an objective, interpretable classification criterion for gust-induced load complexity that does not rely on coarse hand-crafted parameters like flight attitude, while remaining inspectable by experts.

Method: Encodes a large set of experimental observations using a machine-learned representation, then applies a summarization procedure to select a minimal subset of highly significant exemplars that define a similarity-based classification criterion for all observations.

Result: On a database of 3480 pressure-load measurements from random gusts over six flight attitudes, the approach identifies nine fundamental response types that recur across multiple attitudes, and their transient responses yield physical insight into the underlying fluid mechanics.

Conclusion: An objective similarity-based exemplar classification can replace coarse labels such as flight attitude, offering interpretability for experts and serving as a basis for more refined experiments and physical understanding of gust-induced loads.

Abstract: Is it possible to find an objective classification criterion that organizes the complexity of gust-induced loads across many flight conditions? And one that remains as interpretable as a labelling based on coarse parameters, such as the flight attitude? Our approach encodes a large number of experimental observations through a machine-learned representation and applies a summarization procedure to select a minimal subset of highly significant exemplars. The exemplars provide a similarity-based objective classification criterion of all the observations, they can be more conveniently inspected by experts and can become subject of more refined experiments. We demonstrate the approach on a database of 3480 pressure-load measurements induced by random gusts on a flying-wing model across six flight attitudes. We find nine fundamental response types that recur across multiple attitudes; analysis of a type's transient response enables physical intuition into the underlying fluid mechanics.

</details>


### [229] [Learning Under Treatment-Induced Label Indeterminacy with Expert Annotations of Counterfactual Outcomes: A Case Study in Neurological Prognostication](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12477)
*Xiaobin Shen,Chloe Y. H. Huang,Jonathan Elmer,George H. Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper addresses the problem of evaluating and training clinical prediction models when treatment decisions render the clinically relevant outcome unobservable for some patients. Using post-cardiac-arrest prognosis data (2,497 patients, 1,429 with indeterminate outcomes), it proposes a framework that separates evaluation across "certain" and "uncertain" (expert-guessed counterfactual) cases, and a model able to trade off between the two label types. It shows that models with similar AUROC can differ greatly in Brier score and uncertain-case probability estimates, and that improving uncertain-case alignment costs certain-case accuracy—tradeoffs standard evaluation hides.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Clinical prediction models typically assume outcomes are cleanly observed for all patients, but treatment decisions often make the clinically relevant outcome permanently unobservable. This creates a mismatch between the labels used for training/evaluation and the true clinical question, and conventional metrics may ignore important failure modes precisely for the patients whose prognosis matters most.

Method: The authors use a post-cardiac-arrest prognostication cohort (2,497 patients: 1,068 certain and 1,429 uncertain/indeterminate cases, with expert-provided counterfactual outcome guesses for uncertain cases). They propose (1) an evaluation framework that explicitly splits evaluation between certain and uncertain cases, since available target labels differ; and (2) a simple neural prediction model that uses target labels from both certain and uncertain cases in a way that permits explicit tradeoff between them. They compare the proposed neural model against tabular baselines using AUROC, Brier score, and probability estimates.

Result: Models with similar certain-case AUROC can differ substantially in certain-case Brier score and in their probability estimates for uncertain cases. For the proposed model, improving alignment with uncertain-case target labels generally degrades accuracy on certain cases, exposing an explicit tradeoff that standard evaluation conceals.

Conclusion: When treatment decisions determine whether clinically meaningful outcomes remain observable, conventional evaluation metrics can miss important failure modes in exactly the patients for whom prognostic support matters most. Evaluation must account for both certain and uncertain cases rather than assuming cleanly observed outcomes.

Abstract: Clinical prediction models are often developed as if the outcome of interest were cleanly observed for every patient. This assumption fails when treatment decisions make the clinically relevant outcome permanently unobservable. As a case study of this problem, we consider post-cardiac-arrest neurological prognostication using a cohort of 2,497 patients, including 1,429 patients whose outcomes were rendered indeterminate by treatment decisions. These patients with indeterminate outcomes were reviewed by independent clinical experts, who provided their guesses of counterfactual outcomes about what would have happened to the patients. We refer to these patients as uncertain cases. We also have patients for whom we observe their clinically relevant outcomes; we refer to these patients as certain cases. We propose a framework for evaluating prediction models that explicitly splits the evaluation between certain and uncertain cases. Here, we cannot easily evaluate both types of cases in a uniform manner as the available target labels differ. We then propose a simple prediction model that uses target labels from both certain and uncertain cases in a manner that allows us to trade off between them. Across the proposed neural model and a collection of tabular baselines, models with similar certain-case AUROC can nevertheless differ substantially in both certain-case Brier score and their probability estimates for uncertain cases. Improving alignment with target labels of uncertain cases for our proposed model generally comes at the cost of worse accuracy on certain cases, highlighting an explicit tradeoff that standard evaluation conceals. These results show that when treatment decisions determine whether clinically meaningful outcomes remain observable, conventional evaluation metrics can miss important failure modes in the very patients for whom prognostic support matters most.

</details>


### [230] [When Can You Trust Offline Evaluation of Equal-Cost Top-k Allocation? A Controlled, Reproducible Benchmark and Practitioner's Guide](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12489)
*Binshuang Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper benchmarks six off-policy evaluation estimators for deterministic top-k targeting rules on five public datasets, finding that weak overlap, the optimizer's curse (reuse bias), and out-of-fold propensity estimation are the dominant failure drivers, and that only four estimators remain practically distinct after propensity flooring.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Organizations allocating resources under a budget need to estimate the value of a deterministic top-k targeting rule before deployment from logged data. Off-policy evaluation promises this, but top-k rules eliminate action averaging, so weak overlap directly invalidates estimates. The paper aims to characterize which failure mechanisms (logging sharpness, optimizer's curse, propensity error) dominate and which estimators are robust.

Method: Benchmark six off-policy estimators (IPS variants, doubly-robust, and two "tuned hybrids") across five public datasets and two synthetic known-effect sweeps, validated against a non-simulated paired reference for mechanism attribution. Logging is synthesized with propensities floored at 0.02, ensuring bounded weights. Analyses decompose overlap into logger-target action alignment vs. logging sharpness via effective sample size, test cross-fitting of the outcome nuisance alone vs. honest policy-level splitting, and stress propensity estimation with out-of-fold estimates.

Result: (1) Weak overlap is governed by logger-target action alignment, not logging sharpness; sharpening a logger built from the target's own score barely moves overlap, while action disagreement collapses it. Effective sample size ranks risk across logging environments but is weak at ranking candidates within a single log and its cut point does not transfer. (2) Cross-fitting the outcome nuisance alone does not fix the optimizer's curse and can worsen reuse bias; honest policy-level splitting works only by changing the estimand to the learning procedure's value, not by de-biasing the full-sample policy. (3) Propensity-estimation error is the largest measured degradation: it hurts IPS most, leaves doubly-robust almost unchanged, and can invert the overlap diagnostic. The propensity floor reduces the two tuned hybrids to their untuned parents, leaving four practically distinct estimators.

Conclusion: For evaluating deterministic top-k policies, practitioners should prioritize honest action-level alignment between the logging and target policies and careful propensity estimation, while treating cross-fitting alone as insufficient for the optimizer's curse. The benchmark is released using only public data.

Abstract: Organizations decide whom to treat under a budget and want to know what a targeting rule would have earned before deploying it. Off-policy evaluation promises this from logged data, but the deployable rule is a deterministic top-k policy: it removes all averaging over actions, so weak overlap hits the estimate directly. We benchmark six estimators across five datasets and two known-effect sweeps, and validate the mechanisms against a non-simulated paired reference. First, weak overlap is governed by logger-target action alignment, not by logging sharpness alone: what governs support is the logger's probability of the target's actions. Sharpening a logger built from the target's own score barely moves overlap over the tested range; action-level disagreement collapses it. Effective sample size ranks this risk across logging environments, but is weak at ranking candidates within the single log a practitioner holds, and its cut point does not transfer. Second, the optimizer's curse is not fixed by cross-fitting the outcome nuisance. When the rule is fit on the data used to evaluate it, cross-fitting the nuisance alone leaves the reuse bias in place and makes it worse. Honest policy-level splitting avoids the reuse by targeting the learning procedure's value -- a change of estimand, not a de-biasing of the full-sample policy. Third, propensity-estimation error is the largest degradation we measure: an out-of-fold estimate hurts IPS more than any other stress we apply, leaves doubly-robust estimation almost unchanged, and can invert the overlap diagnostic itself. Logging is synthesized and propensities floored at 0.02, so every failure occurs with bounded weights; the floor also reduces the two tuned hybrids to their untuned parents, leaving four practically distinct estimators, and all exact-value surfaces are synthetic or semi-synthetic. We release the benchmark; public data only.

</details>


### [231] [Exploring Oversmoothing with Householder Matrices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12514)
*Bhaskar Karol*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces Householder Graph Neural Network (HouseGNN), which replaces standard GCN hidden-state updates with a Householder reflection estimated from the aggregated neighborhood message, followed by GroupSort, to combat oversmoothing in deep GNNs while preserving node-wise Euclidean norms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep GNNs suffer from oversmoothing: as depth increases, node representations progressively collapse toward a low-information subspace because the normalized graph propagation operator is repeatedly applied directly to hidden representations. The work seeks an alternative update mechanism that avoids this norm/energy decay and information loss.

Method: HouseGNN uses the aggregated neighborhood message only to estimate a reflection direction, then updates the node embedding via a Householder reflector followed by GroupSort, yielding a piecewise orthogonal layer. Three properties are proved: the Householder reflector is scale- and sign-invariant in the message; every internal layer preserves the node-wise Euclidean norm; and pairwise inter-node distances can change through mismatch between node-wise orthogonal operators.

Result: It is proven that: (i) each internal layer preserves the node-wise Euclidean norm; (ii) the Householder reflector is scale- and sign-invariant in the message; and (iii) pairwise distances between nodes can change due to mismatch between node-wise orthogonal operators. These properties suggest HouseGNN can retain representation energy and expressiveness across arbitrary depth.

Conclusion: HouseGNN offers a norm-preserving, piecewise orthogonal alternative to standard GCN propagation that theoretically mitigates oversmoothing by keeping node representations on the sphere while still allowing pairwise distances to evolve through node-specific orthogonal transformations.

Abstract: Deep graph neural networks(GNNs) suffer from oversmoothing- a progressive collapse of node representation towards a low information subspace as network depth increases because the normalized graph propagation operator is repeatedly applied directly to the hidden representations. In this work we study Householder Graph Neural Network (HouseGNN). Rather than updating the hidden state like standard GCN, HouseGNN uses the aggregated neighbourhood message solely to estimate a reflection direction; the node embedding is then updated by a Householder reflector followed by GroupSort, yielding a piecewise orthogonal layer that preserves Euclidean norm at every node and at every depth. We prove three core properties: (i) every internal layer preserves the node-wise Euclidean norm; (ii) the Householder reflector is scale scale and sign-invariant in the message; and (iii) pairwise distance between nodes can change through mismatch between node-wise orthogonal operators.

</details>


### [232] [GENADA: efficient generative time series adversarial attack framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12535)
*Michael Baronov,Denis Vorobev,Margarita Rusanova,Petr Sokerin,Alexey Zaytsev*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GENADA is a generative adversarial attack for time-series models that produces adversarial perturbations in a single forward pass, matching the attack quality of iterative gradient-based baselines while being faster at inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Time-series deep learning models are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, but existing gradient-based iterative attacks are computationally expensive because they repeatedly backpropagate through the victim model to compute input gradients. The authors aim to reduce this computational burden while maintaining attack effectiveness.

Method: The paper proposes GENADA, which learns a generative model that directly produces deceptive perturbations in a single forward pass, along with a training procedure for it. Both single-step and iterative generative attack variants are introduced. Validation is performed on several neural models and datasets in the time-series domain, using a controlled, low-dimensional setting.

Result: GENADA achieves attack quality comparable to strong iterative gradient-based baselines while requiring substantially less time to generate perturbations during inference.

Conclusion: A learned generative attack (GENADA) provides an efficient alternative to iterative gradient-based adversarial attacks for time-series models, trading negligible quality loss for significant inference-time speed-up.

Abstract: Deep learning models are widely used for time series analysis in domains such as healthcare, finance, energy systems, and environmental monitoring. However, these models remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks, where small input perturbations cause severe degradation in predictive performance. Commonly used gradient-based attacks, iterative first-order methods, are computationally burdensome, as they repeatedly backpropagate through the victim model to compute input gradients during a number of iterative refinement steps. We propose a GENerative ADversarial Attack (GENADA) that learns a generative model to produce deceptive perturbations directly in a single forward pass and a procedure to train it. Variants include single-step and iterative generative attack schemes. The validation considers attacks on several neural models and datasets in the time-series domain, a controlled, low-dimensional setting. Empirically, GENADA achieves comparable attack quality to strong baselines while requiring less time to generate perturbations during inference.

</details>


### [233] [Scaling Automatic Research Agents via World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12564)
*Xiyuan Yang,Sheikh Sarwar,Jingru Cheng,Zhan Shi,Duanshun Li,Huiyuan Chen,Haiyang Zhang,Chenlei Guo,Jingrui He,Zhenyu Liao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: WMRL is a reinforcement learning framework for AutoResearch agents that replaces costly environment execution with a world model to remove the training bottleneck. It adds Online Debiasing and Inverse-Variance Denoising to correct the imperfect world model's rewards, achieving 3-4x faster training and outperforming larger open-weight agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Post-training (especially RL) is central to recent AutoResearch agents, but scaling RL faces a fundamental tension: agent generation is cheaply batched and shares compute, while environment execution (sandbox/real machine time) is exclusive and dominates training cost as trajectories grow, becoming the bottleneck.

Method: The authors propose World Model RL (WMRL), which replaces environment execution with a world model to eliminate the execution bottleneck. Because the world model's rewards can be corrupted by bias and noise, WMRL is equipped with two mitigations: Online Debiasing (offsets bias) and Inverse-Variance Denoising (suppresses noise). They prove both mitigations strictly improve the convergence guarantee.

Result: WMRL accelerates training by 3-4x across tasks and agent scales while exceeding standard RL baselines. Post-trained 4B and 9B agents outperform much larger open-weight agents (48B and 120B) on held-out benchmarks. The method also transfers to post-training embodied VLA policies.

Conclusion: WMRL effectively resolves the compute scaling tension in AutoResearch RL by substituting a world model for environment execution, with principled debiasing and denoising mitigations. It delivers significant training speedups, improved downstream performance over larger models, and generalizes beyond AutoResearch to embodied VLA post-training.

Abstract: Automating empirical research is a long-standing direction of AI. Recent automatic research (AutoResearch) agents bring this goal within reach, as modern LLMs show the capability to independently implement solutions and learn from the execution outcomes. Behind these gains, post-training (especially RL) plays a central role. In this paper, we identify a fundamental tension when scaling RL for these agents: the two components of every AutoResearch trajectory (agent generation and environment execution) scale in very different manners, since all generation shares compute through batching, while each execution occupies its exclusive sandbox and real machine time. As a result, the environment execution dominates the training cost and becomes the bottleneck as trajectories grow. To resolve this tension, we propose World Model RL (WMRL), which replaces environment execution with a world model to remove this bottleneck. Additionally, the world model can be imperfect, as its rewards are corrupted by bias and noise. Therefore, we further equip WMRL with two mitigations, Online Debiasing and Inverse-Variance Denoising, which offset the bias and suppress the noise respectively. Theoretically, we prove that both mitigations of WMRL strictly improve the convergence guarantee. Empirically, WMRL accelerates training by 3-4x on various tasks at different agent scales, while exceeding the performance of standard RL baselines. Moreover, our post-trained 4B and 9B agents outperform much larger open-weight agents of 48B and 120B on held-out benchmarks. Beyond AutoResearch, WMRL also transfers to post-training embodied VLA policies, which demonstrates the generalizability of our method.

</details>


### [234] [Prof-K: Probabilistic One-Pass Filtering for Efficient Top-k Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12573)
*Tadeusz Dziarmaga,Witold Sikora,Łukasz Struski,Jacek Tabor,Marcin Mazur*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Prof-K is a fast, scalable, distribution-agnostic top-k selection algorithm that uses a single-pass random sampling approach to estimate an adaptive threshold, buffers a small candidate set, and recovers the true top-k elements with probability at least 1-ε, achieving 1.5x-10x speedups over PyTorch topk and RadiK.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Top-k selection is fundamental across databases, information retrieval, signal processing, and modern ML workloads (sparse activations, attention pruning). As data sizes grow, existing exact methods incur high memory/compute overhead, while approximate methods rely on brittle heuristics that degrade under adversarial or heavy-tailed inputs.

Method: Prof-K performs a single-pass filtering procedure: (1) a small random sample estimates an adaptive threshold, (2) the N input elements are streamed once into a compact buffer against this threshold, and (3) an exact top-k routine on the buffer recovers the true top-k elements with probability at least 1-ε. It derives high-probability guarantees for correctness and buffer size, plus an approximately optimal sample size as a function of N and k. A recall relaxation (e.g., 95%) offers a principled accuracy-speed trade-off.

Result: Prof-K achieves 1.5x-10x speedups over highly optimized PyTorch topk and recent RadiK implementations, with the largest gains in the large-scale, small-to-moderate-k regime where prior methods struggle most. Its guarantees hold independently of input distribution, ensuring robustness to adversarial settings. It is demonstrated to reduce cost in training BatchTopK Sparse Autoencoders, where top-k selection is a significant portion of training cost.

Conclusion: Prof-K provides a fast, scalable, distribution-agnostic top-k algorithm with probabilistic correctness guarantees, outperforming existing exact and approximate methods while remaining robust to adversarial and heavy-tailed distributions, and enabling a principled accuracy-speed trade-off that directly benefits ML workloads such as BatchTopK SAE training.

Abstract: Top-k selection is a fundamental computational primitive with applications spanning databases, information retrieval, signal processing, and modern machine learning workloads, including sparse activations and attention pruning. As data sizes grow, existing approaches become inefficient: exact methods incur high memory and compute overhead, while approximate methods often rely on brittle heuristics that degrade under adversarial or heavy-tailed inputs. In this paper, we introduce Prof-K, a fast, scalable, and distribution-agnostic top-k algorithm with probabilistic correctness guarantees. Prof-K performs a single-pass filtering procedure: a small random sample estimates an adaptive threshold, the N input elements are streamed once into a compact buffer, and an exact top-k routine on this buffer recovers the true top-k elements with probability at least 1 - $ε$, where $ε$ > 0 is user specified. We derive high-probability guarantees for correctness and buffer size, together with an approximately optimal sample size that minimizes overhead as a function of N and k. Empirically, Prof-K achieves 1.5x-10x speedups over the highly optimized PyTorch topk and recent RadiK implementations, with the largest gains in the large-scale, small-to-moderate-k regime where prior methods struggle most. Unlike previous approaches, these guarantees hold independently of the input distribution, ensuring robustness to adversarial settings. By relaxing the recall target (e.g., recovering 95% of the true top-k values), Prof-K additionally provides a principled accuracy-speed trade-off. We further demonstrate its impact on training BatchTopK Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), where top-k selection constitutes a significant portion of the training cost.

</details>


### [235] [Vero: Can AI Agents Build Formally Verified Software Repositories?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13522)
*Zhe Ye,Hantao Lou,Yuechun Sun,Peiyang Song,Zhengxu Yan,Timothe Kasriel,Qingyang Zhang,Kaiyu Yang,Soonho Kong,Jingxuan He,Dawn Song*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Vero is the first repository-level benchmark for joint implementation and proof synthesis, containing 43 multi-module Lean 4 instances. Frontier agents fully solve only 27/43 instances, showing a large gap remains in repository-scale verified code generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI agents generate code without any correctness guarantees. Verified code generation—producing both an implementation and a machine-checked proof—offers a stronger path to trustworthy software. Existing benchmarks are limited: they either focus on individual functions or only evaluate proof generation for already-provided implementations. It remains unknown whether agents can make coherent implementation and proof choices across real, multi-module codebases.

Method: The authors build Vero, a benchmark of 43 multi-module instances sourced from real-world repositories spanning Python, Dafny, Verus, and Coq, covering domains from cryptographic protocols to distributed systems. Each instance is a multi-module Lean 4 repository with predetermined API interfaces, manually curated formal specifications, and reference implementations, supporting both proof-only and code-and-proof evaluation modes. Vero includes an audit mechanism allowing agents to formally prove unsatisfiability of provided specifications or incorrectness of reference code, surfacing and correcting latent errors during curation. The authors evaluate frontier coding-agent configurations with Lean toolchain access.

Result: The strongest agent fully solves only 27 of 43 instances and closes no specifications on the hardest repositories.

Conclusion: Vero provides a concrete testbed for measuring progress toward repository-scale verified software synthesis, where current agents still fall short. The benchmark, curation pipeline, and evaluation harness are publicly released.

Abstract: AI agents are increasingly used for programming, but do not provide any guarantee on the correctness of generated code. Verified code generation, in which an agent produces both an implementation and a machine-checked proof of its specification, offers a stronger path toward trustworthy AI-generated software. Existing benchmarks in this direction either focus on individual functions or only evaluate proof generation with provided implementations. It is still an open question whether agents can make coherent implementation and proof choices across real multi-module codebases. To bridge this gap, we introduce Vero, the first benchmark to evaluate joint implementation and proof synthesis at the repository level. Vero contains 43 multi-module instances sourced from real-world repositories spanning Python, Dafny, Verus, and Coq, and covering diverse domains from cryptographic protocols to distributed systems. Each instance consists of a multi-module Lean 4 repository with predetermined API interfaces, manually curated formal specifications, and reference implementations, supporting both proof-only and code-and-proof evaluation modes. To improve benchmark reliability, Vero also includes an audit mechanism where agents are allowed to formally prove unsatisfiability of provided specification or incorrectness of reference code, which surfaces and corrects latent code and specification errors during curation. We evaluate frontier coding-agent configurations with Lean toolchain access. The strongest agent fully solves only 27 of 43 instances and closes no specifications on the hardest repositories. Vero provides a concrete testbed for measuring progress toward repository-scale verified software synthesis, where current agents still fall short. We release the benchmark, curation pipeline, and evaluation harness at https://github.com/sunblaze-ucb/vero.

</details>


### [236] [Represent, Then Generate: Multimodal-Conditioned Time-Series Generation under Irregular Missingness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12592)
*Haochen Zhang,Jiaheng Guo,Yu-Chao Huang,Nicholas Knoz,Tianlong Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ReCoGen is a two-stage framework that decouples multimodal condition representation from signal generation, using per-modality masked autoencoders (Stage I) to produce missingness-tolerant tokens and a flow-matching generator (Stage II) that fuses these tokens with static conditions to synthesize unobserved physiological signals. It achieves state-of-the-art downstream utility across 16 settings on three benchmarks, often matching or exceeding real-signal utility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Continuous physiological monitoring relies on signals that are often invasive, expensive, or unavailable. Conditional generation can synthesize missing signals from co-recorded signals and clinical variables, but existing generators handle only a single conditioning modality and degrade when faced with the heterogeneous, irregularly missing mix of time-variant signals and static covariates typical of real clinical data.

Method: ReCoGen uses a two-stage design. Stage I trains one masked autoencoder per time-variant modality, distilling each condition into a compact, missingness-tolerant token sequence. Stage II trains a flow-matching generator that fuses these frozen per-modality tokens with static conditions via learnable cross-attention and a dual token-plus-AdaLN routing scheme, synthesizing the target signal. Ablations isolate the conditioning path components.

Result: Across three physiological benchmarks (continuous glucose monitoring on AI-READI; arterial blood pressure generation on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV), ReCoGen achieves the best downstream utility on all sixteen (dataset, task, metric) settings, surpassing six representative conditional generators; on thirteen of the sixteen, its utility reaches or exceeds utility measured on the real signal (treated as an approximate anchor, not a ceiling).

Conclusion: ReCoGen converts routinely collected signals into informative surrogates for invasive or unavailable ones, advancing less invasive, lower-cost continuous clinical monitoring. The gains stem from the conditioning path: learnable cross-attention over frozen per-modality encoders and the dual token-plus-AdaLN route for static conditions.

Abstract: Continuous physiological time series underpin modern clinical monitoring, yet many of the most informative signals are invasive, expensive, or simply unavailable for a given patient. Conditional generation offers a remedy: an absent signal can be synthesized from co-recorded signals and routine clinical variables. Existing generators, however, are built around a single conditioning modality and degrade when forced to handle the heterogeneous, irregularly missing mix of time-variant signals and static covariates seen in practice. We propose ReCoGen (Represent Conditions, then Generate), a two-stage framework that decouples multimodal condition representation from target generation. Stage I trains one masked autoencoder per modality, distilling each time-variant condition into a compact and missingness-tolerant token sequence. Stage II trains a flow-matching generator that fuses these tokens with static conditions to synthesize the target signal. Across three physiological benchmarks, including continuous glucose monitoring on AI-READI and arterial blood pressure generation on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV, ReCoGen attains the best downstream utility on all sixteen (dataset, task, metric) settings, surpassing six representative conditional generators; on thirteen of them its utility also reaches or exceeds the utility measured on the real signal, a reference we read as an approximate anchor rather than a ceiling. Ablations trace the gains to the conditioning path: learnable cross-attention over the frozen per-modality encoders, and a dual token-plus-AdaLN route for the static conditions. ReCoGen thus turns routinely collected signals into informative surrogates for invasive or unavailable ones, a step toward less invasive, lower-cost continuous clinical monitoring.

</details>


### [237] [Predicting When Random Low-Dimensional Reparameterizations Train Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12597)
*Andrew Cheng,Ali Eslamian,Jie Cheng,Mehdi Zargham,Qiang Cheng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper studies how large the latent dimension must be for random low-dimensional reparameterization of neural network training/fine-tuning to succeed, derives a quadratic master formula predicting the residual from curvature and displacement, and introduces Random Mapping Networks (RaMaN) with memory-efficient structured maps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Neural networks can be trained or fine-tuned via random low-dimensional reparameterization (small latent vector mapped to full parameter update through a frozen random map), but the practical question of how large the latent search space must be to reach a low-loss region remains open. The work aims to provide a theoretical predictor for this dimension and to make the approach memory-efficient.

Method: The authors reformulate the known accessibility transition in an equivalent conic form centered on the statistical dimension of the polar cone for compact convex targets. The main contribution is an orientation-resolved quadratic master formula predicting the random-slice residual from both the curvature spectrum and the reference-to-solution displacement profile, yielding a self-consistent isotropic-orientation predictor and recovering the earlier Gaussian-width quadratic bound in a radius-only specialization. They introduce Random Mapping Networks (RaMaN) using structured Hadamard or seed-regenerated Gaussian maps to avoid O(dP) storage, plus matrix-free curvature approximations and sweep-free dimension selection.

Result: In controlled quadratic and neural-curvature experiments, the orientation-resolved predictor closely tracks measured transition locations and outperforms orientation-agnostic approximations when displacement direction matters. End-to-end experiments show sharp, protocol-dependent training transitions across image and language models.

Conclusion: The latent dimension needed for successful random-slice training is predictable via a conic/statistical-dimension framework refined by an orientation-resolved quadratic master formula, and RaMaN makes random low-dimensional reparameterization practically viable with drastically reduced memory, showing protocol-dependent transitions in real image and language model training.

Abstract: Neural networks can often be trained or fine-tuned through random low-dimensional reparameterization, where a small latent vector is mapped into a full parameter update by a frozen random map. This raises a practical question: how large must the latent search space be to reach a low-loss region? We first express the known accessibility transition in an equivalent conic form, centered for compact convex targets at the statistical dimension of the polar cone. Our main theoretical contribution is an orientation-resolved quadratic master formula that predicts the random-slice residual from both the curvature spectrum and the reference-to-solution displacement profile. It yields a self-consistent isotropic-orientation predictor and, in a conservative radius-only specialization, recovers the earlier Gaussian-width quadratic bound. Building on this analysis, we introduce Random Mapping Networks (RaMaN), which instantiate the predicted latent dimension using structured Hadamard or seed-regenerated Gaussian maps. These constructions avoid the O(dP) storage of dense random maps and reduce optimizer-state memory from O(P) to O(d). We also develop matrix-free curvature approximations and sweep-free dimension selection. Across controlled quadratic and neural-curvature experiments, the orientation-resolved predictor closely tracks measured transition locations and outperforms orientation-agnostic approximations when displacement direction matters. End-to-end experiments further show sharp, protocol-dependent training transitions across image and language models.

</details>


### [238] [The Boolean Power of ReLU](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12617)
*Pablo Barceló,Floris Geerts,Matthias Lanzinger,Klara Pakhomenko,Jan Van den Bussche*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: On finite simple undirected graphs with a single Boolean node feature, the Boolean queries expressible in Σ-MPLang (for any collection Σ of eventually constant activation functions and arbitrary real coefficients) form a strict subclass of those expressible in ReLU-MPLang. This settles an open problem by showing ReLU-MPLang is strictly more powerful than trReLU-MPLang for Boolean queries.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To settle the recently posed open problem of whether ReLU-MPLang is more powerful than trReLU-MPLang for Boolean queries, i.e., whether the truncated ReLU activation can match full ReLU in expressiveness over Boolean-featured graphs.

Method: The authors analyze the expressiveness of message-passing languages (MPLang) over finite simple undirected graphs with one Boolean feature. They characterize the Boolean queries definable using eventually constant activation functions (e.g., truncated ReLU) with arbitrary real coefficients, and compare this class against the queries definable with full ReLU, proving strict containment.

Result: They prove that ReLU-MPLang is strictly more expressive than Σ-MPLang (including trReLU-MPLang) with respect to Boolean queries on Boolean-featured graphs, establishing a strict subclass relationship.

Conclusion: ReLU-GNNs are strictly more expressive than {TrReLU, id}-GNNs for Boolean queries on Boolean-featured graphs, meaning the truncated ReLU activation is inherently less capable than ReLU in this setting.

Abstract: We prove that, on finite simple undirected graphs equipped with a single Boolean node feature, the Boolean queries expressible in $Σ$-MPLang, for any collection $Σ$ of eventually constant activation functions and with arbitrary real coefficients, form a strict subclass of the Boolean queries expressible in ReLU-MPLang. We thereby settle a recently posed open problem: whether ReLU-MPLang is more powerful than trReLU-MPLang when it comes to Boolean queries. In particular, this implies that ReLU-GNNs are strictly more expressive than {TrReLU,id}-GNNs with respect to Boolean queries on Boolean-featured graphs.

</details>


### [239] [Structure-preserving uncertainty quantification for GENERIC dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12624)
*Zequn He,Celia Reina*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces Structure-Preserving Epistemic Neural Networks (S-PENNs), a framework for uncertainty quantification in scientific machine learning models with hard architectural constraints, instantiated for GENERIC dynamics. By attaching lightweight epinets to constrained components of a pretrained model, S-PENNs guarantee physically admissible sampled realizations (preserving thermodynamic laws) and, combined with split conformal prediction, provide finite-sample marginal coverage intervals at one to three orders of magnitude lower cost than deep ensembles.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Uncertainty quantification for hard-constrained (structure-preserving) machine learning models is limited: standard UQ methods can violate the encoded admissibility conditions, require architectural modifications, or impose substantial computational cost. Existing approaches fail to preserve physical constraints while providing calibrated, affordable uncertainty estimates.

Method: The authors propose S-PENNs, a general framework that preserves the structural constraints of a pretrained model by attaching lightweight epinets to its constrained components, so every sampled realization remains physically admissible by construction. They instantiate the framework for GENERIC dynamics, yielding thermodynamically consistent rollouts, and combine it with split conformal prediction as a post-hoc calibration method to obtain prediction intervals with finite-sample marginal coverage guarantees.

Result: Across three numerical examples—a harmonic oscillator coupled to a heat bath (ODE), an idealized chemical motor (ODE), and a one-dimensional viscoplastic model (PDE)—S-PENNs produce thermodynamically consistent stochastic realizations and well-calibrated prediction intervals while reducing computational cost by roughly one to three orders of magnitude compared to deep ensembles.

Conclusion: S-PENNs successfully deliver physically admissible, well-calibrated uncertainty quantification for GENERIC dynamics at markedly lower computational cost. Although focused on GENERIC, the framework can be extended broadly to scientific machine learning models in computational mechanics with hard or soft constraints.

Abstract: Structure-preserving machine learning embeds physical structure directly into model architectures, yet uncertainty quantification (UQ) for such hard-constrained models remains limited because standard UQ methods may violate the encoded admissibility conditions, require architectural modifications, or impose substantial computational costs. In this work, we propose Structure-Preserving Epistemic Neural Networks (S-PENNs), a general framework for UQ in scientific machine learning models with hard architectural constraints, and instantiate it for GENERIC (General Equation for Non-Equilibrium Reversible-Irreversible Coupling) dynamics. S-PENNs preserve the structural constraints of a pretrained model by attaching lightweight epinets to its constrained components, ensuring that every sampled realization remains physically admissible by construction. When applied to GENERIC dynamics, such a proposed framework yields thermodynamically consistent rollouts that preserve the first and second laws. Furthermore, we combine S-PENNs with split conformal prediction as a post-hoc calibration method to produce prediction intervals with finite-sample marginal coverage guarantees. We validate S-PENNs on three numerical examples: a harmonic oscillator coupled to a heat bath and an idealized chemical motor, both governed by ODEs, and a one-dimensional viscoplastic model governed by PDEs. Across all three examples, S-PENNs produce thermodynamically consistent stochastic realizations and well-calibrated prediction intervals while reducing the computational cost by about one to three orders of magnitude compared to deep ensembles. Although the present study focuses on GENERIC dynamics, S-PENNs can be extended more broadly to scientific machine learning models in computational mechanics with either hard or soft constraints.

</details>


### [240] [CAKE: Compiler-Agent Co-Design for Frontier Kernel Evolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12629)
*Zihao Ye,Yingyi Huang,Hongyi Jin,Bohan Hou,Junru Shao,Zhongming Yu,Jinqi Chen,Meghan Cowan,Shiyi Cao,Shanli Xing,Hanfeng Chen,Vinod Grover,Tianqi Chen,Luis Ceze*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CAKE is a compiler-agent co-design that gives GPU kernel agents a typed, hardware-explicit IR (CAKE IR) exposing warp roles, memory movement, synchronization, and pipelines. The harness co-evolves with the agent, turning recurring failures into verifier rules, primitives, model calibrations, and tactics. CAKE enables agents to beat tuned baselines (1.144x on Flash-KMeans B200) and produce validated kernels (2.05x on Kimi Delta Attention), targeting NVIDIA Ampere–Blackwell GPUs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: GPU kernel agents and GPU programming languages have advanced separately, making expert kernels hard to reproduce. Agents treat the compiler as an opaque black box (receiving only errors, correctness, and timing), while existing DSLs either hide critical scheduling decisions or expose them via difficult layout abstractions. This gap motivates a co-designed IR and agent harness.

Method: Introduces CAKE IR, a typed, hardware-explicit schedule representation exposing warp roles, memory movement, synchronization, and pipelines, with support for verification, cost modeling, and localized diagnostics. The harness itself evolves by converting recurring failures into verifier rules, IR primitives, model calibrations, and reusable optimization tactics. The system separates single-shape evolution from library generalization and dispatch, and targets NVIDIA Ampere through Blackwell.

Result: On matched implementation-hidden Flash-KMeans clean starts on B200 with an 80M-token budget, the best CAKE IR candidate runs at 1.144x the tuned FlashML baseline vs. 0.928x for direct CUDA/PTX. Agent-generated Kimi Delta Attention achieves 2.05x geometric-mean speedup over official FlashKDA with end-to-end serving validation. Dispatcher-backed KNN and KMeans improve performance 1.42x–2.12x across 400+ shapes, with four kernel changes available as upstream PRs.

Conclusion: A compiler-agent co-design with a hardware-explicit, typed IR and a self-improving harness lets agents surpass hand-tuned baselines and produce production-quality, validated kernels. The approach generalizes across workloads via dispatcher-backed libraries and is upstreamed into real kernel codebases.

Abstract: GPU kernel agents and GPU programming languages have advanced separately, leaving expert kernels difficult to reproduce. Agents usually treat the compiler as a fixed black box and receive only errors, correctness outcomes, and timing, while existing DSLs either hide critical scheduling decisions or expose them through difficult layout abstractions. We present CAKE, a compiler-agent co-design in which agents author CAKE IR, a typed, hardware-explicit schedule representation. CAKE exposes warp roles, memory movement, synchronization, and pipelines while supporting verification, cost modeling, and localized diagnostics. The harness itself evolves: recurring failures become verifier rules, IR primitives, model calibrations, and reusable optimization tactics. In matched implementation-hidden Flash-KMeans clean starts on B200, the best CAKE IR candidate at an 80-million-token budget runs at 1.144x the tuned FlashML baseline, compared with 0.928x for direct CUDA/PTX. Beyond this benchmark, agent-generated Kimi Delta Attention achieves a 2.05x geometric-mean speedup over official FlashKDA and passes end-to-end serving validation. Dispatcher-backed KNN and KMeans improve performance by 1.42x to 2.12x across more than 400 shapes, and four kernel changes are available as upstream PRs. CAKE targets NVIDIA GPUs from Ampere through Blackwell and separates single-shape evolution from library generalization and dispatch.

</details>


### [241] [Interpretable Causal Discovery via Causal-Effect Constraints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12640)
*Cixuan Zhang,Guy Van den Broeck,Benjie Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a Bayesian method for conditional causal discovery that performs posterior inference over causal graphs and parameters subject to an event (e.g., a large causal-effect constraint), using rare-event estimation techniques to overcome the challenge of low posterior mass.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Causal discovery should not only infer causal edges but also interpret and explain observed or hypothesized phenomena, such as particularly large causal effects. Existing Bayesian causal discovery methods struggle when the conditioning event has small posterior mass, motivating the need for an approach capable of inference conditional on rare events.

Method: The authors cast conditional causal discovery as Bayesian inference, targeting the posterior over causal graphs and parameters given an event (a causal-effect constraint). They adapt rare-event estimation techniques, specifically using a particle population that is gradually driven toward the constrained region while maintaining samples approximating the conditional posterior in the joint graph-parameter space.

Result: Empirical evaluation on synthetic graphs validates the accuracy of the approach at both small and large scales. A case study on the Sachs protein dataset demonstrates how the method provides pathway-level summaries to aid scientific exploration.

Conclusion: The proposed rare-event estimation framework enables accurate conditional Bayesian causal discovery even for low-probability events, and offers interpretable, pathway-level insights for scientific applications such as biological network analysis.

Abstract: Causal discovery aims to uncover the underlying causal relationships given data generated from a system. The goal, however, is not merely to predict causal edges given data, but also to be able to interpret and explain either observed or hypothesized phenomena, such as a particularly large causal effect. We consider this task of conditional causal discovery and cast it as a Bayesian inference problem, in which we target the posterior over causal graphs and parameters conditional on an event such as a causal-effect constraint. Unfortunately, this poses a computational challenge: existing approaches to Bayesian causal discovery struggle when the event has small posterior mass. To address this, we adapt rare-event estimation techniques to perform inference the joint graph-parameter space. Our method gradually drives a particle population toward the constrained region while maintaining samples that approximate the conditional posterior. Empirical evaluation on synthetic graphs validates the accuracy of our approach at small and large scales, and we show in a case study on the Sachs protein dataset how our method can be used to aid scientific exploration by providing pathway-level summaries.

</details>


### [242] [Training Under Challenge: Executable Certificates and Challenge-Closed Optimality for Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12655)
*Farhang Yeganegi,Arian Eamaz,Mojtaba Soltanalian*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes "Training Under Challenge," a framework of executable certificates that construct alternative solutions to test whether a trained neural network checkpoint is actually optimal, revealing otherwise-invisible cases of local traps, representation limits, or trainer mismatch.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: A flat training curve alone is uninformative: it cannot distinguish a true global optimum from a local trap, a representation-limited solution, or a mismatch between network and trainer. There is a need for a principled, verifiable way to certify or falsify the optimality of a checkpoint without relying solely on loss stagnation.

Method: The authors introduce an executable-certificate framework called Training Under Challenge, where predeclared, architecture-valid procedures generate complete alternative candidates in the same certified class and reevaluate the same objective. Lower-valued candidates serve as replayable witnesses lower-bounding the empirical global-optimality gap. A resource-indexed challenge-power modulus characterizes the largest gap compatible with passing a finite challenge suite. For squared loss, block-decrease operators make coverage checkable and provide uniform and realized-residual bounds.

Result: They prove a converse frontier showing a first-order ReLU trainer can hit infinitely many exact conditional head optima while still converging to a non-global point absent coverage. On a channel-gated ResNet-18 distillation problem with a known optimum, eight internal challenges cover all 240 audited output directions, with realized-residual bounds within factors of 1.74–3.02 of the true gap. Paired predictive certificates separate decoder under-use from representation insufficiency, and quantized-denoising studies demonstrate diagnosis, repair, and current-state recertification.

Conclusion: The framework shows that flat training curves are insufficient evidence of optimality, and that executable challenges with justified coverage provide practical, checkable lower bounds on the optimality gap, enabling diagnosis and repair of suboptimal checkpoints.

Abstract: A flat training curve does not reveal whether a neural network has reached a global optimum, is locally trapped, is representation-limited, or is mismatched to its trainer. We introduce Training Under Challenge, an executable-certificate framework in which predeclared, architecture-valid procedures construct complete alternatives in the same certified class and reevaluate the same objective. Any lower-valued candidate is a replayable witness that lower-bounds the checkpoint's empirical global-optimality gap. Passing a finite suite is only suite-relative; global-gap conclusions require a separately justified coverage mechanism. We define a resource-indexed challenge-power modulus that characterizes the largest gap compatible with passage. For squared loss, current block-decrease operators make coverage checkable and yield uniform and realized-residual bounds. We prove the converse frontier: without coverage, a first-order ReLU trainer can reach infinitely many exact conditional head optima while converging to a non-global point. On a channel-gated ResNet-18 distillation problem with known optimum, eight internal challenges cover all 240 audited output directions, and realized-residual bounds lie within factors of 1.74--3.02 of the true gap. Paired predictive certificates separate decoder under-use from representation insufficiency, while quantized-denoising studies demonstrate diagnosis, repair, and current-state recertification.

</details>


### [243] [Demand Transfer Estimation at Scale via Restricted Logit Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12680)
*Lakshya Garg,Deep Narayan Mishra,Swapnil Yadav,Haoan Wang,Sujal Alugubelli,Karthik Kumaran,Anupriya Sharma*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces a scalable method for estimating Demand Transfer (DT) coefficients—the fraction of a removed target item's demand that shifts to each remaining item—enabling assortment optimization over item universes exceeding 1 million items, instead of forecasting demand per-assortment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing assortment optimization requires learning a customer choice model and computing expected demand separately for every possible assortment, which is inefficient for large item universes spanning many categories. The authors seek an approach that forecasts item demand independently while applying adjustments capturing substitution effects between items.

Method: The authors propose a framework centered on estimating Demand Transfer (DT) coefficients, which quantify the percentage of a target item's demand redirected to each other item when the target is removed from the shelf. The method applies independent demand forecasts and corrects them using these coefficients, and is designed to scale to very large assortments (1M+ items).

Result: Experiments on data and historical transaction data across multiple locations within categories show that, when reasonable assumptions about substitution behavior hold, the procedure accurately estimates underlying DT coefficients and improves demand forecasting.

Conclusion: The proposed DT coefficient estimation approach is accurate and scalable, providing an efficient alternative to per-assortment forecasting for assortment optimization in large-scale retail settings.

Abstract: Item demand forecasting is an integral component of store assortment optimization. Existing literature focuses on learning a suitable customer choice model and using this model to determine the value of an objective function (i.e. expected demand) with respect to an assortment proposal. However, for large item universe with many categories, this approach can prove inefficient, needing a separate demand forecast for every possible item assortment. An alternate approach exists whereby we combine the efficiency of forecasting item demand independently, while at the same time applying adjustments to the independent forecasts that account for the relations between item demand and the availability of other similar items on the shelf.
  Central to this approach is the estimation of Demand Transfer (DT) coefficients. These DT coefficients represent the percent of a particular target item's (item that the customer walked in the store to buy) demand that is redirected to each other item in the universe should the target item be removed from the shelf. We introduce an approach that allows us to compute these DT coefficients on large item universes (assortments having 1 million+ items). Experiments on data as well as historical transaction data for multiple locations within categories demonstrate that when certain reasonable assumptions about substitution behavior are satisfied, our procedure is able to accurately estimate underlying DT coefficients and lead to improvements in demand forecasting.

</details>


### [244] [Finding the Needle in a Haystack: Test-Time Analog Circuit Representation Adaptation for Bayesian Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12687)
*Fin Amin,Sounak Dutta,Paul D. Franzon*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TTARO is an online deep-kernel Bayesian optimization framework that adapts analog circuit representations at test time using newly observed figure-of-merit labels, aligning the search space with the optimization objective and reducing regret AUC by 15.2% vs. BO and 20.7% vs. DKL on average.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Representation-based Bayesian optimization for analog circuit topology search typically freezes circuit embeddings after encoder training, creating a mismatch between representation learning (which optimizes for structure encoding/reconstruction) and the figure of merit actually being optimized. This paper aims to close that gap by adapting embeddings during the search.

Method: TTARO starts from pretrained circuit embeddings and jointly learns a nonlinear feature transformation plus a Gaussian-process surrogate using FoM labels of circuits evaluated so far. After each new evaluation, it updates both the representation and the surrogate before selecting the next candidate, continually incorporating newly observed FoM labels.

Result: Across 40 encoder/kernel/acquisition settings, TTARO reduces regret AUC by an average of 15.2% relative to Gaussian-process BO over fixed embeddings and by 20.7% relative to Deep Kernel Learning, outperforming the prior art in most settings with reductions as large as 46.7%.

Conclusion: By continually adapting representations to newly observed FoM labels, TTARO aligns the search space with the optimization objective as BO progresses, significantly improving analog circuit topology search efficiency over fixed-embedding BO and DKL baselines.

Abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) is a sample-efficient framework for analog circuit topology search, where evaluating each candidate topology can require costly simulation. However, representation-based BO methods typically treat circuit embeddings as fixed after encoder training. This creates a mismatch between representation learning and optimization: embeddings learned to encode or reconstruct circuit structure are not necessarily organized according to the figure of merit (FoM) being optimized. This paper introduces Test-Time Analog Representation Adaptation for Bayesian Optimization (TTARO), an online deep-kernel BO framework that adapts circuit representations throughout the search process. Starting from pretrained circuit embeddings, TTARO jointly learns a nonlinear feature transformation and a Gaussian-process surrogate using the FoM labels of the circuits evaluated so far. Following each new evaluation, TTARO updates the representation and surrogate before selecting the next candidate. We compare TTARO with conventional Gaussian Process-based BO over fixed embeddings and with Deep Kernel Learning (DKL), which learns the representation only from the initial evaluated designs and keeps it fixed throughout the remainder of the search. By continually incorporating newly observed FoM labels into representation learning, TTARO aligns the search space with the optimization objective as BO progresses. In our experiments, TTARO reduces regret AUC by 15.2% on average relative to BO and by 20.7% relative to DKL across 40 encoder/kernel/acquisition settings, outperforming prior art in most settings with reductions as large as 46.7%.

</details>


### [245] [The Impact of Temporal Context Length and Encoding Strategies on Self-Supervised ECG Representation Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12695)
*Ahmed Sameh,Ramzi Al-Sharawi,Yogatheesan Varatharajah*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A controlled study on ECG self-supervised learning finds that longer input horizons (5–10 min) and continuous encoders outperform short 16-second snapshots and vector-quantized tokens for rhythm detection and patient-level retrieval.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: ECG self-supervised models are typically trained on short signal windows and increasingly on discretized tokens, but it is unclear whether these design choices discard information required for rhythm inference and longitudinal consistency in ambulatory recordings. The authors aim to quantify the impact of input horizon and front-end representation while holding other factors constant.

Method: The study uses the Icentia11k single-lead ECG dataset, varying (i) input horizon across 16 s, 1 min, 5 min, and 10 min, and (ii) front-end representation between continuous convolutional patch embeddings and fixed vector-quantized tokens, while keeping the Transformer backbone and training protocol identical. Models are evaluated via downstream abnormal rhythm detection and patient-level retrieval probing cross-session stability. Code and pretrained models are released.

Result: Increasing temporal context beyond 16-second snapshots improves transfer performance and retrieval accuracy, with 5- and 10-minute models performing best, indicating better capture of slow-varying rhythm dynamics and individual-specific structure. Continuous patch embeddings outperform discretized tokens across all horizons, suggesting quantization discards clinically relevant waveform detail.

Conclusion: ECG foundation models should emphasize extended temporal context and continuous encoders for clinical prediction and similarity-based applications, rather than short windows and quantized tokenization.

Abstract: Self-supervised electrocardiogram (ECG) models are often trained on a few seconds of ECG signal and, increasingly, on discretized token sequences. It remains unclear whether these choices sacrifice information needed for rhythm inference and longitudinal consistency in real-world ambulatory recordings. We present a controlled study on the Icentia11k single-lead dataset that varies (i) the input horizon (16 seconds, 1 minute, 5 minutes, and 10 minutes) and (ii) the front-end representation (continuous convolutional patch embeddings vs. fixed vector-quantized tokens), while holding the Transformer backbone and training protocol constant. Representations are assessed by downstream abnormal rhythm detection and by patient-level retrieval that probes cross-session stability. Our results show that increasing temporal context beyond 16-second snapshots yields stronger transfer and higher retrieval accuracy, with the strongest performance achieved by the 5- and 10-minute models, indicating improved capture of slow-varying rhythm dynamics and individual-specific structure. Across all evaluated horizons, continuous patch embeddings outperform discretized tokens, suggesting that quantization can discard clinically relevant waveform detail. These findings motivate ECG foundation models that emphasize extended context and continuous encoders for clinical prediction and similarity-based applications. Our code and pretrained models are publicly available at https://github.com/muha-0/ecg-ssl-representation-learning.

</details>


### [246] [Understanding Backdoor Vulnerabilities in Vertical Federated Learning: The Gap Between Research and Practice](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12962)
*Ziqi Zhao,Jialin Lu,Junjie Shan,Junyuan Zhang,Shuya Yang,Ka-Ho Chow*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper exposes a gap between reported VFL backdoor attacks/defenses and real-world practicality, showing that prior near-perfect results rely on unrealistic assumptions and flawed evaluations. It redefines realistic threat models and workflows and introduces BVBench, a backdoor-centric benchmark for fair, practical evaluation, demonstrating the fragility of current understanding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vertical Federated Learning's asymmetric information structure enables backdoor attacks, but prior work reports near-perfect attack success rates and effective defenses that fail under realistic conditions. This reveals a fundamental gap between research claims and actual practice, motivating a systematic, practice-oriented re-examination of backdoor vulnerabilities in VFL.

Method: The paper conducts a systematic, practice-oriented study identifying methodological and evaluation shortcomings in existing VFL backdoor research. It redefines threat models under realistic constraints, proposes practical backdoor workflows, and introduces BVBench, a backdoor-centric benchmark with state-of-the-art baselines for fair, practical, and comprehensive evaluation.

Result: Existing approaches overlook key practical constraints and rely on unrealistic prior knowledge, with limitations hidden by poorly designed evaluation practices. BVBench provides strong evidence of the fragility of the current understanding of VFL backdoor risks, establishing a foundation for future research. (Explicit quantitative metrics are not stated in the abstract.)

Conclusion: A fundamental gap exists between VFL backdoor research and practice. BVBench steers the field toward uncovering practical vulnerabilities and developing more meaningful defenses, replacing unrealistic assumptions and flawed evaluations with realistic threat models and benchmarking.

Abstract: Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) enables organizations holding complementary features of shared entities to collaborate and train models. In this setting, the initiator can withhold information about the learning task, while other contributors participate without exposing their local datasets, creating an asymmetric information structure aligned with growing privacy demands. However, this asymmetry is a double-edged sword. Among various threats, backdoor attacks are particularly concerning because VFL not only enables malicious contributors to poison the model during training, but also allows them to activate the backdoor at inference time to manipulate predictions. Although prior work has reported near-perfect attack success rates and proposed effective defenses, we find that most findings fail to hold under realistic conditions, exposing a fundamental gap between research and practice. In this paper, we present a systematic, practice-oriented study of backdoor vulnerabilities in VFL, revealing this gap in both methodological design and evaluation practices. We show that existing approaches overlook key practical constraints and therefore rely on unrealistic prior knowledge. Furthermore, these limitations have remained hidden due to poorly designed evaluation practices in the literature. To bridge this gap, we redefine threat models under realistic constraints, propose practical backdoor workflows, and introduce BVBench, a backdoor-centric benchmark that enables fair, practical, and comprehensive evaluation, preloaded with state-of-the-art baselines. BVBench provides strong evidence of the fragility of the current understanding of VFL backdoor risks and establishes a foundation for steering research toward uncovering practical vulnerabilities and developing more meaningful defenses.

</details>


### [247] [A Contract-Grade Verifier for LLM-Generated GPU Kernels, and a Native Blackwell Backward for the Gated-Linear-Recurrence Family](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12700)
*Rishi Shah,Rishav Shrestha*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Paper introduces a contract-grade verifier with 12 tolerance-free adversarial gates to properly test machine-generated GPU kernels, revealing that 39.5% of kernels previously accepted as correct are broken and 62.1% violate at least one property; it also validates the authors' own Blackwell tcgen05 GDN backward kernel.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current correctness reporting for language-model-generated GPU kernels relies on a single loose test (a few random inputs at one fixed shape, closeness to a reference), which misses silent bugs such as wrong NaN/infinity handling, run-to-run nondeterminism, shape-dependent failures, and fp16 accumulation errors. The field's reported high correctness rates are therefore misleading.

Method: The authors build a contract-grade verifier consisting of twelve adversarial gates, each encoding a property a correct kernel must satisfy, several of which are tolerance-free so no threshold choice can dismiss a failure. The verifier is applied outward to audit 2,638 machine-generated kernels already accepted by a public system's harness, and inward to verify the authors' own first native Blackwell tcgen05 training backward kernel for the gated-linear-recurrence (GDN) family, including the reverse-state stage.

Result: The verifier finds 39.5% of previously accepted kernels broken beyond any tolerance argument and 62.1% with at least one violation. The standard test accepts 1,487 kernels the verifier rejects, versus only 14 the other way. The finding is defended by a 7/7 positive control, a threshold-calibration sweep, 98.5% agreement with the reference benchmark's own correctness code, and a stratified hand-audit. The authors' GDN kernel is independently verified against a double-precision oracle and used to train five family members.

Conclusion: The correctness signal behind reported progress in kernel generation is far weaker than the numbers suggest; adopting a set of tolerance-free contracts would close most of the gap between reported and actual correctness.

Abstract: Systems that generate GPU kernels with language models report high correctness rates. Those rates come from a single loose test: run the kernel on a few random inputs at one fixed shape and accept it if the output is close to a reference. A kernel can pass that test and still be silently wrong. It can return an ordinary number where the true answer is a NaN or an infinity, differ from run to run, break when the shape changes, or accumulate in fp16 where the reference keeps an fp32 total. We build the instrument that checks correctness properly: a contract-grade verifier of twelve adversarial gates, each a property a correct kernel must satisfy, several of them tolerance-free, so no choice of threshold can explain a failure away. Aimed outward, the verifier audits 2,638 machine-generated kernels that a public system's own harness had already accepted as correct. It finds 39.5% broken beyond any tolerance argument and 62.1% carrying at least one violation. The field's standard test accepts 1,487 kernels the verifier rejects, against only 14 the other way. We defend the finding four independent ways: a 7/7 positive control, a threshold-calibration sweep, 98.5% agreement with the reference benchmark's own correctness code, and a stratified hand-audit. Aimed inward, the verifier judges a kernel of our own: the first native Blackwell tcgen05 training backward for the gated-linear-recurrence (GDN) family, including the reverse-state stage the field still runs on a fallback. We establish its correctness independently, against a double-precision oracle, and train five family members through it. The correctness signal behind reported progress in kernel generation is far weaker than the numbers suggest, and a set of tolerance-free contracts would close most of the gap.

</details>


### [248] [Federated Compositional Muon Optimizer for Matrix-Wise Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12710)
*Wang Yan,Feihu Huang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes FedCoMuon, a federated compositional Muon optimizer for distributed matrix-wise compositional optimization, plus a variance-reduced variant FedCoMuon-VR, achieving O(ε^{-3}) sample complexity and state-of-the-art empirical performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Muon optimizers are effective for matrix-wise models but are not well-suited to hierarchical (compositional) structured problems; existing FedMuon algorithms also have higher sample complexity. The authors aim to fill this gap by designing a federated Muon-based optimizer tailored to compositional optimization problems.

Method: The proposed FedCoMuon combines compositional gradient tracking with orthogonalized momentum to solve distributed matrix-wise compositional optimization. A variance-reduced variant, FedCoMuon-VR, is further developed using a momentum-based variance reduction technique. Convergence is analyzed under non-i.i.d. and non-convex settings.

Result: FedCoMuon-VR achieves a lower sample complexity of O(ε^{-3}) for finding an ε-stationary solution compared to existing FedMuon algorithms. Experiments on robust federated learning and task-distributed risk-sensitive meta learning show the methods are competitive with existing compositional baselines and achieve the best reported accuracy in several settings.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that FedCoMuon and FedCoMuon-VR effectively extend Muon optimizers to federated compositional optimization, with theoretical guarantees of improved sample complexity and strong empirical performance across federated learning and meta learning tasks.

Abstract: Muon, a more recently developed optimizer, is useful for matrix-wise models in AI areas. Although many works have studied Muon and its variants, these methods are still not particularly well-suited for hierarchical structured problems. To fill this gap, we propose an effective federated compositional Muon (FedCoMuon) optimizer to solve distributed matrix-wise compositional optimization problems. Specifically, our FedCoMuon optimizer builds on compositional gradient tracking and orthogonalized momentum. Moreover, we propose a variance reduced variant of FedCoMuon (FedCoMuon-VR) based on a momentum-based variance reduced technique. In theory, we analyze the convergence properties of our algorithms under the non-i.i.d. and non-convex settings. In particular, we prove that our FedCoMuon-VR obtains a lower sample complexity of $O(ε^{-3})$ for finding an $ε$-stationary solution than the existing FedMuon algorithms. Extensive numerical experiments on robust federated learning and task-distributed risk-sensitive meta learning show that our proposed methods are competitive with existing compositional baselines and achieve the best reported accuracy in several settings.

</details>


### [249] [EEG Decoding Using CNN and LSTM Network](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13285)
*Athanasios Karagounis*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a hybrid CNN + bidirectional LSTM deep learning model for motor imagery EEG classification, achieving robust two- and three-class decoding and promising subject-independent performance on public and private datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motor imagery BCIs enable flexible brain-device communication for stroke and neurodegenerative patients, but reliable MI-EEG decoding is hard because EEG signals are noisy and only weakly informative. Deep learning can learn representations directly from EEG, yet its use for MI-EEG feature learning remains limited.

Method: A hybrid deep-learning architecture combining a convolutional neural network (CNN) and a bidirectional long short-term memory (bi-LSTM) network. The CNN learns high-level spatial and temporal representations directly from raw MI-EEG, and the bi-LSTM models temporal dependencies among the extracted features. Evaluated on a public dataset and a privately acquired dataset from an EEG acquisition system, including subject-independent decoding.

Result: The CNN+bi-LSTM architecture shows robust performance for two- and three-class motor-imagery classification and demonstrates promising subject-independent decoding capability.

Conclusion: The hybrid CNN and bi-LSTM model is an effective approach for MI-EEG decoding, offering reliable classification performance and strong generalization across subjects.

Abstract: Motor imagery (MI) brain--computer interfaces (BCIs) have emerged as a promising approach for establishing flexible communication pathways between the human brain and external devices , particularly for individuals affected by stroke or neurodegenerative disorders. Reliable decoding of motor-imagery electroencephalography (MI-EEG) remains challenging because EEG recordings contain substantial noise and exhibit complex, weakly informative relationships with the underlying brain activity. Although deep learning provides an effective means of learning representations directly from EEG signals, its application to MI-EEG feature learning remains comparatively limited. This study introduces a hybrid deep-learning architecture that integrates a convolutional neural network (CNN) with a bidirectional long short-term memory (bi-LSTM) network. The CNN is used to learn high-level spatial and temporal representations directly from raw MI-EEG recordings, whereas the bi-LSTM models temporal dependencies and relationships among the extracted features. The proposed approach is evaluated using both a publicly available dataset and a privately acquired dataset obtained with an EEG acquisition system. The experimental results indicate that the CNN\&bi-LSTM architecture provides robust performance for both two- and three-class motor-imagery classification and demonstrates promising subject-independent decoding capability across the evaluated methods.

</details>
