### [250] [Perturbation-based Regional Interpretability through Subtraction Mapping (PRISM): naming-error dissociations in language models and post-stroke aphasia](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12717)
*Xiang Guan,Roger D. Newman-Norlund,Yong Yang,Saeed Ahmadi,Regan Willis,Nadra Salman,Kalil Warren,Srihari Nelakuditi,Chris Rorden,Leonardo Bonilha,Julius Fridriksson*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces PRISM, a perturbation-based subtraction-mapping framework that adapts human neuroimaging methods to large language models, and demonstrates parallel, replicable phonemic-specialization dissociations across perturbed transformers and post-stroke aphasia brains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mechanistic interpretability of LLMs lacks spatially resolved, falsifiable tools for testing whether internal components specialize for distinct cognitive operations. The authors aim to establish such a tool by mapping a rigorous human-neuroimaging analysis framework onto transformer networks.

Method: Building on the Brain-LLM Unified Model (BLUM), PRISM maps seven clinical Philadelphia Naming Test categories onto layer-perturbed LLaVA-1.6-Vicuna-13B, subtracts error classes pairwise, and treats each perturbation seed as a subject in a group analysis with threshold-free cluster enhancement along the layer axis. A structurally matched analysis is run on 213 chronic post-stroke aphasia patients via correlation-difference lesion-symptom mapping, with replication on held-out splits. The designs match in subject dimension (seeds/patients), spatial dimension (layers/parcellated cortex), and thresholding, but differ in the contrast operator (within-subject error-proportion difference vs. between-subject correlation difference).

Result: Both substrates recover a robust, replicating phonemic-favoring dissociation—a deep layer cluster in the LLM and a frontal-perisylvian cortical cluster in patients. The semantic-favoring direction appears as a consistently signed but non-significant trend in both.

Conclusion: PRISM provides a falsifiable, spatially resolved test of functional-specialization claims in transformer language models, with parallel evidence across artificial and biological substrates. A confirmatory ROI-level causal intervention (PRISM Stage 3) is deferred to future work.

Abstract: Mechanistic interpretability of large language models lacks spatially resolved, falsifiable tools for testing whether internal components are specialized for distinct cognitive operations. We adapt subtraction analysis, the standard framework of human neuroimaging, from biological brains to perturbed transformers, and apply the same logic to both substrates in parallel. Building on the Brain-LLM Unified Model (BLUM), which showed that layer-perturbed LLaVA-1.6-Vicuna-13B error profiles match the lesion patterns of aphasic patients, we develop PRISM (Perturbation-based Regional Interpretability through Subtraction Mapping). PRISM maps the seven clinical Philadelphia Naming Test categories, subtracts error classes pairwise, and treats each perturbation seed as a subject in a group analysis with threshold-free cluster enhancement along the layer axis. We run a structurally matched analysis on 213 chronic post-stroke aphasia patients using correlation-difference lesion-symptom mapping, and replicate both sides on held-out splits. The designs match in subject dimension (seeds, patients), spatial dimension (layers, atlas-parcellated cortex) and thresholding, but the contrast operator differs: a within-subject error-proportion difference for the LLM, a between-subject correlation difference for the cortex. Both substrates recover a robust phonemic-favoring dissociation, a deep layer cluster and a frontal-perisylvian cortical cluster, both replicating; the semantic-favoring direction is a consistently signed but non-significant trend on both. PRISM thus gives a falsifiable, spatially resolved test of functional-specialization claims in transformer language models. A confirmatory ROI-level intervention (PRISM Stage 3) licensing the strongest causal-mechanism claim is left to subsequent work.

</details>


### [251] [MAG: MAnifold Guided Semi-Supervised Multi-modal In-Context Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12724)
*Zirui Cheng,Xun Xu,Tiankai Chen,Fady Rezk,Bowen Zheng,Xiaodong Shi,Shijie Li,Kangkang Lu,Bharadwaj Veeravalli,Nancy F. Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MAG is a semi-supervised framework that selects multi-modal ICL demonstrations by propagating relevance scores over a graph built from unlabeled data, pseudo-labeling only the most impactful samples to cut inference cost, then selecting final demonstrations using both visual and textual features.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Few-shot ICL with MLLMs is highly sensitive to demonstration quality/coverage, and while unlabeled multi-modal data is plentiful, exploiting it for demonstration selection remains an open problem, especially in label-scarce settings where existing selection approaches degrade.

Method: MAG formulates demonstration selection as semi-supervised propagation on a multi-modal graph. Stage 1 propagates relevance scores to identify a compact set of high-impact unlabeled samples for pseudo-labeling, minimizing MLLM inference cost. Stage 2 selects final demonstrations using multi-modal relevance, with textual representations driving propagation and both visual and textual modalities informing final selection.

Result: Across eight multi-modal benchmarks, MAG consistently outperforms strong baselines in label-scarce regimes, achieving significant gains while using only a limited pseudo-labeling budget.

Conclusion: Unlabeled multi-modal data can be efficiently leveraged to improve ICL demonstration selection; textual features are most effective for relevance propagation, while combining visual and textual modalities yields the highest-quality demonstrations, making MAG a practical solution for label-scarce multi-modal ICL.

Abstract: Few-shot in-context learning (ICL) with multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) enables task adaptation without parameter updates, but its performance is highly sensitive to the quality and coverage of the selected demonstrations. While unlabeled multi-modal data is abundant, it remains elusive how to exploit them for ICL. We propose MAG (MAnifold-Guided semi-supervised in-context demonstra- tion selection), an efficient framework that leverages unlabeled data to improve multi-modal ICL. MAG formulates demonstration selection as a semi-supervised propagation problem on a multi-modal graph and adopts a two-stage strategy: (i) relevance score propagation identifies a compact set of high-impact unlabeled samples for pseudo-labeling, reducing MLLM inference cost; (ii) multi-modal relevance is used to select the final demonstrations. We show that textual represen- tations are more effective for relevance propagation, while both visual and textual modalities are crucial for high-quality demonstration selection. Experiments on eight multi-modal benchmarks demonstrate that MAG consistently outperforms strong baselines in label-scarce regimes, achieving significant gains with a limited pseudo-labeling budget.

</details>


### [252] [A Cloud-Edge System for Multimodal Clinical Screening in Resource-Constrained Rural Settings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12745)
*Hei Ting,Chan,Chenwei Wu,Xueshen Liu,Zesen Zhao,Boyuan Zheng,Luis Filipe Nakayama,Michael G. Morley,Liyue Shen,Jiasi Chen,Z. Morley Mao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A cloud–edge hybrid architecture pairs lightweight edge models that compress medical data into structured outputs with a cloud LLM that synthesizes clinical summaries. An LLM orchestrator dynamically chooses diagnostic tools, achieving near-full tool recall, cloud-level accuracy, low invariant latency, and 4–15× token cost reduction under bandwidth-constrained rural conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Specialist-level medical AI remains inaccessible in resource-constrained rural settings because of scarce bandwidth, limited compute, and the need to integrate heterogeneous data modalities for clinical decisions.

Method: A cloud–edge collaborative architecture: (1) lightweight, domain-specific edge models transform raw medical data into compact structured outputs; (2) a cloud LLM synthesizes these outputs into clinical summaries; (3) an LLM-based orchestrator dynamically selects diagnostic tools based on patient context to ensure broad modality coverage while skipping irrelevant inputs. Evaluated on 20 multimodal clinical cases (cardiac, obstetric, trauma, screening) under three simulated network profiles (500 kbps–5 Mbps).

Result: The hybrid system achieves 98–99% diagnostic tool recall with 92–96% precision, matches or exceeds cloud-only baselines on clinical accuracy, and keeps latency bandwidth-invariant at 25–35 s with 4–15× lower token cost.

Conclusion: Architectural design plays a key role in enabling efficient multimodal integration and improving factual grounding relative to cloud-only approaches under deployment constraints.

Abstract: Medical AI has demonstrated specialist-level diagnostic accuracy, yet these capabilities remain largely inaccessible in resource-constrained rural settings where bandwidth is scarce, compute is limited, and clinical decision-making requires integrating heterogeneous modalities. We introduce a cloud--edge collaborative architecture that addresses these constraints: lightweight, domain-specific models on the edge transform raw medical data into compact structured outputs, while a cloud LLM synthesizes these outputs into clinical summaries. An LLM-based orchestrator dynamically selects diagnostic tools based on patient context, promoting comprehensive modality coverage without processing irrelevant inputs. We evaluate on 20 multimodal clinical cases spanning cardiac, obstetric, trauma, and screening scenarios under three simulated network profiles (500,kbps--5,Mbps). The hybrid system achieves 98--99% diagnostic tool recall with 92--96% precision, matches or exceeds cloud-only baselines on clinical accuracy, and maintains bandwidth-invariant latency (25--35,s) at 4--15x lower token cost. These results highlight the role of architectural design in enabling efficient multimodal integration and improving factual grounding compared to cloud-only approaches under deployment constraints.

</details>


### [253] [Decentralized Multi-Player Q-Learning in Episodic Markov Decision Processes with Information Asymmetry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12753)
*Larissa Xu,King Bi,William Chang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper studies decentralized multi-player RL in episodic tabular MDPs under three information asymmetries (unobserved actions/common rewards, observed actions/independent rewards, unobserved actions/independent rewards). It proposes mQ-learning and mQ-learning-intervals for Problems A and B with regret O~(√(H⁴ S A_joint T)), and mEXC/mEXC-Bellman for Problem C with regret O~(H (S A_joint)^(1/3) T^(2/3)), matching centralized single-agent rates up to log factors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understand whether decentralized multi-player RL can perform as well as centralized learning when players act under information asymmetry (no communication, but pre-agreed protocol), and to characterize the regret achievable for different observability/reward structures.

Method: For Problems A and B, propose optimistic Q-learning-style algorithms mQ-learning and mQ-learning-intervals that align players' value estimates using confidence intervals over the joint action space. For Problem C, propose two-phase explore-then-commit algorithms mEXC and mEXC-Bellman that first explore to learn the model, then commit to the optimal joint policy.

Result: Problems A and B achieve regret O~(√(H⁴ S A_joint T)); Problem C achieves O~(H (S A_joint)^(1/3) T^(2/3)). These match the centralized single-agent Q-learning rate of Jin et al. (2018) up to logarithmic factors, though A_joint grows exponentially in M, so bounds are most meaningful for small M or small action sets.

Conclusion: Decentralized multi-player RL under information asymmetry can match centralized joint-action benchmarks (up to logarithmic factors), with the unobserved-actions/independent-rewards case (C) incurring a worse T^(2/3) rate than the T^(1/2) rate of cases A and B, and all bounds limited by the exponential growth of the joint action space in M.

Abstract: We study decentralized multi-player reinforcement learning in episodic tabular Markov decision processes (MDPs) under three forms of information asymmetry: (A) unobserved actions with common rewards, (B) observed actions with independent rewards, and (C) unobserved actions with independent rewards. Players cannot communicate during learning but may agree on a protocol a priori. For Problems A and B we propose \texttt{mQ-learning} and \texttt{mQ-learning-intervals}, achieving $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{H^4 S A_{\text{joint}}\, T})$ regret, where $H$ is the horizon, $S$ the state count, $T = KH$ the total steps, and $A_{\text{joint}} = \prod_{i=1}^M |\mathcal{A}_i|$ the joint action space across $M$ players. For Problem C we give \texttt{mEXC} and \texttt{mEXC-Bellman}, two-phase explore-then-commit algorithms with regret $\tilde{O}(H (S A_{\text{joint}})^{1/3} T^{2/3})$. Against the centralized joint-action benchmark, decentralized learning under information asymmetry matches the single-agent Q-learning rate of \cite{jin2018q} up to logarithmic factors. Because $A_{\text{joint}}$ grows exponentially in $M$, the bounds are most meaningful for small $M$ or small per-player action sets.

</details>


### [254] [Concept Drift Detection and Adaptive Retraining of Malware Classification Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13465)
*Christofer Washington Berruz Chungata,Martin Jurecek,Katerina Potika,William B. Andreopoulos,Mark Stamp*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper evaluates automated concept drift detection for malware classification using three methods (OCSVM, MK-Means, MMD) across four learning models and three retraining scenarios, showing drift-aware retraining matches periodic retraining accuracy while greatly improving efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Malware classification models degrade over time due to concept drift caused by attackers continually modifying malware. Retraining is expensive, so the authors seek an automated way to detect when retraining is actually needed, avoiding unnecessary retraining while maintaining accuracy.

Method: Three concept drift detection techniques are compared: a novel One-Class Support Vector Machine (OCSVM) approach, a previously studied Minibatch K-Means (MK-Means) technique, and Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD). Experiments use four learning models (Multilayer Perceptron, Random Forest, Support Vector Machines, eXtreme Gradient Boosting). Three scenarios are evaluated: static (no retraining), periodic (constant retraining), and drift-aware (retrain only on detected drift). Accuracy vs. efficiency tradeoff is analyzed using Pareto Front analysis.

Result: All three drift detection techniques achieve classification accuracy comparable to periodic retraining while requiring substantially fewer model retrainings. The OCSVM-based drift-aware retraining generally outperforms the MK-Means and MMD approaches.

Conclusion: Concept drift can be accurately detected in malware classification models, enabling efficient drift-aware retraining that preserves accuracy while markedly reducing retraining cost compared to periodic retraining.

Abstract: Concept drift refers to changes over time in the statistical properties of data, as compared to the data that was used to train a learning model. Machine learning models for malware detection or classification are particularly susceptible to performance degradation caused by concept drift, as attackers constantly modify existing malware. In this chapter, we analyze two machine learning-based approaches to automated concept drift detection-a novel approach based on One-Class Support Vector Machines (OCSVM) and a previously-studied technique based on Minibatch K-Means (MK-Means). For comparison we also consider Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD), a statistical technique for detecting changes in multidimensional data. We conduct an extensive series of experiments comparing the effectiveness of four learning models, namely, Multilayer Perceptron, Random Forest, Support Vector Machines, and eXtreme Gradient Boosting. For each of these models, we consider three distinct scenarios: A static scenario where no model retraining occurs, a periodic scenario where models are constantly retrained irrespective of concept drift, and a drift-aware scenario where models are only retrained when concept drift is detected. Under the drift-aware scenario, we analyze the tradeoff between accuracy and training efficiency using Pareto Front analysis. We find that all three concept drift detection techniques achieve classification accuracy comparable to periodic retraining, while offering substantially greater efficiency in terms of the number of models that must be retrained. In addition, drift-aware retraining based on our OCSVM technique generally outperforms the MK-Means and MMD approaches. Overall, these results provide strong evidence that we can accurately detect concept drift in malware classification models.

</details>


### [255] [Beyond Outcome Rewards: Step-Level Self-Distilled Policy Optimization for Deep Search Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12764)
*Haoze Wu,Chuqiao Kuang,Tianyi Zhuang,Xiaoguang Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SSPO extends on-policy self-distillation to deep search agents by using web-extracted Evidence Anchors as privileged step-level information, converting teacher-student disagreement into step-level advantage weights inside GRPO applied only to incorrect trajectories, outperforming GRPO with only ~5% overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep search agents involve long trajectories but receive only a sparse outcome reward, making credit assignment difficult. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) provides dense token-level teachers, but applying it to search agents creates a tension: the teacher has privileged information (e.g., the correct answer) whose distribution differs from the student's exploration-based reasoning, so naive distillation transfers this information asymmetry instead of improving search strategy.

Method: Two contributions: (1) Evidence Anchors — concise, step-level evidence snippets extracted from the web — serve as privileged information capturing key reasoning steps without revealing the full answer path. (2) Step-Level Self-Distilled Policy Optimization (SSPO) converts teacher-student disagreement into step-level advantage weights within GRPO, applied exclusively to incorrect trajectories. The outcome reward determines the direction of policy change, while the teacher modulates its magnitude at each step; correct trajectories are left untouched to preserve diversity.

Result: On Qwen3-8B, SSPO consistently outperforms GRPO on BrowseComp, GAIA, and FRAMES. It surpasses or matches GRPO trained with twice as many gradient steps while adding only ~5% per-step overhead from a single additional forward pass.

Conclusion: SSPO effectively transfers privileged evidence-based guidance into step-level policy updates for search agents, decoupling update direction (from outcome reward) from update magnitude (from teacher disagreement), improving sample efficiency and performance at minimal computational cost.

Abstract: Deep search agents operate over trajectories spanning dozens of steps, yet standard reinforcement learning provides only a single outcome reward per trajectory, which is far too sparse for effective credit assignment. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) addresses this by using the model's own logits as dense token-level teachers, but extending it to search agents introduces a fundamental tension: the teacher, having access to privileged information such as the correct answer, produces a distribution that differs systematically from the student's exploration-based reasoning, and naive distillation causes the student to inherit this information asymmetry rather than learn better search strategies. We resolve this tension through two contributions. First, we construct Evidence Anchors, which are concise, step-level evidence snippets extracted from the web, as privileged information that captures key reasoning steps without revealing the entire answer path. Second, we propose Step-Level Self-Distilled Policy Optimization (SSPO), which converts teacher-student disagreement into step-level advantage weights within GRPO, applied exclusively to incorrect trajectories. This design decouples what to update from how much to update: the outcome reward determines the direction of policy change, while the teacher modulates its magnitude at each step. Correct trajectories are left untouched, preserving their diversity. On Qwen3-8B, SSPO consistently outperforms GRPO across BrowseComp, GAIA, and FRAMES, surpassing or matching GRPO trained with twice as many gradient steps while adding only about 5 percent overhead per step from a single additional forward pass.

</details>


### [256] [CoMedBench: A Multi-Source Benchmark of Synthetic Medical Data Fidelity and Downstream Utility](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12805)
*Akanta Das,Al Amin Farhad,Mrinmoy Sarkar Anto,David Rehkopf,Ayin Vala,Tanmoy Sarkar Pias*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CoMedBench is a reproducible benchmark for evaluating synthetic clinical data generators across 37 dataset–task pairs (20 static tabular, 17 temporal ICU time-series) from seven public sources, measuring both statistical fidelity and downstream task utility. It finds synthetic data preserves most signal on tabular tasks (up to ~97% AUROC utility), while temporal ICU tasks are harder and more generator-sensitive (64–95% retention).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real electronic health records are hard to use for ML development due to privacy regulation, IRB review, data-use agreements, and re-identification risk. Synthetic data could preserve useful clinical structure while reducing privacy exposure, but prior studies evaluate only a single generator, one dataset, or one narrow task, making it unclear when synthetic data can (or cannot) support model development.

Method: Introduce CoMedBench, a reproducible benchmark applying a common clinical-validity framework and a shared training/evaluation engine to a family of generators. It spans 37 dataset–task pairs across two modalities (20 static tabular, 17 temporal ICU time-series) drawn from seven public sources: MIMIC-III, MIMIC-IV, eICU, UCI ML Repository, CDC BRFSS diabetes (2015), NHANES (1999–2014), and pycox survival datasets (GBSG, METABRIC). It evaluates statistical fidelity and task utility by comparing models trained/tested across real and synthetic data, using reference generators CoMed-CTGAN and CoMed-TVAE.

Result: Synthetic training data preserves most downstream signal. Tabular: CoMed-CTGAN retains 90.6% mean AUROC utility (synthetic-to-real ratio), rising to 97.3% for CoMed-TVAE. Temporal ICU tasks: CoMed-CTGAN retains 81.6% AUROC and only 64.0% AUPRC (imbalance-sensitive), while CoMed-TVAE retains ~95% AUROC.

Conclusion: Synthetic data is largely viable for tabular clinical tasks, with strong generators recovering nearly all real-data signal. Temporal ICU tasks are more challenging and generator-sensitive, especially under imbalance-sensitive metrics like AUPRC, indicating that generator choice and modality matter greatly for preserving task-critical signal.

Abstract: Access to clinical data is essential for developing reliable healthcare machine learning systems, but direct use of electronic health records is constrained by privacy regulation, institutional review, data-use agreements, and the risk of re-identification. Synthetic data promises a practical alternative: it can preserve useful statistical and clinical structure while reducing exposure of sensitive patient records. Prior studies often evaluate a single generator, one dataset, or a narrow downstream task, making it difficult to know when synthetic data can support model development and when it fails to preserve task-critical signal. We introduce CoMedBench, a reproducible benchmark that evaluates a family of generators under a common clinical-validity framework and one shared training and evaluation engine, spanning static tabular and temporal downstream tasks on established critical-care datasets. In total the benchmark spans 37 dataset-task pairs across two modalities consists of 20 static tabular and 17 temporal ICU time-series-drawn from seven public data sources: three intensive-care databases (MIMIC-III, MIMIC-IV, and eICU) together with the UCI Machine Learning Repository, the CDC BRFSS diabetes cohort (2015), NHANES (1999-2014), and the pycox survival datasets (GBSG and METABRIC). The benchmark evaluates both statistical fidelity and task utility by comparing models trained and tested across real and synthetic data. In these settings, synthetic training data preserves most of the downstream signal: on tabular tasks the reference generator CoMed-CTGAN retains a mean AUROC utility (the synthetic-to-real performance ratio) of 90.6%, rising to 97.3% for the strongest generator, CoMed-TVAE. Temporal ICU tasks are harder and more generator-sensitive: CoMed-CTGAN retains 81.6% (AUROC) and only 64.0% under the imbalance-sensitive AUPRC, whereas CoMed-TVAE still retains ~95% (AUROC).

</details>


### [257] [HiRoute: Hierarchical Routed Prompt Tuning for Safety Alignment of Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12821)
*Fangzhou Chen,Shiji Zhao,Mengyang Wang,Qihui Zhu,Ranjie Duan,Maoxun Yuan,Xingxing Wei*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HiRoute is an input-adaptive hierarchical prompt-tuning framework that separates category-agnostic safety control from category-specific response guidance, using a lightweight router and a mixture of prompt experts to improve LLM safety while reducing over-refusal and preserving helpfulness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing parameter-efficient safety alignment methods based on prompt tuning rely on a single global prompt or externally selected prompt modules. These static designs fail to maintain a cross-category safety boundary while generating constructive, risk-specific responses and avoiding over-refusal of benign inputs. The goal is to make safety alignment adaptive to input risk without hurting general task performance.

Method: HiRoute uses an input-adaptive hierarchical prompt-tuning framework. It first trains a lightweight hierarchical router on frozen LLM representations to jointly detect harmful intent and predict multi-label risk scores. Then it freezes both the backbone model and the router, and applies preference optimization with alternating gradient updates to learn a shared coarse-grained prompt and a set of fine-grained prompt experts as continuous embeddings. At inference, benign inputs bypass the safety branch, while risky inputs use the shared prompt combined with a router-weighted mixture of risk-specific prompt experts.

Result: Experiments on three instruction-tuned models show HiRoute achieves high safety rates across multiple safety benchmarks while preserving safe-response helpfulness, reducing over-refusal, and maintaining competitive performance on general-purpose tasks.

Conclusion: HiRoute demonstrates that separating category-agnostic safety control from category-specific response guidance via adaptive hierarchical prompt tuning effectively strengthens LLM safety alignment with better helpfulness, lower over-refusal, and maintained general capability.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to harmful requests and jailbreak attacks. Parameter-efficient safety alignment methods based on prompt tuning typically rely on a single global prompt or externally selected prompt modules. Such static designs struggle to maintain a cross-category safety boundary while generating constructive responses tailored to specific risks and avoiding over-refusal of benign inputs. To address these limitations, we propose HiRoute, an input-adaptive hierarchical prompt-tuning framework that separates category-agnostic safety control from category-specific response guidance. HiRoute first trains a lightweight hierarchical router on representations extracted from a frozen LLM to jointly detect harmful intent and predict multi-label risk scores. It then freezes both the backbone model and the router and uses preference optimization with alternating gradient updates to learn a shared coarse-grained prompt and a set of fine-grained prompt experts as continuous embeddings. At inference time, benign inputs bypass the safety branch, whereas risky inputs are processed using the shared prompt together with a router-weighted mixture of risk-specific prompt experts. Experiments across three instruction-tuned models show that HiRoute achieves high safety rates across multiple safety benchmarks while preserving safe-response helpfulness, reducing over-refusal, and maintaining competitive performance on general-purpose tasks.

</details>


### [258] [Fast A/B/n Testing: Exact Multi-Policy Comparison via Tree-Coupled Feedback Sharing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12831)
*Yuxiao Wen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces Tree-Coupled A/B Testing (TCAB), an exact feedback-sharing design for comparing J adaptive, history-dependent contextual-bandit policies nearly for the price of one, by coupling policies through a tree whose edge mismatches determine the extra reward queries beyond T.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Platforms increasingly need to compare many adaptive decision policies (ranking, recommendations, pricing, LLM agents), but each reward-bearing interaction is costly or risky. Standard A/B/n testing requires JT outcomes for J policies over T rounds, which is prohibitively expensive; the paper seeks a design that retains exact per-policy trajectory laws while minimizing total reward queries and improving the cost–precision frontier.

Method: TCAB constructs a predictable tree connecting current policy histories at each round, maximally couples each parent–child context–action law, and shares one reward within each component of matched tree edges. The number of reward queries follows the pathwise identity N(T) = T + Σ_{t,e} D_{e,t}, where D_{e,t} records mismatches on tree edge e at round t, so expected cost equals T plus cumulative tree-edge total variation. The design is conditionally optimal among exact edge-local designs on the selected tree, and a current-round minimum-spanning tree is myopically optimal among tree designs.

Result: For fixed J, sublinear pseudo-regret of every policy plus almost-sure uniqueness of the oracle action imply E[N(T)] = T + o(T), versus JT for independent runs. The paper also provides finite-sample variance bounds for pairwise policy contrasts. Experiments on reward-model evaluation, multiple-choice language-model evaluation, and adaptive search policies show substantial improvements in the cost–precision frontier.

Conclusion: TCAB enables exact comparison of many adaptive policies at near the cost of a single policy, asymptotically requiring only T + o(T) reward queries as policies converge to the oracle action, with finite-sample variance guarantees, and delivers strong empirical cost–precision gains.

Abstract: Online platforms increasingly compare many adaptive decision policies---ranking systems, recommendation algorithms, pricing rules, and language-model agents---while each reward-bearing interaction can be costly or risky. A direct A/B/n design gives each of $J$ policies its own horizon-$T$ trajectory and therefore uses $JT$ outcomes. We introduce Tree-Coupled A/B Testing (\TCAB), an exact feedback-sharing design for arbitrary history-dependent contextual-bandit policies. At each round, a predictable tree connects the current policy histories; every parent--child context--action law is maximally coupled, and one reward is shared within each component of matched tree edges. Every policy retains exactly its standalone finite-horizon trajectory law, even though the policies are deliberately dependent. If $D_{e,t}$ records a mismatch on tree edge $e$ at round $t$, the number of reward queries satisfies the pathwise identity $N(T)=T+\sum_{t,e}D_{e,t}$ and hence equals $T$ plus cumulative tree-edge total variation in expectation. This cost is conditionally optimal among exact edge-local designs on the selected tree, and a current-round minimum-spanning tree is myopically optimal among tree designs. For fixed $J$, sublinear pseudo-regret of every policy and almost-sure uniqueness of the oracle action imply $\mathbb{E}[N(T)]=T+o(T)$, versus $JT$ for independent runs. We also obtain finite-sample variance bounds for pairwise policy contrasts. Experiments on reward-model evaluation, multiple-choice language-model evaluation, and adaptive search policies demonstrate substantial improvements in the cost--precision frontier.

</details>


### [259] [A Compositional Theory of Curvature in Probabilistic Circuits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12869)
*Hrithik Suresh,Sahil Sidheekh,Shelar Parth Vijay,Yasir Z,Sriraam Natarajan,Narayanan Chatapuram Krishnan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper shows that global sharpness regularization in Probabilistic Circuits (PCs) is misspecified because curvature is compositional. It proves each sum node's Hessian trace contribution factorizes into a circuit flow term and a local sharpness term, then introduces an adaptive sharpness-aware regularizer targeting nodes by local curvature, recovering generalization while keeping closed-form EM updates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Recent work regularizes the global trace of the Hessian of the log-likelihood to bias PCs toward flatter, better-generalizing optima. However, the authors observe that PCs have inherently compositional curvature, so treating sharpness as a single global regularizer is misspecified and can cause depth bias and underfitting.

Method: The authors prove a factorized decomposition of the Hessian trace: each sum node's contribution equals its circuit flow (how heavily the node is used) times a local sharpness term determined by its output distribution. Using this insight, they design an adaptive sharpness-aware regularizer that penalizes nodes based on intrinsic local curvature rather than a global trace, while preserving closed-form EM updates.

Result: Empirically, the targeted adaptive regularization recovers the generalization that global sharpness regularization sacrifices, while retaining the robustness and other benefits of sharpness-aware learning.

Conclusion: Global sharpness regularization is misspecified for PCs due to their compositional curvature and depth bias. An adaptive, node-level sharpness-aware regularizer grounded in the flow–sharpness decomposition corrects this, improving generalization without losing closed-form EM updates or robustness.

Abstract: Probabilistic Circuits (PCs) are generative models that support exact inference and, unlike deep neural networks, admit an exact and tractable measure of loss-surface curvature: the trace of the Hessian of the log-likelihood. Recent work regularizes this trace globally to bias learning toward flatter, better generalizing optima. We show that treating sharpness as a global regularizer can be misspecified for PCs, whose curvature is inherently compositional. We prove that each sum node's contribution to the Hessian trace factorizes exactly into its circuit flow, which measures how heavily the node is used, and a local sharpness term determined by its output distribution. This decomposition provides insights into why global sharpness regularization is depth biased and can lead to underfitting. Building on it, we introduce an adaptive sharpness aware regularizer that penalizes nodes based on intrinsic local curvature and preserves closed form EM updates. We also show that empirically, this targeted regularization recovers the generalization that global regularization sacrifices while retaining the robustness and benefits of sharpness aware learning.

</details>


### [260] [Sustaining Plasticity via Learnable Wavelet Activations in Continual Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12874)
*Zeyang Zhang,Tieliang Gong,Junyan Lu,Weizhan Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a learnable wavelet activation function that splits activations into low- and high-frequency components to counter spectral bias in continual learning, combined with dynamic wavelet injection and a stability regularizer, achieving state-of-the-art results across benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Plasticity loss severely impairs sequential task learning in continual learning. Existing fixed-form activation functions are biased toward low-frequency variations, while learnable activations allow unconstrained updates that cause catastrophic forgetting. Neither approach adequately addresses the spectral bias that underlies plasticity loss.

Method: The authors introduce a learnable wavelet activation that decomposes the activation into explicit low-frequency and high-frequency components to combat spectral bias. They add a dynamic wavelet injection mechanism that adaptively boosts plasticity for new tasks, plus a regularization strategy preserving stability of previously learned knowledge. A loss-driven injection trigger is formally derived to guide when injection occurs.

Result: The theoretical analysis proves the hybrid wavelet architecture is structurally necessary for efficient L2 approximation and shows the decoupled learning-rate mechanism restores plasticity for high-frequency information. Extensive experiments show superior trainability and generalization throughout learning, with state-of-the-art performance on diverse continual learning benchmarks.

Conclusion: The learnable wavelet activation with dynamic injection and stability regularization effectively mitigates plasticity loss, offering both theoretical guarantees and strong empirical performance, establishing it as a robust solution for continual learning.

Abstract: Plasticity loss has emerged as a critical challenge in continual learning that significantly hinders the acquisition of sequential tasks. While optimizing activation designs offers a potential solution, current fixed-form functions suffer from an inherent spectral bias towards low-frequency variations, whereas learnable variants permit unconstrained updates that induce catastrophic forgetting. To address these limitations, we propose a novel learnable wavelet activation that decomposes the activation function into low-frequency and high-frequency components to explicitly counter spectral bias. Furthermore, we employ dynamic wavelet injection to adaptively enhance plasticity for new tasks, alongside a regularization strategy to ensure the stability of previous learned knowledge. Theoretically, we provide rigorous mathematical guarantees for the proposed framework, proving the structural necessity of the hybrid wavelet architecture for efficient $L^2$ approximation and demonstrating that the decoupled learning rate mechanism successfully restores network plasticity for high-frequency information. Additionally, we provide a formal derivation of the loss-driven injection trigger mechanism to precisely guide the injection. Extensive empirical evaluations demonstrate that our approach maintains superior trainability and generalization throughout the learning process and achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse continual learning benchmarks.

</details>


### [261] [Robust data-driven discovery of fractional differential equations via weak formulations and Pareto-based subset selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12879)
*Pongpisit Thanasutives,Yoshinobu Kawahara*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Weak-Pareto is a method for discovering fractional PDEs from noisy data by combining a weak (adjoint-consistent) formulation that suppresses noise amplification with Pareto-based subset selection over both discrete term types and continuous fractional orders. It outperforms strong-form and neural baselines in support recovery and runtime across several benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Discovering fractional PDEs from data is hard because fractional differentiation amplifies high-frequency measurement noise, and the fractional derivative orders are unknown a priori. Existing pointwise (strong-form) approaches are noise-sensitive, and fixed dense dictionaries of candidate orders complicate model selection.

Method: Weak-Pareto combines (1) an adjoint-consistent weak formulation that moves fractional operators from noisy measured fields onto smooth test functions, turning noise-sensitive pointwise differentiation into smoothing integration (full suppression for linear RHS terms, partial for nonlinear terms); (2) coefficients fitted by ridge regression inside a branch-aware differential-evolution search over continuous fractional orders; and (3) support-size selection at the validation-error-complexity elbow using Pareto-based subset selection over discrete term types and continuous orders.

Result: The variance of fixed linear RHS weak features vanishes under grid refinement, while noise amplification in pointwise fractional features grows with derivative order. On fractional advection-diffusion, reaction-diffusion, and Burgers benchmarks, Weak-Pareto recovers parsimonious structures from clean and noisy data. It retains correct support at every tested multiplicative-noise level (strong-form counterpart largely fails once noise appears), and this advantage persists under additive Gaussian noise. Ablations show the weak library drives noise robustness and continuous-order Pareto search avoids the support-selection failure of a dense fixed dictionary. On advection-diffusion, Weak-Pareto gives more consistent operator recovery and substantially lower runtime than a contemporary neural baseline.

Conclusion: Weak-Pareto's adjoint-consistent weak formulation and continuous-order Pareto subset selection together enable robust, parsimonious discovery of fractional PDEs from noisy measurements, outperforming strong-form and neural approaches in accuracy, noise robustness, and efficiency.

Abstract: Fractional partial differential equations describe nonlocal dynamics, but discovering them from noisy data is difficult because fractional differentiation amplifies high-frequency measurement noise and the derivative orders are unknown. We propose Weak-Pareto, which combines an adjoint-consistent weak formulation of fractional terms with Pareto-based subset selection over discrete term types and continuous fractional orders. For linear right-hand-side terms, the adjoint transfers fractional operators from measured fields to smooth test functions, replacing noise-sensitive pointwise differentiation with smoothing integration; for nonlinear terms, the noise-suppression effect is partial yet useful. Coefficients are fitted by ridge regression within a branch-aware differential-evolution search over the orders. The support size is then selected at the validation-error-complexity elbow. We show that the variance of fixed linear right-hand-side weak features vanishes under grid refinement, whereas noise amplification in pointwise fractional features increases with derivative order. Across fractional advection-diffusion, reaction-diffusion, and Burgers benchmarks, Weak-Pareto recovers parsimonious structures from clean and noisy measurements. In controlled advection-diffusion and Burgers comparisons, it retains the correct support at every tested multiplicative-noise level, whereas the unregularised strong-form counterpart largely fails once noise is introduced; this advantage persists under additive Gaussian noise. Ablations show that the weak library drives noise robustness and that continuous-order Pareto search avoids the support-selection failure of a dense fixed dictionary. On the advection-diffusion benchmark, Weak-Pareto yields more consistent operator recovery and substantially lower measured runtime than a contemporary neural baseline.

</details>


### [262] [Adaptive $k$ Nearest Neighbors Classifier via Granular Ball Computing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12903)
*Xiaoyu Lian,Shuyin Xia,Hongxuan He,Lifeng Shen,Guoyin Wang,Xinbo Gao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes an adaptive KNN method based on granular-ball computing that dynamically determines the effective k value using a granular-ball representation of the training data, improving both accuracy and efficiency over existing KNN variants.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The k value selection in the classic k-Nearest Neighbor algorithm significantly affects performance, yet a fixed k is often suboptimal. The authors aim to adaptively and efficiently determine k to improve robustness and classification performance.

Method: The method has two stages. (1) Training stage: the dataset is coarsely partitioned into granular balls to reduce data-distribution complexity, then the Fisher criterion controls ball splitting and stopping to yield a multi-granularity granular-ball representation. (2) Prediction stage: the nearest granular ball is located via a weighted distance mechanism, an adaptive neighborhood is built around the test sample, and the effective k is set dynamically to the number of samples in that neighborhood, providing stable local group information for noise robustness.

Result: Experiments show the proposed method outperforms existing KNN variants across multiple datasets in both accuracy and efficiency, with open-sourced code for reproducibility.

Conclusion: The adaptive, efficient KNN via granular-ball computing effectively overcomes the fixed-k limitation, dynamically selecting the neighborhood and k value based on the nearest granular ball, leading to improved accuracy, robustness against noise and local perturbations, and better efficiency.

Abstract: The $k$-Nearest Neighbor~(KNN) algorithm is widely used across various tasks. The selection of the $k$ value is a key issue because it significantly impacts performance. In this paper, an adaptive and efficient KNN approach via granular-ball computing is proposed. The method consists of two stages. \textcolor{black}{In the training stage, the dataset is first coarsely partitioned to reduce the complexity of data distributions within a granular ball, and then the Fisher criterion is introduced to control ball splitting and stopping, yielding a multi-granularity granular ball representation. In the prediction stage, the nearest granular ball is first located through a weighted distance mechanism, and an adaptive neighborhood is then constructed around the test sample. The effective $k$ value is dynamically determined by the actual number of samples contained in this neighborhood. The neighborhood induced by the nearest granular ball provides more stable local group information, thereby improving robustness against noise and local perturbations.} Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing KNN variants across multiple datasets in terms of both accuracy and efficiency. The code has been open-sourced for reproducibility: https://github.com/lianxiaoyu724/Adaptive-GBKNN.

</details>


### [263] [EGRL: Edge generation-guided relation-aware learning for RNA-protein interaction prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12906)
*Danyu Li,Ling Zhou,Rubing Huang,Xian Zhong,Bin Zou,Kui Jiang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EGRL is a novel GNN-based framework for RNA-Protein Interaction prediction that introduces implicit meta-path learning, multi-relation-aware attention, a soft-edge graph generator for cold-start nodes, and a multi-feature fusion predictor. It achieves competitive overall performance and significantly outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods in cold-start settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RPI detection via wet-lab experiments is costly and slow, motivating DL-based computational prediction. Existing GNN-based RPIP methods rely on homogeneous graphs or handcrafted meta-paths, which limits their ability to handle data sparsity and generalize to cold-start scenarios involving unknown molecules.

Method: EGRL combines four key components: (1) implicit meta-path learning to capture relational semantics without handcrafted paths; (2) a multi-relation-aware attention mechanism for adaptive fusion of interaction patterns; (3) a graph generator that predicts potential ("soft") edges to support cold-start nodes; and (4) a multi-feature fusion predictor for final interaction scoring. The framework is jointly trained using a primary task loss and an auxiliary generator loss.

Result: On four benchmark datasets, EGRL achieves competitive overall performance. In cold-start settings, it attains AUROC of 0.867 and AUPR of 0.861 on unknown molecules, representing improvements of 8.6% in AUROC and 5.0% in AUPR over prior state-of-the-art methods.

Conclusion: EGRL effectively addresses data sparsity and cold-start generalization in RPI prediction through implicit relational learning and soft-edge generation, delivering superior performance on unknown molecules. The code will be released soon.

Abstract: RNA-Protein Interactions (RPIs) are critical for regulating cellular functions. While traditional wet-lab experiments for RPI detection are costly and time-consuming, Deep Learning (DL) methods provide an efficient computational alternative for RPI Prediction (RPIP). In particular, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are promising, as they naturally model RPI networks. However, existing GNN-based methods often rely on homogeneous graphs or predefined meta-paths, which limit their ability to handle data sparsity and to generalize to cold-start scenarios involving unknown molecules. To address these limitations, we propose Edge Generation-guided Relation-aware Learning (EGRL), a novel framework with several key components: implicit meta-path learning to capture relational semantics without handcrafted paths; a multi-relation-aware attention mechanism for adaptive fusion of interaction patterns; a graph generator that predicts potential ("soft") edges to support cold-start nodes; and a multi-feature fusion predictor for final interaction scoring. EGRL is jointly trained with a primary task loss and an auxiliary generator loss. Comprehensive evaluations on four benchmark datasets demonstrate that EGRL achieves competitive overall performance. More importantly, it exhibits superior generalization in cold-start settings, achieving an Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.867 and an Area Under the Precision-Recall curve (AUPR) of 0.861 on unknown molecules, corresponding to improvements of 8.6% in AUROC and 5.0% in AUPR over prior state-of-the-art methods. The code will be released soon.

</details>


### [264] [Revisiting Overestimation Bias Problem of Q-learning: Settling Large Discrete Action Space via Action Intersection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12912)
*Pu Li,Tao Tan,Hong Xie,Xiaoyu Shi,Mingsheng Shang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses the overestimation bias of Q-learning in large action spaces by introducing an "action intersection" strategy that semi-decouples Q-value and action estimation, enabling tunable bias (from under- to overestimation) via a data-sharing fraction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large action spaces increase randomness in Q-value estimation, causing existing overestimation-correction paradigms to hit bottlenecks: the coupling paradigm (same Q-function for action selection and value estimation) suffers persistent positive bias, while the decoupling paradigm (two independent Q-functions) suffers persistent negative bias.

Method: Proposes an action intersection strategy that enables semi-decoupling: (1) two Q-functions share a tunable fraction of trajectory data; (2) when a sample is shared, updates follow the coupling paradigm, otherwise the decoupling paradigm. Key properties are a large bias range (varying the sharing fraction shifts bias from underestimation to overestimation) and fine granularity (intersection size can be finely tuned).

Result: Deep RL experiments show the method drastically outperforms several SOTA baselines; tabular experiments explain why the method achieves superior performance.

Conclusion: Action intersection is a simple yet powerful strategy to relieve the overestimation biases of both coupling and decoupling paradigms in large action spaces, offering fine-grained bias control and state-of-the-art empirical performance.

Abstract: This paper considers the overestimation bias problem of Q-learning in the setting of a large action space, for the purpose of relieving the bottleneck of existing methods. We find that the large action space increases the randomness in Q-value estimation. The randomness makes two paradigms that drive the major literature on the overestimation problem have their own bottlenecks: the coupling paradigm, i.e., the optimal action and its Q-value are estimated with the same Q-function, always has a positive bias. This is because randomness leads to some actions having abnormally high estimated values than their true values, and the coupling methods prefer these actions. The decoupling paradigm, i.e., the optimal action and its Q-value are estimated with two independent Q-functions, always has a negative bias. This is because randomness increases the estimation gap between the two independent Q-tables for the same action. This paper shows that action intersection can be a simple yet powerful strategy to relieve these bottlenecks. The action intersection strategy enables semi-decoupling via two designs: (1) it allows two Q-functions to share a certain fraction of trajectory data; (2) if a data sample is shared, each Q-function is updated using the coupling paradigm; otherwise, using the decoupling paradigm. Two properties make the action intersection strategy powerful: (1) attaining a large bias range, i.e., varying the data sharing fraction, the estimation bias varies from underestimating to overestimating; (2) fine granularity: the action intersection size can be made arbitrarily finer to enable finer control. We consider two experiment settings, i.e., tabular and deep RL, deep RL experiments show that our method outperforms several SOTA baselines drastically; tabular experiments reveal why our method can achieve superior performance.

</details>


### [265] [Towards Socially Compliant Navigation in Deep Reinforcement Learning via Proxemics-Based Reward Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12917)
*Takieddine Soualhi,Jacques Saraydaryan,Laetitia Matignon*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a proxemics-based reward function for deep reinforcement learning (DRL) social robot navigation, modeling personal space as radial Gaussian-mixture fields from Hall's theory to deliver a dense, interpretable social signal that improves social compliance without sacrificing navigation efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing DRL crowd navigation methods emphasize task-centric objectives (e.g., reaching goals efficiently) and underrepresent social compliance, leading to behaviors that may not respect human social norms in crowded environments.

Method: The authors model each human's personal space as a radial Gaussian-mixture field derived from Hall's proxemics theory and compute a robot-centric local cost over the robot's field of view. This reward is integrated into established DRL navigation methods and evaluated in simulation across multiple crowd scenarios, reward baselines, and crowd densities.

Result: The proposed reward consistently improves social metrics in simulation while maintaining competitive navigation performance relative to the compared reward models.

Conclusion: A dense, interpretable proxemics-based social reward can enhance social compliance in DRL social navigation without degrading navigation efficiency, offering a practical improvement for robot navigation in crowded environments.

Abstract: Developing effective robot navigation methods in crowded environments is essential for real-world applications. Although recent deep reinforcement learning (DRL) methods have improved navigation performance in crowded environments, they often focus primarily on task-centric objectives and underrepresent social compliance objectives. In this paper, we introduce a novel proxemics-based reward formulation for DRL social navigation that provides a dense, interpretable social learning signal while maintaining navigation efficiency. Our approach models each human's personal space as a radial Gaussian-mixture field derived from Hall's proxemics theory and computes a robot-centric local cost over the robot's field of view. We integrate the proposed reward into established DRL navigation methods and evaluate it in simulation across multiple crowd scenarios, reward baselines, and crowd densities using both navigation metrics and social metrics. Results show that the proposed reward consistently improves social metrics in simulation while maintaining competitive navigation performance relative to the compared reward models.

</details>


### [266] [Momentum as Residual-Driven Multiplier Correction for Deep Learning Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12925)
*Zhixin Ren,Yau Lyu,Congrong Li,Liping Zhang,Shengbo Eben Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes an ADMM-inspired momentum (AIM) framework that explains momentum as a multiplier-like correction from a residual-penalty splitting, unifies residual penalty (update geometry) and objective subproblem approximation (acceleration form), and uses it to design RADAR, a stochastic optimizer achieving consistent gains across vision, language, and RL tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Momentum-based optimizers are ubiquitous in deep learning, but the relationships among momentum recursion, update geometry, and acceleration remain only partially understood, limiting principled optimizer design.

Method: The authors develop AIM, an ADMM-inspired momentum framework based on residual-penalty variable splitting that interprets momentum as a multiplier-like correction driven by the splitting residual. AIM recovers the exponential moving average of gradients from an ADMM-style multiplier update and decouples two mechanisms: the residual penalty governing update geometry, and the approximation of the objective-related subproblem governing acceleration form. Building on AIM, they propose RADAR combining relativistic adaptive geometry, decoupled residual correction, and second-order momentum filtering, with convergence established via variance-perturbed Lyapunov drift analysis.

Result: Experiments on supervised vision learning, language modeling, and reinforcement learning demonstrate that RADAR achieves consistent improvements over strong adaptive optimizer baselines.

Conclusion: The AIM framework clarifies the link between momentum recursion, update geometry, and acceleration, and the derived RADAR optimizer provides a unified, principled, and empirically effective alternative to existing adaptive momentum optimizers.

Abstract: Momentum-based optimizers are widely used in modern deep learning, yet the relations among momentum recursion, update geometry, and acceleration remain only partially understood. We develop an $\textbf{A}$DMM-$\textbf{I}$nspired $\textbf{M}$omentum (AIM) framework based on residual-penalty variable splitting, which interprets momentum as a multiplier-like correction driven by the splitting residual. AIM recovers the exponential moving average of gradients from an ADMM-style multiplier update and separates two mechanisms that are usually intertwined in practical optimizers: the residual penalty determines the update geometry, whereas the approximation of the objective-related subproblem determines the acceleration form. Building on AIM, we propose $\textbf{R}$elativistic $\textbf{A}$daptive gradient $\textbf{D}$escent with $\textbf{A}$ccelerated $\textbf{R}$esidual (RADAR), which combines relativistic adaptive geometry, decoupled residual correction, and second-order momentum filtering to improve the update direction and momentum estimation. We establish stochastic convergence through a variance-perturbed Lyapunov drift analysis. Experiments on supervised vision learning, language modeling, and reinforcement learning show that RADAR achieves consistent improvements over strong adaptive optimizer baselines.

</details>


### [267] [H-VAEP and H-xT: Valuing Offensive On-the-Ball Actions in Handball by Estimating Probabilities](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12926)
*Julius Broermann,Oliver Müller,Michael Döring,Jochen Baumeister*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper adapts two soccer action-valuation frameworks (xT and VAEP) to handball, creating Handball-xT (H-xT) and Handball-VAEP (H-VAEP), evaluates them on five seasons of Bundesliga tracking-derived event data, and releases the code for club deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional handball player evaluation relies on box-score metrics or heuristic indices that fail to credit multi-player build-up play. Since soccer analytics has successfully used xT and VAEP but these frameworks have not been adapted to handball, the authors aim to fill this gap.

Method: Using five seasons of tracking-derived event data from the Handball Bundesliga, the authors develop H-xT with a handball-native court zoning layout (shown via simulation to be more robust than standard rectangular grids) and H-VAEP by tailoring its feature space and selecting context length to limit team-identity leakage. The models are then evaluated for stability, discriminativeness, and intuitiveness of ratings.

Result: The handball-native zoning makes H-xT systematically more robust than rectangular grids, and H-VAEP produces exceptionally stable, discriminative, and intuitive player ratings that effectively highlight build-up play.

Conclusion: The authors successfully adapt xT and VAEP to handball, demonstrating improved zoning robustness and high-quality ratings, and release their complete code repository to help professional clubs deploy the models.

Abstract: Traditional player evaluation in professional handball relies on basic box-score metrics or heuristic indices, which fail to credit the multi-player build-up chain. While football (soccer) analytics has adopted Expected Threat (xT) and Valuing Actions by Estimating Probabilities (VAEP), these event-based action valuation frameworks have not yet been adapted to handball. In this paper, we present the first comprehensive adaptation and evaluation of xT and VAEP for handball, utilizing five seasons of tracking-derived event data from the Handball Bundesliga. We develop Handball-xT (H-xT) using a handball-native court zoning layout, demonstrating via simulations that it is systematically more robust than standard rectangular grids. We optimize Handball-VAEP (H-VAEP) by tailoring its feature space and selecting the context length to limit team-identity leakage. Our evaluation shows that H-VAEP yields exceptionally stable, discriminative, and intuitive player ratings that highlight build-up play. Finally, we release our complete code repository to help professional clubs deploy these models.

</details>


### [268] [Multi-perspective Imbalance-Conscious 6G Beamforming Optimization and Performance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12929)
*Chukwunonso Henry Nwokoye,Blessing Oluchi Iloka,Chikwue V. Umeugoji,Christopher Anene Egemba,Nnenna D. Duroha*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A systematic ML study of 6G-IoT beamforming optimization (6GBO), comparing supervised and unsupervised methods. Network features outperform device, environmental, and vision features for prediction, while clustering is driven mainly by deployment environment and device type; bandwidth, IoT sensors, and mobility show the highest feature importance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To systematically investigate how machine learning can optimize 6G-IoT beamforming, and to determine which feature groups (network, environmental, device, vision) carry the strongest predictive power while also exploring unsupervised approaches that can enhance 6GBO.

Method: Supervised and unsupervised ML approaches. Supervised: compared predictive power of network, environmental, device, and vision feature groups using imbalance-aware experiments evaluated by recall, F1-score, and ROC-AUC. Unsupervised: clustering of network scenarios via K-means, DBSCAN, and hierarchical clustering, assessed using Elbow, Silhouette score, and Davies-Bouldin Index. Explainability analysis was also performed for feature importance.

Result: Network features exhibit better prediction power than device, environmental, and vision features (per recall, F1-score, ROC-AUC). Clustering is primarily influenced by deployment environment and device type rather than mobility-based attributes. Bandwidth, IoT sensors, and mobility show the highest global feature importance across feature groups.

Conclusion: Network features are the most predictive for 6GBO, and unsupervised clustering reflects environment/device characteristics. Future work will apply deep learning and reinforcement learning to predict throughput/latency and optimize rewards based on performance indicators such as SNR enhancement.

Abstract: The study presents a systematic machine learning (ML) study of 6G-IoT beamforming optimization (6GBO) using supervised and unsupervised approaches. We compared the predictive power of network, environmental, device, and vision feature groups for 6GBO. Additionally, it addressed other unsupervised perspectives that can enhance 6GBO, including clustering network scenarios using methods such as K-means, DBSCAN, and hierarchical clustering. Several imbalance-aware experiments revealed that network features possess better prediction power than device, environmental, and vision feature groups, as evidenced by their recall, F1-score and ROC-AUC values. For unsupervised ML exploration (assessed using Elbow, Silhouette score, and Davies-Bouldin Index methods), the results indicate that the deployment environment and type of device primarily influence clustering, rather than mobility-based attributes. Furthermore, the explainability analysis showed that bandwidth, IoT sensors, and mobility possess higher global feature importance across the feature groups. In the future, we would apply deep and reinforcement learning techniques to predict throughput/latency or to optimize rewards determined by performance indicators like SNR enhancement

</details>


### [269] [Diagnosing JEPA World Models with Action-Conditioned Predictive Consistency](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12939)
*Guo An,Zijing Wu,Honghua Dong,Yuhao Yan,Zixuan Gui,Haochong Chen,Shanzhao Ruan,Xiang Wang,Yurong Ling,Qi Tian*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces Action-Conditioned Predictive Consistency (ACPC), a bisimulation-based diagnostic that measures how much a clean history and a visually perturbed version of it diverge after being rolled forward under identical action sequences. It proves this divergence upper-bounds perturbation-induced changes in multi-step prediction error and planner cost, and operationalizes it via two complementary measures: Invariance Radius (IR) and Separation Rate (SR).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) predict in a compact latent space, which reduces pressure to model nuisance appearance but does not guarantee robustness to visual perturbations, since perturbed inputs can still alter encoded representations and subsequent action-conditioned predictions. Bisimulation formalizes the desired property: two observations should map to the same state only when their action-conditioned consequences agree. There is a lack of a principled diagnostic to measure whether world models satisfy this robustness property.

Method: The authors formalize Action-Conditioned Predictive Consistency (ACPC) as a diagnostic measuring divergence between a clean history and a visually perturbed view after rolling both forward under the same action sequence. They prove this divergence bounds the perturbation-induced change in multi-step prediction error and planner cost. They then define two aggregate measures built on pairwise ACPC: Invariance Radius (IR), summarizing clean-perturbed rollout spread, and Separation Rate (SR), checking whether different states remain distinguishable after rollout.

Result: Experiments on four visual control tasks show that pairwise ACPC predicts perturbation-induced prediction and cost changes. On the LeWM model, the IR-SR screen transfers across tasks, and the joint diagnostic remains informative under blur and resize perturbations. PLDM exhibits similar diagnostic trends under a different architecture.

Conclusion: ACPC provides a principled, bisimulation-grounded diagnostic for assessing visual perturbation robustness in joint-embedding world models, with the IR-SR measures offering complementary and transferable insights across tasks, architectures, and perturbation types (e.g., blur, resize).

Abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn world models that predict in a compact latent space rather than in pixels, reducing the pressure to model nuisance appearance. Yet this provides no guarantee against visual perturbations: they can still alter the encoded representation and affect subsequent action-conditioned predictions. Bisimulation captures this requirement precisely: two observations should be treated as the same state only when their action-conditioned consequences agree. Guided by this criterion, we introduce Action-Conditioned Predictive Consistency (ACPC), a diagnostic that measures how far a clean history and a visually perturbed view of it diverge after being rolled forward under the same action sequence. We prove that this divergence bounds the perturbation-induced change in multi-step prediction error and planner cost. Building on pairwise ACPC, we define two complementary measures: the Invariance Radius (IR) summarizes clean-perturbed rollout spread, while the Separation Rate (SR) checks whether different states remain distinguishable after rollout. Experiments on four visual control tasks show that pairwise ACPC predicts perturbation-induced prediction and cost changes. On LeWM, the IR-SR screen transfers across tasks, and the joint diagnostic remains informative under blur and resize. PLDM exhibits similar diagnostic trends under a different architecture.

</details>


### [270] [CardioState-JEPA: Delay-Aware Cross-Modal Learning of a Shared Cardiac Representation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12944)
*Hamza Shafiq,Hung Manh Pham,Bin Zhu,Pan Zhou,Jun Hu,Aaqib Saeed*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CardioState-JEPA is a cardiac foundation model that learns a single shared latent representation jointly from ECG, PPG, and PCG signals using a physiology-aware joint-embedding predictive architecture, and it achieves strong gains across unimodal downstream tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: ECG, PPG, and PCG capture complementary (electrical, mechanical, hemodynamic) views of the same cardiac cycle, but existing cardiac foundation models are single-modality and fail to exploit the shared underlying physiology. The work also addresses the scarcity of synchronized multi-sensor recordings and the temporal offsets between modalities.

Method: Maps heterogeneous waveforms into a common token space, encodes them with a single shared Transformer, and pretrains by predicting masked latent cardiac states (JEPA-style). A learned delay aligner handles cross-modal temporal offsets by matching signals at corresponding cardiac time. Training proceeds in two stages: first learning within-modality structure from abundant unimodal data, then using paired data to align modalities in latent cardiac time.

Result: As a frozen encoder across 25 downstream tasks, it improves average PPG classification by 8.2 AUROC points, PCG murmur detection by 18.8 AUROC points, and ECG classification by 15.5 AUROC points over the best self-supervised signal baseline, and matches or exceeds cardiac models trained with privileged clinical text or supervised labels on several ECG benchmarks.

Conclusion: Heterogeneous cardiac signals can mutually supervise a single foundation model of cardiac physiology, establishing a shared cross-modality representation that transfers to diverse downstream cardiac tasks.

Abstract: Electrocardiography (ECG), photoplethysmography (PPG), and phonocardiography (PCG) provide complementary views of the same cardiac cycle, yet existing cardiac foundation models are trained for a single sensing modality, leaving the shared physiology across sensors unexploited. We introduce CardioState-JEPA, a cardiac foundation model to learn a single shared representation jointly across ECG, PPG, and PCG, built on a physiology-aware joint-embedding predictive architecture. The model maps heterogeneous waveforms into a common token space, processes them with a single shared Transformer encoder, and learns by predicting masked latent cardiac states, placing the pretraining target on shared physiology rather than sensor-specific waveform appearance. To handle the temporal offsets between electrical, mechanical, and hemodynamic events, cross-modal prediction uses a learned delay aligner that matches signals at the corresponding cardiac time. Because synchronized multi-sensor recordings are scarce, CardioState-JEPA first learns within-modality structure from abundant unimodal data and then uses paired data to align modalities in latent cardiac time. Evaluated as a frozen encoder across 25 downstream tasks spanning ECG, PPG, and PCG, our encoder improves average PPG classification by 8.2 AUROC points, PCG murmur detection by 18.8 AUROC points, and ECG classification by 15.5 AUROC points over the best self-supervised signal baseline and matches or exceeds cardiac models trained with privileged clinical text or supervised labels on several ECG benchmarks. These results establish that heterogeneous cardiac signals can mutually supervise a single foundation model of cardiac physiology.

</details>


### [271] [I-SDPO: Instance-Level Adaptive Self-Distillation Policy Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12957)
*Yubo Zhang,Xinhong Ma,Zezhong Tan,Ziqiang Dong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: I-SDPO adaptively routes between GRPO and privileged self-distillation per instance: all-incorrect rollout groups use dense teacher supervision, while any-success groups stay under GRPO, avoiding persistent imitation and achieving large accuracy gains on SciKnowEval.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: GRPO learns only from within-group reward differences, yielding no useful signal when all sampled responses are incorrect. Privileged self-distillation supplies dense token-level supervision but, if applied throughout training, becomes a biased low-variance surrogate that opposes reward-improving updates once the policy can already produce successful trajectories. The authors seek a mechanism that uses imitation only where relative rewards are uninformative, while withdrawing teacher influence as the policy improves.

Method: I-SDPO (Instance-Level Adaptive Self-Distillation Policy Optimization) makes a single routing decision per input instance, shared across that instance's rollout group. Instances whose groups are all incorrect are trained with a privileged self-distillation objective; instances with any successful rollout remain under GRPO. A local analysis characterizes when teacher and reward directions align, showing a non-vanishing biased distillation weight induces an optimization bias floor, and the routing rule automatically lowers the expected distillation rate as success probability rises (no hand-designed schedule).

Result: On SciKnowEval, I-SDPO achieves the best result in all four scientific domains and raises average mean@16 accuracy from 56.67% (GRPO) to 70.31%, with a maximum per-domain gain of 18.24 points.

Conclusion: Adaptive, capability-dependent teacher reliance via instance-level routing overcomes both GRPO's lack of signal on all-incorrect groups and the bias/variance failure mode of persistent self-distillation, yielding substantial and consistent accuracy improvements.

Abstract: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) learns from reward differences within a rollout group, but receives no useful relative signal when every sampled response is incorrect. Privileged self-distillation can fill this gap with dense token supervision, yet applying it throughout training creates a different failure mode: the teacher is a biased, low-variance surrogate for the reward objective, so persistent imitation can oppose reward-improving updates after the policy becomes capable of producing successful trajectories. We introduce I-SDPO (Instance-Level Adaptive Self-Distillation Policy Optimization), which treats teacher reliance as capability-dependent. I-SDPO makes one routing decision per input instance and shares it across that instance's rollout group: all-incorrect groups use a privileged self-distillation objective, whereas any-success groups remain intact for GRPO. This design uses imitation only where group-relative rewards are uninformative. A local analysis characterizes when teacher and reward directions align and shows that a non-vanishing biased distillation weight induces an optimization bias floor. The routing rule automatically reduces the expected distillation rate as success probability rises, withdrawing teacher influence without a hand-designed schedule. On SciKnowEval, I-SDPO obtains the best result in all four scientific domains and improves average mean@16 accuracy from 56.67% with GRPO to 70.31%, with a maximum domain gain of 18.24 points.

</details>


### [272] [The Objective Is the Bottleneck: Latent World Models Encode What Their Planners Cannot Use](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12959)
*Joyjeet Singh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper shows that failures in long-horizon planning with latent world models are caused by the planner's cost objective (squared latent distance), not prediction degradation. Simply replacing the objective, with no retraining or GPU, nearly eliminates the horizon dependence of planning success.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Latent world models are typically judged by prediction quality, so long-horizon planning failures are usually attributed to predictor degradation. The authors challenge this assumption on a reproduction of LeWorldModel on TwoRoom.

Method: Reproduce LeWorldModel on TwoRoom and diagnose the source of long-horizon planning failure. Measure prediction error at long horizons, the correlation of squared latent distance with true distance, and position recoverability from frozen embeddings via a ridge probe. Test across the authors' released weights and four checkpoints.
