Then replace only the planning objective (e.g., with a head learned from frame separation alone) and re-evaluate goal-reaching success.

Result: The predictor is not the limit: imagined state 75 steps ahead is only 0.189 as wrong as a frozen-world baseline, while the planner never imagines beyond 25 steps. Squared latent distance tracks true distance at r=0.426, saturates by ~80 arena units, and decreases beyond 120, so moving away from the goal can lower cost. A ridge probe recovers position from the frozen embedding at R^2=0.9922. The pathology appears in the authors' released weights and across all four checkpoints, where long-horizon success rank-orders with metric quality and inversely with prediction accuracy. Replacing only the objective lifts goals reached at offset 100 from 26.0% to 98.0% (matching 98.0% at offset 25), reaching 92.0% under a third of the budget. The learned head predicts spatial distance worse than a position probe (r=0.819 vs 0.9897) yet plans better, charging 24% more to cross the dividing wall than squared latent distance (which charges 4% less), indicating it learns reachability rather than proximity.

Conclusion: The binding constraint in long-horizon planning is the planner's objective, not the predictor. The best cost is not the most accurate metric; a cost that encodes reachability rather than proximity substantially improves long-horizon planning with no retraining and no additional compute.

Abstract: Latent world models are judged by how well they predict, so when planning fails at long horizons the natural reading is that the predictor degrades. On a reproduction of LeWorldModel on TwoRoom we show the binding constraint is the planner's objective instead.
  The predictor is not the limit: its imagined state seventy-five environment steps ahead is still only 0.189 as wrong as assuming the world froze, while the planner never imagines beyond twenty-five. The objective is. Cross-entropy-method planning minimises squared latent distance, which tracks true distance at r = 0.426, saturates by about eighty arena units and decreases beyond a hundred and twenty, so moving away from the goal can lower the cost. The information is present throughout: a ridge probe recovers position from the frozen embedding at R^2 0.9922.
  The pathology is the method's, not one reimplementation's. It is present in the authors' released weights, and across four checkpoints long-horizon success rank-orders exactly with metric quality and inversely with prediction accuracy.
  Replacing only the objective, with nothing retrained and no GPU, lifts goals reached at offset 100 from 26.0% to 98.0%, equals the 98.0% at offset 25, and reaches 92.0% under a third of the budget: planning stops depending on the horizon. The best cost is not the most accurate. A head learned from frame separation alone predicts spatial distance worse than a position probe (r = 0.819 against 0.9897) yet plans better, charging 24% more to cross the environment's dividing wall where squared latent distance charges 4% less. It has learned reachability, not proximity.

</details>


### [273] [Comment on "Modeling rapid language learning by distilling Bayesian priors into artificial neural networks"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12974)
*Orr Well,Idan Tarshish,Nur Lan,Roni Katzir*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper critiques McCoy & Griffiths (2025)'s claim that MAML distills a Bayesian prior into ANNs. It argues MAML only initializes weights favorably without changing the objective, and that no interpretation successfully establishes that the model implements a Bayesian learner; empirically, M&G's model overfits and generalizes poorly compared to genuine Bayesian learners.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: McCoy & Griffiths (2025) claim that Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning can distill a Bayesian prior into artificial neural networks, supported by empirical results showing meta-trained networks match a Bayesian learner's formal-language learning abilities. This paper scrutinizes whether that claim is sound under standard or permissive interpretations of what constitutes a prior, and whether MAML actually reproduces Bayesian behavior.

Method: The authors provide a conceptual analysis of M&G's procedure versus the standard definition of a (Bayesian) prior. They show the meta-learning algorithm only favors weight initializations and leaves the learning objective unchanged, so no prior is instilled in the objective. They then evaluate a more permissive interpretation—treating the whole system as a Bayesian learner—and identify the challenges it faces. Finally, they empirically assess how well MAML approximates Bayesian learning results, examining generalization to unseen data.

Result: Under the standard interpretation of a prior, M&G's procedure does not instill one—it merely initializes network weights favorably while leaving the objective function unchanged. The permissive interpretation, which treats the system as whole as implementing a Bayesian learner without an explicit prior, faces nontrivial challenges. Empirically, unlike genuine Bayesian learners, M&G's MAML-trained model overfits and generalizes poorly to unseen data.

Conclusion: M&G's claim that MAML distills a Bayesian prior into ANNs is unsupported: the procedure does not change the objective under the standard prior interpretation, the permissive interpretation is problematic, and the resulting model does not exhibit the robust generalization characteristic of genuine Bayesian learners.

Abstract: McCoy & Griffiths (2025, henceforth M&G) suggest that a Bayesian prior can be distilled into Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) through Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML, Finn et al., 2017). They support this empirically by showing that meta-trained networks demonstrate formal language learning abilities comparable to Yang & Piantadosi (2023)'s Bayesian learner, significantly outperforming standard ANNs. We point out that under the standard interpretation of a prior, M&G's procedure does not actually instill one; it merely initializes network weights favorably, leaving the objective function unchanged. We then consider a more permissive interpretation, where the system as a whole can be seen as implementing a Bayesian learner even without an explicit prior in the objective. We show that this interpretation faces nontrivial challenges. Finally, we assess how well MAML approximates the empirical results of Bayesian learning, showing that unlike genuine Bayesian learners, M&G's model overfits and generalizes poorly to unseen data.

</details>


### [274] [Learning the Mathematical Property for Designing Low Mutual Coherence Binary Sensing Matrices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12982)
*Rekha,Santosh Singh,S. K. Neogy*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a learning-based method to construct a binary sensing matrix with low mutual coherence for compressive sensing, using a neural network whose loss function is directly built on the mutual coherence mathematical property, without relying on any dataset or specific application.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Perfect recovery of sparse signals in compressive sensing depends on the sensing matrix satisfying properties such as restricted isometry property (RIP), null space property (NSP), and spark property (SP). These are NP-hard and computationally challenging to solve, so practical construction requires a sensing matrix with low mutual coherence. The authors aim to achieve this without using large-scale training datasets or a specific application.

Method: A neural network framework is used to construct a binary sensing matrix with low mutual coherence. The matrix entries are generated through a shared underlying rule. The novelty is that the loss function is defined directly using the mutual coherence mathematical property/constraint, rather than being learned from data, and the architecture is simple with no large-scale training datasets.

Result: The proposed technique constructs a binary sensing matrix with low mutual coherence for perfect signal recovery. It brings a drastic reduction in computational cost compared to solving NP-hard properties, and provides generality, robustness, and reduced storage requirements. This is claimed to be the first use of a mathematical property to define the loss function in this context.

Conclusion: Using a mathematical property (mutual coherence) as the loss function in a neural network framework enables the construction of a low-coherence binary sensing matrix without datasets or application specificity, achieving generality, robustness, and reduced computational and storage requirements for compressive sensing.

Abstract: In this research work, we are constructing the sensing matrix, which is essential for the success of the compressive sensing technique. We have chosen a learning-based technique for the construction of the sensing matrix. The novelty and uniqueness of the proposed technique is that it does not use any data set and also does not use a specific application. It uses the mathematical property/constraint for the construction of the sensing matrix for the perfect recovery of the signal. The perfect recovery of signals is an old and still very challenging problem in real-world applications. In late 2000, compressive sensing became a popular mathematical tool for the perfect recovery of sparse signals. The core of the compressive technique is the construction of the sensing matrix, which satisfies certain special properties such as restricted isometry property (RIP), null space property (NSP), and spark property (SP). All these properties are NP-hard problems and hence computationally challenging to solve. For all practical purposes, the construction of the sensing matrix needs to achieve low mutual coherence to achieve the perfect recovery of the signals. We have used a neural network for the construction of the sensing matrix, and this framework constructs a binary sensing matrix with low mutual coherence. The entries in the matrix are generated through a shared underlying rule. The proposed architecture is simple and does not use large-scale training data sets. Such uniqueness and novelty bring a drastic reduction in computational cost, and also, for the first time in literature, the use of a mathematical property for defining the loss function. In this proposed research work, the mutual coherence property has been used in the neural network framework. Such a neural network framework brings generality, robustness, and reduces storage requirements.

</details>


### [275] [Balanced Adaptive Prototype Selection for Scalable TabPFN Inference on Large-Scale Tabular Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12989)
*Mahboobe Jadid,Melika Rezaye Garkani,Ali Mousavi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BAPS is a prototype-selection framework that builds compact, information-preserving contexts to let pretrained TabPFN scale to million-row tabular datasets without retraining, achieving ~1,953× context compression (512 prototypes) while keeping strong predictive performance and calibration on HIGGS and SUSY.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pretrained tabular foundation models such as TabPFN perform well but are limited by small inference contexts, preventing their use on large-scale (million-row) datasets. The authors seek a practical, training-free way to bridge this scalability gap.

Method: BAPS selects a compact set of prototypes that jointly preserve five criteria: representative structure, informative decision boundaries, local density, class balance, and feature-space diversity. This is done without modifying or retraining the pretrained model, and the selected prototypes form the input context for TabPFN inference.

Result: On the million-row HIGGS and SUSY datasets, using only 512 prototypes retained strong predictive performance and reliable calibration, equivalent to roughly a 1,953-fold reduction in context size. All experiments ran CPU-only (Intel Core i7, 16 GB RAM, no GPU).

Conclusion: Effective context construction is a practical mechanism for extending pretrained tabular foundation models to million-scale datasets, enabling scalable inference without model modification or retraining.

Abstract: Pretrained tabular foundation models have demonstrated strong predictive capability; however, their application to large-scale datasets remains constrained by the limited inference context. This paper introduces Balanced Adaptive Prototype Selection (BAPS), a framework for constructing compact, information-preserving contexts for scalable TabPFN inference. Without modifying or retraining the pretrained model, BAPS jointly preserves representative structure, informative decision boundaries, local density, class balance, and feature-space diversity. Experiments on the million-row HIGGS and SUSY datasets show that 512 prototypes retain strong predictive performance and reliable calibration, corresponding to an approximately 1,953-fold context compression. All experiments were conducted on an Intel Core i7 CPU with 16 GB RAM and no GPU acceleration. These findings establish effective context construction as a practical mechanism for extending pretrained tabular foundation models to million-scale datasets.

</details>


### [276] [Incremental Evaluation and Training in Relational Deep Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13023)
*Jakub Peleška,Gustav Šír*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes an incremental, multi-episode evaluation and training framework for Relational Deep Learning (RDL) to address the temporal, continuously-evolving nature of real-world databases that static single-episode benchmarks ignore. It shows temporal concept drift is common, and that transfer learning via incremental fine-tuning is both feasible and effective, outperforming expensive from-scratch training under a new near-future accuracy metric.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prevailing RDL evaluation uses static, single-episode dataset snapshots, which overlook the time-evolving nature of real multi-tabular databases and fail to measure how model performance changes as new data accumulates. There is a need to assess and improve temporal robustness and adaptability of RDL models under continuous data growth.

Method: Introduce an incremental, multi-episode evaluation and training paradigm. Use established large-scale datasets to analyze data evolution and model training dynamics, detect temporal concept drift, and apply multiple incremental fine-tuning (transfer learning) regimes. Propose a new temporal evaluation metric prioritizing near-future accuracy, and compare incrementally fine-tuned models against from-scratch trained baselines.

Result: Temporal concept drift occurs in the majority of predictive tasks. Transfer learning is feasible and highly effective in the RDL setting. Incrementally fine-tuned models consistently outperform standard, expensive, from-scratch trained baselines under the near-future accuracy metric.

Conclusion: Incremental, multi-episode training with transfer learning is a practical and superior alternative to retraining RDL models from scratch as databases evolve, offering stronger near-future predictive performance and better temporal adaptability.

Abstract: Relational Deep Learning (RDL) models multi-tabular databases as temporal heterogeneous graphs to enable end-to-end representation learning. However, prevailing RDL evaluation practices rely on static, single-episode dataset snapshots, overlooking the continuous, time-evolving nature of real-world databases. Consequently, current RDL benchmarks fail to capture how model performance changes as new data accumulates over time. To address this limitation, we introduce an incremental, multi-episode evaluation and training paradigm to assess and improve the temporal robustness and adaptability of state-of-the-art RDL models. Using established large-scale datasets, we examine data evolution and model training dynamics, demonstrating that temporal concept drifts occur in the majority of predictive tasks. We present multiple incremental training regimes for fine-tuning the models and demonstrate that transfer learning is both feasible and highly effective in the RDL setting. Alongside a new temporal evaluation metric that prioritizes near-future accuracy, we show that our incrementally fine-tuned models consistently outperform the standard, expensive, from-scratch trained baselines.

</details>


### [277] [On the global feature importance for interpretable and trustworthy heat demand forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13039)
*Milan Zdravković*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper applies ante-hoc Explainable AI to evaluate the global feature importance of ML models used to forecast heat demand in District Heating Systems, aiming to improve model interpretability and trustworthiness to meet communal standards, customer satisfaction, and liability requirements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Facilitate interpretability and trustworthiness of heat demand forecasting ML models used in intelligent District Heating System control, addressing challenges related to communal standards adherence, customer satisfaction, and liability risks.

Method: Employs the ante-hoc Explainable AI methodology through four feature-importance approaches: (1) intrinsic interpretability of Gradient Boosting, and post-hoc methods including (2) Partial Dependence, (3) Accumulated Local Effects, and (4) SHAP. Notably, none of the selected methods rely on feature permutation or perturbation, avoiding bias from introducing random unrealistic data values.

Result: Provides a discussion of the resulting global feature importances with assessment of complementarities among methods where applicable, including specific interpretations in the context of district heating processes.

Conclusion: The proposed permutation-/perturbation-free explainability methodology supports interpretable and trustworthy heat demand forecasting models in District Heating Systems, suggesting its suitability for meeting communal standards, customer satisfaction, and liability constraints.

Abstract: The paper introduces the ante-hoc Explainable AI methodology to assess the global feature importance of the Machine Learning models used for heat demand forecasting in intelligent control of District Heating Systems, with motivation to facilitate their interpretability and trustworthiness, hence addressing the challenges related to adherence to communal standards, customer satisfaction and liability risks. Methodology includes use of four different approaches, namely intrinsic interpretability of Gradient Boosting method and selected post-hoc methods, namely Partial Dependence, Accumulated Local Effects and SHAP. None of the selected methods assume feature permutation or perturbations which can introduce bias due to introduction of random unrealistic values of data instances. Discussion of results is provided, including the assessment of complementarities where applicable, with specific interpretations in context of the district heating processes.

</details>


### [278] [Latent On-Policy Self-Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13040)
*Guibin Zhang,Jiayang Lyu,Ran Sun,Xinlei Yu,Haoyu Zhao,Qibing Ren,Shuicheng Yan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LOPD makes the privileged context of an on-policy self-distillation teacher learnable end-to-end from experience, using retrieved experiences composed into latent tokens plus a privileged-margin objective, outperforming RLVR and OPSD baselines on agentic tool use and code generation with substantially fewer rollouts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enabling agents to internalize experience into their policy is central to self-evolving AI. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) helps by using a privileged self-teacher for dense supervision, but existing methods rely on designer-specified privileged artifacts (answers, feedback, skills, trajectories), limiting end-to-end learnability and scalability for continual self-improvement.

Method: Introduce Latent On-Policy Self-Distillation (LOPD), which makes the teacher's privileged context learnable end-to-end from experience instead of hand-crafting it. LOPD retrieves relevant experiences and composes them into continuous latent tokens that condition a self-teacher; the student generates trajectories from task/interaction history and receives dense token-level supervision at every visited prefix. A privileged-margin objective is added to stabilize and regulate the learning of the latent context.

Result: LOPD shows strong performance, outperforming RLVR and representative OPSD methods (OPSD, SDPO, Skill-SD) on both agentic tool use and code generation; and high learning efficiency, surpassing GRPO and Skill-SD with less than 30% of their rollout budget. Ablations show making privileged context learnable is necessary for these gains.

Conclusion: LOPD represents a step toward a more scalable and self-directed paradigm for agent evolution, replacing hand-crafted privileged contexts with end-to-end learnable latent context regulated by a privileged-margin objective.

Abstract: Enabling agents to learn from experience and internalize it into their policy has become a central problem in self-evolving AI. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) offers an effective pathway by using a privileged self-teacher to provide dense supervision on the student's own trajectories; however, existing methods still rely heavily on designer-specified privileged artifacts (e.g., answers, feedback, skills, or trajectories), limiting the end-to-end learnability and scalability required for continual self-improvement. In this work, we introduce Latent On-Policy Self-Distillation (LOPD), which, rather than proposing another hand-crafted OPSD variant with a newly prescribed form of privileged context, makes the teacher's privileged context itself learnable end-to-end from experience. Technically, LOPD retrieves relevant experiences and composes them into continuous latent tokens that condition a self-teacher, while the student generates trajectories from the task and interaction history and receives dense token-level supervision at every visited prefix. We further introduce a privileged-margin objective to stabilize and regulate the learning of latent context. Empirically, LOPD demonstrates (I) strong performance, outperforming RLVR and representative OPSD methods including OPSD, SDPO, and Skill-SD across both agentic tool use and code generation; and (II) high learning efficiency, surpassing GRPO and Skill-SD with less than 30% of their rollout budget. Ablation studies further provide direct evidence that making privileged context learnable is necessary for realizing these gains. Together, these results position LOPD as a step toward a more scalable and self-directed paradigm for agent evolution.

</details>


### [279] [A Multispectral Framework for the Detection of Calcium Carbide-Induced Ripening and Shelf-Life Estimation in Climacteric Fruits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13073)
*Gurbhit Chaurakoti,Harshit Kumar,Hani Kumar,Anurag Singh,Ram Asrey*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A non-invasive multispectral (410–940 nm, AS7265x sensor) framework using PCA + XGBoost distinguishes calcium carbide-ripened mango and banana from safely ripened fruits, with accuracy/recall of 95%/0.67 (mango) and 81%/0.74 (banana), and estimates ripening percentage and shelf life.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Illegal industrial-grade Calcium Carbide (CaC2) ripening of climacteric fruits (mango, banana) leaves toxic arsenic and phosphorus residues, posing health risks; a safe, non-invasive detection method is needed for food safety.

Method: Spectral reflectance captured at 18 wavelengths (410–940 nm) using the AS7265x spectral triad sensor. Feature engineering combines inter-method spectral variance, wavelength intensity ratios, and environmental parameters (temperature, humidity). PCA reduces dimensionality (retaining >90% variance in 5–7 components), and three independent XGBoost models perform ripening-method classification, shelf-life estimation, and ripening-progression estimation.

Result: Mango: 95% classification accuracy with 0.67 carbide-class recall. Banana: 81% accuracy with 0.74 carbide-class recall. CaC2-treated samples show sharper spectral intensity drops in the visible region, consistent with accelerated chlorophyll degradation and carotenoid development.

Conclusion: The proposed instrumentation and data-driven approach effectively distinguishes CaC2-ripened fruits from naturally/ethephon-ripened ones non-invasively, while enabling estimation of ripening progression and remaining shelf life, supporting food-safety screening.

Abstract: Significant health risks are associated with the illegal, yet commonly practiced use of industrial-grade Calcium Carbide (CaC2) for ripening climacteric fruits like mango and banana, which leaves behind trace residues of arsenic and phosphorus. To address this, the proposed study explores a novel, non-invasive multispectral framework for distinguishing safely ripened fruits (naturally ripened and ethephon-induced) from calcium carbide-ripened samples, while also estimating their ripening progression (in percentage) and remaining shelf life (in days). The spectral profiles of mango (Mangifera indica) and banana (Musa acuminata) at 18 discrete wavelengths in the visible-near infrared (NIR) range (410 nm - 940 nm) are studied using the AS7265x spectral triad sensor. CaC2-treated samples exhibit sharper spectral intensity drops in the visible region, consistent with accelerated chlorophyll degradation and carotenoid development. To characterize these physiological changes, the feature engineering strategy integrates inter-method spectral variance, intensity ratios at distinct wavelengths, and environmental parameters including temperature and humidity. Dimensionality reduction using Principal Component Analysis (PCA) retains >90% of spectral variance within the first 5-7 components. The resulting feature set is used to train three independent eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost)-based learning algorithms for ripening method classification, along with quantitative estimation of remaining shelf life and ripening progression. A classification accuracy of 95% along with carbide class recall of 0.67 is observed for mango samples, while the model achieves an accuracy of 81% and carbide class recall of 0.74 for banana. This instrumentation and data-driven approach demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed non-invasive framework.

</details>


### [280] [Learning Discrete Decisions for MIPs with Constraint-Aware Diffusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13079)
*Vincenzo Di Vito,Mehdi Taghizadeh,Deepjyoti Deka,Kaarthik Sundar,Ferdinando Fioretto*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces Constrained Graph Diffusion (CGD), a learning-based framework that combines a graph diffusion generative model with a training-free feasibility projection operator to approximate solutions to mixed-integer optimization (MIO) problems, then solves the remaining continuous subproblem with numerical solvers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mixed-integer optimization problems are computationally challenging because they require jointly determining discrete and continuous decisions under complex combinatorial constraints. The authors aim to accelerate these problems while maintaining feasibility and solution quality.

Method: CGD uses a graph-based generative diffusion model to learn and sample the discrete decisions of an MIO problem. During reverse diffusion, a training-free feasibility projection operator steers intermediate samples toward the feasible set. Once discrete variables are generated, the remaining continuous optimization is solved efficiently with existing numerical solvers. The approach is problem-agnostic, supporting different problems via suitable projection operators.

Result: On optimal transmission switching for ACOPF and discrete portfolio optimization, CGD achieves substantial improvements in feasibility and solution quality over learning-based baselines, and speedups up to 425x over state-of-the-art MINLP numerical solvers.

Conclusion: CGD provides a scalable, problem-agnostic framework for approximately solving mixed-integer optimization problems by decoupling discrete generation from continuous solving, yielding large speedups while improving feasibility and quality over existing learning-based methods.

Abstract: This paper proposes a novel learning-based approach to approximately solve instances of mixed-integer optimization problems. These problems are computationally challenging, as they require jointly determining discrete and continuous decisions while satisfying complex combinatorial constraints. The proposed method relies on a graph-based generative diffusion model that learns the discrete component of mixed-integer optimization problems while integrating a training-free feasibility projection operator directly into the reverse diffusion process to steer intermediate samples toward the feasible set throughout generation. Once the discrete decisions are generated, the remaining optimization reduces to a continuous problem that can be solved efficiently (relative to the original problem) using existing numerical methods. The resulting framework named Constrained Graph Diffusion (CGD), is problem-agnostic and can accommodate a broad class of mixed-integer optimization problems through suitable projection operators. We evaluate CGD on optimal transmission switching for ACOPF and discrete portfolio optimization, demonstrating substantial improvements in feasibility and solution quality over learning-based baselines while achieving speedups of up to $425\times$ over state-of-the-art numerical solvers for MINLPs.

</details>


### [281] [Sampling Luck Masquerades as Allocation Gain: Auditing Test-Time Budget Allocation for Neural Combinatorial Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13087)
*Jinhyung Bae*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper audits and recalibrates a common evaluation convention in neural combinatorial optimization (NCO): reporting the best of many sampled solutions with an identical sample count per instance. It shows an apparent ~2% gain from non-uniform budget allocation is a phantom caused by in-sample evaluation, but that a real, pre-registered gain (~11.5% for AM) emerges under distribution shift.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: NCO solvers conventionally allocate the same number of samples to every instance and report the best-of-k. It is unknown whether redistributing a fixed total budget across instances would improve results, and existing in-sample evaluation practices may produce spurious (phantom) gains that would incorrectly support such allocation methods.

Method: The authors measure the possible benefit of non-uniform sample allocation across three pretrained solvers (POMO, AM, SymNCO) on TSP-100. They compare oracle allocation computed and evaluated on the same stored samples (in-sample) against out-of-sample evaluation, and calibrate the in-sample bias using an instance-wise null where the true gain is zero by construction. Under distribution shift (uniform + clustered instances), they run a pre-registered confirmatory experiment with a held-out-statistics-guided allocation policy, a negative control (POMO), a frozen distribution-label baseline, and an exploratory policy charging a 20-sample probe against the budget.

Result: In-distribution, an oracle in-sample allocation reports 2.2-2.6% gains with CIs excluding zero, but out-of-sample the same gains are indistinguishable from zero (0.457%, 0.015%, -0.512%). The in-sample bias does not shrink with more samples or instances. Under distribution shift, the pre-registered primary endpoint shows a best-of-k improvement of 11.5% (AM, 95% CI [7.4, 19.7]) and 12.0% (SymNCO replication), while the negative control (POMO) shows -0.3% [-0.7, 0.24]. The gain exceeds a frozen distribution-label baseline by 4.2 points [1.9, 7.7]. Charging a 20-sample probe retains 3.4% (AM) and 4.6% (SymNCO).

Conclusion: The customary in-sample procedure produces phantom ~2% allocation gains that do not generalize, an artifact the authors' correction removes. However, under distribution shift the correction preserves a genuine gain, demonstrating that non-uniform budget allocation can be beneficial when instance difficulty varies. The authors provide a correction procedure, a reporting checklist, and release data, code, and the pre-registration record.

Abstract: Neural combinatorial optimization (NCO) solvers report the best of many sampled solutions per instance, and the sample count is, by convention, identical for every instance. Whether a non-uniform allocation of a fixed total budget would buy anything has not been measured. We measure it, and we audit the measurement itself.
  First, on in-distribution workloads the allocation headroom is not detectable. Across three pretrained solvers (POMO, AM, SymNCO) on uniform TSP-100, an oracle allocation computed and evaluated on the same stored samples reports a 2.2-2.6% gain with intervals excluding zero; measured out of sample the same gain is indistinguishable from zero (0.457, 0.015, -0.512 percent). Following the customary in-sample procedure, all three solvers would have supported a published 2%-level gain that does not exist. We calibrate this bias against an instance-wise null in which the true gain is zero by construction; over the ranges we test it does not shrink with more samples or more instances.
  Second, the same correction that removes the phantom gains preserves a real one. Under distribution shift (a workload mixing uniform and clustered instances), a pre-registered confirmatory experiment finds that allocation guided by held-out sample statistics improves best-of-k by 11.5% (AM, primary endpoint; 95% CI [7.4, 19.7]) and 12.0% (SymNCO, replication) at equal evaluation budget, with the signal-acquisition cost not charged; a pre-registered negative control (POMO, an order of magnitude more robust to shift) shows -0.3% [-0.7, 0.24]. The gain exceeds a frozen distribution-label baseline by 4.2 points [1.9, 7.7]. An exploratory policy charging a 20-sample probe against the same budget retains 3.4% (AM) and 4.6% (SymNCO).
  We give a correction procedure and a reporting checklist, and release all data, code, and the pre-registration record.

</details>


### [282] [FlowLOB: Efficient and Controllable Limit Order Book Generation with Flow Matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13096)
*Zhuohan Wang,Andreea Bacalum,Ollie Olby,Carmine Ventre,Namid Stillman*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FlowLOB is a conditional flow-matching generative model of limit order book trajectories that is computationally efficient (only 10 ODE-solver steps), realistic, controllable, and transfers zero-shot to unseen instruments, outperforming diffusion and agent-based baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LOB simulators—both agent-based and deep generative—only partially satisfy the key practitioner requirements: realistic market dynamics, computationally efficient sampling, controllable scenario generation, and generalization to unseen instruments. Prior generative models (e.g., diffusion) require many function evaluations, and agent-based models are hard to calibrate or control.

Method: The authors propose FlowLOB, a conditional flow-matching generator of LOB trajectories trained on multiple HKEX symbols at three sampling frequencies (0.1s, 1s, 10s) using tick-relative representation. Leveraging the common formulation of flow and diffusion models, both are trained with identical data, architecture, and budget, and sampled via the same fixed-step ODE solvers, enabling a controlled comparison. Flow matching reaches best quality at 10 ODE steps, while diffusion requires many more. Controllability is tested distributionally by checking whether changing a condition moves the generated statistic toward the corresponding real tail regime. Ablations cover network architecture and learning rate.

Result: Flow matching attains best quality with only 10 ODE-solver steps vs. diffusion's many more function evaluations. FlowLOB improves realism over four baselines (two learned, two agent-based) in most distributional metrics at the finer sampling frequencies. It satisfies the distributional counterfactual controllability criterion in most settings, and both realism and control effects transfer zero-shot to a held-out symbol.

Conclusion: Conditional flow matching is a more sample-efficient and fidelity-preserving alternative to diffusion for LOB simulation, delivering a practitioner-friendly simulator that is realistic, computationally efficient, controllable, and generalizable to unseen instruments.

Abstract: Limit order book (LOB) simulators are most useful to practitioners when they combine realistic market dynamics, computationally efficient sampling, controllable scenario generation, and the ability to generalize beyond the instruments seen during training---properties that existing agent-based and deep generative simulators provide only partially. We present \textbf{FlowLOB}, a conditional \textbf{flow}-matching generator of \textbf{LOB} trajectories, trained on multiple Hong Kong Exchange (HKEX) symbols at three sampling frequencies ($0.1$s, $1$s, $10$s) in tick-relative representation that transfers to unseen instruments. Because flow and diffusion models admit a common formulation, we train both with identical data, architecture, and budget, and sample both through the same fixed-step ODE solvers, yielding a controlled comparison of sampling efficiency and fidelity. Flow matching attains its best quality with only $10$ ODE-solver steps, whereas diffusion needs many more function evaluations to approach the same fidelity. At this efficient operating point, FlowLOB improves realism over baselines, two learned and two agent-based models, in most distributional metrics at the two finer sampling frequencies. We evaluate counterfactual controllability with a distributional test that asks whether changing a scenario condition moves the generated statistic toward the corresponding real tail regime; FlowLOB satisfies this criterion in most tested settings. Both realism and control effects transfer zero-shot on a held-out symbol. We additionally conduct ablation studies on the network architecture and the learning rate.

</details>


### [283] [Branch and Bound for Relational Verification of Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13118)
*Kota Fukuda,Zhenya Zhang,Guanqin Zhang,Jianjun Zhao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SaBRe introduces a branch-and-bound framework for verifying neural networks against relational specifications (e.g., global robustness), featuring relational neuron splitting and a dual-formulation-based selection strategy, and it outperforms baselines across 817 verification problems on ACAS Xu, MNIST-F/C, CIFAR, and GTSRB.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Verifying relational specifications (e.g., global robustness) for neural networks in safety-critical CPS is essential but technically harder than trace properties like local robustness. Existing sound convex over-approximation methods are inherently incomplete, can raise false alarms, and therefore need effective abstraction refinement.

Method: The authors propose SaBRe, a branch-and-bound (BaB) framework that iteratively splits the verification problem until all sub-problems are verified. Its key innovations are: (1) splitting relational neurons rather than individual neurons, and (2) a relational neuron selection strategy based on the dual formulation of the verification problem to efficiently choose the relational neuron that maximizes refinement from splitting.

Result: SaBRe was evaluated on 817 verification problems across ACAS Xu, MNIST-F, MNIST-C, CIFAR, and GTSRB. It outperforms different baseline approaches in both the number of solved instances and verification efficiency.

Conclusion: The proposed relational-neuron-splitting BaB framework with a dual-based selection strategy effectively refines abstractions for relational neural network verification, as demonstrated by superior performance over baselines.

Abstract: Verification of neural networks against relational specifications, such as global robustness, is crucial for safety-critical applications of cyber-physical systems (CPS), given their increasing adoption of AI components. Compared to simple trace properties (e.g., local robustness), verifying relational specifications requires reasoning about the relationship between multiple network inferences, which brings significant technical challenges. Existing research has explored abstraction techniques based on sound and convex over-approximation of neural network outputs; however, since these approaches are inherently incomplete and may raise false alarms, they further underscore the need of effective abstraction refinement.
  In this paper, we propose a branch-and-bound (BaB) framework to mitigate the issue, which iteratively splits the problem until all sub-problems are verified. Specifically, our BaB framework features splitting of relational neurons rather than individual neurons as prior works do, and as the core of our technique, we devise a relational neuron selection strategy based on the dual formulation of the verification problem, which allows us to efficiently select the (most likely) optimal relational neuron that maximizes the refinement brought by problem splitting. We evaluate SaBRe on 817 verification problems across ACAS Xu, MNIST-F, MNIST-C, CIFAR and GTSRB. The results show that SaBRe outperforms different baseline approaches, in terms of the number of solved instances and verification efficiency, which demonstrates the effectiveness of our proposed techniques.

</details>


### [284] [ProME: Prototype-Margin Environments with Repair-Aware Selection for Group-Robust Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13190)
*Qianqian Wang,Yunshan Li,Dawei Huang,Wenwu Gong,Lili Yang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ProME (Prototype-Margin Environments) jointly aligns environment inference and classifier selection with the deployed predictor by splitting prototype margins at the median to build balanced environments, then ranking candidates via a group-balanced linear head on group-annotated validation data, achieving state-of-the-art worst-group accuracy under the same label access.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Group-robust learning must preserve accuracy on rare subpopulations when training-group labels are unavailable, but existing methods infer environments with a separate reference model and select representations before fitting the deployed classifier, so both decisions are misaligned with the predictor actually used at deployment.

Method: The authors formulate the task as the endogenous environments with repair-aware selection (ERAS) problem. ProME constructs approximately balanced environments by splitting prototype margins at their median along the training trajectory, then fits a group-balanced linear head on group-annotated validation data to rank resulting predictors by validation worst-group accuracy. They also derive a worst-risk bound over inferred environments that transfers to oracle groups under an explicit alignment condition.

Result: Prototype margins enrich shortcut-conflicting examples, and classifier repair reshapes candidate evaluation. ProME achieves the highest average worst-group accuracy among compared methods with the same group-label access.

Conclusion: Jointly aligning environment inference and representation/classifier selection with the deployed predictor improves group-robustness, with theoretical guarantees tying inferred-environment risk to oracle groups under an alignment condition.

Abstract: Group-robust learning is crucial for maintaining accuracy on rare subpopulations when training-group labels are unavailable. However, existing methods often infer environments from a separate reference model and select representations before fitting the classifier used at deployment, leaving both decisions misaligned with the deployed predictor. In this work, we formulate group robustness without training-group labels as the endogenous environments with repair-aware selection (ERAS) problem, and propose ProME (Prototype-Margin Environments) to align both decisions with the deployed predictor. ProME splits prototype margins at their median to construct approximately balanced environments along the training trajectory, and fits a group-balanced linear head on group-annotated validation data to rank the resulting predictors by validation worst-group accuracy. We theoretically bound the worst risk across the inferred environments for a fixed predictor and partition, showing that this bound transfers to the oracle groups under an explicit alignment condition. Extensive experiments show that prototype margins enrich shortcut-conflicting examples, classifier repair reshapes candidate evaluation, and ProME achieves the highest average worst-group accuracy among the compared methods with the same group-label access.

</details>


### [285] [Beyond Simulated Benchmarks: Evaluating Motion Representations for Fall Detection Under Real-World Data Scarcity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13197)
*Timilehin B. Aderinola,Ilaria D'Ascanio,Luca Palmerini,Lorenzo Chiari,Jochen Klenk,Clemens Becker,Brian Caulfield,Georgiana Ifrim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper systematically compares motion representations (interval-based, kernel-based, symbolic, and foundation model) for wearable fall detection under real-world data scarcity, showing that high-capacity models overfit simulated data while a symbolic representation augmented with physically-grounded impact descriptors degrades least under domain shift and extreme scarcity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world falls are extremely rare (≈100,000 monitoring days per 100 falls), yielding severely limited labelled data, so models trained on abundant simulated falls report high lab performance but generalise poorly to real-world deployment.

Method: The authors compare interval-based, kernel-based, symbolic, and foundation model representations of accelerometer signals; they add an interpretable symbolic baseline that converts short motion segments into symbolic sentences augmented with physically-grounded impact descriptors. Evaluation uses FallAllD (simulated) and FARSEEING (real-world falls) with cross-validation, controlled data scarcity, and cross-dataset transfer.

Result: Highly parameterised kernel and foundation models excel on simulated data but degrade severely under data scarcity and domain shift. The interval-based representation achieves the strongest absolute real-world performance, while the augmented symbolic representation shows the smallest degradation under domain shift and retains detection sensitivity under extreme scarcity, albeit at lower precision.

Conclusion: Evaluating beyond simulated benchmarks is essential; representation choice is critical for deployable fall detection given the scarcity of real-world data, and lightweight symbolic representations with physically-grounded descriptors offer a robust trade-off under domain shift and extreme scarcity.

Abstract: Falls are a major health concern for older adults, and wearable sensors have been widely explored for detecting falls and enabling timely intervention. However, real-world falls are extremely rare: collecting 100 of them requires an estimated 100,000 days of monitoring, resulting in severely limited labelled data for training machine learning models. Consequently, many approaches rely on simulated datasets, often reporting high laboratory performance but limited real-world generalisation. We present a systematic evaluation of motion representations for wearable fall detection under real-world data scarcity. Using accelerometer signals, we compare interval-based, kernel-based, symbolic, and foundation model representations. As an interpretable baseline, we additionally investigate a lightweight symbolic representation that converts short motion segments into symbolic sentences augmented with physically-grounded impact descriptors. Experiments use FallAllD, a simulated falls dataset, and FARSEEING, a clinically verified real-world falls dataset. Through cross-validation, controlled data scarcity, and cross-dataset transfer, we examine how representation choices affect robustness under realistic deployment. Our results reveal that highly parameterised kernel and foundation models excel on simulated data but degrade severely under both data scarcity and domain shift. Although the interval-based representation achieves the strongest absolute real-world performance, augmenting a symbolic representation with physically-grounded impact descriptors yields the smallest degradation under domain shift and retains detection sensitivity under extreme scarcity, albeit at lower precision. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating beyond simulated benchmarks and show that representation choice is critical for deployable fall detection given the scarcity of real-world data.

</details>


### [286] [TANGCO: Learning Topology-Aware Capacity Allocation for Overload-driven Cascading Failures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13212)
*Orkun Irsoy,Leman Akoglu,Osman Yagan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces TANGCO, a topology-aware graph neural network policy for allocating a fixed capacity budget across nodes to resist load-redistribution cascades. Trained via policy-gradient learning through a cascade simulator, it outperforms hand-designed heuristics across synthetic and real networks and transfers to unseen topologies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In networked systems (power grids, traffic, cloud clusters), node overloads can trigger cascading failures. Allocating a fixed capacity budget to resist cascades is hard because no optimal allocation is known and the fail-or-survive objective is non-differentiable and piecewise constant, defeating exact and gradient-based optimizers. The goal is a scalable, transferable allocation method that beats hand-designed heuristics.

Method: TANGCO uses a graph neural network (GNN) policy trained end-to-end through a cascade simulator with policy-gradient (reinforcement) learning and a heuristic anchor to stabilize learning. A pre-trained variant, TANGCO^pre, learns on synthetic graphs and then allocates on unseen real networks with no per-target training. Free-vector variants (without the GNN) serve as ablations to isolate the contribution of graph representation versus numerical search.

Result: TANGCO improves on the best of four hand-designed heuristics in all 450 synthetic instances and in 40 of 45 real-network conditions, with robustness gains of 1.6% to 246%. Learned policies transfer to unseen graphs within a family and partially across related topologies; TANGCO^pre matches per-network training on unseen real networks. Training scales near-linearly with graph size. Free-vector variants stay close to heuristics, showing the GNN carries the gain. Analysis yields an improved closed-form heuristic and identifies regimes where topology-aware learning is necessary.

Conclusion: A topology-aware GNN policy trained via policy gradients effectively allocates capacity to resist cascading failures, surpassing hand-designed heuristics and transferring across and between graph families. The graph representation is essential for the gains, and analysis of learned allocations advances closed-form heuristics while clarifying when learned policies are still required.

Abstract: Networked systems, from power grids to traffic networks and cloud clusters, carry loads across nodes with limited capacity. A node whose load exceeds its capacity fails and sheds its load onto its neighbors, which can trigger a system-wide cascade. We study how to allocate a fixed capacity budget across nodes to resist these cascades under local load redistribution. The problem is difficult because no optimal allocation is known, and the fail-or-survive objective is non-differentiable and piecewise constant, so exact and gradient-based optimization methods do not directly apply. We introduce TANGCO (Topology-Aware Neural Graph-Guided Capacity Optimization), which uses a graph neural network policy trained through the cascade simulator with policy-gradient learning and a heuristic anchor. We evaluate TANGCO on five synthetic graph families and five real networks spanning power, road, air, and Internet topologies. The learned policy improves on the best of four hand-designed heuristics in all 450 synthetic instances and in 40 of 45 real-network conditions, with robustness gains ranging from 1.6% to 246%. The learned policies transfer to unseen graphs within a family and partially across related topologies, and TANGCO$^{pre}$, pre-trained on synthetic graphs, matches per-network training on unseen real networks. Training scales near-linearly with graph size, and TANGCO$^{pre}$ allocates on a new network with no per-target training, matching the deployment cost of a hand-designed heuristic. Free-vector variants without the GNN, stay close to the heuristics, so the graph representation carries the gain beyond numerical search. Finally, analysis of the learned allocations identifies when local risk is sufficient, leads to an improved closed-form heuristic, and reveals the regimes where a topology-aware learned policy remains necessary.

</details>


### [287] [History-informed Lagrangian Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13215)
*Tianshuo Zhang,Xianglei Xing,Wenzhe Zhai,Jia Gao,He Cao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HiLNN forecasts long-horizon mechanical system evolution from position-only data by using a recurrent encoder to infer latent history context that reconstructs hidden velocity and adapts Lagrangian parameters, trained end-to-end with differentiable RK4 rollout and energy regularization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Forecasting long-horizon evolution of mechanical systems from position-only observations is difficult because hidden velocities and trajectory-specific physical parameters must be inferred simultaneously. Existing physics-guided networks like Lagrangian Neural Networks guarantee physical plausibility but require complete state inputs and cannot adapt to changing system parameters.

Method: The paper introduces History-informed Lagrangian Neural Networks (HiLNN). A recurrent encoder extracts a latent context from position history; this context reconstructs the unobserved initial velocity and adaptively modulates the mass matrix, potential energy, and damping coefficients of a structured Lagrangian system. A differentiable RK4 rollout scheme enables end-to-end optimization under multi-step trajectory supervision and energy-consistency regularization.

Result: Empirical evaluations across conservative, dissipative, and heterogeneous variable-parameter systems show HiLNN attains superior long-term prediction accuracy and maintains precise energy profiles compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

Conclusion: HiLNN effectively combines history-informed latent inference with structured Lagrangian priors, overcoming the limitations of complete-state dependence and parameter rigidity, and delivers accurate, physically consistent long-horizon predictions. Source code is publicly available.

Abstract: Forecasting the long-horizon evolution of mechanical systems from position-only observations is a pivotal yet difficult task, as hidden velocities and trajectory-specific physical properties must be inferred simultaneously. Although physics-guided neural networks like Lagrangian Neural Networks (LNNs) guarantee physical plausibility, they generally require complete state inputs and lack adaptability to changing system parameters. To break these limitations, we introduce History-informed Lagrangian Neural Networks (HiLNN). Grounded in the insight that temporal position sequences implicitly encode underlying dynamics, HiLNN employs a recurrent encoder to extract a latent context from history. This context not only reconstructs the unobserved initial velocity but also adaptively modulates the mass matrix, potential energy, and damping coefficients of a structured Lagrangian system. By leveraging a differentiable RK4 rollout scheme, the entire pipeline is optimized end-to-end under multi-step trajectory supervision and energy-consistency regularization. Empirical evaluations across conservative, dissipative, and heterogeneous variable-parameter systems show that HiLNN delivers superior long-term prediction accuracy and maintains precise energy profiles compared to state-of-the-art baselines. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/yingtian22/History-informed-LNN.

</details>


### [288] [Knowledge-guided Pattern Discovery via Coupled Tensor Factorizations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13234)
*Gaute Johannessen,Geert Roelof van der Ploeg,Evrim Acar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a knowledge-guided tensor factorization method that couples real (noisy, multiway) data with simulated data from computational models via coupled tensor factorizations, improving pattern discovery in metabolomics while exposing model-data mismatches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multiway datasets from complex systems (e.g., metabolomics, brain imaging) are noisy and hard to interpret. Existing tensor factorization approaches are mostly data-driven and ignore valuable prior knowledge encoded in computational models of these systems.

Method: A knowledge-guided approach using coupled tensor factorizations with linear coupling, jointly analyzing real data and simulated data generated from a computational model of the system.

Result: Experiments on real metabolomics measurements show that guiding the analysis with simulated data improves pattern discovery performance and reveals potential discrepancies between the real data and the computational model.

Conclusion: Combining real data with computational-model-generated simulated data through coupled tensor factorization is a promising way to harness prior knowledge, yielding better patterns and insights into model-data disagreements.

Abstract: In order to understand complex systems such as the human metabolome or human brain, different sensing technologies are used, generating complex data. These datasets are often multiway, i.e., with more than two axes of variation such as a subjects by metabolites by time array. While tensor factorizations have successfully revealed interpretable patterns from such complex data, they have so far been mainly data-driven. On the other hand, there is more to data -- there are computational models (of these systems), which are rich sources of prior information. In this paper, we introduce a knowledge-guided approach that brings together data and computational models by jointly analyzing real data and simulated data (generated using a computational model) using coupled tensor factorizations with linear coupling. Our experiments on real metabolomics measurements demonstrate that guiding the analysis of such noisy data with simulated data improves the pattern discovery performance while also revealing potential discrepancies between data and computational models.

</details>


### [289] [Novel Knowledge-Guided Generative Methods for Synthetic Transcriptomic Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13256)
*Francesca Pia Panaccione,Sofia Mongardi,Marco Masseroli,Pietro Pinoli*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper benchmarks generative models for synthetic transcriptomic data generation, introducing MK-TGAN, a multi-kernel Graph Neural Network-based GAN that integrates prior biological knowledge via gene graphs, and shows it outperforms alternatives in realism and biological utility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Biomedical research increasingly depends on data-intensive tools, but dataset quality and availability are constrained by class imbalances, biases, and ethical/legal restrictions. Synthetic data generation offers a way to overcome these limitations while capturing real-world gene patterns useful for downstream tasks.

Method: The authors perform a comparative analysis of generative models for transcriptomic data, specifically benchmarking three Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) variants that incorporate prior biological knowledge using gene graphs. They introduce MK-TGAN, a multi-kernel, Graph Neural Network-based GAN that exploits knowledge graphs through graph neural networks.

Result: Prior knowledge integration strategies improve generative performance. MK-TGAN consistently produces synthetic samples with superior realism and biological plausibility compared to other methods.

Conclusion: Incorporating prior biological knowledge through gene graphs enhances synthetic transcriptomic data generation, and MK-TGAN is the most effective model among the benchmarks for producing realistic, biologically plausible, and useful synthetic data.

Abstract: As biomedical research increasingly relies on data-intensive tools, the quality and utility of datasets are critical. Challenges such as imbalances, biases, and ethical or legal constraints often limit access to high-quality data. Synthetic data generation can help overcome these limitations. Here, we present a comparative analysis of generative models for transcriptomic data, investigating strategies to incorporate prior biological knowledge via gene graphs. This ensures that synthetic data capture real-world gene patterns, maintaining their usefulness for downstream tasks. In particular, we introduce and benchmark three variants of the Generative Adversarial Network. Among the alternatives, MK-TGAN - an innovative multi-kernel, Graph Neural Network-based model - stands out for its performance in terms of both the realism and utility of the generated data. Unlike other methods, MK-TGAN leverages prior knowledge graphs by exploiting graph neural networks. Our results show that prior knowledge integration strategies improve performance, and that MK-TGAN consistently produces synthetic samples with superior realism and biological plausibility.

</details>


### [290] [Virtual Temperature Sensors in Power Transformers Using Neural Ordinary Differential Equations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13260)
*Berk Hadzhamolla,Alexander Johannes Stasik,Signe Riemer-Sørensen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a physics-aware Neural Ordinary Differential Equation (Neural ODE) framework to forecast power transformer thermal behavior from real-world time-series data, addressing limitations of computationally expensive numerical methods, transformer-specific lumped-parameter models, and data-hungry black-box ML approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing thermal modeling approaches are insufficient: FEM/CFD are accurate but computationally expensive and impractical for real-time or large-scale use (especially with unknown geometries); lumped-parameter thermal models rely on transformer-specific constants and struggle to capture dynamic responses under varying conditions; purely data-driven machine learning (ANN, CNN, LSTM) requires large high-quality datasets and can yield physically inconsistent or uninterpretable predictions.

Method: The authors develop a physics-aware Neural ODE framework that models thermal system dynamics in continuous time, providing smooth trajectory prediction and a natural representation of continuously evolving thermal behavior. A key contribution is embedding simplified heat-transfer equations directly into the Neural ODE formulation, combining physical priors with learned dynamics.

Result: Evaluated on datasets from fifteen transformers across different regions of Norway with varying designs and cooling mechanisms, the framework demonstrates a standardized, physics-aware, and robust forecasting capability across heterogeneous transformer units.

Conclusion: The physics-aware Neural ODE framework offers a practical, scalable, and physically grounded alternative for transformer thermal forecasting, enabling reliable predictions across diverse transformer designs without requiring detailed geometry or large volumes of training data.

Abstract: Accurate modeling and forecasting of power transformer thermal behavior are critical for reliability, asset lifetime, and optimized power system operation. Numerical approaches such as finite element methods (FEM) and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) offer high fidelity but are computationally expensive, require complex mesh generation, and are often impractical for real-time or large-scale applications, particularly when transformer geometries are unknown. Lumped-parameter thermal models are more practical but depend on transformer-specific thermal constants and may fail to capture dynamic responses under varying operating and environmental conditions. Purely data-driven machine learning methods, including artificial neural networks, convolutional neural networks, and long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, have shown success in forecasting transformer temperatures but typically require large volumes of high-quality training data and may produce physically inconsistent or uninterpretable results. This paper develops a physics-aware Neural Ordinary Differential Equation (Neural ODE) framework for forecasting transformer thermal behavior from real-world time-series data. Neural ODEs model system dynamics in continuous time, providing smooth trajectory prediction and a natural representation of continuously evolving thermal dynamics. A key contribution is the integration of simplified heat-transfer equations directly into the Neural ODE formulation. The model is evaluated across datasets from fifteen transformers in different regions of Norway with varying designs and cooling mechanisms. The results demonstrate that the developed Neural ODE framework provides a standardized, physics-aware, and robust forecasting approach for heterogeneous transformer units.

</details>


### [291] [Into the ORBIT for Time Series: Training Regimes for Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13262)
*Hongjie Xia,Yiding Liu,Yifan Hu,Peiyuan Liu,Zewei Dong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces ORBIT, a controllable pre-training paradigm for time series foundation models, along with Falcon-2.0 architecture and Rank-Guided Cross-Depth Alignment, achieving strong zero-shot forecasting results.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Time series foundation models have focused on architecture while neglecting training regimes, leading to poorly controlled pre-training distributions regarding domain imbalance, context length, prediction horizon, and missing data.

Method: ORBIT combines Bootstrap Multi-Level Sampling (controlling dataset exposure, records, target variables, context windows, and horizons) with Omni-Range Incremental Training (varying context/horizon in one stage). Falcon-2.0 is a univariate encoder-only Transformer with missingness-aware triple-channel patch tokenization and parallel patch prediction, trained with Rank-Guided Cross-Depth Alignment using late-layer representations as stop-gradient teachers.

Result: Evaluations on GIFT-Eval and fev-bench show strong zero-shot forecasting performance across diverse domains and frequencies.

Conclusion: Making the pre-training distribution explicit and controllable via ORBIT, combined with the Falcon-2.0 design and cross-depth alignment objective, yields competitive zero-shot forecasting without extra inference cost.

Abstract: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) have advanced primarily through architectural innovation, while training regimes for large-scale heterogeneous corpora remain under-explored. As a result, pre-training distributions are often poorly controlled with respect to domain imbalance, context requirements, prediction horizons, and missingness. We introduce ORBIT (Omni-Range Bootstrap Incremental Training), a training paradigm that makes this distribution explicit and controllable. ORBIT combines Bootstrap Multi-Level Sampling, which controls dataset exposure and samples records, target variables, context windows, and prediction horizons, with Omni-Range Incremental Training, which varies context lengths and prediction horizons throughout a single training stage. Under ORBIT, we train Falcon-2.0, a simple univariate encoder-only Transformer with missingness-aware triple-channel patch tokenization and parallel patch prediction. We further introduce Rank-Guided Cross-Depth Alignment, a training objective that uses late-layer representations as stop-gradient teachers for shallow layers without additional inference cost. Evaluations on GIFT-Eval and fev-bench demonstrate strong zero-shot forecasting performance across diverse domains and frequencies.

</details>


### [292] [Large-scale Testing Global Optimization Methods with Black-box Adversarial Attacks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13296)
*Wojciech Zarzecki,Jarosław Arabas*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper argues that black-box adversarial attack (BBAA) tasks can serve as much-needed high-dimensional benchmarks for global optimization, and demonstrates several evolutionary algorithms and metaheuristics working effectively on example BBAA problems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current global optimization benchmark suites are too small and rely on a few analytical functions dating back to the 1970s, creating a risk of biasing the development of optimization methods. Modern machine learning challenges, particularly black-box adversarial attacks, offer a richer and more relevant testing ground in high-dimensional spaces.

Method: The authors frame black-box adversarial attack problems as global optimization tasks and apply several types of evolutionary algorithms and other metaheuristics to solve example BBAA problems, demonstrating their efficiency.

Result: Multiple evolutionary algorithms and metaheuristics are shown to be efficient in solving example black-box adversarial attack problems, supporting the viability of BBAA as a global optimization benchmark in many-dimensional space.

Conclusion: BBAA tasks provide valuable, modern, high-dimensional benchmarks for global optimization, and their adoption is a step toward aligning global optimization research with the needs of contemporary machine learning.

Abstract: Existing global optimization benchmark suites are of a moderate size and are based on a small number of analytical functions that date back even to the 1970s. This causes a risk of biasing the development of global optimization methods. We argue that the tasks related to the black-box adversarial attack (BBAA) can serve as valuable global optimization benchmark in many-dimensional space. We demonstrate the efficiency of several types of evolutionary algorithms and other metaheuristics in solving example BBAA problems. Thus, we take a step towards convergence of global optimization methods to the challenges and needs that arise in the modern machine learning field.

</details>


### [293] [The Time Value of Evolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13297)
*Matthew Siper,Ahmed Khalifa,Julian Togelius*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces Lineage-Value Policy Gradients (LVPG), a long-horizon actor-critic method that assigns credit to mutations based on their future lineage potential rather than immediate returns, improving finite-budget evolutionary search for trading policy discovery.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Immediate-return control in evolutionary search penalizes mutations through weak immediate offspring even when they open productive future lineages, making high-fitness regions unreachable. The authors formalize this as the "time value of evolution" that immediate-return methods are blind to.

Method: LVPG is a finite-horizon Markov decision process framework with a long-horizon actor-critic architecture. It decouples search control into specialized policy heads over a shared generative backbone: a bootstrapped critic head estimates finite-horizon lineage potential from multi-step mutation trees, and an actor head dynamically modulates mutation intensity over the remaining search budget. Evaluation uses 90 paired runs with matched operators, lineage supervision, folds, seeds, and budgets.

Result: Path-based long-horizon credit assignment substantially accelerates finite-budget search, increasing validation best-so-far AUC by 0.394 Sharpe units compared to immediate-return optimization. LVPG also produces fewer temporary regressions and recovers from them more often, yielding more selective non-monotonic search and stronger policies under identical resource constraints.

Conclusion: Finite-horizon lineage value enables more selective non-monotonic search and stronger policies than immediate-return optimization, demonstrating that accounting for the time value of evolution improves automated trading policy discovery within identical resource constraints.

Abstract: In evolutionary search, a weak child can be a valuable ancestor that makes high-fitness regions reachable. Immediate-return control is blind to this delayed utility, penalizing mutations through their immediate offspring even when they open productive future lineages. We formalize this hidden dynamic as the time value of evolution within a finite-horizon Markov decision process. To exploit it, we introduce Lineage-Value Policy Gradients (LVPG), a long-horizon actor-critic framework for automated trading policy discovery. Our architecture decouples search control into specialized policy heads over a shared generative backbone: a bootstrapped critic head estimates the value of finite-horizon lineage potential from multi-step mutation trees, while an actor head dynamically modulates mutation intensity over the remaining search budget. We isolate the impact of long-horizon credit assignment against immediate-return optimization across 90 paired runs under matched operators, lineage supervision, folds, seeds, and budgets. Path-based credit assignment substantially accelerates finite-budget search, increasing validation best-so-far AUC by 0.394 Sharpe units. LVPG also produces fewer temporary regressions than immediate-return optimization and recovers from them more often. Finite-horizon lineage value yields more selective non-monotonic search and stronger policies within identical resource constraints.

</details>


### [294] [A Probe Direction Is a Property of Its Prompt](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13329)
*Valentin Noël*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper shows that a widely used activation-based method for detecting whether a model "knows it is being evaluated" is not robust: the reported score depends heavily on which specific prompt is chosen to signal evaluation, not on the model itself. The apparent sign and trend with scale are artifacts of prompt choice, and even a direction carrying no evaluation information reproduces much of the published scores.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Recent work treats evaluation-awareness as a latent state readable from activations by contrasting "evaluation-announcing" prompts with non-announcing ones. If this sense of being tested correlates with capability or dangerous behavior, we want to measure it. However, the method has an unspecified degree of freedom—the exact wording of the evaluation-announcing prompt—whose influence on the measurement has not been examined. The authors aim to test whether the instrument's readings are driven by the model or by the arbitrary prompt choice.

Method: The authors systematically vary only the "evaluation-announcing" prompt while holding the task text fixed, then measure how the contrastive direction's separation score changes across prompts and across models of different scales. They decompose the variance in reported scores to quantify how much is attributable to the model versus the prompt and their interaction. They also test the surface-form separability of the prompt split (e.g., whether the direction is learnable from wording alone), and compute how many prompts are needed for a defensible between-model comparison.

Result: The reported score—and even whether it trends upward or downward with model size—follows the chosen prompt rather than the model. Two published studies with opposite signs of the scale trend are both reproducible from a single design by prompt choice alone. Variance decomposition shows the model accounts for only a small share of the variance; most lies in how each model responds to each specific prompt. Collecting more evaluation items cannot fix the measurement, but varying prompts can. A direction carrying no information about evaluation still reproduces a substantial fraction of each published score because the split is largely separable from surface form alone.

Conclusion: A single-prompt design cannot support comparisons between models, since the score is confounded by prompt wording and surface form. The authors conclude that varying prompts is necessary and provide the number of prompts required for a defensible comparison.

Abstract: A model that behaves differently when it senses it is being tested would undermine the evaluations we rely on, so recent work has sought to read that sense directly from a model's activations. The standard instrument contrasts activations on prompts that announce an evaluation against prompts that do not, and reports how well the resulting direction separates held-out cases. That number is then compared across models and correlated with scale. We observe that the instrument has a free parameter its readings do not disclose: "a prompt that announces an evaluation" is not a prompt but a choice among many, and nothing in the method fixes which. Holding the task text fixed and varying only that choice, we find that the reported score, and even the direction in which it trends with model size, follows the prompt rather than the model; two published studies that disagree about the sign of that trend are both reproducible from a single design, by choice of prompt alone. Treating the prompt as a facet of a measurement design rather than an implementation detail, we find the model under study accounts for a small share of the variance in the number reported about it, and most of the rest lies in how each model responds to each prompt: collecting more evaluation items cannot repair the measurement, while varying prompts can. A further check finds that the split these probes are scored on is largely separable from surface form alone, so a direction carrying no information about evaluation at all still reproduces a substantial fraction of each published score. We conclude that a single-prompt design cannot support comparison between models, and we give the number of prompts a defensible comparison requires.

</details>


### [295] [Training AI Scientists to Replicate Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13331)
*Damon Falck,Samer Sabri,Anja Surina,Thom Foster,Anya Sims,Sam Devlin,Dylan Rogers,Tantum Collins,Kaloyan Aleksiev,Louis Kirsch,Edward Hughes*

Main category: cs.LG
