TL;DR: The paper introduces Replica, a scalable benchmark/task space for replicating scientific papers, paired with an auto-generated rubric-based judge. The authors post-train Faraday, a 27B "AI Scientist" agent that uses coding agents as tools, which outperforms Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 on replication tasks and shows more scientifically-principled behavior.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Replicability is essential for scientific knowledge but requires hypothesis-driven exploration similar to open-ended research. The authors aim to enable AI agents capable of long-horizon scientific innovation without complex harnesses, using paper replication as a tractable proxy task.

Method: They build Replica, a scalable task space of paper-replication tasks. For reward signal, they introduce an auto-generated rubric-based judge with low noise that aligns with human assessments of replication quality. They then post-train Faraday, a 27B-parameter agent that uses coding agents as tools.

Result: Faraday surpasses Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 on held-out replication tasks. Qualitative analysis shows Faraday adopts a more scientifically-principled approach in individual rollouts.

Conclusion: The results provide a stepping stone toward AI agents capable of long-horizon scientific innovation without requiring complex harnesses.

Abstract: The replicability of papers is a cornerstone of scientific knowledge, ensuring the reliability of existing results and providing a base for further experiments. The act of replication typically illuminates details that were previously underspecified, and thus requires similar hypothesis-driven exploration to open-ended research. In this work, we develop Replica, a scalable task space for paper replication. To provide reward signal, we introduce an auto-generated rubric-based judge that has low noise and agrees with human assessment of replication quality. We post-train Faraday, a 27B-parameter "AI Scientist" agent that leverages coding agents as tools, surpassing the performance of Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 on held-out replication tasks. Qualitative analysis of individual rollouts reveals that Faraday adopts a more scientifically-principled approach. We believe that our results provide a stepping stone towards AI agents capable of long-horizon scientific innovation without requiring complex harnesses.

</details>


### [296] [Neural Quadratic Forms: A Unified Minimal Model for Sudden Learning and Scaling Laws](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13335)
*Liu Ziyin,Yizhou Xu,Tomaso Poggio,Isaac Chuang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Neural networks trained by gradient descent can exhibit abrupt step-like loss drops despite a smooth cost, and smooth power-law losses. The authors show this behavior emerges from a symmetry: interchangeable units in a layer lead to a universal quadratic form Tr[WW^T A(x)] near zero weights, determined by a single structure matrix A per architecture. Training dynamics reduce to a Lotka–Volterra equation whose modes switch on sequentially, causing plateaus and power laws.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Explain why seemingly smooth gradient descent on smooth costs produces step-like, plateau-and-drop training dynamics, and why training losses follow power laws across very different architectures—suggesting a common low-dimensional mechanism described by a few collective variables.

Method: Leverage the permutation symmetry of interchangeable layer units (relabeling leaves the layer invariant), combined with smoothness and the condition that a unit's gradient vanishes at the origin, to derive a universal leading-order expansion of the cost about near-zero initial weights: the quadratic Tr[WW^T A(x)]. All architecture-specific detail is absorbed into a single structure matrix A(x). Define the order parameter M = WW^T and close the training dynamics on it; when data matrices share an eigenbasis, the dynamics reduce to a Lotka–Volterra system whose modes activate sequentially.

Result: Plateaus appear as a singular limit of a smooth flow, with smaller initial weights separating switch-on times further. When many modes are unresolved, these sequential events merge into a power law in training time with a theory-predicted exponent. Numerical results confirm the predictions across multiple training methods and architectures (perceptrons, attention layers, mixtures of experts, convolutions).

Conclusion: A symmetry-driven universal form unifies the training dynamics of diverse architectures, reducing them to a single-mode-sequential Lotka–Volterra picture; this explains both plateau-drop and power-law loss behaviors as limits of the same smooth flow, with quantitative predictions that match experiments.

Abstract: Neural networks trained by gradient descent on a smooth cost function can nevertheless learn in steps: the cost holds on long plateaus and then drops abruptly. Meanwhile, training losses instead follow smooth power laws. Variants of both behaviors occur in architectures with very different microscopic structures, which is the signature of a few relevant collective variables. We show that a symmetry fixes what those variables are: a network layer is a sum over interchangeable units, so relabeling the units leaves it unchanged; given smoothness and the condition that a unit's gradient vanish at the origin, symmetry then enforces a universal leading form for the expansion about the near-zero weights present at the start of training, the quadratic $\Tr[WW^{\top}A(x)]$, in which every architectural detail is confined to a single ``structure matrix" $A(x)$ that we compute for each architecture. Perceptrons, attention layers, mixtures of experts, and convolutions become one model at different $A$. Its training dynamics then close on the ``order parameter" $M=WW^{\top}$ and, whenever the data matrices share an eigenbasis, reduce to a Lotka--Volterra equation whose modes switch on one after another. The smaller the initial weights, the further apart the switch-on times, and the plateaus appear as a singular limit of a smooth flow; when many modes are unresolved the same events merge into a power law in training time whose exponent the theory predicts. We confirm both numerically across training methods and architectures.

</details>


### [297] [Where You Measure Decides What You Measure: Position Selection in Ablation-Based SAE Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13337)
*Valentin Noël*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Sparse autoencoder latents are conventionally evaluated by ablating them at their maximally-activating token, but this measurement position is chosen implicitly by the dictionary itself. The authors show this convention causes different dictionaries for the same model to be compared at different tokens, and introduce a one-line correction fixing the evaluation token across dictionaries, which removes most of the apparent "disagreement" between latents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The standard causal-evaluation protocol for sparse autoencoder latents (measure the effect of ablating a latent at the token where it fires hardest) has no fixed reference position: the position is implicitly selected by the dictionary under evaluation, not by the experimenter. This makes cross-dictionary comparisons measured at different tokens, conflating dictionary differences with positional differences, and the choice is almost never reported.

Method: The authors analyze two Google sparse autoencoders for the same model, matching latents by decoder similarity to show even near-identical latents select different maximal-activation tokens. They then train six autoencoders from a single initialization differing only in fitting choices, so latents correspond across dictionaries, and compare variance decomposition under the usual protocol versus a protocol that fixes a single evaluation token per latent. They also vary corpus size across a sixteenfold range and audit five published papers against a proposed reporting protocol.

Result: Matched latent pairs from the two Google dictionaries pick different measurement tokens for a large share of even nearly identical latents. In the controlled six-dictionary setting, apparent disagreement attributed to the dictionaries drops from 7.6% and 11.9% of variance to near zero once all dictionaries are measured at the same token. Larger corpora make dictionaries agree less about where to measure, not more, so the problem grows with scale.

Conclusion: A causal number (ablating a latent) reported without its measurement position describes the token it was taken at as much as the latent itself. The correction is a one-line change: report the measurement position, and fix it across dictionaries to make results comparable across papers.

Abstract: Sparse autoencoders are meant to name the things a language model computes, and the usual way to check that a latent matters is to switch it off and see what changes. But a latent fires at many tokens, and the effect has to be measured at one of them. The convention is to measure where the latent fires hardest. That choice is almost never reported, and it is not made by the experimenter: it is made by the dictionary under evaluation. Change the dictionary and the measurement moves to a different token. We show this is not a detail. Take two sparse autoencoders released by Google for the same model and match their latents by decoder similarity: even among the pairs the two dictionaries encode almost identically, they pick different tokens for a large share of them. Two dictionaries compared under the usual protocol are therefore very often compared at different places. To separate the convention from the dictionaries we train six autoencoders from one initialisation, differing only in fitting choices, so that a latent means the same thing in each. Most of the variance such a comparison reads as "these dictionaries disagree about this latent" turns out to be the position instead: it falls from 7.6% and 11.9% of variance to near zero once every dictionary is measured at the same token. More evaluation data does not rescue it. Across a sixteenfold range of corpus sizes the dictionaries agree less about where to measure, not more, so the problem grows with scale. The correction is one line of evaluation code. We give the protocol an ablation-based causal number must report to be comparable across papers, and an audit of five published papers against it. In short: a causal number reported without its position describes the token it was taken at as much as the latent it was taken from.

</details>


### [298] [Simulation-to-real transfer learning for infrared spectroscopic chemical sensing and analysis from molecules to complex samples](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13341)
*Yusen Tan,Yixuan Chen,Zheng Fang,Pan Liu,Yifan Li,Qinyu Guo,Zhedong Lin,Yuqiang Li,Xiangxiang Zeng,Tong Wang,Jun Xia*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: UltraIR is a 100M+ parameter foundation model for infrared spectroscopy, pretrained on ~60 million simulated IR spectra via spectral reconstruction, molecular fingerprint similarity alignment, and functional-group prediction, then adapted to downstream tasks. It outperforms conventional ML and task-specific deep-learning baselines across many chemical sensing tasks and transfers effectively to limited-label and zero-shot real-world settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: IR spectroscopy is widely used for chemical sensing, but extracting reliable chemical information is difficult: conventional interpretation is labor-intensive, prior-knowledge-dependent, and hard to scale, while most ML methods are task/dataset-specific and require large labeled training sets with poor transferability. A general-purpose, transferable model is needed.

Method: UltraIR is a foundation model (100M+ parameters) enabling simulation-to-real transfer learning. It is pretrained on ~60M simulated IR spectra using three objectives: spectral reconstruction, molecular fingerprint similarity alignment, and functional-group prediction. It is then adapted to downstream tasks using task-specific labels or targets.

Result: UltraIR outperforms conventional machine-learning and task-specific deep-learning baselines across functional-group prediction, molecular structure elucidation, physicochemical property prediction, mixture-component identification/quantification, bacterial classification, medicinal-herb geographic origin traceability and constituent quantification, microplastics classification, and soil property prediction. It performs strongly with limited labeled experimental spectra and in zero-shot inference across FTIR spectrometers and laboratories.

Conclusion: UltraIR provides a route to adaptable, data-efficient chemical sensing from complex real-world samples, demonstrating strong generalization and cross-instrument/laboratory transfer for IR spectroscopy analysis.

Abstract: Infrared (IR) spectroscopy is widely used for chemical sensing, but extracting reliable chemical information from spectra remains challenging. Conventional interpretation is labor-intensive, relies on prior knowledge and reference spectra, and is difficult to scale, whereas most machine-learning methods are tailored to individual tasks or datasets, require large labeled training sets, and transfer poorly across analytical objectives and experimental datasets. Here we introduce UltraIR, a foundation model for IR spectroscopy with more than 100 million parameters that enables simulation-to-real transfer learning for chemical sensing and analysis from molecules to complex samples. UltraIR is pretrained on approximately 60 million simulated IR spectra using spectral reconstruction, molecular fingerprint similarity alignment, and functional-group prediction, then adapted to downstream objectives with task-specific labels or targets. Across functional-group prediction, molecular structure elucidation, physicochemical property prediction, mixture-component identification and quantification, bacterial classification, medicinal-herb geographic origin traceability and constituent quantification, microplastics classification, and soil property prediction, UltraIR outperforms conventional machine-learning and task-specific deep-learning baselines. It performs strongly with limited labeled experimental spectra and in zero-shot inference for the same analytical task across Fourier-transform infrared spectrometers and laboratories, providing a route to adaptable, data-efficient chemical sensing from complex real-world samples.

</details>


### [299] [When Local Variance Optimality Is Not Enough: RoPE-Aligned Q/K Rotations for Dynamic 4-Bit Quantisation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13365)
*Shuhan Wang,Yilin Luo,Nan Xu,Chi Wang Cheung*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper investigates whether RoPE-compatible pairwise (two-dimensional) rotations can outperform full-head Hadamard mixing in rotation-based post-training quantisation. The authors prove no other single-head orthogonal map commutes with RoPE for distinct frequencies, derive a head-shared pairwise angle that minimises a pooled-covariance surrogate, and empirically show that this pairwise configuration does not improve accuracy over full-head mixing in dynamic W4A4KV4 quantisation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Rotation-based post-training quantisation uses full-head orthogonal transforms to reduce outlier-induced error, but RoPE partitions each attention head into 2D frequency pairs. This raises whether a transform respecting the RoPE decomposition can improve on full-head mixing by matching the structural prior while reducing outlier effects.

Method: The authors first state the converse of prior work: for distinct frequencies, no single-head orthogonal map other than per-pair rotations commutes with RoPE. For a head-shared parameterisation, they derive the rotation angle minimising the larger channel variance under a pooled-covariance, position-averaged surrogate, verify the implementation attains this analytic minimum, and evaluate the pairwise configuration via interpolation between two-channel and full-head mixing.

Result: The head-shared pairwise rotation does not improve accuracy in dynamic W4A4KV4; across four checkpoints it raises perplexity at short and long context lengths versus full-head Hadamard. Composing pairwise rotation with Hadamard meets the ±0.05-PPL criterion under the default estimator, and estimating the shared angle from K alone improves pairwise-only on every checkpoint but still underperforms full-head mixing. Along the interpolation, K range, relative quantisation error, and perplexity degradation decrease as mixing support increases.

Conclusion: Optimality for a structured surrogate (position-averaged second moment of pooled covariance) does not reduce quantisation error when the surrogate and two-channel mixing support are misaligned with the dynamic quantiser's tokenwise group-range scale-setting statistic. Full-head mixing remains preferable for this quantisation setup.

Abstract: Rotation-based post-training quantisation commonly applies an orthogonal transform across an entire attention head to reduce outlier-induced error. RoPE instead partitions each head into two-dimensional frequency pairs, raising the question of whether a transform respecting this decomposition can improve on full-head mixing. Prior work has established the per-pair rotations that commute with RoPE. We state the converse result that, for distinct frequencies, no other single-head orthogonal map commutes with RoPE. For the head-shared parameterisation used in our experiments, we then derive the rotation angle that minimises the larger channel variance under a pooled-covariance, position-averaged surrogate and verify that the implementation attains its analytic minimum. The evaluated head-shared pairwise configuration does not improve accuracy in the tested dynamic W4A4KV4 setting. Across four checkpoints, replacing the full-head Hadamard with this configuration increases perplexity at both short and long context lengths. Composing the pairwise rotation with the Hadamard satisfies the selected $\pm0.05$-PPL interval criterion under the default estimator. Estimating the shared angle from K alone improves pairwise-only on every checkpoint but does not close its gap to full-head mixing. The analytic objective controls a position-averaged second moment of a pooled calibration covariance, whereas the dynamic quantiser sets its step from a tokenwise group range. The pairwise transform also has only two-channel mixing support. Along a controlled interpolation from two-channel to full-head mixing, K range, relative quantisation error, and perplexity degradation decrease as support increases. These results show that optimality for a structured surrogate need not reduce quantisation error when the surrogate and mixing support are misaligned with the quantiser's scale-setting statistic.

</details>


### [300] [Reduced Matrix Multiplication: Input-Adaptive Matrix-Product Reduction for LLM Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13426)
*Zixuan Lan,Yanhong Li,Jiawei Zhou*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RMM is a training-free, input-adaptive method that reduces Transformer matrix multiplications by selecting informative slices along contraction dimensions, offering a predictable accuracy-efficiency trade-off without modifying weights.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Transformer language models deliver strong performance but suffer from high inference cost due to repeated high-dimensional matrix multiplications. The goal is to cut this computational burden without retraining or altering model weights.

Method: RMM (Reduced Matrix Multiplication) reduces Transformer matrix products by adaptively selecting informative slices along the contraction dimensions of matrix multiplications at inference time, controlled by a simple retention-ratio parameter, and validated with custom CUDA kernels on an NVIDIA A100.

Result: Across 1B–70B models, reduction tolerance varies by model family, task, component, and retention ratio, generally improving with scale; RMM stays robust under moderate reduction for discriminative, generative, and long-context tasks, and also transfers to multimodal vision-language inference. Mechanistic ablations show attention-side computations are far more reducible than MLP components, and wall-clock benchmarks confirm practical runtime gains, especially at longer sequence lengths.

Conclusion: RMM provides a scalable, weight-free direction for input-adaptive inference-time optimization, with predictable accuracy-efficiency trade-offs and practical speedups on real hardware.

Abstract: Transformer-based language models achieve strong performance but incur substantial inference cost due to repeated high-dimensional matrix multiplications. We propose Reduced Matrix Multiplication (RMM), a training-free, input-adaptive inference method that reduces Transformer matrix products by selecting informative slices along their contraction dimensions, without modifying model weights. Under a simple retention-ratio control, RMM provides a smooth and predictable accuracy-efficiency trade-off. Across language models ranging from 1B to 70B parameters, we find that reduction tolerance depends on the model family, task, component, and retention ratio, although it often improves with model scale. Under moderate reduction, RMM remains robust across the evaluated discriminative, autoregressive generation, and long-context settings. We further show that the same principle extends to multimodal vision-language inference. Mechanistic ablations reveal a structural asymmetry within Transformers: attention-side computations are substantially more reducible than MLP components. Finally, wall-clock benchmarks with custom kernels on an NVIDIA A100 show that these computational savings can translate into practical runtime gains, especially at longer sequence lengths. Together, these results position RMM as a scalable direction for input-adaptive inference-time optimization.

</details>


### [301] [Symmetry-Breaking De Novo Crystal Generation via Markovian Jump Diffusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13457)
*Van Khoa Nguyen,Alexandros Kalousis*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SbCD proposes a diffusion-based generative model for crystals that, inspired by spontaneous symmetry breaking, generates full crystallographic specifications by reversing from lowest-symmetry priors and explicitly modeling inter-space-group transitions via a Markovian jump-diffusion process, outperforming symmetry-preserving baselines on MP20 and MPTS-52.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing generative models for crystals fail to produce complete crystallographic specifications, limiting their ability to capture global symmetry and structural dependencies; state-of-the-art methods generate only up to site symmetries and sample space groups from empirical distributions, rather than learning them jointly.

Method: The authors propose Symmetry-breaking Crystal Diffusion (SbCD), a diffusion-based framework that generates full structure specifications by reversing a process starting from lowest-symmetry priors. It uses a Markovian jump-diffusion process to model symmetry-breaking dynamics, enabling explicit inter-space-group transitions in a physically motivated way.

Result: In de novo generation experiments on MP20 and MPTS-52, SbCD substantially outperforms its symmetry-preserving counterpart, demonstrating improved generative performance for crystalline materials.

Conclusion: Explicitly incorporating inter-space-group transitions through a symmetry-breaking diffusion process offers a principled and promising approach for generative modeling of crystalline materials.

Abstract: Generating crystals has recently attracted significant interest due to their broad applications in materials science. However, existing generative models struggle to produce complete crystallographic specifications, limiting their ability to capture global symmetry and structural dependencies. In particular, current state-of-the-art approaches generate crystals only up to site symmetries and rely on sampling space groups from empirical distributions during generation. Inspired by \emph{spontaneous symmetry breaking} in physics, where crystals break symmetries under external conditions, we propose a novel diffusion-based framework that generates full structure specifications by reversing from the lowest-symmetry priors. Our method leverages a Markovian jump-diffusion process to model these symmetry-breaking dynamics, enabling it to traverse different space groups in a physically motivated manner. Our model, dubbed \emph{Symmetry-breaking Crystal Diffusion} (SbCD), introduces a principled approach to explicitly incorporate inter-space-group transitions into the generative process. In de novo generation experiments on MP20 and MPTS-52, SbCD outperforms its symmetry-preserving counterpart by a substantial margin, offering a promising perspective for generative modeling of crystalline materials.

</details>


### [302] [Doubly Robust Estimation of Causal Effect on CVR with Targeted Regularization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13461)
*Jiayi Dan,Bo Li,Lu Deng,Yong Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a new doubly robust causal effect estimator for post-click conversion rate (CVR) built on semiparametric theory, achieving faster convergence than nuisance parameter estimation, and pairs it with a targeted-regularization framework for stability, validated on synthetic and real data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Estimating the causal effect on post-click conversion rate (CVR) is practically important, but applying standard causal inference methods to clicked samples suffers from sample selection bias and inflated variance because non-click data are excluded. Recent "ideal loss" approaches in CVR prediction optimize parameters using an unbiased estimate of the full-sample loss, yet unbiasedness of the loss does not guarantee unbiasedness of the final estimator, leaving a theoretical gap.

Method: The authors revisit the problem through semiparametric theory and develop a doubly robust causal effect estimator specifically designed for chain-structured outcomes like CVR. They derive its theoretical properties in detail, showing it attains a faster convergence rate relative to nuisance parameter estimation, making it more robust when flexible nonparametric estimators (including neural networks) are used. They further design a targeted-regularization framework to improve numerical stability and practical applicability.

Result: Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world data demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed method. The authors also find that naively combining loss debiasing with standard causal estimators underperforms their method, underscoring the need for an estimator tailored to the CVR-style objective with solid theoretical guarantees.

Conclusion: A dedicated doubly robust estimator for CVR-style chain-structured outcomes, grounded in semiparametric theory, provides faster convergence, robustness to flexible nuisance estimators, and superior practical performance over naive combinations of loss debiasing and standard causal estimators.

Abstract: Post-click conversion rate (CVR) is a key metric in various scenarios including e-commerce and advertising, reflecting the efficiency and user experience in the second stage of the conversion process. Estimating the causal effect on CVR is therefore of great practical importance. However, directly applying existing causal inference methods to clicked samples introduces sample selection bias and increased variance due to the exclusion of non-click data. Recent studies on CVR prediction introduce "ideal loss", which optimizes model parameters using an unbiased estimate of the loss over the full sample. Nevertheless, there is no guarantee that unbiasedness of the loss implies unbiasedness of the final estimator.
  We revisit this challenge from the perspective of semiparametric theory. Specifically, we develop a new doubly robust causal effect estimator for chain-structured outcomes such as CVR, and derive its theoretical properties in detail. It achieves a faster convergence rate compared to nuisance parameters estimation and is therefore more robust when using flexible nonparametric estimators, including neural networks. Based on these theoretical findings, we further design a framework based on targeted regularization to improve numerical stability and practical applicability.
  Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world data demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of our method. In addition, we find that naively combining loss debiasing with standard causal estimators underperforms our method, highlighting the necessity of developing the new estimator tailored to this CVR-style objective with solid theoretical guarantees.

</details>


### [303] [Active-Trace Complexity Bounds for Moreau--Yosida Unadjusted Langevin Sampling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13467)
*Yuchen Xin,Zhihua Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper analyzes MYULA for composite sampling and shows the leading discretization error is governed by a "reference active trace" rather than the worst-case curvature bound d/λ, improving complexity from Õ(ε⁻³) to Õ(ε⁻²) for common structured penalties.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing MYULA complexity results rely on the global curvature bound d/λ of the Moreau envelope, which is overly pessimistic for structured nonsmooth penalties (lasso, group, total variation). The authors aim to sharpen convergence guarantees by identifying a sharper, problem-specific quantity that controls the discretization error.

Method: The authors decompose the MYULA iteration error and show it is controlled by the "reference active trace" B_ref, defined as the average of a_λ = tr H_λ (the trace of the a.e./weak Hessian of the Moreau envelope g_λ) along the heat substep of one update started from π_λ. They prove an iteration complexity bound in terms of B_ref, the constant M_λ (an a.e. upper bound for a_λ), the strong convexity m, L_f, and τ_f, measured in √m W₂ to π_λ. They also establish a Moreau-bias bound √m W₂(π_λ, π) ≤ G²λ/4, and use curvature-tube estimates for piecewise-linear, lasso-type, group, and total-variation penalties to show B_ref is independent of λ.

Result: Up to logarithmic factors, N ≲ (1/m)[L_f + (τ_f + G² + B_ref)/ε_alg² + M_λ/ε_alg] iterations ensure √m W₂(μ_N, π_λ) ≤ ε_alg. The Moreau bias is bounded by √m W₂(π_λ, π) ≤ G²λ/4, so choosing λ ≍ ε/G² yields an end-to-end guarantee for π. The universal bound B_ref ≤ d/λ gives Õ(ε⁻³); for structured penalties, curvature-tube estimates make B_ref independent of λ, yielding Õ(ε⁻²) for the same classical MYULA kernel.

Conclusion: By replacing the global curvature bound d/λ with the reference active trace B_ref, the paper achieves refined MYULA complexity guarantees and, for common structured penalties, recovers Õ(ε⁻²) — matching sharper rates without modifying the algorithm.

Abstract: We study the Moreau--Yosida unadjusted Langevin algorithm (MYULA) for the nonsmooth composite target \[ π(dx)\propto \exp\{-f(x)-g(x)\}\,dx, \qquad x\in\mathbb R^d, \] where \(f\) is \(m\)-strongly convex with \(L_f\)-Lipschitz gradient and \(g\) is convex and \(G\)-Lipschitz. Let \(g_λ\) be the Moreau envelope of \(g\), \(π_λ\) the corresponding smoothed target, and \(a_λ=\operatorname{tr}H_λ\), where \(H_λ\) is the a.e./weak Hessian of \(g_λ\). We show that the leading MYULA discretization error is controlled by the reference active trace \(B_{\mathrm{ref}}\), the average of \(a_λ\) along the heat substep of one MYULA update started from \(π_λ\), rather than by the global curvature bound \(d/λ\). If \(M_λ\) is an a.e. upper bound for \(a_λ\), then, up to logarithmic factors, \[ N \lesssim \frac{1}{m} \left[ L_f + \frac{ τ_f+G^2+B_{\mathrm{ref}} }{ \varepsilon_{\mathrm{alg}}^2 } + \frac{M_λ}{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{alg}}} \right], \qquad τ_f:= \sup_x\operatorname{tr}\nabla^2 f(x), \] iterations suffice to ensure \(\sqrt m\,W_2(μ_N,π_λ)\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{alg}}\), where \(μ_N\) is the law of the \(N\)-th iterate and \(W_2\) is the quadratic Wasserstein distance. We also prove the Moreau-bias bound \[ \sqrt m\,W_2(π_λ,π) \leq \frac{G^2λ}{4}. \] Thus, choosing \(λ\asymp\varepsilon/G^2\) gives an end-to-end guarantee for \(π\). The universal estimate \(B_{\mathrm{ref}}\leq d/λ\) yields \(\widetilde O(\varepsilon^{-3})\) accuracy dependence. For the structured piecewise-linear, lasso-type, group, and total-variation penalties considered here, curvature--tube estimates make \(B_{\mathrm{ref}}\) independent of \(λ\), yielding \(\widetilde O(\varepsilon^{-2})\) for the same classical MYULA kernel.

</details>


### [304] [Synthetic Persona Pretraining: Alignment from Token Zero](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13482)
*Julian Minder,Viktor Moskvoretskii,Raghav Singhal,Difan Jiao,Andy Arditi,Shaobo Cui,Yiderigun Borjigin,Kartik Bali,Stefan Krsteski,Harsh Raj,Huu Nguyen,Jannik Brinkmann,Ashton Anderson,Roland Aydin,Robert West*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces Synthetic Persona Pretraining (SPP), a method that installs a value-aligned assistant persona from the very start of pretraining (token zero) rather than after, showing it improves alignment, jailbreak robustness, and constitution following without hurting capabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current alignment and the assistant identity are typically introduced only after pretraining, once behavioral priors are already fixed. This makes values a thin overlay rather than deeply rooted, leaving models vulnerable to misalignment. The authors seek a paradigm where the desired persona is installed from the beginning of pretraining.

Method: Synthetic Persona Pretraining (SPP) has three stages: (1) annotate pretraining documents with value-aligned first-person reflections derived from a normative value constitution; (2) pretrain with standard cross-entropy loss on both the standard documents and their reflections, installing the desired persona among many others; (3) post-train on user-assistant dialogue data to bind the persona to the assistant identity ("persona binding"). Models up to 3B parameters are pretrained on 500B tokens.

Result: SPP improves constitution following and jailbreak robustness and reduces misalignment rate in out-of-distribution moral dilemmas, while preserving capabilities. Early intervention matters: introducing SPP only at the end of pretraining yields weaker constitution adherence, no shift in value priorities, and less aligned choices in dilemmas. The advantage depends on persona binding and increases with pretraining budget.

Conclusion: Shaping values early is critical for alignment, and pretraining-time persona interventions (SPP) are an effective approach, outperforming late-stage or post-pretraining-only alignment.

Abstract: As language-model-based AI is increasingly deployed in autonomous settings, aligning its goals and values with those of humans becomes critical. Today, alignment, and the assistant identity itself, are typically introduced only after pretraining, once behavioral priors are already established. This can make values a thin overlay, rather than deeply rooted, and facilitate subsequent misalignment. Pursuing a different paradigm, we introduce Synthetic Persona Pretraining (SPP), which installs the desired assistant persona from token zero in pretraining. First, we annotate pretraining documents with value-aligned first-person reflections derived from a normative value constitution. Second, we pretrain via the standard cross-entropy loss on standard pretraining documents as well as their reflections, which installs the desired persona among a multitude of other personas. Finally, we post-train on user-assistant dialogue data, which binds this desired persona to the assistant identity, a process we call persona binding. By pretraining models up to 3B parameters on 500B tokens, we show that SPP improves constitution following and jailbreak robustness, and reduces the misalignment rate in out-of-distribution moral dilemmas, while preserving capabilities. Early intervention matters: compared with alignment from token zero, introducing SPP only at the end of pretraining yields weaker constitution adherence, does not shift value priorities, and leads to less aligned choices in dilemmas. This advantage depends on persona binding and, importantly, increases with pretraining budget. Overall, our results show that shaping values early is critical for alignment and establish pretraining-time persona interventions as an effective approach to do so.

</details>


### [305] [Sparse Orthogonal Regression Technique: A Spectral Framework for Equation Discovery, Approximation, and Integration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13504)
*Sabin Roman,Ljupco Todorovski,Saso Dzeroski*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SORT is a sparse spectral framework that learns orthonormal-basis expansions directly from noisy, irregularly sampled data via L1-regularized regression, used mainly for data-driven discovery of ODEs and also for nonlinear approximation and integral estimation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing data-driven equation-discovery methods (symbolic regression, grammar-based discovery, SINDy-style sparse identification) rely on selecting terms from finite libraries or grammars. When the library misses a problem-specific nonlinearity, these methods fail brittly. There is a need for a complementary representation that avoids brittle term selection and captures vector fields compactly in a problem-adapted spectral basis.

Method: SORT uses sparse orthogonal regression: vector fields are represented in chosen orthogonal bases and learned as sparse coefficient expansions. Expansion coefficients are estimated directly from observations via L1-regularized regression, avoiding explicit quadrature or analytic inner-product evaluation. This yields a compact spectral representation that can later guide searches for simpler analytic forms.

Result: Across dynamical-system experiments, SORT matches or improves upon library-based sparse-regression baselines when the basis is well adapted to the problem, and degrades more stably under sparse sampling, noisy derivative estimates, and representation mismatch. Dominant low-order coefficients persist as model order increases, supporting order-consistent model growth. Examples show that a finite library missing a problem-specific nonlinearity can fail while SORT's representation remains usable. The same learned expansion also supports nonlinear approximation and estimation of complex, high-dimensional integrals via coefficient readout.

Conclusion: SORT provides a reusable intermediate representation for system identification, approximation, and integration. It shifts the challenge from brittle selection among generic terms to explicit basis design tailored to the problem domain, making basis design an explicit part of the scientific modeling problem.

Abstract: We develop the Sparse Orthogonal Regression Technique (SORT), a sparse spectral framework for learning orthonormal-basis expansions from noisy and irregularly sampled data. SORT estimates expansion coefficients directly from observations using L1-regularized regression, avoiding explicit quadrature or analytic inner-product evaluation. The central application is data-driven discovery of ordinary differential equations: vector fields are represented in chosen orthogonal bases and learned as sparse coefficient expansions. This provides a complementary route to symbolic regression, grammar-based discovery, and SINDy-style sparse identification by first recovering a compact spectral representation, which can later guide searches for simpler analytic forms. Across the dynamical-system experiments, SORT matches or improves upon library-based sparse-regression baselines when the basis is well adapted to the problem, and shows more stable degradation under sparse sampling, noisy derivative estimates, and representation mismatch. Specific examples illustrate why this representation is useful: if a finite library misses the problem-specific nonlinearity, the resulting model can fail. SORT is not immune to mismatch, but it shifts the problem away from brittle selection among generic terms to basis design adapted to the problem domain. The experiments also show that dominant low-order coefficients persist as model order increases, supporting order-consistent model growth. Beyond equation discovery, the same learned expansion supports nonlinear approximation and estimation of complex, high-dimensional integrals by coefficient readout. Overall, SORT provides a reusable intermediate representation for system identification, approximation, and integration, while making basis design an explicit part of the scientific modeling problem.

</details>


### [306] [Intern-S2-Preview: Scientific Agentic Foundation Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13505)
*Lei Bai,Jiaqi Cao,Chiyu Chen,Guanzhou Chen,Kai Chen,Guangran Cheng,Erfei Cui,Xuanlang Dai,Shengyuan Ding,Shangheng Du,Yanhui Duan,Yue Fan,Youqing Fang,Quan Gan,Yuanyuan Gao,Jiaye Ge,Lixin Gu,Yuzhe Gu,Qipeng Guo,Junjun He,Xin Hong,Ming Hu,Zhouqi Hua,Haian Huang,Junhao Huang,Zixian Huang,Minxi Jin,Lingkai Kong,Alexander Lam,Zehao Li,Zonglin Li,Tianhao Liang,Dahua Lin,Junyao Lin,Tianyang Lin,Zhouhan Lin,Jiangning Liu,Jin Liu,Kuikun Liu,Wenran Liu,Yifei Liu,Yuhong Liu,Yuhong Liu,Zhoumianze Liu,Ziyan Liu,Ziyu Liu,Haijun Lv,Han Lv,Chengqi Lyu,Le Ma,Ningsheng Ma,Zerun Ma,Haoyang Peng,Runyu Peng,Jifei Shan,Zixin Shang,Kou Shi,Xiang Shi,Qisheng Su,Xuerui Su,Hao Sun,Xiao Sun,Yanan Sun,Yu Sun,Huanze Tang,Yinghao Tang,Wenhui Tian,Zhongbo Tian,Bingli Wang,Haomin Wang,Jiarui Wang,Jingzhi Wang,Rui Wang,Xiquan Wang,Yi Wang,Zhecan Wang,Ziyi Wang,Zun Wang,Rubin Wei,Lianyi Wu,Wen Wu,Yue Wu,Yuhan Wu,Zhenyu Wu,Zijian Wu,Shuhao Xing,Jun Xu,Xingle Xu,Xuenan Xu,Xiangchao Yan,Ziang Yan,Bowen Yang,Danni Yang,Lin Yang,Zhiqi Yang,Qian Yao,Haochen Ye,Peng Ye,Jinhui Yin,Jiashuo Yu,Dingbo Yuan,Fei Yuan,Yuhang Zang,Bo Zhang,Chao Zhang,Chen Zhang,Hongjie Zhang,Junming Zhang,Wenlong Zhang,Wenwei Zhang,Yiming Zhang,Zhuo Zhang,Ziyang Zhang,Haiteng Zhao,Penghao Zhao,Yibo Zhao,Zhonghan Zhao,Zhihang Zhong,Bowen Zhou,Peiheng Zhou,Xin Zhou,Xinyu Zhou,Yunhua Zhou,Dongsheng Zhu,Yicheng Zou*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Intern-S2-Preview is a series of scientific agentic foundation models (up to 397B parameters) built through scientific multimodal pre-training plus a unified post-training pipeline (SFT, multi-task RL, agentic RL, on-policy distillation). It adds time series forecasting and a separate Memory Decoder path for cheap scientific specialization, achieving competitive/leading results across scientific, multimodal, agentic, and general benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scientific discovery demands AI that can reason over heterogeneous scientific evidence, interact with tools/environments, and sustain progress over long task horizons—capabilities lacking in general-purpose models. The work aims to build foundation models specialized for multimodal scientific understanding, reasoning, generation, and long-horizon agentic tasks.

Method: A two-stage pipeline: (1) scientific multimodal pre-training on rendered scientific documents, interleaved image-text data, and scientific corpora; (2) unified post-training comprising supervised fine-tuning, scalable multi-task RL, black-box and white-box agentic RL, and on-policy distillation. Efficiency/stability is handled via partial rollout with off-policy correction, adaptive length regularization, online speculative decoding, robust multi-task optimization, and trace-aware experience assembly. Architecturally, Intern-S2-Preview-397B extends time series modeling to numerical forecasting, and a separate Memory Decoder (Memory Decoder) path enables rapid scientific specialization without modifying the frozen 397B backbone.

Result: Intern-S2-Preview-397B achieves competitive or leading results on scientific, multimodal, agentic, and general benchmarks. Time series modules improve scientific signal understanding/forecasting on SciTS. Separately, Intern-MemDec-4B raises Biology-Instructions average score from 56.92 to 60.32 without touching the frozen 397B backbone.

Conclusion: The Intern-S2-Preview series demonstrates that combining scientific multimodal pre-training, a unified RL-heavy post-training pipeline, and modular extensions (time series forecasting, memory-augmented lightweight adapters) yields strong, versatile scientific agentic models, with the Memory Decoder offering an efficient path to domain specialization on a frozen large backbone.

Abstract: Scientific discovery increasingly requires AI systems that can reason over scientific evidence of heterogeneous modalities, interact with scientific tools and environments, and sustain progress across long task horizons. We present Intern-S2-Preview, a series of scientific agentic foundation models designed to support multimodal scientific understanding, reasoning, generation, and long-horizon tasks. The training pipeline begins with scientific multimodal pre-training over rendered scientific documents, interleaved image-text data, and diverse scientific corpora. Starting from the pretrained checkpoint, we apply a unified post-training pipeline consisting of supervised fine-tuning, scalable multi-task reinforcement learning (RL), black- and white-box agentic RL, and on-policy distillation. This pipeline is supported by practical techniques that improve rollout and training stability and efficiency, including partial rollout with off-policy correction, adaptive length regularization, online speculative decoding, robust multi-task optimization, and trace-aware experience assembly for agentic tasks. At the architecture level, Intern-S2-Preview-397B extends time series modelling from efficient long-sequence understanding to numerical forecasting, while Memory Decoder is studied as a separate memory-augmented path for rapid scientific specialization without modifying the frozen 397B backbone. Evaluations across scientific, multimodal, agentic, and general-purpose benchmarks show that Intern-S2-Preview-397B achieves competitive or leading results in multiple settings. The time series modules improve scientific signal understanding and forecasting on SciTS, while the separate Intern-MemDec-4B extension improves the Biology-Instructions average score from 56.92 to 60.32 without modifying the frozen 397B backbone.

</details>


### [307] [Intervention-Aware Clinical World Model for Post-Op Outcome Forecasting in Cardiology](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13518)
*Yunsung Chung,Yingshuo Liu,Abboud F. Hassan,Han Feng,Mary M. Maleckar,Nassir Marrouche,Jihun Hamm*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes an intervention-aware clinical world model that models post-procedure recovery as an evolving structured latent state updated through asynchronous, time-ordered events (procedural context, covariates, elapsed time, physiological embeddings), using follow-up imaging only for training-time supervision. Applied to atrial fibrillation ablation on DECAAF-II, it achieves AUROC 0.756, AUPRC 0.777 for recurrence prediction and a scar-extent MAE of 2.971 percentage points without needing follow-up MRI at inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most clinical prediction models treat outcomes as a one-step mapping from baseline to a future endpoint, ignoring the irregular, asynchronous trajectory of post-intervention events (clinical observations, medication changes, repeat interventions, physiological measurements) that can shift risk over time. The authors aim to capture this temporal structure and make predictions that update with accumulating evidence.

Method: A clinical world model encodes baseline imaging into a 3D spatial latent state, then sequentially evolves this state using time-ordered post-intervention events: procedural context, static covariates, elapsed time, and peri-event physiological embeddings. Follow-up imaging is used only as a training-time supervision signal via a latent forecasting objective. The framework is validated with repeated internal cross-validation on the DECAAF-II dataset, supporting recurrence-risk queries at multiple horizons and retrospective editing of blanking-period records.

Result: On atrial fibrillation ablation, irregular 90-day post-procedure records provide clinically meaningful recurrence-risk evidence. The model achieves AUROC 0.756 and AUPRC 0.777 for recurrence prediction, and a scar-extent MAE of 2.971 percentage points while requiring no follow-up MRI intensities at inference time.

Conclusion: Modeling post-intervention recovery as an evolving latent state over asynchronous events improves long-term recurrence-risk prediction and enables horizon-based queries and input editing, all without needing follow-up imaging at inference.

Abstract: Many clinical prediction models treat post-intervention outcomes as a one-step mapping from baseline measurements to a future endpoint. However, recovery after a procedure often unfolds as an irregular trajectory: clinical observations, medication changes, repeat interventions, and physiological measurements are recorded asynchronously and can change risk assessment over time. We propose an intervention-aware clinical world model that represents each patient with a structured latent state and evolves it through time-ordered post-intervention events. The model first encodes baseline imaging into a 3D spatial latent state. It then updates this state using procedural context, static covariates, elapsed time, and peri-event physiological embeddings. Follow-up imaging provides training-only supervision through a latent forecasting objective. We apply the framework to atrial fibrillation ablation. During the 90-day recovery window, irregular post-procedure records provide clinically meaningful evidence for long-term recurrence risk. In repeated internal cross-validation on DECAAF-II, our model achieves AUROC 0.756 and AUPRC 0.777 for recurrence prediction. It also achieves a scar-extent MAE of 2.971 percentage points without requiring follow-up MRI intensities at inference. The learned state supports recurrence-risk queries at different horizons and retrospective input editing of blanking-period records.

</details>


### [308] [The data geometry of masking diffusion: Certified-optimal schedules via unmasking growth complexity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13520)
*Martin J. Wainwright*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces Unmasking Growth Complexity (UGC), a path-resolved measure of data geometry for masking diffusion in discrete sampling, which yields a unified analysis of unmasking schemes, optimized schedules, and certified-optimal samplers with strong dimension-dependent gains over coarse schedules.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Masking diffusion is a key framework for discrete sampling, but existing analyses lack a unified, geometry-aware measure connecting discretization error (KL) to sampling schedule design. The authors seek to understand how data geometry should shape adaptive unmasking schedules and to obtain provably near-optimal samplers with guaranteed error.

Method: They define the path-resolved UGC measure whose local increments control KL discretization error, providing a unified treatment of Bernoulli-subset and fixed-cardinality unmasking. In log-reveal-odds coordinates they derive optimized single-block and multi-block schedules. They estimate UGC increments from samples via KL increments along coupled reveal trajectories, yielding certified-optimal samplers. They also connect aggregate UGC mass to multivariate dependence measures and perform a fine-partition limit analysis linking the squared integral of the square-root UGC density to the sharp leading-order Euler discretization error.

Result: The construction yields samplers achieving a prescribed KL error with high probability and iteration complexity within a constant factor of the oracle procedure. In the fine-partition limit, the squared integral of the square-root UGC density determines the sharp optimal discretization error. Examples show substantial dimension-dependent gains over coarse schedules, including ~Ω(√d) improvements with only a constant number of adaptively placed blocks.

Conclusion: UGC provides a principled, geometry-aware foundation for discrete masking diffusion, unifying theory, enabling certified-optimal adaptive schedules, and demonstrating significant dimension-dependent improvements over coarse schedules.

Abstract: We study masking diffusion for discrete sampling and introduce a path-resolved measure of data geometry called the \emph{unmasking growth complexity} ({\textsf{UGC}\xspace}). Its local increments directly control Kullback--Leibler (KL) discretization error, yielding a unified analysis of Bernoulli-subset and fixed-cardinality unmasking schemes. In log-reveal-odds coordinates, this structure yields optimized single-block and multi-block schedules, and quantifies the gains from adapting computational effort to data geometry. Crucially, we show how {\textsf{UGC}\xspace} increments can be estimated from samples via KL increments along coupled reveal trajectories. This leads to \emph{certified-optimal} samplers that achieve a prescribed KL error with high probability and iteration complexity within a constant factor of the corresponding oracle procedure. Collapsing the \ugc path yields the aggregate {\textsf{UGC}\xspace} mass, which connects to classical multivariate dependence measures and complexity measures from previous analyses of discrete diffusion. In the fine-partition limit, the squared integral of the square-root {\textsf{UGC}\xspace} density determines the sharp leading-order optimal Euler discretization error. Examples exhibit substantial dimension-dependent gains over coarse schedules, including $\widetildeΩ(\sqrt{d})$ improvements achievable with a constant number of adaptively placed blocks.

</details>


### [309] [DARTree: Speculative Diffusion Decoding with Autoregressive Draft Trees](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13524)
*Tianyi Li,Yaxin Luo,Xinyi Shang,Zhiqiang Shen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DARTree is a training-free speculative decoding method that turns a pretrained autoregressive correction head from a single-chain into a tree-based verification process, achieving state-of-the-art acceptance length and speedup across math, code, and chat benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion-based drafters predict token blocks in parallel with low latency, but their distributions are marginal (position-wise) rather than conditioned on tokens along each draft path. Existing approaches trade off: recurrent correction adds causal conditioning but only along a single chain, while diffusion-based tree construction broadens candidate coverage but lacks per-branch correction. The goal is to combine causal correction with tree-based candidate coverage without retraining.

Method: DARTree extends a pretrained AR correction head from chains to trees. It first constructs a fixed-width candidate tree by expanding and scoring all nodes at each depth in a single batch, then applies best-first pruning only to select the verification tree, decoupling AR-head inference from sequential heap operations. The method is training-free.

Result: Across seven math, code, and chat benchmarks, DARTree achieves the highest average acceptance length and speedup in all four model--temperature configurations. It accepts up to 12.97 tokens per verification round (98.6% more than DFlash and 27.9% more than Domino in the same setting) and reaches up to 9.73x lossless speedup over locally measured autoregressive decoding.

Conclusion: By unifying AR-head causal correction with tree-structured candidate expansion, DARTree substantially improves verification efficiency and decoding speed while remaining lossless and training-free.

Abstract: Speculative decoding losslessly accelerates autoregressive language models by verifying multiple draft tokens in parallel. Diffusion-based drafters further reduce proposal latency by predicting an entire token block in parallel, but their position-wise distributions are marginal rather than conditioned on tokens selected along each draft path. Existing recurrent correction incorporates causal information along a single draft chain, whereas diffusion-based tree construction broadens candidate coverage without carrying this correction along individual branches. We introduce DARTree, a training-free speculative decoding method that extends a pretrained AR correction head from chains to trees. DARTree first constructs a fixed-width candidate tree by expanding and scoring all nodes at each depth in a single batch, and then only applies best-first pruning to select the verification tree, decoupling AR-head inference from sequential heap operations. Across seven math, code, and chat benchmarks, DARTree achieves the highest average acceptance length and speedup in all four model--temperature configurations, accepting up to 12.97 tokens per verification round, 98.6\% more than DFlash and 27.9\% more than Domino in the same setting, and reaching up to 9.73$\times$ lossless speedup over locally measured autoregressive decoding.

</details>


### [310] [Exponential Convex Calibration Dimension for the Multi-Label Jaccard Measure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13549)
*Mingyuan Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper studies calibration and regret for the Jaccard (IoU) score in multi-label classification, proving that exact calibration requires exponentially many prediction coordinates (between 2^(s-1) and 2^s - 1), while any fixed additive regret tolerance can be achieved with polynomial-dimensional convex surrogates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The Jaccard score is a standard loss in multi-label classification and binary segmentation, but its calibration properties were poorly understood. The authors aim to characterize how many prediction coordinates are needed to exactly calibrate the Jaccard loss, and whether practical polynomial-dimensional convex surrogates can achieve small Jaccard regret.

Method: The authors prove nonsingularity and affine dimension results for the Jaccard, shifted-loss, and ordinary loss matrices using a finite MinHash Gram representation combined with Boolean Möbius inversion. They establish calibration dimension bounds CCdim between 2^(s-1) and 2^s - 1, using a factorially weighted distribution with 2^(s-1)+1 supported outcomes and Bayes-optimal reports for the lower bound. They then construct two polynomial-dimensional surrogates: an F1-to-Jaccard regret transfer giving bounded asymptotic regret, and a MinHash square-loss surrogate (direct and signed variants) achieving additive regret floor alpha with explicit dimension guarantees.

Result: The Jaccard, shifted-loss, and ordinary loss matrices are nonsingular, and loss columns have affine dimension 2^s - 1. Exact calibration requires exponential dimension: 2^(s-1) ≤ CCdim(L^Jac) ≤ 2^s - 1. An F1-to-Jaccard transfer yields a polynomial-time rule with asymptotic Jaccard regret at most 3 - 2√2. A MinHash square-loss surrogate attains Jaccard-regret floor alpha uniformly over arbitrary conditional label distributions, with dimension O((s^2 + s log(1/ρ))/α^2) for the direct construction and O((s + log(1/ρ))/α^2) for the signed variant, holding with probability at least 1 - ρ.

Conclusion: There is a fundamental trade-off: zero-regret (exact) calibration of the Jaccard loss requires exponentially many coordinates, but every fixed additive regret tolerance admits polynomial prediction dimension. This resolves the tension between the theoretically exponential calibration cost and the practical feasibility of strong Jaccard learners.

Abstract: The per-instance Jaccard score, or intersection over union (IoU), is standard in multi-label classification and binary segmentation. With $s$ labels, its loss matrix has $2^s$ outcomes and reports. Under the convention $\mathrm{Jac}(\varnothing,\varnothing)=1$, we prove that the Jaccard score, shifted-loss, and ordinary loss matrices are nonsingular and that the loss columns have affine dimension $2^s-1$. The proof combines a finite MinHash Gram representation with Boolean Möbius inversion. For exact calibration, we prove $2^{s-1} \leq \mathrm{CCdim}(L^{\mathrm{Jac}}) \leq 2^s-1$. The lower bound uses a factorially weighted distribution with $2^{s-1}+1$ supported outcomes and Bayes-optimal reports. Consequently, every exactly calibrated convex surrogate requires exponentially many prediction coordinates. We also give two polynomial-dimensional approximation guarantees with explicit regret transfers. A new $F_1$-to-Jaccard transfer turns an existing $(s^2+1)$-dimensional $F_1$ surrogate into a polynomial-time rule with asymptotic Jaccard regret at most $3-2\sqrt{2}$. For any $α>0$ and $0<ρ<1$, a MinHash square-loss surrogate attains Jaccard-regret floor $α$ uniformly over arbitrary conditional label distributions. With probability at least $1-ρ$, the direct construction has dimension $O((s^2+s\log(1/ρ))/α^2)$, while a signed variant has dimension $O((s+\log(1/ρ))/α^2)$. Thus zero-regret calibration requires exponential dimension, whereas every fixed additive regret tolerance admits polynomial prediction dimension.

</details>


### [311] [Defensive Boosting for Online Probabilistic Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13554)
*Georgy Noarov,Aaron Roth*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces the Defensive Booster, an efficient online forecasting algorithm that simultaneously guarantees Brier score competitiveness with the span of a weak hypothesis class and error reduction under smooth weak-learning conditions, outperforming existing methods in speed and predictive accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing online boosting approaches give only one of two desirable guarantees: online gradient boosting competes in Brier score but fails without an accurate predictor in the span, while online weak-to-strong boosting drives error to zero only under a weak-learning condition. The goal is a single algorithm achieving both guarantees efficiently.

Method: The authors propose a defensive forecasting algorithm (Defensive Booster) that operationalizes the dual view of boosting. When randomized classification error stays high, mistake weights form a smooth reweighting on which every weak hypothesis has low edge, certifying ex-post that the weak-learning condition fails. A strongly adaptive variant extends both guarantees to every time interval. The algorithm accesses only one weak learner rather than maintaining large ensembles.

Result: On adaptive sequences, Brier score is competitive with the best span prediction at the same rate as online gradient boosting; under the smooth weak-learning condition, Brier score and randomized classification error match online classification boosting rates. Experiments on synthetic and real data streams show strong predictive performance (often improving over baselines) with orders-of-magnitude faster runtime.

Conclusion: The Defensive Booster unifies the competing guarantees of online gradient boosting and weak-to-strong boosting in one efficient algorithm, providing robustness regardless of weak-learning condition satisfaction, with practical speed and accuracy advantages demonstrated empirically.

Abstract: We study online probabilistic forecasting of binary outcomes chosen by an adaptive adversary. Given an online learning algorithm for a weak hypothesis class $H$, we would like to efficiently obtain two incomparable guarantees that existing online boosting techniques provide separately. Online gradient boosting competes in Brier score with the best predictor induced by the span of $H$ on every sequence, but promises nothing when the span does not contain an accurate predictor. Online weak-to-strong boosting drives classification error to zero under a weak-learning condition, but promises little when that condition fails.
  We give a simple defensive forecasting algorithm, the Defensive Booster, that obtains both guarantees. On every adaptive sequence, its Brier score is competitive with the best prediction induced by the span of $H$ at the same rate as online gradient boosting; simultaneously, whenever the realized transcript satisfies the smooth weak-learning condition, its Brier score and randomized classification error satisfy the same rate guarantee as online classification boosting. This is achieved by operationalizing the "dual view" of boosting: When the algorithm's randomized classification error is persistently high, its mistake weights form a smooth reweighting on which every weak hypothesis has low edge, yielding an ex-post hard-core certificate that the weak-learning condition fails. We also develop a strongly adaptive variant, which satisfies both guarantees on every time interval. The Defensive Booster is very efficient: it accesses just one weak-class learner, whereas the prior online boosting methods we compare against maintain large weak-learner ensembles. Experiments on synthetic and real data streams demonstrate its strong predictive performance (sometimes substantially improving over all prior baselines) coupled with orders-of-magnitude faster runtime.

</details>


<div id='cs.IR'></div>

# cs.IR [[Back]](#toc)

### [312] [Test-Time Optimization of Query Embeddings with Ranking Aware Reward Maximization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12569)
*Tianyu Chen,Jiaxing Wu*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: TTT-Embed distills test-time ranking rewards into a lightweight learned vector in a frozen encoder's output embedding space, making rewards reusable without touching model weights or the index. A single scope parameter (global/task/query) trades reusability against specificity under a fixed reward budget, achieving large nDCG@10 gains on MTEB retrieval tasks while generalizing to unseen queries/tasks and fixing catastrophic forgetting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing dense retrievers discard test-time ranking rewards (from rerankers or LLM judges) after a single query. Making rewards reusable via weight updates requires parameter access (impossible for closed-source models) and is computationally prohibitive. The paper aims to retain the benefit of ranking rewards while avoiding weight modification and enabling budget-efficient adaptation for any embedding model, including closed-source APIs.

Method: TTT-Embed freezes the base encoder and optimizes a lightweight learned vector directly in the model's output embedding space, driven purely by scalar ranking scores assigned to the retriever's own candidate documents. It needs no model weights, ground-truth labels, or index changes. A single scope parameter controls reward reuse at global, task, or query level, creating a principled trade-off between reusability and specificity under a fixed reward computation budget.

Result: Across five embedding models and 15 MTEB retrieval tasks, TTT-Embed improves test-time retrieval by up to +8.36 nDCG@10. Learned states generalize to unseen queries (+8.57 nDCG@10) and unseen tasks (+4.71 nDCG@10). TTT-Embed also resolves catastrophic forgetting: with base weights fully frozen, it recovers degraded general capabilities by up to +8.00 nDCG@10 (surpassing the original base model) while preserving in-domain specialization. As the reward budget scales, the optimal sharing scope shifts dynamically from global-wise to task-wise to query-wise.

Conclusion: Ranking rewards can be treated as a reusable test-time state, distilled into an embedding-space vector without weight or index modification. This enables budget-efficient, specificity-controlled adaptation for any embedding model, including closed-source APIs, with strong gains, cross-query/task generalization, and recovery from catastrophic forgetting.

Abstract: Dense retrievers rank documents using vector similarity between a frozen encoder and a precomputed index. While test-time ranking rewards from a reranker or LLM judge can improve results, existing methods discard this signal after a single query. Updating the retriever's weights makes rewards reusable, but this requires parameter access, which is unavailable for closed-source models, and is computationally prohibitive. We propose TTT-Embed (Test-Time Tuning of Embeddings), a framework that distills ranking rewards into a lightweight, learned vector within the output embedding space of a frozen model. This vector is optimized purely from scalar ranking scores assigned to the retriever's own candidate documents, requiring no access to model weights, ground-truth labels, or modifications to index. A single scope parameter controls rewards reuse (global, task, or query), enabling a principled trade-off between reusability and specificity under a fixed reward computation budget. We demonstrate that as the available reward budget scales, the optimal sharing scope shifts dynamically from global-wise to task-wise and finally to query-wise. Evaluated across five embedding models and 15 MTEB retrieval tasks, TTT-Embed improves test-time retrieval by up to +8.36 nDCG@10. Crucially, the learned states generalize effectively to unseen queries (up to +8.57 nDCG@10) and unseen tasks (up to +4.71 nDCG@10). Furthermore, TTT-Embed successfully resolves catastrophic forgetting: by leaving base weights entirely frozen, it recovers degraded general capabilities (up to +8.00 nDCG@10, even surpassing the original base model) while preserving in-domain specialization. These results establish ranking rewards as a reusable test-time state, enabling budget-efficient adaptation for any embedding model, including closed-source APIs.

</details>


### [313] [Knowledge Synthesis Review Framework: Task-Level Benchmarking of LLM-Based Systems for Multi-Source Evidence Synthesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12741)
*Wafa Shafqat,Mark Patterson,Steven N. Liss*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: The paper introduces the Knowledge Synthesis Review (KSR), a human-in-the-loop framework that decomposes evidence synthesis into screening, extraction, analysis, and synthesis, benchmarks LLMs on each task against expert standards, and routes tasks to the best-performing model under expert validation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evidence in rapidly evolving fields is fragmented across heterogeneous sources of varying quality, making timely synthesis difficult. While LLMs could accelerate synthesis, their reliability across the distinct cognitive tasks of a review is uncertain, necessitating a framework that governs LLM assistance without sacrificing rigor or accountability.

Method: The authors benchmarked GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and NotebookLM on a 244-document subset of a 1,893-document corpus on AI and work spanning four source types, against an expert gold standard with 92.2% agreement (kappa = 0.80). KSR decomposes synthesis into screening, extraction, analysis, and synthesis, evaluates LLM-based systems on each task, routes each task to the best performer, and applies continuous expert validation. A post-cutoff contamination check was performed to rule out inflated results from prior model exposure.

Result: No single system led on all tasks. Claude Sonnet 4 had the highest screening accuracy (82.8%) and GPT-5 the highest recall (91.8%) at the cost of specificity. Extraction exceeded 90% agreement for titles and sources but degraded on author and reference fields. Performance was weakest on interpretive analysis and cross-source synthesis, where expert judgment remained essential. The contamination check found no evidence of inflated performance. Applied to the full corpus, the routed workflow revealed cross-source asymmetries and blind spots (e.g., worker well-being, small firms, the Global South) that single-source synthesis would miss.

Conclusion: KSR provides a transparent, auditable, model-agnostic framework for governing LLM assistance in research synthesis while preserving human accountability, and highlights that expert judgment remains indispensable for interpretive and cross-source analysis.

Abstract: Evidence in rapidly evolving fields is fragmented across academic studies, industry reports, policy documents, and media sources that differ in quality, structure, and purpose, making timely synthesis difficult. Large language models (LLMs) may accelerate this work, but their reliability across the distinct cognitive tasks of a review remains uncertain. We introduce the Knowledge Synthesis Review (KSR), a human-in-the-loop framework that decomposes evidence synthesis into screening, extraction, analysis, and synthesis, benchmarks LLM-based systems on each task against expert reference standards, and routes each task to the best-performing system under continuous expert validation. We evaluated GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and NotebookLM on a 244-document benchmark subset drawn from a 1,893-document corpus on AI and work spanning four source types, against a gold standard with high inter-rater reliability (92.2% agreement, kappa = 0.80). No system led on all tasks. Claude Sonnet 4 achieved the highest screening accuracy (82.8%) and GPT-5 the highest recall (91.8%) at the expense of lower specificity. Extraction exceeded 90% agreement for titles and sources but degraded in author and reference fields. Performance declined most in interpretive analysis and cross-source synthesis, where expert judgment remained essential. A contamination check on post-cutoff documents showed no evidence that prior exposure inflated results. Applied to the full corpus, the routed workflow surfaced cross-source asymmetries and blind spots that single-source synthesis would miss, including worker well-being, small firms, and the Global South. KSR offers a transparent, auditable, model-agnostic framework for governing LLM assistance in research synthesis while preserving human accountability.

</details>


### [314] [DrEM: Dual-Side Robust Ensemble Ranking from Noisy User Preference Predictions in Video Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12778)
*Canwei Huang,Tiantian He,Xiaoxiao Xu,Jun Zhang,Ziran Deng,Weike Pan,Chunjie Chen,Kaiqiao Zhan*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: DrEM is a dual-side robust ensemble ranking framework for industrial video recommendation that mitigates prediction noise in pxtrs, using a risk-denoising robust loss and a preference-preserving ranking consistency regularizer, validated by offline experiments and online A/B tests.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In multi-stage industrial video recommendation, ensemble ranking fuses multi-task predictions (pxtrs) into a ranking score. Since true user satisfaction is unobservable, pxtrs serve both as input features and as sources for constructing proxy preferences. However, pxtrs are noisy predictions, and this noise propagates to downstream learning on two sides: on the supervision side it flips proxy preferences and introduces erroneous gradients, while on the feature side it destabilizes ranking scores. Existing methods treat pxtrs as reliable and ignore this noise.

Method: DrEM proposes two complementary components: (1) a risk-denoising robust loss that corrects the empirical risk using an estimated preference flip probability, and (2) sampling perturbations from the prediction noise distribution combined with a preference-preserving ranking consistency regularizer to improve feature-side output stability. The authors also derive an approximate distribution of the prediction noise and prove the robust loss remains superior under flip probability estimation error.

Result: Extensive offline experiments and large-scale online A/B tests demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of DrEM compared to existing ensemble ranking approaches.

Conclusion: Treating pxtrs as reliable signals causes prediction noise to degrade both supervision and feature sides of ensemble ranking. DrEM's dual-side denoising framework, with theoretical guarantees on noise distribution approximation and robustness to estimation error, effectively addresses this issue and achieves validated improvements in real-world video recommendation systems.

Abstract: Industrial video recommendation systems typically adopt a multi-stage architecture. At the ensemble ranking stage, multi-dimensional user preference predictions (pxtrs) from an upstream multi-task model are fused into a unified ranking score to reflect user satisfaction. Since users' true satisfaction is difficult to observe directly, ensemble ranking models commonly use pxtrs both as input features and as a source for constructing proxy preferences. However, as outputs of an upstream prediction model, pxtrs inevitably contain prediction noise, which propagates to downstream learning across two sides. On the supervision side, noisy pxtrs may flip proxy preferences and introduce erroneous gradients. On the feature side, pxtr noise may propagate through model inputs and destabilize ranking scores. Existing ensemble ranking methods typically treat pxtrs as reliable signals and overlook such prediction noise. To address this, we propose DrEM, a dual-side robust ensemble ranking framework. Our DrEM introduces a risk-denoising robust loss that corrects the empirical risk using estimated preference flip probability. Meanwhile, it samples perturbations from the distribution of prediction noise and introduces a preference-preserving ranking consistency regularizer to improve feature-side output stability. Theoretically, we obtain an approximate distribution of the prediction noise and prove that the robust loss remains superior under flip probability estimation error. Extensive offline experiments and large-scale online A/B tests demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of our DrEM.

</details>


### [315] [A Comprehensive Empirical Evaluation of Vector Database Systems for Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search: Performance, Quality, and Resource Trade-offs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12812)
*Ashen Rashmiks,Tiroshan Madushanka*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: A systematic empirical benchmark of seven vector databases (FAISS, Qdrant, Milvus, Weaviate, Chroma, pgvector, LanceDB) across six datasets and over 4 million vectors, measuring 15 metrics covering retrieval quality, query performance, and resource utilization, with an open-source benchmarking framework.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vector databases are critical infrastructure for AI applications such as RAG, semantic search, and recommendation systems, yet there is a lack of comprehensive, reproducible benchmarks that jointly evaluate retrieval quality, query latency, throughput, and resource utilization.

Method: A systematic empirical evaluation of seven systems using six diverse datasets (SIFT, GIST, MS MARCO, GloVe) totaling over 4 million vectors with dimensionalities from 96 to 960. Fifteen metrics were measured across three categories: retrieval quality (Recall@K, Precision@K, MRR, NDCG@K, Hit Rate@K), query performance (latency percentiles, QPS, cold-start latency), and resource consumption (index build time, memory, storage).
